## 5.5 PRESENTATION AND DISCLOSURE

The purpose of a general purpose financial report is to communicate financial information about an entity that is useful to its existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors in making decisions about providing resources to the entity. These users need information about the economic resources of the entity, claims against the entity and changes in those resources and claims. They also need information about how efficiently and effectively the entity’s management and governing board have discharged their responsibilities to use the entity’s resources.

To be useful, the financial information included in the general purpose financial report needs to be relevant and faithfully represent what it purports to represent. Accordingly, an entity’s disclosures about its contracts with customers should be entity-specific, relating to its products and reflecting the way the entity operates. The entity explains its revenue recognition policies and the impact of those policies on the entity’s financial position and financial performance.

Because a disclosure is entity-specific, different entities may emphasise different aspects of the specified disclosures, aggregate or disaggregate to different levels of detail or in different ways, use different descriptions, use different presentation methods or make more extensive or fewer disclosures. However, an entity’s disclosures will ultimately need to be sufficient to meet the following disclosure objective:

The objective of the disclosure requirements is for an entity to disclose sufficient information to enable users of its financial statements to understand the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue and cash flows arising from its contracts with customers.

To achieve the disclosure objective, HKFRS 15 requires an entity to disclose qualitative and quantitative information about its:

• Contracts with customers;

• The significant judgements made in relation to its contracts with customers, and changes in those judgements; and

• Assets recognised from the costs to obtain or fulfil a contract with a customer.

Some of the disclosures specified by HKFRS 15 may also be specified by another HKFRS (e.g. HKFRS 9 Financial Instruments or HKAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements). There is no need to present the same disclosure twice.

### 5.5.1 Contracts with Customers

An entity discloses the following amounts for the reporting period:
- • Revenue recognised from contracts with customers, separately from other sources of revenue.
- • Impairment losses (in accordance with HKFRS 9 Financial Instruments) on receivables and contract assets arising from contracts with customers.
(These disclosures are specified by HKFRS 15 to provide context for other specified disclosures.)

In addition, HKFRS 15 requires an entity to disclose the following information about its contract with customers:
- • Information about the disaggregation of revenue (see Section 5.5.1.1).
- • Information about contract balances (see Section 5.5.1.2).
- • Information about the entity’s performance obligations under its contracts (see Section 5.5.1.3).
- • Information about the transaction price allocated to outstanding performance obligations (see Section 5.5.1.4).

#### 5.5.1.1 Disaggregation of Revenue

To help users of the financial statements understand the composition of the revenue from contracts with customers recognised in the current period, HKFRS 15 requires an entity to disclose:

• Revenue recognised from contracts with customers disaggregated into categories that depict how the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue and cash flows are affected by economic factors; and
• Sufficient information to enable users of financial statements to understand the relationship between disaggregated revenue and any operating segment revenue information that has been disclosed in accordance with HKFRS 8 Operating Segments.

Examples of possible categories include the type of good or service, geographical region, market or customer type, contract type, contract duration, timing of transfer of goods or services and sales channels. Exhibit 5.18 illustrates an example of these disclosures. An entity may present the required information in a different manner; for example, it may be difficult to show the relationship between disaggregated revenue and segment revenue in this manner due to differences in the manner operating segment revenue is determined.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-38.png)
When selecting the type of category or categories to use to disaggregate revenue, an entity considers how information about the entity’s revenue has been presented for other purposes, including all of the following:
- • Disclosures presented outside the financial statements (e.g. in earnings releases, annual reports or investor presentations).
- • Information regularly reviewed by the Chief Operating Decision Maker (e.g. the board of directors or the CEO) for evaluating the financial performance of operating segments.
- • Other similar disclosures or information that is used by the entity or users of its financial statements to evaluate the entity’s financial performance or make resource allocation decisions.

#### 5.5.1.2 Contract Balances

The purpose of the disclosures about an entity’s contract balances is to explain the relationship between the amount of revenue recognised in a reporting period and the changes in the entity’s contract assets and contract liabilities. These disclosures provide users of the financial statements with information useful to assessing the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue and cash flows arising from an entity’s contracts with customers. For example, disclosure of the amount of revenue recognised in the reporting period relating to performance obligations satisfied or partially satisfied in previous periods provides relevant information to users about the timing of revenue recognition that was not a result of performance in the current period and, therefore, useful information to understanding the current period operating results and on predicting future revenue levels.

Exhibit 5.19 summarises the information an entity must disclose about its contract balances.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-39.png)
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-40.png)
Changes in an entity’s balances of contract assets and contract liabilities could result from:
• Changes due to business combinations;
• Cumulative catch-up adjustments to revenue that affect the corresponding contract asset or contract liability, including adjustments arising from a change in the measure of progress, a change in an estimate of the transaction price (including any changes in the assessment of whether an estimate of variable consideration is constrained) or a contract modification;
• Impairment of a contract asset;
• A change in the time frame for a right to consideration to become unconditional, that is, for a contract asset to be reclassified to a receivable; and
• A change in the time frame for a performance obligation to be satisfied, that is, for the recognition of revenue arising from a contract liability.

HKFRS 15 does not require entities to all present disclosures about contract balances in the same manner. As such, an entity will need to consider how best to present information about its contract balances in its financial report. For example, some entities may present a reconciliation between the opening and closing contract liabilities balance; others may elect to communicate similar information in a different form. Exhibit 5.20 illustrates an example of these disclosuresL the form, location and extent of disclosures will vary from entity to entity.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-41.png)
#### 5.5.1.3 Performance Obligations

The disclosures about an entity’s performance obligations in its contracts with customers provide users with more context to understanding the entity’s revenues because the entity is required to relate its revenue accounting policies to its contracts with customers. With respect to its performance obligations in contracts with customers, HKFRS 15 requires an entity to disclose:
• When the entity typically satisfies its performance obligations;
• The significant payment terms;
• The nature of the goods or services the entity has promised to transfer, highlighting any performance obligations to arrange for another party to transfer goods or services, that is, if the entity is acting as an agent;
• Obligations for returns, refunds and other similar obligations; and
• Types of warranties and related obligations.

For example, Tellev may disclose the following information to satisfy, in part, the requirement to provide information about the nature of goods or services it has promised to transfer and when it typically would satisfy performance obligations in those contracts:

> **Telecommunication Services**
> Revenue from mobile and landline calls is recognised on completion of the call. Revenue from unlimited data services packages is recognised on a straight-line basis over the period of service. Revenue from capped data services packages is recognised as data is consumed during the period of service.

#### 5.5.1.4 Transaction Price Allocated to the Remaining Performance Obligations

An entity discloses the aggregate amount of the transaction price allocated to the unsatisfied or partially unsatisfied performance obligations at the end of the reporting period and an explanation of when it will be recognised as revenue; this explanation may be provided qualitatively or on a quantitative basis using appropriate time bands. This disclosure applies also to wholly unperformed contracts. In addition, the entity must explain qualitatively whether any consideration from its contracts with customers has not been included in the transaction price, for example, because it is subject to the variable consideration constraint, and is, therefore, not included in the disclosure of the aggregate amount of the transaction price allocated to the unsatisfied or partially unsatisfied performance obligations at the end of the reporting period.

An entity need not disclose this information if the performance obligation is part of a contract that has an original expected duration of one year or less or if the entity recognises revenue in an amount that corresponds directly with the value to the customer of the entity’s performance completed to date, for example, entity bills a fixed amount for each unit of electricity consumed. An entity that does not disclose this information because it has taken advantage of the practical expedient must disclose that fact.

##### Illustrative Example 14 – Adapted from IFRS 15 Illustrative Examples, Example 43

Granite Limited (Granite) enters into a contract with customer Silicon Limited (Silicon) to construct an office building by 31 December 20X2, which it has identified as being a single performance obligation that it satisfies over time. The promised consideration is HK$12 million, and at 30 June 20X1, Granite has recognised HK$4 million of that amount as revenue. Granite estimates the construction projects will possibly take two months longer to complete than planned due to poor weather conditions.

Granite might prepare the following note disclosure in its financial statements to disclose the aggregate amount of the transaction price allocated to the partially unsatisfied performance obligation at the end of the reporting period and an explanation of when it will be recognised as revenue:

‘At 30 June 20X1, the aggregate amount of the transaction price allocated to the remaining performance obligation is HK$8 million. Granite will recognise the revenue as the building is completed, which is expected to occur over the next 18–20 months’.
---- 
### 5.5.2 Significant Judgements in the Application of this Standard

HKAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements requires an entity to disclose its significant accounting policies, judgements and sources of estimation uncertainty.

Because of the importance of understanding ‘revenue’ to a user’s decision making, HKFRS 15 specifically requires an entity to disclose the judgements that significantly affect the determination of the amount and timing of revenue from contracts with customers, and changes in those judgements. These disclosures must include the judgements, and any changes in those judgements, used in the determining (1) the timing of satisfaction of performance obligations and (2) the transaction price and amounts allocated to performance obligations.

To provide users with an understanding of the timing of revenue recognition, an entity discloses:
- • With respect to performance obligations satisfied over time, the methods it uses to recognise revenue and an explanation of why the selected method provides a faithful depiction of the transfer of goods or services; and
- • With respect to performance obligations satisfied at a point in time, the significant judgements made in determining when a customer obtains control of the good or service.

To provide users with an understanding of the amounts of revenue recognised, an entity discloses information about the methods, inputs and assumptions used for:
- • Determining the transaction price (including estimating variable consideration, adjusting the consideration for the effects of the time value of money and measuring non-cash consideration);
- • Assessing whether an estimate of variable consideration is constrained;
- • Allocating the transaction price, including estimating stand-alone selling prices of promised goods or services and allocating discounts and variable consideration to a specific part of the contract; and
- • Measuring its obligations for returns, refunds and other similar obligations.

In addition, an entity adopting a practical expedient relating to the non-adjustment of consideration for the time value of money must disclose that fact.

##### Apply and Analyse 7

Tellev is proposing to make the following note disclosure in the notes to its financial statements: ‘Where two or more deliverables are sold under a single contract, each deliverable is accounted for as a separate unit of account. Consideration on the contract is allocated to each deliverable based on the relative standalone selling prices. The consideration is limited to the amount that is not contingent upon the delivery of additional items or meeting other specified performance obligations’.

Evaluate whether Tellev has disclosed information about its judgements that significantly affect the determination of the amount and timing of revenue from contracts with customers that is sufficient to meet the disclosure objective of HKFRS 15.

###### Analysis

Tellev has not disclosed information about its judgements that significantly affect the determination of the amount and timing of its revenue that is sufficient to enable users of its financial statements to understand the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue and cash flows arising from its contracts with customers. This is because:
- • The disclosure that consideration on the contract is allocated to each deliverable based on the relative stand-alone selling prices and it is constrained to non-contingent consideration that is generic and non-specific to Tellev and, accordingly, does not provide the user with an understanding of the judgements Tellev uses to determine the transaction price of its contracts with customers;
- • The disclosure tells users that variable consideration is constrained, but it does not explain how Tellev has determined it should exclude contingent consideration from its estimate of variable consideration; and
- • The disclosure tells the user the allocation is based on stand-alone selling prices but does not explain how Tellev determines the stand-alone selling prices.

### 5.5.3 Assets Recognised from the Costs to Obtain or Fulfil a Contract with a Customer

In addition to disclosures about the contracts with customers and the significant judgements an entity makes relating to those contracts, HKFRS 15 requires information to be disclosed about any capitalised contract costs. These disclosures help users to understand the types of costs recognised as assets and how those assets are subsequently amortised or impaired.

With respect to capitalised contract costs, an entity discloses:
- • The judgements made in determining the amount of the costs incurred to obtain or fulfil a contract with a customer;
- • The method it uses to determine the amortisation for each reporting period;
- • The closing balances of assets recognised from the costs incurred to obtain or fulfil a contract with a customer, by main category of asset (e.g. costs to obtain contracts with customers, pre-contract costs and setup costs); and
- • The amount of amortisation and any impairment losses recognised in the reporting period.

In addition, an entity adopting a practical expedient relating to the immediate expensing of incremental costs of obtaining a contract must disclose that fact.

### OPENING CASE

HOME SUPPLIES

Home Supplies Limited (Home Supplies) is a retail company offering a range of general merchandise for the family home, including furniture, appliances and electronics. It has a chain of 22 retail stores located in shopping malls throughout Hong Kong and mainland China, and has in recent years, extended its international presence by opening stores in other parts of Asia, including Singapore and Malaysia.

Each retail store is leased by Home Supplies from the shopping mall owners. Also, each retail store is designed and fitted out the same way to ensure customers are familiar with the placement of the product in all stores. Home Supplies has the exclusive use of all retail stores for the duration of the respective leases and has control over the nature of the operations during the period of use, including the products offered to customers.

As part of Home Supplies’ products, including furniture and electronics, such as televisions, Home Supplies offers free next-day delivery and installation for all ‘large’ items. Home Supplies has a warehouse in Hong Kong and mainland China that act as distribution centres, where Home Supplies’ delivery trucks are loaded daily for delivery. Home Supplies’ delivery trucks are used only for delivering ordered products and are parked overnight in the loading dock area neighbouring the warehouse. Home Supplies is planning to provide delivery and installation services in Singapore and Malaysia in the future.

In the last year, Home Supplies undertook steps to diversify and expand its operations in two ways. First, Home Supplies purchased a parcel of land in Guangzhou to build a ‘mega’ store. The five-storey building will include Home Supplies’ full product range, as well as a food eatery. Home Supplies will also use the store to introduce its new products, which will include baby furniture, toys and video games. Second, Home Supplies introduced online shopping for a range of appliances. The online shopping store is operated out of the mainland China warehouse, which required a refurbishment to contain a designated office space where online orders are received, packaged and distributed.

### OVERVIEW

In a lease arrangement, one entity (the lessee) promises to pay another entity (the lessor) for the right to use the lessor’s asset for a specified period of time. How are leases recognised and measured in general-purpose financial statements? Consider the case of Home Supplies, which leases all its retail stores from shopping mall owners. When and how should Home Supplies recognise, measure, present and disclose the assets arising from the leases (i.e. its rights to use the retail stores) and the liabilities arising from the leases (i.e. its obligations to make lease payments in return)? Should Home Supplies’ key financial ratios differ depending on whether it owns the retail stores compared to leasing them? Should the same rules apply to all kinds of leases, irrespective of the terms of the leases or the values of the underlying assets? For example, if Home Supplies decides to lease low-value assets for a short period (e.g. computers to operate its online business), should it be allowed to account for these leases differently from the long-term leases of the higher value retail stores?

This chapter addresses the recognition and measurement of leases from the perspective of the lessee and the lessor. You will gain an understanding of the complexities in recognising and measuring leases in financial statements of lessees and lessors. By the end of this chapter, you will have gained an understanding of when a lease exists and how leases are required to be recognised, measured and presented in financial statements, together with the types of information disclosed and how that helps ensure lessees and lessors provide relevant information that faithfully represents lease agreements.

## 9.1 OVERVIEW

This chapter examines the definition, recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure requirements relating to lease agreements specified in HKFRS 16 Leases. HKFRS 16 is a recent accounting standard, effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2019.

The objective of HKFRS 16 is for lessees and lessors to provide relevant information in a manner that faithfully represents lease arrangements. This information gives a basis for users of financial statements to assess the effect that leases have on the financial position, financial performance and cash flows of an entity.

Exhibit 9.1 provides a flowchart illustrating the process of lease accounting from the lessee’s and the lessor’s perspectives. Both first identify whether a lease exists and then extract its components from the lease agreement. The process then differs because a lessor is required to classify a lease as a finance or as an operating lease and a lessee does not. Subsequently,
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-42.png)
the lessee and lessor make decisions relating to recognition, initial measurement, subsequent measurement and the presentation and disclosure of the impact of leases on their financial position, financial performance and cash flows.

In this section, you will gain an understanding of the lease agreements to which HKFRS 16 applies and be introduced to some of the terminology to describe the parties to, and the key terms of, a lease agreement.

### 9.1.1 Scope
HKFRS 16 applies to all leases except for:
• Leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources (HKFRS 6 Exploration for and Evaluation of Mineral Resources specifies the accounting for rights to explore for mineral resources) (see Chapter 26);
• Leases of biological assets within the scope of HKAS 41 Agriculture held by a lessee (see Chapter 26);
• Service concession arrangements within the scope of HK(IFRIC)-Int 12 Service Concession Arrangements (see Chapter 26);
• Licences of intellectual property granted by a lessor within the scope of HKFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers (see Chapter 5); and
`HKFRS 16.3–4`
• Rights held by a lessee under licensing agreements within the scope of HKAS 38 Intangible Assets for items, such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights (see Chapter 11). For leases of other types of intangible assets, a lessee may, but is not required to, apply HKFRS 16..

### 9.1.2 Terminology

Throughout this chapter, you will be introduced to terminology pertinent to HKFRS 16. Before proceeding further, it will be beneficial to understand some introductory terms associated with a lease agreement relevant to the lessee, lessor or both (Exhibit 9.2).

#### Lessor
The lessor (i.e. the owner/supplier) is an entity that provides the right to use an underlying asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. How this arrangement is reflected in the lessor’s financial statements depends on whether the lease is a finance lease (a lease that transfers substantially all the risks and rewards incidental to ownership of an underlying asset) or an operating lease (a lease that does not transfer substantially all the risks and rewards incidental to ownership of an underlying asset)

#### Lessee
The lessee (i.e. the tenant/renter) is an entity that obtains the right to use an underlying asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. The lessee recognises for the duration of the lease term a right-to-use asset in its financial statements, representing its right to use the underlying asset for the lease term, and a lease liability that reflects the obligation to make future lease payments in return for the right to use the underlying asset.

#### Lease
A lease is a contract, or part of a contract, that conveys the right to use an asset (the underlying asset – The asset that is the subject of a lease, for which the right to use that asset has been provided by a lessor to a lessee, e.g. a building) for a period of time in exchange for consideration. A contract is an agreement between two or more parties that creates enforceable rights and obligations.

The terms and conditions of a lease will normally include:
• An inception date – The earlier of the date of a lease agreement and the date of commitment by the parties to the principal terms and conditions of the lease;
• A commencement date – The date on which a lessor makes an underlying asset available for use by a lessee;
• A lease term – The non-cancellable period for which a lessee has the right to use an underlying asset; and
• Details of the lease payments – The payments made by a lessee to a lessor relating to the right to use an underlying asset during the lease term.

Each of these will have implications for the timing of recognition and amounts recognised in the financial statements of the parties to the lease.

## 9.2 IDENTIFYING A LEASE

When a customer and supplier enter into a contractual arrangement, determining the nature of the contract is important. By determining the nature of the contract, each party is better able to identify its rights and obligations arising from the contractual relationship and how to account for these rights and obligations. For example, if the supplier promises to transfer goods or services to the customer, the obligation (to fulfil this promise and the revenue that is generated as the promise is fulfilled) is to be accounted for under HKFRS 15. If, however, the supplier (i.e. the lessor) promises the customer (i.e. the lessee) the right to use one of the lessor’s assets for a period of time, HKFRS 16 will govern the terms of that contract. Given the different accounting treatment for various contract types, the contracting parties must accurately identify whether the contractual arrangement is, or contains, a lease.

### 9.2.1 Application of HKFRS 16
To determine whether HKFRS 16 applies, an entity must assess whether a contract to which it is a party is, or contains, a lease. A contract is, or contains, a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration. An entity makes this assessment at the inception (as distinct from at commencement) of a contract and again during the contract but only if the terms and conditions change.. 

An entity must, therefore, assess whether there is an identified asset; for which there is a right to control its use and for a period of time.

For the purposes of the following discussion, the two parties to the contract are referred to as the supplier (the potential lessor) and the customer (the potential lessee).

#### 9.2.1.1 Identified Asset

An identified asset can be explicitly or implicitly specified in a contract. An example of an identified asset being implicitly specified is if the contract requires the supply of a motor vehicle of a particular make and model for use by the customer but does not require one particular motor vehicle held by the supplier, as identified by registration number, to be the motor vehicle supplied.

Furthermore, an identified asset can be a physically distinct portion of a larger asset (e.g. a floor of a building). In the case of Home Supplies, it must determine whether each retail store it occupies is an identified asset within each shopping mall, which it is likely to be. In contrast, a capacity or portion of an asset that is not physically distinct (e.g. permission to sell from a mobile cart in designated areas of a shopping mall) is not an identified asset for the purposes of HKFRS 16 unless it represents substantially all of the capacity of the asset (e.g. the shopping mall, which it is unlikely to be) and, as such, provides the customer with the right to obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from use of the asset.. 

If the supplier has the substantive right to substitute the asset at any time throughout the period of use, it would also not be an identified asset for the purposes of HKFRS 16 because the customer does not have the right to use the specific asset; rather, the customer has a right to use an unspecified asset. Exhibit 9.3 outlines the criteria to be satisfied for a supplier to possess a substantive right of substitution.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-43.png)
For example, consider a lease in which the shopping mall owner has a right to relocate a retailer to another store within the mall if the mall owner is able to lease out the original store to another retailer for a greater return. In this example, the shopping mall owner can substitute alternative assets throughout the period of use because they have the right to move a lessee to another store and benefit economically from such asset substitution, given their ability to generate greater returns by doing so.

For the supplier’s substitution right to be substantive, it must exist for the duration of the contract. For example, if the supplier can only substitute an asset after a future date or the occurrence of a future event, the supplier’s substitution right will not be substantive. In addition, if the asset is to be replaced if it becomes faulty or a technical upgrade becomes available, this does not prevent the asset from being an ‘identified asset’.. 

As a practical expedient, there is a presumption in HKFRS 16 that if the customer cannot readily determine whether the supplier’s substitution right is substantive or not, it is treated as being not substantive..





# Implement and monitor business strategy

## Opening Case
### DEEPHARBOUR HK COMPANY LIMITED

A brand-new Hong Kong-based container shipping company, DeepHarbour HK Company Limited, has just established its business to operate out of Victoria Harbour. It will service countries throughout the entire Asia-Pacific region.

This is a private company founded with HK$5 billion, with a board of directors. It has hired a chief executive officer, chief financial officer and chief information officer. To commence operations, the company intends to invest HK$1.5 billion to acquire 100 ships approximately 200 m in length, another HK$500 million in self-loading/unloading technology and HK$250 million in sophisticated navigation and communications IT systems.

Industry competitors include large international shipping lines, some of whom have been in business for decades.

Management is now tasked with establishing a business strategy for the fledgling organisation. This will require a comprehensive assessment of multiple factors, from the perspective of the many internal and external stakeholders the organisation will serve.

Stakeholders will include shareholders, capital market stakeholders including banks and major creditors, product market shareholders that include members of DeepHarbour HK’s supply chain to its shipping fleet, as well as the customers that employ shipping services. These customers are expected to come primarily from Hong Kong’s clothing, electronics and jewellery industries, as well as industries in the Asia-Pacific region that will be exporting their wares to Hong Kong.

Its organisational stakeholders will include the 500 employees that DeepHarbour HK intends to hire at the start of operations, and the community at large in terms of adhering to, for example, environmental regulations (such as allowable pollution emissions and rules on where ballast water discharge is acceptable under environmental regulations concerning ballast water). The global shipping industry faces a number of challenges, including narrow profit margins, global environmental initiatives, security and safety of employees and cargo and a competitive landscape with many ships competing for customers. Management is optimistic that some of these issues will improve over the next five years.

How does management establish a long-term strategy that will benefit the organisation in the face of intense international competition in the shipping industry? What factors does it need to consider in terms of how it allocates scarce resources to achieve its corporate goals?

Furthermore, management needs to build flexibility into its strategy so that DeepHarbour HK can respond swiftly to changes in its business environment – including new technologies, customers and competitors. One thing is certain; no business today is able to stand still for very long before it is overtaken by new developments.

Is there a particular model that might provide the new company with a basis upon which to build and execute a strategy that works best for them? This chapter will examine the strategic, financial and operational strengths that DeepHarbour HK can draw upon when implementing this strategy.

### OVERVIEW

This module reinforces the ability to evaluate alternative business strategies in a range of circumstances, as well as the capability to advise on optimal decisions. Building on past modules, students will be able to construct processes to implement projects and evaluate the appropriate course of action across ethical dilemmas.

This chapter and this module build on the knowledge gained in all of the preceding modules, but especially the financial lessons of Modules 2 and 7. Together, these three modules provide a strong, cohesive basis for financial and business management.

A major overall learning objective for this chapter is to introduce students to the principles involved in an organisation’s quest to implement and monitor its business strategy in a competitive and constantly changing international environment.

In particular, students will learn about:
- • The functional strategies necessary for management and employees to implement the organisation’s strategy.
- • The key issues that need to be addressed by management as its business strategy is implemented.
- • How a business can collect and analyse relevant data and information – including big data – for strategic decision making within the company in order to monitor and, as necessary, modify or adapt that strategy to changing internal and/or external conditions.
- • How various organisational methodologies and processes might impact variations in business models.

Another important objective of this chapter is to enable students to evaluate and advise on the strategic capability of an organisational entity, including its financial strategy.

This will involve learning how to evaluate the likely consequences of strategic options and use that information to recommend strategies designed to meet the organisation’s objectives.

## 1.1 DEVELOPING BUSINESS STRATEGY

The development of a strategic plan for any organisation is both a significant undertaking as well as being the first step in sustaining and growing the business. Traditionally, the board and management develop the organisational strategy, with the board mandated to approve the strategy.

A company’s business strategy involves its own dynamic plan to gain and sustain a competitive advantage in the particular market in which it competes. Thus, the organisation must engage in forecasts about which markets are attractive and how it can offer unique value to customers in those markets by offering resources and capabilities that won’t be easily imitated or replaced by competitors. This is particularly so in industries undergoing rapid change or disruption. Some organisations are natural monopolies, while others provide essential services, such as governmental organisations. Those forecasts can be used to formulate a plan which will allow them to gain or maintain a competitive advantage.

Business strategy must be dynamic and respond to change, including new technologies, changing demands of customers and new competitors.

Developing a business strategy should take into account four factors:

1. Where to compete?
	The organisation needs to recognise the attractiveness of a geographic and/or industrial market or a certain customer segment in the targeted markets. This requires an external analysis, to assess the competition and forces that are shaping industry competition. It also requires a customer analysis to determine what the organisation’s customers really want and/or need.

2. How to offer unique value relative to competitors in targeted markets?
	This represents the firm’s value proposition and the reason why an organisation succeeds with a set of customers. The unique value the organisation offers need not necessarily be financial. A not-for-profit firm, for example, may seek to improve society through services or expertise. Both for-profit and not-for-profit organisations benefit from strong strategic management. Strategic management often requires firms to acquire resources – such as land or equipment – and human capabilities (for example, employees, management) to deliver that unique value.

3. What are the resources or capabilities needed to deliver unique value?
	What does the organisation need to have and what does it need to do? A for-profit firm might, for example, need to consider whether they will benefit most from offering low-cost products or product differentiation – or perhaps both simultaneously.

4. How must the organisation capture value and sustain its competitive advantage?
	Consistently generating above-average profits through a strategy that creates barriers to imitation means that competitors are either unable to imitate or find it too costly to imitate that strategy.

Any organisation – whether it is new or well established, requires a business strategy or plan that is reflective of the organisation’s mission. The strategy will assist it in gaining and sustaining a competitive advantage in its market. This is particularly important when the organisation faces challenges or disruption. This strategy incorporates elements of its mission, which outlines the organisation’s primary purpose and the core values that it promotes, along with the vision of its leaders.

### Mission Statement

An organisation’s mission outlines its primary purpose and often specifies details that include the business field(s) in which it aims to compete and the customers and broader stakeholders in the community or communities that it serves.

As organisations grow, they may develop formal mission statements, which expand on the stated mission and define the core values that a firm promotes. Mission statements may be inspirational for employees and management in pursuit of the corporate mission.

The mission of the organisation pulls together several criteria, including:
- • Values, or the shared beliefs of its members;
- • Vision, or the central strategic excellence position to be sought; and
- • Other purposes that may be related to the organisation’s stakeholders, such as stockholders, employees, suppliers, the community, the public and customers.

A strong mission statement often begins with considering three important questions, including:

1. What business are we in? Defining the business involves more than identifying its industry or its products or services. This process begins by considering its primary stakeholder groups. This might include customers, employees, investors, the local community and others. A consideration of what specific stakeholder needs are to be met by the company, and how that will be accomplished – for example, through specific products or services or support – is also useful.

2. What do we want to achieve? The answer to this question should not be too focused, such as ‘our mission is to grow earnings per share by 15% each year’. While such a goal may be valid for the short term – for example, a year – it might not be a sustainable achievement over time. A better goal might be to create sustained growth in shareholder value. Good mission statements may focus on outcomes (for example, market share, growth, etc.), processes (such as innovation, quality, speed, etc.), or a particular feeling the leadership hopes to evoke (such as being identified as the best place to work, or the most loved by its customers).

	A good mission statement should only focus on one or two goals for each important stakeholder group.

3. What values and principles guide us? This question focuses on where a mission statement connects with and communicates shared values. This can include two or three core values, such as the value of a customer connection, exciting innovation, or disciplined investing and cost control. A good mission statement will also communicate a company’s aspirational values, or what they want to be in the future. This could involve a goal of, for example, building a better community or society, or providing development opportunities for all of its employees.

For example, the corporate mission of our fictionalised company DeepHarbour HK is:
> ‘to exceed customer expectations by delivering a premium shipping service using modern technology with timely, efficient and personalised service that is reliable and predictable, that builds loyalty with our global customers, and supports the local communities in which we do business’.

#### Apply and Analyse 1

Consider the factors that DeepHarbour HK Company Limited, the fictional Hong Kongbased start-up shipping company, may need to take into account as it develops its initial business strategy.

##### Analysis

There are multiple factors that DeepHarbour HK will need to take into account with respect to its business strategy, including:

1. Where to compete? DeepHarbour HK wishes to initially compete in the Asia-Pacific region, which encompasses an enormous trading region. Does DeepHarbour HK want to expand that reach, for example in its first five years, to include parts of the European Union and the Atlantic region? An external analysis may help to assess the competition and other factors affecting the shipping industry.

2. How will DeepHarbour HK offer unique value in those targeted markets? For example, does the firm want to distinguish itself through customer service? Advanced technology in loading and unloading cargo? Or, are there other efficiencies that can distinguish it from competitors?

3. What resources or capabilities does DeepHarbour HK require to deliver on its unique value? For example, should DeepHarbour HK increase staffing to deliver a unique customer service? Or should it invest more heavily in technology than its competitors?

4. How might DeepHarbour HK sustain a competitive advantage, to thrive financially in a highly competitive global shipping industry? Perhaps there are advantages in a new cost structure at the beginning of its operations that will provide an advantage over its more established competitors using less efficient models.

### 1.1.1 Relationship Between Functional Strategy and Overall Business Strategy

An organisation’s overall business strategy, expressed at a macro level, must often be tailored by individual functional units to work at a practical level.

A functional strategy undertaken by a corporation involves decisions about how to effectively implement the business unit strategy within various functional areas of the business. These areas can include, for example, finance, operations, product development, information technology, sales and marketing and customer service.

In our hypothetical case, newly formed DeepHarbour HK Company Limited has announced plans to invest HK$1.5 billion to acquire 100 ships. How does it intend to finance those capital purchases? Will it purchase the ships outright, or lease them, or a combination of those strategies? How will it raise the money – for example, through debt or equity? In the latter case, perhaps a decision will be undertaken to allow for at least partial public ownership of the new company. These constitute functional strategies for financing the business.

With respect to sales and marketing, a functional strategy will examine factors such as the degree to which DeepHarbour HK is prepared to invest in technology, such as a website and other forms of social media to advertise its new business, or rely on its personnel to make cold calls and send e-mails, etc., to try and attract customers. This decision will involve an allocation and commitment of the company’s resources.

Firms that do not have the resources and capabilities necessary to implement the strategies they are considering may need to acquire, improve, change or otherwise create them. Resource allocation thus becomes an important aspect of strategy. After deciding how it would like to offer unique value, the resources necessary to build those capabilities must be allocated by the company.

Formulating a strategy requires selecting which actions the company will take in order to execute its overall corporate strategy and, where applicable, the appropriate business unit strategies. In order to do so, the organisation’s internal structure, including its personnel, its systems, style and culture, should be designed to facilitate the execution of that strategy.

If a company’s functional strategies do not align with its overall business strategy, then the execution of the business strategy will likely be flawed throughout the organisation, negatively affecting profitability, creating inefficiencies that weaken customer relations, as well as relations with internal and external stakeholders. For example, poorly established human resource policies could make a company unattractive for employees and result in higher employee turnover. Inattentive environmental practices could hurt the organisation’s relationship with its community.

A strategic plan needs to proceed through a logical series of steps that reflect the organisation’s grand strategy. These five steps include:

1. Development of the vision/mission, which is the central concept for the organisation’s future development. This should encompass the shared beliefs of members of the organisation; other purposes related to the organisation’s stakeholders (including owners, employees, customers, suppliers, the community, etc.); and the position of strategic excellence that the organisation is trying to achieve at its centre.
2. Identifying the corporate goals that the organisation is trying to achieve, along with the distinctive capabilities that the organisation possesses to help it accomplish that.
3. Identifying how progress toward those goals and success in achieving the corporate objectives will be measured.
4. Identifying the various specific corporate strategies – including functional, business and cultural strategies – by which the organisation aims to achieve its objectives.
5. Development of detailed action plans designed to implement the corporate strategies, along with a determination of how progress towards achieving those goals will be monitored by senior executives.

This is a healthy process because it enables the company and its employees to feel positive about its work and direction.

1.1.2 Models of Business Strategy

Given the importance of business strategy, many models have been developed to help guide organisations in developing their strategic approach. Several of these models of business strategy are discussed in this section and include:

• Porter’s Five Forces
• McKinsey and Company 7 S
• BCG growth–share matrix
• PEST analysis
• Value chain
• Ansoff matrix
• POPIT model

#### 1.1.2.1 Porter’s Five Forces

Strategy professor Michael Porter developed a model for conducting industry analysis called the Five Forces that Shape Industry, frequently called ‘Porter’s Five Forces’. See Exhibit 1.1.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-44.png)
Porter’s assessment is that five forces affect industry attractiveness and profitability, as follows:
1. Rivalry among industry competitors
2. Bargaining power of suppliers
3. Threat of potential new entrants
4. Threat of substitutes
5. Bargaining power of buyers

These five forces, combined, define an industry’s structure and shape the competitive interactions – and potential profitability – of companies within a particular industry. Even though industries might appear to differ significantly, the principles that determine their underlying drivers of profitability are often the same.

##### 1) Rivalry Among Industry Competitors

For most industries, there is a direct relationship between the level of competition among industry participants and the level of profitability or losses – the latter because aggressive competition can lead to drastically lower prices. Some industries do not have strong price competition, and instead its members establish rivalries based on brand, which depends on other variables such as strong marketing, advertising and innovation. There are five factors which tend to determine the intensity of competition between established firms in a particular industry. These are:

1. Seller concentration – This refers to the number of and the size distribution of firms that are competing within a particular market.

2. Diversity of competitors – The presence of companies that are dissimilar in their origins, objectives, costs and strategies helps to ensure there will be price competition.

3. Product differentiation – In industries where products are highly differentiated, such as in pharmaceuticals, restaurants and management consulting, price competition tends to be relatively weak, even in situations where many firms are competing. In contrast, in industries such as agriculture, where many products, particularly those that are organic, are basically the same, price becomes the sole basis for competition and profits tend to be squeezed.

4. Excess capacity and exit barriers – Excess capacity of a particular product can cause firms to cut prices in order to liquidate that inventory and attract new businesses. If that is coupled with barriers to exit, for instance if workers in a particular industry that is perhaps unionised are protected against being laid off when economic times are bad, this can seriously reduce industry profitability.

5. Cost conditions – This refers to scale economies and the ratio of fixed to variable costs. The determination of how low prices can go when excess capacity causes price competition will be largely determined by the organisation’s cost structure.

##### 2) Bargaining Power of Suppliers

The key issues when determining the relative power held by an industry’s producers and its suppliers are the relative bargaining power that producers and suppliers hold, as well as the degree to which individual firms are free to switch between different input suppliers. This is similar to the way a relationship between producers and buyers would be analysed, with the exception being that the buyers in this case are the industry’s individual firms and the suppliers are the producers of inputs.

The bargaining power of suppliers is largely influenced by size and scale. Commodity suppliers are usually smaller companies selling to large manufacturing companies that lack bargaining power. That is why commodity suppliers often seek to boost their bargaining power in numbers, such as through labour unions or farmers’ marketing cooperatives or specialised industry groups such as OPEC for oil producing countries.

##### 3) Threat of Potential New Entrants

Whether or not an industry is open to new participants can be a major determinant of profitability for the participating firms. If entry is open and unrestricted, profitability will be at competitive levels. Even a threat of new participants entering the industry may be enough to ensure that existing participants keep their prices at competitive levels. New firms from outside the industry may be drawn to industries that are capable of earning a return on its capital that exceeds its cost of capital.

On the other hand, if there are barriers to entry in a particular industry (i.e. a significant barrier to entry would be if potential new entrants faced a unit cost disadvantage compared to existing participants), the established firms will hold an advantage compared to their counterparts in other industries featuring unrestricted entry. Principle sources of barriers to entry in an industry include:

• Capital requirements – If the capital costs required to get a new business set up are extremely large, this can discourage the establishment of new companies, and leave the field open for only the largest, established organisations.

• Economies of scale – In industries that are capital or research or advertising intensive, efficiency requires a large-scale operation. New entrants to an industry like the automotive industry face a difficult choice of either entering on a small scale and accepting the reality of high unit costs or commencing on a large scale and having to bear the costs of underutilised capacity.

• Absolute cost advantages – Established firms may have a unit cost advantage over new industry entrants irrespective of their size and scale. Furthermore, absolute cost advantages to early entrants in a particular market often result from the acquisition of low-cost sources of raw materials.

• Product differentiation – Existing brands may have a significant advantage when a new company tries to introduce a product in an industry, such as consumer electronics, where strong brand loyalty between the company and customer has already been established. The new company must then spend a disproportionately higher amount on advertising and promotion in an effort to reach those same customers.

• Access to channels of distribution – New businesses producing consumer goods may succeed in manufacturing them, but then be denied access to channels of distribution by, say, major retailers, who won’t provide shelf space.

• Governmental and legal barriers – Industries that are protected by government and/ or legal restrictions, such as banking and broadcasting in some countries, can be effectively covered by such protection.

• Retaliation – Expectations regarding possible retaliation by established firms can also serve as a barrier to entry for potential new entrants. Retaliation could come in the form of, for example, aggressive price-cutting, litigation or more aggressive than normal sales or advertising campaigns.

• Effectiveness of barriers to entry – Industries protected by high entry barriers, such as capital requirements, tend to earn above-average rates of profit.

##### 4) Threat of Substitutes

The existence or absence of substitute products is a key factor in determining the price that consumers are willing to pay for a particular product. If close substitutes are lacking, such as for products like petrol or cigarettes, then consumer demand will be relatively insensitive, or inelastic with regard to the price they are willing to pay. In contrast, if there are close substitutes available for a product, price increases would likely create demand elasticity whereby consumers are willing to purchase those alternative products. The extent to which substitutes depress prices and profits depends on the tendency of buyers to substitute between alternatives.

The Internet has also provided a new source of substitute competition that has proved devastating for a number of established industries.

##### 5) Bargaining Power of Buyers

The firms in an industry compete in two types of markets: for inputs and outputs. Both markets create value for buyers as well as sellers. Input markets feature the purchase of raw materials, components, labour services and financial services by individual firms. Output markets feature the sale of goods and services by firms to their customers, such as consumers, distributors or manufacturers.

Value sharing in terms of profitability between buyers and sellers depends on the relative economic power of each party. Key factors that determine the strength of the buying power that a firm faces from its customers are buyers’ price sensitivity and the firm’s relative bargaining power.

##### Buyers’ Price Sensitivity 
Four major factors determine the extent to which buyers will be sensitive to the prices charged by an individual firm in a particular industry, including:

1. Buyers will be more sensitive about the price they are willing to pay as that item becomes a greater proportion of total cost.
2. The less differentiated the products of the supplying industry, the more willing the buyer will be to switch suppliers on the basis of price.
3. The more intense the competition among buyers, the greater will be their eagerness for price reductions from their sellers.
4. The more critical an industry’s product to the quality of the buyer’s product or service, the less sensitive buyers will be to the prices they are charged.

###### Relative Bargaining Power

Bargaining power rests, ultimately, on the relative strength of each participating party’s ability to negotiate. The credibility and effectiveness with which buyers and sellers to a transaction are able to negotiate with each other will determine the balance of power between them. The key factor is the relative cost to each when a transaction is not completed. The relative expertise of each party in managing its position is a secondary factor. The bargaining power of buyers relative to sellers is influenced by several factors, among them:
- • Size and concentration of buyers relative to suppliers. The smaller the number of buyers and the bigger their purchases, the greater the cost of losing one. The size of one organisation compared to the other is another important consideration.
- • Buyers’ information. The better informed buyers are about suppliers and their prices and costs, the better they are able to bargain.
- • Ability to integrate vertically. In refusing to deal with the other party, the alternative to finding another supplier or buyer is to do it themselves.

##### Illustrative Example 1

As DeepHarbour HK Company Limited establishes its global shipping business out of Hong Kong’s Victoria harbour, it – like the organisation’s more experienced competitors will encounter the challenges of Porter’s Five Forces. Some of the challenges they might face, as defined by Porter’s Five Forces are:

Rivalry among industry competitors – Existing global shipping lines cannot be expected to be pleased about facing a new rival in the field, and are likely to take advantage of their size, existing customer base and experience to try and outsmart the new business. For example, there is a danger that DeepHarbour HK could face a ‘price war’ as competition pushes prices down.

Threat of potential new entrants – When a new organisation such as DeepHarbour HK enters an industry, established firms may face several barriers to entry, including the fact that its established competitors already have a unit cost advantage as a result of factors such as product differentiation and existing access to channels of distribution, among others.

Bargaining power of buyers – Established competitors may be in a stronger position with respect to their bargaining power with groups such as labour unions for employees. Since DeepHarbour HK is offering the same service as its competitors, the more willing buyers of those services might switch suppliers on the basis of price, which could represent a significant advantage for competitors.

Bargaining power of suppliers – Suppliers to the shipping industry, such as a business that repairs ships in a fleet, provides petroleum for their journeys, or provides fresh water for the crew, among other services, could band together to have greater bargaining power.

A smaller start-up like DeepHarbour HK could be susceptible to this pressure in a way that a larger, more established company would not.

Threat of substitutes – As a start-up company, DeepHarbour HK faces the disadvantage of not having the name recognition that its major industry competitors have, some of whom will have been in business for many years, if not decades. Consequently, the organisation will face pressure to be very good, very fast in terms of providing shipping services, at a competitive price, that its clients can depend on. They will not possess the margin of error that a larger competitor who has been servicing a client for many years, and has built up a reservoir of goodwill, will have. If a long-established company makes a major error on one shipment, for example, the client of that firm is much more likely to stay, given the long history between the two parties. But if that same error is committed by a start-up like DeepHarbour HK, the customer is much more likely to quickly partake in the services of a competitor.
