#### 1.1.2.2 McKinsey and Company 7 S Model of Organisational Alignment 
The McKinsey and Company ‘7 S model of organisational alignment’ contains the seven important organisational elements: strategy, structure, systems, staffing, skills, style and shared values. All organisations face regular decisions on how to establish and/or maintain their company based on these variables (Exhibit 1.2).
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-45.png)
Strategy refers to the plan, process and related activities that create and sustain a competitive advantage for a firm in its target markets.

Structure answers two critical questions for an organisation: ‘Who does what?’ and ‘Who reports to whom?’

Systems describes key processes that span a firm’s organisational structure.

Staffing refers to the human resource management processes in the organisation.

Skills refers to the abilities of individuals within an organisation, along with how well that firm has combined those individual talents to build capabilities (such as processes) for competitive advantage.

Style refers to the interpersonal relationships between the management and employees of an organisation.

Shared values refer to priorities, values and virtues that members of an organisation view as being important. Along with style, this is another key factor that comprises the culture of an organisation.

##### Apply and Analyse 2
Evaluate how the individual elements of the McKinsey and Company 7 S model might influence planning for the business of DeepHarbour HK Company Limited, the fictional Hong Kong-based start-up shipping company outlined at the beginning of this chapter.

Analysis

Strategy – The stated goal for DeepHarbour HK, as it begins operations, is to establish a business strategy that will provide it with the best chance to achieve a sustained excellent financial and operational performance, along with a competitive advantage over more experienced rivals in a global shipping industry.

Structure – The structure that DeepHarbour HK establishes might be a traditional hierarchical structure or a more informal, flat structure. This will be an important element of the operations because the structure assigns accountability for tasks and provides a measure of performance by a particular organisational unit.

Systems – The systems that DeepHarbour HK establishes will coordinate and control the work of different units. For example, information systems will track containers or shipments as they are loaded, en route, which ships they are on, and their arrival at the destination.

Staffing – For DeepHarbour HK, staffing will encompass recruitment, hiring, training, compensation and deployment of new employees. As the organisation begins operations, some of those processes will be used to measure employee performance and to assess the need for additional or specialised training.

Skills – The talents of employees hired at DeepHarbour HK will be utilised to build processes that can provide the new organisation with a competitive advantage over international fleets that will compete for its business.

Style – DeepHarbour HK’s intent is to hire the best people from a technical standpoint, however technical skills alone may not be adequate. The newly hired staff must be prepared to work together and in pursuit of a common goal. Style is an intangible attribute that all companies, especially early in their development, must be mindful of, to give it the best chance to achieve its business strategy. Management will need to consider style in its strategy development.

Shared values – Deep Harbour HK’s senior management will need to be cognisant of shared values as they hire new staff because this will be a key factor in the culture of their organisation.
---- 

#### 1.1.2.3 BCG Growth–Share Matrix

The Boston Consulting Group (BCG) ‘growth–share matrix’ uses industry attractiveness and competitive position to compare the strategic positions of different businesses or units within a diversified firm to measure how they contribute to value creation. However, it uses a single indicator to represent each of these dimensions: industry attractiveness is measured by rate of market growth on the vertical axis and competitive advantage by relative market share (the business unit’s market share relative to that of its largest competitor) on the horizontal axis. The four quadrants of the BCG matrix predict patterns of profits and cash flow and indicate strategies to be adopted (Exhibit 1.3).

![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-46.png)
For example, a business unit with a high growth rate, but low relative market share is placed in the upper left quadrant. If the unit has both a high growth rate and high relative market share, it is placed in the upper right quadrant. A unit with both a low growth rate and low relative market share is placed in the lower right quadrant because it is considered to add little profitability to the organisation’s overall business portfolio. The fourth quadrant, represented by a unit that has high relative market share, but low growth, attracts minimal investment.

The simplicity of the BCG matrix is both its limitation and its usefulness. It can be prepared easily and offers a clear picture of a firm’s business portfolio in relation to important strategic characteristics.

However, the simplicity of this model could also present potential disadvantages. Consider, for example, an organisation that specialises in selling luxury cars, which few can afford. This company may lead the world market for luxury car sales, but only sells a very small portion for example, one to three per cent of the world’s cars in total.

Under the BCG matrix, the relative market share relative to the automobile industry might make it appear unfavourable. But on the other hand, its position as a market leader in the niche segment of the industry in which it competes would likely have the opposite effect. As a result, this matrix is useful when considered in context rather than used in isolation.

##### Apply and Analyse 3

Evaluate how the four quadrants of the BCG matrix might be applied to a large fictional grocery business with multiple locations and online business, All-In-One Grocers & More Co Ltd, that expands its operations into new business units that sell pharmaceuticals, electronics and sporting goods.

Analysis

Upper left quadrant (high growth, low market share) – Groceries, the core industry of All-in-One Grocers & More, are experiencing rapid market growth in many countries as new foods are introduced and many jurisdictions are experiencing a growing middle class, with thousands of additional people who can now afford to purchase a greater variety of groceries for their families. However, the relative market share of All-In-One Grocers & More may be low. It is unclear as to whether this unit could increase its relative market share.

Upper right quadrant (high growth, high market share) – Due to growing customer demand for new pharmacological products, the pharmaceutical industry is very profitable in many jurisdictions. The pharmaceutical unit of All-in-One Grocers may experience the benefit of both a high market growth rate for their industry and a relatively high market share within the jurisdiction they are competing in. Therefore, the pharmaceutical unit might be classified as a ‘star’ performer in terms of the profitability it might generate for the organisation.

Lower left quadrant (low growth, low market share) – Electronics is a fast-paced industry that honours a new and cutting edge of technology, which means that many electronic devices go out of style and are no longer in favour, leaving a potential surplus of low-value goods that are hard to sell. If the electronics unit of All-In-One Grocers ends up holding a large inventory of devices/products that have both a low market growth rate and a relatively low market share within the electronics industry, such a unit would be classified as a ‘dog’ within the BCG matrix. It could potentially negatively impact the company as a whole.

Lower right quadrant (low growth, high market share) – The sporting goods unit of All-in-One Grocers may offer the best example of a business unit selling well-known products that will usually maintain a relatively steady demand. All-in-One Grocers may even succeed in earning a relatively high market share for the sale of their sporting goods compared to its competitors. However the growth rate for this industry will likely remain low. Therefore the challenge for All-in-One Grocers will be to try and keep generating cash flow from a low-growth industry that can be used to finance the rest of the business.

##### Apply and Analyse 4

Also evaluate how the four quadrants of the BCG matrix might be applied to the opening case of this chapter involving DeepHarbour HK Limited, based on the industry study the new company’s management undertakes as part of its due diligence prior to commencing operations. How might you apply the potential findings to the four quadrants using this model?

Analysis

Upper left quadrant (high growth, low market share) – The shipping industry already contains several long- established international organisations. While there is an increased demand for shipping as a form of commerce and more countries grow their middle class, it is questionable whether a new player can enter the market and earn a sufficient share of the shipping industry to remain in business.

Upper right quadrant (high growth, high market share) – There is a growing, emerging middle class in many countries in Asia. Accompanying that economic demand has been a marked rise in the demand for goods and services, necessitating increased international shipping in Asian waters to export these items. This may be an excellent time for a start-up like DeepHarbour HK to commence operations.

Lower left quadrant (low growth, low market share) – The overhead of a shipping company, including the costs of adopting ever-changing technology, such as newer and faster unloading systems, and information systems for head office, along the heavy labour expenses associated with hiring a staff of 500 employees as DeepHarbour HK intends to do, may make this a risky proposition for a start-up company in the industry. Moreover, suppliers have already formed their allegiances with the larger, more established international companies and may be reluctant to risk new ones with a start-up.

Lower right quadrant (low growth, high market share) – DeepHarbour HK’s location in Hong Kong places it at the centre of growing trade and shipping commerce among Asian countries. While the initial plans for this new business are to expand its reach into the entire Asia-Pacific region, it has strong competition from much more seasoned and long-operating companies in the waters beyond the South China Sea. Perhaps DeepHarbour HK will need to settle on more modest plans to become more of a smaller, regional shipping company. This could provide it with a stable, albeit more steady income for many years as it commences operations.

#### 1.1.2.4 PEST Analysis

The PEST analysis model (the acronym stands for political, economic, social, technological) is an environmental scanning framework that classifies external influences by source. It covers four key factors that are most important and most likely to shape the competitive conditions that an organisation and its industry face. They are as follows:

1. Political – Including, for example, variables such as licensing by authorities, taxation and trademarks and intellectual property requirements in a particular jurisdiction.
2. Economic – This takes into account variables such as the costs of labour, capital and energy, and the level of economic activity impacting the organisation/industry, which could affect, for example, demand and supply.
3. Social – This factor considers social attitudes toward the organisation and the business in which it competes. This may be an indication of the types of customers a particular business may attract.
4. Technological – This examines how technology and technological changes impact the business and organisation.

Sometimes this framework is extended, and is referred to as PESTEL, when an organisation takes into account environmental and legal considerations, as many increasingly do in their operations. The additional ‘EL’ factors are as follows:

• Environmental – This takes into account environmental considerations such as greenhouse gas emissions restrictions, carbon taxes or cap-and-trade requirements, among other factors that may impact business operations.

• Legal – This factor covers legal considerations, such as labour laws, including health and safety regulations/standards, consumer protection laws, taxation laws, environmental laws, operating by-laws and other legal variables that a business may need to consider when operating in a particular jurisdiction.

##### Apply and Analyse 5

How might the expanded PESTEL analysis model apply to the opening case involving DeepHarbour HK? What political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal factors might the new organisation encounter in its competitive environment as it commences operations?

Analysis

• Political – As DeepHarbour HK will be servicing ports in many countries within the Asia-Pacific region, it will need to keep a close eye on political developments in those countries, because instability and/or military conflict in any of those jurisdictions could close ports and cost business. From an administrative standpoint, there may also be licensing requirements, carrying various degrees of complexity, in certain international ports.

• Economic – The international shipping industry is very competitive and capital-intensive and, as noted in the opening case, DeepHarbour HK intends to invest HK$1.5 billion in an initial fleet of 100 ships. But management must weigh that expensive commitment against what it views as the potential long-term benefits of establishing a new shipping line in the Asia-Pacific region, with countries that feature some of the fastest rates of growth in the world.

• Social – As a company that is running a fleet of ships that require costly fuels to operate, DeepHarbour HK’s environmental impact will likely be closely scrutinised in various jurisdictions that it serves. Factors such as allowable pollution emissions, and water ballast discharge regulations can be expected to impact its operations. There may also be carbon related taxes or fees in certain jurisdictions.

• Technological – DeepHarbour HK’s management team will need to determine how various new technologies will impact the organisation’s operations and financial health. These include self-loading and unloading automated systems, and management information systems and software for its head office and fleet of ships. Similarly, the costs of implementing such technologies needs to be factored in – the organisation has budgeted HK$500 million in self-loading/ unloading technology and another HK$250 million in sophisticated navigation and communications IT systems.

• Environmental – Deep Harbour HK’s environmental impact as a shipping company will be considerable. As noted in the social analysis, factors such as allowable pollution emissions, water ballast discharge regulations, carbon taxes or other environmental/financial considerations will impact the organisation’s operations to a certain degree in all jurisdictions.

• Legal – Deep Harbour HK’s management must be aware of, and prepared to adhere to, the local laws in the various countries within the Asia-Pacific region that it will be operating in. Special attention must be paid to factors such as taxation laws, particularly in Hong Kong, where the corporate head office is located, employment and labour laws, including health and safety regulations/standards, environmental impact laws, licences, advertising and marketing laws, and privacy laws, among others. Although many laws in most countries might be similar, in areas such as the environment, or licencing, there may be significant differences. Even at sea, there may be jurisdictional legal issues that arise.

#### 1.1.2.5 Value Chain

The ’value chain’ for an industry is the sequence of activities that transform raw materials into finished products, with each subsequent key activity adding value to the activity before it, thus contributing to the value chain (Exhibit 1.4).
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-47.png)
Some organisations have their own value chains, as distinct from the value chain of the industry they compete within. Companies that participate in many or all stages of the industry value chain from exploration to final sale are highly ‘vertically integrated’. Those that participate in only one activity are considered to be ‘vertically specialised’.

There are two types of activities in the value chain – primary activities and support activities. Primary activities include the following activities:

• Inbound logistics – This refers, for example, to activities such as purchasing and supply chain management.
• Operations – This encompasses various organisational activities, depending on the type of business or industry it competes in, including production and administrative duties carried out by employees.

• Outbound logistics – This refers, for example, to the distribution of a product or service rendered by the organisation.

• Marketing and sales – This includes advertising and selling strategies designed to make the organisation’s product or service stand out in the market and to consumers.

• Servicing – This covers the organisation’s policies and strategies for interacting with its client base, even after a sale, such as when follow-up warranty work is completed.

Support activities include the following factors:

• Infrastructure – This refers to the basic foundation of an organisation, including its strategic and risk management, internal and external relations, financial activities, and governance, among other critical activities.

• Human resource management – This covers issues such as employee recruiting, training and skills development, performance management, and promotions.

• Technology development – This includes operational activities such as an organisation’s information management systems, its design of proprietary technology, and technology related sales.

• Procurement – This covers activities that include, for example, acquiring goods and services critical to the organisation through negotiation strategies, supply chain coordination and database and inventory management.

##### Apply and Analyse 6

Evaluate how the primary and support activities in Porter’s value chain might apply to the operations of DeepHarbour HK Company Limited.

Analysis

There are two types of activities in the value chain – primary activities and support activities. Primary activities for DeepHarbour HK include the following activities: inbound logistics (for example, purchasing and supply chain management), operations, outbound logistics (for example, dealing with distribution of a product or service), marketing and sales and servicing.

Inbound logistics – This category covers the efforts DeepHarbour HK will need to make to obtain container cargo supplies from Hong Kong businesses – such as the clothing, electronics and jewellery industries that DeepHarbour HK plans to serve.

Operations – This category refers to a number of activities regarding the running of a new company such as administrative duties of management in the head office, as well as field operations that will involve the transporting of container goods on ocean voyages undertaken by the DeepHarbour HK fleet.

Outbound logistics – This category describes the process by which container cargo supplies will be loaded on to DeepHarbour HK’s fleet and delivered to various ports in the Asia-Pacific region.

Marketing and sales – This category covers activities by DeepHarbour HK to recruit and sell its business services to new customers, including strategies designed to allow DeepHarbour HK to stand out from its older, more established competition and attract new clients.

Servicing – This category covers DeepHarbour HK’s servicing strategy to its clients. For instance, the organisation may end its responsibility for delivery at the harbour, or it might decide to maintain secondary delivery services inland to ensure that the contents of its containers arrive at a specific destination. It may also involve follow-up to ensure that the goods were delivered undamaged, and providing compensation for damages en route.

Support activities for DeepHarbour HK include the following factors: infrastructure, human resource management, technology development and procurement. Here is a sampling of how these support activities can assist the organisation in undertaking its primary activities.

Infrastructure – DeepHarbour HK’s infrastructure will determine how efficiently the organisation is able to execute its inbound and outbound logistics in terms of, for example, being able to load and unload cargo containers on its fleet of ships. DeepHarbour HK will need to have both the proper personnel and information systems for efficient management of those operations.

Human resource management – DeepHarbour HK plans to hire 500 new employees to commence business. The organisation’s marketing and sales strategy, as well as the quality of its servicing, including the potential for services continuing to the client after delivery, will depend on the competency and skill of the individuals hired.

Technology development – DeepHarbour HK plans to spend HK$500 million on self-loading and unloading technology, plus another HK$250 million in sophisticated navigational and communications IT systems. That technology will be an essential component to smooth running operations, as the company moves container cargo to multiple jurisdictions in the Asia-Pacific region.

Procurement – DeepHarbour HK’s procurement practices, for example, its ability to make a deal with suppliers to save costs on internal supplies to feed the crew during ocean voyages, or the company’s ability to procure the right technology systems at a good price, will also have a direct bearing on the efficiency of its operations.

#### 1.1.2.6 Ansoff Matrix

The Ansoff matrix is a simplistic model that uses quadrants to cover four different potential growth strategies for an organisation to choose, depending on four underlying factors. The two variables listed vertically on this quadrant cover organisations that are competing in existing markets versus those trying to establish new markets. The horizontal variables cover organisations that are dealing in existing products compared to those who are developing new products.

The four growth strategies are as follows:

1. Market penetration – For an organisation that is trying to grow by offering existing products that will allow them to sell into existing markets, the strategy they develop will involve market penetration and the ability to increase its share of that market. This is likely the least risky growth strategy of the four listed in the Ansoff matrix.

2. Product development – For an organisation attempting to grow by developing new products for an existing market, their strategy will involve product development that provides them with the opportunity to become competitive in that market.

3. Market development – An organisation that is attempting to grow by offering existing products, but make inroads into new markets, such as a new country, will need to develop a strategy that is centred on market development.

4. Diversification – An organisation that is attempting to grow by entering new markets, while also offering new products for those markets, will need to be innovative and develop a business diversification strategy. This is likely to be the most difficult, and risky, growth strategy of the four quadrants in this model.

##### Apply and Analyse 7

Provide an example for each quadrant in the Ansoff matrix of the type of company for which the growth strategy described might be most applicable.

Analysis

Market penetration – The fictional organisation DeepHarbour HK Company Limited covered in this chapter is attempting to grow by offering a transportation service on the high seas to service various countries throughout the Asia-Pacific region. DeepHarbour HK’s container shipping service, the routes it will travel and the Pacific Rim markets it will serve are all well established. Thus, the growth strategy of DeepHarbour HK fits the definition of market penetration under the Ansoff matrix.

Product development – Let’s say that a fictional company is developing a digital readout for a barbeque tank that will indicate how much propane is left in that tank. That is an example of an organisation developing a new product that will be sold to an established market, since the barbeque is a common tool used around the world. Those two variables – a company that is attempting to grow by offering a new product for an existing market – would fit the product development quadrant definition under the Ansoff matrix.

Market development – In contrast to the product development quadrant, some organisations wish to grow by offering an existing product or service, but then sell that into a new market that is not established. For example, pretend that several Caribbean countries have decided to do what tropical Dubai has done, in building a large dome that can be kept cold for people who want to ski indoors. A ski manufacturer in a cold northern climate with long winters who has done business at home for years, but develops a new growth strategy with contracts to sell to those Caribbean countries enclosed, cold domes, would have an existing product line that they were trying to sell into new markets.

Diversification – The most difficult quadrant in the Ansoff matrix would be occupied by an organisation that is offering a new product for new markets. A hypothetical example would be a company that develops an expensive, body covering clear umbrella, complete with a GPS tracking device. Such an umbrella would be effective. It would be virtually guaranteed to keep somebody dry during a driving rainstorm and, with the GPS device, it is unlikely that this umbrella, an object people are often prone to forget, will get lost. But would there be a market for such an expensive umbrella? Both the new product and new market to match it with would be a risky idea.

#### 1.1.2.7 POPIT Model

The POPIT (acronym for people, organisation, processes, and information and technology) model is a simple business architecture model that an organisation can use to conduct a strategic analysis of its operations when faced with decision making and choices necessary to effect change.

This model is shaped like a pyramid represented by four triangles (Exhibit 1.5). ‘Organisation’ is at the top of the pyramid and the base consists of three variables or factors, including ‘People’, ‘Information and Technology’ and ‘(Business) Processes’.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-48.png)
The ‘Organisation’ triangle examines the organisation’s management and employee structure, their roles and responsibilities and how well that is co-ordinated, as well as the resources available to do the job and the corporate culture and rules that need to be followed.

The ‘People’ triangle examines details that include current job descriptions, employee skills, motivation and knowledge, and whether those variables match up to the changes that are required. A detailed assessment of those factors can assist management in making any necessary adjustments.

The ‘Information and Technology’ triangle assesses whether the organisation’s hardware and software systems are producing the information and support necessary, or whether changes are required to keep the organisation up to date with the business competition and other pressures it faces.

The ‘Processes’ triangle studies the organisation’s existing processes, including those involving its value chain, to determine how well they are documented and followed, which ones are most critical to operations and what changes may be required to bring them up to date.

##### Apply and Analyse 8

Evaluate how each of the triangles in the POPIT model pyramid might affect DeepHarbour HK Company Limited if, two years after commencing operations, the organisation is not penetrating the Asia-Pacific region shipping market at anywhere near the rate that it planned to, and its leaders need to conduct a major analysis of operations to determine what changes are necessary.

Analysis

Organisation – Under this triangle at the top of the POPIT model pyramid, it would be necessary to study DeepHarbour HK’s organisational structure to determine whether the company has been established in a way that will maximise its chances of achieving the goals set out in its business strategy. In this instance, DeepHarbour HK has been unable to successfully penetrate the Asia-Pacific commercial shipping region. This would involve an analysis of the overall corporate structure of key managers and employees, including whether there is a more efficient way of utilising their talents to achieve success.

People – This triangle in the POPIT model, one of three in the base of the pyramid structure, would examine in further detail the role of DeepHarbour HK’s employees, including whether they have the skills, motivation and knowledge to perform the tasks required in an effort to achieve the organisation’s goals. For example, there may be an issue with motivation that prevents certain people in the sales and marketing area from advocating for the company as they should in order to secure new clients. Or there may be issues with the way clients are being treated, which is causing a drop-off. This analysis of the people in the organisation could lead to an important change to maximise the chances of improvement in the pursuit of strategic goals.

Information and technology – This triangle in the POPIT model, one of three in the base of the pyramid structure, assesses the role of DeepHarbour HK’s information systems, including its hardware and software, and whether the problems preventing the company from expanding as it should have anything to do with technology. For example, there could be issues with the computer systems that affect the time it takes for the automated loaders and unloaders to do their respective jobs, which is negatively impacting the clients that DeepHarbour HK is able to secure. An analysis of these factors could lead to important changes that help improve the organisation’s chances of achieving its goals.

Processes – This triangle in the POPIT model, one of three in the base of the pyramid structure, will study DeepHarbour HK’s current processes to determine whether changes are necessary to put it back on track to achieve its strategic goals. This will, for example, involve assessing the infrastructure of the company’s fleet, the logistics it uses for ship voyages and its procurement practices, among others, to determine where improvements need to be made to better enhance DeepHarbour HK’s chances for greater market penetration.

### 1.1.3 Strategic Capability

David Fater, in Essentials of Corporate and Capital Formation (Wiley, 2010), writes that ‘an organisation’s grand strategy is its blueprint for building, exploiting and renewing the positions from which superior performance results’. He also notes that, ‘. . .excellence by itself is not enough. Excellence in areas of strategic significance (for example, that determine the outcome of competition in the marketplace) is what is needed’.

Strategic capability, or the competitive strengths of an organisation, is an important factor in the ability to execute business strategy. The strategic business plan should be dynamic, rather than static, for the firm.

A strategic business plan includes the following components:

1. Evaluate the business environment within which the firm operates.
2. Identify the firm’s core competencies and potential growth opportunities.
3. Formulate a strategic business plan for turning the firm’s core competencies into sustainable competitive advantages, and develop robust processes for implementing and sustaining the business plan and financial strategy.

The processes that organisations use to develop a business strategy can differ dramatically. In some cases, not enough time is spent on strategy formulation, and some strategies can be based only on recent experience and limited information. Furthermore, the competitive landscape is sometimes changing so quickly that recent experience and limited information are the norm.

A strategic management process for formulating and implementing strategy requires both a thorough external and internal analysis. Conducting an analysis of the company’s external environment and its internal resources and capabilities provides a formal structure for executives to understand those criteria (Exhibit 1.6).

The primary purpose of the strategy formulation process is to specify the high-level plan and set of actions the company will need to take to achieve a competitive advantage. After determining the plan for competitive advantage has been formulated, it is necessary to develop another, more detailed plan to put into action the firm’s strategy using specific actions. The focus should be to make key strategic choices through the strategic management process.

#### 1.1.3.1 SWOT Analysis

A SWOT analysis is an analysis of an organisation’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (‘SWOT’). To drive strategic planning, it may be useful to conduct this type of analysis at a high level or for any component of the business.

The first two assessments – strengths and weaknesses – are typically determined by an analysis of internal attributes. The final two assessments – opportunities and threats – will be uncovered by an analysis of the external environment.

SWOT assessments should take into account a wide variety of factors, including financial, competitiveness, technological, management, and skills, a macro-assessment of the industry and market within which it operates, and the organisation’s customers and rivals.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-49.png)
For some organisations, the external environment might include the commitment to corporate social responsibility (CSR) – which covers environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues. In the contemporary business world, financial profit and corporate social responsibility can no longer be considered mutually exclusive entities.

##### Illustrative Example 2

When conducting a SWOT analysis of DeepHarbour HK Company Limited, an assessment could be made based on the following factors:

###### Strengths
• Do we have a service that will create value for customers?
• Do we have a unique level of service and/or technology that cannot be duplicated by our competition?
• Can we offer a competitive price and remain profitable?
• Do we have the necessary information technology and systems to function efficiently?

###### Weaknesses
• Can the level of our services be imitated/duplicated by our competitors?
• Are we trying to do too much in too many places or are we too specialised?
• Are we proposing services to a market that is already over-saturated?
• Do we lack the financial resources to develop our shipping company to where we want it to go?

###### Opportunities
• Is there a long-term market for our service appealing to, say, a particular industry?
• Have we spotted an opportunity that puts us ahead of current trends compared to our competitors?
• Can we attract unique talent that our competitors cannot?
• In starting a business at a later date than our competitors, are there certain technological advances that we can leverage earlier than they can?

###### Threats
• Will we face increasing competition in our industry, including in our own geographic location?
• Can we be undercut in our pricing strategy by a large competitive field that serves to drive down prices?
• Do our services face the risk of quickly becoming obsolete in the face of technological advancements?
• Could our business be upended by environmental risks?

### 1.1.4 Financial Capability

A properly conceived financial strategy is a crucial element of the financial plan. This strategy needs to be determined by senior management and monitored on an ongoing basis to ensure that it continues to meet the organisation’s changing requirements. The strategy must be comprehensive in terms of covering and promoting all of the organisation’s core operations. It should also serve to advance the goals and objectives of each business unit.

For example, risk management, including a determination of acceptable risk exposures, represents a key aspect of an organisation’s financial policy. The financial strategy should provide risk management guidelines and establish how such activities will be monitored in an effort to prevent exposing the organisation to financial – or even catastrophic – loss.

Management must decide, for instance, whether currency exposures will be managed and, if so, how actively they will be managed and the extent to which the firm is willing to take speculative positions in the pursuit of its business and financial objectives.

Financial strategies often centre on decisions such as how growth is to be attained. For example, organisational growth can be achieved through various strategies, including:

• Diversification of its products or business lines;

• Acquisition of another company for growth or diversification purposes;

• Strategic alliances with another organisation; or

• International expansion to achieve economies of scale, or access key resources, or provide new skills.

Another key decision could involve vertical integration, which determines whether it is more profitable for an organisation to make or buy a particular product. Another contemporary decision that many businesses need to make involves whether to manufacture something in its home country or to outsource, or offshore it to a jurisdiction where costs – primarily labour-related – are lower.

Organisations must continually reassess, update and revise their strategic business plan and financial strategy in a competitive and fluid global marketplace. The organisation’s financial capabilities should be assessed in detail as part of a wider SWOT analysis of corporate strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. Factors to be assessed might include financing, earnings prospects, strength of the corporate structure, statement of financial position and cash flow, among others.

Financial Planning Model Preparing a financial planning model requires the organisation’s top management to make several investment and financial policy decisions (Exhibit 1.7). These decisions impose constraints on the financial model’s outputs that must be recognised during its preparation. Investment decisions are crucial to an organisation’s continuation, but they may also create substantial risk when such activities are material to the organisation and senior members may have little experience with that type of investment.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-50.png)
Some important investment and financial policy decisions are:
- • Investment policy decisions: These involve identifying the investment decisions to be evaluated as part of the financial planning process. Typically, these involve large capital expenditures such as building a new manufacturing facility, entering a new line of business or acquiring another firm.
- • Financial policy decisions, including:
	- °Capital structure decisions: Capital structure decisions determine management’s targeted capital structure and its willingness to use financial leverage.
	- °Financing decisions: Financing decisions determine the acceptable type of financing in addition to the availability of such financing – including retained earnings, equity, preferred stock, commercial loans and/or long-term debt.
	- °Payout decisions: Payout decisions identify the firm’s dividend and stock repurchase policies for the sales period.

The diagram below illustrates the financial planning process. As noted, the organisation’s various departmental and other budgets, along with its investment and financing plans, originate from the corporate financial plan, which serves as the foundation for those documents. The financial plan, in turn, executes the corporate strategic plan.

### 1.1.5 Operational Capability

An organisation will need to formulate, and then implement, strategy at three different levels: at the corporate level, at a business unit or product level and at a functional level (Exhibit 1.8).
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-51.png)
Corporate strategy refers to decisions that are made by senior corporate executives about where to compete in terms of industries and markets, as well as the support and approval of the board of directors who set the direction and hire the CEO to execute them.

Business unit strategy is made at the level of the strategic business unit. This refers to business units in an organisation that typically has its own profit and loss responsibility. The individual in charge of each business unit will address how to gain and sustain advantage in that particular market. Different functions, such as product development, operations, information technology, sales and marketing and customer service, may also reside within each business unit.

A functional strategy should align with the overall business unit strategies to effectively implement the business unit strategy.

#### Who Is Responsible for Business Strategy?

The organisation’s strategic leaders are typically those individuals who develop strategy through the strategic management process. Strategic leaders are responsible for both formulating and explaining the corporate strategy, in addition to providing motivation so that all employees are able to understand and execute the strategy.

Deliberate strategies are implemented as a result of a careful analysis of markets, customers, competitors and a firm’s resources and capabilities. For example, executives at a retail chain might decide it is in the organisation’s best interests to move to upscale retailing if they determine they cannot compete successfully with other firms in their industry offering lower prices.

The organisation’s business plan should incorporate all of the firm’s existing businesses, as well as plans for potential new lines of business, including that which is beneficial to conduct online. It should promote and refine existing core competencies as well as the development of new competencies.

An organisation’s business strategy is the driving force behind all of its subsequent decisions.

The organisation’s business strategy ultimately determines the firm’s lines of business, the products it will sell, its method of producing them and the geographic markets in which the business will compete.

An organisation’s business strategy also defines its competitive position within its industry. In order to be successful, a firm must have a good strategy and a management team that can implement it. Management should, therefore, always be striving to produce a strategy that gives the firm a sustainable competitive edge.

Overall, the strategic plan provides high-level direction to management for making business decisions and guidance about what the firm will and will not do. The strategic plan covers all areas in the firm, such as operations, marketing, finance, information systems and human resources management. The plan determines the lines of business in which the firm will compete and the relative emphasis the executives wish to place on each business activity.

It also identifies major details such as:
• Areas for investments in productive assets.
• Capital expenditures.
• The acquisition of a firm or the launch of a new line of business.
• Potential mergers, alliances and divestitures that management may seek to strengthen the firm’s business portfolio.

Flexibility is an important factor in a rapidly changing global business environment where even carefully laid plans of established companies are in danger of becoming obsolete without proper and ongoing monitoring.

That is why a SWOT analysis, as discussed in the previous sections, is an important component of an organisation’s business strategy, particularly as the analysis applies to the external factors of opportunities and threats. Factors to be considered include, but are certainly not limited to:

• Are potential new markets gaining in importance and old ones diminishing?
• Are new technologies making the traditional technologies the organisation has depended on in the past obsolete, or perhaps even changing the way business is done entirely?
• Does the organisation need to adapt to a new or rapidly changing regulatory environment?
• Do global or regional shortages of resources affect the way the organisation needs to do business?

With strategic objectives that are both specific and measurable, an organisation can revise them periodically and cope with change and renewal without having to make wholesale changes to its strategic plan.

#### Knowledge Check Questions

##### Question 1

The McKinsey and Company ‘7 S model of organisational alignment’ contains seven important organisational elements, including strategy, structure, systems, staffing, skills, style and shared values.

Identify which of the following describes what the ‘softer’ attributes of style and shared values contribute to organisational alignment with respect to achieving business goals.

- A Style and shared values are an indicator that employees get along together, and individuals who share similar personal attributes are also likely to share similar business aspirations. 
- B Style and shared values are both indicators of efficiency and efficient organisations are more likely to achieve their stated business strategy.

## 1.2 IMPLEMENTING BUSINESS STRATEGY

This section examines the process involved in implementing, or putting into practice, a business strategy, along with the potential impact and consequences that various strategic options might have on the organisation as it does so.

The previous section focused on developing the business strategy for an organisation. Once strategy has been determined, the organisation needs to ensure strategic, financial and operational capability so that all parts of the organisation can work together to execute the strategy.

Traditionally, corporate strategic decisions are determined by senior management with the support and approval of the board of directors. This involves decisions about how the organisation will compete, industries and markets it will compete in and how it will allocate its resources.

Typically, management then develops a more detailed strategy for individual business units to achieve those strategic objectives. Individual business units may (or may not) be responsible for determining how best to implement components of the strategy, depending on the structure of the organisation.

Effective strategic implementation typically requires the following:

• The functional strategies within the organisation (i.e. research and development, operations, sales and marketing, human resource management) are well aligned with delivering the unique value identified in the overall strategy. Measuring how effectively functional activities are being performed to support the overall strategy will contribute to the success of implementation.
• The organisation’s structure – including its systems, staff, skills, style and shared values (for example, culture) – are designed to handle the execution of this strategy.

### 1.2.1 Implementation Process

The development of key resources and capabilities needed to deliver unique values should be part of an organisation’s strategic implementation plan.
The strategic implementation plan involves having the organisation develop a set of processes or capabilities within each individual function (for example, that could include research and development, operations, sales, service or human resources) and then ensuring that such capabilities align with the unique value the organisation hopes to offer its stakeholders.

Effective implementation of an organisation’s business strategy requires forging an alignment among the external environment, the strategy and the internal elements of the firm. Implementation is as much a matter of alignment as it is of execution.

Alignment means that the important elements of the organisation are in the proper relationship with each other – in other words, they fit well together and reinforce each other. In an aligned organisation all of the elements support this strategy.

The McKinsey and Company 7 S model discussed earlier can support strategy implementation for the organisation as well as for divisions, groups or departments. For example, an organisation might review employee compensation to identify where the compensation does not match the business strategy. Moving a sales force from commission-based compensation to a new salary structure represents a significant change and could result in important implications in terms of employee motivation and customer service. It might raise questions such as:

• How will the compensation change affect the company’s ability to attract and retain its sales force?
• Will high sales performers still be appropriately compensated under a salary-based arrangement?
• Will the new compensation system align with the values of the organisation?

To use this tool most effectively organisations should follow these five steps:

1. Identify the current state of the organisation and misalignments.
	Interviews and surveys are powerful tools for managers in this regard. Management, or perhaps consultants or other outsiders for larger companies that can afford it, will rely on a mix of interviews and other sources. The goal is to create a picture of the 7 S variable elements in the company as they currently exist.

2. Rank order misalignments based on the importance of misalignment with strategy.
	After having accurately identified the current state of the organisation, along with any misalignments, managers will often be able to identify a misalignment or multiple misalignments, both within each of the 7 S variables themselves, as well as between the different elements in the model.

	It is easy to get frustrated or feel overwhelmed as a result of those findings. However, managers need to take that information and be able to ask the right questions in order to be able to reduce the list of misalignments down to the few that really need to be changed.

	Those questions include:
- • Which misalignments keep us from reaching our strategic goals?
- • Which misalignments dissipate rather than build a competitive advantage?
3. Develop plans to create alignment.
	While some of the misalignments will be company specific (particularly those that involve elements of style, which are often difficult to codify, or shared values, which take a long time to influence and change), managers and consultants should be open to looking at how other companies have solved these problems.

	There is, for example, no need for an executive team to start all over again in terms of compensation. Benchmarking other organisations, or divisions within their own company, provides a starting point from which companies can customise their own solutions.

4. Understand how the proposed change affects other elements in the model.
	This examines how changes in one variable affect others in the 7 S model. For example, moving a sales force from being under a system of being paid pure commission to a new salary structure represents a huge change, and could result in important implications in terms of staff motivation. It raises questions such as:

	• How will the company attract and retain a sales force to fit the new pay scheme?
	• What new skills will existing salespeople need to learn?
	• Where will the new system conflict with shared values?

	Programmes within an organisation can be doomed but this would rarely be as the result of the change in compensation alone. Failure, when it does occur, is usually from pushback as a result of impact on the other six ‘S’ variables.

5. Adjust plans accordingly.
	After managers see the effort required to create realignment within the entire 7 S model, they may need to adjust their business plans accordingly. The previous example noted that changing the compensation system may result in the need to simultaneously work on new hiring and retention plans. The changes to compensation may also precede and signal an important change in shared values within the organisation.

### 1.2.2 Consequences and Impact of Strategic Options

Each of the functional areas within an organisation – for example, human resources, sales and marketing, operational units and research and development – may, in turn, be responsible for developing their own tactics and a path forward to help execute the business unit strategies.

Strategic decision making and execution therefore involve precision within the organisation. Business unit managers must understand the overall corporate strategy in order to ensure that the strategies they develop match the overall corporate strategy.

#### 1.2.2.1 Impact on Stakeholders

Every organisation has a set of both internal and external stakeholders to whom it is accountable – and who can therefore influence business strategy. Four primary stakeholder groups for organisations include:

1. Capital market stakeholders (including shareholders, banks, etc.);
2. Product market stakeholders (including customers, suppliers);
3. Organisational stakeholders (including employees); and
4. Community stakeholders (including communities, government bodies).

Different stakeholder groups may have conflicting views regarding the appropriateness of different strategic decisions. For example, shareholders of an organisation may be presented with the option of lowering the company’s product costs by closing down its domestic production and moving production offshore, where labour is cheaper. This would require reducing many of its local employees.

Both the employee stakeholder and community stakeholder groups in locations where production is currently located will naturally perceive this move as negative. However, shareholders and customer stakeholder groups may applaud this decision on the grounds this could increase profits for shareholders, or lower prices for customers, or perhaps both. It might enable the company to maintain the business in the face of competitive pressure. Because of conflicts like this, organisations need to ensure their strategic actions follow accepted ethical standards for business activity.

#### Illustrative Example 3 – Impact on DeepHarbour HK

Let us look at the example of our fictional company, DeepHarbour HK Company Limited, whose corporate strategy is to commence operations with 100 ships in the Asia-Pacific region. The organisation’s mission statement, as noted previously, is ‘to exceed customer expectations by delivering a premium shipping service using modern technology with timely, efficient and personalised service that is reliable and predictable, that builds loyalty with our global customers and supports the local communities in which we do business’.

The senior executives of DeepHarbour HK, backed by its board, have set an overall agenda for the organisation, as well as a philosophical theme of being known as a company that delivers a high-quality customer service that utilises efficiencies and technology for its business clients. They must determine what capabilities are necessary to deliver the unique value they set out to achieve. Also, where should the company’s resources be most heavily allocated, in order to achieve that goal? For example, should DeepHarbour HK spend big on staffing expenses to deliver a unique customer service experience? Or does it opt to go with a lean staff – particularly during its start-up phase, to invest more heavily in technology than its competitors?

Each of DeepHarbour HK’s business units – the company will commence operations with operations in Hong Kong, but plans to expand to Shanghai and Tokyo within the first two years as the company grows – must then develop a business strategy to determine how the company will achieve its mission statement and earn a niche as a leading container cargo carrier in Asia-Pacific ocean nations.

Then the key functional areas within each of the organisation’s business units including accounting, human resources, sales and marketing and operations – must, in turn, develop their own tactics to align with the strategy of that business unit.

For example, while DeepHarbour HK has already announced it will commence operations with 500 employees, in future, management and the human resources department must determine how many employees will be optimal for a business that is expected to expand rapidly. It must also recruit the right employees who are capable of fulfilling the mission of providing a ‘timely, efficient and personalised service’, where those employees should be located, and whether any roles should be filled by outsourcing rather than directly hiring employees.

Implementation of one strategy may affect how another strategy is executed. Some customer service roles at DeepHarbour HK can be outsourced to an external service provider (to a third-party call centre, for example), resulting in a business that is more flexible in an economic downturn, since it would have fewer employees on its payroll during a period of economic weakness. However, this outsourcing may reduce the ability of DeepHarbour HK to provide an exceptional service, which is expected to be one of its key differentiators. Therefore, the interrelationship between two different strategies should be considered.

A marketing strategy will be required to advertise the availability of those services, particularly since DeepHarbour HK is new to the container shipping industry, compared to its more seasoned competitors. The finance department will be responsible for conducting a cost-benefit analysis of strategies that might be considered in coming years, such as whether the time is right to finance and purchase new ships or whether to make an investment in additional new technologies, such as those that permit ships to self-load and unload cargo.

Each of these execution/tactical decisions needs to be filtered through individual business unit managers to ensure that is consistent with their strategy and that the business unit strategy in turn supports the overall strategy or direction set by senior management in conjunction with the board of directors. Recommendations for future strategic options must also be filtered through the same lens – does this ultimately help fulfil the entity’s overall strategic objective? If so, it signals that parts of the organisation are pulling together to fulfil corporate goals, which is positive for internal and external stakeholders.
---- 
#### 1.2.2.2 Consequences if Business Strategies Are Not Coordinated

An organisation’s business unit strategies should support the overriding corporate strategy and its functional strategies should, in turn, reinforce and provide appropriate tactics for executing the business unit strategies.

If this does not happen, the organisation is likely to lack clear direction and certainly will not be able to launch a coordinated effort to achieve its goals. This could also result in significantly reduced profit, financial loss or operational inefficiencies. Furthermore, this may seriously impact an organisation’s ability to conduct research and development to enhance its viability as a business that is a going concern.

For example, DeepHarbour HK’s mission statement, as already noted, pledges to ‘to exceed customer expectations by delivering a premium shipping service using modern technology with timely, efficient and personalised service that is reliable and predictable, that builds loyalty with our global customers, and supports the local communities in which we do business’.

Therefore, it is important for both the human resources and the information technology (IT) departments of the organisation’s business unit – and expected future business units in other geographic venues in the Asia Pacific – to deliver on that promise.

If, say, the IT department makes a bad decision, for example, they purchase systems that fail to perform properly and therefore fail to adequately service the customer; or the human resources department does not hire employees sensitive to the expected customer relations experience, then the company will have implemented a tactic that directly contradicts its overall strategy.

#### Illustrative Example 4

Evaluate the considerations of potential stakeholders that DeepHarbour HK Company Limited would need to take into account as it develops its overall corporate strategic business plan.

Answer

DeepHarbour HK’s capital market stakeholders would include external stakeholders such as financial shareholders of the private company. If it later becomes a publicly listed organisation, that might expand in the future to include a large public ownership in all or part of the company. It would also include the banks with which DeepHarbour HK does business and which may potentially be large creditors.

The new company’s product market stakeholders also refer to external stakeholders, including members of its supply chain who would, for example, help supply its shipping fleet as well as the customers who DeepHarbour HK will be shipping containers on behalf of.

Organisational stakeholders include internal stakeholders such as the employees that DeepHarbour HK elects to hire. The organisation will have a duty to those employees to provide them with a fair and honest corporate governance system as well as a safe environment as is possible in which to work.

Community stakeholders are external stakeholders and include, for example, government bodies in each jurisdiction that DeepHarbour HK operates, whose regulations may require DeepHarbour HK to adhere to rules involving factors such as pollution emissions and where to discharge its ballast. The community at large in the jurisdictions in which the shipping company operates is another external stakeholder that must be paid close attention to, particularly with respect to pollution emissions close to land or in the vicinity of its harbour. Negative publicity from the community at large can be very damaging, even fatal for a business, particularly one that is just starting up and hasn’t yet established a solid reputation.

#### Apply and Analyse 9

DeepHarbour HK Company Limited’s mission statement is ‘to exceed customer expectations by delivering a premium shipping service using modern technology with timely, efficient and personalised service that is reliable and predictable, that builds loyalty with our global customers, and supports the local communities in which we do business’.

Advise what the new organisation must do to effectively coordinate all three levels of strategic planning – at the corporate (executive) level, the business unit (management) level and at the functional level.

Analysis The actions of several departments at the functional strategic level within DeepHarbour HK will be key to the execution of a co-ordinated strategy that fulfils the direction established in the organisation’s mission statement and in its overall corporate strategy.

Human resources – The organisation has promised to ‘deliver timely, efficient personalised service’ to all of its stakeholders. Therefore, much of the onus will be on human resources to hire staff members who are capable of delivering on that promise. The human resources department will also likely be asked to contribute to future decisions about optimal levels of staffing.

Information technology – DeepHarbour HK has promised to ‘utilise the latest in technology to most efficiently address’ the business requirements of its clients. This means that the purchase of information systems and other technology, such as self-loading/unloading equipment is critical: for example, it must be as modern and efficient as possible. Accounting – The accounting department needs to calculate costs precisely so that the financial resources of the new company are spent wisely in pursuit of its corporate goals. The accounting department’s calculations will be critical for conducting a cost-benefit analysis of financial issues expected to arise in the future, such as the optimal number of ships DeepHarbour HK needs to maintain in its fleet in order to maximise profit.

Sales and marketing – Acquiring new clients and making a positive impression about the organisation’s services and the benefits of shipping with DeepHarbour HK, a start-up, will be the responsibility of sales and marketing professionals. They will need to coordinate and execute a strategy – for example, that might be a website, online ads, cold calling or a combination of all of those – to obtain the clients necessary to get the business up and running in order to provide the ‘timely, efficient and personalised service’ promised by executives in the corporate strategy.

## 1.3 MONITORING BUSINESS STRATEGY

Strategic change and realignment take a long time to be successfully implemented, but the job is not done when that occurs. Ongoing monitoring is required. Strategic managers need a way to be able to effectively measure their organisation’s progress against the strategic goals that have been established.

Monitoring of adherence to business strategy is important for success. When the organisation’s leaders fail to monitor its business strategies, the organisation can lose sight of how it is performing relative to the goals it has set. Monitoring enables management to see when strategies are working and when adjustments may be helpful.

An effective measurement system is an essential element of solid strategy implementation, designed to help everyone in the organisation, from top management on down to front-line employees, understand how their daily work contributes to strategic success.

### Line of Sight Principle

The line of sight principle is an approach that helps managers create measurement systems to overcome the limited perspectives of individual organisational members. The notion behind this principle is that individual members of an organisation should easily be able to connect their daily work and tasks to the overall strategic goals of the organisation.

For example, imagine the dilemma faced by a vice-president of a cosmetics company. It is 10:10 a.m. and she has arrived late at her office, delayed by construction and multiple lane closures on the freeway that brought ground traffic to a near standstill for hours, frustrating motorists. She is now running very late for a 10:00 a.m. meeting to discuss a critical new product line expansion. The sales and research and development teams are already in the meeting room, ready to help her make key decisions that will determine the course of the organisation’s sales strategy for the next fiscal year.

But then things get worse. Just as the vice-president prepares to head into the delayed meeting, she receives a message from a senior manager facing an emergency with the organisation’s largest customer that the manager says must be resolved quickly because the customer is threatening to leave.

The question is not ‘what is most important?’, for it is clear that both of the matters at hand demand her immediate attention. The more relevant question is ‘under the circumstances, what must she do first?’

The line of sight principle recognises that grand strategies are realised only as individual managers and employees make conscious decisions about how to allocate the valuable resources they control. They don’t just happen.

The following four-step approach can be taken to build line of sight into a corporate strategy:

Step 1: Consider what is most important. List the abstract and broad goals and objectives of the organisation. For example, are the goals related to the creation of shareholder value? Cutting-edge innovation? World-class customer service? Or a great place to work?

Step 2: Identify the tangible strategy that reaches that objective. For example, does the organisation intend to create shareholder value through a premium price or through cost leadership? An organisation needs to coordinate its resources under each of those major strategic positions, in order to achieve those goals of meaningful differentiation or low cost. Considerations such as the need for division or functional managers to determine the resources and capabilities under their direct control and how each area can use those to assist in implementing the larger corporate strategy, establishes the line of sight for the organisation’s respective divisions or functions.

Step 3: What specific activities do various work groups within the organisation perform that use and can strengthen those resources? Such daily work activities in most organisations are responsible for its most basic functions such as paying bills and facilitating sales to keep the company running, as opposed to the higher activities related to developing and enhancing the organisation’s strategic capabilities. But a common key for all work performed, both at a work group level, as well as for higher level activities, is to be able to prioritise what needs to be done first. When that has been determined, work group tasks can then be further subdivided such that each individual involved should be able to understand how their personal work ties in with and helps execute the organisation’s strategy.

Step 4: Determine which measure among the organisation’s various activities illustrates how work is supposed to be carried out. For example, many organisations have customer call centres. These are treated as cost centres, which execute the function of providing customer support and assistance as required. Often employees in those call centres are told the corporate objective is to keep the calls as brief as possible in order to maximise the number of calls over a specified period of time. This works well if the organisational strategy is cost leadership, but if the key resource is promoting the brand, getting customers off the phone quickly does little to build brand or achieve that goal.

The organisation should have clear metrics, or ways to measure whether its business strategy is being successfully implemented. One strategy tool suggests some useful metrics that functional area leaders, as well as the CEO and members of the top management team, can use to determine how effectively strategies are being implemented.

These include:

• Financial metrics, to determine how well the organisation is meeting its financial targets to satisfy shareholder/investor demands, as part of an analysis on current performance;

• Customer metrics, to determine how well the organisation is meeting customer service needs and product desires, or external performance processes;

• Process metrics, to determine how well the organisation is performing its key business (internal performance) processes; and

• Innovation metrics, to determine how well the organisation is performing as a means of helping to ensure future growth, developing new products or future performance.

### Illustrative Example 5

Developing a sound business strategy and then having the ability to successfully implement that strategy are two very important and necessary pre-requisites for any organisation to be able to succeed. But today’s fast-paced business world doesn’t leave much of a window to enjoy that success, unless organisations are able to continually monitor that strategy and determine if and where adjustments are necessary.

In order to be able to monitor in real-time or an on-going basis whether the business strategy is succeeding, organisations need clear metrics to measure. List some of the key metrics that DeepHarbour HK Company Limited will need to measure after it develops and implements a new business strategy.

Answer

Financial metrics – DeepHarbour HK will need to have metrics in place to help the organisation to continually evaluate how well it is meeting shareholder and investor demands, as part of its ongoing analysis on current performance. Examples of financial metrics include net cash flow, liquidity, earnings per share, return on investment, and net present value, among others.

Customer metrics – The organisation will need metrics to continually determine how well it is meeting its customer needs and other external performance processes that have been established. Examples of customer metrics include customer satisfaction surveys, brand awareness, customer loyalty and customer profitability.

Process metrics – DeepHarbour HK will need metrics to continually determine how well the organisation is performing its key business or internal performance processes. Examples of process metrics include employee satisfaction surveys, employee turnover, response time to customer concerns and safety record.

Innovation metrics – As mentioned, even after the initial business strategic plan has been successfully implemented, the organisation will require the use of metrics to be able to continually determine how well it is performing. This measurement will help enhance the chances of future growth and future performance. Examples of innovation metrics include rate of adaptation to new technologies, rate of new service sales and rate of new product development sales.
