### 1.3.1 Data Collection

Hard, indisputable facts that reflect performance critical to the business and operating unit level of the organisation are measures that are easily converted to financial results to determine return on investment. Without impact data, a credible return on investment (ROI) calculation cannot be delivered.

One unique feature about business impact data is that they are often very easy to measure. Hard and soft data measures at this level often reflect key measures that are found in numbers easily available throughout an organisation. For example, a typical large organisation will have hundreds or even thousands of business measures reflecting output, quality, costs, time, job satisfaction and customer satisfaction, among many other variables.

#### Types of Data

A distinction is made in two general categories of data: hard data and soft data.

Hard data are quantitative, undisputed measurements that are gathered from functional areas within an organisation. They are the most desirable type of data to collect. The ultimate criteria for measuring the effectiveness of the organisation’s management and performance rest on hard data items, such as productivity, revenue and profitability.

Hard data are:
• Easy to measure and quantify
• Relatively easy to convert to monetary values
• Objectively based measures of organisational performance
• Credible measurements

Hard data can be grouped into five major categories – including output, costs, time, quality and technology – and are typical performance measures in almost every organisation (Exhibit 1.9).
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-52.png)
There are times when hard, rational numbers simply do not exist. For example, it may be challenging to quantify specific aspects of the business, such as employee innovation. When this is the case, soft data may be meaningful in evaluating projects. Soft data tend to be less quantifiable and more subjective in nature.

Common types of soft data can be categorised or subdivided into six areas including: work habits, initiative/innovation, customer service, employee development/advancement, work climate/job satisfaction and image (Exhibit 1.10). There are multiple other ways to divide soft data into categories depending on the intent of the data collection and the type of organisation.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-53.png)
#### Hard Data and Soft Data Measures in Practice

Both hard and soft data are typically collected through measuring attributes of the business. Examples of hard data include revenue, productivity and profitability, as well as measures of quality, costs and time. Hard data from a particular program might result in improvements in the output of a work unit, section, department, division or the entire organisation. This data can be gathered statistically, often through reports provided by internal technology systems. When these values are monitored, changes can easily be measured by comparing outputs before and after a program or change are instituted to identify improvement.

Soft data such as attitude, motivation and satisfaction are more difficult to gather and analyse than hard data. However, some measures may be obtained through customer and employee satisfaction surveys, employee award voting (for example, employee of the month), department complaints, use of whistleblower tools (for example, a whistle-blowing telephone or email hotline) or through observation. Soft data is helpful when hard data is unavailable, or it can be used to supplement hard data.

#### Illustrative Example 6

DeepHarbour HK Company Limited is considering adding some data sources to support its analytical activities. Provide specific recommendations of hard data variables and soft data variables that might provide more insight into DeepHarbour HK’s business operations.

##### DeepHarbour HK Hard Data

Category: Output New Accounts Generated: A regular statistic (for example, monthly) to measure the rate at which DeepHarbour HK is able to attain new customers.

Category: Costs Overhead Costs: The cost of labour related to ship maintenance relative to the number of ship journeys that DeepHarbour HK’s fleet undertakes.

Category: Time On-time Shipments: The percentage of container shipments that reached the destination ports on time (as measured within a specified number of hours).

Category: Quality Incidents: Number of accidents – for example, hard landings, spills, injuries, loss of cargo at sea.

Category: Technology Hardware and/or software malfunctions: Incidents where DeepHarbour HK’s self-loading/ unloading technology fails to perform as expected.

##### DeepHarbour HK Soft Data

Category: Work Habits Violations of safety rules: Since safety violations are very serious, measurement of safety rules violations could be enhanced by regular inspections, supplemented by a whistleblowing hotline.

Category: Initiative/Innovation New Services: Measurement of the addition of new auxiliary services, such as freightforwarding, at the ports it services.

Category: Customer Service Customer Satisfaction: Monitoring customer satisfaction through regular surveying and reporting of results.

Category: Employee Development/Advancement Promotions: The number of employees promoted versus new hires may be an indication of work environment and career opportunities at DeepHarbour HK.

Category: Work Climate/Job Satisfaction Grievances: Frequent employee complaints could be an indication of a poorly operating work environment.

Category: Image Reputation: Media mentions of DeepHarbour HK may be tracked as an indication of corporate reputation.

#### Data Collection at Different Stages of the Strategic Cycle

Implementing a strategy

Before an organisation’s strategy can be successfully implemented it must first be well researched. This will require collecting hard data about the industry in which it is competing, including profitability, sales trends and performance figures for leading competitors, to the extent that information about individual companies is publicly available. This data will then need to be combined with analysis and expert predictions about the future direction of the industry or market.

Monitoring a strategy

When an organisation begins to monitor its strategy, it will have access to actual performance data. This will include the various categories of hard data and soft data outlined in this chapter, as applicable to a particular organisation. Hard data would measure factors such as output (for example, completion rate, units produced, items sold), the costs to produce such goods and/ or services, and the precise time it takes to produce units of a product, as well as measures of quality and efficiency, such as wastage, error rates and the costs of fixing errors. Soft data will be harder to collect, but it can be sourced by questionnaires, word of mouth, etc., to provide specific, albeit more subjective, information about the company’s performance, such as the quality of customer service it provides, corporate image, innovation and work habits of employees.

Modifying a strategy

When an organisation determines that it needs to modify its strategy, data collection will combine elements of both the implementing a strategy and monitoring a strategy stages. Various methods of data collection could be used in this situation but many senior managers might want to compare their performance data with that of successful competitors – to the extent such information for those companies is available – to understand how those organisations are managing to thrive by comparison.

Similar to the implementation stage, data collection will centre on both hard and soft data, including output (for example, completion rate, units produced, items sold), the costs to produce such goods and/or services and the precise time it takes to produce units of a product, as well as measures of quality and efficiency like wastage, error rates and the costs of fixing those errors. Soft data will include, for example, an attempt to quantify the quality of customer service, corporate image and innovation.

### 1.3.2 Data Analysis

Data analysis is a formal approach to extracting meaning from business data. Multiple metrics may be analysed to determine whether an organisation’s business strategy is on track. New technologies provide organisations with far greater amounts of data than ever before.

An organisation’s data provides a valuable source of reliable, analytical information, upon which data can be interpreted and decisions made, including whether the mandate presented by the organisation’s business strategy is being fulfilled.

Information can be sourced from multiple internal and external–based sources. For example, internal sources for financial forecasts include historical cash flows and a record of suppliers’ prices. External sources of economic or financial data might include interest rates and currency data for the jurisdiction(s) in which the organisation operates.

Non-financial data measures could come from many sources, including information gathered through employee and/or customer satisfaction surveys, employee turnover, brand recognition measures, customer complaints or accident or injury data. Many companies, for example, carefully track employee injuries as a way to actively look for strategies to improve the company’s safety record.

Such systems often rely on source information obtained online. For example, past seasonal data collected from a time-series analysis can pinpoint cyclical fluctuations to help analysts distinguish between short-term and long-term trends and the degree to which that impacts the overall business strategy of the organisation.

Key performance indicators (KPIs) are performance measures that an organisation tracks. KPIs serve many functions, including as an early warning system about emerging difficulties or challenges that might lie ahead for the organisation. They can be used organisation-wide or for individual divisions or projects.

KPIs can track and measure many metrics, typically to support profit, revenue and cash flow, or sales goals. They can also track measures of customer service and satisfaction. KPIs may help determine whether strategic objectives related to operational efficiency, productivity, value creation, safety and environmental impact are being met.

Some organisations use a collection of indicators, sometimes known as a ‘dashboard’, to monitor key important indicators for the business. There are many tools available, including as part of specialised software, to help organisations capture and track their data more effectively.

The strength of KPIs is that they have multiple uses. They can, for example, be custom-designed to suit an organisation’s philosophy and strategy, such that senior executives are going to want to learn and analyse various key metrics first. And while they provide a snapshot at the present time of multiple important items, perhaps of a financial, consumer or social responsibility nature, KPIs can also serve to provide an early warning sign of impending trouble.

A large appliance retailer, for example, may still enjoy buoyant sales of televisions, but various financial ratios may, at the same time, be indicating a steady multi-year downward trend as more consumers opt for viewing opportunities online instead of through cable TV. This would serve as an early warning sign to the organisation that at least part of the business may no longer be profitable in coming years.

Another organisation may be conscious of both the financial and social responsibility aspects of its business. Management there would, like the aforementioned appliance retailer, want to keep a keen eye on their financial ratios, but also track various environmental and social KPIs, such as pollution/waste and the public perception about whether that organisation is a good corporate citizen.

#### Data Analysis at Different Stages of the Strategic Cycle

##### Implementing a strategy

Implementing an organisational strategy will involve analysing hard data about the industry, including profitability, sales trends and performance figures for leading competitors, to the extent the latter information is publicly available. The implementation stage will also require analysis of soft data that takes into account predictions for the market in which the company is operating, particularly if there is a risk that the product(s) or service(s) rendered could become obsolete in the foreseeable future. If that industry is in decline, analysis of past results will be of limited value.

##### Monitoring a strategy

When an organisation begins to monitor its strategy, it will have real-performance data available to analyse. This will include the various categories of hard data and soft data outlined in Section 1.3.1 as applicable to a particular business. Hard data would measure variables such as output (for example, completion rate, units produced, items sold), the costs to produce such goods and/or services, time of production, along with measures of quality and efficiency, such as wastage, error rates and the costs of fixing those errors. Soft data will include multiple measures, including the quality of customer service the organisation provides, measures of corporate image, innovation and the work ethics of its employees.

##### Modifying a strategy

When the need arises to modify a strategy – perhaps because the organisation’s initial strategy has uncovered certain inefficiencies, or because of a need to adapt to international economic and market conditions, or both – the organisation’s data analysis will need to combine elements of both the implementing a strategy and monitoring a strategy stages. Various strategies could be followed, but many senior managers might want to carefully analyse their comparative data with that of its successful peers – to the extent such information is available – to understand potential differences as a guide to making modifications.

Similar to the implementation stage, data analysis when modifying a strategy will centre on hard and soft data, including output (for example, completion rate, units produced, items sold), the costs to produce such goods and/or services and the precise time for production, as well as measures of quality and efficiency like wastage, error rates and the costs of fixing those errors. Soft data analysis will include, but certainly not be limited to, measuring the company’s perceived performance in terms of the quality of customer service it provides, its corporate image, innovation and the work habits of its employees.

### 1.3.3 Big Data Considerations

‘Big data’ refers to the huge quantities of data that technology has made available to many organisations. The availability of such data, through various sources, including online transactions, mobile devices, social media and connected equipment, has affected organisational strategies in a major way. There is a much greater ability to monitor, sometimes in real-time, whether aspects of the business strategy are succeeding. Increasing use of data collected from online sources and advances in artificial intelligence also changes the way that data can be used.

However, even with increased technological abilities, many organisations remain technologically hampered in their ability to access or use data. The opportunities that large quantities of data represent are not always understood or appreciated throughout an organisation. Although much of this information is often very useful, it is not always in a form that organisations can use directly.

#### Data Harvesting

Social media harvesting is a way to collect data from social media platforms automatically and in a way that doesn’t attract attention. By employing simple programming tools, researchers can extract relevant messages from social media platforms for research or commercial purposes. Harvesting social media data differs from traditional communication methods (for example, surveys) in several ways.

First, it is by nature unobtrusive in that it will not attract attention. It is a method of collecting and studying social behaviour without affecting it. Therefore, harvested data may be more objective and reliable than that obtained from surveys and experiments. Second, harvesting social media is an automatic process, employing computers to collect and code data automatically.

Third, social media data is usually obtained on a real-time basis, in fine-grained detail, and with a tremendous amount of information available on a global scale. Social scientists have long been skilled at being able to collect data inconspicuously. Organisations have long routinely tracked the purchases of their customers. Banks, for example, are able to analyse their credit card transactions to glean a lot of data about their clients. Social media harvesting of data takes this activity to a larger level because of the global nature of the data that is available to organisations. This data can also be analysed on a microscopic behavioural scale.

#### Big Data Considerations at Different Stages of the Strategic Cycle

##### Implementing a strategy

As noted in Sections 1.3.1 and 1.3.2, the research required to implement an organisational strategy can be very detailed and involve collecting hard data about the industry, including profitability, sales trends and performance figures for leading competitors. This stage will also require analysis of soft data that takes into account future predictions for the market in which the company is operating,

With large quantities of data available, gathering the relevant information for the implementation stage of a corporate strategy can be very challenging. Without knowing how to prioritise that information or hone in on the information that is most important, senior management may end up wasting a lot of valuable time when speed is of the essence in getting the organisational strategy up and operating.

However, when the proper methodologies for collecting and prioritising the most relevant information have been established, this data can be used to an advantage as an important tool to provide information that can assist the organisation to implement and revise corporate strategies in various ways, including but not limited to:

• Evaluating whether key procedures remain consistent with the corporate strategy.
• Identifying misalignments in procedures with the corporate strategy, and if any, to prioritise which misalignments need to be corrected first.
• Analysing through modelling how realignments in corporate practices might impact the organisation’s internal operations.
• Analysing through modelling how realignments in corporate practices might impact corporate stakeholders.

##### Monitoring a strategy

Monitoring an organisation’s strategy is a key stage in the business cycle, because this determines what is working or what isn’t and can also pinpoint elements of the strategy that need to be improved.

The availability of significant data with respect to the organisation’s actual performance both in terms of the hard data and soft data variables outlined in Sections 1.3.1 and 1.3.2 can provide senior management with a significant advantage, provided that information is used skillfully. However, the sheer volume of data reported will not be of equal value. It will have varying degrees of relevance, and management must be able to discern which of those variables provides the most meaningful feedback to help them determine the elements of their strategy that are performing well and those that are not.

##### Modifying a strategy

When an organisation determines that there is a need to modify its business strategy, senior management will need to make decisions about how to execute those changes based on a wide array of both internal and external performance data.

This will yield numerous calculations for management to analyse that will include hard data variables about the performance of its own company and, presumably if the information is public, also about its competitors. Soft data variables may also be available about competitors, to be used for comparative purposes.

In order to make decisions that will yield the right improvements or modifications to its corporate strategy, management will need to be able to determine which data points are most relevant to executing those changes in a reasonable timeframe. Otherwise it runs the risk of over-analysing too much information – much of which may yield few, if any, tangible results.

This data can also be used as a key organisational tool to assist in monitoring corporate strategies in ways that include, but are not limited to:

• Analysing financial metrics – for example, in determining whether an organisation’s projected targets for shareholder returns are being achieved.

• Analysing customer metrics – for example, in assessing whether customer servicing and product targets are being met.

• Determining whether process metrics, such as internal operational efficiency goals, are being satisfactorily achieved.

• Assessing innovation metrics – for example, to determine if new products or services are being produced in the quality, quantity and in the timeframe intended.

#### Ethics in Practice 1 – Informed Consent

Data collected through online mediums such as social media platforms, including blogs and online social networks, is growing and evolving.

The large quantities of personal information available on social media create multiple risks, including the possibility of an organisation, its management and employees being caught by surprise and having unwanted private data exposed. Furthermore, such data might be publicised out of context, in a manipulated fashion.

A series of key ethical questions thus arise, particularly around the protection of individual privacy when such data is being collected and analysed. For example, are individuals being properly informed about the data that is being collected from, say, their online social media sites, even though such sites are publicly available? What permissions may need to be granted to conduct this type of research? Where must the line be drawn with respect to an individual’s right to remain anonymous, versus the public’s right to be able to see such information in certain circumstances?

Informed consent is another key issue that raises concerns about the boundaries of allowing information to be used by service providers. If the terms of use require that the service provider has the right to use personal information for revenue purposes, can that information then be used by organisations that are seeking new clients to sell to or provide services to?

Each country will have their own separate laws to deal with situations like that.


## SUMMARY

• An organisation’s business strategy provides it with a plan to gain and sustain a competitive advantage in the industry and market they are participating in.

• Strategy professor Michael Porter’s ‘Porter’s Five Forces’ model for conducting industry analysis consists of five variables: rivalry among industry competitors; bargaining power of suppliers; threat of potential new entrants; threat of substitutes; and the bargaining power of buyers.

• The McKinsey and Company ‘7 S model of organisational alignment’ contains seven important organisational elements: strategy, structure, systems, staffing, skills, style and shared values.

• The BCG growth share matrix uses quadrants of high or low market growth and relative market share to compare the strategic positions of different businesses or units within a diversified firm to measure how each contributes to value creation.

• The PEST (political, economic, social, technological) analysis model assesses how political, economic, social and technological factors shape the competitive conditions that an organisation and its industry face.

• The value chain model measures the sequence of events that an organisation uses to transform raw materials into finished products and how primary activities in that process (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales and service) are enhanced by the firm’s infrastructure, human resource management, technology development and procurement practice.

• The Ansoff matrix uses quadrants to illustrate four potential growth strategies, including: market penetration, product development, market development and diversification.

• The POPIT model, which is an acronym for ‘people, organisation, processes, information and technology’, is used by a business to conduct a strategic analysis of its operations when faced with decisions necessary to effect change.

• A strategic business plan involves evaluating the business environment within which the firm operates; identifying the firm’s core competencies and potential growth opportunities; and then formulating a plan designed to turn the firm’s core competencies into a sustainable competitive advantage.

• An organisation will need to formulate, and then implement, a strategy at the corporate level, at a business unit or product level and at a functional level.

• Many organisations have a wide-ranging set of stakeholders to whom they are accountable, including investors, bankers, customers, suppliers, employees, the government and community at large, among others.

• Successful strategic implementation takes a lot of time and effort, but the job is not done when that occurs as ongoing monitoring is required to measure the organisation’s progress towards achieving its strategic goals.

• An organisation requires clear metrics, including financial metrics, customer metrics and process metrics, to measure whether its business strategy is being successfully implemented.

• Data collection and analysis involves the collection of both hard data, which are quantifiable and easy to measure, and soft data, which tend to be more subjective in nature.

• ‘Big data’ refers to the huge quantities of data that technology has made available to many organisations through online and other sources.

• Monitoring a business strategy against actual performance data provides key information for management to determine where its strategies are working well or where adjustments may be needed.

## OPENING CASE

DEEPHARBOUR HK COMPANY LIMITED

As you will recall from Chapter 1, the case study involves DeepHarbour HK Company Limited, a fictional Hong Kong-based container shipping company that will operate out of Victoria Harbour and service countries throughout the entire Asia-Pacific region, including Australia and New Zealand in Oceania.

This chapter will examine various business strategies, including for the fictional DeepHarbour HK and the risks attached to those strategies. For example, how does management analyse whether the strategies it is establishing are leading to a performance as intended in a way that will allow the organisation to succeed in the face of intense international competition? Will those strategies allow management to respond swiftly to changes in its business environment as new challenges, including new technologies, customers and competitors, arise?

## OVERVIEW

Chapter 2 will focus on determining how to **analyse organisational strategies**, including understanding the **risks** involved in executing that strategy. It will also explain how to **monitor and analyse** the organisation’s performance against that strategy, including the primary considerations that need to be taken into account while making that assessment.

This will build on the knowledge gained in Chapter 1, which was to introduce students to the principles involved in an organisation’s quest to implement and monitor its business strategy in a competitive and constantly changing international environment.

In particular, students will learn how to:

• Analyse an organisation’s objectives, including the ethical factors that need to be taken into consideration, as it develops its strategic management systems.

• Describe the environment in which an entity operates including the main economic, legal, political, social, technological, international and cultural forces that are putting pressure upon it.

• Explain the external and internal factors which can impact an entity’s ability to achieve its strategic aims.

• Identify the implications for stakeholders, including for shareholder value, of the potential consequences of choosing between multiple strategies.

• Identify the risks attached to the alternative strategies (including attributes to risk, security and cyber security) and explain how an organisation can make a strategic choice based on an understanding of those variables.

• Adapt business strategy to successfully address change.


## 2.1 STRATEGY FORMULATION

Determining the right strategy for an organisation is a difficult undertaking, particularly in the modern twenty-first century global business environment, where multiple external and internal variables, influenced by the need to service a wide range of stakeholders, need to be taken into account.

Corporate strategic decisions cover three dimensions of an organisation’s scope. They include: product range (which covers the firm’s product scope), the firm’s presence along the industry value chain (representing its vertical scope) and the geographical markets in which the organisation will compete (its geographical scope).

With respect to product scope, some companies define their businesses broadly. For example, they may state that they wish to become a leading company in a particular industry.

Others will define that mission more narrowly and specifically, perhaps focusing on a particular specialty they wish to pursue and develop to make their brand better known.

The scope of a firm’s business is likely to change over time. For example, an organisation may want to place more or less emphasis on its core business at a particular point in time. Some businesses decide to refocus on their core businesses. Others have divested themselves of supplementary businesses that were not central to their main business.

Similar trends can be seen regarding the vertical scope, or range of vertically linked activities of business organisations. Vertical integration occurs when a firm extends its activities into the preceding (or succeeding) stages of the production process. A single integrated firm will incorporate those activities in-house. This is viewed as a way of improving coordination and reducing risk.

In contrast, some businesses have opted for a trend that involves outsourcing and de-integration, which may involve the use of multiple, specialised firms working together. In the pharmaceutical industry, for example, firms were traditionally highly vertically integrated and involved in all stages of their production process. These activities included basic research on drug formulation, through the various stages of the business, from the manufacture of active chemical ingredients to packaging and marketing of the product. But in the 1980s, the pharmaceutical industry began de-integrating certain services. Companies initially outsourced chemical manufacture; then that outsourcing expanded to encompass additional activities, including product formulation, clinical trials and some basic research.

The geographical scope refers to the breadth of an organisation’s activities around the globe, which may include, broadly, the number of jurisdictions in which the company operates or it may include particular activities that are internationally dispersed. For example, a company’s manufacturing operations may be carried out in a separate country from where its head office is situated.

#### The Role of Strategic Planning in Success

Four key characteristics of a corporate strategy that is conducive to success include: goals that are simple, consistent and long term; having a profound understanding of the competitive environment; having an objective appraisal of resources and a strategy for effective implementation. These factors, as shown in Exhibit 2.1, are covered in detail throughout this chapter.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-55.png)
The topic of effective strategic implementation was discussed in detail in Chapter 1 of this module.

#### Goals that Are Simple, Consistent and Long Term

Many traditional and online businesses have a sole focus, which is to excel in one, clear area for which the public identifies them. These organisations have name, brand and image recognition that most people can readily identify with, such as the manufacture of a famous athletic shoe, or online sites to purchase or trade goods, among scores of other potential examples.

#### Having a Profound Understanding of the Competitive Environment

Many organisations have arisen designed to harness the power of the Internet. A large number of the companies that have enjoyed the most success in their endeavours were those that recognised early on how certain aspects of daily life and commerce, such as dating and buying and selling, would increasingly become online activities, fueled at least in part by a new generation that is fully conversant with technology and would demand changes.

#### Having an Objective Appraisal of Resources

A good organisational leader understands their capabilities, but equally important they also understand the skills and talents they lack strength in. Accordingly, they seek assistance in those areas to build a strong and complementary team.

#### A Strategy for Effective Implementation

Good leaders know that pure technical talent is rarely enough, standing on its own, for a business to succeed. Several other business attributes need to be present – including a strong finance team to ensure cash flow and profitability, expert marketers, human resource specialists who can hire the right team of people, and many other professionals. This group of people, combined with the raw talent and technical skills of those who produce the product or service at the core of the business, provide the synergies necessary for an organisation to compete in a tough, globally oriented world economy.

### 2.1.1 Corporate Objectives

An organisation’s strategy will reflect its corporate objectives. For example, with respect to scope, organisations will, on occasion, decide to either extend or reduce their scope because they believe this to be in their best interest. It is reasonable to assume that in the case of for-profit firms, changes in firm boundaries are designed to create value for its shareholders, either by increasing revenue or by reducing costs – or perhaps ideally by achieving both.

Three concepts that are key to analysing corporate strategic decisions and shifts in the scope of an organisation’s activities over time include:

• Economies of scope: These exist when an organisation uses a resource across multiple activities, and in the process of doing so uses less of that resource overall than when those same activities are carried out independently. Economies of scope create the potential for multi-business firms to gain cost advantages over more specialised businesses. This is different from the notion of economies of scale, which refers to the reductions in unit costs that result from an increase in the output of a single product.

• Transaction costs: Organisations acquire inputs, and they also sell their output on markets. Markets have a cost: for example, the effort involved in finding a supplier or a buyer entails search costs, making an agreement involves negotiating, then drawing up a contract, and subsequently monitoring what was promised is actually being delivered, and maybe even enforcement of the contract through arbitration or litigation, will normally entail additional transaction costs. However, in many instances, these transaction costs can be avoided. When the firm extends its activities to encompass the activity undertaken by the seller or buyer, what was a market transaction previously would then become a transfer within the firm. As a result, an organisation is more likely to extend its corporate scope as the transaction costs in the market increase.

• Costs of corporate complexity: Market transaction costs can be eliminated as an organisation extends its boundaries. However, an organisation that internalises its business transactions faces the costs of corporate complexity because extra demands are placed on the organisation’s managers and its management systems as a result of having to manage a greater number and diversity of transactions internally. This also imposes extra costs that may be greater than any savings realised from the elimination of transaction costs as well as economies of scope. These additional costs of corporate complexity will escalate further the more the organisation diversifies to add various different types of business activity.

These three concepts allow executives of an organisation to evaluate corporate strategies that take into account the merits of specialisation, compared to a broader corporate scope. In the case of product scope, an organisation might need to consider, for example, whether it is more efficient to have metal cans, plastic containers and glass bottles produced by three separate companies, or whether efficiency would be increased if there was a single diversified packaging company capable of producing all three.

With respect to vertical scope, an example would be consideration about whether it is more efficient to have three independent companies – one that produces steel, another that rolls the steel into a sheet and yet a third producing steel cans – or whether it is better to have a single company operating across all three stages of production.

#### Apply and Analyse 1

Explain what factors DeepHarbour HK, the fictional Hong Kong-based start-up shipping company, will need to analyse as it aligns its organisational strategy with its corporate objectives.

Analysis

DeepHarbour HK’s organisational strategy will need to closely correlate with the corporate identity it carries. The shipping company must be cognizant of the need to establish and then preserve its reputation for providing timely, quality service throughout the Asia-Pacific region. It must have a disaster plan should something go seriously awry, such as a spill of a hazardous substance.

The organisation will also need to determine how broadly or narrowly it wishes to define its strategic goals. For example, it might wish for a broad declaration to, for example, aim to become a leading company in terms of shipping volume, or that declaration could become narrower in focus, such as a determination to develop its brand recognition as a company that provides a superior service.

DeepHarbour HK will also need to determine whether it wishes to focus solely on its core business or whether there are supplementary activities it wishes to pursue, such as providing land transportation delivery services from the ports of entry that it sails to. There could be a risk element to expanding the business into additional areas, such as the greater potential for a serious incident and resulting legal issues.

### 2.1.2 Operating Environment and Factors Affecting Strategic Success

As an organisation commences and grows its operations it will encounter real-world opportunities and challenges in the industries and markets it is competing in and face many new strategic decisions.

#### Strategy Vehicles for Achieving Strategic Objectives

An organisation often relies on key strategy vehicles to assist it enter what it views as an attractive market(s) in an effort to build the resources and capabilities needed that will allow it to deliver unique value to its stakeholders.

An organisation may decide to pursue various strategies in pursuit of key corporate objectives, including future growth. These strategies include:

• Diversification, which may involve adding to its product inventory or a new line of business. An organisation might want to consider diversification from its core business to also sell supplementary products. For example, some large grocery stores have diversified from their staple product, food, to add a pharmaceutical section and/or sales of basic clothing.

• Acquisition of another company to grow or diversify, or to acquire key resources. Many large organisations grow and stay ahead of their competitors by acquiring smaller firms with specific niche expertise and incorporating them into their business.

• Strategic alliance with another organisation to access new resources and capabilities through an exclusive relationship with another firm. Rather than acquire a new company, a strategic alliance involving an exclusive contractual arrangement with another organisation can also provide access into new markets and expand a company’s reach.

• Vertical integration through either making a product in-house, thus keeping the production process ‘vertical’, or purchasing from an outside source. For example, what is the trade-off involved in the extra expense to manufacture a product on-site versus outsourcing it but losing a degree of autonomy? Could that external company be depended on to provide a swift response if, say, there was a sudden upsurge in customer demand?

• International expansion to achieve economies of scale, access key resources or learn new skills. Some companies use this as a key strategy in order to achieve a competitive advantage and expand their global presence. This decision would require a careful analysis of risks and benefits, including a financial determination to calculate the optimal point at which any extra revenue generated by expanded international operations would exceed the additional expenses required to do business in those new jurisdictions.

Stakeholder implications and the potential benefits and risks associated with the diversification, acquisition of another organisation, strategic alliance with another organisation, vertical integration and international expansion strategies discussed in this section will be considered later in this chapter.

### 2.1.3 Strategic Planning Process

Strategic plans tend to cover a multi-year period – for example, over three to five years, or perhaps longer in specific circumstances, although in a fast-paced global economy time frames have generally tended to be shortened. Plans combine both ‘top-down’ initiatives and directives from higher levels of the organisation, as well as strategy proposals from the ‘bottom up’, that are received from managers or employees at lower levels in the corporate hierarchy.

Strategic planning is an ongoing process that is reviewed and approved on a regular basis, often annually. As an organisation adapts to changing circumstances in the workplace, new strategies are often developed and existing strategies are revised.

The principal stages of a typical strategic planning cycle are as follows:

• Planning: The chief executive officer (CEO), chief financial officer (CFO) or other senior leaders typically initiates the strategic planning process with some clear indications of strategic priorities. Other groups may provide input and forecasts to assist in this process. On the basis of this framework of priorities and planning assumptions, the different organisational units (including divisions and functional departments) will also create their respective strategic plans.

• Approval: The organisation’s strategic plans are presented to the board of directors for discussion and approval. This is one of the key corporate oversight responsibilities of the board. The original plans may be revised before they receive final approval.

• Execute: Once the organisational plan is approved by the board of directors, it can then be executed throughout the company.

• Review: The strategic plan should be reviewed on a regular basis, typically annually. The findings of that review are then incorporated into a revised and/or updated strategic plan in the next strategic planning cycle. Longer-term strategic plans (for example, a 20-year plan) might be reviewed less frequently given their long-term focus.

#### Strategic Management Systems

The strategic management system of an organisation reflects key components of the framework under which the company operates, including its operational plan and capital expenditure budget.

Operational planning in an effort to achieve a business objective is a very comprehensive process. It includes setting performance targets and planning marketing, sales, and other activities, as well as establishing efficient productivity levels. Performance management and resource allocation are also important elements of the strategic implementation process. It is especially important that these activities be well coordinated in a large organisation with many departments and specialised areas of personnel where coordination is likely to be more of a formal process than in a smaller company with only a handful of people.

Capital expenditure budgets are financial documents that detail the organisation’s financial objectives through planned spending on capital assets for long-term growth. Capital expenditure budgets for a strategic planning period allocate funds among various business segments and/or geographic regions (for a multinational company), and provide important financial details about the organisation’s strategic priorities. Capital expenditure budgets are also aggregated to the corporate level as part of the overall organisational plan.

### 2.1.4 Ethical Considerations

The term ethics describes a society’s ideas about what actions are right and wrong. Generally accepted ethical rules include considering the impact of one’s actions on others, being willing to sometimes put the interests of others ahead of personal interests and being willing to follow the same rules expected of others.

Business ethics describe actions that are perceived to be right or wrong within the context of a business environment. An organisation’s business ethics will be guided by multiple factors, including the laws in the various jurisdictions in which it operates, its obligations to its various stakeholders and the personal beliefs of its management and employees about what is right or wrong, among other factors.

However, in business as in society, ethical values are not moral absolutes, and they can vary across societies. Even within the same society, business ethics, including the way ethics are perceived and practiced in individual organisations, can differ.

#### Types of Ethical Conflicts in Business

While business generally produces many potential ethical conflicts, most such conflicts involve three related areas: agency costs, conflicts of interest and informational asymmetry.

#### Agency Costs

Many relationships in business are agency relationships. In such a relationship, agents can be bound both legally and ethically to act in the best interests of their principal.

For example, a financial manager has an agency obligation to act honestly and to also ensure their subordinates act honestly with respect to financial transactions involving their respective clients.

#### Conflicts of Interest

Conflicts of interest often arise in agency relationships when the agent’s interests are different from those of the principal. Such conflicts of interest are typically resolved in one of two ways. Sometimes complete disclosure is sufficient. Alternatively, the conflicted party can withdraw from serving the interests of one of the parties, which the law sometimes requires.

#### Information Asymmetry

Information asymmetry exists when one party in a business transaction has information that is unavailable to the other participating parties. For example, the seller of a building probably knows much more about its real condition than the prospective buyer. Information asymmetry is common in business. The ethical issue is how information should be provided to parties to a transaction.

#### The Importance of an Ethical Business Culture 
The legal system and market forces often impose substantial costs on individuals and institutions that engage in unethical behaviour, including the prospect of significant financial losses, legal fines, criminal convictions and jail and bankruptcy.

Ethicists argue, however, that laws and market forces are not enough. It is also important to create an ethical business culture in the firm, with company leaders setting the tone for ethical behaviour and to do what is considered ‘right’ at all times. This helps to provide everyone working for the organisation with a set of principles to help them identify issues and make good ethical judgements, especially in an international organisation that may face a variety of issues in multiple jurisdictions where ethical implications might be viewed differently.

#### Corporate Culture and Ethics 
A strong ethical culture helps to provide an employee with the confidence to act or behave in a manner that they believe is ethically correct when they encounter a difficult and complex situation, without any ambiguity or concern about how others in the organisation will react.

## 2.2 STRATEGIC DECISION IMPACTS

Many businesses are largely global and serious tensions elsewhere can affect the broader business and operating environment. Management needs to take into account how multiple variables in a complex global operating environment might impact the performance of its business.

### 2.2.1 Operating Environment

The operating environment affects business success and management will need to factor several variables into business decisions.

#### 2.2.1.1 General Environment 
Business opportunities and threats were discussed in detail in Chapter 1. This provides a straightforward way for management to approach the general environment in which the business operates, including changes and trends that may require adaptation. This is illustrated in Exhibit 2.2.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-56.png)
1. Complementary products or services are products and services that can be used in tandem with those in another industry, creating synergies whereby the value of those items together is worth more than each separately. For example, the automotive industry and the oil and gas industry complement each other.

2. Technology changes within an industry can potentially reshape an organisation’s landscape, and sometimes also that of the society at large along with it, even quite substantially. Early adopters of new technology are often able to gain greater market share and earn higher profit margins than those who are late to adopt.

	The rapid growth of new and evolving technologies also means that management must be on guard against change. Industries and customer preferences can be very volatile. The identity of an organisation’s customers is sometimes changing. Several companies have decided to diversify into new products as technology has evolved.

3. General economic conditions

	General economic conditions affect most organisations. For the purposes of strategic success, several underlying economic factors are important, including:

	a. Changing macroeconomic forces – for example, the rate of growth of an economy’s gross domestic product (GDP) – whether the GDP is growing at a healthy pace or whether it is stagnating or in recession, will have a direct impact on the profitability prospects of most organisations.

	b. Interest rates affect the cost of capital and through their effect on the broader economy may influence demand for an organisation’s or industry’s products or services.

	c. Currency exchange rates, which reflect the relative value of one currency to another, can have a significant impact on the prices that customers will pay for products from another country, directly affecting profitability.

	d. Inflation, if resulting in a consistent rise in underlying prices, can create negative impacts for firms to keep pace with rising prices. Deflation is a different, but also potentially challenging, business scenario as falling prices can make it difficult to plan future investments.

4. Demographic forces reflect changes in the basic characteristics of a population, including changes in average age, gender, income and ethnicity over time. These changes can have a significant influence on organisations involving, for instance, basic shifts in the product and geographic markets that firms target.

5. Ecological/natural environment can also be a source of change for many industries.

	For example, long-term changes in climate and weather patterns may affect how businesses can operate. Many jurisdictions have laws to protect their environment and to punish violators.

	Current trends in the natural environment have also had a major impact on the public’s perception of how business affects the environment. Many firms have responded to that demand by implementing new sustainable initiatives that are environmentally focused.

6. Global forces such as new technologies in communications and transportation have resulted in dramatic changes and trade barriers among many nations have fallen substantially. These changes have resulted in firms with expanded international operations and producing and selling across national borders.

7. Political, legal and regulatory forces

	Changing or evolving laws and regulations may require organisations and industries to rethink strategy, sometimes unexpectedly. Therefore, it is imperative that management and the board analyse and understand the political processes, laws and regulations, and the potential risks associated with them, that could potentially shape and constrain their organisation and industry.

	The political, legal and regulatory forces that an organisation will encounter in a particular jurisdiction represents country risk. The world’s different legal systems and tax codes represent a patchwork of systems that can vary substantially from country to country. These differences can affect an organisation’s strategic financial decisions, such as what assets the organisation needs to acquire, how to organise the firm and what capital structure to use, and must, therefore, factor into a strategy for operating in foreign countries.

8. Social/cultural forces

	Social and cultural values and attitudes, which can be very different in countries around the globe, often shape the overall landscape in which an organisation competes. Management must understand differences among consumers in each country, and sometimes even in different regions of the same country. When there are conflicts between cultural norms and ethical business practices, management will need to provide leadership for their organisation to take the best course of action.

	Cultural views and attitudes are powerful forces that bind people together and define a particular society. Cultural views also shape business practices and people’s attitudes toward business. Management needs to be aware of cultural views and attitudes when planning and assessing international operations.

#### 2.2.1.2 International Considerations 
Globalisation refers to the removal of barriers to free trade and the integration of national economies, which has also led to the world’s financial system becoming highly integrated, along with the production of various goods and services.

Multinational corporations have an international reach, and may purchase raw materials from one country, obtain financing from the capital markets in another country, produce finished goods with labour and capital equipment from a third country and sell finished goods in several other countries.

When an organisation operates in multiple countries, it can help extend the life of a product beyond what it might have been if available only in one country. Thus, the organisation can better leverage its long-term investment in that product. This can help the company achieve better economies of scale in manufacturing, marketing or research. Economies of scope might also be achieved as competing in multiple markets can allow organisations to spread their costs across more units in multiple product categories.

Operating in more than one country can also provide firms with a measure of diversification against both economic and natural disaster, should one location experience a major setback.

### 2.2.2 External Factors

An external analysis should enlighten managers about the competitive forces that influence the profitability of particular markets and industries, as well as the opportunities and threats that exist. In addition, it should provide information about what customers want and what they are willing to pay to meet their needs.

#### Industry Analysis

One of the central questions for management to determine is which markets or industries to compete in. Understanding the Porter’s Five Forces that shape industry competition, as discussed in detail in Chapter 1, is one of the starting points for developing strategy.

A framework helps managers think about how the company can increase its bargaining power over suppliers and buyers, impede other entrants to the market, reduce the rivalry with its competitors and reduce the threat of substitute products or services.

Establishing the organisations that are competing with each other draws upon the principle of substitutability, which has two dimensions: substitutability on the demand side and substitutability on the supply side. For example, are consumers willing to substitute one brand of luxury car for another or are they willing to substitute a luxury car for a mass-market brand on the basis of a lower price for the latter? This will help ascertain whether a company is competing only against other luxury car makers or whether it is competing against the larger automotive industry.

The same considerations apply to geographical boundaries. The criterion for whether the management of an organisation should consider themselves as competing in a single global market or in a series of separate national or regional markets is also substitutability.

If customers are willing and able to substitute a product, such as cars that are available on different national markets, or if manufacturers are willing and able to divert their output among different countries to take account of differences in margins, then the market for that industry is global.

#### Customer Analysis

An analysis of an organisation’s customers or its potential future customers must take into account the customers’ needs, including a determination of sensitivity to price changes. Management can make better decisions about how to offer unique value to its customer base by determining various segments of customers who have similar needs. For example, in the automobile industry, some customers want stylish cars that are powerful, luxurious and with the newest technology. Others want economy cars for basic transportation.

#### Data Analysis

The term ‘big data’, has been used to describe the availability of huge quantities of data that technology has made available to many organisations. Data can provide valuable insights when developing a corporate strategy, especially in terms of helping management filter through critical information necessary for a comprehensive industry or customer analysis or emerging trends.

The use of data is covered comprehensively in Chapter 1, Section 1.3.3, including a description of how data can help an organisation and a discussion of some of the ethical issues involved with accessing such information. An important risk associated with data is the risk of data loss. That risk is covered in more detail later in this chapter.

### 2.2.3 Internal Factors

Management also needs to closely examine multiple internal factors in connection with the firm’s ability to properly execute its business strategy. The following mechanisms for coordination can be found in an organisation:

- • Rules and instructions: A basic feature of the firm is the existence of general employment contracts under which individuals agree to perform a range of duties as required by their employer. Rules and instructions provide its members with grounding in terms of describing what activities need to be performed and broadly outlining how to do them.

	Rules and instructions need to be followed in order to achieve corporate goals because they establish a blueprint for members of the organisation to follow. For example, if an organisation’s strategy is to double its sales of product X over the course of the next calendar year, then it must:

	- °Establish certain rules for its sales staff to follow, with respect to, for example, requiring a minimum number of online and/or phone calls or visits, on a daily or weekly basis;
	- °Determine which geographic areas need to be covered and which staff members are responsible for each of those areas;
	- °Determine which companies and/or industries those calls need to be directed to; and
	- °Ensure that training is carried out on a timely basis so staff members are always familiar and ready to sell the latest products with full knowledge of its capabilities.

- • Routines: Where activities are performed on a recurrent basis, coordination based on mutual adjustment and rules becomes institutionalised within organisational routines. Routines establish procedures for how employees and management will carry out those activities in practice.

	Just as a winning soccer team needs to have routines in place like regular practices, and drills to hone their skills, and the players need to have the discipline to follow those routines and work hard every day in order to achieve its goal of winning a championship, so must the employees of a business follow certain routines to achieve their strategic goals. For example, if it is the stated goal of a retailer to be recognised for providing exceptional customer relations, the staff of that organisation also needs to follow certain routines. They must be attentive to customer needs, in a pleasant manner, without being overly aggressive or intrusive. Service representatives must be knowledgeable about the retailer’s products and services, and its policies with respect to customer returns. Those routines should be enhanced through regular training sessions, to ensure there is cohesion and consistency among all employees in approaching such duties.

- • Mutual adjustment: This describes the mutual adjustment required of individuals who are engaged in related tasks. Mutual adjustment describes the team effort required to coordinate everybody working together and making allowances for various styles to successfully carry out the strategy.

	A professional basketball team will have skilled players – among the world’s elite – at the guard, forward and centre positions. But a team that is of championship calibre will have much more than that. They will be able to field a cohesive unit of players with different playing styles who can capitalise on each other’s strengths to achieve symmetry on the court.

	The same is true of a business organisation. An airline whose strategic goal is to rise to the top of its industry in earnings will need a team of professionals. Although finance professionals with strategic planning skills will be front and centre in this endeavour, they must successfully work with other managers and board members with different working styles and skills in order to have a cohesive, functioning unit. But that alone will never ensure profitability because the pilots and attendants on the airplane, and the baggage handlers and check-in personnel at the airport, must also coordinate different working styles and skills in order to provide a quality customer experience to make the airline appealing to a public willing to pay for its services.

These three mechanisms coordinate well together and also build on each other, in terms of helping an organisation execute its business strategy.

#### Identifying Resources

It can be difficult to draw up an inventory of a firm’s resources. The corporate statement of the financial position typically provides a limited view of a firm’s resources, as it comprises mainly financial and physical resources. In order to take a wider view of a firm’s resources it is helpful to identify three principal types of resources, tangible, intangible and human resources, in an effort to understand their potential for achieving strategic success in line with the organisational goals. This is illustrated in Exhibit 2.3.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-57.png)
Tangible resources are easier than intangible resources to identify and evaluate because financial resources and physical assets are identified and valued in the firm’s financial statements. The measures are not necessarily foolproof because strategically relevant information can be obscured, even on the statement of financial position. For example, historical cost valuation may provide little indication of an asset’s current market value.

For many organisations, intangible resources prove to be more valuable than tangible resources. Yet intangible resources tend to remain largely invisible in corporate financial statements. The undervaluation, or even exclusion, of intangible resources can create a very large and growing divergence between companies’ valuations based on book value and their stock market valuations.

For example, brand names and other trademarks all represent a form of reputational asset: their value is delivered through the confidence they instill in customers. The value of an organisation’s brands can be increased by extending the range of products over which that company markets its brands. Intellectual property, including patents, copyrights, trade secrets and trademarks, comprise technological and artistic resources where ownership is defined in law.

The firm’s human resources comprise the expertise and effort offered by its employees. Most firms devote considerable effort to appraising their human resources, including paying attention to that requirement at the initial hiring stage, when potential employees are evaluated in relation to the requirements of their job. Many organisations have also established assessment centres specifically for the purpose of providing comprehensive, quantitative assessments of the skills and attributes of individual employees.

#### Apply and Analyse 2

Identify and describe the factors that DeepHarbour HK must take into account as it conducts a thorough analysis of the tangible resources, intangible resources and human resources available to that organisation.

Analysis

Tangible resources – DeepHarbour HK’s tangible resources will include its investment of HK$1.5 billion to acquire 100 ships, HK$500 million in self-loading/unloading technology and another HK$250 million in sophisticated navigation and communication systems. When those resources have been acquired and the business has commenced operations, it will be possible to measure whether those resources are being put to the best use or whether they can be used more profitably. For example, perhaps over time the focus on operations in the Asia-Pacific region will change and it will be deemed more profitable to expand the geographic scope of those operations to maximise use of the organisation’s tangible resources in fleet and technology.

Intangible resources – DeepHarbour HK will not be likely to have many intangible resources as the organisation commences operations. But if, over time, the company achieves the desired level of success it strives to provide clients through its services, it might develop valuable reputation and goodwill.

Brand names, copyrights and other trademarks may also develop value over time as DeepHarbour HK expands its operations and perhaps diversifies into supplementary businesses, including trucking services from its fleet of ships in port to various client destinations. It is also possible that the organisation will develop proprietary technology or intellectual property of value with respect to modifications made to its self-loading/ unloading technology and/or navigation and communication systems.

Although intangible resources may be a future consideration, this should not be overlooked during the strategic planning stages.

Human resources – The degree to which DeepHarbour HK is able to develop much of the overall value of the organisation will be dependent on the effort, dedication, knowledge and expertise of the personnel it hires at all levels.

The exercise of hiring executives, managers and employees and selecting the board of directors will be an important investment for DeepHarbour HK – just as the organisation’s commitment to acquire tangible assets, including its fleet of ships and operating systems, represents a financial investment.

Good hiring practices represent an integral part of strategic planning DeepHarbour HK should have, well ahead of actual hiring, comprehensive, quantitative assessments of the skills and attributes that are required of management and employees, as well as documented job appraisal criteria, to maximise the chances of hiring and retaining personnel who will properly represent the values of the organisation. This will also contribute significantly to the goodwill value (an integral intangible resource) that DeepHarbour HK is able to build over time.
