## Opening case
MIDDLE KINGDOM AIRLINES LTD

You work for Middle Kingdom Airlines Ltd (MKAL), an international airline that is registered and based in Hong Kong offering scheduled passenger and cargo services to more than 50 countries.

You are part of the organisation’s finance department with responsibilities for risk management and hedging.

In the normal course of business, Middle Kingdom Airlines Ltd is exposed to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates, interest rates and jet fuel prices. These exposures are managed by the finance department with the use of derivative financial instruments, in accordance with corporate board policies.

According to corporate policy, derivative financial instruments are to be used solely for financial risk management purposes and the company does not use derivatives for speculation. Derivative financial instruments, which constitute a hedge, mitigate the company’s exposure to market risk by compensating change in the market value of the hedged items. Management regularly reviews exposure to foreign exchange rates, interest rates and jet fuel price movements and adjusts positions in accordance with company guidelines.

MKAL manages different types of risks in the following ways:

A. Credit risk Middle Kingdom Airlines Ltd normally grants a credit term of 30 days to customers or it follows the local industry standard. In certain circumstances the receivable is partially protected by bank guarantees or other collateral.

B. Liquidity risk The company monitors liquidity and compliance with lending covenants, so as to ensure sufficient liquid funds and funding lines from financial institutions are available to meet liquidity requirements over both the short and long term.

C. Foreign currency risk The company’s revenue streams are exposed to foreign exchange rate fluctuations because they are denominated in a number of foreign currencies. To manage this exposure, assets are, where possible, financed in those foreign currencies in which net operating surpluses are anticipated, thus establishing a natural hedge. The foreign currencies the company is using are the US dollar, euro, Australian dollar, Singapore dollar, renminbi and Japanese yen. The risk is that economic, political or other events could have a materially negative effect on one or more of these currencies.

D. Interest rate risk The primary cause for the company’s cash flow exposure to interest rate risk is attributable to long-term borrowings at floating interest rates. In order to manage the interest rate risks that arise from liabilities, the company can use interest rate swaps to maintain what they deem to be the proper fixed rate and floating rate exposure. An analysis of changes in interest rates for variable rate instruments is used to assess the company’s interest rate risk.

E. Commodity price risk (fuel price risk) Fuel is one of the biggest components of Middle Kingdom Airlines Ltd’s operating cost. Fuel accounted for 30.7% of the company’s total operating expenses in 20X9. Exposure to fluctuations in the fuel price is managed by the use of fuel derivatives. The profit or loss generated from these fuel derivatives is dependent on the combination of contracts that generate payoffs in any particular range of fuel prices.

## 3.1 Major Types of Financial Risk
There are many sources of financial risk and several major types of financial risk. This section describes some of the important risks that may be faced by an organisation.

An organisation’s risks arise from a variety of activities undertaken by an organisation. Risk assessment helps to determine the priorities and controls required by an organisation. The risks discussed here are those typically managed or assessed by treasury. These major treasury-related risks include:
- • Market risks, through purchases, sales and financing activities;
- • Credit risks, through commercial and financial market transactions;
- • Operational risks, through people, systems or processes; and
- • Liquidity risks, through an organisation’s ability to maintain financial assets and the risks and returns on invested assets.

One of the key risks facing investors and other financial stakeholders is the financial risk they take when investing in an organisation that might, for a variety of reasons, subsequently end up unable to meet its financial obligations, causing financial loss. Organisations face many sources of financial risk in their daily operations, including interest rate risk, foreign exchange risk and commodity price risk, liquidity risk or capital risk (which in turn involves market, credit and operational risk), which will be studied in more detail in this section.

Financial risk could also arise as a result of unexpected financial or economic changes – possibly as a result of political or other factors – in a host country or international jurisdiction in which the organisation is doing business.

Financial risk to the cash flows of stockholders results from the way the organisation’s assets have been financed. Thus, the treasury function encompasses financial risk management, along with cash management and liquidity management. Among the most common risk management activities faced by a treasury department are foreign exchange risk, interest rate risk, commodity pricing risk, credit risk and operational risk. These are discussed in the sections that follow.

### 3.1.1 Interest Rate Risk
Interest rate risk is the possibility of a change in interest rates that has a negative impact on a company’s ability to finance its operations and profitability. Whenever an organisation borrows money or extends credit it may incur interest rate risk. Although a large, financially healthy company might have better financial capacity to absorb potential losses arising from interest rate risk, it can affect all organisations. It is an even more serious issue for organisations with substantial debt outstanding, because they are sensitive to even a small boost in interest expense and have less financial capacity to absorb the potential loss. Such an increase could negatively affect their cash flows and profit or loss. Moreover, that could potentially cause the company to break certain lending covenants with respect to, for example, the interest coverage ratio that needs to be maintained.

The organisation also must be concerned, albeit less critically, with respect to its forecasts. When interest rates change, this will impact the reliability of longer term forecasts beyond the first few months of a year when trying to determine the expected return on investment for cash on hand available for investment purposes. If the forecast interest rate changes during the year, the organisation’s budgeted interest income may be inaccurate.

The serious cash flow problems that interest rate volatility can cause, as well as the potentially negative impacts on budgeted interest income, illustrates the importance of having a treasurer, finance manager or other appropriate person define an organisation’s financial risk management objectives and the necessity to have strategies in place in order to mitigate such risk.

Financial, economic or political shocks sourced from any number of factors can create volatile and unpredictable interest rates, which in turn introduce additional risk to economies, markets, industries and individual businesses. The unpredictability of interest rates in financial markets has the potential to create major uncertainty and risk around the world.

Interest rate risks, which can have a material impact on profit or loss as rates increase or decrease, arise from various financial transactions, including extending credit, long-term borrowing to fund new projects or fixed income securities’ portfolio holdings. For global organisations the exposures that need to be managed are impacted by both domestic and foreign variables. Interest rate risks are, therefore, a key factor in many organisational financial decisions.

Asset-liability management involves the matching of assets and liabilities so that interest rate exposure is minimised, thereby reducing the potential adverse impact on the organisation. For example, in a **financial** institution setting, asset-liability management involves matching customer loans or mortgages with customer deposits. In a **non-financial** organisation, this might mean matching funding (such as long-term funding) with long-term assets (such as plant expansion).

Matching of assets and liabilities may take place on the basis of **maturity**. A measure such as duration can be used to reflect interest rate sensitivity. The securitisation of assets, such as receivables or mortgages, might be a strategy that can be used in situations where the organisation needs to raise cash. This could assist an organisation in improving its liquidity and reducing the need to seek additional funding.

Some non-financial organisations have exposure to interest rate mismatches through financing programmes for their customers or through internal financing for projects. Non-financial institutions might also be able to reduce interest rate exposure by building an awareness of asset-liability management within parts of their organisation that are involved in such activities, and then using that knowledge to reduce exposure to potential interest rate mismatches wherever possible.
### 3.1.2 Foreign Exchange Risk
An organisation’s financial fortunes, and even the firm’s value, can be heavily influenced by international factors, such as political and global economic events that are beyond its control, which can lead to unexpected changes in foreign exchange rates. Foreign exchange, or currency risk, is, therefore, a key financial risk faced by multi-national corporations in particular, but its effects can also impact domestic companies that conduct business abroad. Foreign exchange risk arises through various sources, including financial/operational transactions, translation of financial statement items and the activities of competitors.

#### 3.1.2.1 Transaction Risk
A transaction is exposed to currency risk when exchange rates change unexpectedly, causing a change in the value of an organisation’s monetary (contractual) cash flows. Such exposures are straightforward to spot and manage. This can be done through executing offsetting transactions within the company or else through hedges in the external financial market.

For example, an organisation that imports will buy its goods at prices that are determined in foreign markets. Then it will sell those goods to domestic customers at prices that are determined in the domestic market. **Importers** tend to gain from a real appreciation of the domestic currency or lose from a real depreciation of that currency.

Conversely, an **exporter** would tend to gain from a real depreciation of the domestic currency and lose from a real appreciation of that currency. How much the firm gains or loses depends on the organisation’s pricing policies and the price elasticity of demand for its products.

#### 3.1.2.2 Translation Risk

Translation (accounting) exposure refers to changes in a firm’s financial statements as a result of changes in currency values. This can leave the organisation open to translation, or accounting exposure, whereby the consolidated financial statements of the parent company, for example, will bear the impact of exchange rate changes in subsidiaries.

Thus, translation exposure is a very important measurement to the firm’s managers if, say, their compensation schedule is correlated with financial performance. Hedging translation exposure to currency risk may also be important in situations that involve meeting profit forecasts, fulfilling loan covenants or to maintain a credit rating.

Translation exposure is applicable, particularly in instances involving multinational organisations that are operating in many countries with a range of currencies.

The functional currency of an organisation is, generally speaking, the primary currency with which that business operates – for example, the currency in which the business generates its revenues and costs and expenses. Generally, the functional currency of an organisation will be the domestic currency of the parent company and that currency will be reflected in the company’s financial statements.

The presentation currency (reporting currency) of an organisation is the currency used in its financial statement presentation to stakeholders and the public. There are situations where the functional currency will need to be translated for financial presentation purposes. This might occur if, for example, an organisation conducts a materially significant amount of business in a foreign country and currency.

#### 3.1.2.3 Economic Risk

Economic risk refers to the exposure that an organisation faces as it conducts business in a global business environment, where various changes in the business, political or other conditions, such as natural weather disasters that affect one or more countries, can materially impact an organisation’s operations.

Currency risk is a key element of economic risk. Currency risk can arise due to changes in future cash flows resulting from unexpected changes in exchange rates, whether these cash flows are monetary or non-monetary. Economic exposure can be further considered as the transaction exposure from financial assets and liabilities and the operating exposure of non-financial assets. There will also be operational exposure to currency risk resulting from a change in the **value of non-monetary assets or operating cash flows** due to changes in currency values.

Exhibit 3.1 shows some sample exchange rates.

#### Illustrative Example 1
The opening case involving MKAL illustrates how an organisation can face potentially significant currency translation risks. For example, the opening case documents how MKAL uses six foreign currencies: US dollar, euro, Australian dollar, Singapore dollar, renminbi and Japanese yen. Any or a combination of those currencies could be subject to external shocks that could negatively affect MKAL’s business transactions in the respective countries to which they apply.

For example, assume that a financial crisis simultaneously affects two countries in the European Union (EU), necessitating an emergency financial bailout for each nation at risk, and that severely depreciates the value of the euro. Assuming also that a significant portion of MKAL’s annual flights take place within the EU, this may also depress economic activity and therefore MKAL’s annual revenues in euros.

Since MKAL has the advantage of its global operations and the use of other currencies, it might try to compensate for the loss in euro revenue by attempting to earn more of its annual revenue in other jurisdictions where the local currency is stronger. If, for example, the US dollar is strong, and the US dollar might appreciate in response to the depreciation of the euro, MKAL’s management might want to examine the viability of conducting further flights and generating more passenger revenue in the US.

### 3.1.3 Commodity Price Risk
Commodity price risk is the probability of changes in the price of a commodity that is a component of an organisation’s business. Commodity price risk occurs from contract pricing or sales involving goods such as metals (for example, gold or silver), energy (for example, oil or natural gas) or agricultural products (for example, wheat or soybeans) whose prices can fluctuate, often unexpectedly. These fluctuations can have a major positive or negative impact on financial results. Commodity price risk affects consumers and end users such as manufacturers, governments, processors and wholesalers.

Quantity risk arises through the requirement for commodity assets or the ability to sell adequate quantity. Although quantity is closely tied to price, quantity risk remains an issue because supply and demand are critical with respect to commodities in production or operations.

Typically, commodity risk involves products that must be purchased or sold, but it can also arise indirectly through prices of ingredients in the supply chain that are themselves affected by commodity prices. Commodity exposure can also arise even if the organisation is a non-commodity business should there be inputs or products and services that have a commodity component. This commodity price risk is wide ranging; it affects consumers and end users such as manufacturers, governments, processors and wholesalers.

Depending on the size and scale of the organisation, commodity risk might be managed by the treasury department or by another internal group that focuses specifically on the commodity element of the business.

### 3.1.4 Liquidity Risk
Liquidity risk refers to the risk that an investor holding an instrument might not be able to convert it into cash with the promptness required to conduct a transaction in the financial market. This is significant because lack of liquidity can lead to, or exacerbate, financial losses in market transactions.

For example, if the market is liquid, a business asset can quickly be converted into cash without any loss of value. Conversely, in an illiquid market, it will take time to convert an asset into cash or else there will be a loss of value in the conversion.

Multinational corporations that have access to liquid international markets can have advantages over domestic firms without access to those same financial resources. However, for all organisations it is vitally important to continually monitor liquidity and be aware, in real-time, of any risks that exist.

Closely related to liquidity management, which includes forecasting and ensuring cash availability, is working capital, which involves managing an organisation’s current assets and current liabilities. Working capital, and its relationship with liquidity management, is discussed in detail in Chapter 6, Working Capital Management.

### 3.1.5 Capital Risk
Capital risk refers to the risk that an investor – such as an investor in stocks and bonds – faces of losing all or part of their original investment amount. There are several components to capital risk, discussed in the following paragraphs.

Credit-related strategies carry the potential for multiple risks, including suffering a credit loss as a result of an incorrect assessment of risk. The consequences can be very serious for an individual investor or an organisation, including a deterioration of credit quality leading to a capital loss, to an outright default by an issuer.

The quality of capital assets and the timing of their purchase and sale in the market require careful consideration. Market risk, credit risk and operational risk, as elements of capital risk, will be studied in more detail in this section.

#### 3.1.5.1 Market Risk

The risks discussed in the previous section, such as interest rate risk, foreign exchange risk, commodity risk, liquidity risk, arise from financial markets. However, market risk is a term commonly applied to non-diversifiable or systematic risk, which is a risk that is **shared by all assets** in the market. Systematic risks arise through market-wide events, such as an unexpected change in real economic growth, government spending or general investor sentiment regarding the value of assets. Systematic risks cannot be managed by diversification. Systematic risk was covered previously in Module 7.

The component of an asset’s risk that can be diversified by holding a portfolio with many assets is known as unsystematic risk. Unsystematic risk is also called non-market risk or diversifiable risk. For a share of stock, that component of total risk that is diversifiable is also known as company-specific risk. Unsystematic risks include labour issues, CEO changes, company-specific commercial successes or any other event that is unique to a single asset or company.

Total risk (or variance) is composed of systematic and unsystematic risk:
> Total risk = Systematic risk + Unsystematic risk
For example, assume that an organisation in Hong Kong invests in a portfolio of stocks denominated in British pounds (GBP). The component parts of systematic risk and unsystematic risk are illustrated in Exhibit 3.2 to show how the systematic risk factors (which are non-diversifiable) remain fixed at **21.9%**. The standard deviation of the portfolio suggests the organisation’s total risk, taking into account both systematic and unsystematic risk factors (the latter being diversifiable). This risk decreases from 40% to about 23% as the portfolio of stocks held in GBP increases from one stock to 26 stocks. The key assumption is that an increase in the number of stocks held improves diversification.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-59.png)
A commonly used measure of market risk within banks and large corporations is value-at-risk. Value-at-risk is a systematic methodology that is designed to estimate the potential financial loss for a given period of time, based on statistical estimates of probability at a predetermined confidence interval. Value-at-risk is commonly used to estimate risk in a portfolio of assets or exposures. (See Module 7, Chapter 6.)

For example, a Hong Kong based company holds a portfolio of investments with a value-at-risk of HK$2 million a year with a 95% confidence interval. This means there is a 95% chance (probability) that the amount at risk of loss will be HK$2 million or less over the next year and a 5% chance it will be greater.

In the current regulatory environment, expected shortfall, which estimates likelihood of losses that are larger than the estimates from value-at-risk, is often used.

#### 3.1.5.2 Credit Risk

Credit risk is the risk arising from an organisation through its commercial and financial market activities. For example, a business may extend trade credit to customers, use derivatives for hedging and borrow. Credit risk is a concern whenever an organisation is owed money or relies on other organisations for payment of some kind. Credit risk can also be affected by the legal environment and whether funds are owed on an aggregate or individual basis. When a borrower’s credit rating or risk deteriorates, this can also give rise to credit risk, through the reduced ability to issue debt or borrow. Finally, credit risk can originate with owning of securities issued by another organisation.

Credit risk involves the probability that some component of funds due could be at risk, and, naturally, this risk is more difficult in different legal or regulatory regimes such as those in other countries.

Counterparty risk arises from the **potential non-performance** of counterparties in transactions or contracts, such as derivatives. Counterparty risk exists during settlement and during the pre-settlement period. In the pre-settlement period, if a counterparty **defaults or fails to deliver** its obligations, it might be necessary to replace a contract at less favourable market prices. Counterparty risk is also particularly important during the settlement process. Settlement risk arises at the time payments under a contract occur, particularly cross-payments between counterparties. This has the potential to result in large losses because if a counterparty fails during the settlement process, the entire amount of the payment between counterparties may be at risk. Since the 2008 financial crisis, local authorities have established rules to reduce settlement risk. These include some settlements through a central counterparty, similar to an exchange clearinghouse.

The credit manager in an organisation must be able to correctly assess credit quality independently of the assessments that are widely available, such as those provided by credit rating agencies. The assessments provided by third parties, although often very useful, are not infallible and therefore need to be supplemented by an independent analysis. Independent sources of information may also include a prime supplier or a related company.

An accurate assessment of credit risk can be a complex undertaking, since credit quality is fluid. It can deteriorate relatively quickly, particularly if there is a concurrent liquidity, economic or financial event impacting a business. In their pursuit of credit strategies, management in an organisation must be aware of this and be comfortable with the additional risks that such strategies involve.

Credit exposure in concentrated sectors can lead to concentration risk. For example, some organisations have a great deal of exposure due to industry or geographic influences. Concentration risk can be managed in an investment portfolio, but in other areas it may be more challenging. Since success may result from concentrating efforts in specific industry, geographic or product areas, this risk can be recognised if not eliminated.

#### 3.1.5.3 Operational Risk

Operational risk arises from multiple sources, including human error and fraud, processes and procedures, and technology and systems. Operational risks often are interrelated and may be caused by a combination of events. For example, an organisational weakness that permits an electronic funds transfer to occur fraudulently may be related to its personnel (as a result of human error or fraud), technology (through technology and systems risk) or processes.

Operational risk can be **one of the most significant risks** facing an organisation due to the varied opportunities for losses to occur. Even if the odds of a certain risk being realised are low, losses may be substantial when they do occur. For example, many large trading losses have occurred due to operational failures. This section discusses the operational risks that affect finance and treasury in particular.

Due to the size and volume of treasury and finance transactions, the **potential damage of a large error or fraud is serious**, and this could be compounded in certain organisations where there is pressure to outperform competitors and/or earn significant profit.

The critical issues that impact how organisations around the world respond to operational risk are very complex and diverse. For example, operational risk is a key determinant for global financial institutions in their efforts to comply with the pronouncements of the Basel Accords.

## 3.2 Managing Interest Rate Risk
Interest rates are a key input to many financial decisions as even small changes to interest rates can impact profitability. Interest rate risk must, therefore, be managed carefully within the organisation. This section elaborates on the importance of interest rate risk and examines preventative measures that can be taken to mitigate interest rate risk.

### 3.2.1 Importance of Managing Interest Rate Risk
Interest rate risk is complex. It includes absolute interest rate risk (arising from exposure to either an increase or decrease in interest rates), yield curve risk (changes in the relationship between short-term and longer-term interest rates) and reinvestment or refunding risk.

The absolute interest rate risk faced by an organisation arises from exposure to either an increase or decrease in interest rates. Due to its visibility and potential for affecting profitability, most organisations closely monitor their absolute interest rate risk as part of their overall risk assessment.

Due to its financial focus, the treasury department/function is both a source of risk and a moderator of risk for the organisation. For example, treasury may be involved in transacting financial derivatives as a strategy to mitigate interest rate risk. It is important that both senior management and the board of directors clearly understand the various risks that treasury is involved with managing, including the risks that it specifically creates.

### 3.2.2 Mitigating Measures
Organisations can use various financial strategies to mitigate the potential damage that interest rate risk can cause. The sources of interest rate risk were discussed earlier in this chapter. This section considers alternatives for managing interest rate risk.

**Enhanced cash flow management** may permit an organisation to maintain cash balances for longer periods of time. There are several ways an organisation can do this. It can make more effective use of its account payable policies, including re-evaluating the credit terms it offers clients and tightening its collection practices. It can introduce favourable changes to customer payment schedules to also speed up the collection process. It can also make changes to improve both efficiency and speed, such as encouraging electronic payments.

These measures can, in turn, **reduce the need for funding** and therefore exposure to interest rates, particularly in countries where there is less liquidity and there is additional difficulty in moving funds. Another strategy to reduce interest rate exposure might include **global cash netting**, where one part of the organisation functions as an in-house cash management bank, providing intercompany lending and borrowing.

If hedging against changes in interest rates is needed, there are several derivatives-based strategies that can be used.

#### 3.2.2.1 Forward Rate Agreement (FRA)

A forward rate agreement (FRA) is an over-the-counter agreement between two parties, a notional borrower and a notional lender, to lock in an interest rate for a short period of time – typically one month or three months – beginning at a future date. The notional nature of this agreement is important because the contract amount itself does not change hands between the counterparties, nor does any lending or borrowing occur.

FRA rates are determined by the relationship between shorter-term and longer-term interest rates. Most FRAs are for short time periods, either one month or three months. It is possible to enter into an FRA that begins in nine months and expires in twelve months (9 × 12) or that begins in one year and expires in two years (12 × 24). The notation sets the effective (beginning) and termination dates of the FRA, with each date being the number of months from the present month. For example, 3 × 6 refers to an FRA covering a period starting in three months and ending in six months. Exhibit 3.3 shows a sample of FRA rates.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-60.png)
A borrower buys an FRA contract to protect against rising interest rates, while a lender sells an FRA to protect against declining interest rates. Counterparties to an FRA can continue to borrow or invest through normal channels. It is often the case that a borrower, for example, contracts the FRA with a counterparty that is not its lender. The FRA provides interest rate protection against changes in rates as measured by the reference rate specified in the contract but not the ability to borrow/invest.

Should interest rates rise and a buyer has purchased an FRA, the counterparty will pay the difference in the amount that the market interest rate is greater than the reference rate. The reference rate is typically based on a recognised market interest rate such as the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) or Euribor. These rates will be specified in the FRA contract.

If interest rates should increase and the buyer is using the FRA as a hedge on the interest rate for the amount it is borrowing, it will pay the increased interest rate to the lender and then should be able to offset the additional cost through the counterparty’s payment under the FRA. There may be a difference between the interest rate charged by the lender and the interest rate covered by the FRA, in which case the offset will not be perfect.

If interest rates instead decrease, the buyer will need to pay the difference between this lower rate and the FRA-specified reference rate to the FRA counterparty. This will offset, or add to, the reduced interest rate that needs to be paid to the lender. Therefore, regardless of which direction actual interest rates (the reference rate) subsequently go, the purchaser of an FRA will have secured or locked in a fixed reference rate, though the organisation may face a different rate in its borrowing (or investing) transactions.

The following formula illustrates how settlement amount is calculated under an FRA contract
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-61.png)
The paying party discounts the settlement amount against the reference rate and pays this amount to the other party. The formula for discounting the settlement amount is:
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-62.png)
A number of date conventions are used in an FRA. The contract date is the start date of the agreement. The expiry date is when the difference between the market rate and the reference rate is determined (end of the agreement). The settlement date is when the payment is made; this is also the first day of the underlying period (period covered by the FRA). Finally, the maturity date is the last day of the underlying FRA period.

These dates are shown in the sample timeline in Exhibit 3.4. In the exhibit, the FRA contract term is three months, running from 1 January to 1 April. The underlying period is three months, from 3 April to 3 July.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-63.png)

#### Illustrative Example 2

Middle Kingdom Airlines Ltd (MKAL) has multinational operations and expects to borrow HK$25 million in one year’s time to finance a refit of mechanical systems on some of its equipment, and it will need funds for a period of one year. The current market interest rate for equivalent financing is currently 5.00%, and given current market conditions MKAL’s treasurer expects there will be an increase in market rate to 6.00% when MKAL needs to borrow.

In order to lock in at the current rate of 5.00%, MKAL’s treasurer will need to enter into a 12 × 24 FRA at 5.00% as determined by the HIBOR reference rate. The FRA settlement amount will be determined by the 12 month HIBOR rate in one year’s time. Assume that in one year the HIBOR rate has increased to 5.80%. Therefore, prior to discounting, the bank counterparty to the FRA determines that it owes HK$200,000 to MKAL, which is calculated as:
> HK$25,000,000 x (365 Days in Contract / 365 Days in Year) x (0.058 Reference Rate - 0.050 Contract Rate) = HK$200, 000

The final step in the process is for the bank to calculate its discounted payment to MKAL. The **discounted payment** is HK$189,035.92, which is calculated as
> HK$200, 000/(1 + 365 / 365 x 5.80%) = HK$189,035.92

#### 3.2.2.2 Interest Rate Swap

Banks are major participants in the very large swap market. Swaps provide corporate treasurers with a great deal of flexibility to select the instrument’s notional amount, its duration and its floating benchmark rate. Furthermore, a swap between an organisation and its bank can be liquidated any time. This can be accomplished by payment and receipt of the net present value of future cash flows on the notional amount of the swap, at the market rate.

Swaps are contractual agreements frequently used to manage interest rate risk on floating or fixed-rate assets or to retool an exposure to better suit an organisation’s risk tolerance.

Interest rate swap terms range from 1 to 15 years but are commonly around 5 years. They can be used for managing a company’s longer-term exposure arising from longer projects. The key principle behind interest rate swaps is that they enable an organisation to make a change to the interest rate risk of a loan or investment without changing the underlying loan or investment itself.

#### Illustrative Example 3

As noted earlier in the chapter, MKAL’s exposure to interest rates arises from its strategy of borrowing for long-term projects at floating rates. As a result, interest rate swaps are then used to change the interest rate profile of interest-bearing financial liabilities to maintain an **appropriate level of fixed rate and floating rate components**.

MKAL’s treasurer may need to finance a new passenger boarding and baggage project. The treasurer is considering a fixed rate financing for HK$1 million. However, because HK interest rates are expected to stay low or even fall further, floating rate financing would be preferable.

Below is an illustration showing the financing MKAL would be using.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-64.png)
MKAL enters into an interest rate swap with a bank. Under the terms of the swap, it receives a fixed rate, and it pays a floating market reference rate (plus a spread of 1.5%) on HK$1 million. The fixed rate received under the swap helps to offset the fixed rate paid to the lender. Rates for the first year of the swap are shown here:
![](DraggedImage-65.png)
The details of this swap are negotiated between the company and the bank. Given
the rates provided by the interest rate swap MKAL has entered into and its HK$ financing, the resulting MKAL exposure is exposure to floating HK$ interest rates. The company continues to make payments to its lender. By receiving fixed rates, the hedging results in paying lower rates in Q1 and Q2, but MKAL pays higher rates in Q3 and Q4. MKAL has effectively converted fixed rate debt into floating rate payments, permitting it to benefit somewhat if interest rates should fall. However, MKAL’s swap payments will rise if the market reference rate rises.

#### 3.2.2.3 Interest Rate Option

The two basic types of options available to mitigate risk are puts and calls. A put option on interest rates provides protection to the option buyer from declining rates, as defined by the contract terms and reference rate. The reference rate is established in the option contract as the benchmark against which the potential benefits to the option buyer are measured. A call option on interest rates provides protection to the option buyer from rising rates as defined by the contract terms and reference rate.

Options are available in the over-the-counter market, typically directly transacted with a bank, and they are also traded on exchanges (exchange-traded or listed options). The contract value, term and strike price of a listed option is standardised, whereas these terms are customised for an over-the-counter option.

The business of options is analogous to the role of insurance. One party pays to reduce or eliminate risk, while the other party accepts that risk in exchange for an option premium.

Interest rate option contract details include the following features:
- • Strike price. A strike price refers to the interest rate in the option contract.
- • Reference rate. The reference rate refers to the market interest rate that is referred to in the contract.
- • Expiry. The expiry date is the date that an option contract expires, if it has not been exercised.
- • Contract or notional amount. The contract or notional amount refers to the amount that contract terms cover (or the notional amount of a fixed income security).
- • Exercise. Exercise terms refer to how and when a particular contract by an option buyer can be exercised – for example, whether such a contract must be settled by cash or if there are conditions under which delivery of an underlying asset is permitted.

A European-style option can be exercised only at expiry and an American-style option can be exercised any time until expiry.

An option is said to be in-the-money (ITM)  when it is **profitable** for the option buyer to exercise it.

An option is said to be out-of-the-money (OTM) when it is **not profitable** for the option buyer to exercise it.

An option is said to be at-the-money (ATM) when one would be** approximately indifferent **whether to exercise it or transact at market.

In hedging, it is common for the option exercise price to be compared to the forward price for assessing whether it is in-the-money. An option that is in-the-money will be more expensive than an option that is not in-the-money, presuming the other attributes of the options are the same.

- • Interest rate cap. With a cap, borrowers may establish a ceiling interest rate above which they will no longer wish to borrow. They will then receive the difference between the market rate and the cap rate.
- • Interest rate floor. Establishing a floor rate allows lenders to establish a minimum interest rate below which they do not wish to lend. They will then receive the difference between the floor rate and the market rate.
- • Swaption. A swaption is an option on a swap. It typically allows a swaption buyer to enter into an underlying swap during a specified period of time. The underlying swap attributes are predetermined, including notional amount, maturity and fixed and floating rates that are used as benchmarks.

#### Illustrative Example 4

As you are aware, MKAL’s treasurer is considering some new financing for a new passenger boarding and baggage project. The treasurer is considering HK$ floating rate financing, because HK interest rates are expected to stay low or fall further. The bank is willing to offer competitive short-term financing, with a quarterly rate reset, for two years, which covers the project adequately. Since rates will be reset quarterly, an increase in rates will result in higher interest costs that must be passed along to the cost of the project.

The treasurer enters into an interest rate cap with the bank, in conjunction with floating rate financing. The cap and the financing do not have to be with the same bank, although they are in this scenario. The interest rate cap is a series of quarterly interest rate call options. (If MKAL wanted to protect against falling interest rates, it might use an interest rate put instead of a call.)

At each quarterly rate reset, the cap rate is compared to the reset rate. The treasurer is comfortable with floating rates unless the interest rate rises above 6.00%. The cap is structured so that 6.00% is the cap rate. If interest rates exceed the cap rate, the bank will pay MKAL the difference for that quarter. If rates do not exceed the cap rate, the bank will pay MKAL nothing. For this protection, MKAL pays a fee (cap premium) to the bank.

At the first quarterly rate reset, the market benchmark is 6.15%, which is higher than the cap rate at 6.00%. As a result, MKAL will use the cap and the bank will pay MKAL the difference between the market benchmark (6.15%) and the cap rate (6.00%), prorated over the number of days in the quarter.

At the second quarterly reset, the market benchmark is 5.85%, which is lower than the cap rate at 6.00%. As a result, the cap will not be used and MKAL will take advantage of the lower financing in the market for the quarter.

#### 3.2.2.4 Interest Rate Futures

Futures contracts are **similar to forwards** in that they deliver a certain security (or cash) at a predetermined date and price, known as the futures price. Futures contracts differ from forward contracts in a few key respects.

Futures contracts are similar to forwards but traded on a regulated exchange, which sets the details of the contract. The exchange facilitates transactions of investors who want to buy (long) or sell (short) contracts. In addition, it also guarantees that payments will be honoured at maturity, through the exchange clearinghouse. The futures contract is standardised and the exchange specifies the asset underlying the contract and the method (e.g. quality, quantity, location) of delivery. Most futures contracts don’t permit customisation. Gains or losses are marked-to-market, or realised, daily.

The quote represents the price at which delivery will take place in the future. The futures market thus may provide a convenient way for market participants to lock-in a future interest rate.

#### Illustrative Example 5

Consider a futures contract that allows the futures buyer to lock in an interest rate on HK$1 million; if the buyer wishes to lock in the interest rate on a larger amount, then additional contracts of HK$1 million increments must be used. The exchange quotes prices derived from a baseline index of HK$100, with a decline in futures price for periods further in the future, corresponding to higher interest rates further into the future. The difference between the baseline index and the quoted price (HK$100 − the price) is the interest rate on the contract. Sample futures contracts prices are:

June HK$95.500
September HK$95.255
December HK$94.990
March HK$94.550

Presuming that the interest rates above are similar to those faced by the hedger, a corporation with a large receivable expected in December might use a futures contract to lock in the rate at which it can invest a sum of money for the following 90 days, thus removing the risk of lower interest rates. Based on the sample prices shown, the rate would be 5.01% (100 – 94.990).

In order to lock in at a 5.010% rate, the company would buy a December futures contract. This protects against a further decline should interest rates decline below 5.01% by December. When funds are received by the corporation, it would close out the futures contract and invest through its normal channels (e.g. at a bank or investment dealer). If rates had risen, the futures contract would have fallen in value and a loss on the futures contract would be offset by higher investment rates. If rates had fallen, the futures contract would have risen in value and a gain on the futures contract would help to offset the lower investment rates. It will be important for the treasurer to ensure that the interest rates faced by the company are similar to those underlying the futures contract.

Given the certain rates provided by the futures contract, the resulting exposure is to the fixed interest rate of 5.01% for the benchmark rate for 90 days beginning in December. If rates rise above that rate for the 90-day term beginning in December, the futures contract will fall in value and the company will have a loss on the futures contract. If rates fall below that rate for the 90-day term beginning in December, the futures contract will rise in value and the company will have a gain on the futures contract. The hedging results in locking in the rate of 5.01%.
---- 
There are dozens of different interest rate futures contracts and new contracts are regularly added based on market demand. Futures contracts may be listed for specific interest rates or debt securities (e.g. government bonds). As you learned in Module 7, bond prices and yields move inversely. For example, futures contracts are traded on the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), which is the Hong Kong dollar-denominated rate for trades between local banks at 11:00 a.m. (Hong Kong time) daily. HIBOR is calculated from quotes provided by a set of Hong Kong banks designated by the Hong Kong Association of Banks (HKAB) and rates are published for terms of up to 12 months. Like its peers in other countries, it forms the basis for many transactions, including futures contracts and interest rate swaps.

Bond and interest rate futures can be used as a strategy to hedge bond and interest rate risk, change portfolio asset allocation or alter portfolio duration, without the need to buy or sell the underlying bonds. Bond futures are useful for tactical asset allocation strategies employed by professional money and portfolio managers. They can also assist in the management of exposure to long-term interest rates.

Presuming there has been no change in the willingness of the organisation’s lenders to extend credit, a borrower can sell a bond futures contract in order to protect against the prospect of increasing interest rates, which will cause bond prices to drop. This can be done provided that the underlying interest in the bond futures contract being sold is similar to the exposure. Should interest rates increase, meaning that the bond price will decrease, the gain realised on the futures contract should somewhat offset the increase in market interest rates. Conversely, should interest rates decline, meaning that the underlying bond price goes up, the loss realised on the futures contract should be able to offset the decrease in market interest rates.

## 3.3 Managing Foreign Exchange Risk
Foreign exchange risk is often an unavoidable risk facing a multinational corporation, or any organisation – even one that is exclusively based in one country, but is conducting business internationally. External economic and political circumstances will conspire to create foreign exchange risk that is beyond their control. The sources of foreign exchange risk were discussed earlier in this chapter. This section considers alternatives for managing foreign exchange risk.

### 3.3.1 Importance of Managing Foreign Exchange Risk
Foreign exchange risk is an integral part of many businesses. Many organisations in a global economy, whether they are based in one country or in multiple jurisdictions, have transaction exposures to currency risk through contracts denominated in a foreign currency. Their domestic currency value depends on a foreign exchange rate. If an organisation mismanages its foreign exchange risk, unforeseen business, political or other risks in one part of the world could leave the company financially exposed and it could face serious financial losses as a result of an unfavourable exchange rate.

As a result, financial managers within the organisation are provided with motivation to hedge against currency risk. This would reduce any unevenness in their divisional financial results. However, currency hedges come at a cost and divisional exposures throughout various parts of the business might offset one another. A globally diversified organisation or other companies might have some operational flexibility to use to their advantage. For example, the treasury department can elect to take an integrated approach to financial risk management by netting off the various exposures that are maintained in the organisation. This would avoid having to take offsetting positions and it would also minimise financing costs.

A forward price is based on the spot price with an adjustment for the forward date that may result in the forward rate at a discount or premium to the spot. There is an active market where financial institutions actively trade forwards and rates provided to customers reflect interest rates and profitability. An example of a forward is provided in Section 3.2.2.1.

For example, covered interest arbitrage takes advantage of an interest rate differential that is not fully reflected in the forward premium. If there is any disequilibrium in interest rate parity, this provides an opportunity for banks engaged in arbitrage to borrow in one currency, invest in the other currency and cover the difference in the spot and forward markets. This no-arbitrage condition then ensures that the two currency markets are in equilibrium (although there may be transaction costs).

### 3.3.2 Mitigating Measures
Multiple strategies can be used to mitigate foreign exchange risk. For example, foreign exchange forwards, futures, swaps and options can be used to reduce foreign exchange risk. Hedging can reduce the adverse consequences of currency risk by creating currency exposures that offset an organisation’s underlying exposures.

#### 3.3.2.1 Currency Forward

Forward contracts are commonly used in foreign exchange hedges. With a forward contract, an organisation purchases a predetermined amount of a foreign currency for delivery at a specific date and rate. The forward allows an organisation to lock in the exchange rate for settlement in the future, typically with its bank. The bank requires credit availability, with payment due on the forward (settlement) date. The bank will usually allocate a portion of the company’s credit facility to outstanding forward contracts until contracts are settled and the forwards are closed out. The forward contract is an over-the-counter transaction, because there is no centralised trading location and transactions are customised for the hedger.

Forward transactions can fully eliminate risk by locking in at present the price or rate at which a transaction will be made in the future. If, however, there is a favourable shift in price or rates, the organisation will not be able to benefit as a result of having locked in the price or rate of a transaction.

For example, consider a Hong Kong based company set to receive CA$1 million. The Canadian dollar is currently trading at CA$1 = HK$5.84. If the organisation is concerned about a decline in the Canadian dollar, its goal might be to lock in today at an exchange rate at which it will be able to sell those Canadian dollars.

The price of a currency on the maturity date (its forward price) is composed of the spot price, plus an adjustment for the interest rate differential between the two currencies (which may be a positive or negative adjustment). The currency with the higher interest rate trades at a discount in the forward market, while the currency with the lower interest rate trades at a premium.

Foreign currency interest rates affect forward foreign exchange rates. For example, if the foreign currency interest rate is lower than the domestic interest rate, the foreign currency should be less expensive in the forward market (than in the spot market). As an example, if the spot price of euro per US dollar is 0.7350 and there is a discount of 30 points (0.0030) for a one-year forward contract, then the ‘all-in’ forward rate would be 0.7320.

A forward contract with a ‘window’ of settlement dates can provide additional flexibility by permitting a range of settlement dates. The company can use the outstanding contract at the forward rate according to the specifications in the contract. This contract may be slightly more expensive than a standard forward exchange contract but makes it much easier to match incoming customer payments to the terms of the contract. For example, a company is expecting a foreign currency payment in early September, but the date is not clear. The company books a window forward for 1 to 15 September, providing it with a range of dates to settle, rather than one date.

#### Illustrative Example 6

Consider a retailer in Hong Kong that has booked a contract with a furniture supplier in Copenhagen, Denmark, to provide bedding and other household furniture to its stores over a two-year contract. When that contract was booked six months ago, the retailer has promised to pay local expenses in Denmark of Danish kroner (DKK) 25 million. The spot rate was then HK$2.00/DKK. Therefore, their expected Hong Kong dollar cost was

DKK25,000,000 × HK$2.00/DKK = HK$50,000,000.

That retailer has a short position in the Danish kroner.

Today, however, assume the kroner has appreciated by 25% from HK$2.00/DKK to HK$2.50/DKK. This increases the cost of the furniture from HK$50 million to DKK25 million × HK$2.50/DKK = HK$62,500,000. The 25% appreciation of the Danish kroner has increased the Hong Kong dollar value of their kroner obligation by 25%, or HK$12.5 million.

In the hedged position, the underlying short kroner position is offset by the long kroner forward contract. The net result is an obligation of HK$50 million regardless of what happens to the HK$-per-kroner exchange rate.

The hedged position is the sum of the two exposures. If the spot rate rises, the gain on the forward hedge would offset exactly the loss on the underlying position. Conversely, if the spot rate falls, the loss on the forward hedge would exactly offset the gain on the underlying position. The Hong Kong retailer would be able to exchange HK$50 million for DKK25 million regardless of what happened to the exchange rate.

#### 3.3.2.2 Currency Futures

A currency future is similar to a forward exchange contract. Both currency futures and forwards are contracts with a predetermined delivery date and price. However, there are significant differences between the two types of transactions. Currency futures trade on financial exchanges and usually have standard transaction amounts, currencies and expiration dates. Forward transactions are customised to meet client needs. Flexibility is, therefore, a big difference between the two types of transactions and a corporate treasurer needs to take both flexibility and cost into consideration when choosing whether a futures or forwards contract best meets the organisation’s requirements.

These contracts are normally handled through a brokerage firm, which typically charges a commission. Brokers and exchanges also have requirements for margin and the futures hedger may be required to provide additional funds if the underlying futures position declines in value. Margin consists of an initial deposit, based on the contract size and type of position, and maintenance margin, based on subsequent market movements. All futures contracts are marked to market daily, with the underlying margin accounts debited or credited daily with gains or losses. If the balance of the margin account drops too far, then the contract buyer must contribute additional funds to the margin account or risk the futures position being closed out by the broker.

Like other futures contracts, currency futures have standardised contract sizes and expiry dates. Therefore, a futures-based hedging strategy will usually not precisely match the underlying currency exposure. If a good match is required, a forward contract can be used.

Consider a company that requires EUR450,000 for a future payment. The exchange offers futures contracts of EUR100,000. As a result, the company must buy either four contracts (EUR400,000) or five contracts (EUR500,000). Further, the projected currency requirement date may differ from the futures contract expiry date. As a result, the standardised currency futures contract may result in an imperfect hedge for many users.

#### 3.3.2.3 Currency Swap

With a currency swap transaction, two parties are able to exchange payments and effectively change the nature of an asset or liability. Similar to an interest rate swap, the underlying exposure is not changed. Periodic payments are usually required between counterparties to currency swaps over the term of the swap, and a currency swap covers a longer period than a foreign exchange swap.

A currency swap is similar to a combination of a loan and an investment. With a currency swap, an exchange takes place at the commencement of the transaction in order to obtain the desired currency. Each party will then make regular periodic interest payments on the currency that has been received. In return, they will receive periodic interest payments on the currency they have given up. Usually because the payments are in different currencies, they are not netted. There is no foreign exchange risk on the principal amount because an exchange back to the original currencies will occur upon the maturity of that swap transaction.

Sometimes a currency swap involves a change in currency only. Where there is a currency basis swap (or a floating-to-floating swap), there is a change in both the currency and in the floating interest rate, which is known as the basis. A currency swap most commonly involves a change in both the currency and the rate – namely from a floating rate to a fixed rate or, the reverse, from a fixed rate to a floating rate.

A currency swap can be used for many purposes. For instance, the need for such a transaction might originate with a long term foreign currency debt issue that the organisation has. With a foreign currency swap, the transaction could convert a payment in a foreign currency to a payment in the domestic currency. Alternatively, a currency swap transaction could lock in the cost of existing foreign currency debt or it could be used to change the revenue stream on an asset.

Here is an example of how a currency swap works.

A tool company headquartered in Hong Kong plans to spend £5 million in six months’ time to invest in a new plant in London. The organisation’s treasury department has already accumulated British pounds to invest in the plant.

However, until such time that the investment needs to be made (in six months’ time), the company will require Hong Kong dollars to meet its daily operating expenses. The current, or spot, exchange rate is HK$10.00 = £1.00. To protect the value of its British pound investment six months in the future, as well as to maintain the interim cash flow it requires in Hong Kong dollars, the organisation conducts a swap transaction with two components.

In the first component of the swap, the tool company concludes a purchase with its primary financial institution for HK$51 million in exchange for selling £5.1 million it has accumulated. This will be transacted at the spot exchange rate of HK$10.00 = £1.00.

In the second component of the swap, the company agrees to sell back HK$51 million in exchange for £5 million, at a forward rate of HK$10.20 = £1, to be executed in six months’ time when the British currency is required for its capital investment.

The interest rate differential will be the difference between HK$10.20 and HK$10.00, or 0.02 × HK$51 million = HK$1,020,000. The tool company will earn that amount over the intervening six month period through its currency swap agreements. It will also protect the value of its foreign currency investment should the British pound depreciate any further against the Hong Kong dollar.

#### 3.3.2.4 Currency Option

Currency options can be used by organisations as a form of insurance to compensate for adverse currency movements caused by unfavourable changes in the underlying exchange rate that could be caused by any number of factors beyond its control.

Financial options are available in two variations – calls and puts. A currency call option gives the option buyer (holder) the right to buy the underlying currency at the exercise price (exchange rate) on or before the expiration date, depending on the exercise privileges in the option contract. The seller (writer) of the option has the obligation to deliver the specified currency at the exercise price and in exchange receives an option premium from the option buyer.

Exercising a currency call option may be advantageous or disadvantageous under certain circumstances.

For example, consider a small investor in Hong Kong who is concerned about the value of the Australian dollar rising. The investor purchased a call option on Australian dollars (AU$) that provides the right to buy AU$10,000 at an exchange rate of AU$1.00 = HK$5.43 on or before its expiry on June 1. By June 1, the Australian dollar has fallen against the Hong Kong dollar to an exchange rate of AU$1.00 = HK$5.22. It would not be advantageous for the investor to exercise that call option because the exercise price (exchange rate) exceeds the current market value of the Australian dollar. Since the investor owns the call option, it can be used or allowed to expire. If the investor wants to buy Australian dollars, it will be more favourable to buy them at current exchange rates and let the call option expire. To illustrate, if the call option was exercised, the purchase of AU$10,000 would cost HK$54,300 (HK$5.43 × 10,000), compared to only HK$52,200 (HK$5.22 × 10,000) if AU$10,000 had been purchased in the current market.

If the AU$ had appreciated to AU$1.00 = HK$5.70 on June 1, then it will be financially beneficial to exercise the call option and purchase AU$10,000 at AU$1.00 = HK$5.43 at a cost of HK$54,300 (HK$5.43 × 10,000), compared with a cost of HK$57,000 (HK$5.70 × 10,000) on the open market.

The gain to the investor in exercising the call option under those circumstances would be HK$57,000 − HK$54,300 = HK$2,700. This gain is not known in advance, since the market can move unexpectedly. The option premium paid by the AU$ call option buyer is to compensate the option seller for this risk.

Conversely, a currency put option gives the put buyer the right to sell the underlying currency at the exercise price. The option writer takes on the obligation to buy the specified currency at the exercise price, if the option buyer decides to use the put option.

The benefits and costs of the put option are similar to those for the call option buyer. The put buyer gets the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying currency.

Consider a seller of AU$. The seller would be in an advantageous position if they owned a put option with the right to sell AU$10,000 at an exchange rate of AU$1.00 = HK$5.43 on or before June 1. If, on June 1, the AU$ has fallen against the Hong Kong dollar to an exchange rate of AU$1.00 = HK$5.22, the seller could, by taking advantage of the exercise option, realise a return of HK$54,300 (HK$5.43 × 10,000), compared to a return of only HK$52,200 (HK$5.22 × 10,000) if A$10,000 had instead been purchased on the open market.

The gain to the seller in exercising the put option under those circumstances would be

> HK$54,300 − HK$52,200 = HK$2,100.

However, if the seller has the right to sell A$10,000 for HK$5.43, on or before June 1, and then on June 1 the exchange rate has appreciated to A$1.00 = HK$5.70, it will not be financially beneficial to exercise the put option and sell A$10,000 at A$1.00 = HK$5.43 because a price of HK57,000 (HK$5.70 × 10,000) could otherwise be attained if AU$10,000 had been sold on the open market.

The loss to the seller in exercising the put option under those circumstances would be

> HK$57,000 − HK$54,300 = HK$2,700.

Currency option values are a function of several variables. With the exception of volatility, each of these determinants of option value is readily observable. The strike price and expiry date are stated in the option contract, and the underlying exchange rate and the foreign and domestic interest rates are widely known and traded. The volatility of the underlying currency is not directly observable, but it is an important component of option valuation.

Option premiums consist of two components of value: intrinsic value and time value dependent on time until expiration. Together, these are the market value of the option. Similar to an insurance premium, an option buyer pays the option premium to the option seller (writer) resulting from exercise of the option by the option buyer.

The intrinsic value of an option is its value, if any, if exercised at current market prices. If an option is out-of-the-money, its intrinsic value is zero. If an option is in-the-money, its intrinsic value is equal to the difference between the exercise price and the value of the underlying asset. The time value of an option is the option’s market value (its premium) minus its intrinsic value or

> Option value = Intrinsic value + Time value

The holder of a call option gains when the underlying currency appreciates beyond the exercise price, but the holder cannot lose more than the option premium paid if the underlying currency depreciates instead. The holder of a put option gains when the underlying currency depreciates beyond the exercise price, but the holder cannot lose more than the option premium paid if the underlying currency appreciates instead. It is this asymmetry, similar to insurance, that gives options their unique place in risk reduction.

#### Illustrative Example 7

An investor purchases a call option that allows her to purchase 100 shares of ELL, a publicly traded stock at an exercise price of US$35 a share (US$3,500 for 100 shares), any time prior to the option’s expiry in six months. The current stock price is US$38 a share. The investor pays US$4.20 a share (US$420 for 100 shares) for the call option. This is the option’s premium.

Because ELL stock is trading at US$38, the call option is currently in-the-money. The call option’s value of US$4.20 consists of both intrinsic value and time value. The option provides an exercise price that is better than the current stock price, so the intrinsic value is US$3 (the difference between the US$35 exercise price and US$38 market price). The remaining premium (US$1.20) is time value, which is based on the probability of exercise prior to expiry.

A collar strategy combines the purchase of an option and the sale of an option that both have the same expiry date and the same currencies. A collar strategy is frequently used for managing foreign exchange risk. Foreign exchange collars often are used to reduce the cost of hedging using options. The two options, combined, then provide an exchange rate range for the user. The structure is highly customised for the hedger.

Forward foreign exchange contracts and currency futures are easier and less expensive to engage in than options and so are favoured by organisations with many treasury operations with more conservative risk profiles. Options are more expensive to purchase in the short-term and require closer monitoring due to the potential for losses and the lack of hedge.
