## 3.7 Risk Management Framework
Organisations, and corporations in particular, have become more risk-focused in their financial activities in recent decades, in part as a result of major crises but also due to the increased global nature of competition and an awareness of risk. The introduction of capital adequacy requirements through the Basel Accords was a major milestone in financial risk management at the bank level, and this has continued to evolve. Some experts noted that this international convergence of capital measurement and standards represented a means of ‘managing risk at the source’ and resulted in increased focus on risk and its sources.
### 3.7.1 Process for Managing Risk
An organisation’s hedging strategy is undertaken to allow treasury or finance officials to try and manage financial market fluctuation risks that occur when, for example, interest rates or exchange rates change, as well as to manage other critical business risks, including credit risk, or non-financial risks, such as with respect to energy or climate change. The term hedging is a generic term used for transactions or contracts, including forwards, futures and options, that are designed to offset financial market exposures, but it can also be used to apply to the broader strategy of an organisation.

A large multinational organisation that is operating in many countries and is dealing with various global currencies may by its very nature have a natural hedging strategy in place because a downturn in the economy and/or in the value of the currency of one or several countries might be offset by the strength of the economy and/or the value of the currency in another country, or several other countries in which it has operations.

For example, a large global corporation based in the United Kingdom that has major operations in the United States, as well as throughout the European Union (EU) and in Hong Kong, will be able to offset the negative effects of a potential financial crisis in the EU affecting the euro with its operations in the US, in US dollars, and in Hong Kong, in HK dollars.

The same is true for a national or multinational organisation that is involved with multiple industries because the impact of a downturn in the economic cycle of one sector or industry could be mitigated by the strength in another sector or industry in which that business operates.

For example, if a large multinational organisation is diversified into three major industries – oil and gas exploration, gold mining and agricultural supplies – a severe downturn in energy prices is likely to hurt the business division dealing in oil and gas through steeply declining prices, but the organisation’s mining and agricultural industries may not be affected by the same global or domestic causes that are hurting oil and gas. The same may be true if either gold mining or agricultural supplies are impacted by negative market conditions, as those same conditions may not affect the company’s other two divisions.

The business operations of an organisation may also contain natural hedges such as, for example, when a treasury department has established fixed-rate deposits to offset fixed-rate loans and/or floating-rate deposits to offset variable rate loans.

Derivatives are contractual agreements, the value of which are dependent on, or derived from, a reference asset or rate. Derivatives act as a risk transfer mechanism from organisations that want to reduce and redistribute risk to other participants in capital markets that are willing to accept it.

The objective of an organisation’s hedging strategy is to try and reduce or eliminate risk associated with market changes to an acceptable level. This strategy is not designed to try and outperform the market. A successful hedging strategy may provide the treasurer or finance official with some certainty with respect to costs or revenues for a limited period of time, perhaps one or more fiscal periods. It generally provides a temporary solution to changes in interest or exchange rates, although sometimes this protection can extend longer. This provides organisational officials with time to find business solutions to help them adjust to major changes to market rates.

The derivatives strategy of an organisation will reflect its objectives, risk tolerance and governance policies. The potential use of derivatives will also be affected by specific issues, such as the organisation’s time horizon for derivatives (for example, whether that accommodates long-term hedging versus short-term hedging), as well as its ability to accurately forecast cash flows, cash requirements and financial markets.

#### 3.7.1.1 Strategy

A variety of risk management strategies have been noted in this chapter. The main strategy approaches to hedging are as follows:
• Not to hedge the exposure.
• Hedge the exposure through business practices.
• Hedge the exposure with a derivative.

If hedging with derivatives, a treasurer must decide on what level of exposure to hedge, as well as what derivatives are acceptable.

Decisions about hedging vary between industries and companies. There are no specific rules about what and how to hedge, though the considerations have been discussed. Ultimately, hedging decisions have to include consideration of the cost. An organisation that hedges absolutely everything will face costs and practicalities that may be prohibitive and that may reduce or eliminate profitability. An organisation could choose not to hedge at all, with a decision to pay or receive the spot or cash price for revenue and expense items. However, the resultant net income for each period would make management appear to be a spectacular failure, success or average for the period, depending on how the markets fared during that particular time period.

In practice, few organisations hedge all known exposures. Organisations typically only hedge a portion of exposures. Hedging less than 100% avoids having hedged too much if some exposures are delayed or don’t materialise, due to a business slowdown for example. Development of a hedge ratio is discussed later in this section. Typically, organisations choose a middle ground, hedging exposures that are of greatest concern and in keeping with the risk tolerance of its owners or stakeholders.

#### 3.7.1.2 Policy

An organisation’s hedging policy provides specific directions regarding appropriate methods for its financial risk management activities. For example, processes in the finance or treasury department will outline how transactions are confirmed and settled, with individual procedures conducted by various individuals.

The policy should specify what, if any, derivative products are acceptable and whether an organisation is permitted to use forwards, futures, swaps, options or a combination of strategies. This policy should also specify whether derivative products can be bought or sold, particularly with respect to options and related derivatives.

In summary, forward contracts and futures are easier and less expensive to engage in than options and so may be favoured by organisations with simpler finance or treasury operations and conservative risk profiles. Options are more expensive in the short term and require closer monitoring.

Sample matters potentially covered by risk-related policy might include:
• Amount to hedge (e.g. benchmark hedge ratio), including percentages for known exposures and forecasted exposures (e.g. over the next 12 months) with a regular review (e.g. annual).
• Authorised types of derivatives (e.g. forwards) and time limits for maturity/expiry.
• Dollar limits for individual transactions (e.g. derivatives) and transactions in aggregate.

• Authorisation to transact, approve and confirm derivatives transactions.

• Compensation for hedging performance (e.g. prohibition of bonuses based on hedge performance).

• Regular review and update to reflect ongoing changes in a company’s business.

• Approval of business transactions creating new exposures (e.g. transactions in foreign currencies or granting of credit).

• Approval of risk management policies (e.g. board of directors).

Illustrative Example 12

A fictional medium-sized but fast-growing gaming software development company in Hong Kong, ASAC Mista Co Ltd, which has HK$2 million in annual global revenues, wants to ensure that its international transactions in multiple currencies are properly protected as part of a comprehensive organisational risk management strategy. This strategy, along with any updates, must ultimately be approved by the company’s board of directors.

One of the key components of ASAC Mista’s risk management strategy involves hedging of its foreign currency transactions through derivatives. However, management does not want the company to exceed certain guidelines so it has established a limit of HK$100,000 per transaction involving futures or forwards contracts, upon the approval of the treasury manager, chief financial officer (CFO) or chief executive officer (CEO). ASAC’s policy does not include swaps or options, which are not currently used by ASAC. All of these transactions must not exceed a one-year time limit for maturity, unless specifically authorised for a longer duration by both the CFO and CEO.

Company policy also prohibits executive compensation, specifically bonuses paid on top of salary, from being linked directly to hedging performance. This is to ensure that there is no conflict of interest between professional decision-making and personal interest.


### 3.7.2 Risk Budgeting
The various financial risks faced by a business are analogous to a portfolio of assets and liabilities. Decisions about hedging specific risks are typically governed by an organisation’s hedging strategy and specific policies, discussed in this chapter.

#### Illustrative Example 13

Most organisations desire to limit potential losses from financial exposures. For example, as you learned earlier in the chapter, Middle Kingdom Airlines Ltd (MKAL) expects to borrow US$25 million in one year’s time to finance a refit on some of its equipment, and it will need funds for approximately one year. MKAL’s treasurer anticipates that rates may rise and the company wants to hedge its exposure to rising interest rates using a forward rate agreement (FRA) to lock in the rate.

By locking in the cost of financing for the year that funding is likely to be required, the company has set its cost of funds. If rates decline, the company will not benefit on the amount covered by the FRA. If rates rise, the company will not be adversely affected for the amount covered by the FRA.

By limiting potential losses arising from higher-than-expected interest rates, MKAL may have the ability to withstand greater fluctuations in other parts of its business. For example, it is also exposed to the cost of aviation fuel, as well as a number of foreign currencies through its operations in 50 countries. Certainty in MKAL’s cost of funds for the refit project may give it some resilience to withstand other financial risks.

### 3.7.3 Hedge Ratio
The benchmark hedge ratio guides the percentage of exposures to hedge. It may vary by currency, for example, if there are differences in the ability to forecast requirements for individual currencies. A forecast with more confidence can drive a higher hedge ratio, while a forecast with lower confidence may drive a lower hedge ratio.

There are no specific rules that determine how much of an organisation’s exposure should be hedged. Many organisations hedge one-half to two-thirds of their exposure and some do not hedge at all. The percentage of their exposure to hedge often depends on a number of factors, such as:

• The risk culture of an organisation, including its risk tolerance;

• Jurisdictional rules on hedge accounting and reporting requirements; and

• Industry norms in the industry/sector in which the organisation competes.

When considering an appropriate hedge ratio, one strategy is to hedge 100% of known or booked exposures, and then halve it for each subsequent year (100%, 50% and 25%).

For example, if known exposures for the current year are EUR1 million, EUR500,000 of forecasted euros would be hedged over the next rolling 12-month period and EUR250,000 would be hedged over the following 12-month period . This declining benchmark hedge ratio for longer forecast periods is justifiable on the assumption that the level of forecast accuracy declines over time, so that one should hedge against the minimum amount of exposure that will almost certainly occur.

#### Illustrative Example 14

MKAL’s approach to hedging is based on historical variability of forecasted versus actual cash flows. For the past several years, the company policy has been to hedge 80% of forecasted cash flows. MKAL’s treasurer is reviewing the company’s approach to hedging, and you have been asked to compare the past few months of forecast against actual cash flows from one of the businesses to see whether the current hedge ratio of 80% remains valid.

Based on a review of MKAL’s January to June results, the forecasted and actual cash flows occurred as shown in the table below for the first half of the year:
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-69.png)
MKAL’s forecast appears to be consistently higher than the actual cash flow, with the difference ranging from 5% to 10% of the forecasted amount. This appears to provide a good level of forecasting accuracy.

As a result, MKAL’s decision to use a benchmark hedge ratio in the range of 80%
to 90%, if it can be presumed that future forecasted cash flows will continue to have a high level of accuracy, appears valid. A hedge ratio of this level would provide a hedge for almost all of the exposure. One consideration may be that if actual cash flows are consistently below forecasted cash flows whether that indicates any change in the business (e.g. slowing). Another consideration might be to extend the analysis for a full year, to see whether any other trends emerge.
### 3.7.4 Macro Hedge
A macro hedge strategy is a portfolio strategy that can be used to mitigate risk from many potential sources – including financial, economic or political events – to the assets held by the company. The term is used in several different ways but often signifies an approach to hedging that does not necessarily focus on individual constituents but rather the exposures as a whole. For many organisations, this is the most practical approach to hedging.

If a risk management strategy considers financial risk over an organisational or portfolio view and potentially over a longer time horizon than the current fiscal period, it could be considered a macro hedge. Also known as dynamic hedging, new hedges are put in place as maturing or expiring ones roll off. In addition, hedges might be closed out and new hedges established.

Management of financial risk should not be a one-time affair. Exposure to risk changes over time with changes in exchange rates, interest rates, commodity prices and the geographic and product mix of the firm. Under a macro hedge strategy, managers should monitor and regularly reassess the firm’s risk management policies, strategies and positions in light of changing market, industry and company conditions. Both financial and real assets (such as commercial real estate) might be considered together.

Engineering a macro-hedging strategy requires significant forecasting skill and expertise, along with access to market trading platforms and wide-ranging data that can be used as a predictor of market trends and events such as the direction of interest rates and the movement of equities, currencies, commodities and other variables, which are expected to materially impact the value of the organisational assets. This type of forecasting is often found in financial institutions.

#### Illustrative Example 15

MKAL’s exposure to interest rate risk arises from long-term borrowings at floating interest rates. Interest rate swaps are used to manage many of the interest rate risks arising from interest-bearing liabilities by currency to maintain an appropriate fixed rate and floating rate exposure.

Some of MKAL’s capital projects involve very specific timing on cash flows and most projects consist of a number of deliverables, such as building construction, capital components and technology. For these projects, MKAL uses a macro approach to hedging. The treasurer assesses the forecasted cash flows associated with its major cash flows and hedges the largest exposures individually. Smaller exposures are grouped together and hedged in aggregate, without managing each one individually.

This approach may result in under-hedging or over-hedging some of MKAL’s exposures. However, the risk of over-hedging or under-hedging is considered to be manageable.

### 3.7.5 Hedge Effectiveness

Perfect matching of an exposure to an instrument intended to mitigate that exposure is not always possible. The change in the fair value of the hedging instrument does not always perfectly offset the change in the value of the hedged item. This difference is called hedge ineffectiveness.

In currency forward contracts, which can be customised for amount and delivery date, there should be a very high level of effectiveness, since an organisation can hedge its specific requirements relatively easily. Hedging interest rates that are not actively traded will be a little more challenging. Hedging some commodity products may be quite challenging, since their price may depend on physical location and quality, and in some cases there may be no actively traded market that properly represents the organisation’s exposure. In all cases, an organisation needs to balance the cost of hedging with the likelihood of the hedge being effective at mitigating risk.

Hedge effectiveness is a hedging issue as well as an accounting issue. As you learned in Module 11, under HKFRS 9, it is required that a hedged item and the hedging instrument maintain an economic offset. If hedge ineffectiveness becomes too large, this could indicate that a hedge relationship is no longer effective and an entity may need to cease applying hedge accounting.

There are several techniques for considering the effectiveness of a hedge under consideration.

Measures of instrument sensitivity can be a useful way to measure potential for risk and hedge effectiveness. For example, a duration strategy provides an estimate of the sensitivity of fixed income securities’ prices to small changes in interest rates. Duration is also sometimes used for assessing gaps between assets and liabilities, because a timing mismatch is a source of interest rate risk. Duration strategy has certain limitations – for example, it works better for small changes in rates.

A hedge may not adequately offset or protect an organisation against its underlying exposure in situations involving a mismatch between the organisation’s exposure and the hedge. A hedging strategy is also limited because not all financial risks can be hedged, and even when hedging does occur the offset to the company’s actual exposure might be imperfect and/ or costly. Several factors must be taken into account when deciding whether to hedge. These include an analysis of the potential costs associated with a hedge compared to potential losses that might occur if the hedge is not undertaken, as well as an assessment of the opportunity costs associated with forgone gains when a hedge is attempted.

Basis risk is a consideration when contracts used to hedge differ from the organisation’s exposure – for example, exposure to an administered borrowing rate (for financing a project) hedged with a euro futures contract.

When considering hedge effectiveness, it is important to exclude the portions of the fair value of a forward contract (or a futures contract) attributable to the cost of carrying or forward differences (i.e. the difference between the spot rate and the forward rate).

In the case of exchange rates, this is an interest rate differential. In the case of commodities, it is usually attributed to financing, storage and insurance costs, while in interest rates, it is a function of the relationship between short- and long-term interest rates (yield curve).

## 3.8 Accounting Implications of Hedging Instruments
Throughout this chapter, we have considered the application of different hedging approaches including adjustments to the way business is conducted, as well as hedging using forwards, futures, options, swaps and credit derivatives. This section covers the implications of the business finance decisions made in the course of managing financial risks. 

Hedging requires an entity to assess the risks it is exposed to and determine the extent to which it should mitigate those exposures by entering into counteracting exposures. To effectively hedge risk exposures, an accountant must understand the major variables that contribute to the value of that exposure, such as interest rates, foreign currency exchange rates and commodity prices.

Entities can choose to maintain their exposures and not to undertake hedging. There may not be enough advantage to undertake hedging, which is not without its cost. As discussed in Section 3.7.1, sometimes the exposures of an entity provide a natural hedge, where one aspect of the business involves exposure to certain risks and another aspect of the business involves a mitigating exposure.

If an entity engages in hedging, it may decide to apply hedge accounting in accordance with HKFRS 9 (or the reporting rules of another country in which it reports). Hedge accounting seeks to replicate the risk mitigation of hedging in the financial statements of the entity by reducing volatility in profit or loss or the statement of financial position.

Hedge accounting, as specified in HKFRS 9, follows a relatively straightforward concept, which is to account for a hedged item (an exposure of the entity) and a hedging instrument (such as a swap) together, and in a similar way, to produce an accounting outcome that reflects the economics of the hedge relationship. If the hedged item and the hedging instrument are perfectly matched, the accounting outcome will reveal the chosen offset of exposure. You may wish to review Module 11, Chapter 13, which covers the accounting treatment of different types of derivatives.

Hedge accounting is voluntary, so even if an entity uses hedging instruments such as derivatives to hedge its exposures from an economic point of view, the entity might accept volatility in profit or loss arising from the hedging instruments. Without applying hedge accounting, all hedging instruments and hedged items would continue to be accounted for separately, as per relevant accounting requirements, discussed in detail in Module 11, Chapter 13.

For short-term hedges, given that hedge accounting can be complex, with documentation requirements and numerous accounting entries for transactions, it may be reasonable to record gains and losses as they occur and use hedge accounting only for longer-term hedges.

The various financial instruments that organisations use in a hedging strategy may result in accounting differences. The accounting treatment depends on the rules in the jurisdiction where the head office or the office responsible for financial reporting is located. If there is a need to report in another country, this could involve a different accounting treatment.

However, in most cases, decisions about hedging are made with economic interests first, and the choice of instrument often depends on it meeting the organisation’s requirements at a reasonable cost. These requirements include the ability to transact an appropriate notional amount on the right underlying asset or benchmark.
### 3.8.1 Forwards

A forward contract sets a rate today for an exchange to take place on a specified date in the future. Forward contracts are traded on currencies, interest rates and commodities. For example, a foreign exchange forward contract is a bilateral agreement to purchase or sell a predetermined amount of currency for a future delivery date. Most forward contracts have a specific delivery date and will mature within one to two years, although there is no theoretical maximum maturity date.

Forward exchange contracts are the most frequently used form of hedging, for two reasons. First, they are very inexpensive, having a modest transactional cost usually built into the price. Second, they are an over-the-counter product and so can be precisely tailored to a company’s individual needs. However, they also lock a company into the forward rate, providing no opportunity to participate in future favourable price movements. Finally, unlike futures contracts that trade on an exchange, there is typically no requirement for margin or cash flows until the forward maturity date.

It is rare for a hedging instrument to perfectly match all risks associated with a hedged item. To avoid causing ineffectiveness resulting from changes in the time value of money, under HKFRS 9 an entity can remove changes in the forward rates that would otherwise affect the valuation of forward contracts such that only movements in spot rates are hedged.

A forward rate agreement (FRA) might be used to hedge an exposure such as bank borrowing, based on a different benchmark rate. Because the benchmarks are economically related, a relationship can be established between the two benchmarks. For example, one benchmark might typically be about 10 basis points higher than the other benchmark. As a result, it may be necessary to use different quantities of the FRA against the exposure of the hedged item, in order to maintain an effective hedge relationship from an accounting perspective. It would also need to be considered against the economic (risk mitigation) impacts of adjusting the FRA notional amount.

![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-70.png)
### 3.8.2 Futures
Futures contracts are contracts for the future delivery of assets such as securities, foreign currencies, interest cash flows or commodities. Organisations use these contracts to reduce, or hedge risk exposure caused by fluctuation in factors such as foreign exchange rates or commodity prices.

A futures margin is a small deposit used to control a larger position in the futures contract. It is a performance bond that helps to ensure the performance of both the futures buyer and seller. Exchanges determine a minimum margin, depending on the contract size and type of position. Exchange members (brokers) may require an additional margin.

Futures contracts are re-priced on a daily basis and each margin account is debited or credited with the day’s losses or gains. When the market value of a futures position declines, an additional margin may be required. Failure to respond to a margin call may result in the position being closed out at the expense of the account holder. The gain or loss pertaining to a futures contract is realised daily throughout the life of the contract, through adjustments to the margin account, whereas the gain or loss on a forward is typically realised at maturity.

Margin is designed to absorb potential subsequent losses on the open futures position. The amount of margin required depends on exchange rules and whether the position is hedging or speculative. Margin rules may change based on the futures exchange’s perceptions of risk. Failure to respond to a margin call may lead the broker to close out the futures position by offsetting the contracts outstanding at the account holder’s cost.

Exhibit 3.6 summarises the advantages and disadvantages of futures contracts.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-71.png)
When futures contracts are first entered into, they typically have zero fair value because the forward price at that time and the futures price are equal. Futures markets are liquid and contracts are transacted at market value. With futures contracts, the fair value movement of the futures contracts are recognised.

If the hedged item is already subsequently measured at fair value through profit or loss, an entity will often forgo applying fair value hedge accounting (because both the hedging instrument and the proposed hedged item are already subsequently measured at fair value through profit or loss). If the hedged item and the futures contract are already subsequently measured at fair value through profit or loss, foregoing fair value hedge accounting saves the entity the effort of preparing hedge documentation and disclosures.

As you learned in Module 11, Chapter 13, the hedging instrument and the hedged item are economically related if their respective fair values generally move in opposite directions in response to the same hedged risk, but the hedged item and the hedging instrument may not share the same variable. As long as the two variables are economically linked, and they generally move similarly in response to the same market movement, they are economically related and meet the qualifying criteria for hedge accounting.

#### Illustrative Example 17

Middle Kingdom Airlines Ltd, based in Hong Kong, is exposed to the price of aviation fuel, which in turn is related to crude oil prices. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude or Brent Sea crude prices may be used as benchmarks in more refined fuels, such as aviation fuel. WTI is a widely tracked benchmark with alternatives for hedging using derivatives. Even if a hedged item, such as the requirement for fuel, is based on Brent Sea crude and hedged with a futures contract based on WTI, this relationship does not necessarily fail the economic relationship test, from an accounting perspective. This is because the price of Brent and WTI are still expected to move in the same general direction.

However, the company considering hedging crude oil with futures contracts may find there are differences in delivery specifications between Hong Kong (where the crude oil requirements are) and New York (one of the hubs where crude oil futures contracts are actively traded). These differences may make the hedge less effective than if it were identical to the exposure. With financial futures, such as currency or interest rate futures, the hedge will likely match the exposure more closely (other than quantity) because the underlying financial assets are similar or identical.
### 3.8.3 Swaps
A swap is a derivative instrument in which there is an exchange of one stream of cash flows for another. The exchange may be notional or actual. Currency swaps are contractual agreements between two parties that provide for an exchange of currencies. The advantage of swaps is that they provide organisations with flexibility in their financing choices by allowing them to transform the nature of their obligations at low cost without repurchasing or renegotiating those obligations. Swaps trade primarily in the over-the-counter market between large financial institutions and with customers.
The decision-making process in hedging supports the reasons for undertaking the hedge. There are many considerations besides financial and reporting requirements. For example, a swap may fit an organisation’s hedging requirements because it is customised to offset the hedger’s exposures to borrowing and the cost of funds, thus enabling the original debt relationship to be maintained. For example, a swap can be entered into with a bank, while maintaining the existing debt with the original lenders.

Swap transactions are common components of fair value hedge relationships. Common fair value hedge relationships involving swaps include converting a fixed rate liability into a floating rate liability using an interest rate swap, perhaps because the entity is able to obtain better variable interest rates due to changes in the market. Another example is the conversion of a floating rate instrument using a benchmark rate such as bank prime to another benchmark such as the Hong Kong Interbank Offer Rate (HIBOR) using an interest rate swap.

Common to all fair value hedges is that they do not eliminate cash flow volatility. Instead, they either create cash flow volatility or maintain it, but referenced to a different variable.

The definition of a derivative illustrates that there is typically little or no initial net investment. Any net investment upfront would be minor in comparison to the exposure the entity obtains from entering into that derivative contract. For example, on an interest rate swap an entity might agree to exchange fixed interest payments with floating interest payments on a notional amount of HK$5 million. On day one, the obligation to pay fixed interest payments to the counterparty is equal to, and the opposite of, the right to receive floating interest payments from the same counterparty (in other words, the derivative is ‘at market’). However, over time the fair value of the pay-fixed leg will vary in comparison to market rates. That variance will be multiplied by the notional amount of the contract. Therefore, a 1% move in interest rates could have a HK$50,000 impact on profit or loss.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-72.png)
#### Illustrative Example 18 (tbc)

Belvue Limited entered into an interest rate swap, paying a floating rate in exchange for receiving a fixed rate, in combination with a loan. As a result of the interest rate swap, Belvue introduced the fair value volatility of the swap onto its statement of financial position, as follows.

Belvue currently has a loan paying 6% fixed interest on a borrowed amount of HK$5 million for a remaining term of three years. If Belvue were to borrow that same amount in the current market it would be able to negotiate an interest rate of 4% and Belvue thinks those market rates are likely to decrease further. Instead of renegotiating its loan with the bank, Belvue decides to enter into an interest rate swap with another bank whereby it pays that bank a floating rate of interest in exchange for receiving a fixed rate of interest equal to the amount Belvue pays its lender.

In combination with the fixed interest payments on the loan, Belvue would ultimately be exposed to a variable rate of interest. On entering the contract, the present value of the remaining interest cash flows is HK$832,527 (this would become the ‘receive leg’ on the derivative from Belvue’s perspective). To ensure the derivative is ‘at-market’ on this day, the counterparty computes a variable rate of interest that would apply to the ‘pay leg’ to ensure the net present value of the derivative is zero. Using software, the counterparty determines this rate to be 6.26% (the market rate of 4% plus a rate specific to Belvue of
### 3.8.4 Options
Options can be used to reduce risks associated with commodity prices, interest rates, foreign exchange rates and equity prices. The use of options for hedging has economic as well as accounting implications. As discussed earlier in this chapter, a purchased option involves the payment of an option premium, while the sale of an option generates an option premium.

In the decision-making process in hedging, options have an advantage over forwards and futures contracts in that they allow a buyer to exercise an option or let it lapse, thereby allowing a treasurer to take advantage of favourable price movements without being limited by a forward or futures price. Against this major benefit is perhaps the biggest problem with a cost of premium imposed by the option seller. The time value component of an option premium declines as expiry approaches, and more rapidly just prior to expiry unless there is a chance of the option being in-the-money prior to expiry.

In practice, treasurers tend to buy options that are relatively far out of the money, since these options are less expensive, but doing so means that they retain some market risk, since the probability of the out of the money option being exercisable is small, even if the market moves substantially. Because of the premium, options appear to be the most expensive alternative; however, one must also factor in the opportunity cost of using forward exchange contracts or currency futures where one cannot take advantage of favourable price swings. Options also require closer monitoring than other strategies, since one must judge exactly when to exercise them.

Options are available from both exchanges and the over-the-counter market. An organisation can therefore source an appropriate option from standardised exchange-traded options or more customised over-the-counter options.

With respect to options, there are exceptions to all fair value through profit or loss for financial instruments qualifying as a hedging instrument. Written options, unless the written option is designated in a hedge relationship, is used to offset a purchased option and the combination of the two is not a net written option.

For example, an option writer provides the option purchaser the right to sell (put) a liability back to the option writer. The writer will receive an option premium for writing the option but is otherwise exposed to potentially unlimited losses because the purchaser can put the liability back to the option writer at the option holder’s discretion, regardless of the market value of the liability. The option writer will be obligated to assume the liability, regardless of the cost to the option writer. Therefore, a written option (or net written option) increases an entity’s risk as opposed to reducing it. This is why written options (or net written options) are prohibited from qualifying as hedging instruments.

As a result, the use of an option-based strategy such as a foreign exchange collar has accounting implications. A combination of a written option and a purchased option will be considered a net written option (and not quality for designation) if the entity receives a net premium and if, except for the strike price, the critical terms of the options are not the same or the notional of the written option is greater than the purchased option.
![](Study/QP/new%20LP/Doc/DraggedImage-73.png)
#### Illustrative Example 19

To see how the value of an option is derived from the value of an underlying asset, consider an individual who owns an option to buy one share of company XYZ’s stock for HK$50 per share. Today is the option’s expiry date and if that option is not exercised today, it will expire as worthless.

If the price of company XYZ’s stock is less than HK$50 per share, it does not make sense to exercise that option. Similarly, if the stock price is exactly HK$50, there is no benefit to be had from exercising that option. However, if the price is above HK$50, there will be a benefit from exercising the option.

The value of the option at expiry would be the difference between the market price of company XYZ stock and the exercise price of the option. For example, if the XYZ stock is trading for HK$80 per share in the market, then the option is worth HK$30 (HK$80 stock price − HK$50 exercise price = HK$30) to the option holder. This value is known as intrinsic value. If the option had additional time left until expiry, it may have additional value (time value) and the option’s value might be greater than HK$30.
### 3.8.5 Credit Derivatives
Credit derivatives are contractual agreements on credit performance. They permit banks, pension funds and others to manage their credit risks. The most common credit derivative is a credit default swap (CDS). With a CDS, a protection buyer pays a protection seller a periodic fee to cover a specified period of time for assuming the credit exposure of an underlying asset (reference entity). The protection seller makes payments to the protection buyer if a specified credit event occurs. If that happens, the protection seller pays the protection buyer.

That payment is linked to the decline in the market value of the reference entity, which can be almost any asset or index, but is usually a corporate bond, from the credit event. Credit events are defined in the CDS contract. Such events typically include bankruptcy, a material default or a debt restructuring of the reference entity. A CDS thus acts as a form of insurance against credit risk for the protection buyer.

Credit derivatives markets reflect the assessment of risk by market participants. As a result, prices of transactions between relatively sophisticated participants, such as transactions involving credit default swaps, may provide insight into the market’s assessment of an issuer’s riskiness and serve as a useful addition to other credit risk measures.

Credit derivatives tend to be used by larger organisations and the decision-making process for their use is not only financial. There may be legal and sovereign (country) considerations, and definitions within the legal framework are important. Since most credit derivatives are customised, the attributes can be tailored for the specific risks faced by the organisation.

As discussed in Module 11, Chapter 13, in detail, from an accounting perspective, hedging instruments such as credit derivatives are designated into relationships to manage risks arising on hedged items. In order to do so, the risk component must be reliably measurable. An example of a reliably measurable risk component for credit derivatives might include a market quoted credit risk index that is related to the credit derivative under consideration.

## Summary
• Major types of financial risk include interest rate risk, foreign exchange risk, commodity price risk, liquidity risk and capital risk.

• Asset-liability management involves the matching of assets and liabilities so that interest rate exposure is minimised, thereby reducing the potential adverse impact on the organisation.

• A forward rate agreement (FRA) is an over-the-counter agreement between two parties, to lock in an interest rate for a **short period** of time. The FRA provides interest rate protection against changes in rates as measured by the reference rate specified in the contract.

• Interest rate swaps, which are similar to a long-term portfolio of FRAs, may be a strategy especially suited for managing a company’s **longer-term exposure** arising from longer projects.

• The two basic types of options available to mitigate risk are puts and calls. A put option on interest rates provides protection to the option buyer from **declining** rates, as defined by the reference rate. A call option on interest rates provides protection to the option buyer from **rising** rates as defined by the reference rate.

• Foreign exchange forwards, futures, swaps and options can be used to reduce foreign exchange risk. Hedging can reduce the adverse consequences of currency risk.

• Forwards and futures contracts allow an organisation to lock in a rate or price for future delivery.

• Forward transactions can fully eliminate risk by locking in at present the price or rate at which a transaction will be made in the future.

• A currency future is similar to a forward exchange contract, except that it trades on an exchange. Each contract has a standardised size, expiry date and settlement rules.

• Option buyers pay an option premium for risk reduction, while option sellers receive an option premium and take on an obligation under the contract.

• Swaps permit the exchange of cash flows, currencies or commodity prices and can be used to refine risk to an acceptable level or change from a fixed rate to floating (or vice versa).

• The Basel Accords represent an agreement between central banks of major countries to develop consistent minimum standards for banking institutions in those countries. The introduction of capital adequacy requirements was a major milestone in financial risk management.

• Derivatives are contractual agreements, with their underlying value dependent on or derived from a reference asset or rate. They act as a risk transfer mechanism from an organisation that wants to reduce risk and redistribute it to other participants in the capital markets willing to accept it.

• Economic and accounting considerations are not only financial but also qualitative factors, such as the ability to customise the hedge to fit the exposure.
