## OPENING CASE

MIDDLE KINGDOM AIRLINES

Middle Kingdom Airlines (MKAL), an international airline that is registered and based in Hong Kong, offers scheduled passenger and cargo services to more than 50 countries. You are part of the organisation’s finance department with responsibilities for risk management and hedging.

You first learned about MKAL in Chapter 3, Financial Risk Management. MKAL monitors its liquidity carefully and must ensure it maintains compliance with its lending covenants.

This ensures sufficient liquid funds and adequacy of funding from financial institutions to meet MKAL’s liquidity requirements over both the short term and long term. As a member of MKAL’s finance department, treasury activities are important components of your work.

Because of the nature of its business, MKAL is exposed to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates, interest rates and jet fuel prices. These exposures are managed by the finance department, in accordance with corporate board policies.

## OVERVIEW

This chapter introduces the key activities of treasury, including its operations and important external relationships, as well as a look at some of the changes as a result of the internationalisation of the Chinese renminbi.

In a small company, treasury responsibilities are handled by the accounting or the finance department, but as a company grows the need for specialised treasury services increases.

In a larger company, which will often also be multinational, treasury services are more likely to be required to make strategic decisions for activities such as consolidating and managing multiple bank accounts, cash and working capital management, internal funds transfer pricing transactions, investment management, interest rate management and foreign exchange exposure, among other key activities.

An organisation’s treasury professionals participate with key financial community members, including bankers, regulators, insurers, rating agencies and investors. These relationships are important because they benefit the organisation as a whole.

Finally, the internationalisation of the Chinese renminbi has major implications for treasury and business generally. Hong Kong is a major financial centre in Asia with a significant reliance on financial services. It stands to benefit from the changes that are occurring in China as well as in Asia more broadly.

## 4.1 TREASURY OPERATIONS

Smaller organisations and those with less complex finance requirements may manage their responsibilities through either the accounting department or the finance department. Such a structure works well with limited bank accounts, relatively straightforward foreign exchange requirements and little requirement for specialised market or investment knowledge.

Typically, larger organisations have greater requirements for treasury expertise. A larger company will often also be multinational or a large conglomerate, necessitating treasury services in multiple facets of its operations. This will include activities such as consolidating and managing multiple bank accounts, cash and working capital management, internal funds transfer pricing transactions, investment management, interest rate management and foreign exchange management, among other key activities.

Treasury is also actively involved in the financial stewardship of an organisation’s assets, including risk management activities – a role that is closely associated with corporate governance. Treasury also functions to execute the strategic decisions of management and the board of directors, on behalf of the organisation’s stakeholders. The management of treasury involves strategic decisions that impact how an organisation will achieve its objectives.

Organisations that do not have adequate financial management are at a disadvantage by virtue of having to compete in an aggressive global economy without the necessary proficiencies. Within this global context, the management of corporations has become increasingly transparent, and shareholders and stakeholders demand adequate financial accountability.

For the many companies that have global activities, competitors may be international and equipped with a different set of economic circumstances that are available to them. Although organisations can generally control risk factors that are internal, it is impossible for them to control the many external factors that impact their international business activities. A profitable company can be quickly and adversely impacted by changes in exchange rates, interest rates and commodity prices. As a result, it is important to manage treasury and the inherent risks and opportunities that it faces appropriately.

Just as all parts of an organisation typically affect treasury, either directly or indirectly, the efficient and effective functioning of treasury also provides implicit benefits throughout an organisation. For example, the organisation may, as a result, benefit from access to a lower cost of funds, debt optimisation, control of risk, increased liquidity and the benefit of strategic financial planning expertise.

Most organisations undertake some treasury activities within finance or accounting. Not every organisation is large enough to have a dedicated treasury. This chapter looks at the activities and relationships that might be undertaken or managed by an organisation’s treasury. It is helpful if you think of the roles themselves, rather than where in an organisation the treasury activities are undertaken.

### 4.1.1 Key Objectives

Managing availability of cash is usually a key objective for almost any organisation, but it is far from being the only key objective. The more complex the organisation, the more activities there are that may fall within the scope of treasury.

The role of treasury involves ultimately ensuring that a company has sufficient cash available at all times to meet the needs of its primary business operations. However, its responsibilities range well beyond that single goal. It also has significant responsibilities in the following areas:

• Funding. Treasury’s role includes ensuring critical funding is available, which usually involves building and developing relationships with the investment and financial communities. The sell side includes intermediaries that help debt issues and equities get to the market, such as investment banks and brokers. In exchange for fees, they provide introductions and relationships to potential investors on the buy side. The buy side includes institutional investors, such as hedge funds and pension funds, which are potential buyers of new issues. Treasury’s relationships with investors is discussed in more detail later in this chapter.

• Investments. The investment of organisational funds typically falls to treasury. Such investments often involve short-term or excess operating funds for which security of funds and maintaining adequate liquidity for upcoming cash requirements are the main objectives.

• Financial risk management. Treasury develops financial risk management strategies and implements hedging tactics in adherence to policies in order to mitigate or manage the company’s financial risks. Interest rates on debt obligations may vary directly with market rates, which present a problem if market rates are rising. Foreign exchange positions could also be at risk if exchange rates suddenly worsen. The topic of financial risk management is addressed in more detail in Chapter 3, Financial Risk Management.

• Cash management. Treasury staff use the information obtained from cash forecasting and working capital management activities to ensure that sufficient cash is available for operational needs. The efficiency of this area is significantly improved by the use of technology, both at the organisation level and the bank level, which is discussed in more detail in Chapter 5.

• Cash forecasting. Treasury’s role in cash forecasting is the creation of forecasts, including both short-term and long-term forecasts, of cash flows from disparate sources including operating groups and subsidiaries, as well as from accounting and tax. Forecasts are used for determining optimal maturity dates for short-term investments or issuing debt, for example. Most organisations with multiple currencies may also forecast by currency to assist with hedging. The topic of cash forecasting is covered in more detail in Chapter 5.

• Managing working capital. Managing working capital includes the treasury’s role in the oversight of changes and trends in current assets and current liabilities and providing guidance as needed. Working capital may change as a result of changes in customer credit policy or revenue growth. Working capital management is addressed in more detail in Chapter 6, Working Capital Management.

• Credit ratings. When a company issues marketable debt or other securities, a credit rating will likely be sought as a part of that process. The company’s financial condition will be reviewed and a credit rating assigned. The treasury liaises with the credit rating agency and responds to information requests from the credit review team, providing additional information over time. The treasury’s relationships with ratings agencies topic is addressed later in this chapter.

• Bank relationships. The relationships with banks and other financial institutions represents a key component of the treasury’s activities. These relationships encompass the organisation’s financial and operating results, availability of credit, fees for products and services and other related issues that may arise. In addition, specialised bank expertise for foreign exchange hedging, debt issuance, payments, cash management services and others can also affect the relationship. The subject of the treasury’s relationships with bankers is addressed later in this chapter.

• Credit policies. The granting of credit to customers may be within the responsibilities of the treasury department. Alternatively, it may be handled by accounting or it may be a specialised internal function. If treasury is not involved in granting credit, it may have an advisory role in developing credit granting policies. It is useful for treasury to provide input to credit policy, if not to directly manage it, since it gives treasury some control over the amount of working capital (and its associated risk) held in accounts receivable. This topic is addressed in more detail in Chapter 6.

• Corporate finance. If a company engages in corporate finance activities such as acquisitions or mergers on a regular basis, then treasury may have expertise in some facets of these acquisitions, such as components of due diligence or integration of treasury systems. Expertise in the integration of treasury systems from acquired companies into those of the acquirer helps to manage the many risks associated with complex transactions. In larger organisations, this may include a core of acquisition integration and IT experts. This topic is addressed in more detail in Chapter 11, Business Combinations.

• Insurance. Another activity is the maintenance of many types of insurance on behalf of the company. This responsibility may be given to treasury because it fits within risk management activities. Treasury’s management of insurance, particularly if it is on behalf of the group, represents a further centralisation of risk management activities and this may result in the development of a level of insurance expertise in treasury. The treasury’s relationships with insurers topic is discussed in more detail later in this chapter.

• Management advice. Treasury staff monitor market conditions constantly and therefore treasury is an excellent in-house resource for management should they need information about interest rates that the company is likely to pay on new debt offerings, the availability of debt financing or probable terms that equity investors will want in exchange for a new offering.

From the preceding discussion, it is clear that treasury’s traditional goal of maintaining cash availability has been superseded by a wide range of activities in investing, debt issuance, risk management, working capital management, as well as taking the lead role in dealing with banks and credit rating agencies. Treasury occupies a central, if sometimes underappreciated, role in the finances of large or complex organisations.

As an organisation grows beyond its domestic market and becomes multinational in scope, it must develop a financial control system that is capable of managing its international transactions and the currency risk exposures of its operating units, as well as managing those functions for the corporation as a whole. The treasury function of the multinational corporation fulfils this role. It serves as a corporate bank that manages cash flows within the corporation and also between the corporation and its external partners.

Treasury operates as a financial clearinghouse for other parts of an organisation. In large companies, an international or regional treasury may provide specific services to its corporate group anywhere in the world. Treasury performs several functions that are pertinent to both domestic and international operations, including:

• Determining the organisation’s overall financial goals and financial strategy.
• Managing domestic and international trade.
• Financing domestic and international trade.
• Consolidating and managing the financial flows of the organisation.
• Identifying, measuring and managing the organisation’s exposures to financial price risks, particularly its currency risk exposures.

Treasury is responsible for establishing policies and procedures to cover the proper internal coordination between the organisation’s various operating divisions, as well as coordinating the organisation’s interactions with its various external stakeholders, including customers, suppliers, investors and governments in venues where it does business. The treasury function is unique within an organisation. It may act as a cost centre, providing services to other parts of the organisation, or it may be a profit centre, operating on behalf of different parts of the organisation and charging them for services.

#### 4.1.1.1 Governance

Management and the board play a vital role in the development of an appropriate set of written financial and risk management policies – as formal documents – to guide treasury activities. Management typically develops treasury policies, while the board of directors has responsibility for their approval. Once policies for management and staff have been developed, specific strategies can be generated that are acceptable to the organisation and are consistent with the policies.

The board of directors of an organisation is responsible for the oversight of its management, which requires a lot of knowledge and understanding about the implications of prospective transactions amidst complex financial products, a strict and changing regulatory environment and global competition. One of the challenges of an organisation is to ensure that the board has enough specific knowledge and understanding about the salient risks and issues that an organisation faces in order to participate in decision making at a strategic level.

Treasury’s role in the stewardship of assets is closely associated with corporate governance. Treasury functions to execute the strategic decisions of management and the board of directors, on behalf of the stakeholders of an organisation. The governance structure helps to determine whether the strategic goals of an organisation are carried out through the organisation’s policies, processes and procedures.

#### 4.1.1.2 Treasury Risk

An organisation’s approach to treasury and risk management should be based on the critical metrics that its board of directors, management and shareholders determine are appropriate for the organisation, including the financial strategies that are relevant to the organisation’s business, funding or tax situation. The following factors should be thoroughly understood:

• Financial risks, including market risks, credit risks and operational risks, that are being taken by the organisation in the course of business.
• Operational controls in place to protect the organisation against fraud and theft, including payment fraud.
• Acceptable financial instruments and strategies for managing financial risks.
• Risks associated with any financial instruments or strategies.
• Risks associated with working capital strategies.
• Risk measurement methodologies and their relationship to corporate policy.
• The implications associated with acceptable exposure, risk or loss limits.
• Recognition that it might not be possible to quantify potential losses with certainty.
• Financial results, as reported and why.
• Risks related to the organisation’s funding structure, including relationships with key debtors and creditors.

Financial risk management was discussed in Chapter 3. The next section covers some of the operational and strategic considerations in treasury management.

### 4.1.2 Approaches to Treasury Management

Every treasury operation is somewhat a reflection of the organisation that it serves, and there are various approaches that can be taken towards operationalising the strategies deemed appropriate for a particular organisation. For example, a large government entity may have a very different approach than a multinational organisation operating in dozens of countries.

Treasury typically manages substantial funds in its transactions. Its procedures are critical and time-sensitive, and must be performed precisely. Issues such as whether to outsource treasury operations or certain aspects of treasury operations, such as technology systems used to manage treasury and its transactions, or whether to maintain specific staff in-house and outsource other functions may need to be considered. Treasury may be expected to be a profit centre, generating returns beyond its costs, or alternatively as a cost centre, with the mandate to provide treasury-related services for other parts of the organisation. Appropriate treasury metrics to manage performance must be tailored to an organisation’s requirements, including required reporting and accountability to its stakeholders.

Another key issue involves whether and how much to centralise or decentralise operations. Oversight of the treasury function is easier when this function is highly centralised. Conversely, it is more difficult to monitor when this function is distributed over multiple locations or countries. Treasury activities may involve complex pricing and terminology that is difficult for non-treasury specialists, so there may be real advantages to centralising operations into a small, well-trained group. This section looks at important decisions related to an organisation’s approach to treasury, such as the degree of centralisation of treasury activities.

#### 4.1.2.1 Roles

Treasury professionals have several key roles to fulfill. Especially in a larger organisation, these important responsibilities allow treasury to perform functions akin to that of an ‘internal bank’.

##### Foreign Exchange Exposure Reduction

As you learned in Chapter 3, most organisations are affected directly or indirectly by foreign exchange exposure. Entirely domestic businesses may be affected when the currency of an international competitor (or supplier) weakens (or strengthens).

Foreign exchange exposure arises from many commercial and financial transactions of an organisation. Some exposure reduction techniques are easier to implement in a centralised treasury environment, for example, taking advantage of natural opportunities for hedging including:
• Netting currencies between related companies or operations.
• Changes to purchasing and/or processing.
• Transfer exchange rate risk (e.g. to central treasury).

Currency netting involves aggregating foreign exchange payments and receipts that are made between parts of an organisation, or with outside organisations, to reduce the necessity for external purchase and sale activities.

Potential benefits include a reduction of payments and therefore costs of foreign exchange transactions, wire transfers and delays in accessing funds. Potential disadvantages include lack of control for group members and the methodology used to price and time hedge transactions.

When there is a mismatch between foreign currency assets and liabilities, there is a potential for loss. The risk of debt denominated in a foreign currency may be reduced if the borrower has offsetting assets denominated in the same currency, such as an income-producing subsidiary. A centralised treasury can take advantage of natural hedges between assets and liabilities, thus reducing the risk to the group as a whole.

For example, an organisation with a foreign currency debt is susceptible to foreign exchange rate changes. Without a hedge or natural offset, if the currency of the debt increases in value, the market value of the debt increases. However, if the organisation has adequate revenues in the same foreign currency to make its foreign currency debt payments, the organisation might have a natural hedge. Provided that the foreign currency revenues are anticipated to continue for the term of the debt, the organisation may be able to take advantage of both the foreign currency borrowing and reduction of currency risk on foreign currency sales.

A potentially unknown variable is how customer demand and revenues might change in response to exchange rates. Foreign currency revenues may be sensitive to exchange rates, particularly those that involve major changes. Changes in exchange rates that impact revenues may affect the organisation’s ability to service debt denominated in a foreign currency.

Transferring exchange rate risk from individual business units or operating subsidiaries is another opportunity for managing exchange rate risk. For example, treasury can set an exchange rate that passes that risk on to treasury, especially for small transactions that would be difficult to hedge for the subsidiary. Treasury can aggregate the exposures and set up hedging, if appropriate, on the net balance.

Exposure reduction strategies may be impacted by local legal, tax or reporting considerations, and therefore they require careful consideration prior to implementation.

##### Treasury Policy

Treasury policies are developed specifically by organisations to assist decision-making. Policies cover common treasury activities in large organisations, such as foreign exchange hedging, debt issuance, investing and other similar ones. Treasury activities are conducted in accordance with policy, supervised by senior management, and oversight is provided by the board of directors.

For example, a treasury policy addressing specific aspects of foreign exchange hedging might include:

• Percentage of known exposure to hedge.
• Acceptable hedging instruments.
• Changes to purchasing and/or processing.
• Transfer exchange rate risk (e.g. to central treasury).

Currency netting involves aggregating foreign exchange payments and receipts that are made between parts of an organisation, or with outside organisations, to reduce the necessity for external purchase and sale activities.

Potential benefits include a reduction of payments and therefore costs of foreign exchange transactions, wire transfers and delays in accessing funds. Potential disadvantages include lack of control for group members and the methodology used to price and time hedge transactions.

When there is a mismatch between foreign currency assets and liabilities, there is a potential for loss. The risk of debt denominated in a foreign currency may be reduced if the borrower has offsetting assets denominated in the same currency, such as an income-producing subsidiary. A centralised treasury can take advantage of natural hedges between assets and liabilities, thus reducing the risk to the group as a whole.

For example, an organisation with a foreign currency debt is susceptible to foreign exchange rate changes. Without a hedge or natural offset, if the currency of the debt increases in value, the market value of the debt increases. However, if the organisation has adequate revenues in the same foreign currency to make its foreign currency debt payments, the organisation might have a natural hedge. Provided that the foreign currency revenues are anticipated to continue for the term of the debt, the organisation may be able to take advantage of both the foreign currency borrowing and reduction of currency risk on foreign currency sales.

A potentially unknown variable is how customer demand and revenues might change in response to exchange rates. Foreign currency revenues may be sensitive to exchange rates, particularly those that involve major changes. Changes in exchange rates that impact revenues may affect the organisation’s ability to service debt denominated in a foreign currency.

Transferring exchange rate risk from individual business units or operating subsidiaries is another opportunity for managing exchange rate risk. For example, treasury can set an exchange rate that passes that risk on to treasury, especially for small transactions that would be difficult to hedge for the subsidiary. Treasury can aggregate the exposures and set up hedging, if appropriate, on the net balance.

Exposure reduction strategies may be impacted by local legal, tax or reporting considerations, and therefore they require careful consideration prior to implementation.

##### Treasury Policy

Treasury policies are developed specifically by organisations to assist decision-making. Policies cover common treasury activities in large organisations, such as foreign exchange hedging, debt issuance, investing and other similar ones. Treasury activities are conducted in accordance with policy, supervised by senior management, and oversight is provided by the board of directors.

For example, a treasury policy addressing specific aspects of foreign exchange hedging might include:
• Percentage of known exposure to hedge.
• Acceptable hedging instruments.
• Authority for foreign exchange hedging decisions.
• Responsibility to approve hedging transactions.
• Controls for separation of duties.
• Minimum quality of bank for transacting foreign exchange hedges.

##### Funds Transfer Pricing

Funds transfer pricing, which requires decisions about how to price internal transactions, is part of the strategy to be determined.

A transfer price is a price that is established within the organisation on an intra-company sale. Transfer prices in most countries need to be set as if they were arm’s length transactions between unrelated parties, even though this transaction is occurring within the company.

A convenient way to determine an arm’s length price for this purpose is to use market prices. However, the corporate treasury has some latitude in setting transfer prices when market prices are not available on transfers of intermediate goods or services.

Transfer pricing decisions undertaken by treasury should be made to benefit the firm as a whole, but are likely to face pressure from individual units within the company that are subject to performance standards and have incentives to maximise their sales prices and to minimise costs. Treasury must ensure fairness throughout the organisation – for example, that the managers of the individual business units are not unjustly penalised or rewarded by transfer prices that diverge from market prices.

A transfer price is a price set on an intra-company sale, for example, from one subsidiary of a company to another subsidiary. While there is often a business purpose for the sale, it is typically governed by local tax rules that may require transfer prices be set as if they were arm’s-length transactions between unrelated parties to prevent an unwarranted shifting of profit from one tax centre to another.

Treasury transfer pricing is a similar concept. It involves treasury facilitating a transaction with subsidiaries or operational groups, with treasury taking the role of an in-house bank. Market prices may be the most convenient for this purpose. The corporate treasury has some latitude in setting transfer prices when market prices are not available on transfers of intermediate goods or services. Treasury policy and corporate guidelines will guide whether a small margin can be added to the price or rate passed along to the subsidiary.

Treasury transfer pricing should benefit treasury and the organisation as a whole. However, individual units are subject to performance standards with incentives to maximise sales revenues and minimise costs. This can create disputes within the organisation if treasury determines transfer prices purely for profitability. Instead, treasury must ensure that individual business units are not unjustly penalised or rewarded by transfer prices that diverge from market prices.

Divisional costs of capital are also a consideration when treasury is involved in financing for a group. Disputes can arise among operating divisions over funding rates and investment hurdle rates. Operational managers typically seek funding rates that optimise projects or initiatives but may have limited involvement with financial markets. Treasury is typically involved in the financial markets daily. As a result, treasury is best situated to set transfer prices such as exchange rates and interest rates.

##### Management Advice

Treasury staff monitor market conditions constantly and can therefore serve as an excellent in-house resource for management should they need information about expected changes in interest rates, exchange rate forecasts or the credit spread that the company is likely to face on new debt offerings. Their relationships on behalf of the company with bankers, ratings agencies and investors can serve the company well in assessing the availability of funding and probable terms that investors will seek in exchange for their investment in the company.

##### Cost Centre Versus Profit Centre

The treasury department has evolved from a simple cost centre within the organisation, seen as generating expenses for personnel and equipment, to a valuable profit centre with the potential capability of generating substantial revenue.

The advent of faster technology has been a big enabler in this evolution, as treasury management works with real-time information to assist with cash management, liquidity, risk management and other key decisions that impact revenues and profitability. Technology in cash and treasury management, including real-time data services, online banking systems, virtual or online banking and the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) global messaging network, among other uses, are covered in more detail in Chapter 5.

##### Illustrative Example 1

After five years of solid but modest financial success, a medium-sized fictional video game production company based in Edinburgh, named HCHW (Scotland) Co Ltd, which makes video games for distribution, has acquired an international competitor from South Africa and has seen its revenue increase by a magnitude of ten. The organisation has also since grown by number of employees and complexity. It has become a major international game producer. The acquisition was possible because of the competitor’s financial difficulties and it has resulted in a more complex business structure and additional debt.

HCHW (Scotland)’s finance team has always maintained treasury activities. However, during its five years of growth as a medium-sized organisation, treasury’s asset-liability management strategy was primarily concerned with hedging variables such as interest rate risk and foreign currency risk, as well as minimising the cost of funding, in order to protect the value of existing investments and to preserve the organisation’s cash flow and liquidity. Thus, treasury was more of a cost centre than a profit centre.

However, with its acquisition of a South African competitor and subsequent growth, HCHW (Scotland)’s emphasis for its treasury department has changed. With more of an international presence in the video game market and additional investments in international currency reflecting the increased size of the organisation, the strategy for its treasury department has shifted to a focus on profitability. Thus, the treasury department has been mandated to become a profit centre in its own right.

---- 
#### 4.1.2.2 Decentralised Treasury

Complete Decentralisation

Individual locations manage their own bank accounts, foreign exchange transactions, customer credit, payables, borrowings and investments. Subsidiaries and operating groups manage their own cash positions. When balances are small, there is little gain from concentrating cash into a single account. A variation of this strategy is to centralise accounts by currency and country (e.g. HK dollars are kept in Hong Kong, while US dollars are kept in the US). This variation creates some efficiencies but also additional record-keeping.

Degrees of Centralisation

In its development, a company may pass through a series of phases where centralisation gradually occurs over time from dispersed to centralised treasury functions. Centralisation is usually a process through several decision points as a company increases the geographic scope and scale of its operations. Some companies move through the phases in reverse, due to divestitures and spinoffs, where previously centralised activities are again handled at the local level.

Transition from complete decentralisation to the introduction of some netting and hedging may be triggered by an event, such as a large foreign exchange loss that could have been prevented by a proper hedge transaction. The transition to centralised investments may arise when the scale of operations has resulted in so many bank accounts that cash is not being effectively pooled and invested. At this stage, it is common to first create local cash pools (pooling cash by country), then to progress to an international cash pool in order to further aggregate cash for investment purposes. The ability to pool cash across countries becomes more restrictive and depends on country rules.

With complete centralisation, there is an integration of accounts receivable and payable portions of working capital into treasury. In many companies, there may be considerable resistance to this loss of independence, on the grounds that working capital should remain under local control. Centralisation typically requires technology support such as the prior installation of an enterprise resources planning system. Thus, even very sophisticated companies may not completely centralise all treasury and working capital activities.

4.1.2.3 Centralised Treasury

Many organisations have centralised their treasury operations, rather than have divisions or subsidiaries each operating their own treasury or finance functions. An organisation with significant worldwide financial exposures may find that centralising its treasury has certain benefits, including streamlining cash management, foreign exchange, commodity sales or purchases and hedging transactions among worldwide members.

Centralised treasury centres are sometimes located in favourable tax environments. There may also be tax issues, such as transfer pricing, as well as tax incentives available from the host country. However, tax is not necessarily the driving factor. Other important considerations include banking services, costs of the local labour market, skills and language, telecommunications infrastructure and ease of accessibility.

When the treasury function is centralised, transactions can be handled in higher volumes by a smaller number of highly skilled staff. Under such conditions, there is generally better management oversight. Internal audit staff can review operations in a single location more easily than if they were scattered throughout multiple locations.

Another advantage for having a centralised treasury function may arise when an organisation uses an enterprise resources planning (ERP) system similarly implemented throughout the company. An ERP system processes all of the transactions used to run all key operations of a company. All of the information required to calculate cash forecasts and foreign exchange positions can potentially be derived from components of the system.

In a situation where the organisation has multiple subsidiaries and each of those subsidiaries uses its own ERP or accounting system, a centralised treasury may provide less of an advantage. It will be necessary to work around those limitations or for treasury to be more decentralised. It may make more sense to assign a small treasury staff to each subsidiary who is an expert in using the local system to extract information.

Having a centralised banking staff can also be advantageous in a situation where an organisation operates in few geographical venues and has relatively few banking relationships. However, if it is dispersed over multiple locations, each with its own banking rules, a decentralised treasury function with expertise in its own respective jurisdiction might be best. Also, the larger the organisation, typically the greater the number of banks and bank accounts.

Given the 24-hour day and far-flung operations, there may be instances where a fully centralised treasury department of a multinational corporation finds it advantageous to use a regional treasury centre to ensure treasury services are available as needed in the vicinity of major organisational subsidiaries. Regional treasury centres are usually located in major financial centres including Hong Kong, Singapore or Tokyo in Asia, Amsterdam or London in Europe and Toronto or New York in North America. The cost of regional treasury centres is substantial and increases with the number of treasury centres.

Moreover, there can be significant costs associated with a centralised treasury, which can make this type of arrangement uneconomical for smaller organisations, unless it is offset by substantial cost savings. Furthermore, many operating subsidiaries may feel they are losing control and independence over their financial transactions and relationships when such transactions are centralised.

The greater the complexity and number of bank relationships, services and bank accounts, the easier it will be for centralisation in one treasury centre. However, when there are operations in many countries, in multiple time zones, and perhaps operations in areas with currency or banking controls, more specialised or local treasury services may be warranted in order to support the operations of the organisation.

The following describe the functions of a centralised treasury.

##### Centralised Netting and Hedging

If large cash balances are languishing in some accounts, or other accounts are incurring overdraft charges, a more centralised approach may be helpful. With centralised netting and hedging, the role of the organisation’s treasury department is to net payments made between its subsidiaries. Treasury must also hedge the organisation’s major risks with respect to interest rates and foreign exchange. The organisation’s local venues maintain responsibility for managing their own investments, borrowings and payables, as well as for customer credit and bank accounts.

##### Centralised Investments

The responsibility of an organisation’s centralised treasury staff also consists of consolidating and managing all, or most of its bank accounts. This includes the tasks of both pooling and investing funds in those accounts. Payables and customer credit management are also still the responsibility of local offices. Treasury centralises cash into a concentration account, using automated services such as sweeps or notional pooling. Treasury also has responsibility for investments, ensuring adherence to the corporate investment policy. Local managers are responsible for disbursements.

##### Centralised Working Capital Management

In addition to prior centralisation, the central treasury staff centralises credit granting and uses a payment factory for centralised payables management that handles all payables for all company subsidiaries. This improves the overall planning for cash outflows. Treasury pools cash into one or more concentration accounts, invest them and manage disbursements.

This structure optimises investment income and gives treasury considerable control over the accounts payable portion of working capital. Due to the costs and infrastructure usually involved, this is typically restricted to large organisations. Cross-border centralisation is more complex and may involve legal and tax restrictions, depending on the countries involved. In this case, companies may centrally manage widely traded currencies, such as euros and US dollars, while allowing regional control over other currencies.

While the most centralised of these strategies appears to be the most efficient approach for cash concentration, it may not be the most cost-effective. An organisation with relatively few subsidiaries and low account balances may not need a central treasury. Doing so to manage cash may add more overheads than will be offset by increased interest income or reduced interest expense.

##### Centralised Cash

Centralising cash management on a group-wide basis is known as cash pooling. Cash pooling is a technique and, although banks offer it as a service, does not require specialised services. This permits a group, such as a treasury, to take responsibility for all the liquidity requirements of its subsidiaries. The debit and credit cash balances of subsidiaries can be aggregated, with some contributing cash balances and some using cash balances, in the same way bank accounts of a single organisation can be aggregated. This creates an internal market for cash, with some subsidiaries acting as lenders and some subsidiaries acting as borrowers. The net result should involve saving bank charges including fees, commissions and interest rate spreads (the difference between the bank’s lending and deposit rates). Cash pooling over multiple subsidiaries captures the bank’s interest rate margin, thus reducing interest expense or increasing interest income for the organisation as a whole.

The benefits of centralising cash go beyond reducing interest expense. Cash pooling also provides a group of subsidiaries or operating units the ability to benefit from financial markets, even those that are relatively small. Their size would typically prohibit smaller operating groups from obtaining wholesale pricing for financing and investments, as compared with the ability of treasury operating on behalf of a group. Cash pooling permits the treasurer to support all of the operating units through the financial markets with economies of scale. The treasurer then organises an internal refinancing of each subsidiary on the same financing terms that the group receives.

Technology provides numerous advantages for cash pooling. Since cash pooling can be operated by banks as services, the logistical and administrative work increases but at a much slower rate than the funds under management or the number of subsidiaries or bank accounts included in the pool. Instead, treasury will typically require more specialised skills and technology to support its operations, including systems, services and data. These topics are discussed in more detail later in Section 4.2 of this chapter, as well as in Chapter 5.

Centralisation has many benefits, but it can result in a reduced ability of individual group members to undertake projects that might be beneficial to the overall success of the organisation. Individual unit managers may fail to optimise liquidity management, local borrowing or customer credit management, for example, therefore missing opportunities to the detriment of the whole. As a result, it may be prudent to consider how local financial or treasury interacts with central treasury and to ensure adequate responsibility is provided to management.

##### Centralised Investment Management

Many organisations manage excess liquidity in the form of cash and short-term assets in the money market, which is the wholesale market for cash, liabilities and short-term fixed income securities. This facilitates both short-term investing of excess cash and short-term funding for borrowers.

Money market investments typically meet the following attributes:

• They have a relatively short term to maturity – typically from overnight (one day) to about a year.

• They are of low-risk, high-credit quality.

• Their liquidity requirements vary depending on the investor; however, the requirement is usually for high liquidity.

Commonly used financial instruments for managing excess short-term cash include bank deposits, certificates of deposit, commercial paper, bankers’ acceptances, treasury bills and other government securities, as well as money market mutual or pooled funds.

For the most part, the money market is a dealer market. Dealers trade among themselves and with customers in a virtual dealer marketplace. Participants in the money market include banks and other financial institutions, governments, fund managers, investment dealers, corporations, insurance companies and central banks.

##### Centralised Foreign Exchange

Depending on its structure, the centralised treasury may undertake passive strategies in addition to netting cash and currency requirements as appropriate. Alternatively, it may provide a more active role, offering services and products in the same way that a financial institution would. In effect, the central treasury can operate as an in-house bank to other parts of the organisation.

Centralised Interest Rate Management

Interest rates drive many financial decisions and changes in rates can impact margins.

One alternative for managing interest rate risk is to organise business activities to minimise sources of interest rate exposure. Residual risks can then be evaluated and managed according to acceptable operational techniques. Centralising cash flows can dramatically reduce interest rate exposure in a large organisation.

Interest rate exposure can be reduced by combining both business exposures and processes. However, various legal, tax or regulatory consequence may arise, particularly when transactions are cross-border or involve foreign currencies. Such considerations may need to be taken into account.

There are various techniques that have been successfully used to reduce an organisation’s interest rate exposure. Global cash netting is one technique. This involves having one part of the organisation act as an in-house cash management bank that provides intercompany lending and borrowing. Another technique is enhancing cash flow management through better payment and collection mechanisms. Both of these techniques can be used by treasury to enhance cash collection and reduce interest rate exposure for a group of companies or a large organisation.

##### Illustrative Example 2

A Hong Kong-based import-export company has subsidiaries in Canada, the United Kingdom and Australia. With multinational netting, the organisation believes it can realise net savings. The Canadian and Australian subsidiaries both sell some of their product line in US dollars and regularly accumulate the US dollars. The US dollars are needed for capital expansion by Hong Kong.

The Hong Kong head office aggregates US dollars from the Canadian and Australian operations, which can be utilised by the group. A surplus of US dollars can be used to create a loan for another part of the business that otherwise would be borrowing from a bank. The contributing subsidiaries are paid a rate of interest commensurate with a US dollar deposit and the internal borrower pays a rate of interest to borrow the funds. The arrangement may be relatively complex depending on the legal and tax issues facing the company for the countries involved.
---- 
##### Illustrative Example 3

MVBC Manufacturing (Vancouver) Ltd is a Canadian-based organisation that has had cash flow and liquidity problems over the past six months. To resolve these issues, the treasury department has introduced several new processes in an effort to improve its cash flow management through enhanced payment and collection mechanisms. These include:

• Implemented faster customer payment schedules to increase the speed with which accounts receivable are collected, reducing the payment period from net 45 days to net 30 days. This policy is also intended to reduce reliance on borrowing and the costs associated with borrowing.

• Set up a mandatory electronic payments system to speed collections and prevent the possibility of lost or held up paper cheques.

• Established new credit terms and policies, including even more strict collection policies for payers who have a record of falling behind on payments, from net 45 days to net 20 days.
---- 
#### Apply and Analyse 1

TPT-HK Electrical Engines Co Ltd is a growing manufacturer of train engines based in Hong Kong. Over the past three years, TPT-HK has significantly expanded its presence through its subsidiaries to 64 countries around the globe, including jurisdictions with both developed and emerging economies. Up until now, TPT-HK has run a decentralised treasury function, but senior financial officials are now being tasked by the company’s board to weigh the potential advantages and potential disadvantages of switching to a centralised treasury management function.

Here are some important factors that TPT-HK management might take into account when deciding whether to centralise its treasury management operations.

• TPT-HK implemented a new enterprise-wide management information system a year and a half ago. This coordinated system produces financial and accounting records directly into decision-making and reporting modules to create its consolidated financial statements.

• TPT-HK operates in countries with varying political and regulatory systems, and in many of those jurisdictions senior managers and executives have cultivated close relationships with both government and banking officials, which has helped the company succeed locally.

• As TPT-HK has expanded in size and geographic presence, the volume of its treasury transactions and the value and complexity of those transactions has increased.

• The treasury department of TPT-HK has, in the past, experienced inefficiencies, including a lack of coordinated information available for making investment and hedging decisions. Those inefficiencies have increased as the organisation’s geographic reach has expanded.

Analyse the factors that senior finance officials need to take into account when making their decision.

##### Analysis

TPT-HK’s financial and treasury officials need to balance the potential reasons in favour of centralisation against the potential disadvantages of switching from a decentralised treasury. Here are some of the factors to be considered on both sides.

Factors that might favour a continuation of the decentralised treasury:

• If TPT-HK’s systems, such as its accounting system or if it has an enterprise resource planning system, are very different across the organisation and do not coordinate well together, then a centralised treasury function could be less advantageous than retaining a decentralised treasury.

Assessment: Since TPT-HK implemented its new, organisation-wide management information system, it is much less efficient for the company to continue with a decentralised treasury function. The technology now supports centralisation of many treasury activities. This factor favours centralisation.

• Is TPT-HK located in any emerging economies that have currency controls in place? If so, maintaining a small local treasury staff in that jurisdiction might be more advantageous than withdrawing personnel in favour of a centralised function. A local staff might be able to better continue cultivating and maintaining strong banking relationships in that country.

Assessment: TPT-HK, through its global reach of operating in 64 countries, works with many different types of government and economic systems. Having authoritative senior local treasury personnel in certain venues, particularly in countries where special currency controls are in place, has been beneficial. Such personnel are in the best position to advise the management on the unique factors required to make a local treasury decision. This factor favours decentralisation.

• Do instant decisions about investments, access to banks, etc., need to be made in multiple time-zones? In that instance, it may be advantageous to have somebody in the TPT-HK’s treasury department who is local and who understands how to deal with the authorities and perhaps with the unique regulatory environment in that jurisdiction. In other words, does the corporate culture support fast decision making by those who are in the field and closest to the situation?

Assessment: Senior TPT-HK treasury managers have, through the years, cultivated good relationships with government entities and with bankers and other financiers in certain locations, and those relationships have helped the organisation’s success in those markets. Therefore, there are concerns that a centralised treasury system with decision makers located elsewhere could erode those ties and the positive influence they bring. This factor favours decentralisation.

• Are the transactions conducted by TPT-HK sufficiently large that they would be better handled in one central location? If the cash account balances are not high, then continuing with a decentralised treasury might be a preferable way of managing overheads.

Assessment: When TPT-HK was smaller and possessed less of a global reach, its transactions were of a relatively modest size. Today however, as TPT has significantly expanded its global presence, along with the size of its treasury transactions and the number of global currencies it works with, a decentralised treasury operation has become less efficient. This factor favours centralisation.

Factors that could possibly favour moving to a centralised treasury function:

• Has TPT-HK lost investment opportunities in the past because potential investment funds were scattered across its subsidiaries in many venues, rather than in one location where a coordinated treasury investment strategy for cash management could be developed and executed?

Assessment: As TPT-HK has grown both in size and in the scale of its transactions in recent months, senior finance and treasury officials have become increasingly concerned that potential investment opportunities are being lost as a result of a lack of coordination and therefore speed in treasury decision making. This factor favours centralisation.

• Will a centralised approach make it less likely that TPT-HK will experience mismatches, and therefore a potential risk for loss, between foreign currency assets and liabilities? If so, having a centralised treasury function can result in overall risk mitigation to the company, with treasury being able to take advantage of natural hedges or offsets between assets and liabilities.

Assessment: TPT-HK’s finance and treasury officials strongly believe that a centralised treasury approach will maximise both investment and hedging opportunities for the organisation because they will be able to assess and analyse information sooner and act faster in making related decisions. This factor favours centralisation.

• Will centralising cash flows materially reduce TPT-HK’s risk of interest rate exposure by combining business exposures and processes, taking into account legal, tax and regulatory impacts, particularly those involving foreign currencies or cross-border transactions?

Assessment: TPT-HK’s recent global expansion has made management cognisant of the multiple legal, tax and regulatory regimes they face in each of the countries in which they do business. Management believes that centralising cash flows best maximises their investment returns, their chances of materially reducing interest rate and foreign currency exposures, and minimises funding costs. This factor favours centralisation.

• Will having a centralised treasury function, by virtue of being able to coordinate a major strategy such as an aggregated hedging programme, be able to prevent TPT-HK from experiencing negative events such as a large foreign exchange loss?

Assessment: TPT-HK officials do not believe that any strategy can completely protect the organisation from experiencing a negative event such as a large foreign exchange loss. However, they believe that having a centralised treasury and the ability to execute a coordinated international strategy, such as an aggregated hedging programme, can reduce the chances of major losses occurring. This factor favours centralisation.

When finance officials at TPT-HK weigh their assessment of each of these factors, with six of the eight favouring a centralised treasury function, they conclude that, on balance, the decentralised treasury approach the organisation has used in the past is no longer appropriate now that its subsidiaries are operating in multiple jurisdictions around the world. They also recognise that the TPT-HK’s treasury department needs to make crucial investment and hedging decisions on large dollar amounts in many international currencies, and those decisions need to be made quickly, with coordinated information.

Management concludes the time is right to centralise TPT-HK’s treasury function.

## 4.2 KEY EXTERNAL RELATIONSHIPS

Treasury’s management of the firm’s cash flows has both an internal and an external dimension. Individual business units transact with other units within the firm as products are moved through the corporate value chain. As discussed in the previous section, treasury may manage transfer payments associated with these intercompany transactions, and treasury is involved in setting or negotiating internal transfer prices on these intra-firm transactions.

Consolidating these operations allows treasury to monitor and forecast the organisation’s need for funds, minimise transaction costs, manage exposures to operating and financial risks and take advantage of financial market opportunities as they arise.

Managing financial relationships with an organisation’s bankers, regulators, insurers, rating agencies and investors is a key function of the multinational treasury (see Exhibit 4.1). On a day-to-day basis, the treasury must manage the firm’s cash management and liquidity. Managing cross-border relationships is more difficult than managing domestic relationships because of cross-border differences in laws, business and accounting conventions, banking, language and political systems. Bank and insurance products are important tools in managing the costs and risks of international business and they may differ by country.

Treasury may also have a role managing internal relations with operating divisions when management advice or transaction recommendations are required. Treasury monitors market conditions and is an excellent internal resource for management for obtaining information about funding trends, availability of debt financing or probable terms that equity investors will demand in exchange for a new offering.
---- 
**Bankers**: A mutually beneficial and transparent relationship between the organisation and its bankers is a critical factor towards achieving access to funding, payments, hedging and cash flow and liquidity management for daily operations.

**Regulators**: A strong relationship with regulators helps to assure authoritative bodies that the organisation is adhering to applicable laws and regulations.

**Insurers**: The relationship with insurers is important because insurance is often a key element of an organisation’s risk mitigation strategy.

**Rating agencies**: For organisations with rated debt, establishing an open and transparent relationship with rating agencies is crucial to maintaining the organisation’s credibility with existing and potential investors.

**Investors**: Building a positive relationship with financial investors, including maintaining open and transparent communication, is an essential element in an organisation’s financial success.
---- 
Treasury’s role is often focused on external issues that involve financial markets, investors, creditors, financial institutions and rating agencies. Given the breadth of these relationships, a wide variety of skills may be developed by the treasury team. As noted previously, treasury monitors markets almost constantly and is a tremendous in-house resource for perspectives such as information about the rates a company is likely to pay for new financing, availability of funding or probable terms that private placement investors will demand. This expertise can be highly beneficial to management in other parts of the organisation.

The following relationships managed by treasury are discussed in the sections to come:

• Bankers that facilitate most financial transactions including funding.

• Regulatory organisations that set reporting accounting requirements, both in Hong Kong and internationally.

• Insurers, which provide an important risk management function.

• Rating agencies that guide investors and issuers.

• Investors, including the institutional investor community.

### 4.2.1 Bankers

Financial institutions such as banks function as financial intermediaries, delivering various financial services and taking care of non-financial activities. Financial institutions may act as principals, buying or selling currencies, debt or investments for or from their own account. They may also act as brokers, in which case a commission for buying or selling may be payable. There are many services offered by banks, and these vary by bank and by country, including:

• Processing receipts and disbursements.
• Debt and equity issuance and advisory services.
• Investments.
• Foreign exchange products and hedging advisory services.
• Hedging products, including derivatives.
• Custodial and trustee services.

Financial institutions provide these varied services through in-house experts, whose skills and relationships are managed by the account manager or relationship manager assigned to an organisation. Although financial institutions often provide informal advice to treasury, their main area of expertise is their own portfolio of products and services. As a result, their understanding of each organisation and its unique attributes may be limited.

Managing an organisation’s banking relationships constitutes a key part of the treasury department’s responsibilities. A large company in particular may deal with multiple banks, so the treasurer may need to manage a number of relationships. The most critical relationship will be with the company’s relationship bank.There may be one or more relationship banks, depending on the extent and geography of the organisation’s business. The treasurer will typically maintain frequent discussions with his or her contacts there.

Bank relationship management is more complex, with a greater number of banks and bank accounts. A large organisation may have hundreds of bank accounts across dozens of banks.

One of the most inefficient activities in bank relations is maintaining up-to-date lists of bank account signatories – that is, authorised signatories for different types of transactions. This is an important organisational control and usually falls to treasury. A bank may require not only a signature card containing the signatures of all signatories but also a board resolution approving the signers. Each bank needs similar information in a different format, so standardising the reporting required by each bank is ideal.

This can be an operational problem for treasury when an organisation has hundreds of bank accounts spread among multiple banks in various jurisdictions and where staff turnover results in an authorisation updating process before trades and transactions can occur.

Some efficiencies have been introduced into this process by banks. However, because the requirements still vary by country and a large organisation may be transacting with many entities, it remains challenging. In a larger treasury, one person may be tasked with managing the bank relationships, with a regular procedure to review and update authorised signatories.

In addition to signatory management, the treasury staff must integrate information from bank accounts into its treasury management system, so that it has immediate access to bank transactional information. These accounts will typically reside in different countries with different banking systems and sometimes there is a lag in the availability of information. Depending on the complexities, it can take weeks or months to go through a detailed integration, which involves establishing communication channels, configuring formats and setting up exchange encryption and signing keys. Systems must also be tested. Monitoring the integration progress, which also involves information technology professionals, is a major ongoing task for an organisation’s treasury staff, particularly in a larger company with a significant number of bank accounts and continuous account activity.

Treasury staff will be familiar with account statements or reporting that is provided at regular, periodic intervals, such as daily and monthly. Account statements itemise critical details, such as the organisation’s transactions with the bank, along with fees for processing transactions and other services provided. This is discussed in more detail in Chapter 5.

The structure of banking in a region provides advantages and disadvantages for treasury. A powerful bank can foster a close relationship with customers, effectively monitor their performance and facilitate growth through activities such as lending, debt issuance and cash management. This is important for smaller and mid-size firms without direct access to the capital markets. Banks provide an information advantage and may be in a better position than broader capital markets to see opportunities, fund risky projects or provide financing in stages over a company’s growth.

As noted earlier, relationships with banks and other financial institutions are a key component of treasury’s activities. These relationships involve an organisation’s financial and operating results, availability of credit, fees for products and services, and other related issues that may arise. In addition, specialised bank expertise for foreign exchange hedging, debt issuance, payments, cash management services and other activities can also deepen the relationship.

Banks offer a wide variety of services, but many of those services are centred on cash management. Global banks are large and usually active in many markets, including wholesale money markets. They undertake activities as a result of their own liquidity management arising from banking business and activities in financial markets. They may be active in trading several segments of the wholesale markets on behalf of their own and customer positions, thus developing clout and expertise in these areas in the process. Regional or smaller financial institutions may be more interested in liquidity and interest rate risk management.

In working capital management, banks are active participants, providing financing through factoring and forfaiting. As a reminder, factoring is the discounted sale of a receivable with a shorter term. Forfaiting is the discounted sale of a receivable with a longer term. Banks provide important funding as well as reduce credit risk for the customer.

This sale of trade or bankers’ acceptances is transacted at a discount to face value, based on the riskiness of the transaction to the bank. Such a transaction is termed discounting, with or without recourse. Discounting with recourse means that the bank does not accept the risk of the buyer not paying when due. The seller could be liable to pay face value if the buyer defaults. Discounting without recourse means that the bank accepts the risk of the buyer not paying when due. As a result, interest rates and fees for discounting without recourse are higher, all else being equal. Letters of credit can be discounted in some countries but not in others. These topics will be covered in more detail in Chapter 6.

In its relationships with its banks, the treasurer should have an excellent knowledge of the debt and loan covenants imposed on the company. There should be frequent communication with its banks regarding any approaching debt or loan covenant violations. A prolonged covenant violation can result in additional covenants, higher fees or an interest rate increase. Lenders may impose fees in response to a covenant breach to improve the rate of return on the loan. If treasury, and in particular the treasurer, spends time cultivating these relationships early on, it is more likely to be granted a waiver of a covenant violation if it is possible.

Another important factor related to debt covenants is the length and depth of a company’s relationship with a lender. Long-term relationships may have unintended benefits. However, if the treasurer dropped a long-term relationship bank in favour of a lower-priced transactional lender and there are later issues, there is not a long history of business to use as a negotiating factor.

Maintaining adequate cash is perhaps the most important objective of treasury.

A discussion of banking relationships with treasury would not be complete without a mention of the importance of cash aggregation services used by many treasuries. Banks offer several cash aggregation services, and these are typically governed by local country laws and bank rules. These techniques are described in more detail in Chapter 5.

Pooling, notional pooling and zero balance accounts are techniques, typically using bank services, to offset cash shortfalls in some accounts with excess cash in other bank accounts. Entities or accounts that require cash can effectively be funded by those with excess cash. Interest is paid or earned on the net amount and, in turn, allocated to the entities or accounts making up the group.

Pooling refers to bank services that aggregate cash from various bank accounts, either on a notional or actual basis, into a main account where funds can be utilised more efficiently. Notional pooling means that subsidiaries’ account balances are not actually transferred, but the group’s bank recalculates credit or debit interest based on the notional balance of the overall entity. Physical pooling means that subsidiaries’ account balances are actually transferred and earn or pay interest accordingly. Zero balancing of a subsidiary bank account transfers the balances into a concentration account each day, managed at the group level with funds physically moved between accounts.

In general, notional techniques may reduce the intercompany transactions (e.g. loans and deposits) that need tracking and recording. As a result, notional techniques may result in a lower cost of administration for treasury. There are restrictions and legal and tax considerations that should be explored for cash aggregation prior to initiation. The term pooling is also used to refer to an organisational strategy where a central treasury acts as an in-house bank to other parts of the organisation.

The centralisation of cash management and the methods used, such as those discussed here, do not depend solely on financial criteria but also on treasury management style (for example, decentralised or centralised), regulatory and tax rules in the relevant countries and the cost of banking services to manage cash more efficiently.

International cash management techniques are the same as those used domestically, provided that services are available. However, the challenges arising with cash pooling are more complex in an international environment. The availability of services and the legal and regulatory considerations will vary by country and these need to be assessed individually.

These techniques are discussed in more detail in Chapter 5.
