The cash flows from the project can be determined after adjusting after-tax income for non-cash depreciation and the net change in working capital. You will explore working capital in more detail in Chapter 6.

## 5.3 SHORT- AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCING

The financing of an organisation involves the management of short-term obligations, such as bank loans, potentially combined with medium-term and long-term financing including debt and equity. The management of short-term and medium-term obligations requires an understanding of the needs of the organisation throughout the year for its borrowing and credit requirements. There are many forms of financing and the financial manager must evaluate the cost of each available type.

In this chapter, we will consider short-term and medium-term financing. Traditional forms of short-term funding include the use of a range of instruments such as bank loans, commercial paper, bankers’ acceptances, trade credit, overdrafts, leasing and credit cards. These approaches have been supplemented with funding techniques directly using accounts receivables and inventory as collateral. Traditional forms of medium-term funding include revolving credit facilities and bank loans, supplemented by some types of bonds. In Chapter 7 you will look at longer-term financing options.

The objective of an organisation’s financial policy is to maximise the value of the firm through its financing choices, given the firm’s investment decisions. Each organisation will need to make decisions about critical items, such as the appropriate mix of debt and equity capital, the maturity structure for its debt, the markets in which capital is denominated and issued and its strategy for financial risk management. The implementation of financial policy will depend on the organisation’s access to capital.

### 5.3.1 Financing Working Capital and Fixed Assets

In order to fully understand the strategies that organisations may choose to finance working capital, it is important to recognise that some working capital needs are short term in nature and that others are longer term. The amount of working capital that an organisation requires tends to fluctuate over time – for example, its volume of sales might tend to rise and fall during different business seasons.

A toy company, for instance, might build up its finished goods inventories in the spring and summer in preparation for shipping its products to retailers in the early fall ahead of the upcoming end-of-year holiday season. In that instance, working capital will remain high throughout the fall as finished goods inventories are sold and converted into accounts receivable. They will then decline in January as receivables are collected. At that point, the seasonal pattern would begin anew, with the same types of fluctuations reflecting seasonal working capital needs.

Typically, an organisation will still have some inventory on hand, even during slow business cycles. Similarly, it will have some cash on hand, in addition to holding some prepaid expenses from customers. There will also be a certain percentage of accounts receivables outstanding. Thus, even during slow times, an organisation will still possess a minimum level of working capital on its accounting records.

In determining its financing decisions, an organisation must balance profitability and risk in reaching a decision on how the funding of current and non-current assets is divided between short-term and medium-term sources of funds. Although there are no rules, short-term financing typically covers up to one or two years, medium-term approximately two to five years, and long-term five years and over. This chapter considers options for short-term and mediumterm financing. Long-term financing is covered in Chapter 7.

There are three basic strategies that a firm can follow to finance its business, presuming that it will need a combination of working capital and fixed assets. Each of those three basic financing strategies might be appropriate at certain intervals in an organisation’s life cycle.

These alternative strategies are:

1. The maturity matching strategy, which matches the expected life of assets with funding maturities. The maturity matching strategy is especially important for the financial services industry. Financial institutions such as banks may match assets with funding maturities in order to meet their liquidity requirements and to manage interest rate exposure. This can also be a key strategy for organisations that require fixed assets (also sometimes referred to as capital assets) – for example, equipment that becomes a long-term asset whose value is amortised over time rather than immediately expensed – that need to be refinanced in the future. If interest rates rise over the interim, initial short-term financing might be insufficient to cover the costs of refinancing when the need arises, perhaps leading to a higher cost of funds and potentially negative economic consequences.

2. The long-term funding strategy, which relies on long-term debt to finance both working capital and fixed assets. A long-term funding strategy might be appropriate to finance, for example, an organisation’s permanent working capital requirements, or to finance its purchase of fixed, or capital assets, among other needs. A longer-term funding strategy might become a higher priority for an organisation later in its business cycle, when its history provides it with more competitive longer-term funding options. It may also be the strategy pursued by organisations with major capital projects or those that are in capital-intensive industries.

3. The short-term funding strategy, which finances an organisation’s seasonal working capital needs, along with some of its permanent working capital and fixed assets through short-term debt. Short-term funding may be an appropriate strategy to meet, for example, an organisation’s seasonal working capital requirements, as well as other needs. A younger company might prioritise short-term financing, particularly if short-term rates are lower than longer-term rates, as its limited organisational history may provide a better opportunity to get competitively priced financing in the shortterm market.

#### 5.3.1.1 Maturity Matching Strategy

Maturity matching strategy uses the principle that the maturity of a liability should match the maturity of the asset that it funds. Short-term assets such as working capital are financed with short-term financing, while longer-term assets such as fixed assets are financed with longer-term financing. In Exhibit 5.4, the wavy line indicates total financing required for seasonal working capital needs and permanent working capital and fixed assets. The wavy line in this illustration slopes upward because of an assumption that the business represented in Exhibit 5.4 is a going concern that will continue to grow over time. As organisations grow, they need additional working capital as well as more long-term productive assets.
![](DraggedImage-85.png)
As shown in Exhibit 5.4, all seasonal working capital needs are funded with short-term borrowing. As the level of sales varies seasonally, short-term borrowing fluctuates with the level of seasonal working capital required.

Long-term financing is used to fund all of an organisation’s permanent working capital and fixed assets. This strategy uses the basic technique of matching asset and liability maturities – where the maturity date of a liability should match the maturity date of the asset it is funding. This serves to reduce the company’s asset financing risk.

#### 5.3.1.2 Long-Term Funding Strategy 
A long-term funding strategy is a conservative strategy where long-term debt and equity are used to fund fixed assets, permanent working capital and transitory working capital. This means that long-term debt is used to finance both working capital and fixed assets, reducing the risk of financing. Exhibit 5.5 illustrates a long-term funding strategy.
![](DraggedImage-86.png)
Using a long-term funding strategy, long-term liabilities and equity are used to fund short-term working capital, longer-term working capital and fixed assets. As a result, funding is provided by longer-term liabilities with some certainty. If there is excess cash as a result of seasonality, it can be invested in short-term securities.

#### 5.3.1.3 Short-Term Funding Strategy 
The short-term funding strategy is more aggressive, since it uses short-term debt to finance all seasonal working capital needs and a portion of permanent working capital and fixed assets. Exhibit 5.6 illustrates a short-term funding strategy.
![](DraggedImage-87.png)
Using a short-term funding strategy, short-term working capital, such as that used for seasonal inventory purchases, plus some of the longer-term working capital and fixed assets, are financed using short-term liabilities. As a result, the organisation is borrowing at generally lower interest rates, thus lowering its costs.

The downside to this strategy is that a portion of an organisation’s long-term assets must be periodically refinanced over their working lives, which can pose a significant refinancing risk because the firm might not be able to obtain new financing when it is required.

### 5.3.2 Short-Term Financing

Temporary cash shortfalls are a part of the operations for many organisations, such as those that are seasonal. In the event of a cash shortfall or a negative balance, such as an overdraft or overdrawn account, the firm may need to arrange funding. There are several potential strategies for doing so. For example, the company could attempt to arrange financing through a loan at bank prime, draw down its existing operating line of credit with a financial institution or negotiate with a lender for short-term borrowing arrangements. It might also have the option of issuing short-term debt such as commercial paper or bankers’ acceptances. Typically, these short-term strategies can be arranged relatively quickly, easily and without significant costs or regulatory obstacles. They also usually involve flexible instruments that can be easily rolled over or repaid, if needed. The availability of short-term financing alternatives depends on local financial institutions as well as a country’s regulators.

A short-term financing strategy relies on short-term debt to finance all seasonal working capital as well as a portion of permanent working capital and fixed assets. The most important types of short-term instruments used in practice are accounts payable, short-term bank loans and commercial paper.

Accounts payable (trade credit) comprise a large portion of the current liabilities of many businesses. Accounts payable are incurred when managers do not pay for purchases with cash on delivery, but instead carry the amount owed as an account payable. Depending on the credit policy of the vendor, this can delay payment for 30 days (or more). Of course, if a company is consistently late paying those invoices, it may lose the privileges of trade credit, so the relationship must be managed with care.

Any discount offered should be considered in the context of the discount’s value. A discount received for early payment reduces the cost of the purchase (and therefore the cost of goods sold), but it also reduces the organisational funds available for other purposes.

### Illustrative Example 4

A firm orders HK$1,000 worth of raw materials daily. Its local supplier extends a 30-day credit policy with no discount for early payment. As a result, the firm will be receiving HK$30,000 financing from this supplier in the form of a trade credit (HK$1,000 × 30 days) for these accounts payable.

#### 5.3.2.1 Lines of Credit

Lines of credit are offered by financial institutions and provide access for borrowers to meet short-term funding requirements up to a maximum amount (credit limit) and term. Lines of credit are common and easy to use.

Lines of credit are either secured (backed by collateral such as accounts receivable) or unsecured (based on the credit quality of the borrower). A revolving line of credit permits the borrower to borrow and repay as needed, subject to the credit limit and any other terms of the line. The interest rate charged on a line of credit is typically a benchmark rate (such as bank prime) plus a spread that represents the borrower’s creditworthiness.

Lines of credit may require payment of a commitment fee to keep the line available, which may be required whether the line is used or not. Unlike a loan, the borrower typically makes interest payments but not payments of principal. Restrictions may prevent a line of credit from having an outstanding balance maintained throughout the year. Organisations that use their line of credit regularly may therefore be required to pay it down in its entirety at least once per year for a minimum specific term, depending on the terms of the agreement. This helps assure the lender that the line of credit is not being used for long-term financing. Changes in policy at the lending financial institution may also cause the line of credit to be cancelled, in which case the organisation may have to find an alternative source of credit.

The line of credit provides relatively easy access to additional credit when it is required, which is preferable to an organisation taking on additional debt (beyond what is currently required) in order to ensure access to funds.

An informal line of credit is an agreement between a borrower and the bank permitting access to credit up to an agreed-upon limit. The applicable interest rate depends on the credit quality of the borrower. For example, assume that a company sets up an informal line of credit with its bank for HK$1,000,000 over two years. This line of credit will permit the company to borrow up to HK$1,000,000 between now and two years hence. If the company borrows HK$200,000 next quarter, its remaining credit limit available (for the remaining term) is HK$800,000 (HK$1,000,000 less HK$200,000 utilised).

Some banks offering lines of credit (or other credit products) may require the borrower to maintain a compensating balance in a bank account. These funds, which need to be held by the bank, add to the cost of the borrowing. When compensating balances are needed to receive or maintain a loan, the opportunity cost of maintaining the balance must be included in calculations of the cost of funds.

A formal line of credit is also known as a revolving credit. Under a revolving credit, the bank has a contractual obligation to lend funds to the organisation up to a preset limit. In exchange, the organisation must pay a yearly fee, which is commonly a percentage of the unused portion of the entire credit line, in addition to the interest expense on the amount borrowed.

### Illustrative Example 5

One of MKAL’s banks requires it to hold a 10% compensating balance against its line of credit. These funds are held in an account that pays no interest. If MKAL borrows HK$100,000 at an 8% stated interest rate, it will have to maintain a compensating balance of HK$10,000 (10% of HK$100,000).

Because MKAL cannot use these funds while a compensating balance, the effective amount borrowed is HK$100,000 − HK$10,000 = HK$90,000. Since the corporation must still pay interest on the entire loan amount of HK$100,000, its interest expense is HK$8,000 (8% on HK$100,000). Thus, the effective cost of the loan is HK$8,000/HK$90,000 = 8.89%.

### Illustrative Example 6

MKAL has a formal credit line of HK$10 million over five years with one of its banks. The interest rate on the loan is 6.00%. Under the agreement, the organisation must pay 75 basis points (0.75%) on the unused amount as its yearly fee.

If MKAL does not borrow under the line of credit during the year, it will pay the bank 0.75% multiplied by HK$10 million or HK$75,000 for each year of the agreement. If MKAL were to borrow $4 million against the credit line immediately, that fee would drop to HK$45,000 (0.75% of the HK$6 million unused portion).

MKAL will also have to pay an annual interest rate of 6.00% on the HK$4 million borrowed (HK$240,000 interest). Therefore, the effective interest rate on that loan for the first year will be equal to HK$285,000 (HK$240,000 interest plus HK$45,000 fee) on HK$4,000,000, i.e. 7.13%.

#### 5.3.2.2 Overdrafts

An overdraft facility on a current account is the business tool for adjusting to unexpected cash shortfalls, to a limit. Given their high interest charges (and often additional fees), they are most appropriate to use infrequently, for example to protect the organisation from an important payment being rejected. Smaller organisations may find they can obtain overdrafts only by posting collateral, making the overdraft more of a secured loan. In many cases, the overdraft facility on a current account is arranged at the time the account is opened and its availability is dependent on the banking system where the account is located.

#### 5.3.2.3 Accounts Receivable

Accounts receivable financing is an important source of funds for small- and medium-sized businesses. Accounts receivable can be financed in two ways. First, an organisation can secure a bank loan by pledging (assigning) its accounts receivable as security, although it retains ownership of the assigned receivables. Should the organisation default on its bank loan payments, this allows the bank to collect through the receivables as they come due to cover any cash shortfall. If there is still an amount owing to the bank after it has collected from the organisation’s assigned receivables, the organisation remains legally responsible to pay the remaining amount owing on its loan.

Second, an organisation can sell its receivables to a factor, being an individual or a financial institution, such as a bank or a business finance company that buys accounts receivable without recourse at a discount. The term ‘without recourse’ means that once the receivables are sold, the factor bears all the risk of collecting the money due from the receivables.

The firm that sells the receivables has no further legal obligation to the factor.

The advantage of selling receivables to a factor is that the organisation gets money from the receivables immediately rather than having to wait to be paid as the receivables come due.

#### 5.3.2.4 Procurement Cards

A procurement card programme, similar to a credit card, can be used for smaller company payments. While the procurement card can be structured as a debit card, where charges are debited directly from the company’s bank account, this does not support a company’s short-term financing efforts, so most are structured as credit cards.

The payer will be billed monthly for those charges by the bank managing the procurement card programme, charging interest on any late payment. The bank will then remit those funds to the payee within a few days.

Procurement cards are an alternative method of payment for an organisation to pay funds to its suppliers because it introduces certain efficiencies and prevents having to go through the lengthy procedure of issuing a purchase order and then matching supplier invoices to receiving documents before effecting payment, which can also be an expensive process.

A signed credit card agreement with an authorised credit card processor is typically required. The company may also need to pay a processing fee for the services provided in the procurement card programme. The specifics will depend on the card provider. Credit card fees depend on the issuer and type of card and spend volumes of an organisation but can be 2% or more. This fee to the credit card processor is much higher than that charged for debit card transactions, where the payor’s bank account is debited directly as a result of the card transaction. Many business-to-business transactions by credit card are limited due to the fees that would be paid by the organisation collecting via credit card, because the fees become substantial for larger transactions. Procurement cards (or purchasing cards) have similarities to credit cards but are often used by organisations because they provide more control over their use, such as the types of charges for which the card can be used.

#### 5.3.2.5 Bankers’ Acceptances

Bankers’ acceptances (BAs) are issues of corporate debt that have been accepted – meaning guaranteed by a bank – which raises their market appeal with investors. BAs are created when a bank lends to a corporation, adding its own guarantee, or acceptance, to become a liability of the financial institution. The newly issued BA is then sold to investors. Although BAs originate as a result of corporate indebtedness, they become classified as bank obligations and trade on the strength of the guaranteeing bank. There are some differences in the use of BAs in different countries around the world.

#### 5.3.2.6 Commercial Paper

Commercial paper is unsecured debt that is issued by a company with a fixed maturity ranging from days to several months. In the US, which is the largest market for commercial paper, the maximum maturity is 270 days. Commercial paper can be used to meet short-term working capital obligations. It is commonly sold at a discount from face value. A company can sell commercial paper directly to institutional investors or through a dealer in exchange for a small commission.

Commercial paper issuance is limited to relatively well-known, high-quality companies rated by one of the major credit rating agencies. As a result, interest rates on commercial paper are usually competitive and relatively low. Credit rating agencies are discussed in more detail later in Section 5.5.4.

Most commercial paper issuers sell this instrument on a regular basis – some even do so daily. They either issue their own commercial paper as a source of funds or purchase the commercial paper of other firms for their short-term investment portfolios, providing liquidity for the organisation. An organisation’s demand for commercial paper financing depends on its need for short-term funds at the time, as well as the commercial paper interest rate relative to other borrowing rates.

Buyers of commercial paper include banks, insurance companies, mutual funds and corporations. Although commercial paper maturities generally extend to 270 days, most issues have a maturity of less than 60 days, and there is trading in the secondary market.

The commercial paper buyer (lender) has no claim on assets of the issuer in the event of default. However, the default rate on commercial paper is low, since a firm of lesser credit quality will generally not be able to borrow in the commercial paper market, especially when market conditions and the economy are weak.

#### 5.3.2.7 Leasing

Under a leasing arrangement, an organisation will pay a leasing company a fixed amount, including principal and interest. In return, the leasing company will purchase a specific asset, such as an automobile, for that organisation.

The leasing option can be an option for organisations that want to ensure some of their assets are unencumbered to serve as collateral for other loans or debt. Because of the potential security provided by the underlying (leased) asset, leasing may be accessible for companies that would otherwise have difficulty obtaining financing.

Aggregating purchases of multiple items under one lease can reduce the documentation burden for the lender and therefore the cost. Multiple existing leases can be repaid and re-leased through a larger single lease, thereby potentially obtaining a slightly lower financing cost. A company is typically obligated to make all payments through the end of a lease term, even if it no longer needs the equipment being leased, although the details depend on the specifics of the lease agreement.


### Apply and Analyse 2

Maintaining cash flow is the lifeblood for any business, and senior management always wants to be able to control the factors that determine its cash flow. For finance officials at MKAL, maintaining cash flow is difficult because airline fuel represents about 40% of the organisation’s expenses, and the cost of airline fuel is subject to multiple complex international political, military and economic factors that are beyond its control.

Let us assume a scenario whereby international political and military threats combine to create a sudden spike of 20% in aviation fuel. There are pros and cons of using three financial strategies – including a line of credit commercial paper, and leasing – to maintain cash flow at a level that operations are not threatened. Describe the pros and cons for each of the financial strategies that senior financial managers at MKAL need to consider.

Analysis

#### Line of Credit

##### Pros

• Administrative ease: MKAL could turn to its financial institution for short-term funding to cover a specific amount and term needed to cover any anticipated shortfall. This could be advantageous in a situation where the events leading to the aviation fuel spike are temporary.

• Interest rates may be relatively low if MKAL has a good working relationship and strong credit history with its financial institution.

• Payment terms tend to be flexible. For example, MKAL could pay the loan down when financial circumstances improve. This once again assumes that the underlying adverse factors causing the spike in aviation fuel prices are temporary.

• In certain situations, the funding might not require collateral, so MKAL would not need to put at risk any of its assets.

##### Cons

• A line of credit beyond a certain amount often needs to be secured with collateral, which would require MKAL to put certain assets at risk if the underlying economic conditions do not improve. This could potentially make its financial situation much worse.

• There may be a commitment fee attached to the line of credit.

• The line of credit may have a time limit at which the entire amount must be paid down entirely, with a further specified period before a new line of credit can be set up. If the underlying financial conditions that caused the increased price in aviation fuel are not resolved by then the line of credit would have only limited effectiveness as a strategy.

#### Commercial Paper 
##### Pros
• Commercial paper is an effective financing strategy in a situation involving a cash shortfall that needs to be bridged in order to meet short-term working capital obligations. This could be a viable strategy for MKAL should aviation fuel costs representing roughly 40% of corporate expenditures soar to new heights due to factors beyond the organisation’s control.
• As commercial paper is unsecured debt, there is no collateral required to obtain this short-term financing.
• The effective interest rate paid for commercial paper can be very low for an organisation with a strong credit rating.

##### Cons
• This form of debt is typically only available for between one to nine months, and more often towards the shorter end of that range. If the economic conditions that caused MKAL to seek short-term financing through commercial paper persist for up to a year or longer, the organisation might need to seek another financing strategy.
• Although commercial paper is usually purchased at a discount from face value, it is a form of debt that MKAL would need to pay an effective interest rate for in order to secure this financing. This could be an added business stress if global conditions keep airline fuel costs high beyond the term of the commercial paper and MKAL cannot find a new equilibrium through ticket prices with its paying customers.

#### Leasing
##### Pros
• Leasing could allow MKAL to borrow a substantive amount, at comparable market rates since its underlying assets, particularly its airline fleet, have a high value. This could cover a cash shortfall caused by markedly higher aviation fuel costs that constitute a significant proportion of its annual expense obligations.
• It may be possible to create a large single lease for multiple existing leases on assets. This could provide an administrative benefit for an organisation like MKAL with a large fleet of high value assets.

##### Cons
• The leasing option could cause MKAL to lose some autonomy over its primary assets, namely its fleet of airplanes.
• This form of financing might create a perception to market analysts and other industry observers that MKAL is experiencing financial difficulty.

### 5.3.3 Medium-Term Financing

The management of medium-term obligations requires an understanding of the borrowing and credit requirements of the organisation throughout the year. While there are many forms of financing, the traditional forms of medium-term funding include revolving credit facilities and bank loans, supplemented by some types of bonds.

#### 5.3.3.1 Revolving Credit Facility

Alternatively, as discussed in the previous section, an organisation can establish a short-term or medium-term revolving credit facility or credit line on which the organisation can draw for financing as required. The firm will only pay a commitment fee on the undrawn amount, as discussed in the previous section.

In addition to the credit spread, a utilisation fee will be added depending on the percentage of credit drawn. If the firm has to finance a specific investment, it will put in a term loan that will be less flexible than the revolving credit facility. Usually, under the term loan, the borrower will not be allowed to re-borrow any repaid amounts.

#### 5.3.3.2 Bank Loans

Bank loans are an important financing tool for many organisations. Depending on the term to maturity, these loans may help meet short-term or medium-term financing. When securing a bank loan, the firm and the bank negotiate the amount, the maturity and the interest rate of that loan, as well as any binding covenants that might be included. After an agreement is reached, both parties sign the debt contract, which is sometimes referred to as a promissory note.

Commercial loans are short-term loans that are relatively easy to set up. They can also be used for medium-term financing. The bank provides funds for the period specified and the interest rate is the bank’s refinancing rate plus a margin negotiated between the two parties. The margin generally ranges from 0.10% to 1.50% per year depending on the borrower’s creditworthiness, since there are no other guarantees.

Another important loan characteristic is whether the loan is secured or unsecured. The loan is secured if the organisation backs it with an asset, called collateral. An unsecured loan is when the lender does not receive any collateral from the borrower. When an organisation borrows over the short term, it will often use current assets like accounts receivable or inventory as collateral, which tends to appeal to lenders, as these types of working capital are generally highly liquid.

When loans are secured with collateral, this should normally provide the borrower with an opportunity to borrow at a lower interest rate, because if the borrower defaults, the lender can simply liquidate the collateral and use the cash generated from that sale to pay off at least part of the loan. The more valuable and liquid the asset pledged as security, the lower the interest rate on the loan.

Although the specifics vary by country and by bank, bank loan documentation typically includes all of the key details of the loan, including the amount, maturity and purpose of funds, how funds will be accessed by the borrower (e.g. one single payment, or on request), the interest rate (and whether it is fixed or floating), the frequency of interest payments, rules for computation of interest and any fees to be paid, reimbursement or amortisation features and any early repayment options. The loan documentation also includes potential guarantees and pledges and any covenants.

Covenants in the loan agreements are chiefly regarding accounting ratios, financial decisions and share ownership to be maintained by the borrower, including:

• Positive covenants – Where the organisation agrees to maintain specified capital or legal structure or ratios.

• Negative covenants – Where the organisation agrees to restrict dividends paid, new debt or specific transactions (e.g. the purchase of its own equities), or to prevent the pledge of specific assets (e.g. negative pledges).

• Pari passu – A clause in which the organisation provides the lender with a benefit from future guarantees it may provide for other loans.

• Cross default – A clause in which the organisation agrees that if it defaults on another lender’s debt, the organisation’s loan becomes due even without a missed payment or breach of its specific covenants.

The agreement can also include a clause allowing banks to cancel the contract under certain scenarios (e.g. a material adverse change, ownership change, market disruption, etc.), and these should be reviewed very carefully as they can be complex both from a legal and a commerical point of view.

#### 5.3.3.3 Bonds

While many bonds are issued with longer-term maturities, a number of issues of medium-term maturity also make their way to market. As a result, these types of bonds can play an important role in financing. This section will cover a few types that may be pertinent to medium-term financing.

A bond is generally issued with a fixed interest rate. The bond indenture document itemises features of the bond issue, some of which are intended to benefit the investor. Restrictions that the company imposes on itself, such as limitations on capital expenditures or dividends, make the bond more attractive to investors. Terms may call for a sinking fund into which the issuer contributes funds periodically, ensuring that there will be cash at the bond’s maturity date to pay off all the bondholders. A conversion feature may allow a bondholder to exchange bonds for stock, but in a way that avoids watering down the ownership percentages of existing shareholders. In rare instances, bonds may be backed by personal guarantees or by a corporate parent.

Other bond features are intended to benefit the issuer. A call feature allows the company to buyback its outstanding bonds at a predetermined price and date, prior to maturity, to take advantage of better refinancing rates, for example. The bondholder may also be positioned last among creditors for repayment in the event of a liquidation, allowing the company to use its assets as collateral for other debt. This may result in the company having to pay a higher interest rate to offset investors’ perceptions of higher risk. The typical bond will have a mix of features that impact investors from both a positive and a negative perspective, depending on its perceived ease of attracting investors, expected future cash flows and the need to reserve assets as collateral for other debt. These features are discussed in more detail in Chapter 7.

Bonds are useful for those organisations large enough to attract investors, since they can be structured to precisely fit a company’s financing needs. A company can issue bonds at times of low interest rates, thereby locking in modest financing costs for a longer period than would normally be possible with other forms of financing. Consequently, bonds can be one of the lowest-cost forms of financing.

Although there are many types of bonds, the following are useful in funding cash shortfalls over the medium-term time horizon:

• Debenture – A bond issued with no collateral, while a subordinated debenture is one that specifies debt that is senior to it (in the case of bankruptcy).
• Real property mortgage bond – A bond backed by company-owned real estate.
• Equipment bond – A bond backed by company-owned equipment.
• General mortgage bond – A bond backed by all company assets.
• Variable rate bond – A bond whose stated interest rate varies with a benchmark indicator such as the bank prime rate. Increases in the benchmark indicator can result in substantial increases in funding costs.

A discussion of additional longer-term bonds is covered in Chapter 7.

## 5.4 TECHNOLOGY IN CASH MANAGEMENT

Although the core of the finance and treasury function remains the safeguarding and provision of financial assets to the rest of the organisation, technology has changed the nature of cash and treasury management. It provides organisations with the ability to electronically extract bank and transaction information, track real-time financial rates and prices, share information between disparate organisations around the globe and automate many routine reporting requirements. This has provided opportunities for treasury to add strategic value to the organisation through the services they provide.

The treasurer is increasingly viewed as a key member of the strategic management team, responsible for focusing on the interrelationship between financial markets and the technical operations of an organisation.

An organisation’s technology infrastructure supports that function and permits the organisation to maintain adequate information and reporting to allow it to make good financial decisions.

Financial and strategic decisions require the support of accurate, timely, secure, consistent, complete and relevant information. Many treasury activities, including cash management, reconciliation, payments and trading activities, as well as the reporting to support these activities, are time sensitive.

Often decisions, such as trading or cash management ones, arise in response to market movements. Other treasury activities, such as capital structure decisions and cultivating a relationship with financial institutions, are less time-sensitive although important strategically. Technology can assist in the analysis required to assess those decisions.

Treasury technology, no matter how effective the systems are, does not serve as a substitute for proactive risk management and due diligence. A contravention of organisational policy can still occur if the organisation is not on alert, and intentional circumvention can also occur.

Common treasury technologies include cash flow forecasting and risk management, real-time and historical data and analytical services, historical price and volume data and links to bank and other partner systems.

Many financial activities are improved when technology is introduced. Cash flow forecasting, which typically includes multiple forecasts by subsidiary, bank or currency, can include bank balance and transactional data (usually automated), with easier reconciliation of transactions through the bank account. Information from receivables collections and payables clearings can also be reconciled with accounting records.

Investments, debt and foreign exchange can often be supported, from planning to execution to processing (straight-through processing), as well as reporting, mark-to-market and hedge effectiveness. Some systems also provide support for documentation related to trade finance activities, and interfaces to tax and other regulatory filings.

Treasury technology provides a number of organisational advantages in terms of providing efficiency and effectiveness. Efficiency improvements may enable treasury staff to spend less time on mundane tasks like bank transactions, data reconciliations and more on value added problem-solving analytics for the organisation and its clients, allowing them to accomplish more.

Reliance on treasury technology systems for financial instrument pricing and trading, and payments is not without risk. Access to files or data can be fraudulently altered or removed. Data and networks might not be properly protected. Systems and networks should be evaluated in light of their vulnerability to sabotage, hacking, fraud and error. A complex system that is understood by only one employee is a potential risk, so this should become institutional knowledge shared by many.

### 5.4.1 Data Services

Real-time data services provide news and market prices, which often includes historical price and volume data, analytical tools and pricing and technical analysis and charting services. Real-time market data are provided by multiple vendors. Not every organisation requires realtime data and there is a cost. Larger organisations may require real-time data (and any ancillary tools that are included with it) because of their transactions or activities in financial markets or their requirement for news. Trading operations, fund managers, and those involved in similar functions typically require real-time market data. Since some data services also enable trades to be executed, appropriate controls should be ensured.

The extent of real-time data usage by an organisation – for example, if it is used for daily foreign exchange trading – means that a backup source of data may need to be considered if there is a risk of data being unavailable at a critical time.

As historical data are often used for internal analysis, it is advisable to confirm what data are available from the services provider. For example, some vendors provide historical data that go back many years, while others are limited.

### 5.4.2 Banking Services

Banking services can be delivered in a variety of ways, depending on the country, financial institution and type of customer. Online banking is widely used for business transactions such as payments, including the ability to transact on mobile devices (e.g. a smartphone). These online banking systems function as proprietary banking platforms, offered by one bank (or banking group) for its customers. For example, users may send payment data to a financial institution, either an individual payment or multiple payments, to initiate local or international payments electronically. Business banking services are typically slower to offer new technologies than retail banking.

Electronic services provided by financial institutions vary greatly, reflecting the needs of finance and treasury in vastly diverse organisations in a global environment. Business banking services include the following:

• Account electronic balance and transaction reporting.

• Payment initiation, including wire transfers and automated clearinghouse (ACH) initiation.

• Transfers between accounts.

• Initiation of borrowing or investing transactions.

• Initiation of foreign exchange transactions, including orders.

• Electronic data interchange (EDI), an electronic transmission of data and payment that can be transmitted between organisations set up to do so.

Many organisations use the online (electronic or e-banking) system offered by their banks for day-to-day banking services such as reviewing transactions, initiating payments, bill payments or transacting foreign exchange. These platforms are web-based and require user authentication, either through a small device, fingerprint or personal identification number (PIN), or through multiple devices, depending on the bank and the service. Using this interface, a customer will log into each bank’s platform to download information from that bank. This is practical for one or two banks; it becomes more work if the organisation uses multiple banks.

Another alternative is to employ host-to-host (electronic banking) services, where the customer (typically a large organisation) uses software, such as treasury software, to connect and log into the bank’s systems (for example, automatically every morning) to download balance and transaction data from the bank or to upload files to the bank for transactions such as payments. This is a more complex technological setup and typical users will be larger companies using their own technology to send and receive files from the bank and manage the associated banking data.

### 5.4.3 Cash Management Services

Cash aggregation is the collection and utilisation of cash as quickly and efficiently as possible. Depending on the financial institution and the country in which bank accounts are held, cash aggregation services can assist in managing dispersed cash pools for use at a central location. This may help to improve returns on excess cash balances or make cash available for debt reduction or other purposes.

Multiple branches and subsidiaries of a larger organisation often require their own bank accounts for operational purposes, and usually small balances are required to handle unexpected operational payments and local collections. As the number of bank accounts grows, the funds held within those accounts, considered in aggregate, also grow. Centralisation can help with using those funds more efficiently. Availability of cash management services varies by country and financial institution.

Services offered by banks include the aggregation of cash across bank accounts, which can improve control and add efficiency to the administration of bank accounts. Services that address cash aggregation include accounts that offer zero balancing and pooling. As you learned in Chapter 4, these services are often used by treasury operations for cash management.

With zero balancing, individual positive account balances are automatically reduced to zero (or another predetermined balance) by moving funds from each account into a master concentration account, while accounts in deficit are increased (to zero or another target balance). Zero balancing is automated to occur regularly, usually daily, and this process includes individual accounts used for both collections (e.g. receivables) and disbursements (e.g. payables). If cheques can be written on the account, an automated funds transfer can be set up from the master account to cover them. There may be legal and tax considerations depending on the corporate structure. There may also be explicit costs associated with the funds transfers and implicit costs to manage and reconcile. Zero balancing has the benefit of providing access to organisational cash funds that can then be deployed for the best available return by payment against a line of credit, for example.

Pooling services accumulate cash from several bank accounts. To assist with pooling, which can be conducted on either an actual or a notional basis, an organisation may be required to establish credit facilities to cover debit balances within its pooled accounts. In Europe, where several countries use the euro for cross-border transactions, pooling is common, although legal and/or tax restrictions or prohibitions with respect to pooling can complicate international transactions. In contrast, the pooling process is more straightforward if the transaction takes place in only one country.

With physical pooling, funds are moved from pooling accounts into the central account.

Notional pooling means that balance and transaction data are reported and interest is calculated, as if transfers had taken place but no physical movement of funds occurs. The ability to do physical versus notional pooling depends on local country regulations and the corporate legal structure. Some countries prohibit or restrict cash pooling, so expert assistance may be necessary to avoid tax and legal issues.

Lockboxes are locations where payments, such as cheques and electronic payments, are collected. Lockboxes offer advantages for receiving payments, including faster processing of receipts, updating of customer accounts and reporting and data. In addition, the lockbox may speed up cash collection. Wholesale lockboxes are used for business-to-business payments, while retail lockboxes are typically for consumer payments with high volumes and smaller dollar amounts with rigorous processing requirements.

The introduction of the newest Basel Accord (Basel III) is discussed later Section 5.5.5.1, but the implications of liquidity metrics for banks’ funding and lending strategies have resulted in some changes in pricing and services provided to customers. The Basel rules, combined with the banks’ own desire to reduce liquidity risk, have resulted in changes. Although there are other effects, three of the main impacts include:

• The customer loan-to-deposit ratio moving more into balance, to provide a higher degree of liquidity to cover in the event of emergency cash requirements, such as an economic recession, which is significantly higher than normal customer withdrawal demands;
• A focus on retail/small and medium enterprise deposits, including the introduction/ re-launch of deposit products, such as 35-day notice accounts and

• Higher holdings of liquid assets and the disposal of securities that do not improve liquidity, to boost liquidity ratios and provide banks with faster access to cash to cover unexpected circumstances where large amounts of cash are required for holding and/or are in demand for disbursement.

### 5.4.4 Virtual Banking

Virtual or online banks provide financial transactions, typically without traditional branch networks.

In September 2017, the introduction of new ‘virtual banking’ licenses by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is a key milestone marking Hong Kong’s entry into the Smart Banking Era. The major requirements are as follows:

• Ownership: Virtual banks are expected to operate in the form of a locally-incorporated bank. A person who holds more than 50% of the share capital of a virtual bank should be a bank or a financial institution in good standing and supervised by a recognised authority in Hong Kong or elsewhere. If it is not owned by such a bank or financial institution, it should be held through an intermediate holding company incorporated in Hong Kong.

• Physical presence: A virtual bank must have a principal place of business physically located in Hong Kong, although a physical local branch is not required.

• Minimum capital requirement: The requirement of minimum paid-up capital of HK$300 million is applicable to all licensed banks.

• Ongoing supervision and recordkeeping: Virtual banks are subject to the same supervision as conventional banks. They must keep full bookkeeping and accounting records and provide the HKMA with supervisory access to them.

• Risk management: Technology risk is of vital importance to a virtual bank. The general principle is that the security and technology related controls should be fit for purpose. A virtual bank applicant is required to engage a qualified and independent expert to perform an independent assessment of the adequacy of its planned IT governance and systems. Apart from technology risk, the applicant must also go through the eight basic types of risk identified in the risk-based supervisory framework of the HKMA (i.e. credit, interest rate, market, liquidity, operational, reputation, legal and strategic risks) and establish appropriate controls to manage these risks.

• Business plan and exit plan: A virtual bank must be able to present a credible and viable business plan which strikes an appropriate balance between the desire to build market share and the need to earn a reasonable return on assets and equity.

As virtual banking is a new business model in Hong Kong, the HKMA also requires a virtual bank applicant to provide an exit plan in case its business model turns out to be unsuccessful.

Companies intending to apply for a virtual banking licence can refer to the information and the requirements listing out in the HKMA’s Guide to Authorization, particularly Chapter 2 – The Authorization Regime, Chapter 4 – Authorization, and Chapter 8 – Application Procedures.

The HKMA received over thirty applications and eight virtual bank licenses were granted in the first two quarters of 2019. The list of the virtual banks incorporated in Hong Kong as at 30 September 2020 is shown below:

1. Airstar Bank Limited (formerly Insight Fintech HK Limited)

2. Ant Bank (Hong Kong) Limited (formerly ANT SME Services (Hong Kong) Limited)

3. Fusion Bank Limited (formerly Infinium Limited)

4. Livi Bank Limited (formerly Livi VB Limited)

5. Mox Bank Limited (formerly SC Digital Solutions Limited)

6. Ping An Oneconnect Bank (Hong Kong) Limited (formerly Ping An Oneconnect Company Limited)

7. Welab Bank Limited (formerly Welab Digital Limited)

8. ZA Bank Limited (formerly Zhongan Virtual Finance Limited)

The decision to conduct business with a virtual bank, as opposed to a traditional financial institution, affects financial transactions, risk management, and strategy. There are several potential advantages and disadvantages to consider with such a decision.

For example, on the plus side, the decision might prove cost-effective. Because virtual banks have reduced overheads, they may offer business and personal customers comparatively lower fees for banking transactions. Clients might also receive a comparatively higher interest rate on deposits, loans and other financial products. Another potential advantage is that digital banking could provide faster, more efficient, personalised services for clients that prefer an alternative to a traditional banking structure.

The timing may also be beneficial, as banking transactions can take place and also be checked for accuracy on a real-time basis – the latter function in particular may offer an advantage over traditional financial institutions.

There are, however, some potential downsides to dealing with an entity that exists predominantly online. One is the possibility of an outage that causes access to become temporarily unavailable. This could be a serious detriment, particularly if an urgent financial matter arises when time is of the essence. It may also be more challenging to develop relationships with a local representative who can assist when problems arise and need to be resolved quickly.

Another concern is that a virtual bank, being heavily dependent on technology, may be more vulnerable to a cybersecurity attack or loss (or exposure) of customer data. These risks can evolve quickly and should be considered. Virtual banks might also be less attractive for clients that require more complex financial products or services offered by a branch, such as local deposit services.

### 5.4.5 Treasury Management Systems

Many large organisations rely on specialised treasury software solutions or systems to manage many of the tasks and reporting associated with treasury management. Specialised software permits treasury professionals to generate cash flow forecasts, create a variety of reports based on their internal requirements and model different scenarios. Some software includes or integrates derivatives pricing models. Such software can be costly and require additional peripheral technology and training to access data from other systems and banks.

Treasury software is often built on a database, which may reside locally, remotely or in the cloud. The database stores data that can be accessed in different ways. The software may support multiple users and treasury staff in various locations. Technology is an important component of the treasury infrastructure and it typically needs to connect to internal and external systems.

The selection and implementation of treasury technology, including upgrading current systems, requires multiple steps, including planning, potentially preparing a formal request for proposal and implementation and follow-up, as well as the need to upgrade staff skills and provide other appropriate training. These steps are similar to those for implementing other business technology solutions.

Many treasury software components are module-based. Customers purchase a base product or service and then choose additional modules or functions depending on their requirements. This allows for the purchase or subscription of only the modules required, which may reduce cost and complexity.

Typical components include cash management, forecasting, foreign exchange, risk management, bank and Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) interfaces. SWIFT will be introduced in Section 5.4.6. Interfaces enable the user to receive or transmit data. For example, treasury may download balance and transaction data from its bank, directly into the treasury software. Other functionality may facilitate automated reconciliation. Customisation may be required to provide interfaces to an organisation’s other systems and financial institutions interfaces, or to facilitate specific reporting requirements.

Traditionally, software was purchased and run on a local server. Today, many products run under an application service provider (ASP) arrangement. Typically a monthly fee is charged for accessing web-based software in a subscription-type service rather than accessing it on a local server. Upgrades are automatically applied and need not be managed by treasury. Thus an organisation can eliminate the capital cost of acquiring the software and reduce the need for in-house IT to support the system. The downside is that the software is not owned, so if the organisation stops paying the monthly fee, the service ceases, and this may make it difficult to access past data. For legal reasons, it may be important to know where (which country) the data is stored. The system should have considerable controls limit access, provide disaster recovery services and address other security requirements. These added controls are very valuable to organisations, particularly for publicly-listed companies whose executives may be required to personally certify for the efficacy of their internal control systems.

#### 5.4.5.1 Planning, Selecting and Implementing Treasury Software

The successful implementation of new treasury software, despite being expected to improve an organisation’s processes, takes time and effort. Disruptions can occur, and costs and time requirements might expand beyond those that have been forecast.

A cost-benefit analysis associated with implementing new technology may help to support the treasury technology decision and permit financial quantification. A cost-benefit analysis should include considerations about the following types of costs:

• Technology requirements: including software, hardware, network and training.

• Consulting and specialty services: including IT, training and support.

• Hidden costs: including opportunity costs, staff turnover, the potential for there being temporarily less efficiency during implementation and testing, customer complaints and trial-and-error in terms of evaluating the appropriateness of current staff in a new role.

• Purchasing, implementing and operating new treasury software can result in potentially extra costs, including:
- Upgrade requirements for software, hardware, operating systems, networks or any combination thereof.
- New software licence costs. 
- Establishing specific interfaces for various internal/external sources, including the organisation’s accounting systems, financial institutions and its markets/clients.
- The need to revise backup and contingency planning procedures, manuals and other support tools and customised reports as required.
- Internal or external consulting and audit expertise and potential follow-up, including annual maintenance support.
- Training costs for staff. 

Treasury objectives can be an important guide to the determination of an organisation’s specific technology requirements. Typically, this involves gathering relevant information from across the organisation, including an assessment of existing information/data/systems and requirements, any necessary interfaces to communicate with other systems and support for various types of financial instruments and transactions.

Potential risks may include a technology failure due to system or technical flaws that result in instrument mispricing, incorrect access to transaction approval or confirmation, operational risks arising from fraudulent or erroneous reports, vulnerability to hackers or external access to organisational data, or erroneous information downloads. These potential risks help to highlight the importance of planning and involving experts, if needed, when an organisation plans new treasury technology.

The potential benefits for the organisation in terms of new treasury systems that need to be considered include: increased efficiency and speed of operations; increased automation of routine tasks, such as payments reconciliation and reporting, less data re-keying and opportunity for error; the provision of greater cash flow forecasting ability for treasury staff; and new tools that will permit more sophisticated analysis and analytic models in areas such as corporate risk management.

Treasury software can bring some benefits to an organisation, including reducing underutilised cash, a better ability to forecast cash requirements for longer periods of time, automated reconciliations and better controls through the electronic audit trail. Some systems permit initiation of payments, which typically require greater controls and segregation. If reporting rules require evidence, treasury systems may be useful to document compliance. Depending on the treasury system components, there may be other benefits such as interfaces for executing and processing trades, and analytical tools for portfolio and risk management, as well as for reporting.

Where appropriate, a treasury system may provide additional analytics and reporting for the board of directors, management and stakeholders.

#### 5.4.5.2 Spreadsheets

Spreadsheets are commonly used in many financial areas including treasury because they permit users to create formulas and conduct analysis and are relatively easy to use and flexible. As a result, they are used in many organisations for cash flow forecasting, pricing and financial analysis.

However, there are also potential weaknesses with the use of spreadsheets. Financial decisions are sometimes based on erroneous spreadsheet calculations, which can result in significant losses and increased operational risk. Reliance on spreadsheets, combined with a lack of controls, can also create unexpected operational exposures.

When spreadsheets are used for cash flow forecasting, as they often are, it may be inconvenient to rearrange cash flow data for different users, and the resultant data may introduce opportunities for errors.

### 5.4.6 SWIFT

The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) operates a global messaging network that banks use to exchange standardised electronic messages with one another.

The SWIFT network permits large organisations to connect treasury and cash management systems to the SWIFT network. This permits a standard messaging format for multiple banks, rather than maintaining interfaces with each bank in their banking relationships. The standard message format enables an organisation to conduct transactions and receive bank account information from most or all its banks.

SWIFT messages use a SWIFT message type (MT) code to initiate messages in the network. The information is standardised so that it can be read easily. Some common SWIFT MT codes are shown in Exhibit 5.7.

![](DraggedImage-88.png)

Treasury systems can accept and generate these standardised messages, which enable many tasks to be automated.

Several access methodologies permit an organisation to obtain access to the SWIFT system. However, none of the access methodologies permit a company to deal directly with another corporation; it can only send messages through bank intermediaries. SWIFTNet Link software provides the interface. Doing so streamlines a number of treasury transactions, which makes the entire treasury system more cost-effective to operate.

## 5.5 FINANCIAL INTERMEDIATION

A financial system is necessary to distribute surplus money from sources such as governments, organisations or individuals (households) that possess excess funds, to sources with financial requirements that need to be fulfilled.

In direct finance, the financial system functions similarly to a broker’s role. Organisations and individuals with funds to invest are matched with organisations and individuals that need to borrow or sell. An example is the issuance of commercial paper by a multinational corporation, issued through a bank and purchased by a pension fund.

In indirect finance, financial intermediaries such as banks buy securities (e.g. loans) issued by borrowers that include companies, governments and individuals. The banks collect funds, in the form of demand or savings deposits, or issue their own securities to investors. Financial markets act as intermediaries that permit suppliers of capital and users of capital to connect with one another.

Intermediation is an important activity in the financial markets, and one that differs substantially from the role of a broker.

An understanding of financial intermediation is enhanced by understanding the money markets, capital markets and international markets that exist today. Financial intermediaries are the banks, dealers and others that undertake trading in financial instruments on behalf of clients. This makes them an important part of the financial markets in which they operate. Financial intermediaries and markets are affected in a major way by two components, the activity of credit rating agencies, which rate and therefore greatly influence securities offered by major issuers, and the governance structures that underlie issuers, banks and others.

Financial assets and liabilities are bought and sold through financial markets. One of the most important factors for a financial market is liquidity, which indicates how readily an asset’s value can be converted into cash. Highly liquid assets such as US Treasury bills are considered a proxy for cash. In general, markets with higher trading volumes, such as foreign exchanges, tend to have higher liquidity than markets with lower volumes, such as small regional stock exchanges.

Financial markets vary according to maturity:

• Money markets are wholesale markets for financial assets and liabilities of short maturity, usually less than one year.

• Capital markets are markets for long-term financial assets and liabilities, typically with maturities of one year or more.

The distinction between short-term and long-term assets is somewhat arbitrary. In some markets, the distinction is clear. A 20-year government bond is considered a long-term instrument, while a six-month instrument is considered a short-term instrument. However, when a long-term instrument nears maturity, it may trade as a short-term instrument.

Financial market participants typically are issuers or investors in either short-term or long-term securities and sometimes in both. Many longer-term investors, such as pension funds, match the expected terms (or duration) of their liabilities to assets to reduce risk. Financial institutions are often active in shorter-term markets as a result of financial activities such as lending. In many cases, different regulations govern short-term and long-term instruments.

### 5.5.1 Money Markets

Money markets are wholesale markets for financial assets and liabilities of short maturity, with a time frame usually considered to be less than one year. This includes commercial paper and Treasury bills.

Money markets exist in most market economies. Money markets are the short-term component of capital markets, and they are an important source of short-term debt, as well as participating investors and financial institutions.

The existence of money markets provides multiple benefits. Organisations are willing to invest large amounts of idle cash in money market instruments because of their high liquidity and their low default risk. If an organisation’s cash receipts are in excess of its expenditures, that excess cash can be invested in money market instruments over the short term. On the other hand, an organisation might turn to the money markets for short-term borrowing to cover a shortfall resulting from when its cash expenditures are in excess of its cash receipts. Moreover, a portfolio that contains money market securities can provide extra needed cash when some of those instruments are sold.

Various parties, including banks and other financial institutions, along with investment dealers, fund managers, corporations, insurance companies, and central banks and governments all participate in the wholesale money market. Interdealer firms enable or facilitate trading. They act as intermediaries for wholesale transactions between dealers situated at financial institutions.

Because financial institutions – especially larger banking organisations – deal with significant cash management necessitating from their core business and financial management responsibilities, these firms are particularly active in money market activities. In contrast, their smaller competitors might concentrate more on risk management with respect to interest rates, as well as on maintaining liquidity.

Governments of all levels in a jurisdiction, along with their agencies, incur obligations and issue debt to support their activities and finance both short-term and long-term shortfalls of cash. They may also need to invest excess cash in the money market. Thus, governments may be both issuers of and investors in money market securities.

Corporations of all sizes occupy the other major tier of money market participants, both as issuers and as investors. Corporations may use the services of financial institutions to bundle and package assets for security creation to raise funds, or they might issue their own obligations through debt issues.

Many organisations manage excess liquidity in the form of cash and short-term assets in the money market, which is the wholesale market for cash, liabilities, and short-term fixed income securities. It facilitates short-term investing of excess cash and short-term funding for borrowers.

Money market instruments have a relatively short term to maturity (usually under one year), are high quality (low risk), and are usually liquid and therefore easy to buy or sell. Like other fixed income securities, they are subject to credit risk and interest rate risk, as well as foreign exchange risk if they are denominated in a foreign currency. Commonly used financial instruments for managing excess short-term cash include bank deposits, bankers’ acceptances, certificates of deposit, commercial paper, Treasury bills and other government securities, as well as money market fund products.

Exhibit 5.8 illustrates the relationships between financial markets, financial institutions, investors and borrowers.
