### 5.5.2 Capital Markets

Capital markets typically trade longer-term financial assets and liabilities, including equities and most bonds, with maturities of one year or more.

Large firms finance fixed assets such as plants and equipment in these financial markets, where equity and debt instruments are traded. Well-known international stock exchanges such as the NYSE, as well as the London and Tokyo stock exchanges, are capital markets. Compared with money market instruments, capital market instruments not only have longer maturities, they also carry higher risk generally.

In most developed and developing countries, capital markets are the most important providers of capital to businesses. Even though the growth of capital markets across the world has reduced the influence of governments, founding families and commercial banks, some of these stakeholders continue to exert control on companies in many countries. For example, the economies of South America, the Middle East and mainland China are still dominated by governments; controlling interests are still retained by families in countries such as Mexico; and commercial banks continue to be major players in continental Europe and Japan.

Despite this, the trend shows that capital markets have an increasing importance in these countries because they are relied upon to stimulate the creation of new businesses, allocate capital and monitor managerial performance. Capital market growth in these countries is gradually eroding the influence of other stakeholders.

#### 5.5.2.1 Debt Markets

Governments are the most active issuers of international debt, whereas financial institutions such as commercial banks are active issuers of domestic debt. The growth in market value or capitalisation of domestic and international debt and equity markets has followed along with economic growth.

Bonds can be categorised according to whether or not they are issued by a domestic issuer. Domestic bonds are issued by a domestic resident in their own local market. International bonds are traded outside the country of the issuer and can be categorised into types.

Foreign bonds are bonds issued locally by a non-local issuer. They are typically issued in the domestic (local) currency, and subject to local regulation. They are created to attract local institutional investors.

Bonds may be issued in the Eurobond market. A Eurobond is traded in a market outside the borders of the country of the currency of denomination. A Eurobond is called a global bond when it trades in one or more foreign or domestic bond markets as well as in the Eurobond market. The concept of eurocurrencies is covered later in this Section 5.5.3.2.

The United States is the world’s largest domestic debt market, with Eurozone countries, Japan, the UK and mainland China also big domestic debt issuers. Well-known borrowers such as multinational corporations and governments may find their borrowing costs are lower in international than in domestic markets. Smaller borrowers may find funding costs to be lower in the domestic debt market because of the higher information costs faced by international investors.

#### 5.5.2.2 Equity Markets

The equity claim in a firm can take different forms, depending on whether the firm is privately owned or publicly traded, and on the firm’s growth and risk characteristics. Capital provided by the founder(s) of a company, the original owner’s equity, is the basis for the future of the business. Even large global corporations today often started with a founder’s backing.

The growth and investment needs of small businesses will eventually cause them to require more funds.

Some firms that were originally privately owned may be able to become publicly traded companies and issue common stock to ease their need for funding. However, those businesses must be sizable enough or have appeal to investors to be offered to the public. Many private businesses find themselves unable to make this transition to become publicly traded firms. For these businesses, an alternative is to raise equity financing from private investors or to seek funds in the form of venture capital.

Conventionally, a publicly traded firm raises equity capital by issuing common stock at a price the market determines. For a first-time publicly traded firm, this price is estimated by an investment banker and is called the offering price. For an existing company whose stock is already being traded, it is based on the current market price. The common stock issued by a company is usually uniform, with each share receiving the same proportional share of both the cash flows and the voting rights. In some cases, different classes of common stock will provide different cash flows and voting rights.

Companies that are publicly-traded (on a stock exchange, for example) are typically considered to be more liquid than companies that are not. This is because it is easier to buy or sell shares in the company. However, it is more important how actively the company’s shares are traded, since many companies that are publicly-listed have low levels of liquidity due to their shares not being actively bought and sold.

### 5.5.3 International Markets

A company based in Hong Kong or elsewhere might be entirely domestic, or it may have operations that provide it with substantial exposure to international markets. A discussion of international markets follows.

International markets provide the financial manager of a multinational organisation with exciting, although challenging, opportunities to consolidate existing operations, to pre-empt competitors from entry into existing and possible future markets and to protect and expand the value of current and future operations.

International capital markets are more integrated today than in past years. With fewer barriers, market participants are able to narrow cross-market valuation differentials and enforce a single price. This evolution has important consequences for international portfolio diversification and asset pricing, and therefore for the firm’s cost of capital.

There are many international markets, in interest rates, liabilities such as bonds, derivatives, currencies and other financial assets and liabilities. Two of the largest international markets are worth mentioning separately, due to their size and influence. These markets are the foreign exchange market and the eurocurrency market.

#### 5.5.3.1 Foreign Exchange Market

The foreign exchange (FX or forex) market is at the heart of international trade and finance, because it permits the transfer of purchasing power from one currency to another. The foreign exchange market allows investors to move capital toward its most productive uses regardless of the timing of investment or currency of denomination. It is also the world’s largest financial market, with transactions averaging US$6.6 trillion per day in April 2019, up from US$5.1 trillion per day in April 2016, according to the Triennial Central Bank Survey of foreign exchange and over-the-counter derivatives markets as conducted by the Bank for International Settlements.

Foreign exchange markets provide the mechanism for organisations to exchange currencies and hedge unwanted risk arising from changes in currency rates that may affect the market value of an organisation’s assets or liabilities. Hedging foreign exchange risk was covered in detail Chapter 3.

The foreign exchange market also allows speculators to bet on changes in currency values. Currency speculation by international banks and hedge funds ensures that exchange rates represent a consensus of market participants and it also provides additional liquidity to the markets. In addition to being the largest market, the wholesale (interbank) market is also the world’s most operationally efficient market, with very low percentage costs for large transactions between major banks. However, percentage fees on small transactions, such as retail transactions, can be large.

Most foreign exchange trading occurs between large international banks in foreign exchange trading hubs such as London, Tokyo and New York. Hong Kong is also a major financial centre. Major banks account for a majority of the trading. Corporations and governments also conduct major volumes as they manage global commercial and financing activities.

Financial institutions, and especially large banks, are active buying from and selling to others, both for customers and for their own requirements. As a result, exchange rates are typically very responsive to relevant information and news that could cause those rates to fluctuate. Speculation ensures that exchange rates reflect a realistic value of the currency, with speculators taking risks that others would not want.

International foreign exchange markets, where currencies are bought and sold in wholesale amounts, provide the ability for facilitating international trade in goods and services, and they permit organisations with unwanted foreign exchange risk to offset their risk by passing it to others.

#### 5.5.3.2 Eurocurrency Market

Eurocurrency markets are external credit markets that trade deposits and loans in a currency, with trading occurring outside the country issuing that currency. Because these external credit markets originated in Europe, they are referred to as eurocurrency markets. This market is not to be confused with the market for euros, the common currency of much of Europe. US dollardenominated deposits held in a country other than the United States are called Eurodollars. Similarly, the Eurosterling credit market resides outside the United Kingdom and the Euroyen market resides outside Japan. Eurocurrencies, which are highly efficient credit markets, are usually variable-rate deposits with maturities of under five years.

Eurocurrencies are not entirely free from government interference, but the government issuing the currency does not have direct jurisdiction over the deposit or the depositor, and they also tend to have fewer disclosure requirements. However, the banks that trade in eurocurrencies are generally highly regulated entities.

#### 5.5.3.3 Chinese Market

Mainland China’s economy features both government-owned organisations that are subject to government planning, whose goals are primarily social, such as to maintain full employment, and private organisations whose goal is profit and maximising the value of the company for its shareholders. However, since the 1980s, mainland China has developed a market economy with some of the leading capital markets on the world stage.

Major global Chinese exchanges by market capitalisation include the Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite, Shenzhen Stock Exchange and Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The Hang Seng index records daily changes in the largest companies traded in the Hong Kong stock market and is the main indicator of the overall market performance in Hong Kong.

Generally speaking, the shares of publicly-listed Chinese companies that trade on stock exchanges in mainland China are referred to as A-shares. Shares of publicly-listed Chinese companies that trade in Hong Kong dollars in Hong Kong Stock Exchange are referred to as H-shares.

Banks are a dominant industrial sector in the Chinese economy. Two of the largest-ever initial public offerings (IPOs) took place on the Shanghai and Hong Kong Stock Exchanges involving banks in mainland China. These transactions illustrate how important banks in mainland China are to the country’s economy, as well as the key role they play in the global economy.

Mainland China’s equity markets are directed by the China Securities Regulatory Commission. There are various types of shares available, including those available only to domestic individual and corporate shareholders for trade only on Chinese exchanges and those available to foreign investors for trade on either Chinese or certain other exchanges. Regulation is discussed in more detail in Chapter 14, Regulatory Environment.

Mainland China’s economy is also one of the world’s most dominant economies.

Consider, for instance, that four of the world’s 15 largest multinational firms as ranked by revenue in 2016 were based in mainland China. Also, in 2016, mainland China had six of the world’s largest 15 banks ranked by assets, including the four most powerful in the country: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, China Construction Bank, Agricultural Bank of China and Bank of China.

Mainland China’s currency is the renminbi, whose primary unit is expressed in yuan. It is issued and circulated by The People’s Bank of China, which is the central bank of mainland China.

### 5.5.4 Rating Agencies

Credit rating agencies assess the overall creditworthiness of an issuer by providing an issuer or issue rating. The issuer rating is an opinion resulting from analysis that considers whether the organisation has the capability to meet its financial commitments. Rating agencies are mostly for-profit companies that charge for their services and their ratings are usually provided to their subscribers for a fee.

Rating agencies will also provide an issue rating, which assesses the quality of a specific security or debt issue by an organisation. This issue rating assesses the creditworthiness of that particular security, including the risk of possible default.

Only a very small proportion of the many organisations that borrow will have their securities rated. Most will be too small or not creditworthy enough. However, those that are rated tend to be among the dominant organisations in their markets, either by industry, geography or issue type.

Rating agencies typically provide ratings for companies, banks, sovereign states and municipalities. They may rate a specific issue (or type of issue, such as short-term debt) or provide a rating for the issuer. The ratings are proprietary to the rating agency and therefore may be revised at any time.

However, it should be emphasised that although credit ratings are a useful tool, they are not a substitute for an issuer or counterparty risk management assessment or associated due diligence by organisations.

The analysis provided by rating agencies is fairly comprehensive. Three rating agencies that are widely used internationally are Standard & Poor’s, Moody’s and Fitch Ratings.

Exhibits 5.9 and 5.10 show examples of debt ratings for Moody’s. The exhibits are not intended to be comprehensive and are shown as an example only. Ratings are intended for use by subscribers and issuers, who pay for the services of the rating agencies, not the general public. The ratings and their definitions are proprietary to the rating agencies and should be interpreted with supporting research. Criteria and ratings can be changed at any time by the rating agencies.

Each rating agency has its own ratings scales and definitions for various types of securities, ranging from highest to lowest quality. As an example, the highest short-term credit rating offered by Moody’s is Prime 1, shown in Exhibit 5.9. Ratings and definitions are provided by the rating agencies. The tables following show examples of ratings from Moody’s.

![](DraggedImage-90.png)
![](DraggedImage-91.png)

In addition to ratings, companies may also issue watchlists, which alert ratings users to potential events of interest that could change the rating, such as a merger.

Higher credit ratings are generally referred to as investment grade and those below that as speculative grade (or non-investment grade). The distinction between these two types of risk is important to investors, especially institutional investors, who may not be permitted to buy speculative grade securities.

Rating agencies generally rate organisations at their request, which enables that organisation to better reach its target investor market. In doing so, the rating agency will gain confidential information about strategy and operations with which to produce a credit grade. A positive credit grade from an objective credit rating agency will generally provide investors and prospective investors with greater confidence about the organisation. This will impact strategic planning in both the company issuing debt, as well as in the treasury department of the organisation or individual that is doing the investing.

For the company issuing debt, strategic planning will be affected because a higher credit rating should enhance its ability to sell debt securities at a lower interest rate than a competitor with a lower credit rating. The strategic planning for a corporate treasury department or individual investor purchasing the debt securities of that company will need to balance potentially lower interest payments with a higher credit rating, signifying less chance of default.

For an organisation that receives a low credit grade from an objective credit rating agency, the reverse situation will be true. Its strategic planning needs to take into account that a lower credit rating should negatively impact the company’s ability to issue/sell debt securities without having to pay a compensating premium on its interest. The strategic planning of the corporate treasury department or individual investor that is purchasing those debt securities will need to balance potentially higher interest payments with a lower credit rating, signifying a higher chance of default.

### 5.5.5 Governance

Governance refers to the ways in which an organisation’s major stakeholders exert control over that organisation and attempt to ensure they will earn an acceptable return on their investment. Each country’s laws, its regulatory framework, legal institutions and conventions combine as factors to determine stakeholder rights in organisational governance.

Many aspects of an organisation’s economic life are influenced by the following factors:

• Ownership and control of that organisation.
• Opportunities available to its borrowers and investors.
• How capital is allocated internationally.

Although many countries share common characteristics, they are shaped by unique legal, political, social and economic forces. All of these forces impact the ways in which organisations within its boundaries are governed and how they perform. This, in turn, affects the frequency and form of cross-border mergers, acquisitions, divestitures and reorganisations within those borders.

In addition to ratings, companies may also issue watchlists, which alert ratings users to potential events of interest that could change the rating, such as a merger.

Higher credit ratings are generally referred to as investment grade and those below that as speculative grade (or non-investment grade). The distinction between these two types of risk is important to investors, especially institutional investors, who may not be permitted to buy speculative grade securities.

Rating agencies generally rate organisations at their request, which enables that organisation to better reach its target investor market. In doing so, the rating agency will gain confidential information about strategy and operations with which to produce a credit grade. A positive credit grade from an objective credit rating agency will generally provide investors and prospective investors with greater confidence about the organisation. This will impact strategic planning in both the company issuing debt, as well as in the treasury department of the organisation or individual that is doing the investing.

For the company issuing debt, strategic planning will be affected because a higher credit rating should enhance its ability to sell debt securities at a lower interest rate than a competitor with a lower credit rating. The strategic planning for a corporate treasury department or individual investor purchasing the debt securities of that company will need to balance potentially lower interest payments with a higher credit rating, signifying less chance of default.

For an organisation that receives a low credit grade from an objective credit rating agency, the reverse situation will be true. Its strategic planning needs to take into account that a lower credit rating should negatively impact the company’s ability to issue/sell debt securities without having to pay a compensating premium on its interest. The strategic planning of the corporate treasury department or individual investor that is purchasing those debt securities will need to balance potentially higher interest payments with a lower credit rating, signifying a higher chance of default.

### 5.5.5 Governance

Governance refers to the ways in which an organisation’s major stakeholders exert control over that organisation and attempt to ensure they will earn an acceptable return on their investment. Each country’s laws, its regulatory framework, legal institutions and conventions combine as factors to determine stakeholder rights in organisational governance.

Many aspects of an organisation’s economic life are influenced by the following factors:

• Ownership and control of that organisation.
• Opportunities available to its borrowers and investors.
• How capital is allocated internationally.

Although many countries share common characteristics, they are shaped by unique legal, political, social and economic forces. All of these forces impact the ways in which organisations within its boundaries are governed and how they perform. This, in turn, affects the frequency and form of cross-border mergers, acquisitions, divestitures and reorganisations within those borders.

#### 5.5.5.1 International Banking Regulatory Framework (Basel Accords)

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) is a central bankers’ bank based in Basel, Switzerland. The Basel Accords represent a set of international recommendations designed to ensure that banks retain sufficient capital to protect themselves against unexpected losses. The Basel Accords, which are a set of regulations affecting banks, are facilitated by the BIS and the Basel Committee of Banking Supervision. That committee, as of 2019, consists of senior representatives from banking authorities and central banks from Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, mainland China, the European Union, France, Germany, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the United States.

The introduction of capital adequacy requirements was a major milestone in financial risk management. An international convergence of capital measurement and standards represented the management of risk at the source, as some experts put it.

The BIS created the initial set of regulations (Basel 1), which governed the capital adequacy of financial institutions, in 1988. Under Basel I commercial banks were required to have equity capital set aside in reserve as protection against possible losses, with the reserve amount related to the credit risk of the borrower. In situations where banks did not have sufficient equity reserves on hand, they would either have to raise additional capital or eliminate assets to meet the Basel requirements. An updated set of requirements in 2004 (Basel II), introduced three new ‘pillars’ of bank regulation to cover more broadly the risks that commercial banks encounter. These three pillars are minimum capital requirements, a supervisory review of capital adequacy and internal assessment processes, and market discipline through disclosure requirements to encourage sound banking practices.

Having arisen from intentions to strengthen the financial system, capital adequacy allocates more capital to riskier activities. In doing so, capital adequacy addresses credit risk, market risk and operational risk.

The 2008 financial crisis caused banks and their regulators to focus on the viability of the financial industry during crisis periods. The Basel III Accord of 2010 introduced further refinements with an emphasis on capital adequacy, financial leverage and liquidity. The intent of Basel III was to create regulatory policies that are counter-cyclical to economic and financial fluctuations.

The Basel Accords have affected financial institutions worldwide. The increased cost of capital is borne by financial institutions and their customers and stakeholders, but all market participants benefit from having a more secure financial system, and they ultimately pay for its costs.

The Basel Accords attempt to strengthen the soundness and stability of the international banking system in a manner that is both fair and consistent, and that also reduces competitive inequality. They address three sources of risk to the value of a bank’s assets, including credit risk, market risk and operational risk. The Basel Accords also specify minimum capital adequacy ratios that a bank must maintain to address the possibility they could become insolvent should the value of its assets fall below the value of its liabilities.

#### 5.5.5.2 US Dodd-Frank Act

The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010 is US legislation that has had an extensive impact. Due to the importance of US capital markets, its effects are farreaching. Its objectives are to promote financial stability, to end ‘too big to fail’, to end bailout; and to protect consumers from abusive financial services practices. While the Dodd-Frank Act is not the first US financial legislation, it is of central importance due to its focus on systemic risk and its tremendous impact on financial institutions and the financial system. Given the size of US financial markets, it also has the potential to affect banks and their customers in other countries.

Following the financial crisis of 2008, a number of changes were made that affected banks and financial markets, and in turn all organisations that use them. The Dodd-Frank Act introduced a number of new requirements for public companies, including two important provisions with respect to governance of executive compensation.

The first requirement is that companies allow stockholders a non-binding advisory vote on executive compensation policies. This is the so-called ‘say-on-pay’ rule. The aim of this rule is to provide shareholders with a way to send a message to an organisation if there are concerns about its compensation practices.

The second requirement is that organisations need to recover compensation paid to executives related to financial results, should it be determined later that the financial statements upon which the compensation was based are materially restated. The purpose of recalling such compensation (otherwise known as a ‘clawback’) is to discourage instances where executives have a financial incentive to misreport financial results and increase their pay, knowing that such compensation earned could be subject to recall later.

Dodd-Frank is a very extensive law addressing systemic risk that has had an enormous impact on both financial institutions and the financial system in the United States. The Act’s preamble states four wide-ranging objectives to ‘promote the financial stability of the United States’. The goal is to accomplish that by improving accountability and transparency in the financial system, to end the concept of ‘too big to fail’, to protect the American taxpayer by ending bailouts, to protect consumers from abusive financial services practices and for other purposes.

The Dodd-Frank Act created a new oversight entity called the Financial Stability Oversight Council, which has many responsibilities, including identifying systemically important financial institutions – defined as a bank or other institution with at least US$50 billion in assets, and making recommendations regarding heightened prudential standards for those entities in various areas, including overall risk-management, as well as risk-based capital, leverage, liquidity, contingent capital (debt that under certain circumstances can convert into equity) and other categories.

One of the key sections of the Dodd-Frank Act is the Volcker Rule, named for the former chair of the US Federal Reserve (the US central bank). This rule prohibits banking entities from engaging in proprietary trading, meaning that the bank cannot trade on behalf of its own account to generate short-term profits. The rule also prohibits banks from owning or sponsoring hedge funds and private equity funds.

The Volcker Rule also establishes limits and requirements for risky non-bank financial companies that engage in those activities. This rule is intended to discourage banks from engaging in speculative, risky activities and/or activities that are proprietary and represent conflicts of interest, without sufficient safeguards against such risks. The rule is also designed to further reduce the need for potentially costly bailouts from the US taxpayers.

#### 5.5.5.3 Markets in Financial Instruments Directive

The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID) is a European Union (EU) regulation, established in 2007 and updated with MiFID II in 2018 to reflect lessons learned about financial markets in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. The MiFID legislative framework is designed to enhance investor protection across the EU, for clients of financial institutions that provide stocks, bonds and derivatives, among other financial instruments. This regulation also attempts to enhance fairness, efficiency and transparency for such transactions.

The European Securities and Markets Authority notes that investor protection is strengthened in several ways through this legislation, including product governance, provision of independent investment advice, reporting requirements to clients and cross-selling, among other areas.

## SUMMARY

• Successful cash and liquidity management is essential for an organisation to meet both its short-term and medium-term financing requirements to continue operations.

• Forecasting focuses on planning for cash receipts and disbursements so that optimal cash balances can be maintained.

• Short-term forecasting, which focuses on the current business cycle, helps to support the organisation with many day-to-day decisions that are required.

• Medium-term forecasts are typically used to establish an organisation’s performance targets, to focus on specific market and product strategies and to prioritise decisions with respect to capital investment.

• Strategies to fund cash shortfalls are typically: short-term in nature and can be easily repaid or rolled over, as necessary; cheap to issue; and quick and easy to issue.

• Traditional forms of medium-term funding include revolving credit facilities and bank loans, supplemented by some types of bonds.

• Technology in cash and treasury management provides the ability to electronically extract bank and transaction information, track real-time rates, share information between disparate organisations and automate routine requirements.

• Money markets are markets for financial assets and liabilities of short maturity, with a time frame usually considered to be less than one year.

• The primary role of a financial system is to bring together economic agents with surplus financial resources, such as households, and those with net financial needs, such as companies and governments, in financial intermediation.

## Answers to Knowledge Check Questions

Question 1

Although there are many specific reasons that organisations hold cash, they typically fall into three categories: anticipation of transactions, precautionary reasons and taking advantage of opportunities.

Question 2

To successfully conduct day-to-day operations, an organisation must be able to maintain a balance between under-utilised cash balances and adequate short-term resources. Cash and liquidity management is arguably the most important role of a treasury department, to enable the company to fulfil its obligations.

Question 3

The statement of cash flows provides information about cash receipts and payments over a defined period of time. It reports cash effects of past operating, investing and financing activities, the net increase or decrease in cash during the period and the cash at the end of the period. The cash flow forecast looks forward to the future, predicting cash receipts and payments in order to estimate expected cash at a future date.

Question 4

Unlike a loan, for a line of credit the borrower typically makes interest payments but not payments of principal. Restrictions may prevent a line of credit from having an outstanding balance maintained throughout the year. Organisations that use their lines of credit regularly may therefore be required to pay it down in its entirety at least once per year for a minimum specific term.

Question 5

## ANSWERS TO EXAM PRACTICE

QUESTION 1

MKAL has found that around 20% of hotel billings are collected during the month of billing, 70% the month following the billing and the remaining 10% in the next month. Thus, the distribution method is used along with billing information from the accounting department to forecast the expected cash flows each month from the Singapore hotels:
![](DraggedImage-94.png)
MKAL faces serious cash flow risks in the new hotel business. These are risks of non-payment for hotel stays, and the potential variability of cash flows given it is a new business with external partners (hotels).

There are several ways these risks might be addressed. These include adapting the reservation process so that hotel guests pay upfront for their stays (either through an MKAL booking platform or a third-party travel website), thus potentially speeding up collection of funds (collection would be dependent on the website’s contractual agreements). Speeding up collection of funds reduces the risk of non-payment and improves the ability to forecast.

Other options might include discounts for the hotels to provide early payment to MKAL or alternatively special privileges for customers of hotels that agree to pay earlier or according to a specific schedule that MKAL provides.

Finally, additional considerations might include offering non-refundable rates, which allow customers to pay upfront and receive a discount by giving up the ability to cancel. These discounted rates appeal to a specific type of traveller. This strategy might reduce revenues to MKAL (if customers switch from non-discounted to discounted rates) but increases the forecastability of cash flows.

QUESTION 2

The treasurer is interested in treasury management software. Benefits include: increased efficiency and speed of operations; increased automation of routine tasks, such as payments reconciliation and reporting, less data re-keying and opportunity for error; the provision of greater cash flow forecasting ability for treasury staff; and new tools that will permit more sophisticated analysis, along with analytic models for assessment in areas such as corporate risk management.

Potential risks include a technology failure due to system or technical flaws that result in instrument mispricing, incorrect access to transaction approval or confirmation, operational risks arising from fraudulent or erroneous reports, vulnerability to hackers or external access to organisational data or erroneous information downloads.

QUESTION 3

Covenants in the loan agreements are mostly accounting ratios, financial decisions and a description of the share ownership to be maintained by the borrower. The ramifications of such covenants are important because each of them is different. Furthermore, there are several types of covenants. Positive covenants, also known as affirmative covenants, are agreements under which the borrower must adhere to certain conditions. For example, the borrower may be required to adopt a specific legal or capital structure, specific earnings ratios or be required to restructure. Negative covenants impose restrictions on the borrower. For example, a negative covenant might restrict an organisation’s ability to seek and take out new loans. It might limit or prohibit it from participating in certain equity transactions. It might prevent the organisation from pledging certain of its assets to third parties (negative pledges). Alternatively, it could limit the amount the company can pay out in dividends. Pari passu clauses are another type of covenant under which the borrower agrees that should it provide additional guarantees on any future credit, the lender will also benefit from those new guarantees. Cross default clauses are a fourth type of covenant. Under a cross default clause, should the borrower default on another loan – not the specific loan with the lender – the loan defaulted on will spark a cross default clause with the loan arranged with the lender. Even though there is no covenant breach or payment default on the loan with the lender, that loan will nevertheless become payable.

QUESTION 4

In a normal yield curve environment, the interest rate that STNC (France) SE will pay for financing is higher for longer terms than shorter terms. Therefore, the use of short-term financing strategies, such as drawing on a line of credit, obtaining bankers’ acceptances or issuing commercial paper, is likely to be the most beneficial financial strategy for the organisation to fund its lease payment over the short term. However, over a longer period of time, a short-term financing strategy could present STNC with a significant financial risk if rates should increase substantially over that interval. This financing decision will be particularly critical after five years, when the organisation will have an opportunity to exercise an option to renew its lease for another five years. STNC’s management knows that it will then need to finance a 25% lease premium in order to continue operations in the space it leases. Therefore STNC would be wise to hedge its bets and obtain medium-term financing, such as obtaining a bank loan, or issuing a longer-term maturity bond. A longerterm financing strategy is more conservative because it allows STNC to lock in interest rates that treasury and finance officials know will be affordable when the lease renewal option becomes due.

An additional consideration might be the competitiveness of STNC’s financing in either the shorter-term or longer-term market. If STNC is growing and has excellent credit and good cash flows, its lenders may be willing to extend longer-term financing at a competitive rate, which would remove some uncertainty from the business. Finally, STNC management may want to consider whether interest rates are expected to rise or fall (independent of the shape of the yield curve). If rates are expected to rise, STNC might want to fund longer-term in order to protect against rising rates. If rates are expected to fall, STNC might want to fund shorter-term in order to take advantage of lower rates.

## OPENING CASE

WORKING CAPITAL AND THE CHEMICAL MANUFACTURING MARKET

The global chemical manufacturing industry produces a number of chemicals used in industries such as agriculture, construction, electronics, plastic, paper, motor vehicles and transportation. The two largest segments in the industry involve the basic chemical industry and the synthetic chemicals industry.

The basic chemical industry produces various petrochemicals (producing carbon and hydrogen from petroleum and natural gas), gases (industrial gases such as oxygen, nitrogen and helium), dyes and pigments and metal and mineral compounds. The synthetic chemical industry produces common plastic materials such as polyethylene, polycarbonate (PC), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polystyrene. These products are extensively used in the motor vehicle and construction industries as well as production of a number of plastics used in the production of glass and plastic bottles and containers.

Chemical manufacturing entities typically have extensive plant and equipment requirements for the manufacturing process. Competition in the industry is restricted due to the capital needed to establish and maintain a chemical manufacturing plant.

These entities have a long-term contractual relationship with the suppliers of the inputs to their chemical manufacturing processes and the users of the chemical products produced by their processes. As such, these entities have well-established working capital practices and performance metrics relative to other industries and they place a premium on the performance of techniques used to manage accounts receivable, inventory and accounts payable.

HK Flex Ltd (‘HKFlex’) is a synthetic chemical manufacturing entity specialising in the production of polyethylene, PC and PET for use in automobile and parts production in mainland China, Japan and Korea.

Over the past three years HKFlex’s revenue has grown by more than 50%, mirroring extensive growth in the entity’s operating activities and concurrent geographical expansion. Despite this growth, through the flexibility displayed in its working capital management practices, HKFlex has achieved working capital management efficiency metrics consistent with other synthetic chemical manufacturing entities. In particular, over the past three years HKFlex has implemented a range of activities including:

• Improved automation of their manufacturing facilities.
• Changes in inventory management.
• Changes in accounts receivable terms arising from continuous assessment of credit terms.
• Improved supply chain relationships, which have facilitated adjustments to payment methods and terms for automobile and parts manufacturers.
• Reviewing the methods used to finance its working capital via supplier finance initiatives.

## OVERVIEW

In the previous chapter students explored cash and liquidity management techniques that can be used for short-term and medium-term financial management. This chapter extends that analysis by introducing students to the principles of working capital management and includes considerations of the impact of short-term and medium-term investment and financing decisions on working capital.

Working capital is typically divided into two categories: gross working capital and net working capital. Gross working capital is the sum of all current assets, while net working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities.

Working capital management involves the management of both current assets and current liabilities so as to achieve the maximum profitability for the entity as it conducts its operational activities, whilst also managing, concurrently, the solvency of the entity. Entities need to optimise their working capital in a way that does not compromise their future sales or profitability. Similarly, entities need to ensure they have sufficient liquid resources arising from the entity’s operating and financial management investment and financing decisions to continue in business.

The nature and scope of working capital management differs between manufacturing, retailing and service-based entities due to differences in their operational activities and external factors that impact their activities.

Working capital investment decisions involve short-term assets such as cash, inventories and accounts receivable and include choices about: the amount of cash and marketable securities needed to meet day-to-day requirements; the purchasing and use of inventory; and the granting of credit on sales (including the terms of the credit arrangements). These investment activities need to be funded, which then gives rise to funding decisions about whether to use short-term or long-term debt or equity to finance these short-term activities.

In this chapter students will learn about:

• The nature of working capital and the role of working capital management in financial strategies;

• How an entity can calculate the level of working capital investment for a given situation and explain the key factors that determine this level;

• How to calculate and apply relevant accounting ratios to assess liquidity and working capital efficiency; and

• How supply chain finance solutions can be adopted in working capital funding.

## 6.1 WORKING CAPITAL AND THE ROLE OF WORKING CAPITAL MANAGEMENT IN FINANCIAL STRATEGIES

An entity’s working capital is generally regarded as being the amount of capital that has been invested in an entity’s short-term assets.

An entity must implement investment and financing strategies to ensure that it has sufficient liquidity to meet short-term obligations as they fall due so as to not become insolvent, whilst simultaneously looking for opportunities to increase the entity’s profitability through the use of its current assets and liabilities.

The level of current assets is a key factor in an entity’s liquidity position and when current assets exceed current liabilities an entity is generally considered to be in a liquid position. However, the two objectives of liquidity and profitability will often conflict since liquid assets typically give lower returns than the returns expected on long-term assets, and current assets need to be financed. Financing strategies may affect the level of leverage and the type of funding used and may expose the entity to interest rate risk, all of which may impact profitability. Also, a shortage of important current assets such as inventory (by holding low stock levels) and accounts receivable (by restrictions on the issuing of credit) will impact the level of sales and will therefore impact future liquidity and profitability.

To improve liquidity, reduce funding costs for working capital and increase profitability through efficiency in management working capital management typically requires an entity to focus on the following current assets and liabilities, which are regarded as operational rather than financial assets and liabilities of an entity:

• Cash and marketable securities.
• Inventory of raw materials.
• Inventory used as part of in progress production.
• Inventory of finished goods.
• Trade and other accounts receivable.
• Trade and other accounts payable.

In this section, students will be introduced to the concept of working capital, including both gross working capital and net working capital, and will consider the role and key principles of working capital management. This section will also consider the financial impact on liquidity and profitability of alternative investment and funding decisions regarding working capital.

### 6.1.1 Defining Working Capital and Net Working Capital

Working capital is typically divided into two categories:
• Gross working capital, which reflects the sum of all current assets.
• Net working capital, which reflects the difference between current assets and current liabilities.

#### 6.1.1.1 Working Capital

The term working capital (also commonly called gross working capital) refers to an entity’s investment in short-term assets that are necessary for an entity to operate on a day-to-day basis. All entities require a certain amount of cash, inventory and accounts receivable to operate smoothly and to carry out their day-to-day operations.

Entities need to pay particular attention to the levels of current assets and how they are financed. This is important because a trade-off exists between profitability and solvency as the level of current assets increases. To determine the optimal level of current assets, entities need to minimise costs; however, this can impact the trade-off between profitability and solvency.

The level of working capital is typically a function of the sales turnover of an entity. For well-established entities, the level of working capital will generally approximate a constant proportion of sales. However, some entities have unique production cycles or can be seasonal in nature. For these entities their level of working capital will appear to be transitory in nature. Hence, for some entities the overall level of current assets may be volatile over time, which can impact decisions about liquidity and funding choices. Factors impacting the level of working capital will be discussed in Section 6.2.

#### 6.1.1.2 Net Working Capital

Due to differences in entity size, operating activities, industry, ability to access funding and levels of risk aversion, entities differ in relation to their levels of short-term assets and shortterm liabilities. The relationship between short-term assets and short-term liabilities is known as net working capital and is measured as follows:

> Net Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities

Current assets and current liabilities include assets and liabilities that the entity reasonably expects will be either redeemed for cash (current assets) or will be payable by cash (current liabilities) within the short term, 12 months being the usual period. (Note that HKAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements paras. 66-69 uses wider definitions of current assets and current liabilities. In particular, they include the notion of a normal operating cycle for both concepts.)

It is also possible to disaggregate current assets and current liabilities into both operational and financial activities. Operational assets requiring investment and funding include: finished goods; inventory used to create those finished goods for sale or to provide services; accounts receivable; and a minimal amount of cash to provide the liquidity necessary for the entity to operate. On the liability side, operating liabilities that are used to fund these operational investments include: accounts payable (HKAS 1 uses trade and other receivables to refer to accounts payable); unpaid employee wages; and current tax payable. Note that short-term operating liabilities do not include financial debts such as short-term borrowing. This is because all other short-term assets and short-term liabilities include those items that are more financial in nature and are typically not affected directly by the operations of the entity.

The level of net working capital can have a direct impact on an entity’s liquidity and funding and its overall profitability.

The two main objectives of working capital management are to increase the profitability of an entity and to ensure that the entity has sufficient liquidity to meet its short-term obligations as they fall due (in order to be able to continue in business). Attempts to maximise the profitability of the components of working capital may create serious liquidity pressures. Conversely, concentration on liquidity tends to diminish profitability as the entity holds a greater proportion of liquid assets that are relatively lower earning assets.

Management must therefore seek to establish the optimal trade-off between profitability of the current assets employed and the holding of sufficient liquidity to maintain the ability to pay current liabilities as they fall due. An entity needs to ensure it has sufficient liquid resources arising from its operating activities to continue in business by satisfying both upcoming operational expenses and maturing debt.

As will be discussed next, the level of net working capital can be interpreted from both a liquidity and a funding requirement perspective.

### 6.1.2 Net Working Capital and Liquidity

Net working capital reflects the amount of working capital an entity would have left over if it settled its existing short-term liabilities. This approach assumes that net working capital is the excess of current assets relative to current liabilities and is therefore a measure of an entity’s liquidity.

Most entities have more current assets than current liabilities, so net working capital is typically positive for most entities. However, some entities, such as construction companies, can have negative working capital without necessarily facing a liquidity crisis. For example, when materials needed for construction are placed on site in the early stages of a job, the construction entity may have been granted more generous credit terms by their suppliers (accounts payable) than the credit terms it has imposed on its customers (accounts receivable).

As a general rule, the larger an entity’s net working capital, the greater its liquidity. However, it is important to understand the potential implications of such an outcome because the twin goals of liquidity and profitability will often conflict, as discussed below:

• If the level of liquidity is excessive, the entity’s rates of return will be lower, and its profitability may decrease. Funds tied up in cash and excess inventory earn little, marketable securities typically yield low returns and receivable levels that are too high deprive the entity of funds that can be reinvested.

• If the level of liquidity is too low, the entity may not be able to meet its liabilities as they fall due. This may adversely affect the creditworthiness of the entity, and it will face difficulties obtaining funds at a reasonable cost in the future. It may result in the entity needing to borrow at high rates of interest and may ultimately force the entity into insolvency. If the entity’s inventory level is too low, delays in meeting orders may result in lost sales as customers shift to competitors.

### 6.1.3 Net Working Capital and Funding

The amount of working capital an entity needs tends to fluctuate over time as its sales rise and fall with economic cycles and the amount of seasonality in demand for the entity’s products. These fluctuations directly affect the funding requirements of the entity. Consider the following examples:

• Christmas Ornamentals is a privately owned entity that specialises in making Christmas decorations. The entity might build up finished goods inventories in the period from March to June each year as it prepares to distribute its products to retailers in the period from July to September to be ready for sale by retailers in the Christmas holiday season. For the entity producing the decorations, working capital will remain high through the period from July to September as finished goods are sold and converted into accounts receivable. However, working capital will decline in January as receivables are collected, and cash is reinvested in the business. Shortly after, the seasonal pattern will begin again. These fluctuations reflect seasonal working capital needs.

• In contrast, an entity such as HK Flex Ltd, as discussed in the case study, may provide an agreed constant monthly volume of its chemical manufactured products to automobile and parts manufacturers who produce at a constant rate throughout the year. HKFlex will hold only a small amount of finished goods, knowing that the products manufactured in any month will be sold each month. Subject to the credit terms negotiated, HKFlex may expect the accounts receivable to be paid in a consistent continuous manner over the year.

As can be seen, both of these examples have different funding requirements. For the Christmas decorations manufacturer, payments for the finished goods will not be received via accounts receivable until the period from January to March of the following year. In contrast, HKFlex will receive continuous accounts receivable payments throughout the year. Similarly, the Christmas decorator will need to store the finished goods inventory until distribution in July to September each year, whereas HKFlex will hold a small volume of permanent inventory but will continuously distribute its production throughout the year.

The differences between these examples highlight that, due to the different business models and the effects of seasonality and economic cycles, the short-term and long-term funding decisions of entities will be impacted differently. As shown above, some working capital needs are short term, seasonal or transitory in nature, while others are long term, or permanent, in nature. Therefore, it is possible to define working capital via time:

> Total Working Capital = Permanent Working Capital + Transitory Working Capital

Permanent working capital (or long-term working capital) can be defined as the minimum level of investment in working capital needed to sustain the entity’s normal long-term operating level. In contrast, transitory working capital (or short-term or seasonal working capital) can be defined as the level of investment in current assets to cope with seasonal or transitory working capital needs.

A lower working capital requirement can be achieved by reducing any of the three components of current assets (i.e. cash, inventory and accounts receivable) or by increasing accounts payable. Whilst the practice of reducing current assets and increasing current liabilities will decrease the size of an entity’s net working capital, the business practices of the entity will have a direct impact on the net working capital position of the entity and the choices that need to be made to fund any existing working capital requirements.

As discussed in Chapter 5, funding can be undertaken using one of the following approaches:

• Maturity matching funding strategy, which is based on the principle that the maturity of a liability should match the maturity of the asset it funds. Short-term or transitory working capital is funded by short-term financing, whilst long-term assets and permanent working capital are funded using long-term funding.

• Long-term funding strategy, which involves a conservative strategy whereby longterm debt and equity are used to fund fixed assets, permanent working capital, and transitory working capital.

• Short-term funding strategy, which involves an aggressive strategy whereby transitory working capital and a significant portion of the permanent working capital are funded using short-term debt. The remainder of the permanent capital is funded with longterm debt and equity.

In determining its financing decisions, an entity must clearly balance profitability and risk when reaching a decision about the funding of current and non-current assets. Decisions will need to be made about whether funding should be short or long term in nature and the type of funding available.

### 6.1.4 Interpretation and Impact of Net Working Capital

Net working capital can be either positive or negative. There are different ways that a company’s finances can be affected by the calculated net working capital.

So how should positive and negative outcomes for net working capital be interpreted?

#### 6.1.4.1 Positive Net Working Capital

If net working capital is positive (typically because holdings of accounts receivable and inventory exceed accounts payable), liquidity is strengthened, since current assets are easily convertible into cash, and the entity is able to repay its short-term liabilities as they fall. This mitigates the risk of insolvency but harms overall profitability because of the large funding commitment required to fund the excess levels of inventory and accounts receivable. This can lead to higher inventory and financing costs, which can reduce profitability.

Excess amounts of positive working capital can create a drag on financial performance. Current assets that do not contribute to return on equity (such as obsolete inventory and uncollectable accounts receivable) hinder the performance of the entity.

Increasingly managers look to reduce current assets to the level where current liabilities can be funded from the ongoing operations of the business. For example, cash collected from sales is used to settle trade payables and employee benefits.

#### 6.1.4.2 Negative Net Working Capital

If net working capital is negative, this may suggest that accounts payable is larger than accounts receivable and inventory combined. This can occur when an entity has strong bargaining power and can delay payment for its inventory for a period that is longer than the life cycle of the inventory and accounts receivable. If an entity can perform in this way, it is possible to generate large levels of cash and marketable securities as debtors settle their accounts in advance of the entity having to pay for the inventory used.

Negative net working capital can also occur if an entity is carrying large amounts of shortterm debt relative to current assets or if the entity currently is unable to meet the demand for its goods because it has insufficient inventory. This supply shortage can cause a reduction in accounts receivable and may mean that the entity is unable to meet its short-term liabilities as they fall due. This can both harm growth and result in a loss of goodwill towards customers. Also, tighter liquidity, through reduced holdings of cash and marketable securities may harm an entity’s creditworthiness and impact the availability of future funding.

The stability of net working capital during this period was due to the working capital management strategies adopted by HKFlex, involving improved inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable management.

### 6.1.5 Management of Working Capital

Working capital management involves management of both current assets and current liabilities so as to achieve the maximum profitability for the entity as it conducts its operational activities, whilst also managing, concurrently, the solvency of the entity.

The goal of working capital management is to maintain the optimal mix of current assets and liabilities that enables the entity to continue its day-to-day operations and ensures the entity has sufficient liquid resources to continue in business and increase its profitability. Essentially, this involves achieving a balance between the need to minimise the risk of insolvency (liquidity) and the desire to maximise the return on assets (profitability).

The following discussion highlights the primary issues arising from holding an excessive or an insufficient level of working capital.

When there is excessive working capital this may lead to:
• The entity holding assets that do not earn profits for the business resulting in the business failing to earn an appropriate rate of return on its investments;
• The entity holding excessive debtors and having a defective credit policy which, in turn, may lead to a higher incidence of bad debts; and
• A lower rate of return on the entity’s investments, resulting in a reduction in the entity’s share price.

When there is a redundant working capital this may lead to:
• Overall inefficiency in the organisation; and
• Unnecessary building up of inventories, increasing opportunities for theft, waste and other losses, for example, due to inventory becoming obsolete.

When there is insufficient or inadequate working capital this may lead to:
• An inability to create sufficient liquidity to meet short-term liabilities;
• A loss of reputation affecting the ability to obtain future credit facilities;
• An inability to buy in bulk at lower prices; and
• An inability to undertake profitable opportunistic projects.

Working capital management is important due to its potential effect on the long-term profitability of the entity. If inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable are efficiently managed, this should reduce the funding needs of working capital and reduce the cash requirements of running the entity. If appropriate adjustments can be made on a sustainable basis then the funding needs for working capital will be reduced leading to lower debt requirements and the potential for higher dividends to shareholders. Both of these will result in a higher entity value.

Because of their short-term nature, decisions involving current assets and current liabilities are typically more flexible than long-term capital investment decisions. However, entities still need to manage their day-to-day operations diligently, so as not to suffer severe financial consequences, including reputational impacts and insolvency.

Through the use of alternative operating and financial strategies, entities can improve liquidity, reduce funding costs for working capital and increase profitability through efficiency in management of each of the following operating components of net working capital:
• Cash and marketable securities
• Inventory
• Accounts receivable
• Accounts payable

Each entity has to balance the above components to obtain the optimum amount of working capital needed to run the business. Practices involved in the management of each of the above will be discussed in detail in Sections 6.2.2–6.2.5.

When it comes to funding working capital, financial managers need to determine the amount of funding required. If sales are expected to increase, then this will require more inventory for production and may increase the size of existing accounts receivable as existing customers increase their purchases or new customers commence purchasing.

Typically, an entity will have only limited ability to increase the term over which accounts payable can be settled, without the risk of incurring higher costs (losing discounts or having to pay penalties), thus choosing the level of current assets that the entity holds is essentially the same as choosing the amount of net working capital.

There are three alternative strategies used for working capital management: flexible, restrictive and trade-off.

#### 6.1.5.1 Flexible Current Asset Management Strategy

A flexible current assets management strategy involves an entity holding large, and at times excessive, amounts of cash, marketable securities, inventory and accounts receivable. By holding these high balances of current assets, an entity is perceived to have high levels of liquidity and therefore be able to withstand any major threats to the business by virtue of being able to use the assets to smooth fluctuations in business conditions.

This strategy is, however, potentially problematic because:

• Current assets (especially cash and marketable securities) typically provide lower returns than long-term assets such as buildings, land and plant and equipment;

• By investing in current assets, management creates an opportunity cost to the entity by forgoing the higher rate of return it could have earned by investing in long-term assets;

• Excess levels of inventory can have high carrying costs, can become obsolete and will require higher insurance costs; and

• Offering relaxed credit terms may result in higher levels of default among accounts receivable customers.

#### 6.1.5.2 Restrictive Current Asset Management Strategy

A restrictive current assets management strategy involves an entity holding minimal amounts of current assets. This typically requires holding small amounts of cash and marketable securities, keeping inventory to low levels and placing strict credit terms on its customers, thereby restricting access to accounts receivable. By restricting investment in current assets, the entity can use a larger proportion of its capital for investment in higher yielding long-term assets.

However, placing restrictions on current assets may create the following problems:

• Liquidity problems may arise if insufficient cash and marketable securities are held to meet normal and abnormal operating conditions.

• Low liquidity may affect the ability of the entity to meet its accounts payable and other billings as they fall due and may result in the entity needing to use expensive external short-term borrowing. In some cases, if outside funding cannot be secured, the entity may default on some current liabilities and run the risk of being forced into insolvency by creditors.

• Low liquidity may impact the entity’s credit rating and increase its cost of borrowing.

• Low levels of inventory may lead to operational problems if there is insufficient inventory for use in the production process or customer dissatisfaction if there are insufficient finished goods available for sale.

• Restrictions on accounts receivable may impact the level of credit sales as customers may turn to alternative suppliers prepared to offer credit on better terms.

#### 6.1.5.3 Working Capital Trade-Off Strategy

When considering the preferred level of working capital most managers engage in a decision process known as the working capital trade-off. This involves an assessment of the benefits and costs of having low levels of current assets (shortage costs) versus the benefits and costs of holding high levels of current assets (storage costs).

As the level of current assets changes over time managers may need to switch between the practices of flexible and restrictive working capital management to maintain a long run working capital position consistent with the goals and strategic requirements of the entity.

Overall, if applying the working capital trade-off strategy, then an entity will undertake activities involving current assets to try to find the level that minimises the sum of the carrying costs and shortage costs.

When identifying and assessing the working capital strategy being applied by an entity, it should be noted that the working capital strategy and supporting policies of an entity can be characterised into one of the above categories and can be compared with the working capital policies of similar entities. Unfortunately, there are no absolute benchmarks of what may be regarded as flexible, restrictive or otherwise, but the above observations about each of the strategies are useful for analysing the ways in which individual entities approach the operational problem of working capital management.

In the next sections students will consider the key factors that determine the level of working capital, how to calculate the level of working capital investment required for an entity and techniques used in the management of accounts receivable, accounts payable and inventory, in order to improve efficiency.
