## 6.2 KEY DRIVERS OF WORKING CAPITAL

This section will address Learning Outcome 6.02.02 and in particular will focus on how to calculate the level of working capital investment for a given situation and explain the key factors that determine this level. As discussed in Section 6.1, net working capital is the capital required in the short term to run an entity’s day-to-day operations, and it entails the management of an entity’s short-term operating assets and liabilities.

Due to differences in a range of external and internal factors affecting an entity, the level of investment in working capital required differs from entity to entity and industry to industry.

External factors affecting the level of working capital include:
• Business cycle impacts, such as changes in the overall level of economic activity, inflation and the level of interest rates affecting working capital expenditure;
• Technological developments and industry-wide changes in production techniques, for example, improvements in robotics can speed up production and reduce the timing of the production cycles of entities in an industry; and

• Changes in government policy, regulations and taxation can directly affect working capital availability; for example, restrictions on international borrowing, foreign exchange or capital flows may impact the type of money market or capital market securities available for funding working capital.

Internal factors affecting the level of working capital include:
• The nature and size of the business;
• The prospects for growth and expansion of the business;
• The entity’s production cycle, which starts with the purchase and use of raw material and ends with the production and sale of finished goods, – the working capital requirement will be higher for entities with large or complex production cycles;
• The entity’s operating efficiency, which means the optimum utilisation of an entity’s resources at minimum cost – efficiencies can be obtained through both the supply and distribution channels used by the entity where established channels result in lower information asymmetries and co-ordination between entities; and
• Access to money and capital markets – restrictions affecting access to capital markets will restrict liquidity and impact the ability of the entity to fund its operations and may also impact its ability to purchase inventory on credit via accounts payable.

Other entity specific factors include:
• The entity’s cash management strategy – entities with tighter controls and deeper understanding of the timing, size, currency and type of cash inflows and outflows associated with the entity’s operating and financial obligations typically operate with lower costs of working capital due to better liquidity management practices;
• The entity’s inventory management processes – entities with tighter inventory management practices and production protocols have lower working capital requirements than entities without these practices;
• The entity’s credit policy – entities with a liberal credit policy to all customers require higher levels of working capital funding than entities that adopt a strict credit policy and grant credit facilities to few potential customers; and
• The availability of trade credit – entities with access to liberal credit terms from suppliers and banks will have less working capital needs relative to those operating with restrictive terms.

### 6.2.1 Operating Cycle and Cash Conversion Cycle

The operational assets and liabilities of an entity directly impact its working capital requirements. These assets and liabilities can be optimised by an entity to generate profits and liquidity and are directly affected by operational strategies and policies of the entity. This section will introduce two important concepts in working capital management: the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle.

#### 6.2.1.1 Operating Cycle

The operating cycle reflects the time from the receipt of raw materials to the collection of cash typically via accounts receivable for the sale of finished goods made from those materials. The operating cycle can be described in terms of two components: the number of days that sales are tied up in inventory (raw materials, work in progress and finished goods) and the number of days between the date of sale of the finished product until payment is received for the sale. Thus, it reflects the time associated with the inventory conversion period and the accounts receivable collection period.

The operating cycle can be estimated as:
> Operating Cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)

The operating cycle is also known as the working capital cycle.

#### 6.2.1.2 Cash Conversion Cycle

The cash conversion cycle (also known as the net working capital cycle or cash cycle) is the residual time between an entity’s payment for raw materials (via accounts payable) and the end of the operating cycle. It represents the time between an entity’s payment for the initial inventory and its receipt of payment for the sale of the finished goods from the inventory. It can therefore be used to assess the relationship between inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable.

Consider a manufacturing entity such as HKFlex in the Opening Case. The entity buys and receives chemicals used as part of its production process to create finished goods, such as polyethylene, polycarbonate (PC) and polyethylene terephthalate (PUT). The finished goods are held as inventory prior to distribution and sale via accounts receivable to buyers in the automobile and parts industries in mainland China, Japan and Korea. The inventory is paid for in the future by HKFlex using accounts payable but typically before the receipt of accounts receivable from the sale of the finished products. Cash received from accounts receivable is then used to fund the acquisition of raw materials in the future and the conversion costs for a new operating cycle.

Alternatively, consider a retailer. Retailers buy and receive finished goods typically from wholesalers and distributors. These finished goods are held as inventory either as stock in warehouses prior to sale or stock held for sale on the floor of their stores. The inventory is paid for in the future by using accounts payable but typically before the receipt of accounts receivable from the sale of the finished products. Cash received from accounts receivable is then used to fund future finished goods for a new operating cycle.

The cash conversion cycle gives the average time it takes for the entity to receive payment from debtors (accounts receivable) after it has paid its trade creditors (accounts payable). This time period will require financing by the entity. This financing will result in a cost to the entity and therefore needs to be minimised in order to reduce this cost of operations.

The length of the cash conversion cycle can be estimated by considering the number of days that sales are tied up in inventory plus the number of days between the date of sale of the finished product until payment is received for the sale less the number of days until the entity actually pays for its raw materials (otherwise known as the accounts payables period).

The cash conversion cycle can be estimated as:

> Cash Conversion Cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) - Days Payables Outstanding (DPO) = Operating Cycle DPO

The formulas used to calculate DSI, DSO and DPO are discussed in Section 6.3.2.

The operating cycle and cash conversion cycle are shown diagrammatically in Exhibit 6.1, which shows the relationships between the cash inflows and outflows involving the inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable periods. These two cycles are closely related. For example, if an entity pays cash for its inventory, then the operating cycle is identical to the cash conversion cycle. However, most entities buy their inventory on credit, which reduces the amount of time between the cash investment in inventories (accounts payable) and the receipt of cash from the sales of the finished goods (accounts receivable). The longer an entity’s cash conversion cycle, the more working capital it has, and the more cash the entity will need to fund its daily operations.
![](DraggedImage-101.png)

### Illustrative Example 2

Assume the following details:

A number of commercial and residential properties in Hong Kong have a 10-metre granite sculpture on display in the courtyard or the foyer of their buildings. HK Commercial Properties Ltd has recently commissioned HK Statues Ltd, a boutique entity specialising in commercial sculpting and other artisan work, to provide them with a specified number of sculptures.

The following events occur:

• HK Statues Ltd orders granite blocks to be used for the sculptures from its supplier, HK Igneous Ltd. The blocks will be delivered in 15 days.

• HK Igneous Ltd requires payment for the granite to be made on credit terms by HK Statues that allow 75 days from the delivery of the granite.

• From the date of receipt of the granite, it will take HK Statues 120 days to finalise the sculptures and to have them ready for sale to HK Commercial Properties.

• From the date of sale, HK Commercial Properties will have 90 days until they have to pay for the sculptures.

Based on the above information:

• The days sales in inventory (DSI) period is equal to 120 days which represents the period during which the raw materials are converted into sculptures. (Note that the delivery time for the rocks (15 days) is not included in this period as there are no costs involved here and the granite does not become the inventory of HK Statues Ltd until such time as the raw materials have been delivered.)

• The days payables outstanding (DPO) is equal to 75 days which represents the date at which payment will be made for the granite.

• The days sales outstanding (DSO) reflecting the period to collect the accounts receivable is equal to 90 days which is from the date of sale when the goods are finished until payment is made by HK Commercial Properties.

The operating cycle is equal to 120 + 90 days = 210 days.
The cash conversion cycle is equal to 120 + 90 - 75 days = 135 days.

From the date of receipt of the raw materials, HK Statues will receive no payments for the work performed until 210 days later (the operating cycle). After 75 days from the receipt of the raw materials the entity will need to pay for the granite blocks (accounts payable). This payment can be made using borrowed funds during the period of 120 to 210 days. Given the payment is not received until day 210, any borrowed funds will not be repaid until that date. Therefore, the cash conversion cycle represents the period of time for which the entity will require financing.

#### 6.2.1.3 Interpreting and Managing the Cash Conversion Cycle

The cash conversion cycle is an important concept because the length of the cash conversion cycle is directly related to an entity’s liquidity and the amount of capital that an entity needs to finance its working capital.

If the cash conversion cycle is positive this indicates that the operating cycle is longer than the days payables outstanding. In this case, the entity has to wait until the end of the cycle to receive the cash inflow from its accounts receivable payments despite having paid the accounts payable cash outflow earlier. Given that the entity has paid its accounts payable prior to the receipt of the accounts receivable, the entity will need to fund this payment either from existing cash or by borrowing money for the cash conversion cycle period.

If the cash conversion cycle is negative this indicates that the operating cycle is shorter than the days payables outstanding. In this case, the entity does not have to pay its accounts payable (cash outflow) until after the end of the cash conversion cycle (cash inflow). Given that the entity will receive the accounts receivable receipts prior to the payment of the accounts payable, the entity will have surplus cash during this period, will not need to borrow funds to fund the accounts payable payment and can invest the surplus funds in marketable securities or use the surplus to repay existing debt.

The shorter the cash conversion cycle, the lower will be the entity’s reliance upon external sources of costly finance, such as short- and long-term debt. Excessive working capital investments in inventory and accounts receivable can lead to lost interest on marketable securities, excessive interest payments and lost investment opportunities. The longer the cash conversion cycle, the more capital is needed to finance it. Given the above observations, entities need to consider how they may be able to reduce the time period of the cash conversion cycle to reduce the impact on liquidity and capital.

Ideally, an entity should aim to minimise the length of its cash operating cycle, consistent with the need for sufficient liquidity. This can be achieved by using the strategies discussed in the next section to manage the various components of the cash conversion cycle.

The next four sections discuss how cash, inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable management can all be used to improve both the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle of an entity. This is then followed by an example of how an entity can determine its working capital requirements.

### 6.2.2 Cash Management

Cash and marketable securities are one of the most important components of current assets. HKAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows defines cash and cash equivalents.

Every entity should have adequate cash to meet both their expected requirements to conduct their business operations and some precautionary cash to meet potential unexpected requirements. Inadequate cash will lead to production interruptions, while excessive cash remains idle and will impair profitability.

As discussed in Chapter 5, entities hold cash for three primary motives:

• Transactions motive – This is the cash needed to meet day-to-day needs and includes regular payment commitments such as accounts payable, rent, employee benefits, dividends and taxes. Entities need a cash reserve for transactions purposes, with cash set aside for both daily cash outflow and other anticipated cash flow needs.
• Precautionary motive – This cash is held by the business to maintain a ‘buffer’ of cash for contingencies, such as unexpected demands on cash. Forecasts of future cash flow requirements are subject to uncertainty, and unexpected events may occur that require urgent access to cash; for example, if a conveyor belt was to unexpectedly malfunction, an entity may need to urgently engage an engineering consultant to make repairs.

• Speculative motive – This is the cash held for speculative purposes such as to take advantage of an investment opportunity that may suddenly arise, such as purchasing inventory at a discounted price due to the liquidation of a current supplier.

Entities hold cash for use either as physical cash, in the form of coins and notes, as cheques or drafts, directly in bank accounts or in near cash assets, such as term deposits or marketable securities such as certificates of deposit and negotiable bills. Some entities also hold cash in bank deposits as collateral called compensating balance accounts. Banks will often require entities to hold minimal cash balance accounts as partial compensation or as collateral for the loans and other services provided by the banks.

#### 6.2.2.1 Identifying Cash Requirements

Cash flows cannot be predicted with certainty due to problems associated with the accuracy of data inputs (such as problems associated with irregularities in cash flows, unexpected delays in collections and disbursements, defaults and expected cash needs), collection techniques, analysis of data and the unpredictability of approaches.

As discussed in Chapter 5, the primary approaches used by entities to identify their cash needs include:

• Identifying the cash inflows and outflows of the entity by type, amount, timing and currency;
• Matching expected cash inflows and outflows to estimate whether the entity will have a cash surplus or shortfall in any period so as to determine whether the entity will have surplus funds that need to be invested or shortfalls that may require access to funds either through the sale of existing cash-like instruments or through the use of funding such as bank overdrafts;
• Managing the impact on the entity, of a sustained period of negative cash flow, such as deterioration of credit quality, which may impact the entity’s credit rating, the ability to obtain or retain trade credit, transaction costs associated with borrowing and increased interest costs or penalty rates on overdue payments;
• Managing excess cash to avoid lost opportunities to obtain higher investment returns; and
• Managing the operational costs of staff and IT systems used in managing cash via bank accounts, securities and short-term borrowing facilities.

As discussed in Section 6.1, net working capital has a direct impact on an entity’s liquidity. This can also be assessed via the cash conversion cycle where it can be seen that a positive cash conversion cycle requires the entity to use non-spontaneous financing (bank lines, secured financing arrangements and other forms of financing) to support the cash conversion cycle.

In contrast, a negative cash conversion cycle may be favourable for the entity’s cash position because the day’s payables outstanding exceeds the operating cycle. However, caution is needed with this interpretation because a negative cash conversion cycle may indicate that an entity has stretched its average payment period to an unreasonable length and may lose future supply agreements on favourable terms. Non-manufacturing entities are more likely than manufacturing entities to have a negative cash conversion cycle, as they can often carry smaller, faster moving inventory and often sell their products for cash. With a negative cash conversion cycle, excess spontaneous financing can be used for other aspects of the business such as for the acquisition of fixed assets.

#### 6.2.2.2 Managing Cash Requirements

An entity needs to maintain sufficient cash balances to meet the transactional obligations of the entity and its precautionary and speculative cash needs. Cash management is concerned with optimising the amount of cash available, maximising the interest earned by the short-term investment of funds not required immediately and reducing losses caused by delays in the transmission of funds. In doing so, two primary conflicting objectives need to be managed:

• To make the payments when they become due.
• To minimise the cash balances.

The objective of cash management is to maximise an entity’s cash flow at minimal cost through the use of effective and efficient practices and techniques designed to:
• Accelerate and control collections;
• Ensure prompt deposit of receipts;
• Improve control over collection and disbursement methods; and
• Eliminate idle cash balances by investing funds into marketable securities, working capital or project activities.

By holding cash to meet short-term needs, entities may experience an opportunity cost equal to the return which could have been earned if the cash had been invested or put to productive use. This is because cash or cash-like balances typically earn a much lower rate of return than the entity’s productive capacity can generate. However, reducing this opportunity cost by operating with small cash balances will increase the risk of being unable to meet an entity’s financial obligations as they fall due, so an optimum cash balance should be found.

In practice, some caution is needed when implementing cash management strategies as cash flow problems can arise within entities due to a range of possible reasons such as:

• Slow cash collection facilities that create delays between payments by customers and receipt of funds, such as the use of credit cards, cheques or money order transfers. Cash receipts, direct debit and other forms of electronic funds transfer can be used to expedite cash collection.
• In a period of growth, more cash is required for the acquisition and maintenance of non-current assets and for holding greater amounts of inventories and accounts receivable.
• In a period of inflation, an ever-increasing amount of cash is required simply to replace used up and redundant assets.

• Seasonal or cyclical sales may result in cash flow difficulties in periods when cash inflows are lower than cash outflows (for example an entity specialising in the retailing of ski equipment is likely to have less favourable net cash flows during the summer than the winter months).

• A single non-recurring item of expenditure may create a cash flow problem requiring use of precautionary funds if it is not planned for or forecasted in the cash flow budget.

##### Day-to-Day Management of the Cash Float

An important aspect of managing cash involves management of the ‘cash float’, which is the time period between the initiation of a payment and the receipt of the payment. On some occasions this can take up to several days. Typical problems encountered when trying to manage the cash float include:

• The time that it takes from initiation of a payment to the receipt of the payment (known as the transmission delay);
• The delay in depositing any payments received by the seller (known as the lodgement delay); and
• The time taken by a financial institution to clear a presented instruction to pay (known as the clearance delay).

Ideally, entities should look for ways in which the cash float can be minimised. This can be achieved via the use of electronic payment methods or the use of simplifying processes such as netting payments.

The optimal level of cash needed by an entity is a function of the entity’s activity level, efficiency of operations, production and cost structures. Caution is needed to avoid excessively low or high balances.

##### Cash Surpluses and Shortages

Management can forecast cash requirements. These forecasts can be examined to assess whether an entity is likely to experience a period of cash shortages or cash surpluses.

##### Cash Shortages

If cash balances become too small (cash shortages), the entity runs the risk that it will be unable to meet its financial obligations as they fall due, may breach loan covenants and may be unable to continue to purchase inventory which will slow any further production, thereby increasing the risk of further loss. If the entity is unable to honour its accounts payable and debt obligations, it may be forced into insolvency.

Cash shortages can be eased by taking longer to pay accounts payable and negotiating early payment on accounts receivable from customers. If the cash shortage will be sustained, then consideration should be given to using short-term financing alternatives (discussed in Chapter 5) such as:

• Bank loans;
• Commercial paper;
• Overdrafts;
• Accounts receivable and inventory asset backed loans;
• Factoring of accounts receivables; and
• Supply chain finance (to be discussed in Section 6.4.1).

If the deficits are expected to continue into the long term, consideration should be given to postponing capital expenditure and if necessary, closing divisions or selling assets. From a funding perspective, consideration should also be given to issuing long-term equity capital.

##### Cash Surpluses

If cash balances become too high (cash surpluses), the entity may suffer an opportunity loss if the returns on cash are low and the excess cash could have been used in productive pursuits.

Cash surpluses can be managed by taking advantage of discounts through early repayment of accounts payable, providing more generous terms on accounts receivable to defer cash receipts and conversion from cash to investments in marketable securities.

Prior to investing in short-term marketable securities, an entity should consider factors such as:
• The size of the surplus;
• The risk of and yield on the investments;
• Whether to make domestic or international investments; and
• Restrictions regarding the ability to redeem investments early if cash is required.

If the cash surplus is likely to be sustained in the long term, consideration should be given to expanding the business into other markets and/or products and undertaking capital expenditure to add and/or replace existing assets.

### 6.2.3 Inventory Management

Inventories are assets used in the production process and assets acquired for onselling. They can be categorised as:
• Raw materials (inventory that is yet to be used in the production or manufacturing process);
• Work in progress (inventory that is currently being used or transformed in the production or manufacturing process); and
• Finished goods (inventory that has been finalised and is waiting for sale and assets that have been acquired for onselling).

The inventory needs of a production or manufacturing entity differ significantly from those of a service-based entity. A manufacturer will have inventory requirements relating to each of the above three types of inventory and needs to manage the supply, use and storage of completed goods prior to distribution. Retailers typically hold negligible levels of raw materials and work in progress but hold high levels of finished goods in warehouses and available for sale in their retail stores. In contrast, service-based entities typically hold little or no inventory.

Entities need to manage their inventory requirements throughout the year. Some entities experience either cyclical or seasonal inventory requirements. Cyclic inventory is the portion of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods inventory available to meet normal customer demand during normal operating periods. It is one of the more important components of overall inventory management. It is the amount of inventory needed to meet normal customer needs and is also conditional upon the storage capacity of the entity’s warehouses and on its production requirements. This level of inventory normally cycles through periods of two to three months at which time it needs to be refreshed with new inventory.

In contrast, seasonal inventory represents the excess amounts of inventory required to meet demand during particular seasonal periods of the year. For example, consider a soft drink manufacturer which will require access to carbonated water and sugar and colour syrups to manufacture its drinks. Across the whole year there would be an anticipated level of demand for its products that can generally be forecasted. Beyond this level, during summer months there will be a seasonal uplift in demand which may require increased levels of production to meet the seasonal needs. This additional seasonal production will require inventory in excess of the underlying normal cyclical requirements.

Inventory management requires an assessment of the benefits of holding inventory weighed against any costs incurred in purchasing inventory if the optimal inventory levels are to be determined.

For manufacturers and retailers, inventories represent a large investment that does not earn interest or a return until such time as the inventories are sold. The period of time that inventory is held within an entity can be reduced by minimising the holding of raw materials and finished goods and by improving the efficiency of production processes to reduce work-in-progress.

Employing better practices in respect of inventory ordering, storage and delivery methods keeps the level of inventories to a minimum and the working capital used to its lowest practicable level. It is important to avoid both understocking and overstocking of inventory.

On the positive side, holding inventories as raw materials and as work-in-progress allows the entity to have a buffer of inventories to meet production requirements. Insufficient inventory in these categories may lead to delays in production. Also, by holding finished goods as inventory also allows consumer demand to be met without unreasonable delay and the potential loss of sales.

On the negative side, potential costs relating to inventory management include:
• Holding costs, which represent the direct costs of holding the goods in stock, such as administrative costs of keeping stock records, insurance, rent, storage costs and utility charges;
• Costs resulting from large holdings of inventories, including: financing costs; warehousing costs (higher rental costs and/or higher acquisition and maintenance costs); higher costs resulting from protecting the inventory against spoilage; greater losses resulting from theft and a greater risk of obsolescence;
• Ordering costs, including procurement expenses that are incurred each time an inventory purchase is made, such as search costs in finding a suitable supplier, and costs associated with inspections of reordered stocks;
• Replacement costs, including the cost of damaged, obsolete, deteriorated or stolen inventory;
• The cost of the inventory itself;
• The opportunity cost of being out of stock, resulting in lost sales and shutdowns in production; and
• The opportunity cost of cash tied up in inventory.

#### 6.2.3.1 Inventory Decision Models

The principal goal of inventory decision models is to determine the minimum possible annual cost of ordering and stocking amounts for each item. Two major variables are typically used for this purpose:
• The order quantity, that is, the size and frequency of orders. This amount should reflect the optimal level of inventory for each item; and
• The point when reordering should occur (the reorder point), that is, the minimum stock level at which additional quantities should be reordered.

Numerous specialised models and techniques exist to manage inventory levels within entities. Examples of inventory models used by entities include the following:
• Economic order quantity (EOQ)
• Just-in-time (JIT) inventory control
• ABC analysis inventory control

Each of these approaches to inventory management is discussed below.

Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) Model The economic order quantity (EOQ) model calculates the optimal order quantity that minimises the total costs incurred to order and hold inventory by balancing the costs of holding inventory against the costs of ordering fresh supplies.

Exhibit 6.2 shows the inverse relationship between the benefits of holding inventory relative to the costs of being out of inventory. This exhibit highlights four important characteristics of this relationship:
![](DraggedImage-102.png)
• If the quantity of inventory purchases is equal to the cost of carrying the inventory, then the total costs of inventory and the required level of investment in inventory will be at its minimum.
• As inventory increases, the risk of running out of inventory decreases but the cost of storage and handling will increase.
• If the quantity of inventory purchases is decreased, the cost of ordering increases while the cost of carrying decreases.
• If inventory levels are too low this can lead to issues in production, causing a slow-down in the production of finished goods and possibly delays in distribution to buyers.

The EOQ approach is a widely used method of computing the minimum annual cost for ordering and stocking each item.

Assume that an entity has a need to reorder inventory to the inventory level Q in Exhibit 6.3. The level Q reflects the maximum level of inventory required by the entity to meet its customer demand and is also a function of the storage and warehousing capacity of the entity.
![](DraggedImage-103.png)
Consistent with the cyclical inventory requirements of the entity, this inventory (Q) is then used up at a constant rate over a period of time T, at which time the inventory is then reordered back to the level Q and the inventory cycle continues. Any restocking of inventory will occur without delay and inventory will always be restocked in full to the level Q.

Based on the above exhibit, it is possible to estimate the cost of holding inventory, the cost of ordering inventory via restocking, the total inventory cost of holding and ordering inventory and the optimal economic order quantity Q*.
> Average Inventory , A = Q / 2

Holding costs can be estimated as the entity’s average inventory times per-unit holding costs, C:
> Holding Costs = Average Inventory x C = Q / 2 x C

Assume that restocking costs (including the cost of placing orders and other administrative costs) are fixed at a cost equal to F for each order. If the entity has an annual demand for inventory equal to its level of sales D, and if the entity purchases an inventory amount equal to Q each time it places an order, the number of orders during this year will be equal to D/Q. Therefore, total ordering costs can be estimated as:
> Ordering Costs = F x D / Q

Therefore, given for both components of inventory costs (holding costs and ordering costs) the total cost of inventory can be estimated as:
> Total Inventory Costs = Holding Costs + Ordering Costs

Algebraically, this can be expressed as:
>  Total Inventory Costs = Q / 2 x C + F x D / Q

In the above equation, the variable Q represents the order quantity and is assumed to be determined specifically for the needs of each entity.

The EOQ computation takes into account the annual sales rate (D), the unit cost (F) and the cost of holding inventory (C). The minimum total cost occurs when holding costs and ordering costs are equal. Putting holding costs equal to ordering costs and rearranging the equation, the EOQ can be expressed as follows:
![](DraggedImage-104.png)
By using the EOQ approach, if a constant demand for inventory is assumed the following will happen:
• Holding costs will increase as average inventory levels and order quantity increase.
• Ordering costs will decrease as order quantity increases and the number of orders decreases.

The EOQ formula is a widely used method of computing the minimum annual cost for ordering and stocking each item.

##### Determining the Maximum Amount of Inventory with Adjustments for Lead Time and Buffer Inventory

For manufacturers and retailers, inventories represent a large investment that does not earn interest or a return until such time as the inventories are sold. The period of time that inventory is held within an entity can be reduced by minimising the holding of raw materials and finished goods and by improving the efficiency of production processes to reduce work-in-progress. However, as was shown in Exhibit 6.3, it would be a risky strategy for an entity not to reorder inventory prior to fully exhausting the existing inventory.

In practice, many entities choose to hold a minimum level of inventory (known as buffer inventory or safety stock) to reduce or eliminate the possibility of inventory shortages, which may arise because of an unexpected increase in demand or a decrease in supply. By balancing holding costs against the potential costs of running out of inventory it is possible to optimise the level of buffer inventory.

Exhibit 6.4 shows the pattern of inventory levels when an entity chooses to operate with an amount of buffer inventory. In this exhibit, regular economic orders of size Q are placed, based on an average annual demand. The lead time is shown as the period of time between the reorder and delivery of the inventory. During this period the entity must hold sufficient inventory to sustain their production requirements and meet demand. This amount reflects the stock to be depleted during the lead time, which is equal to lead time multiplied by daily usage. Because the lead time is known with some degree of certainty due to past experience and long-term supplier relationships, new orders are placed when inventory levels fall to the reorder level. The entity can meet unexpected demand during the lead time from the buffer inventory held.
![](DraggedImage-107.png)
Determining the Maximum Level of Stock (Q)

The maximum level of inventory is usually achieved when the inventory that was ordered at the ‘reorder level’ of the stock is received by the entity. This inventory is then used in the production process (as raw materials and work in process) or sold (in case of finished goods) and then reordered again at the reorder level. The reorder will take the inventory level back to the maximum level (Q). This process is then repeated on an on-going basis.

The maximum level of stock (Q) can be estimated as follows:
> Maximum Level (Q) = Reorder Level with Buffer Inventory - (Lead Time x Daily Usage) + Reorder Quantity

The formula highlights three major determining factors:

1. The reorder level with buffer inventory – If buffer inventory (or safety stock) is held, the reorder point as shown in Exhibit 6.4 can be calculated as follows:
	> Reorder Point with Buffer Inventory = Lead Time x Daily Usage + Buffer Inventory

	From this formula it is also possible to identify the level of buffer inventory by rearranging the above formula for the reorder point with buffer inventory. This is known as the minimum inventory level.

> Buffer Inventory = Reorder Point with Buffer Inventory - Lead Time x Daily Usage

2. Lead time daily usage – Once an order for inventory is placed, there will be a delay between the time of ordering and the delivery time of the ordered items (known as the inventory’s lead time). Assuming that demand and lead time are constant, to manage inventory levels, new inventory should be ordered when the stock of inventory falls to a level equal to the level of demand for inventory at the lead time.

3. Reorder quantity – When using this approach, the reorder quantity will be the amount of stock that returns the inventory to the maximum level (Q). By using the EOQ model it is still possible to determine an optimum order size. But now new inventory needs to be ordered and received before the level of inventory falls to the buffer inventory (or safety stock) level.

	Hence the average inventory level using the EOQ approach will be:

	> Average Inventory = Half of Regular Order Quantity + Buffer Inventory 
	> = Q/2 Buffer Inventory

This can be used to calculate the expected holding cost for the year.



### Illustrative Example 4

HK Game Traders Ltd decides that if demand for the new product is high, they cannot allow their inventory to fall to zero as this may result in lost sales. Management decides to implement the following two modifications to its inventory management model:

• Introduce a buffer of 20 electronic games to be in stock throughout the period.
• Establish a lead time of two days on all reordering.

With the introduction of the buffer, the average inventory will become 50 + 20 = 70 electronic games.

Assume that the entity is open for business on 250 trading days per annum. Based on the prior information, each order will have 100 games and there will be 20 orders per year. Given HK Game Traders Ltd expects to sell 2,000 new games during the year this represents approximately 8 electronic games per day.

If HK Game Traders decided to establish a two-day lead time (and there was no buffer inventory) this would represent a lead time reorder point of 16 units (2 days × 8 units 16 units). But with the buffer of 20 games the reorder point will become 36 electronic games (2 days × 8 units + 20 units of buffer stock 36 units).

##### Just-in-Time (JIT) Inventory Control

Traditionally, inventory managers stockpiled large amounts of inventory as a buffer against unexpected problems in delivery, manufacturing or distribution. For an entity, this is an expensive strategy due to the holding costs involved. Larger holdings of inventory mean higher levels of inventory storage space are needed, resulting in higher rent and/or property costs, including insurance costs.

When managing inventory, it is critical that coordination exists between entities and their suppliers to avoid uncertainties in supply, dispatching and transportation that could leave the entity with inventory problems. This can be managed via a just-in-time (JIT) inventory control system where inputs of inventory are received only as they are needed in the production process. JIT is designed to improve efficiency and reduce waste in a production process, and to minimise inventory carrying costs.

The main purpose of a JIT approach is to minimise the time that elapses between the delivery and use of inventory by minimising the amount of inventory acting as a buffer between different stages of production. The introduction of a JIT system, may reduce inventory holding costs, ordering costs and manufacturing lead times and thereby also reduce the inventory conversion time. Besides reducing inventory levels and their associated costs, the implementation of a JIT system can lead to management reworking the manufacturing processes to eliminate unnecessary steps and enhance efficiency. In that event, the outcome will be a shorter production cycle and reduced financial investment in inventory.

JIT will require the development of close relationships between the supplier and buyer of the raw materials and finished goods used as inventory. To be successful this will require the supplier to provide goods of agreed quality and reliability in a timely manner and for the buyer to be prepared to enter into long-term purchase agreements. When using a JIT system, suppliers are not selected on the basis of price alone. Important considerations also include a commitment to JIT purchasing and the performance of the supplier in providing quality goods and delivering them as needed.

##### ABC Analysis Inventory Control

ABC analysis is an inventory management approach that divides inventory/suppliers into three categories based on cost per unit and quantity held in inventory or turned over during a specified period of time. The basic principle is that high value items are more closely controlled than low value items. Segregating inventory into three categories allows different management techniques to be applied to each of the segments in order to decrease costs and increase revenue. The three categories are:

• Category A – Consists of items that have a large effect on total inventory value. This category typically comprises approximately 10%–20% of the overall inventory but accounts for about 50%–60% of the total cost of the inventory. Close management of inventory in this category should assist in maximising profitability by providing a positive increase in revenue through a minimal increase in inventory management costs. These items need to have tight inventory control, more secured storage areas and better sales forecasts. It is important to avoid stock-outs on Category A items so they are likely to have frequent reorders.

• Category B – Consists of items that have a lesser effect on inventory value. This category typically comprises approximately 25%–35% of overall inventory, and accounts for about 20%–30% of the total inventory costs. This category requires strict controls and monitoring by inventory control systems. An important aspect of category B is the monitoring of potential evolution toward category A or, to the contrary, toward category C.

• Category C – Includes items that contribute little to total inventory value. This category typically comprises approximately 50%–60% of overall inventory but accounts for about only 10%–15% of the total inventory cost. Although this category represents the greatest use of inventory, the value of these items is very low on a per unit basis and therefore typically is not monitored or assessed as actively as categories A and B. Inventory in this category is typically of low demand and is therefore reordered with less frequency than inventory in categories A or B.

Using the above categories for inventory, ABC analysis can accomplish one of two primary goals – either a reduction in procurement costs or an increase in cash flow by having the right items available for production or available for customer sales.

Alternative classification approaches to the ABC approach include:
• The high-medium-low (HML) inventory approach, which classifies inventory according to unit value, as high, medium or low valued items;
• The fast-slow-non-moving (FSN) inventory approach, which considers the speed at which inventory moves through the system, as fast, slow or non-moving;
• The vital, essential, desirable (VED) inventory approach, which classifies inventory according to the degree of urgency with which the inventory is required; and
• The scarce, difficult and easy to acquire (SDE) inventory approach, which classifies inventory based on the ease with which inventory can be obtained when required.

### 6.2.4 Accounts Receivable Management

Entities typically sell goods and services on credit rather than requiring immediate payment. These credit sales generate accounts receivable. The level of accounts receivable is typically regarded as a function of factors such as the level of sales, the credit terms provided and the riskiness of the individual customers.

The management of accounts receivable involves the management of the trade-off between the profits arising from increased sales on credit and the costs arising from the credit policies adopted, including increased administrative costs in processing, monitoring and reporting the performance of credit applications and the increased probability of bad debts.

To reduce the period of accounts receivable, entities can consider a range of possible approaches, including:

• Offering early settlement discounts to shorten average credit periods and thereby reduce the investment in accounts receivable and the interest costs associated with funding periods of the cash conversion cycle;
• Improving efficiency in collection monitoring and methods, to reduce the number and length of overdue accounts;

• Improving the quality of credit sales, to reduce overdue credit experiences by improving credit assessment processes and reducing credit approvals for poor performing customers (an entity must find the least costly balance between enticing customers, whose use of credit entails costs, and missing opportunities for profitable sales);

• Negotiating reductions in the period of credit availability with existing and future clients; and

• Entering into financial arrangements with a factor or invoice discounter, to improve cash flow and shorten the cash cycle.

Whilst most entities manage their accounts receivable via internal methods, as discussed in this section, some entities also take insurance arranged through brokers or intermediaries against the risk of bad debts. This type of insurance is normally categorised as:

• Whole turnover insurance, which covers any debt below an agreed amount against the risk of non-payment. For example, an entity may have an average accounts receivable balance per annum of HK$25 million, so it may select to insure for a loss equal to 80% of this balance (i.e. HK$20 million); and

• Specific account insurance, which will allow an entity to insure key accounts receivable against default and may be used as insurance against the performance of selected major customers.

#### 6.2.4.1 Establishing a Credit and Collection Policy

An entity’s credit and collection policies determine the amount of risk it is willing to be exposed to from its sales activities. Whether an entity has a lenient or strict credit policy can directly affect the amount of credit exposure it has and therefore the value of its accounts receivable.

An entity’s credit and collection policies can directly influence:

• The amount of trade credit provided;
• The credit limits allowed for customers of different credit standing;
• The period of time credit is allowed;
• The cash discount allowed and the period over which the discount will apply;
• The analytical tools applied to assess the credit quality of clients; and
• The collection strategies to be applied.

Entities can have credit and collection policies that exist on a spectrum, from being either lenient or strict in their application. Entities with a lenient credit and collection policy typically have the following characteristics relative to similarly sized entities that have strict credit and collection policies:

• Higher levels of accounts receivable.
• Often larger discounts and longer discount periods being offered.
• Longer periods until net payment is required.
• Credit being extended to lower credit quality customers.
• Longer collection periods beyond the net period.
• More over-due accounts.
• Higher levels of defaults.

In order to operate its accounts receivable policy, an entity needs to set up a credit analysis system, a credit control system and an accounts receivable collection system.

In formulating its accounts receivable policy, an entity should balance the benefits to be gained from offering credit to customers against the costs of doing so, including administrative costs of debt collection and the costs and effects of easing credit terms, which may increase the potential for future credit losses. In striking the right balance, the entity should ensure that the cost of increased bad debts and the cost of any additional working capital required is less than the increased profits generated by the higher turnover.

#### 6.2.4.2 Establishing the Terms of Sale

When credit is part of a sale, a terms of sale agreement sets out the terms of the credit agreement between the buyer and the seller. The terms of sale agreement specifies when the cash payment is due and the amount of any discount if an early payment is made. The size of an entity’s accounts receivable is affected by the terms of trade (or credit terms) offered by the entity. The two important components of the credit terms are the credit period and the discount rate.

There are three typical approaches to setting the terms of sale, as follows:
• Cash on delivery (COD), where the sale is by cash only and no credit is offered;
• Allowing payment to be deferred and paid in the future on net terms (net), where the number of days credit represents the number of days from the issuance of the invoice until payment needs to be made, for example, net 30 would mean payment is due 30 days from the issuance of the invoice; and
• Allowing payment to be deferred as per net payment, but offering a discount for early repayment, for example, 2.5/10, net 30 would mean payment is due 30 days from the issuance of the invoice, but the entity will offer the buyer a discount of 2.50% on the invoiced amount if they pay within the first 10 days.

##### Credit Period

Most entities prefer to receive cash from sales immediately, so as to shorten their cash conversion cycle and minimise the cost of working capital. However, the practicality of doing business, industry convention and development of trusted relationships in supply chains means that most entities will offer accounts receivable with either net terms or net terms with a discount.

Determining the optimal credit period involves the identification of the time period where the marginal profits on increased sales are exactly offset by the cost of carrying the higher amount of accounts receivable.

Most entities normally follow industry practice in establishing the length of time allowed before payment is expected (the credit period). Both lengthening or shortening the time from the industry benchmark will impact the level of the accounts receivables and the cost of working capital because:

• Extending the credit period will stimulate sales but increase the cash conversion cycle (thereby increasing the cost of working capital by tying up funds in accounts receivables) and also increase the risk of bad debts; and

• Shortening the credit period will reduce the entity’s profits due to reduced sales (as customers find alternative suppliers) but will have the positive impact of reducing the cash conversion cycle and reducing the funding required to service accounts receivable.

##### The Cash Discount

A cash discount is typically offered to customers to encourage them to pay their accounts receivable before the expiry of the credit period. By extending credit, an entity has effectively given a loan to its customers who can defer payment on the terms of their credit agreement until the agreed date for payment. By offering a discount, the entity attempts to encourage early pre-payment of the accounts receivable.

The terms of cash discounts indicate the rate of discount as well as the period for which the discount has been offered. If a discount is offered, the terms would be specified as discount rate/discount period net days. The discount rate specifies the discount that will be granted, the discount period specifies the number of days from the issuance of the invoice until the end of the discount period and the net specifies the number of days from the date of the invoice until total payment must be made if the discount is not used. For example, terms such as 2.5/10 net 30 means the entity will grant a 2.5% discount on the invoice amount if the buyer pays the discounted amount of the purchase within 10 days of the invoice date. Otherwise, the buyer has 30 days from the invoice date to pay the balance in full.

Allowing a discount on sales reduces the profitability on the sales, because it results in a direct loss to the entity (equal to the value of the discount). However, allowing a cash discount may also reduce the accounts receivable collection period (i.e. days sales outstanding – DSO) and thereby reduce the time between the sale and receipt of the accounts receivable. Hence, the optimal discount rate and discount period are established at the point where the cost and benefit are exactly offsetting.

If a discount is offered, it is possible to assess the cost of this implied loan by foregoing the opportunity to take the discount and pre-pay the accounts receivable. The implied interest rate of this loan from the seller to the buyer of the finished goods can be estimated using the effective annual interest rate as follows:
![](DraggedImage-114.png)
where the days credit is the number of days between the end of the net period less the number of days in the discount period.

Ideally, an entity offering a discount to buyers should consider the impact of the discount on their days sales outstanding (DSO). If the discount is acceptable to buyers, this will reduce the number of days until payment but at the same time will reduce the profitability of the accounts receivable position. If the discount is not acceptable to buyers, then the discount will not be taken and there is a risk that the period of time to payment may extend beyond the net period.

If the discount rate is too high, the discount period is too long or the net period is very short relative to the discount period, the annual effective rate will increase and therefore discourage buyers from accepting the discount offer and result in them delaying payment until the end of the net period. By doing so, the discount will have been ineffective, and the supplier will have effectively been granted funding at a higher effective rate.

Hence, when determining the discount an entity is willing to offer, the implied effective rate should be no higher than the entity’s cost of capital. If these effective rates are equal, the seller would be indifferent between offering or not offering the discount.

#### 6.2.4.3 Assessment of Creditworthiness

The process of assessing credit risk and determining credit limits is critical to accounts receivable management and should be detailed in an entity’s credit and collections policy. Assessment of the creditworthiness of a particular customer assists an entity in deciding whether the customer should be extended credit and the maximum amount of credit that should be allowed. In doing so, the entity may apply a range of different qualitative and/or quantitative approaches or, if the customer is already credit rated, use this information as part of their credit assessment.

Subject to the size, frequency and number of transactions performed within any year, customers will need to have approved credit, set an approved credit limit and agree to the terms and conditions upon which the credit is granted. Corporates apply a range of different approaches to performing credit assessments and setting credit limits. Different forms of assessment are typically performed to assess the likelihood that the customer seeking credit will in fact be capable and willing to make the repayment when due. These include decisions made on the basis of references, payment histories, reports from credit bureaus, credit scoring models and credit ratings.

A common qualitative approach to assessing the creditworthiness of customers involves the assessment and use of the ‘5 Cs of Credit’:

• Character – An assessment is made of the reputation of the customer, which should reflect the overall trustworthiness of the customer. A history of an absence of defaults, payment on time and good supply chain relations would provide a positive perception of the customer.

• Capacity – An assessment is made of the financial standing of the customer and whether they will be able to repay existing debt and trade credit.

• Capital – An assessment is made of the capital employed by the customer in order to understand existing levels of leverage and risk associated with its capital structure.

• Collateral – As assessment is made of the type and quality of any existing collateral to be pledged as part of the transaction as well as an assessment of the customer’s existing assets in order to understand which assets can be sold by the customer to service its obligations in the event of a liquidity crisis or default by the customer.

• Conditions – An assessment is made of the purpose of the credit as well as the terms and conditions usually specified as covenants under which the credit is permitted after considering how business, industry and general economic conditions may affect the capacity of the customer to comply with the terms and conditions.

Credit bureaus (such as Dun & Bradstreet and Experian), ratings agencies (such as Standard & Poor’s and Moody’s) and some corporate entities use the 5 Cs approach in combination with proprietary statistical credit scoring models and ratings models.

Credit scoring models typically provide a numerical credit score for each borrower and provide information to allow an entity to distinguish between ’good’ and ’bad’ customers as well as provide an estimate of the probability that the customer may default. Such models are typically used for internal risk assessment by corporate entities and financial institutions. In contrast, credit rating models provide risk classifications for corporate loans, bond issues and countries.

Credit scoring models used by entities as part of their credit risk assessment of customers typically consider information related to the borrower’s ability and willingness to repay a debt obligation based on the agreed terms. This includes information about the borrower (e.g. factors such as liquidity, leverage, profitability, previous credit experience, length of prior borrowing, etc.) that is weighted for each factor considered in the model’s formula, and a credit score is assigned based on the evaluation.

Once credit has been granted, an entity should monitor and periodically review its customers to whom credit has been granted to ensure the customers continue to observe the terms of credit, that they keep within their allocated credit limit and that their credit quality does not deteriorate.

Since the purpose of offering credit is to increase sales and maximise profitability, the costs of debt collection from accounts receivable should not be allowed to exceed the amounts recovered. The entity also needs to achieve a balance between the costs and benefits of different collection procedures or policies. The risks and costs of a customer defaulting will need to be balanced against the profitability of the business provided by that customer. Subsequently, the entity would need to continually monitor and control outstanding accounts.

6.2.4.4 Monitoring Accounts Receivable

There are several different techniques available to entities to manage their accounts receivable.

Because all accounts receivable transactions have the potential to default which may lead to a loss, especially if the accounts receivable is unsecured, entities need to calculate the expected loss from all credit exposures. From an accounting perspective, HKFRS 9 ss.5.1-5.5 cover the expected loss method for financial receivables. HKFRS 9 s.5.5.15 specifically deals with a simplified approach to trade receivables. The expected loss method is covered in Module 11, Financial Reporting. An important aspect of the expected loss method is that receivables containing a material financing element must be assessed to see whether there has been a material change in credit risk since origination.

To monitor accounts receivable, an entity needs to be able to gather the necessary data and apply an appropriate expected loss method to its financial and trade receivables. Entities also need to continuously monitor accounts receivable both in aggregate and at the level of individual entities. Apart from applying the expected loss method, entities can monitor accounts receivable through the use of an aging schedule and by reporting, via a credit utilisation report, the credit exposures relative to limits for differing degrees of credit ratings or customer types.

After establishing a credit policy that states clearly the credit standards regarding who will get extended credit, how much credit will be extended, the credit terms of sale that will apply and the entity’s collection approach, an assessment also needs to be made as to whether the policy is being implemented effectively.

Aged Receivables Analysis

An entity should prepare an aged receivables analysis and implement collection procedures for late payers. To perform this analysis the entity should prepare an aging schedule which organises the entity’s accounts receivable by their age. The aging schedule reveals patterns of delinquency and shows where collection efforts should be concentrated. This allows entities to identify and track overdue accounts and provides a mechanism for the analysis of the quality of an entity’s accounts receivable.

Having populated the schedule, it should be monitored to assess if there are any emerging trends towards a heavier weighting for accounts with longer maturities. The aging schedule can be split into overdue accounts and other accounts. This facilitates direct examination of the overdue accounts.

Effective Average Accounts Receivable Days (Average Collection Period)

The aging schedule can be also used to be calculate the effective average accounts receivable days (sometimes known as the average collection period). The effective average days outstanding is simply a weighted-average measure of the average days outstanding where the weights equal the percentage of total accounts receivable days in each account category of days outstanding.

An entity can compare its effective average accounts receivables days to the typical credit terms offered to its clients, to historical averages and to comparator entities. For example, if an entity had terms of net 90, but the average collection time is 120 days, then the entity has an average collection period 30 days longer than the terms being offered. This may be a one-off anomaly that can be traced to a change in economic conditions. However, if this was a continuous trend over time, then the credit assessment, credit terms and credit collection aspects of the credit policy need to be reviewed.

> Effective Days Accounts Receivable Outstanding = ∑( Age of Account Category in Days x Percentage of Total Accounts Receivable Outstanding for the Account Category)
