#### 6.2.4.5 Monitoring the Accounts Receivable Credit and Collection Policy

Like all policy documents, the credit and collection policy document should be subjected to annual review and where necessary amended to reflect any incremental impacts such as changing levels of default by customers and changes in the concentration of risk. The need for revisions to credit limits may arise as a result of credit limit utilisation analysis or regulatory changes affecting the granting of credit.

An entity’s accounts receivable department is responsible for keeping abreast of all communication, documentation, bookkeeping and pertinent matters concerning collecting payments from customers.

Most customers pay within the period specified in their trade credit agreements and operate within their prescribed limits if performing recurring transactions and due to their supply chain relationship. If required, such customers will from time to time seek revisions to their limits or terms of trade. However, as discussed in Section 6.2.4.4, some customers may delay payment beyond the agreed net period.

Managing the aged portion of an entity’s accounts receivable portfolio requires planned written policy on important collection procedures that will ensure consistent and effective accounts receivable management. The collection policy should include:

• When to contact a customer.
• How to contact a customer (i.e. by phone or in writing).
• When to place an account on credit hold (i.e. suspend the account so no further credit is granted until such time as outstanding balances are resolved).
• How to resolve disputes, deductions, etc.
• When to turn over delinquent accounts to a third-party collection agency and/or initiate legal action.
• When to write off an account and reclassify it as a bad debt.

Whilst it is important for an entity to follow up on outstanding balances, entities need to weigh the strictness of their collection policy against the ongoing relationship with a customer and the level of sales activity. If there are numerous potential suppliers available to the customer, invoking a strict collection policy may cause the customer to turn to alternative suppliers. Accordingly, application of an entity’s collection policy needs to reflect the particular circumstances underlying the customer relationship as well as the nature of the supply chain relationship. As will be discussed in Section 6.4.1 of this chapter, it may be possible to assist both sellers and buyers to achieve outcomes through the use of innovative supply chain finance approaches.

The effectiveness of an entity’s collection policy can be evaluated by the use of relevant benchmarks, including the following:

• Acceptable percentage of receivables by aging.
• Effective days accounts receivable outstanding.
• Acceptable level of bad debt write-offs.

### 6.2.5 Accounts Payable Management

Accounts payable are trade credits provided to entities by their suppliers. When issuing an invoice, suppliers typically offer a period of time until payment is required. Subject to the risk aversion of the supplier and the industry involved, this period may be from five days to three months. During this period no interest is charged on the invoice balance due and the supplier has effectively given the buyer an interest-free loan for the payment period.

Accounts payable is a normal component of doing business and is particularly important for small and medium sized entities that are looking to reduce their cash conversion cycle and reduce their cost of funding. It is important that entities recognise that by holding accounts payable, the entity is able to obtain a form of short-term finance other than by shortterm borrowings such as bank overdrafts. This is particularly useful because the supplier does not charge interest on the amount payable (unless overdue) and does not charge any establishment or rollover fees for the credit facility.

Whilst accounts payable provides benefits to an entity that has been extended credit, from the perspective of the supplier, this interest-free period means that they are deferring acceptance of payment and increasing their own cash conversion cycle (because from the supplier’s perspective the amount owed is an account receivable).

The primary forms of accounts payable are:

• Trade credit or trade payables (credit extended to another business); and

• Bill payables (the amount that must be paid to suppliers for which a negotiable instrument in the form of a bill of exchange has been issued by an entity for future payment of inventory or services that have been provided).

The accounts payable needs of a manufacturing entity differ significantly from those of a retailer or service-based entity. If operating efficiently in relation to inventory management and production efficiency, a manufacturer will require relatively lower levels of inventory in connection to inefficient competitors and, as such, may have lower levels of accounts payable in the form of trade payables and bills payable arising from the purchase of raw materials and work in progress inventory used in the manufacturing process. Retailers purchase most of their stock on credit and therefore typically have high levels of accounts payable. Servicebased entities typically have little to no levels of accounts payable because they are not buying inventory for manufacture or sale.

Suppliers tend to provide strong incentives to their customers (either by offering discounts for paying on time or charging penalties for late payment) for entities to pay on time.

Settlement of trade credit is normally in the form of cash, electronic money transfers via direct debit or by bills of exchange.

As discussed in Section 6.2.4.2, if a discount is offered by a supplier for the early payment of accounts payable, the evaluation of the decision about whether to accept the discount (or not) is similar to the evaluation of the decision as to whether a discount should be offered to customers for accounts receivable.

An entity should consider borrowing via accounts payable only if trade credit is the cheapest form of funding. The cost of trade credit depends on the credit terms. Assuming no quality differences in the supplies available, if an entity has the choice of trade credit available from two or more suppliers, the entity should take the supplies from the entity with the least expensive terms.

The entity incurring accounts payable will need to consider the arrangements it has with each supplier separately to assess whether discounts being offered should be taken via early payment, bearing in mind the potential impact of delaying payment of an invoice beyond the due date of the invoice (known as ‘stretching’). If such delays occur, this may impact the goodwill offered by the supplier in providing an invoice payment period and there is a risk that future discounts may be withdrawn, the invoice period shortened or credit withdrawn.

As a general rule, when considering taking a discount with early payment of an invoice, an entity should evaluate the discount as follows:

• Calculate the ‘non-discount’ days in the credit cycle.

• Divide the result into 365 days to identify the number of annual payment cycles.

• Multiply the number of cycles by the cash discount to calculate the annual value of the discount).

• Compare the annual discount rate to their own cost of capital – if the annualised discount rate exceeds their cost of capital, accept the discount and repay early. Otherwise, the entity should reject and pay on the net terms.

Whilst the best financial outcomes will be sought by the entity, these need to be balanced against the views of the supplier and the financial benefits from either taking the early payment discount or delaying payment (the cost of taking advantage of cash discounts can be calculated by comparing the saving from the discount with the opportunity cost of investing the cash used to make the early payment).

#### 6.2.5.1 Effective Average Accounts Payable Days (Average Payment Period)

An aging schedule can also be constructed for accounts payable. This schedule can be used in a similar way to the aging schedule for accounts receivable to calculate the effective average accounts payable days (sometimes known as the average payables period). The effective average days outstanding is simply a weighted-average measure of the average days until payment is required, where the weights equal the percentage of total accounts payable days in each account category of days until payment is required.

An entity can compare its effective average accounts payable days to the typical credit terms offered to its clients, to historical averages and to comparator entities. Ideally, entities will want this period to be as long as possible without having it threaten existing or potential supplier arrangements.

#### Illustrative Example 8

Bright Spark Electrics is a commercial contracting entity that provides electrical services to commercial properties. The entity is considering entering into a continuing monthly supply contract for electrical wire from a new supplier. The terms of sale are set at 1.75/5 net 30.

Bright Spark Electrics has a WACC of 18%.

1. Evaluate whether Bright Spark Electrics should accept the terms of the supply contract.
2. Assume that Bright Spark Electrics is offered the following terms by an alternative potential supplier that can provide similar quality goods: 4.0/15 net 60. Evaluate whether Bright Spark Electrics should accept this new offer and change supplier.

Answer

1. The terms 1.75/5 net 30 means that Bright Spark Electrics must pay for the electrical wire supplied by no later than 30 days from the date of the invoice. They can, however, receive a 1.75% discount on the invoice price if they pay during the first 5 days. If payment is not made by day 5 there is no discount and the full amount of the invoice must be paid by day 30.

	When considering taking a discount with early payment of an invoice, an entity should evaluate the discount as follows:

	Step 1 – Calculate the ‘non-discount’ days in the credit cycle.

	Non-discount Period = 30 days - 5 days = 25 days

	Step 2 – Divide the result into 365 days to identify the number of annual payment cycles.

	Number of Payment Cycles = 365 / 25 = 14.6 cycles

	Step 3 – Multiply the number of cycles by the cash discount to calculate the annual value of the discount.

	Annual Value of the Discount = 14.6 x 0.0175 = 0.2555 or 25.55%

	Step 4 – Compare the annual value of the discount to the cost of capital – if the value exceeds the cost of capital, accept the discount and repay early. Otherwise, reject the discount and pay on the net terms.

	Given the implied annual discount rate is 25.55% and the WACC is 18% (i.e. almost 1.42 times the cost of capital), Bright Spark Electrics should accept the discount and pay the invoice within 5 days.

	On the other hand, the selling entity should not offer such a generous incentive, as its financial cost is likely to be far greater than any sales benefit.

2. To answer this question requires a comparison between the effective annual rate for each of the offers:
	Original offer: 1.75/5 net 30
	![](DraggedImage-118.png)

It is noted that the following features differentiate the two offers: the second offer has a higher discount, a longer discount period and a longer net period. Alternative offer: 4.0/15 net 60
![](DraggedImage-119.png)

The changes have increased the effective annual discount rate from 29.40 % to 39.25%.

Both offers are acceptable as they both have an annual effective rate that is higher than Bright Spark Electrics WACC.

Assuming the quality of the goods supplied and that the relationship with the supplier can be sustained, Bright Spark Electrics should switch to the new supplier as the benefit relative to the WACC is greater.

### 6.2.6 Determining Working Capital Requirements

As discussed in Section 6.2.2, the working capital requirement (WCR) reflects the amount of funding required to fund the entity based on the cash conversion cycle.

When establishing the WCR of an entity, management must consider a range of possible determining factors, including economic conditions, the industry in which the entity operates, the entity’s supply chain, customer requirements and the entity’s strategic decisions with respect to production, operations and the setting of policies which determine the terms and conditions on which the entity will engage with other entities.

Once the strategic direction of an entity is decided and its policy framework set and implemented, it is possible to utilise several different techniques to determine the WCR for the entity.

The next section will discuss the factors affecting the level of the WCR and also two possible approaches to calculate the WCR of an entity.

#### 6.2.6.1 Factors Affecting the Working Capital Requirement

Several of these factors are discussed in Exhibit 6.5.

As discussed above, entities need to consider a broad range of factors when deciding on an appropriate level of the WCR for their business. In this context, management will need to perform a range of activities, such as:

• Market analysis of the demand for their goods and services and identification of any opportunities for or threats to future growth or constraints that will affect their future ability to make sales, source inventory and engage with suppliers in their supply chain; and
• Developing an understanding of an entity’s internal strengths or weaknesses that may impact sales, production efficiency and product development.

##### Factor - How factors affect working capital requirement
The nature of the business
- The core business activities undertaken by an entity will impact the WCR. For example:
	• Manufacturing companies need more working capital to support the production process, especially if they use imported and costly raw materials.
	• Labour intensive industries require more working capital in order to meet high labour costs.
	• Capital intensive industries need less working capital because of their dependence on property, plant and equipment rather than labour.
- The size of the business
	- Larger entities typically have a higher WCR than smaller entities.
- The operating cycle of the entity
	- As discussed in Section 6.2.1, the operating cycle of the entity is a function of the time that it takes to convert raw materials into finished goods and receive deferred payment from customers. Entities that have a long operating cycle will have a large WCR.
- Business cycle
	- The business cycle affects the WCR differently during periods of growth and recession.
	- During a growth period, increasing sales increases the need for inventory and increases accounts receivable. Hence this period will have a higher WCR than in recession periods.
	- During a recession, WCR requirements will be lower than in growth periods. This is principally because sales will decline as people tend to buy less. Thus, in this phase, the entity will spend less cash on running advertising campaigns and sales promotions. It will also have to keep more stock and sell on credit despite its preference to hold less inventory and accounts receivables.
- Production policy – impacts of timing and complexity of production
	- If production costs are high, this will increase the WCR of an entity. Entities with slow production processes and/or high levels of complexity in their operations will have a longer inventory conversion process and higher DSI than other entities. For example, companies involved in the manufacture of soap will have a lower WCR than cargo ship manufacturers.
- Terms of purchase and sales
	- Entities that purchase inventory on credit and sell on a cash basis will have a lower WCR than an entity that buys inventory with cash and sells goods on credit terms.
- Credit and collection policy
	- Entities with a strict credit and collection policy will typically have a lower WCR than other entities.
- Availability of raw materials
	- Entities with regular access to the supply of quality raw materials can keep less raw materials in stock as they can reorder with confidence and with shorter lead times. This will reduce their WCR. In contrast, if inventory supply of raw materials is irregular then this type of entity will have a higher WCR.
- Earnings capacity and growth opportunities of the entity
	- Entities that are growing and expanding their business activities or have low levels of earnings capacity from existing production will require a higher WCR to sustain their growth requirements.
- The nature of demand
	- Entities operating in highly competitive markers will need to spend cash on advertising campaigns and sales promotion. These entities also need to hold high levels of finished goods for customers wanting product availability and typically need to sell their goods and services on credit terms favourable to the buyer. These factors will increase the WCR.
	- Also, entities subject to seasonal demand will have more variability in their WCR. During busy seasonal periods WCR requirements will be higher than in other periods.
---- 

As discussed in Chapter 1, the above can be performed using a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis or a political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental (PESTLE) analysis.

For example, to manage the levels of net working capital, an entity should consider the following operational goals:
• Set the minimum level of raw material and work in progress inventories necessary to support production. Inventory levels should be managed to avoid production delays and to avoid any redundancy or perishability of inventory.
• Identify and apply the lowest possible production costs that allow the most effective and efficient use of work in progress inventory during the production process.
• Identify and maintain the level of finished goods inventory that considers the tradeoff between minimising the amount of capital invested in finished goods inventory (including storage and maintenance costs) and the desire to avoid lost sales from having no stock available for sale;
• Offer customers terms of sale on trade credit that support sales whilst minimising the cost of this credit (both the financing cost and the risk of non-payment).
• Arrange for collections to be made from customers as quickly and efficiently as possible.
• Delay paying accounts payable as long as possible.
• Manage the payment and receipt of cash so as to have sufficient cash available to cover day-to-day expenses.

Once the strategic direction of the entity is decided and the policy framework set and implemented, it is possible to utilise several different techniques to determine the best level of WCR for the entity.

#### 6.2.6.2 Calculating the Working Capital Requirement

There are several different approaches to calculating the WCR. This section will discuss the following two primary approaches used by managers:
• The percentage of sales approach
• The operating cycle approach
As discussed below, each approach has its own assumptions and can produce different WCR estimates.

##### Percentage of Sales Approach

The percentage of sales method is based on an assumption that the WCR of any entity is a function of the level of sales. If this relationship is believed to be stable over time then as sales increases so too will the WCR by a fixed proportion of the level of sales. The change in the level of implied net working capital will indicate the implied WCR.

The steps involved to perform this analysis are as follows:
1. Obtain details of the entity’s current levels of sales, assets and liabilities.
2. Express current assets and current liabilities as a percentage of the level of current sales.
3. Assess the impact on the level of demand and quantity of sales after conducting a SWOT or PESTLE analysis (e.g. increase in sales by 5% due to increased marketing, or decrease in sales due to an economic recession).
4. Using the percentage of sales estimated in step 2, and the revised level of sales estimated in step 3, re-estimate the levels of implied current assets and current liabilities.
5. Using this revised information, re-estimate the working capital requirement implied at this higher level of sales.

##### Operating Cycle Approach

The operating cycle approach uses the individual working capital components to calculate the expected level of the WCR. In doing so it considers the impact of current assets such as inventory (raw materials, work in progress and finished goods), accounts receivable, prepaid expenses and desired levels of cash for liquidity purposes and current liabilities such as accounts payable, storage costs, wages and any unearned revenues.

The steps involved to perform this analysis are as follows:

1. Identify all current sources of current assets and current liabilities relevant to working capital.

2. Determine expected levels of the current assets and current liabilities.

3. Using this revised information, re-estimate the working capital requirement implied based on the assumptions made in step 2. This involves calculating the level of net working capital after considering all current assets and current liabilities that represent expected cash inflows and outflows along with any additional cash required to meet contingencies.

The operating cycle for IT Box Corporation is 16 weeks:

The cash conversion cycle for IT Box Corporation is 12 weeks:

2. The entity notes the following relative information regarding components of the cash conversion cycle:
![](DraggedImage-126.png)
You should note that the IT products industry has a lower cash conversion cycle than IT Box Corporation. This is due to the combined effects of a lower accounts receivable collection period and a longer accounts payable payment period.

If IT Box Corporation was to attempt to lower its accounts receivable collection period from eight to seven weeks, it would reduce the cash conversion cycle but by one week (8 +7 – 4 11 weeks). However, reducing the accounts receivable collection period may have both positive and negative impacts. The positive impact will be that the cash conversion cycle is reduced resulting in sales being paid for earlier than before by one week, which should improve liquidity and profitability. On the negative side, to achieve the one week reduction may require the use of discounts on sales, less tolerance on overdue accounts, tighter credit control activities and renegotiation of existing and future sales contracts. Whilst at face value each of these impacts sounds reasonable, they could result in a drop off in sales volume that would impact profitability (and subsequently impact the inventory requirements in the future) unless new customers could be found.

What would happen if Box IT Corporation was to increase its accounts payable payment period from four to six weeks? If this was possible, this would decrease the cash conversion cycle by two weeks (8 + 8 – 6 10 weeks). However, the trade payables payment period is less flexible as it is determined to a large extent by an entity’s suppliers. If an entity delays its payment of accounts payable past their due dates, it runs the risk of paying interest on overdue accounts, losing its suppliers or being refused credit in the future. In order to increase the accounts payable payment period, it would require a renegotiation of supply contracts. However, if the industry accounts payable payment period is six weeks and IT Box is currently at four weeks, then it would seem reasonable for suppliers to increase the term on their supply contracts to six weeks.

If we assumed IT Box Corporation was to have success in increasing its accounts payable payment period from four to six weeks, the operating cycle will remain unchanged but the cash conversion cycle will reduce from twelve to ten weeks. The change will cause the sundry creditors to increase from HK$553,846 to HK$830,769 and the net working capital requirement to decrease from HK$4.258 million to HK$3.981 million with a saving of HK$0.277 million or HK$1.440 million per annum (0.277 × 52/10).

## 6.3 ANALYSING LIQUIDITY AND WORKING CAPITAL EFFICIENCY

In this section, consistent with Learning Outcome 6.02.03, students will learn how to use accounting ratios to analyse liquidity and working capital efficiency. Using working capital efficiency ratios, students will estimate the operating cycle and cash conversion cycle and then apply this to the cycles for HK Flex Ltd. Throughout this section we will use the financial statements from 31 December 20X4 to 31 December 20X9 for HK Flex Ltd (as shown in Illustrative Example 1).

### 6.3.1 Liquidity

In the context of working capital, liquidity refers to the ability of the organisation to generate cash internally from business operations or to raise cash externally from financial institutions so that it can meet its cash requirements and discharge its current obligations. Liquidity is critical for all entities. Accordingly, it is important that the liquidity position and relative performance of entities can be assessed. The current ratio and the quick ratio are commonly used for this purpose.

#### 6.3.1.1 Current Ratio

The ability of an entity to meet its short-term financial commitments is normally assessed by comparing current assets with current liabilities using a ratio called the current ratio (also known as the working capital ratio).

The current ratio calculates the relationship between current assets and current liabilities and is calculated as follows:

> Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities

A higher current ratio is considered to be more favourable than a lower current ratio, but the particular current ratio that is considered to be an acceptable ratio for an entity varies from industry to industry. An entity with a comparatively high current ratio will be capable of settling its short-term liabilities as and when they become due.

An improvement in the ratio over time may be due to:

• An improved financial position and it may, therefore, imply improvement in the ability of the entity to discharge its debt and accounts payable obligations; and
• The stock-piling of slow-moving and static raw materials and work in progress inventory or finished goods, which will not be conducive to improving the entity’s financial position.

On the other hand, a lower ratio indicates that the entity may not be able to meet its obligations as they fall due. Consequently, a declining current ratio may indicate a deteriorating financial position. A decline in the ratio may also be due to the disposition of obsolete inventories.

The current ratio does not take into account the composition of the current assets. Due to the inclusion of inventory in the current ratio, this ratio may give a misleading impression of the short-term solvency of the entity, especially if the inventory is slow moving or obsolete. In such instances, the current ratio fails to serve as a realistic index of the short-term solvency or liquidity of the entity. This weakness can be resolved to some extent by the quick ratio.

#### 6.3.1.2 Quick (or Liquid) Ratio

To explore the impact of liquid securities as opposed to all current assets and liabilities, management can review liquidity by considering the level of the quick ratio (which is also known as the liquid ratio or acid-test ratio). This ratio is used to examine the relationship between an entity’s liquid assets and liquid liabilities. The liquid assets usually include all the current assets except inventories and pre-paid expenses and can be calculated as follows:

> Liquid Assets = Current Assets - (Inventory + Prepaid Expenses)

The quick ratio establishes the relationship between liquid assets and the current liabilities and is calculated as follows:

> Quick Ratio = [Current Assets - (Inventories + Prepaid Expenses)](#) / Current Liabilities

The quick ratio is designed to assess how well an organisation is capable of meeting its obligations when they fall due without having to wait for its illiquid assets to be liquidated. In assessing the quick ratio, it is important to treat the ratio as an indicator of the coverage an entity’s liquid assets provide for its current liabilities. For example, if the ratio is 1.50 times, this implies that the entity has HK$1.50 of liquid assets available to cover each HK$1 of its current liabilities.

In normal business conditions, a quick ratio of approximately 1 is, as a general rule, considered by some analysts to be satisfactory and therefore, an entity with liquid assets equivalent to or higher than its current liabilities is said to be in a sound current liquidity position. However, this is a generalisation and subject to debate and exception. In any case, deviations from the general rule of thumb are worthy of further investigation.

Entities with a quick ratio lower than 1 are considered to be less liquid than entities with a quick ratio of 1 or above and less able to meet their obligations when they fall due.

Precautions should be taken when interpreting the quick ratio because not all of an entity’s liquid assets can be redeemed in a timely manner. For example:

• Accounts receivable is considered to be a liquid asset but may not be quickly or fully recoverable due to potential changes in default levels and/or slow payment beyond the current year.
• Pledged deposit accounts are also considered to be liquid assets but may not be redeemable if on maturity the loans against which the deposits are pledged are rolled forward.
• Physical assets held for sale are sometimes assumed to be convertible to cash within 12 months. However, delays in the sale and settlement process, along with potential for legal disputes, may mean that they are not practically convertible to cash within 12 months.

In addition, a quick ratio of less than 1 does not automatically imply poor liquidity. This is best assessed via a comparison of the quick ratio with an industry average and with historical ratios for the entity.

### 6.3.2 Working Capital Efficiency

Another important dimension of liquidity and the efficiency of business operations involves the calculation of the rate at which different short-term assets are converted into cash and how promptly liabilities have been settled. Of particular importance are the current assets and liabilities that are directly linked to the operational activities of the entity. The important ratios used for this purpose are the:

• Inventory turnover ratio
• Accounts receivable turnover ratio
• Accounts payable turnover ratio

Each of these ratios measures the number of cycles of use for each of the above operational areas that can be completed within any given year. The higher the ratio, the more cycles of use that can be completed within a year. Therefore, these ratios can be used to measure efficiency in the accounts receivable, inventory and accounts payable operational activities within an entity.

Working capital efficiency can be assessed by comparing the turnover ratios to those obtained by the same entity across prior periods and to industry averages.

By knowing the turnover ratios, it is also possible to identify the number of days in a year that correspond to each of these turnover cycles. Hence, it is possible to calculate the following:

• The average inventory conversion or holding period, which is known as days sales in inventory (DSI) and measures the number of days an entity can keep operating without the need for new inventory.

• The average accounts receivable collection period, which is known as days sales outstanding (DSO) and measures the number of days before an entity receives payment on its sales.

• The average accounts payable payment period, which is known as days payables outstanding (DPO) and measures the number of days an entity can take before settling its accounts payable.

#### 6.3.2.1 Inventory Turnover and Days Sales in Inventory

As discussed in Section 6.2.3, inventory can be in the form of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. For manufacturing and retailing entities, the supply chain and the logistical and inventory management are all key operational aspects affecting an entity’s ability to generate profit. Manufacturing entities typically invest a large amount of capital in raw material inventory for production purposes, utilise the inventory in the manufacturing process and then store finished goods so as to have the goods available to satisfy customer demand. Inventories are held by a manufacturing entity awaiting processing, transformation, packing, storage and subsequent sale. In contrast, retailing entities typically purchase finished goods ready for sale and store the goods until such time as they are sold.

Cost of goods sold is a key performance metric of an entity, since it measures the ability of an entity to design, source and manufacture goods at a reasonable cost. To capture the cost of inventory used in the sales process, entities can calculate the cost of goods sold (sometimes reported as the cost of sales) which should reflect the cost of direct materials (i.e. the raw materials, work in progress and finished goods) and, where applicable, direct and indirect costs that have been incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition ready for sale (refer to HKAS 2 Inventories, paras. 20-33 for a discussion of the accounting measurement of the fair value and net realisable value of inventories).

Direct costs (excluding materials) include:

• Packaging costs;
• Costs of storage or warehousing of the production up to the point of sale; and
• Direct overhead costs related to production, such as energy costs and rent.

Indirect costs include:

• Salaries of administrators and managers overseeing production;
• Depreciation of equipment used to produce, package or store the product; and
• Equipment used for administrative work (not production).

Examples of costs that should not be included in the cost of inventories (and, therefore, cost of goods sold) are:

• General or administrative costs associated with running the entity;
• Costs associated with sales and marketing; and
• Costs associated with transporting goods after the final sale is complete.

A list of costs excluded from the cost of inventories is provided in HKAS 2, para. 16.

The inventory turnover ratio (also known as the stock turnover ratio or stock velocity) measures the relationship between the cost of goods sold during a period and the average of the cost of inventory at the beginning of the period and at the end of the period. This ratio captures the velocity with which the goods move through the production process and therefore shows the number of times that an entity’s inventory has been cycled during the year. The ratio can be calculated as follows:

> Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Goods Sold / Average Inventorry

As an input to this model, it is necessary to calculate the average inventory which is estimated as follows:

> Average Inventory = (Opening Inventory Balance + Closing Inventoory Balance) / 2

Efficient use of inventory involves a trade-off between the benefits of holding inventory against the cost of the inventory. If an entity is not efficient in its use of inventory the entity will experience losses due to factors such as holding excessive levels of inventory, or the direct costs associated with excessive unused or unsold inventory, such as insurance, rent, utility charges and replacement costs, including the cost of obsolete inventory. Therefore, holding an optimal level of inventory is important such that it meets the necessities of production but avoids the costs of excess inventory or inventory shortages.

A low inventory turnover ratio, under normal business conditions and given a certain level of cost of goods sold, can be a possible indicator of an entity holding large volumes of saleable inventory or alternatively holding slow moving, obsolete or shop-soiled goods of either low value or poor-quality goods which the entity is unable to use or sell. On the other hand, a high inventory turnover ratio may reflect good management through efficiency in the entity’s inventory usage and levels of inventory.

The average inventory conversion period or days sales in inventory (DSI) uses the inventory turnover ratio to calculate the number of days that it typically takes to utilise inventory in one turnover cycle of production for manufacturers or the number of days from purchase of finished goods until their sale to customers. By knowing this amount, we can then assess the efficiency of an entity’s inventory management process.

The DSI is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-131.png)
Because the inventory turnover ratio is a component of and is embedded in the DSI formula, both can be calculated conjointly as follows:
![](DraggedImage-132.png)

This equation is often restated as:
![](DraggedImage-133.png)
To assess the level of DSI, the entity should compare the information to historical trends and comparator industry information. When considering the usage of inventory within an entity, management should consider the efficiency of their production processes. A high DSI may suggest slow processing of inventories or inefficient use of inventory due to holding obsolete inventory. In contrast, a low average usage period will imply efficiency in the inventory management processes of the entity. Management accountants within an entity can disaggregate the cost of goods sold between the various stages of production to provide further information that can be used to assess efficiency. This information is typically not publicly available.

Assessment of the performance of an entity from the view point of inventory management is best assessed via a comparison of the inventory turnover ratio and the DSI to an industry average and to historical ratios for the entity.

It is also possible to assess the efficiency of inventory as it moves from raw materials to finished goods. This will allow assessment of the efficiency at each of the different levels of inventory usage.

##### For Raw Material Inventory
![](DraggedImage-134.png)
In this ratio, the cost of raw materials used during the year is equal to the level of raw materials at the beginning of the year plus any raw material purchases less the level of raw materials at the end of the year and average raw materials reflects the level of raw materials at the beginning the year plus the level of raw materials at the end of year divided by two.

Using this information, it is possible to ascertain the number of days that raw materials are held prior to their use in the production process.
![](DraggedImage-135.png)

This ratio provides information about the average number of days for which raw materials have been kept in storage before they are issued to the production departments. When compared to historical usage, it is useful for identifying whether the inventory comprises obsolete raw materials or fast-moving raw materials. If data is kept, it should be possible to perform this analysis for all different raw materials needed for the production processes.

##### For Work in Progress Inventory

The work in progress inventory turnover and days in which inventory is used as part of work in progress both provide valuable information about the efficiency of production processes for manufacturers and the suitability of the inventory used in the production process. The turnover ratio and subsequently the days sales in work in progress will always be conditional on the type of goods produced, the inventory requirements to produce those goods and the production process utilised. Efficiency would suggest that the turnover ratio will be higher and the days sales in work in progress inventory will be lower relative to other entities operating in the same industry.
![](DraggedImage-136.png)

In this ratio, the cost of work in progress materials consumed during the year is equal to the level of work in progress inventory at the beginning of the period plus manufacturing costs incurred during the period less the level of work in progress inventory at the end of the period. The average work in progress inventory reflects the level of work in progress inventory at the beginning of the year plus the level of work in progress inventory at the end of the year divided by two.

Using this information, it is possible to ascertain the number of days that raw materials are used in the production process.
![](DraggedImage-137.png)

##### For Finished Inventory

The finished inventory turnover and days in which finished inventory is used both provide valuable information about the efficiency of the sales process in the period following production for a manufacturer or whilst goods are for sale for a retailer. The turnover ratio and subsequently the days sales are in finished goods is conditional upon the volume of unsold finished goods, the capacity available to store the finished goods before sales and until delivery and the perishability of the goods produced. Efficiency would suggest that the turnover ratio will be higher and the days sales are in the finished goods inventory will be lower relative to other entities operating in the same industry.
![](DraggedImage-138.png)
In this ratio, the cost of finished goods inventory consumed during the year is equal to the level of finished goods inventory at the beginning of the period plus storage cost incurred during the period less the level of finished goods inventory at the end of the period. The average finished goods inventory reflects the level of finished goods inventory at the beginning of the year plus the level of finished goods inventory at the end of the year divided by two.

Using this information, it is possible to ascertain the number of days that raw materials are used in the production process.
![](DraggedImage-139.png)
#### 6.3.2.2 Accounts Receivable Turnover and Days Sales Outstanding

One of the most commonly used methods of sales by business organisations is credit sales, whereby entities sell their goods and services to customers on credit in accordance with the credit policy specified by the entity’s board of directors.

Accounts receivable can be in the form of:
• Trade credit
• Negotiable bills receivable
• Customer credit

Accounts receivable are an important part of the liquidity of an entity. An entity’s ability to pay its accounts payable and repay debt as they fall due is conditional on its ability to collect the funds that are due to it via accounts receivable arising from sales it has made. If an entity is not efficient in collecting accounts receivable it will have to utilise existing cash or borrow funds instead. For the purpose of calculating the accounts receivable turnover ratio, trade accounts receivable, customer accounts receivable and bills receivable must be aggregated.

The accounts receivable turnover ratio (also known as the debtors turnover ratio, receivables turnover ratio or debtors’ velocity) identifies the relationship between the net credit sales for the year and the average receivables. The ratio indicates the number of times, on average, that receivables are collected during the period. The higher the receivables turnover, the shorter the period of time between an entity making a credit sale and collecting the cash.

To put it differently, this ratio shows the number of times the receivables have cycled during the year in terms of sales. This ratio is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-140.png)
As an input to this model, it is necessary to calculate the average accounts receivable, which is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-141.png)
To identify net credit sales requires all sales to be split between cash sales and credit sales. Whilst management accounting staff working within an entity would be able to make this differentiation and be able to estimate the net sales for the year, this would not be possible for all other users of accounting information. For most entities, cash sales would not be a significant component of their revenue as most sales would be on credit.

By assuming all sales are credit sales, the accounts receivable turnover ratio is typically calculated using sales revenue instead of net credit sales. Therefore, the ratio is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-142.png)
The accounts receivable turnover ratio shows the number of times receivables have turned over during the year in terms of sales. The higher the ratio, the more cycles during the year, suggesting efficiency in accounts receivable collections. Assessment of turnover efficiency is best achieved via comparison of the entity’s accounts receivable turnover ratio with an industry average or historical ratios for the entity.

The average accounts receivable collection period or days sales outstanding (DSO) uses the accounts receivable turnover ratio to calculate the number of days that it typically takes to collect accounts receivable in one turnover cycle. By knowing this amount, we can then assess the efficiency of the collection process. The DSO can also be considered as a measure of the number of days that an entity takes to collect cash after the sale of goods or the provision of services.

The DSO is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-143.png)
Because the accounts receivable turnover ratio is a component of and is embedded in the DSO formula, both can be calculated conjointly, as follows:
![](DraggedImage-144.png)
This DSO equation is often restated as:
![](DraggedImage-145.png)
A high number for the DSO can be compared to the average period of credit extended by the entity and indicates the possibility of an ineffective collection process. In contrast, a low average collection period indicates a shorter time-lag between credit sales and cash collection and suggests an effective collection process.

Assessment of the performance of an entity from the view point of debt collection is best achieved via comparison of the accounts receivable turnover ratio and the DSO with an industry average or historical ratios for the entity.

#### 6.3.2.3 Accounts Payable Turnover and Days Payables Outstanding

As discussed in Section 6.2.5, accounts payable is normally an unsecured, non-interest-bearing current liability, owed by the entity to suppliers for the purchase of trade goods or services. The payment is expected to be made within the next 12 months. An account payable can be in the form of:
• Trade credit or trade payables; and
• Negotiable bills payable.

The accounts payable turnover ratio (also known as the creditors turnover ratio or accounts payable velocity) measures the relationship between the net credit purchase (sometimes cost of goods sold is used when net credit purchase is not available) during a period and the average of accounts payable at the beginning of the period and accounts payable at the end of the period. This ratio captures the number of times an entity’s accounts payable has been turned over during the year and can be calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-146.png)
As an input to this model it is necessary to calculate the average accounts payable, which is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-147.png)

The average accounts payable period or days payables outstanding (DPO) uses the accounts payable turnover ratio to calculate the number of days that it typically takes to pay the suppliers. By knowing this amount, we can then assess the efficiency of an entity’s managing its accounts payable.

The DPO is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-148.png)
Because the accounts payable turnover ratio is a component of and is embedded in the DPO formula, both can be calculated conjointly as follows:
![](DraggedImage-149.png)
This DPO equation is often restated as:
![](DraggedImage-150.png)
A high number for the DPO suggests a long period until accounts payable is settled. Subject to the terms of the accounts payable agreement that the entity has with its supplier, this may be a bad or a good outcome for the entity. For example, if an entity has been granted 90 days to pay for supplies and takes 150 days, the payment is 60 days overdue. Being consistently overdue may affect the relationship with the supplier and may lead to a reduction in credit allowed or loss of the supplier relationship. Alternatively, if the entity can pay at 150 days without any consequences, then the entity is delaying payment, and this may be of advantage to the entity as it delays the use of the entity’s cash. In contrast, a low average collection period will imply efficiency in prompt settlement of accounts payable.

Assessment of the performance of an entity from the view point of accounts payable management is best achieved via comparison of the accounts payable turnover ratio and the DPO with an industry average or historical ratios for the entity.

### 6.3.3 Estimating the Operating Cycle and the Cash Conversion Cycle

In Section 6.2.1, students were introduced to the concepts of the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle. In this section, students will learn how to use the efficiency ratios discussed in Section 6.3.2 in order to estimate both of these cycles.

#### 6.3.3.1 Using Efficiency Measures to Calculate the Operating Cycle and the Cash Conversion Cycle

As discussed in Section 6.2.1 and as shown in Exhibit 6.1, the operating cycle reflects the length of time from the receipt of raw materials to the collection of cash from customers for the sale of finished goods made from those materials. The operating cycle is critical to our understanding of net working capital because it reflects the time period that the business needs to be financed, i.e. from the receipt of raw materials by the business until it is paid for the finished goods it has produced.

By applying the efficiency ratios from Section 6.3.2, the operating cycle can be calculated as follows:

> Operating Cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Ouutstanding (DSO)

As discussed in Section 6.2.1 and as shown in Exhibit 6.1, the cash conversion cycle represents the time between an entity’s payment for the initial raw materials inventory and the entity’s receipt of payment for the sale of the finished goods inventory. The length of the cash conversion cycle can be estimated by considering the number of days that sales are tied up in inventory plus the number of days between the date of sale of the finished product until payment is received for the sale less the number of days until the entity pays for its raw materials.

Consistently, with net working capital, the period of time between payment for the raw materials and collection of the accounts receivable needs to be financed by either short-term or long-term debt or equity.

By applying the efficiency ratios from Section 6.3.2, the cash conversion cycle can also be expressed as follows:

> Cash Conversion Cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Saales Outstanding (DSO) - Days Payables Outstanding (DPO)


### Illustrative Example 12

Using the information in HKFlex’s financial statements, as shown in Illustrative Example 1, calculate the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle for HKFlex at 31 December 20X9 and for years 20X5 to 20X8 and compare these results to those for the synthetical chemical manufacturing industry:

#### Answer

At 31 December 20X9 the operating cycle was:

> Operating Cycle = DSI + DSO = 46.83 + 51.55 = 98.38 days

During the 20X9 financial year, HKFlex required financing for 98 days to cover the period from the receipt of raw materials until the receipt of cash from the collection of accounts receivable.

At 31 December 20X9 the cash conversion cycle was estimated to be:
> Cash Conversion Cycle = DSI + DSO - DPO = 46.83 + 51.55 - 68.53 = 29.85 days

During the 20X9 financial year, HKFlex had to wait 30 days from the point at which it settled its accounts payable until it received the cash from collection of accounts receivable.

Applying the timeline for operating and cash conversion cycles in Exhibit 6.1 to the present example case, the figure below shows both the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle for HKFlex as at 31 December 20X9. ![](DraggedImage-161.png)
![](DraggedImage-162.png)
The results above show that HKFlex had a shorter operating cycle than the chemical manufacturing industry by a median of almost 19 days. Due to the consistency of the DPO during the period, most of the change in the cash conversion cycle is directly attributable to the DSO.

## 6.4 WORKING CAPITAL FUNDING

Traditional approaches to working capital management tend to view management of the components of the cash conversion cycle (inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable) and its financing from only a single perspective, either the buyer’s attempt to defer payment/ reduce payment size or the seller’s attempt to accelerate cash collection.

This often results in pitting one side of the buy/sell transaction against the other and leads to problems if one party has stronger market power than the other (suppliers traditionally are smaller entities than buyers). Applying either of the approaches above can add significant risk to the supply chain, including customer loss, business continuity risk, material cost inflation and supplier viability risk.

Over time, entities developed approaches to enhance the flows of goods and the availability of information in their supply chain using information technology and relationship management techniques. But despite these developments, supply chain managers historically have paid little attention to the financial flows associated with the supply chain.

A number of entities that are heavily reliant upon particular suppliers have found that by also considering the financial flows between the entities involved in the supply chain, it is possible to collaborate and create benefits for each other in relation to inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable transactions and improve working capital outcomes, including the cash conversion cycle.

As discussed in Section 6.1.5, when it comes to funding working capital requirements members of the supply chain have tended to seek solutions using traditional short-term funding products in lieu of exploring the use of products that can link the supply chain directly with the financial requirements of both parties. By aligning the financial flows with other components of the supply chain, i.e. physical and information flows, it is possible to improve cash flow from a supply chain perspective.

The next section will discuss the concept of supply chain finance and show how modern supply chain finance solutions can be adopted in working capital funding.

### 6.4.1 Supply Chain Finance Overview

As discussed in Section 6.2, the management of working capital and the cash conversion cycle involve the management of the operational aspects of inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable. These activities create outcomes that give rise to the cash conversion cycle and the need for financial arrangements to support these activities.

Historically, entities were very focused on their own working capital requirements and, despite having developed quality supply chain relationships, they rarely sought to extend financing opportunities beyond traditional short-term funding financial instruments that were entity specific.

With the onset of the global financial crisis of 2008, as the scarcity of cash and liquidity problems grew, entities started to look for alternative ways to reduce working capital requirements. Whilst looking for alternatives to the traditional approaches discussed above, they explored ways to improve their return on investments without damaging the continuity of their supply chain or introducing new supply risks. In doing so, suppliers, buyers and financial institutions worked together to develop a range of new financial instruments and funding techniques that came to be known as supply chain finance.

#### 6.4.1.1 Supply Chain Finance

Historically, entities would often work independently of their suppliers and/or buyers to seek working capital financing based on their own specific financial needs (e.g. ’buyer companies’ wanting to purchase additional inventory and extend accounts payable terms leading to increased revenues, while the ’supplier companies’ providing raw materials and work in progress inventory or selling finished goods want to reduce the collection period). For example, if funding is accounts receivable, either an accounts receivable loan or factoring may be used. Both of these approaches require a relationship between the selling entity providing the accounts receivable and a financial institution providing the funding. When funding the accounts receivable there is no consideration of the funding requirements of the party which is buying the goods or services. The focus is singularly on the entity taking the loan being able to fund its working capital requirement and recover the accounts receivable so as to be able to repay the loan.

As discussed in Section 6.2 of this chapter, the cash conversion cycle needs to be funded in order for an entity to remain operational and not suffer a liquidity issue. Traditionally, this funding was performed by entities using a variety of different short-term funding approaches as identified and discussed in Section 5.3.1 in Chapter 5. These approaches include the use of a range of short-term financial instruments such as lines of credit, overdrafts, credit cards, commercial paper, negotiable bills of exchange, leasing and bank loans. Other short-term approaches to funding working capital that are directly related to using accounts receivable and inventory as collateral, include:
• Accounts receivable loans;
• Factoring of accounts receivable; and
• Inventory loans.

Exhibit 6.6 shows the relationship between supply chain activities and traditional funding approaches. Under traditional financing approaches both parties (the buyer and the seller) have to find ways to finance their supply chain operations and their cash conversion cycle independently.
![](DraggedImage-165.png)
Exhibit 6.6 highlights how both the buyer and supplier may source funding independently of each other. The financial provider bases its credit decision on the supplier’s/buyer’s credit quality based on information provided by the supplier/buyer. The risk associated with this funding stays with each single party.

Buyers are often larger organisations than suppliers and often have more than one supplier. Because of their larger size, superior credit quality and stronger bargaining power, buyers can typically dictate payment terms (such as extended periods of accounts payable), which may place the supplier at risk. Rather than dictating terms in this manner, especially if there is a limited number of suppliers, it is in the buyer’s interest to coordinate their supply chain interests with those of the suppliers. This allows buyers and sellers to reach appropriate inventory and working capital compromises (including payment terms).

These arrangements can also be extended to include financing arrangements, including those that meet the definition of supply chain finance, that utilise the differences in credit quality between the buyer and supplier.

Supply chain finance (SCF) can be defined as the use of financial instruments, financing processes, risk management practices and technological techniques for optimising the management of cash flows, liquidity and working capital invested in the end to end business supply chain processes and transactions undertaken by an entity.

This definition highlights the fact that supply chain finance is highly dependent on the collaborative relationship between supply chain partners, considers all aspects of the supply chain process and focusses on inter-entity financing optimisation. By merging each of the following elements together, entities are able to not only automate payables and receivables but also to inject much-needed liquidity at various stages of the supply chain through the use of SCF:

• Physical supply chain information
• Financial supply chain data
• Flexible funding methods

What factors have promoted the growth of SCF in recent years?

In the era since the global financial crisis of 2008, the following factors have contributed to significant changes in the way working capital financing occurs and have led to the development of the market for SCF:

• Increased globalisation of business characterised by high levels of competition, which has reduced the availability of historical financing methods for working capital financing.

• Significant improvements by entities in the integration and coordination of material and information flows between customers, suppliers and financial institutions in order to better share the risks and reduce working capital finance requirements.

• Regulatory changes that have reduced capital charges for banks in favour of secured short-term financing used for working capital.

• Automation of purchase order, invoicing and payment processes leading to higher levels of transparency and effectiveness in managing supply chain information flows between buyers and sellers.

• Entry of non-bank financial institutions and disruptor financial institutions to provide financial services at low operating costs using connections to the internet that allow the sharing and transfer of data over an internet network without requiring human-tohuman or human-to-computer interaction via the use of computers and other digital machines that have unique identifiers. (This is otherwise known as the Internet of Things and is discussed in more detail in Module 5, Chapter 3.)

• A rapidly changing range of technological advances including technologies such as the blockchain, cloud computing and big data (discussed further in Section 6.4.2).

• Incentive programmes funded by government spending in favour of working capital funding initiatives.

SCF provides the opportunity to create a win-win-win for the buyer, the supplier and any financial intermediary, third party vendor or corporation involved in providing supply chain finance. SCF typically involves a technology platform that electronically unites the partners to the funding arrangement by providing financial triggers that arise from the activities undertaken in the supply chain. Examples of SCF will be discussed in Section 6.4.1.2.

Using supply chain finance (SCF) brings advantages that are often considered to be win-winwin for the buyers, sellers and finance providers, as shown in Exhibit 6.7.

#### 6.4.1.2 Alternative Types of Supply Chain Finance

Supply chain finance allows both the buyer and supplier to free up their working capital and maintain a higher level of liquidity by introducing an intermediary financial institution, third party vendor or corporation. SCF permits the buyer to withhold the payment for a longer period while the supplier is paid earlier.

Supply chain finance is not a single solution-based mode of financing. A range of alternative SCF approaches exist that can be beneficial to suppliers, buyers and financial institutions.
![](DraggedImage-166.png)
To highlight the characteristics of SCF, three of the primary SCF approaches are discussed below. The approaches are:

• Reverse factoring (or payables financing)
• Dynamic discounting
• Inventory in transit financing

Consistent with the definition of SCF in Section 6.4.1.1, benefits will accrue to both suppliers and buyers from the use of SCF, including the following benefits:

• Extended DPO for buyers or reduced DSO for suppliers, enabling off-balance sheet funding, which increases overall business opportunities, reduces debt and improves credit rating;
• Provision of real-time information through use of an automated invoice solution, enabling improved monitoring of invoices and payment status, thereby enhancing the predictability of cash flows;
• Reduction in working capital and related funding costs, by improving commercial terms and thereby improving cash flows for both the buyer and seller;
• Improved supply chain connections by empowering cooperation amongst buyers and vendors as opposed to rivalry; and
• Improved transparency and reductions in costs associated with disputes and collection and payment processes as a result of process mapping, risk identification and controls via the use of technological platforms.

#### Reverse Factoring (or Payables Financing)

As discussed in Chapter 5, factoring is a form of receivables purchase financing, based on the idea of an entity selling or assigning its unpaid receivables (sales invoices) to a factor (bank or other commercial finance provider) for a payment equivalent to a portion of the face value of the invoices less a fee for offering the service and a charge for the period the invoice is financed. This means that instead of having to wait for payment from their customers (the buyers), the seller can access the funds more quickly. The factor subsequently collects the invoice payment from the seller’s customers.

Factoring can assist in reducing the DSO time whilst at the same time assisting the entity to reduce administration costs because the factor can provide the credit services and the entity will have access to the factor’s expertise in credit analysis and credit control.

In a factoring agreement, the factor will typically advance a large proportion of the face value of accounts receivable, in some cases up to 80% of the invoiced amount. In exchange for accelerated cash receipts from the factor, the entity incurs an interest charge, which can be compared with the cost of short-term borrowing. In addition, a service fee is charged which is usually between 0.5% and 3% of projected annual sales turnover. The terms of the factor agreement are negotiated independently of financing requirements of the buyer.

Unlike a factor agreement, a reverse factor originates from the accounts payable of a buyer with high creditworthiness and a leading (core) position in the supply chain. A reverse factoring agreement (also known as approved payables finance) is a buyer-led financing programme that is designed for designated suppliers in the supply chain. It is the most commonly used of the SCF approaches.

In a reverse factor agreement, the buyer’s creditworthiness (which is typically superior to the supplier’s) is used to enable the supplier to receive an early discounted payment in respect of the supplier’s accounts receivable from the buyer’s finance provider. The buyer will subsequently pay the amount due under the original accounts payable directly to the financial institution at a specified future due date. This due date can be negotiated by the buyer to be later than the original due date specified in the original invoice. The early financing to the supplier is for 100% of the invoice less a discount, which is lower than with conventional trade financing. Due to its higher credit rating, the buyer receives an extended term for payment in a secured supply chain environment.

As shown in Exhibit 6.8, in its simplest form, a reverse financing arrangement includes a process involving a buyer, a supplier, the buyer’s finance provider and a web-based technology 
![](DraggedImage-167.png)
platform (the IT platform is typically hosted by the finance provider). In this process, the seller delivers the requested raw material to the buyer, and then, after validating and approving the receipt of the agreed materials and the invoice from the supplier, the electronic invoice is placed on the platform. The IT platform advises the buyer’s finance provider who subsequently pays the supplier the value of the order at a pre-arranged rate (i.e. the face value of the invoice minus a small percentage which represents the finance provider’s fee and an interest cost for receiving payment before the negotiated payment dates). Subsequently, after a predetermined length of time, the buyer is obliged to pay the finance provider the full value of the goods received.

Reverse factoring reduces costs across the supply chain by allowing suppliers to draw funds using their buyers’ creditworthiness instead of their own. This allows sellers to leverage the buyers’ credit rating to reduce the sellers’ cost of capital, obtain lower cost financing and create a more predictable cash flow. The following observations can be made about the benefits to the supplier from entering into a reverse factoring arrangement:

• The supplier will benefit from participating in the reverse factoring scheme if the reduction in its financing cost from receiving the invoice amount earlier is greater than the financing cost of the extended trade credit to the buyer.

• The ratio of the supplier’s cost of capital and the reverse factoring rate set by the financing institution must be greater than the ratio of the time period the reverse factoring rate used and the actual time reduction in invoice payment to the supplier.

• If the buyer’s current cost of capital equals the reverse factoring rate charged by the bank and this rate is lower than the supplier’s cost of capital, the overall total benefit of the reverse factoring arrangement will be positive irrespective of whether it is beneficial for the supplier.

Incorporating purchase order and invoice data into traditional trade finance and creating new IT solutions around them allows finance providers the opportunity to provide financial products that align with both the buyer’s and the seller’s views of supply chain finance.

Reverse factoring potentially lowers the buyer’s and the seller’s exposures to operational risk as it requires the examination of data on invoices, mapping with procurement orders (purchase orders), mutual mapping of balances of open payables (buyer) and open receivables (seller) to operate effectively. Technological advances have facilitated IT platforms that can cope with large volumes of data and exercise effective controls over transactions.

A reverse factoring agreement allows the supplier to reduce their DSO by receiving early payment from the buyer’s financial institution and the buyer is able to extend the due date of their accounts payable by not paying the agreed amount back to the buyer’s finance provider until a later agreed upon date.
