##### Dynamic Discounting

A common goal of each entity in a supply chain may be to increase sales, which can be facilitated by offering their customers payment options that make purchasing more cost effective.

As discussed in Section 6.2.4, trade credit is a well-known managerial practice whereby a vendor allows a customer to extend payment terms beyond cash payment for goods and services. Trade credit gained popularity as a procurement finance solution, in which two parties involved in a transaction may agree on payment terms whereby payment will be made from the buyer to the seller at some point in the future.

As discussed in Section 6.2.4.2, payment terms for trade credit normally comprise three parts:

• A discount percentage (for instance, 2.5%).
• The period within which the customer will need to pay the invoice to obtain the discount (for instance, 10 days).
• The final day of the net period on which the credit is due for payment unless the payment has been made earlier (for instance, 30 days).

Dynamic discounting has evolved from the previously static ‘take-it-or-leave-it’ trade credit discount approach to an agreement in which both the buyer and the seller can propose terms. These terms can be set on a sliding scale whereby they change subject to the volume or value of the transaction. For example, on the approval of the invoice, suppliers can ask for discounted payment terms that differ for each transaction. Two primary types of dynamic discounting alternatives are possible:

• Supplier-initiated – Where suppliers decide if a discount will be granted on accounts receivable based on the entity’s credit risk assessment and/or industry practice (as discussed in Section 6.2.4.2); and
• Buyer-initiated – Where buyers move first to declare an acceptable discount rate.

In setting the terms for each transaction, caution is needed by both parties.

If sellers of inventory have a large volume of transactions relative to buyers, then these sellers will have large costs associated with flexible payment options relating to credit, billing, collection and bad debts. Smaller companies selling to larger companies often experience low processing costs (due to the small number of clients), but generally need to use very expensive and limited capital to finance extended customer payment terms (required due to the larger companies’ market power), creating cash flow, liquidity and potential funding problems.

If buyers have a large network of suppliers, they will be particularly concerned about the sustainability of these suppliers and therefore whilst they will want to set terms that are beneficial to their entity, they will seek to assist the suppliers to manage their liquidity and funding risks. This needs to be balanced by buyers to ensure they also have sufficient capacity to take advantage of the opportunities afforded by dynamic discounting. This capacity involves the buyer having sufficient productive capacity and funding to utilise the volume of inventory acquired to take advantage of the dynamic discounting and sufficient sales to generate revenue to pay for their accounts receivable from the sale of finished goods.

As shown in Exhibit 6.9, in its simplest form, a dynamic discounting arrangement consists of a process involving a buyer, a supplier, the buyer’s finance provider and a technological webbased technology platform for coordination, (this IT platform is typically hosted by the finance provider). The buyer’s bank independently negotiates terms with its own bank regarding payment to the bank.

By using dynamic discounting, the supplier may decrease its cash conversion cycle by reducing their DSO through early payment from the buyer’s financial institution and the buyer may decrease its cost of products sold by being able to negotiate better terms for its DPO based on seeking improved discounts for early payments, extended discount periods or extensions to the repayment period. Dynamic discounting gives buyers more flexibility regarding how and when to pay their suppliers.
![](DraggedImage-177.png)

### Illustrative Example 14

Plantation Pineapple Wholesalers (PPW) is a pineapple wholesaler that is looking at supplying HK$2.5 million worth of pineapples to HK Fresh Retail (HKFR) a retailer specialising in the sale of fresh fruit and vegetables. PPW proposes terms on the basis of net 30 days.

PPW has a cost of capital of 8.50% and HKFR has a cost of capital of 6.00%.

1. Calculate the breakeven number of days that HKFR will want to be indifferent relative to the supplier’s cost of funds.

2. Show how dynamic discounting can be used by the parties to reduce the cost of finance for the supplier.

Answer

1. Under the original terms of net 30, the cost of funding this position will be:
	> HK$2.5 million x 0.0850 x 30/365 = HK$17, 466.

	The implied number of days that HKFR would be indifferent to this cost, given it has a cost of capital of 6.00%, can be solved as follows:
	> HK$2.5 million x 0.06 x days/365 = 17, 466 Days
	> = (17, 466 x 365)/(2.5 million x 0.06) = 42.5006 or 43 days

2. On presentation of the invoice applying terms of net 30 and confirmation that the goods have been received by the HKFR, PPW can request dynamic discounting of the invoice as follows:
	> Original Invoice = HK$2.50 million

The bank dynamically discounts the invoice and provides finance to PPW at the following rate 6.00% plus bank fee of 0.50%.

PPW obtains supplier finance at 90% of the invoice value with the balance payable at the end of the net period.

The cost to PPW for the supplier finance is equivalent to:
![](DraggedImage-178.png)

Assuming full payment of the outstanding accounts receivable is made using the first payment arrangement, PPW will receive HK$2.50 million after 30 days at a cost of HK$17,466 effectively resulting in net receipts of HK$2,482,534.

Using the alternative payment arrangement, dynamic discounting, PPW will receive HK$2.50 million broken down as follows – HK$2.25 million (90% of invoice) on confirmation via the IT system to the bank and subsequently a further HK$0.250 million at day 30. The total cost of the arrangement equals HK$13,768 effectively resulting in net receipts under the arrangement of HK$2,486,232.

PPW should proceed with the second alternative as it has two distinct relative advantages:

1. PPW can get access to 90% of the funds on confirmation via the IT system rather than wait 30 days under the net 30 terms. This will reduce PPW’s DSO and increases their liquidity – it effectively converts accounts receivable to cash through a more attractively priced non-recourse sale.

2. The effective net receipts after consideration of the cost of capital and HK Bank’s fees is higher for PPW by using dynamic discounting.

#### Purchase Order Finance

Financial distress of suppliers can strongly affect supply chain efficiency. At times small to medium sized suppliers can be constrained in their ability to finance manufacturing expenditure, procure raw materials and service existing accounts receivable before production or shipment of goods to buyers.

Using a recently developed financial arrangement, a buyer can alleviate its supplier’s financial distress by providing finance to the supplier through advancing payment at a discount prior to product shipment. This arrangement is known as a purchase order financing arrangement. This is achieved by the buyer entering into a contract with its finance provider to provide a line of credit for the supplier guaranteed by the buyer, based on a purchase order from the buyer to the supplier.

A purchase order is an order form, issued by a buyer to a seller. When it is accepted by the seller, it constitutes an agreement between the buyer and the seller regarding the price and quantity for a product or service.

Purchase Order Finance can be provided using any number of structural variations such as:
• Purchase orders (confirmed by buyer or unconfirmed).
• Demand forecasts.
• Underlying commercial contracts.

The most commonly used structure involves the use of buyer confirmed purchase orders where a supplier offers a purchase order signed by a buyer as collateral to a financial institution to secure the funds. Because the purchase order is used by the financial institution as collateral, the focus is more on the buyer’s credit standing than on the supplier’s statement of financial position.

As shown in Exhibit 6.10, in its simplest form, a purchase order financing arrangement is a process involving a buyer, a supplier, the buyer’s finance provider and a technological webbased technology platform for coordination, (the IT platform is typically hosted by the finance provider). The buyer’s bank independently negotiates terms with its own bank regarding payment to the bank.
![](DraggedImage-179.png)
Purchase order financing allows the supplier to receive funding from the buyer’s financier upon advice to the financier of the receipt of the purchase order. Funding is provided based on the buyer’s credit rating, which creates a ‘win–win–win’ situation by providing the following benefits:

• The potential for the buyer to have an inventory shortfall due to the supplier’s financial distress is mitigated.
• Financing the supplier’s working capital will allow purchase orders to be fulfilled and assist the liquidity and longevity of the supplier.
• The finance provider receives interest plus any fees on the funding provided to the supplier and repaid by the buyer.

Purchase order finance can reduce operating risk, improve borrowing capacity and result in higher profits for suppliers, especially if use of this type of arrangement encourages buyers to increase purchase order commitments and increase their demand for inventory.

### 6.4.2 Recent Developments

In recent years, principally due to technology developments and the use of SCF as part of the broader supply chain, entities have been able to move from the silo approach of managing working capital and the cash conversion cycle to now using creative financing techniques involving buyers, sellers and finance providers.

Consider a retailer that specialises in the sale of plastic toys. The retailer gets the supply of toys as finished goods from a manufacturer that relies upon suppliers of plastics for production, dyes for colouring and cardboard for packaging. Each of these suppliers relies upon another layer of suppliers of raw materials to provide or manufacture each of their inputs to manufacturing. Each of these activities requires active co-ordination and a continuous flow of purchase orders, invoices and cash settlement activities involving buyer, sellers and their finance providers. The sustainability of each member of the supply chain is conditional on all other members of the supply chain.

Supply chain management recognised the complexity of the relationships involved between all members in each supply chain, the sustainability of the supply chain and increasingly the need to coordinate and support the activities of all members of the supply chain. In doing so, SCF needed to develop to be able to handle not just single transferences of purchase orders and/or invoices between parties and their financing but the capacity to be able to identify large volumes of transactions quickly, efficiently and to recognise transactions that represented the flow of activities between all members of the supply chain.

The providers of SCF products extended beyond the banks of the buyers and sellers to include non-bank financial institutions and a range of non-bank platform providers including FinTech companies specialising in enhanced digital interfaces, simplified implementation processes, new business models (such as those focusing on smaller suppliers, offering auctionbased solutions, and those incorporating dynamic discounting).

The next sections will consider the impact of two primary developments affecting the management of working capital technology-driven solutions including platforms and blockchain technology and the transition to FinTech solutions.

#### 6.4.2.1 Technology Platforms and Blockchain

Since 2000 there has been widespread development of IT platforms used to manage the documentation and payments between parties associated with supply chain transactions typically involving the following two primary working capital management processes:

• The procure to payment process – Developments in the accounts payable process which involve the initial purchase order from the buyer, an invoice from the supplier, receiving the goods or services, paying the seller and accounting for the goods or services. Without the use of technological developments this process would require manual routine matching and approving payments, which is time-consuming and inefficient.

• The order to cash process – Developments in the accounts receivable process which involve the issuance of the invoice by the supplier, payment by the buyer, receipt of the payment by the supplier and subsequent clearance of the payment to the supplier. Without technological developments this process is subject to delays or errors due to manual processes involving invoices being sent before they are reconciled against purchase orders and purchasing systems data, and premature payments or payments of incorrect amounts.

Initial developments in SCF involved the use of web-based systems and purpose-built proprietary IT platforms developed by banks, buyers and sellers within a supply chain. These platforms were integrated with the buyer’s enterprise resource planning (ERP) system through host-to-host connectivity solutions. File transfer protocol (FTP) servers were commonly used as a means of securing data transmission. However, the process of implementing these secure data channels could take up to three months.

Technology is both transforming financial services and creating competitors outside the traditional sectors. Over the past ten years, a number of third-party providers have improved the use of IT platforms in relation to working capital and SCF making use of the following technologies:

• Procurement hubs – Use evaluated receipt contracts, adopt advanced Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) practices and use process automation to integrate ledgers and manage cash.

• Robotic process automation – Automation of repetitive tasks, such as transaction processing and the automation of approval and communication processes, thereby avoiding potentially adverse effects of human error or fatigue (examples include activities from call centre management to inventory control).

• Mobile transactions – Include technologies that facilitate payments via mobile wireless devices, such as smart phone wallets (digital wallets), tablets and wearables to perform transactions.

• Digital documentation – Allows documentation such as purchase orders to be completed on-line typically via a web interface incorporating electronic verification and the use of digital signatures for verification.

• Cybersecurity – Includes the development of technological hardware and software that can be used to protect financial privacy or safeguard against electronic theft or fraud (examples include authentication, biometrics, encryption and tokenisation);

• E-invoicing – Allows conversion from paper-based to electronic invoicing to expedite payment processes.

• Plug and play technology – Where the SCF platform is connected to the buyer’s and/ or seller’s ERP system and automatically extracts all required data for verification purposes. This reduces the possibility of human error through manual processes and also accelerates the verification process.

• Cloud computing – Allows the delivery of a range of computing services over the internet (including the use of servers, storage of information, databases and software). The cloud allows the interrogation of large data sets to perform analytical tasks interrogating the characteristics of inventory, accounts receivable and accounts payable data.

In tandem with the above developments has been the advent of blockchain technology.

Blockchain is a distributed ledger technology (DLT) that allows encrypted data to be stored globally on thousands of different servers and allows all members of a supply chain to share the same ledger which is visible only to participating entities. Access to data on the blockchain is restricted by users.

Blockchain technology uses information about data elements encrypted in blocks of computer code. The blocks are chained together across a shared ledger through cryptology. Blockchain can allow proprietary, centralised databases to be replaced with one single master database, all but eliminating the need to reconcile inconsistent individual records by using DLT.

Blockchain provides a way to verify ownership or to exchange ownership securely and efficiently and transfer money, securities or other assets. Blockchain is increasingly being applied in financial applications such as payment and settlement, supply chain finance, securities trading, insurance and credit reporting.

Blockchain can be used to manage information in relation to all transactions and finance processes related to inventory, payables, receivables and compliance. An inter-entity blockchain to document agreements, authorise, confirm and validate receipt of goods and services, facilitate settlement and process payments could reduce significantly the time needed to validate these steps.

Blockchain can also provide a record of all aspects of the transactions undertaken and thereby provide an audit trail of the transactions and ensure compliance as per the agreed contractual conditions. This will improve controls over working capital processes and speed up the time taken for transactions to occur.

Infrastructure costs could be driven down dramatically by substituting large numbers of proprietary systems with one relatively simple open-source protocol. It would make the SCF IT platforms accessible to a far greater number of companies and make it easier to eliminate paper-based processes.

Through the use of blockchain it has been possible to develop smart contracts which ensure that each part of a transaction is validated the instant it happens, triggering the next required action exactly when it is supposed to occur, until the process is complete. The technology behind smart contracts replaces existing processes that rely upon verification procedures involving time-consuming manual documentary evidence. These processes are replaced with computer programs that automatically execute various functions once electronic evidence is provided to support moving to the next stage.

Additionally, because blockchain transactions are direct and settled almost instantaneously, counterparty risk can be virtually eliminated. Other possible benefits include:

• Reducing the requirement for funds for working capital.
• Self-validating sub-ledgers for receivables and payables.
• Procure-to-pay and order-to-cash integration.
• Reduced chance of fraud.
• A more holistic and real-time view of supply chain flows.
• Increased data points allowing for data interrogation to facilitate better decisions.
• The opportunity to implement efficiencies such as ‘smart contracts’.

Since blockchain allows all kinds of payments to be completed without any bank or other intermediary, integrating blockchain with SCF can save both cost and time, as well as improve business efficiency. One significant use of blockchain technology is through the development of financial technology solutions to working capital issues.

#### 6.4.2.2 FinTech Solutions

Financial technology (FinTech) entities utilise new technology and innovative processes to create digital disruption to financial services that aim to support, enable and compete with traditional financial institutions.

Some FinTech entities are owned and operated by banks, but most are either non-bank financial institutions, technology companies such as Apple and Google, companies that provide infrastructure or technology that facilitates financial services transactions or disruptor companies that are fast-moving companies, often start-ups, focused on a particular innovative technology or process.

As opposed to the high level of regulation and high levels of leverage associated with traditional banking, FinTech entities are often smaller, nimble organisations that propose disruptive innovations for the provision of specific financial services including:

• International money transfer and tracking software;
• Investment platforms and analytical tools;
• Insurance and data analytics to support insurance;
• Audit, risk and regulatory compliance software;
• Sales and trading analysis software;
• Tools to manage billing and track transactions performed via credit cards and bank accounts via mobile banking services;
• Payments processing; and
• Lending and brokerage and underwriting services.

In relation to working capital, FinTech entities act as intermediaries by facilitating transactions between buyers and their suppliers. Many FinTech entities use cloud-based software platforms and can transform manual ‘procure-to-pay’ and ‘order-to-cash’ processes to electronic platforms that incorporate both purchasing management and accounts payable functionality.

Using integrated technology provided by FinTech entities, both the buyer and supplier can improve their cash conversion cycle. Buyers can extend their payables and at the same time accelerate payments to their suppliers. This is achieved by using the technology to reduce the burden of administering these functions. FinTech can be used to close the loop between procurement and accounts payable and provide a structure that streamlines these processes.

FinTech entities typically act like brokers. Their relationships include a network of different banks and non-bank financial institutions that allow them to obtain the best funding solutions for their customers. These financial institutions are not always the existing financial institutions with whom the buyers and sellers have existing relationships. FinTech companies also operate with private investors in the peer-to-peer lending space.

By capturing data about each entity’s transactional history, FinTech companies use technology to determine cash inflow projections, cash outflow projections, procurement forecasts and credit underwriting. By gathering this data, they are able to build a risk profile for an entity to inform potential financiers.


### Illustrative Example 15

HKFlex supplies polyethylene terephthalate to an automobile manufacturer based in Korea according to a purchase order request for 800 kilograms. The goods are delivered and an invoice for US$5.5 million is issued. HKFlex gives the buying entity a discount on the invoice amount at the buyer’s lower cost of capital. Terms of the invoice are 5/10 net 60.

Both HKFlex and the Korean automobile manufacturer have an arrangement in place with a FinTech entity whereby once the Korean automobile manufacturer has approved the invoice a cascade of processes will take place on the FinTech entity’s platform. This process allows HKFlex to obtain a discounted payment at a time of its choosing (even before 10 days), whilst the Korean automobile manufacturer can repay the FinTech entity as late as 60 or 90 days, or even 120 days, a period the more powerful buyer entity often prefers.

For example, assume HKFlex can elect to receive payment for a US$5.5 million invoice in 10 days through the FinTech entity and the buyer can submit payment to the FinTech 120 days after it approves the supplier invoice. The Korean automobile manufacturer has a cost of capital of 5%.

HKFlex seeks early payment from the FinTech after five days. The discount applied by the FinTech entity is:

> US$5.5 million x 0.05 x 10/365 = 7, 534.24658 or US$7,534

Hence, after 10 days the supplier gets US$5,492,466 of the US$5.5 million.

The Korean automobile manufacturer benefits through having an extended payment period, which positively impact its working capital.

In many cases, companies have extended their accounts payable to 120 days through such supply chain financing relationships. This improved working capital funding position can be used by companies to fund growth in new markets.

The use of SCF, technology and FinTech developments have allowed many participants in the supply chain to actively manage their funding requirements for working capital. Participants can work together via SCF arrangements to improve supply chain stability, operating cycle and cash conversion cycle positions, and, in so doing, improve their liquidity, financial performance, risk management and balance sheet efficiency.


#### 6.4.2.3 Cryptocurrency and Bitcoin

Historically, there have been a number of alternative means by which firms can receive accounts receivable and pay accounts payable, such as via the use of cash or acceptable noncash options such as cheques, direct debit or credit accounts, monetary transfer of currency or commodities (such as gold) and payments via loyalty programmes.

Non-cash alternatives are typically used in business transactions, as it is more convenient to use a debit or credit card rather than to hold large amounts of cash. These alternatives, however, result in card companies charging a fee, such as a percentage of the sale, 1 each time a credit or debit card is used in a transaction or by applying a minimum fee in the case of small transactions.

Accompanying the development of technology to assist in monetary transfers has been the development of cryptocurrency (otherwise known as virtual or digital currency) as an online alternative to traditional money. Cryptocurrencies are designed to be accepted by some parties as a means of payment and can be transferred, stored, or traded electronically.

Cryptocurrencies involve a peer-to-peer medium of exchange of monetary value that use computer software running across a network and rely on various established cryptographic techniques (hashing, digital signatures or one-way cryptographic functions) to control access and verify transactions. These techniques are used to generate, manage and verify the exchange of the cryptocurrency, rather than relying on a central authority facilitating the payments system (such as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority) between bank accounts.

Cryptocurrencies are on-line currencies that can be purchased by businesses using monetary currency such as US dollars via exchanges or in some jurisdictions via Automatic Teller Machines (ATMs). They are stored in digital wallets and used to settle transactions for goods or services provided or purchased. They can also subsequently be converted to monetary currency or be retained in digital wallets for future transactions. In addition, cryptocurrencies can be used as a form of investment as the exchange value between the cryptocurrency and the US dollar changes over time or can be used as payment to facilitate transfers between one type of cryptocurrency and another.

There are currently more than 1,000 different types of cryptocurrency. At August 2020, the top five cryptocurrencies included:2
![](DraggedImage-180.png)
Since its introduction in 2009, Bitcoin, and subsequently other cryptocurrencies, have received widespread attention in the media and from investors, many of whom speculate in cryptocurrencies. Developments in information technology, including the use of blockchain, have seen an increase in the proportion of cryptocurrency transactions for business purposes. Cryptocurrency can be used for the following purposes:

##### Purpose - Details
- Growth in business and customer base
	- Use of cryptocurrency may attract new customers, especially when involving on-line shopping or computer-based purchase and sale transactions.
- Money transfers
	- Unlike credit and debit card transactions, use of cryptocurrency attracts much lower fees and can reduce the time and cost associated with traditional transactions.
- No need for banking clearance of payments
	- Transactions can be processed more quickly. Transactions can be facilitated via computer or using a fintech app. Some transactions can be completed and transferred between buyer and seller in less than 10 minutes.
- Capital raising
	- Firms can conduct crowdfunding capital raisings using Bitcoins instead of debt or equity.
- To allow anonymity in transactions
	- Cryptocurrencies are typically stored in a digital wallet and when traded using the wallet, all that is revealed to the vendor is the wallet ID. This protects buyer and seller business’s identity from third parties.
- Facilitate multimember escrow transactions
	- Using blockchain technology for transactions requiring staged approvals before release of funding (e.g. property sales), cryptocurrency can be used to electronically log and record all elements of the transaction before release.
---- 

Given its popularity and volume of transactions, it is worthwhile exploring Bitcoin in a little more detail. Bitcoin’s early success led to a proliferation of competing cryptocurrencies. Many cryptocurrencies are essentially replicas of Bitcoin, while others seek to introduce additional functionality or have different design features. Consider the following – What is Bitcoin, how are the digital tokens obtained and how can it be used for business purposes?

Bitcoin was initially designed in 2008 primarily to send the bitcoin cryptocurrency via blockchain technology. Through the use of its blockchain technology, the designers developed a peer-to-peer payment system that enables users to send bitcoin (BTC) directly to a transacting party without having an intermediary holding the transacting parties accountable.

Bitcoin refers collectively to the entire currency system, whereas bitcoins (BTC) are the units of the currency. The total currency supply is capped at 21 million bitcoins. Each bitcoin can be subdivided into smaller denominations; for example, 0.1 bitcoins and 0.001 bitcoins. The smallest unit is a hundred millionth of a bitcoin (0.00000001 bitcoins).

Bitcoin uses an electronic public ledger approach that indicates the number of bitcoins and their owners at any given time. However, instead of associating names of people with accounts, the ledger only lists Bitcoin addresses (usually a mix of letters and numbers). Each address can be thought of as a pseudonym for a person (or group of people, business, etc.) and the use of pseudonyms is why people can use bitcoins without revealing personal information. Prior to conducting transactions, individuals can place bitcoins into a bitcoin wallet, which contains a record of the user’s addresses and bitcoin keys, which are similar to pin numbers.

Although Bitcoin uses a ledger, identical copies of it are distributed across millions of computers around the world. Consequently, no central point of failure exists and transactions recorded on the Bitcoin ledger are permanent and impossible to erase. Moving bitcoins from one address to another when performing transactions is equivalent to sending an instruction to all of the computers on the Bitcoin network to update each ledger in the same way. To ensure the integrity of the blockchain system all transactions are independently verified before the transaction will proceed.

The Bitcoin network itself acts as the intermediary by verifying the transactions and assuring that no one tries to cheat the system by spending Bitcoins twice or claiming nonpayment. When a transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network, instructing bitcoins to be moved from one address to another, computers on the network check whether the transaction is authorised before making any updates to the public ledger.

How can a user obtain BTC? Once having set up a bitcoin wallet, the user can add to this wallet in one of three primary ways:

1. Purchasing bitcoins via on-line suppliers, person-to-person arrangements, via a bitcoin ATM or via an exchange (exchanges directly connect people buying and selling bitcoins using a sophisticated currency exchange system and are particularly recommended for large transactions).
2. Engaging in transactions with counterparties that result in bitcoins being passed into their wallet.
3. Via bitcoin mining, which involves the use of high-powered computing to solve complex computational math problems that improve the efficacy of the bitcoin blockchain.
4. By miners who verify all transactions conducted using bitcoin via the blockchain technology.

The following illustrative example highlights how bitcoin can be used to pay for a business transaction.

### Illustrative Example 16

Blue Fin Technology is a fintech company that specialises in providing a data application that allows restaurant owners to see the prices of, and to purchase, fish from a range of registered seafood providers. Once the order is placed via the fintech app a delivery driver will collect and deliver the seafood to the purchaser within 3 hours.

The fintech app has been very successful and Blue Fin technology recently engaged a consulting firm HK Data Analytics (HKDA) to provide detailed analysis of sales data and to provide advice regarding expansion into other seafood varieties.

For the services provided, HKDA has sent an Invoice for HK$55,000 that allows for payment via either debit card to HKDA’s bank account or for the use of Bitcoin.

Both Blue Fin Technology and HKDA have bitcoin wallets and have access to Bitcoins for commercial transactions.

Assume the following information: 
US$ price per bitcoin = USD 11,813.49. 
US$/HK$ exchange rate is 1 US$ = 7.75 HK$. 
Debit card fee of 1.50% of sales price\> 
No fees are payable for using bitcoin. 
1. Identify the steps required in order for the transaction to be facilitated using Bitcoin. 
2. Calculate the equivalent bitcoin payment that should be requested such that HKDA will be indifferent between payment by debit card or bitcoin. 

Answer 
1. The following outlines the primary steps involved in completing a Bitcoin transaction.

Step 1
- HKDA sends Blue Fin Technology the code for its Bitcoin address (digital wallet). This address is used by Blue Fin Technology to send the payment to HKDA.
Step 2
- Blue Fin Technology instructs Bitcoin to send X amount of bitcoin to HKDA’s address. The transaction is created and signed using the private key for Blue Fin Technology’s sending address.
Step 3
- The transaction is sent to the network with three key pieces of information; input (Blue Fin Technology’s original source of Bitcoin), amount (to be transferred) and output (HKDA’s Bitcoin address).
Step 4
- The transaction must now be verified using the recently publicised code to HKDA’s digital wallet. To perform this:
	• A number of transactions is bundled together into a block, including the Blue Fin Technology to HKDA transaction, and
	• Miners will verify the transaction
Step 5
- Once verified:
	• The transaction block is added to the blockchain, permanently changing it to reflect the transactions in the block, including Blue Fin Technology’s transfer to HKDA, and
	• The bitcoin is transferred from Blue Fin Technology’s digital wallet to HKDA’s digital wallet.

2. If the payment is made by direct debit, HKDA will receive (after payment of the debit card fee) 55,000 x (1 – 0.0150) = HK$ 54,175. This is equivalent to US$ 6,990.32.
![](DraggedImage-181.png)
To be indifferent between the payment options, HKDA will need to charge 0.59172353 bitcoins for the engagement work performed.

## SUMMARY

• Net working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities. Current assets include inventories of raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods, trade receivables and cash and short-term investments in marketable securities, while current liabilities include trade payables, overdrafts and short-term loans.

• The main objective of working capital management is to manage an entity’s profitability and liquidity through the management of the entity’s net working capital.

• The main drivers of net working capital include an assessment of the impact of changes in the operational aspects of current assets and liabilities including cash, accounts receivable, inventory and accounts payable.

• The cash conversion cycle (also known as the net working capital cycle or cash cycle) is the residual time between an entity’s payment of cash for raw materials (via accounts payable) and the end of the operating cycle. It represents the time between an entity’s payment for the initial inventory and the entity’s receipt of payment for the sale of the finished goods from the inventory. The longer the cash conversion cycle, the greater the amount of investment required in working capital.

• The cash conversion cycle can be used to determine the working capital requirement of an entity as well as to help managers look for ways of decreasing the cash invested in current assets. It captures the relationship between the components of working capital and the flow of cash within an entity.

• The length of the cash conversion cycle depends on the length of:
- Days sales in inventory (DSI)
- Days sales outstanding (DSO)
- Days payables outstanding (DPO)

• Inventories include raw materials, work in progress and finished goods. When analysing inventory, it is important to assess the amount of inventory held in each category, the purpose for which it is being held and the time it is held for.

• The effective management of inventory through the use of decision models such as the economic order quantity (EOQ) approach involves the assessment of the cost of holding inventory relative to the cost of ordering inventory and the need for a buffer level of inventory and specification of an inventory reorder point.

• The effective management of trade receivables requires assessment of the creditworthiness of customers, effective control of credit granted, determination of any discounts to be provided for early payment under terms of sales agreements and the efficient collection of money due. Effective management of receivables can be assisted by factoring, invoice discounting and other forms of supply chain finance.

• The effective management of trade payables principally involves continued development of supply chain relationships, the assessment of discounts offered on accounts receivable by suppliers and the use of supply chain financing instruments, such as reverse factoring, dynamic discounting and purchase order finance.

• Modern technological developments such as blockchain and the development of FinTech entities have assisted with the development and use of SCF by extending payables by buyers and accelerating payments to the suppliers.

- Net working capital = Current Assets – Current Liabilities
- Total working capital = Permanent Working Capital + Transitory Working Capital
- Operating cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)
- Cash conversion cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) - Days Payables Outstanding (DPO) = Operating Cycle – DPO
- Total inventory costs = Holding Costs + Ordering Costs

Algebraically this can be expressed as:
- Total inventory costs = Q / 2 x C + F x D / Q

EOQ model

- Reorder level with buffer inventory = Lead Time x Daily Usage + Buffer Inventory
- Minimum inventory level = Reorder Point with Buffer Inventory - Lead Time x Daily Usage
- Average inventory level = Half of Regular Order Quantity + Buffer Inventory = Q / 2 + Buffer Inventory
- Effective annual rate 
![](DraggedImage-184.png)
- Effective days accounts receivable outstanding = ∑(Age of Account Category in Days x Percentage of Total Accounts Receivable Outstanding for the Account Category)
- Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
- Quick ratio = (current assets - (inventories + Prepaid Expenses)) / Current Liabilities
- Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of goods sold / average inventory
- Days sales in inventory (DSI) = 365 / Inventory Turnover Ratio
- Accounts receivable turnover ratio = (Net Credit Sales / Sales Revenue) / Average Accounts Receivable
- Days sales outstanding (DSO) = 365 / Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio
- Accounts payable turnover ratio = (Net credit purchase / cost of goods sold) / Average accounts payables
- Days payables outstanding (DPO) = 365 / Accounts payable turnover ratio

## Answers to Knowledge Check Questions

### Question 1

Gross working capital refers to an entity’s investment in short-term assets that are necessary to operate an entity on a day-to-day basis. All entities require a certain amount of cash, inventory and accounts receivable to operate smoothly and to carry out day-to-day operations. Note that working capital is defined in terms of the sum of all current assets, so in this case, the two terms are one and the same.

Net working capital captures the relationship between short-term assets and liabilities and is typically measured as follows:

> Net Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities

The level of net working capital can have a direct impact on an entity’s liquidity, funding and on its overall profitability.

Working capital management refers to the management of both current assets and current liabilities so as to achieve the maximum profitability for the entity as it conducts its operational activities, whilst also managing, concurrently, the solvency of the entity.

The goal of working capital management is to maintain the optimal mix of current assets and liabilities that enables the entity to continue its day-to-day operations and ensure the entity has sufficient liquid resources to continue in business and increase its profitability. Essentially, this involves achieving a balance between the need to minimise the risk of insolvency (liquidity) and the desire to maximise the return on assets (profitability).

The profitability objective is consistent with the primary financial management objective of maximising shareholder wealth, while liquidity is needed in order to ensure that financial claims made on an entity can be settled as they fall due to credit terms, higher debt costs and possible liquidation.

### Question 4 
There are alternative strategies an entity can implement to achieve its working capital management outcomes, including the flexible and restrictive current asset strategies. As such the statement is factually incorrect. A flexible current assets management strategy involves an entity holding large and at times excessive amounts of cash, marketable securities, inventory and accounts receivable. 

By holding these high balances of current assets, an entity is perceived to have high levels of liquidity and therefore is able to sustain any large business threats as it is able to use these assets to smooth fluctuations in business conditions.

A restrictive current assets management strategy involves an entity holding minimal amounts of current assets. This typically requires holding small amounts of cash and marketable securities, keeping inventory to low levels and placing strict credit terms on its customers, thereby restricting access to accounts receivable. By restricting investment in current assets, the entity can use a larger proportion of its capital for investment in higher yielding long-term assets.

### Question 5

The operating cycle reflects the time from the receipt of raw materials to the collection of cash, typically, via accounts receivable for the sale of finished goods made from those materials.

The operating cycle can be described in terms of two components: the number of days that sales are tied up in inventory and the number of days between the date of sale of the finished product until payment is received for the sale. Thus, it reflects the time associated with the inventory conversion period and the accounts receivable collection period.

The operating cycle can be estimated as:
> Operating Cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)

The cash conversion cycle is the residual time between an entity’s payment for raw materials (via accounts payable) and the end of the operating cycle. The end of the operating cycle corresponds to the time when the entity receives cash from the sale of finished goods made from those materials (accounts receivable). Therefore, the cash conversion cycle can be estimated as:

> Cash Conversion Cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) - Days Payables Outstanding (DPO)

#### Answer A is incorrect. 
The operating cycle is incorrectly calculated by not including the 2 weeks for raw materials prior to production (3 + 1 + 4 = 8 weeks) and the cash conversion cycle is incorrect after removing days payables outstanding (8 – 6 = 2 weeks).

#### Answer B is incorrect. 
The operating cycle is incorrectly calculated by adding weeks to the correct operating cycle for the days payables outstanding (2+3 + 1 + 4 + 6 = 16 weeks) and the cash conversion cycle is incorrect after removing days payables outstanding (16 – 6 = 10 weeks).

#### Answer C is correct.

Operating Cycle = Days Sales in Inventory (DSI) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)
Operating Cycle (3 + 2 + 1) + 4 = 10 weeks

Cash Conversion Cycle Operating Cycle – Accounts Payables Credit Period
Cash Conversion Cycle 10 – 6 = 4 weeks

The operating cycle is 10 weeks and the cash conversion cycle is 4 weeks 

#### Answer D is incorrect. 
The operating cycle is incorrectly calculated by not including the one week for the finished goods prior to sale (2 + 3 + 4 = 9 weeks) and the cash conversion cycle is incorrect after removing days payables outstanding (9 – 6 = 3 weeks).

### Question 7

For most businesses, the operating cycle is longer than the days payables outstanding and therefore the cash conversion cycle is typically positive. In this case, the entity has to wait until the end of the cycle to receive the cash inflow from its accounts receivable payment despite having paid the accounts payable earlier. Given that the entity has settled its accounts payable prior to the collection of the accounts receivable, the entity will need to fund this payment either from existing cash or by borrowing money for the cash conversion cycle period.

However, a negative cash conversion cycle occurs when the operating cycle is shorter than the days payables outstanding. In this case, the entity will use the inventory and collect the accounts receivable before it will need to pay for the inventory used during the inventory conversion period. Given that the entity does not need to settle its accounts payable prior to the collection of the accounts receivable, the entity will obtain a cash surplus and will need to invest surplus funds into other production, growth in non-financial assets or, at the minimum, acquisition of marketable securities.

From a liquidity perspective, the negative operating cycle can result in a cash surplus for the business which can be problematic if the entity is not able to reinvest this surplus into new activities which can obtain a suitable rate of return for shareholders.

### Question 19

Answer A is incorrect. There is no specific requirement that blockchain must be used as part of all supply chain finance arrangements. Many IT systems used in the arrangements are supplied by the finance entities or independent entities that provide plug and play interactive software.

Answer B is incorrect. Most suppliers typically set their own credit and collection policy which in part require the establishment of the terms by which credit will be granted including the setting of credit limits, the maximum net days payment terms and discounts allowed for early payment. These features usually closely follow industry norms. Using supply chain financial arrangements, such as dynamic discounting, can involve discount rates being set by the supplier and/or the buyer.

Answer C is correct. As discussed in Section 6.4.1.1, supply chain finance (SCF) can be defined as the use of financial instruments, financing processes, risk management practices and technological techniques for optimising the management of cash flows, liquidity and working capital invested in the end to end business supply chain processes and transactions undertaken by an entity.

This definition highlights the fact that supply chain finance is highly dependent on the collaborative relationship between supply chain partners, considers all aspects of the supply chain process and focuses on inter-entity financing optimisation.

Answer D is incorrect. If entities engage in financial arrangements that are independent of the needs of others in their supply chain, this will not constitute as supply chain finance.

### Question 20

Answer A is incorrect. Reverse factoring typically occurs on confirmation of receipt of the invoice from the supplier and the goods by the buyer.

Answer B is incorrect. Use of e-invoicing is not a form of supply chain finance. It simply involves the conversion from paper-based to electronic invoicing to expedite payment processes.

Answer C is incorrect. Accounts receivable loans involve the granting of a loan by a financial institution that uses the accounts receivable of an entity as collateral.

Answer D is correct. Purchase order financing allows the supplier to receive funding from the buyer’s financier upon advice to the financier of the receipt of the purchase order.

### Question 21

Blockchain provides a way to verify ownership or to exchange ownership securely and efficiently and transfer money, securities or other assets. Blockchain is increasingly being applied in financial applications such as payment and settlement, supply chain finance, securities trading, insurance and credit reporting.

Blockchain technology uses data elements encrypted in blocks of computer code. The blocks are chained together across a shared ledger through cryptology. It allows proprietary, centralised databases to be replaced with one single master database, all but eliminating the need to reconcile inconsistent records by using a distributed ledger technology (DLT). DLT allows all members of a supply chain to share the same ledger, which is visible only to participating entities, and to restrict access data on the blockchain to users.

Substituting large numbers of proprietary systems with one open-source, relatively simple, protocol could dramatically drive down infrastructure costs. It would make the SCF IT platforms accessible to a far greater number of companies and make it easier to eliminate paper-based processes.

Blockchain can be used to manage information in relation to all transactions and finance processes related to inventory, payables, receivables and compliance. An inter-entity blockchain to document agreements, authorise, confirm and validate receipt of goods and services, facilitate settlement and process payments could reduce significantly the time needed to validate these steps.

Blockchain can also provide a record of all aspects of the transactions undertaken and thereby provide an audit trail of the transactions and ensure compliance as per the agreed contractual conditions. This will improve controls over working capital processes and speed up the time taken for transactions to occur.

Through the use of blockchain it has been possible to develop smart contracts which ensure that each part of a transaction is validated the instant it happens, triggering the next required action exactly when it is supposed to occur, until the process is complete. The technology behind smart contracts replaces existing processes that rely upon verification procedures involving time-consuming manual documentary evidence. These processes are replaced with computer programmes that automatically execute various functions once electronic evidence is provided to support moving to the next stage.

Moreover, because blockchain transactions are direct and settled almost instantaneously, they virtually eliminate counterparty risk. Other possible benefits include:
• Reducing the requirement for funds for working capital.
• Self-validating sub-ledgers for receivables and payables.
• Procure-to-pay and order-to-cash integration.
• Reduced chance of fraud.
• A more holistic and real-time view of supply chain flows.
• Increased data points allowing for data interrogation to facilitate better decisions.
• The opportunity to implement efficiencies such as ‘smart contracts’.

## OPENING CASE

LONG-TERM FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT

Spark Energy Asia (SEA) is a Hong Kong based energy company primarily involved in the generation, distribution and retailing of electricity. Its primary activities include:

• The operation of a 200 megawatt power coal-fired generator using imported coal;
• The distribution of electricity via poles and wires that require continuing maintenance;
• The retailing of electricity to commercial and retail customers across Hong Kong; and
• The provision of advisory services to other energy companies operating in Cambodia and Laos.

All of SEA’s activities are at various stages of maturity and therefore a range of different funding instruments is needed to fund SEA’s activities. Equity is typically used as part of the funding of all activities undertaken by SEA, but given the long-term nature of both the generation and distribution activities, SEA also uses debt as part of the funding.

At 31 December 20X8, the fair value of total debt is HK$85.525 billion and the debt to asset ratio is 23.70%.

Of the total debt, 65% is in the form of unlisted floating rate notes and fixed coupon bonds issued via the debt issuance programmes with various maturities (80% of the notes have a maturity greater than five years). Bank loans represent 25% of the debt (70% of the bank loans have a maturity of less than five years). Short-term debt in the form of overdrafts and short-term loans represent approximately 10% of the debt, 60% of the debt is fixed rate debt and 40% is floating rate debt.

SEA has a long-term credit rating of BBB+ (an investment grade rating). The average cost of debt on a pre-tax basis for SEA was 5.50% in the year ended 31 December 20X8.

SEA has a cost of equity of approximately 16.50%. At 31 December 20X8 the share price was HK$45.50 and the number of shares on issue was 6,050,000, giving a total market capitalisation of HK$275.275 million. Approximately 60% of the shares are owned by a single family.

In its 20X8 Annual Report, SEA stated that based on its available cash balance and unused committed banking facilities, as well as its ready access to both the loan and debt capital markets, it will have sufficient financing capacity to fund the following three capital expenditure projects:

• Replacement of two generators at its power plant, thereby increasing the capacity and efficiency of operations;
• Continued replacement of poles and wires to improve efficiency in distribution operations; and

• Replacement of existing IT systems within its retail business to improve customer service and better understand consumer consumption patterns.

As SEA evaluated the funding requirements for each of their projects and business segments, they would have considered the revenues the activities were likely to generate and how much it would cost to operate and maintain these activities.

SEA would also have estimated what it would cost to finance each of their projects and their overall operations, i.e. how much they would pay for the debt and the equity used to finance each project incrementally and for the entity as a whole, given the associated risks. This ‘cost of capital’ measure would be incorporated into their investment analysis and applied as a discount rate when assessing projects.

The value of the individual projects can be assessed by discounting the expected cash flows of the projects by the cost of capital. If the sum of the present value of the future net cash inflows is greater than the acquisition costs this should result in a positive net present value for the project and the project would be considered a viable project.

## OVERVIEW

In the previous two chapters, students have explored techniques that can be used when financing an entity’s short-term financing requirements for liquidity and for servicing the working capital requirements of the entity. This chapter extends this analysis by introducing students to the factors that impact the long-term financial management of an entity’s funding, investment and dividend decisions.

As part of making funding decisions about an entity, financial managers need to evaluate the capital requirements of the entity and how to calculate and evaluate the cost of a variety of long-term debt and equity funding instruments. Long-term finance is typically used for major long-term investments. This form of capital is normally more expensive and less flexible than short-term finance due to factors such as the need to develop and apply a dividend policy for the distribution of dividends to shareholders, the timing of equity and debt issuances, collateral requirements, debt covenants and the fact that the long-term structure of interest rates is normally upward in nature. This chapter will explore the key considerations in evaluating a debt issuance programme, how a business can evaluate the cost of equity of a variety of equity instruments and how to analyse approaches to the dividend policy decision, including legal constraints, liquidity and shareholder expectations.

This chapter will also explore how a business can analyse capital structure, leverage and the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). It will examine how cost of capital is used in investment decision making, given that investment decisions are reliant upon receiving sufficient returns to cover the cost of debt and equity funding used for the investment project. Also, the cost of capital is typically used to determine whether the incremental cash flows from a project will increase shareholders’ wealth.

This chapter will demonstrate the interdependence of long-term financial management decisions given that a significant change in any of the decisions can have either a positive or negative impact on an entity’s value. A decision made in one area should always take account of decisions made in the other areas. For example, if an entity chose an expensive source of capital, this would increase the cost of capital for the entity, and would, in turn, reduce the number of viable investments the entity could undertake and potentially adversely affect the ability of the entity to pay dividends to shareholders in the future.

This chapter will also demonstrate the linkages between funding, investment and dividend decisions and discuss alternative frameworks such as optimal capital structure, pecking order theory and FRICTO analysis for the assessment of alternative sources of finance.

## 7.1 DEBT CAPITAL

In this section, students will learn how to calculate the cost of debt for a range of debt capital securities. The section will initially provide an overview of debt finance and then discuss the characteristics of corporate bonds, bank debt, convertible notes and preference shares.

### 7.1.1 Debt

As defined in HKAS 32 s.11, a financial liability is:

1. A contractual obligation:
	a. To deliver cash or another financial asset to another entity or
	b. To exchange financial assets or financial liabilities with another entity under conditions that are potentially unfavourable to the entity

2. A contract that will or may be settled in the entity’s own equity instruments, subject to conditions specified in HKAS 32.

Debt occurs when one party (a borrower or debtor) undertakes a commitment to pay an amount, or a series of amounts, in the future to a second party (a lender or creditor). The amounts owed will include both payments of interest and repayment of principal. Interest is regarded as the consideration for: (a) the time value of money over a particular period of time, as reflected by the risk-free rate, and (b) the credit risk associated with the principal amount outstanding, the seniority of the debt and any adjustments to reflect any embedded optionality.

The terms of a debt obligation are typically specified in contractual obligations between an entity and its lenders. Debt typically has the following main characteristics:

• Borrowed funds are typically received now and repaid in the future as a deferred payment or series of payments. The repayment may involve amortisation of the borrowed amount, repayment of the full amount at a future specified repayment date or a mix of these two approaches, which involves amortisation over time and a lump sum future payment of the remaining outstanding balance.

• Interest is typically paid periodically on outstanding balances at either a fixed or floating rate of interest.

• Depending on the terms of the debt (such as to whether the debt is secured or unsecured) and the law governing default in the relevant jurisdiction, borrowers may default on the payments of interest and/or the repayment of principal.

• In some cases, some instruments that otherwise look like equity, such as preference shares, involve a contract that requires settlement in the entity’s own equity instruments. Based on HKAS 32 this form of settlement will require the instrument to be classified as a debt instrument.

Three economic features clearly distinguish debt from equity:

• Debt is typically issued for a fixed period of time during which time interest must be paid and the principal must be repaid. In contrast, equity is issued in perpetuity.
• Interest paid on debt is tax-deductible in most jurisdictions. In contrast, dividends paid to shareholders are not tax-deductible.

• Debt does not represent an ownership interest. Creditors have no voting power whilst the entity is a going concern.

Often it will be relatively straightforward to classify a financial instrument as a financial asset, a financial liability or an equity instrument. After all, a promise to receive cash (a financial asset) or to pay another entity cash (a financial liability) are very common examples of financial instruments. The classification, measurement and reporting of financial instruments is discussed in detail in HKICPA Module 11 Chapter 12.

Whilst the classification of financial instruments as debt or equity will normally be consistent between accounting and financial management, there are some differences when dealing with more complex instruments. Accounting will normally be conditioned by the definition of a liability in the conceptual framework for financial reporting. That definition requires the existence of a present obligation to transfer assets to another entity for the item to be classified as a financial liability. Financial management will be primarily concerned with the probability, timing and size of cash outflows – even if the cash outflows are not obligatory. Financial management has to consider the availability of the entity’s liquid funds for such outflows and of the markets for refinancing. In short, the purposes of financial reporting and financial management can differ, and rightly so.

When share prices and debt prices rise or fall, investors have to make decisions about whether to hold, sell or buy, and financial managers need to consider the impact of the price change on the entity’s cost of capital. To do this, financial managers have to determine the fair value of each share and debt instrument.

The objective of a fair value measurement is to estimate the price at which an orderly transaction to sell the asset or to transfer the liability would take place between market participants at the measurement date under current market conditions. Ideally an analyst would want to perform financial instrument valuations using observable market traded inputs, but these may not always be available.

HKFRS 13 defines fair value as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. Due to this definition, the price determined is an exit price (assuming a sale). From time to time prices for debt and equity will be directly observable as market prices, while at other times the prices may need to be derived from comparator issuances and in the case of complex financial instruments may require use of a valuation model using unobservable inputs. Each of the above approaches will be discussed in greater detail in Chapter 10.

#### 7.1.1.1 Corporate Debt

As a generality, when an entity borrows money to be paid back at a future date with interest, it is known as debt financing. Interest on debt is typically charged at a simple or compounded rate.

Most entities typically have some form of either short-term or long-term debt. As discussed in Chapter 6, short-term debt is typically used to fund working capital requirements and includes short-term overdrafts, borrowings and debt that have less than 12 months to maturity. In contrast, long-term debt securities typically have a term to maturity greater than 12 months and include bank loans and bond issuances. Entities raise long-term debt for a number of reasons, including to:

• Purchase new fixed assets such as plant and equipment or to expand existing production processes.

• Fund the acquisition of another business.

• Refinance existing debt.

• Repurchase shares in a share buyback as part of a capital restructure.

• Change the portion of long-term debt on issue relative to equity as part of a capital restructure to more towards an optimal capital structure that lowers an entity’s cost of capital.

An entity’s cost of debt is the effective interest rate an entity pays on its debt obligations, including bonds, mortgages and any other forms of debt that the entity may have. When estimating the cost of capital for an entity, what is of particular interest is the cost of an entity’s long-term debt.

The cost of debt is typically measured at the point in time when the analysis is performed and as such should reflect the cost of existing debt issued at that point in time, keeping in mind that interest rates may have changed since the debt was first issued. The cost of debt needs to reflect the cost of both fixed and floating rates of interest. However, arriving at the current cost of debt for each type of debt requires careful consideration because both floating and fixed rates of interest change over time.

For floating rate debt, the rate of interest will always reflect the current rate of interest that the entity is contractually obliged to pay. For example, if the entity has interest payable at three-month HIBOR plus 150 basis points and three-month HIBOR is currently at 2.35% p.a., then the total interest payable will be set at a rate of 2.35% p.a. plus 1.50% p.a., i.e. 3.85% p.a. If HIBOR rises in the future, the overall cost of debt would increase and vice versa. Despite changes in the interest rate, the fair market value of the floating rate debt would remain unchanged because the increased or decreased future cash outflows would be discounted at a rate that reflects the higher or lower interest rate.

In contrast, the interest paid by the borrower on fixed rate debt remains unchanged during the period of the fixed rate borrowing. However, the fair value of fixed rate debt changes when there are changes in the level of interest rates. In order that the interest cost on fixed rate debt fairly represents the current cost of debt for the remaining life of the debt, it is necessary to establish what it would cost to re-issue the debt at its remaining term to maturity at the prevailing interest rate on the measurement date.

Most analysts use the current cost of long-term debt as the appropriate cost of debt for calculations of the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). This is the relevant cost because the WACC is the opportunity cost of capital for the entity’s investors as of today.

The cost of debt can be estimated by considering the interest cost of all individual long-term loans and bonds or by considering the level of interest paid in the current year on the total long-term debt (assuming that the past year’s interest expense is indicative of future years).

Entities can typically deduct interest payments from assessable income for tax purposes. The after-tax cost of interest payments equals the pre-tax cost times 1 minus the tax rate or:

## 7.4 Selecting Between Alternative Sources of Finance



### 7.4.1 Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)

![](DraggedImage-206.png)

![](DraggedImage-207.png)
