#### 7.4.1.3 Using WACC in Practice
As discussed above, in the introduction to Section 7.4.1, an entity’s WACC measures the rate of return debt and equity investors require from an entity, given the entity’s existing business risk and financial strategy. The WACC can be used to assess investment decisions. It can also be reduced so as to minimise the overall cost of funding the entity.

If an entity was to purchase major assets not typically used by the entity and expand their business activities into more risky activities, then its current WACC may be inappropriate.

The new business activities will expose the entity to new business risks and if the funding is done using debt in proportions higher than the current debt to equity ratio, the entity will be exposed to higher levels of financial leverage. Both of these factors may necessitate a reconsideration of the appropriate level for the WACC. Similarly, if the entity was to divest itself of major assets, projects or divisions that relied heavily on external financing, this will change the overall business risks and funding requirements of the entity.

An entity’s WACC is not always the appropriate hurdle rate for its investments. If the entity’s WACC is not appropriate, then consideration should be given to use the WACC and deleveraged asset beta for a comparable entity, which is primarily in the riskier (safer) line of operations as a better risk-adjusted benchmark. Caution should be used if applying comparator information because no two firms have identical levels of business and financial risks. It may be necessary to first **deleverage** all comparator firms and then **leverage** the asset betas of these comparator entities using the debt to equity ratio of the entity being assessed to estimate the appropriate equity beta and cost of equity to apply in the WACC.

### 7.4.2 Competing Theories of Capital Structure

An entity’s capital structure refers to the way that an entity finances its assets through some **combination of financing sources**. There are two main sources of financing that can be used by an entity: **external and internal financing**. External financing could be in the form of borrowing or equity issues, whilst internal financing is related to the use of profits or retained earnings. Entities **continuously invest** to sustain or improve existing growth rates. For these reasons, entities financing decisions are very important.

As discussed in Section 7.2 of this chapter, **M&M (1958)** states that the value of an entity is **irrelevant to how that entity is financed** in a **perfect market**. However, once the assumptions of the perfect capital market are relaxed and we consider the impacts of taxation, financial distress, agency theory and information asymmetry, it becomes obvious that an entity’s value is affected by the capital structure it employs.

In this section, we will discuss two concepts that are used to explain how managers make decisions about the appropriate capital structure for their entity: trade-off theory and pecking order theory.

#### 7.4.2.1 Trade-Off Theory
Trade-off theory considers that entities have a target capital structure that is determined by the **marginal benefits of debt**, such as the tax shield from debt relative to **the marginal costs associated with debt **, such as bankruptcy costs and agency costs.

In this model the value of the leveraged firm can be shown mathematically to be equal to:
![](DraggedImage-209.png)
The marginal benefit of increasing debt declines as debt increases, while the marginal cost of debt increases. By considering the marginal benefits and costs of debt, it is possible for an entity to optimise its overall value by focusing on this trade-off when choosing how much debt and equity to use for financing. By doing so, trade-off theory can be used to identify the optimal mix of debt and equity for a firm. This optimal mix is known as the optimal capital structure and reflects the combination of debt and equity where the cost of capital is minimised whilst the value of the entity is maximised. This is because by minimising the cost of capital and WACC, an entity will achieve its highest possible return on capital.

Trade-off theory implies that entities adjust their capital structure in response to the temporary shocks that cause their leverage to deviate from the entity’s target. As such, entities’ capital structures are optimal when they are determined by comparing the costs against the benefits using debt or equity financing.

##### Marginal Benefits of Debt
The interest rate tax shield has the effect of reducing the pre-tax cost of debt by the amount of the tax shield. This is an important consideration in setting the mix of debt and equity because it will directly impact the cost of capital and hence the WACC of the entity.

The tax benefit is very important. Debt can also provide additional benefits to the entity including the following:
- • By issuing debt the company must give priority to meeting its interest and principal obligations to avoid default and potential bankruptcy. By focusing on the efficiency of the entity’s cash flows, managers may be able to increase the earnings per share, which also brings benefits to the shareholders.
- • By issuing debt the company can control and limit the ability of poor managers wasting earnings (which is needed to service the debt) on personal benefits such as business class travel and excessive office refurbishments, which add no direct value to the entity.

##### Marginal Costs of Debt
The costs of using debt fall into two general categories: bankruptcy costs and agency costs.

Bankruptcy costs, also referred to as costs of financial distress, are costs associated with financial difficulties that a firm might experience because it uses debt financing. Bankruptcy costs can be categorised as being either direct or indirect costs.
- • Direct costs include fees paid to lawyers, accountants and consultants and reflect the transaction costs that must be incurred to facilitate negotiations with lenders and to navigate the bankruptcy process.
- • Indirect costs include costs associated with changes in the behaviour of people who deal with an entity when it becomes financially distressed. Examples include existing customers seeking alternative suppliers further decreasing an entity’s revenue, stress to existing employees about the sustainability of their employment, the removal of discounts and the imposition of tighter credit terms on accounts payable.

Agency costs can arise when:
- • Good projects are passed over due to pre-existing excessive debt leading to an underinvestment problem or a ‘debt overhang’ problem.
- • Managers shift investment to more risky assets and projects and the costs are incurred by the debt holders.
- • Managers give priority to shareholders by borrowing to pay out cash to shareholders as dividends.

As shown in Exhibit 7.11, trade-off theory is based on a recognition that the marginal benefit of further increases in debt (such as taxation) declines as debt increases, while the marginal cost (such as bankruptcy and agency costs) increases. An entity that is optimising its overall value will focus on this trade-off when choosing how much debt and equity to use for financing. As such, trade-off theory suggests that the value of an entity is equal to the value of an entity 100% funded by equity plus the present value of the benefits arising from interest tax shields less the present value of any bankruptcy and agency costs.
![](DraggedImage-210.png)
From Exhibit 7.11 it should be noted that at high levels of debt, the value of the firm with debt declines at a faster rate than the growth in the value of the firm prior to the optimal capital structure that maximises the entity’s value. This is because as the perceived risk of bankruptcy increases, the credit rating of the entity will fall, reflecting the loss in credit quality. Accompanying this fall in credit quality will be an increase in the rate of interest charged for debt, which reduces the firm’s liquidity further and increases the probability of default of the entity. The spiral continues quickly unless remedial action is taken by the entity. Due to this increasing cost of debt, the value of the firm will decrease at a quicker marginal rate than the marginal increase in the value of the firm at lower levels of debt.

#### 7.4.1.4 Pecking Order Theory
Different types of capital have varying required rates of return and issuance costs. As a general rule, under the pecking order theory managers regard internal financing as having the lowest cost of capital, debt is ranked next, followed by the issuance of ordinary shares.

The pecking order theory recognises that different types of capital have different costs and that the differences in these costs affect the financing choices that managers will make when selecting which form of capital to use. This theory suggests that managers will exhaust lower cost sources of finance before moving to capital that requires a higher cost.

The pecking order theory maintains that businesses adhere to a hierarchy of financing sources. Entities will give preference to cheaper internal financing, such as retained earnings and excess liquid assets or ‘financial slack’, when they are available relative to external capital sources, and debt is preferred over equity if external financing is required.

The pecking order theory is based on four significant empirical observations about corporate financial behaviour:
- • Dividend policy is ‘sticky’. Despite temporary fluctuations in profits, entities typically maintain a stable dividend payment.
- • Companies prefer internal financing (retained earnings and excess liquid assets) relative to external financing of debt or equity.
- • If a company must obtain external financing, it will issue the safest low-cost security first.
- • As a company requires more external financing, it will work down the ‘pecking order’ of securities, beginning with debt, convertible securities, preferred shares and, as a last resort, issuing more ordinary shares.

The rationale for the pecking order theory is also founded by considering the information asymmetry that exists between the entity and external investors. This asymmetry arises because the management of the entity knows the true value of the entity’s assets and growth opportunities. In contrast, outside investors can only guess these values and will therefore be concerned if the manager offers to sell equity. Therefore, when managers issue equity instead of riskless debt, outside investors rationally discount the entity’s stock price. To avoid this discount in the share price, managers will follow the pecking order theory.

### 7.4.3 FRICTO Framework
Whilst trade-off theory provides an opportunity to identify the **optimal level **of debt to hold within an entity so as to maximise an entity’s value, the approach does not take account of the impact of the changes in capital structure on financial flexibility, risk, net income the control of the entity. These considerations are considered in the FRICTO (flexibility, risk, income, control, timing and other) framework which provides a helpful, systematic approach to how much **debt** an entity should carry in its capital structure and how this is likely to affect **investment and dividend** decisions within the entity.

The FRICTO framework is often used to examine the potential of each financing alternative and to set a strategy for making financing decisions over several years. The FRICTO acronym (originally FRICT) was first used to describe a framework that evaluates systematically the various factors and trade-offs that need to be considered in making capital structure decisions and their impact. The elements of FRICTO analysis are based upon the pragmatic analytical framework for making financing decisions originally developed by Hunt, Williams and Donaldson (1966).

The six elements of FRICTO analysis that need to be considered are discussed in Exhibit 7.12.
#### Flexibility
Flexibility refers to leaving the entity’s financing alternatives open whereby choices can be made between alternative sources of finance. Issues to consider here include:
- • What financing alternatives are available to the entity?
- • Which alternative funding sources provide the greatest benefit/cost to the entity?
- • What portion of funding has already been utilised and is still available for further drawdown?
- • Are existing covenants likely to impact choices?
- • What do other firms in the same industry do to fund their assets?
- • Will financing choices be affected by the time horizon of projects being undertaken? For example, does it make sense to fund a one-year project with a five-year bond?
- • How will shareholders react to changes in business finance strategy?
- • Will the credit rating be compromised by changes in the debt to equity mix?
#### Risk
Risk refers to the ability of the entity to meet its financial obligations (e.g. interest, principal repayment, lease payments and preferred dividends) even in adverse circumstances. Issues to consider include:
- • Is the entity exposed to high levels of operating or financing leverage that may affect EPS when debt is increased?
- • Will the entity be able to commit to a dividend policy involving regular fixed dividends or growth rates?
- • Do you need to perform sensitivity analysis or stress testing of modelled results?
#### Income
Income refers to the impact of the different financing alternatives on returns to shareholders as measured by earnings per share (EPS) or return on equity (ROE). Issues to consider include:
- • What impact will each financing alternative have on EPS and the ROE?
- • Which financing alternatives will result in the highest EPS and ROE?
- • How does this compare to competitors?
- • Are there any industry attributes such as seasonality in revenue that may directly affect the choice of funding and the impact on income?
#### Control
Control refers to how different financing alternatives affect the ownership control of the entity.
Issues to consider include:
- • Are debt covenants too restrictive and therefore impede the future growth prospects to the entity?
- • If equity finance is used, to what extent will current ownership be diluted?
#### Timing
Timing focuses upon the current economic and capital market environment and refers to the sequencing of financial alternatives (both now and into the future), based upon expectations regarding the future economic and capital market environment and the entity’s performance.
Issues to consider include:
- • What is the current outlook for interest rates and the overall equity market?
- • What phase of the business cycle is the economy at and how will this impact credit spreads?
- • Do investors currently have a preference for debt relative to equity?
- • How long will it take for the company to move from its current capital structure to an optimal level?
- • If the project was delayed, what impact would that have on the raising of capital?
#### Other
‘Other’ refers to anything else related to an entity’s unique situation that is relevant to the financing decision. Each situation is different, but some common ‘other’ considerations may include:
- • Asset structure – Are assets tangible and therefore suitable for use as collateral?
- • Flotation costs – How much will an investment bank charge to float the issue?
- • Speed – How soon will the funds be needed?
- • Management attitudes – Is management conservative?
- • Exposure – Will additional stock increase the stock’s value because of greater exposure or liquidity?
- • Market valuation – Is the stock valued fairly?
---- 
To highlight the process involved in conducting a FRICTO analysis, Kester and Hoover (2005) developed a decision tree as shown in Exhibit 7.13 that can be applied to perform a capital structure analysis. The analysis highlights how each of the six steps is applied and the relationships between questions asked in the decision tree.
![](DraggedImage.jpeg)
As noted by Kester and Hoover (2005), the process of evaluating the FRICTO factors and inevitable trade-offs is ultimately subjective and situational. They note that in its bare essential form, FRICTO analysis involves the classic trade-off in finance: a trade-off between risk and income (return). Hence, the first two elements depicted in Exhibit 7.13 are income and risk. In a simple world (perhaps the one imagined by financial economists), entities choose either debt or equity. Because of financial leverage, debt is usually the financing alternative that results in the highest EPS and ROE. However, as the debt of an entity increases, so does the threat or financial distress and bankruptcy. Recognising this trade-off leads to one way to define optimal capital structure: maximise the level of debt (hence maximising EPS and ROE), subject to maintaining reasonable levels of risk. Since ‘reasonable’ is subjective in nature, the optimal trade-off between income and risk ultimately depends upon the entity’s (more specifically the entity’s owners’) attitude toward risk.

Of course, the world is not just two dimensional, the impact of issuing equity will have consequences on the level of control within the entity and the timing may be unfavourable, or the resulting dilution in voting control may be unacceptable. This may lead to choosing convertible shares or preferred stock. Also, callable bonds, floating rate debt, short-term debt or re-financing of the latter will be preferred when a decline in interest rates is expected. If a recurring need to obtain additional capital is expected in the future, it is important to maintain financial flexibility (adequate reserve debt capacity).

# Opening case
## GLOBAL DAIRY PRODUCTS

In the early 2000s, a small group of agricultural scientists and nutritionists employed by the Singapore-based, research-focused subsidiary of Global Dairy Products, a New Zealand-based milk processing company, discovered a specific protein in milk that caused digestion discomfort and lactose intolerance for a significant number of people. After further research they also found that certain types of cows naturally produce milk that is free of this protein.

Commercialisation of these discoveries enabled Global Dairy Products to issue licences to approved dairy farmers who were then able to market the trademarked milk that distinguished it from conventional milk products. Despite its premium price tag, the product was very well received by consumers, which resulted in significant growth in revenue and profitability for the company – not only in the traditional markets in Oceania, but also through significant export sales to Asia (in particular mainland China) where demand for safe and nutritionally beneficial dairy products had boomed following health scares in mainland China in 2008 caused by product contamination.

This period of rapid growth eventually resulted in the company seeking listing on the New Zealand and Australian Stock Exchanges. At the time of listing, the company’s vision was stated as being ‘an innovative, ethical and socially responsible producer of nutritional dairy-based products’. Key strategic priorities were identified to develop a strong brand of premium dairybased products; to venture into new profitable markets; and to continually invest in research to further expand its technical knowledge and competitive advantage. When listed, the product portfolio and target markets were liquid milk and infant formula for the US and the UK; infant formula, fresh milk and milk powder for China and other Asian countries; and fresh milk, infant formula, milk powder and other dairy products for Australia and New Zealand.

Before the public listing the company had appointed a Hong Kong-based food distribution company to handle all sales to the Asian region. Whilst this arrangement had worked reasonably well in the early years, as export volumes from Asia began to grow much more rapidly than those from traditional markets, the company eventually decided to establish a distribution centre in Hong Kong and to appoint a local executive to manage the Asian region. The appointee, Raymond Li, was given a very high level of autonomy. This was in part because the rapid growth in sales had resulted in the New Zealand management team being under significant pressure.

# OVERVIEW

Chapters 1 and 2 discussed strategy formulation and strategic decision-making. Selecting a strategy is simpler than strategy implementation. Success relies in part at least on the organisation’s performance measurement system to plan, monitor and control progress.

This chapter is concerned with how performance measurement helps achieve goals and objectives through setting targets and measuring and monitoring performance against those targets.

Before exploring performance measurement in detail, however, we need to understand some key terms.

Performance is a complex concept with different meanings for different people and in different contexts. For example, it could include market share, lead time, on-time, customer satisfaction, profitability or return on investment.

Organisations may interpret performance differently, and hence, require different measures. For example, a full-service airline may focus on customer satisfaction while a low-cost airline may monitor labour costs to keep them to an essential minimum.

Performance measurement addresses why and what organisations decide to measure and how to quantify them using appropriate metrics.

Since ‘performance’ is a relative term, the selection of measures to serve as appropriate surrogates for performance can be challenging. When the context is not well defined, the task can be even more difficult.

Performance management refers to the process by which an organisation develops appropriate structures and procedures to bring about organisational changes based on the results of performance measurement.

In effect, performance management extends performance measurement by analysing performance to improve decision-making.

Performance management can be considered an integral part of the overall organisational performance measurement system. That said, this chapter focuses on performance measurement whilst simultaneously considering performance management.

This chapter addresses the following concepts:
• Functions of performance measurement;
• Characteristics of various performance measures and changes to control systems;
• Three important performance measurement models, namely, the balanced scorecard, the performance pyramid and the building block model;
• The application of performance measurement to manage performance; and
• The behavioural and ethical considerations for an effective performance measurement system.

In doing so, the chapter seeks to provide insight on the following questions:
• What do we measure/what is performance?
• What is performance measurement?
• How is performance measurement related to performance management?
• Why do we want to measure performance?
• Is there any truth in ‘if you cannot measure it, you cannot manage it’?

This chapter will illustrate the above concepts with examples from manufacturing, service and retail organisations, as well as the public and not-for-profit sectors, to provide you with a real-world view.

# 8.1 Strategic Control and Governance
This section aims to explain the multiple roles of performance measurement, including its role in strategy implementation and governance. To understand this well, one must start with relevant management theories that have underpinned the design and the use of performance measurement.

Performance measurement is considered to have derived initially from the theory of scientific management and the theory of administration. According to these theories, processes can be standardised, rationalised and managed through planning, coordinating and control by an organisation. Subsequently, the performance measurement literature was influenced by the human relations movement. The theme of the movement is that organisations can be viewed as a social system (a network of relationships that exists between individuals, groups and institutions) and the effect of productivity can be manifested among interpersonal relationships. That said, the most influential theories for performance measurement are behavioural management theory and strategic management theory. Behavioural management theory examines the role of human relationships in greater detail. It focuses particularly on the motivational impact of human relationships on individuals. In comparison, strategic management theory uses the lens of an open system and tries to understand organisational behaviour by examining how the organisation’s internal and external environments influence the choices of strategies. These two theories also shed some light on the importance of governance, studying how organisations should be governed and guided and how undesirable behaviour triggered by self-interest can be avoided.

The current state of performance measurement can be viewed as the product of the above paradigms. However, performance measurement will continue to evolve and adapt to dynamic environments, endeavouring to balance the value and needs of individuals, stakeholders (a widely used term referring to a person or organisation with an interest in something, typically

a business or some other form of organisation), other interest groups and society in general. Because of this, organisations that understand this and utilise performance measurement to proactively manage their performance effectively will be well placed to secure a significant competitive advantage.

The remainder of this section will illustrate the functions of performance measurement and how it is intended to deliver effective strategic control and governance.

## 8.1.1 Aligning Performance Measurement with Objectives
An organisation is a complex entity, consisting of multiple processes and procedures that bind various business units together to carry out the organisation’s functions. One of the challenges an organisation is constantly facing is to manage and coordinate many different moving parts strategically and synergistically to achieve its goals. In this context, performance measurement can be viewed as a central nervous system for the organisation, aligning and synchronising the various parts and checking the pulse of the organisation.

To continually perform well, organisations must adapt their structures and management controls to the changing environment in which they operate. Being an integral part of the management control system, performance measurement is no exception. It must be aligned with the strategy that the organisation has decided to pursue.

Thus, there is no ideal performance measurement system. Each organisation needs to develop a performance measurement system appropriate to its needs and mindful of relevant contextual factors in the environment in which it operates and its chosen strategies. This process can potentially deliver the following benefits:

• Clarify performance expectations and avoid misunderstanding.

Although an organisation’s strategic direction could be developed from the bottom up, strategic formulation usually takes place at the senior management level and is approved in the boardroom. If communication between those who set the strategic direction and those at the operational level charged with implementing that direction is inadequate, it could result in misdirected behaviour and, potentially, value destruction (the financial diminution of owners’ equity caused by operational and/or capital losses). For example, assume that an organisation’s competitive advantage is achieved by minimising production costs and providing speedy delivery of products to customers. Operational managers, unaware of such a strategic planning goal, may insist on additional inspection points in the production process to ensure high-quality products are delivered to customers. This not only leads to extra costs but also lengthens the delivery time to customers.

When performance measurement is linked to the organisation’s strategic objectives, it serves as a strong signal to the operational managers about where and how effort should be focused. Too often, senior management fails to communicate their expectations to those at the operation level in the organisation. For example, goals such as ‘We need to be agile’ or ‘We are committed to technological advancement’ may sound meaningful but can cause confusion at the operational level because they are open to misinterpretation. At times, some types of performance such as capability or learning may not be directly visible or observable by the operational staff. By developing specific performance measures, senior management can make the performance expectations visible for operational managers.

• Better utilise limited resources and focus attention on what matters most.

No organisation has unlimited resources, and hence, each organisation needs a strategy to leverage its resources to create a competitive advantage. Managers are one of the most important resources at an organisation’s disposal, yet they are daily faced with competing demands on their time. If performance measurement is linked to the organisation’s strategic goals and subsequently with the reward system, it will focus managers’ attention on the strategic issues that matter to the organisation. There is a saying ‘what gets measured gets managed, and what gets managed gets done’. Performance measurement intensifies the focus on the strategic issues, highlights the areas that need the managers’ attention most and prompts managers to utilise resources efficiently. If a well-designed performance measurement system is absent, operational managers may choose to focus on their self-interests and maximise their own function’s success at the expense of the overall organisation.

With the aid of information technology, large amounts of performance data, either intra-entity or inter-entity, can be readily collected and made available to decisionmakers. This has led to a proliferation of performance measures. To obtain maximum benefit from its scarce resources, an organisation needs to focus on the critical aspects of its performance when specifying performance measures, instead of every aspect. Failure to do so may result in the specification of performance measures that are counterproductive. To measure everything means to understand nothing.

• Motivate employees and direct their behaviour.

It is generally accepted that well-developed goals and milestones have the effect of encouraging initiatives, tracking progress, promoting competitiveness and creating pride in achievements. A goal is a target established on a measurement scale, such as net profit, sales and customer satisfaction. To establish an effective goal, the target must be reasonably precise and related to the organisation’s strategic goals or objectives. Milestones refer to a series of short-term steps towards long-term goals through which management can monitor actions and their associated results. Both goals and milestones are part of the performance measurement system.

Performance measurement provides a specific, measurable, actionable, relevant and timely basis (also known as SMART) for goal setting and defines what success should be. When goals or milestones are objective and aligned with strategic objectives, employees can see their effort turn into something meaningful, and subsequently, inspire them to accomplish the goals or milestones. On the other hand, if the goals or milestones are vague and subjective, employees may lose their focus and become disengaged in their work. Thus, senior management needs to select appropriate performance measures to inspire employees and encourage desirable behaviour for the benefit of the organisation.

The next section explains the role of performance measurement in planning strategic implementation. It is worth noting that professional accountants play an important role in supporting the organisation’s senior management in the strategy development and implementation process. They are responsible for establishing performance measures that are aligned with strategic objectives to create value and sustain the longevity of the organisation.
## 8.1.2 Managing and Monitoring Strategic Objectives
Performance measurement aims to assess how well the organisation has performed by comparing performance measures to established criteria. This is a vital part of the control process. The key questions to ask during the performance measurement process are whether the organisation is on target to meet its overall objectives and whether an action is needed to change performance to bring the organisation back on target.

Organisations use a variety of terms to describe their performance measurement system, for example, a ‘dashboard’ (like the dials in an aircraft cockpit), a ‘traffic light’ system (green, amber and red to indicate progress) or a ‘scorecard’. Despite different terminology, they all share a similar function, that is, to measure, monitor and manage performance. This section examines how management can use performance measurement to monitor progress and improve performance through targets, trends and benchmarking.

Exhibit 8.1 illustrates the process of measuring and managing performance. It begins with reviewing the organisation’s strategy, identifying the organisation’s goals and specifying critical success factors. Based on the critical success factors, management determines the performance milestones that will reflect progress towards the organisation’s strategic objectives. These are expressed in either quantitative or qualitative terms, such as market share, quality, innovation and customer satisfaction. Subsequently, targets with specific timelines are formulated and applied to monitor strategic progress. This process relies on performance surveillance to identify ’gaps’, ‘deviations’ or ’risks’ and direct any necessary actions to keep business operations under control. As a result of this process, feedback is collected and shared within the organisation to improve corporate learning.

Step 1 Review strategy.
Step 2 Identify milestones of performance (strategic objectives).
Step 3 Set target achievement levels.
Step 4 Monitor the strategic progress.
Step 5 Facilitate feedback and reﬂect learning.
![](DraggedImage-211.png)

It is worth noting that sometimes the phrase ‘recognise and reward achievements’ can replace ‘facilitate feedback and learning’ in Step 5. For these performance measurement systems, an annual bonus is awarded if employees exceed their performance expectations. This type of motivational system, where performance measurement is used as the basis for reward and punishment, can have dysfunctional effects. This topic will be explored in Section 8.5.

Nevertheless, performance measurement has played a significant role in managing and monitoring the achievement of an organisation’s strategic objectives. This can be demonstrated in the following respects:

• By promoting an objective and consistent basis for decision-making and execution.

Decision-making is a recurring theme for management. However, estimates from practitioners and researchers suggest that as many as 50% of all managerial decisions fail due to flawed decision-making practices and an over-reliance on intuition for decision-making. Individuals often combine their own experience, views, insights, self-interest and office politics in forming their judgements, a process that is highly susceptible to bias and personal blind spots. Using data and fact-based information enables managers to overcome reliance on personal factors and make better-informed decisions.

In this regard, the sports industry has done a better job than the general business world. It is a common practice for coaches of highly contested sports to use player data and movement analysis to inform them of the progress of a match and whether a swift change to the game plan is needed. In fact, sports performance analysis based on tactical assessment, movement analysis, video and statistical modelling has been extensively applied in the industry to assist coaches and players in staying atop and optimising performance results. Business decision-making could probably learn from this industry and adopt processes that enable an organisation not just to win but to win consistently.

• By providing early warning signals and improving problem-solving.

Performance measurement can function as an early warning system by warning management of upcoming business risks. Too often, business risks have been simply dismissed as inherent organisational ‘symptoms’ and no action taken until the ‘symptoms’ manifest themselves into problems and eventually crises. By then, the damages are too severe to be undone. The best approach for problem-solving is to identify the problem as early as possible, diagnose the root cause and deal with it accordingly.

With the right performance measures built into the periodic review, small but significant risks can be discovered early and be dealt with before getting out of proportion. For example, the manager of a Hong Kong-based online cosmetic shop is worried about her company’s sales performance in the face of increasing competition from both online and bricks-and-mortar stores. The goal assigned to her for the current year is to increase sales by 10% from the previous year, but the first-quarter results show that the sales are only 1.5% above last year’s number for the same period. If this trend continues, the manager is unlikely to meet her annual target. It would be wise for her to check in with her reporting manager to see what can be done to address the gap before more time elapses. This simple case demonstrates how performance measures can be used to discover, prioritise and rectify problems. Effective performance measurement will cost an organisation much less than a major business overhaul or total failure.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Performance can have different meanings for different people. Performance measurement systems (PMS) should be designed so as to ensure accountability by fostering a deeper understanding of business processes.

Quality expert James Harrington once said, ‘If you can’t measure something, you can’t understand it. If you can’t understand it, you can’t control it. If you can’t control it, you can’t improve it.’ Using performance measurement can provide a better understanding of the business. Through the process of selecting the most appropriate performance measures, managers will gain an understanding of the nuances of the business and its interaction with other parts of the organisation. This experience leads to better knowledge of the process, and hence, a better understanding of how to improve the process so as to create value for the organisation, not by rewarding or sanctioning employees, but by learning and endeavouring to continuously improve business processes.

The discussion above describes a formal control process adopted by most organisations to manage and monitor performance. While there are potential benefits associated with using performance measures, there are also potential risks. For example, choosing a limited number of strategic objectives (e.g. market share, profit margin) to measure performance may encourage managers to ignore other relevant issues. Formality can lead to rigidity, which can cause staff to be disengaged. The effectiveness of performance measurement depends on trust between management and staff. Thus, it is not surprising that some organisations rely on informal controls that are not properly monitored or measured.

## 8.1.3 External Considerations

Performance measurement is typically used for internal planning, implementing, managing and monitoring strategic objectives. It can also be used to provide an external perspective relating to matters such as performance prediction, economic conditions and competitors’ pricing. This section explains the need to consider external considerations in performance measurement and identifies ways in which such considerations could be incorporated in the performance measurement system.

First, an organisation’s strategy is concerned with value creation by the organisation over a period. The organisation’s performance in this regard is relevant to all stakeholders. These include investors, customers, suppliers, staff, regulators and trade unions. Measurement data provided in the annual report presents information about how well the organisation is performing with the resources that have been entrusted to it. Without performance measurement, it would be difficult for stakeholders to determine whether management has accomplished what it set out to do, and therefore, whether they had discharged their responsibilities to all stakeholders for the current period. The stakeholder approach suggests that corporate objectives are, or should be, shaped and influenced by those who have direct involvement or interest in the organisation’s operational activities. Organisations may need to develop performance measures to ensure that the needs of stakeholders are met. Below are some common stakeholder measures:

• Share price and dividend yield.
• Compliance with legislation and government environmental regulations.
• Customers satisfaction.
• Percentage of repeat customers.

Second, performance measurement needs to consider the external environment of the business, as the forces and trends of the external environment affect the future direction of the organisation and influence the strategic choices it needs to make. Often, the considerations may encompass political, economic, sociocultural, technological, environmental and legal aspects, also known as PESTEL. Taking the higher education industry for example, Exhibit 8.2 explains how those considerations may impact a university’s performance measurement.
![](DraggedImage-212.png)

Finally, performance management must benchmark with its global and domestic competitors to identify its competitive advantage and add the most value. Relevant information needs to be collated and updated in a timely fashion so that managers can react quickly and effectively to changing market conditions.

Illustrative Example 1 presents how a leading hotel company has incorporated key external perspectives to make its performance measures relevant to discharging its accountability to the organisation’s various stakeholders.

### Illustrative Example 1

Performance needs to be understood relative to an organisation’s strategy and the industry in which it operates.

The Hong Kong and Shanghai Hotels (HSH) Group specialises in the ownership, development and management of luxurious hotels, as well as commercial and residential properties in key locations in Asia, the United States and Europe. The HSH Group also provides services ranging from tourism and leisure to club management. HSH was established in 1866. It had an annual revenue of HK$6.214 billion in the year ended 2018. HSH is listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
