# 8.2 Performance Measures
In Section 8.1 we examined the roles of performance measurement in implementing an organisation’s strategy, monitoring performance and disclosing accountability. This section will continue the theme but will concentrate on the individual performance measures that are commonly used by an organisation. Generally, the performance measurement process encompasses the following aspects: defining what performance is, selecting performance measures to measure performance, reporting and monitoring performance and taking deliberate action by making changes to improve performance. This section explores the process of selecting different types of performance measures, how these performance measures are employed to interpret performance and how they interact with each other.

## 8.2.1 Strategic Mapping
While many organisations will have developed their respective strategies, goals and objectives, whether they have ensured that these elements are interconnected is another question altogether. As highlighted in the strategic management theory, an organisation’s performance measurement should be designed to ensure its strategy will be achieved. The long-term strategic objectives should be cascaded down to short-term goals and performance measures applied to track the performance progress. Exhibit 8.3 illustrates a typical process of strategic mapping. 
![](DraggedImage-213.png)
A firm’s strategy is often supported by its strategic objectives. The organisation believes that if these long-term goals are met, they will ensure success for the organisation. To enable the organisation to monitor how effectively it is achieving its strategic objectives, organisations frequently establish a series of critical success factors (CSFs) aligned to the strategic objectives. These CSFs provide direction, move motives into action and answer questions such as which areas are important to accomplish the vision or which areas should be given priority in the next five years. However, strategic objectives are broad, non-measurable and cannot be achieved overnight. Thus, they need to be broken down into short-term operational goals, the achievement of which is usually measured by establishing a series of key performance indicators (KPIs) to be pursued by the organisation’s various strategic business units (SBUs).

The short-term operational goals give greater specificity to the strategic objectives and can therefore become the signposts for achieving performance milestones. By accomplishing these short-term operational goals, the organisation is, in effect, progressing toward its long-term objectives. However, if there is no link between strategic planning and operational planning, the organisation is very likely to lose its direction, and subsequently, fail in achieving its overall mission. When setting up short-term performance goals, one should think SMART, which means the goals or targets must be:

• Specific with clear and definite aims;
• Measurable by objective measures;
• Achievable but stretched;
• Relevant to the values and strategic objectives of the organisation; and
• Time specific.

Performance must be measured relative to a target, a trend over time or by comparison to a benchmark. Otherwise, measurement would be meaningless. Once the short-term goals are determined, management can proceed to look for reliable performance measures that capture the progress of the short-term goals appropriately and develop targets accordingly. Once selected, performance measures must be monitored regularly to ensure that they continue to provide useful information. There is little point in an organisation devoting considerable resources to measuring an aspect of performance when it cannot be acted upon, or it is irrelevant for the organisation. Exhibit 8.4 provides an example of strategic mapping for a consulting firm.
![](DraggedImage-214.png)

## 8.2.2 Types of Performance Measures
There are many ways an organisation can categorise its performance measures, for example, financial vs non-financial; quantitative vs qualitative; and leading vs lagging. Financial (quantitative) measures are comprehensively discussed in Section 8.2.4. Non-financial (qualitative) measures are discussed in Section 8.3. A performance measure is considered financial if it can be expressed in monetary terms; for example, revenue is HK$20 million.

A performance measure is non-financial if it is expressed in a form other than a monetary value, such as an 80% customer satisfaction rate or an on-time delivery percentage. Ideally, organisations should establish a range of financial/non-financial and quantitative/qualitative performance measures to achieve goals, control progress and remain competitive. Hence, organisations should try to achieve an appropriate balance between different types of performance measures, recognising that they all have their strengths and weaknesses. This will be discussed later in this section.

Performance measures can also be categorised as leading indicators and lagging indicators. Leading indicators provide real-time actions and are easy to calculate and explain while lagging indicators provide post-event information and are often too late for any effective action. For example, falling sales revenue (a lagging performance indicator) is the consequence of a decline in customer satisfaction (a leading performance indicator).

To understand how to ensure business growth and achieve optimal performance both in the short- and long-term, we will need to examine the functions of financial, strategic and operational controls and the performance measures associated with them. Financial controls focus on using financial measures to assess an organisation’s financial situation and operational efficiency, while strategic controls involve setting performance standards, assessing an organisation’s current strategies and adjusting goals for long-term business growth. In comparison, operational control focuses on executing daily activities to determine whether the organisation’s resources are being used efficiently.


## 8.2.3 Performance Evaluation
Whether an organisation is using one type or a combination of performance measures, a typical performance evaluation involves the five steps in Exhibit 8.5.
![](DraggedImage-215.png)
Once the strategic mapping is complete and the key performance aspects are identified, management will set the standards regarding their expectations. The standards can be based on quantitative criteria like net profits, stock price, dividend rates, return on capital, growth in sales, production cost and efficiency, etc. Alternatively, they may use qualitative criteria, such as capabilities, core competencies, risk-bearing capacity, strategic clarity, flexibility and workability. As the performance is underway, so is the measurement process at a monthly, quarterly or any other preferred intervals. Target performance is benchmarked against actual performance to uncover the reasons for deviations. Depending on the cause of each deviation, organisations can either decide to take actions to correct performance, revise the standard or take no action. As the last step of the process, learning is generated through review and passed to the next round of performance evaluation.

The following sections will provide an overview of the different types of performance measures and how they can be used to interpret performance.


## 8.2.4 Financial Measures
Financial performance is frequently the bottom line for any (for profit) organisation whether or not it has developed any specific strategic objectives. Business analysis will not be viewed as comprehensive if reviews of financial statements are not regularly undertaken.

At the most basic level, financial information provides valuable insights about an organisation’s past performance, and it also enables management to track the trend in financial performance periodically. It also enables management to detect the source of adverse financial performance and undertake preventive actions before they escalate. Moreover, the reason business analysts regularly review an organisation’s statement of cash flows, the statement of financial position and the statement of profit or loss is because financial information can also be used to identify opportunities for growth and expansion assess risks and facilitate assessments of an organisation’s ability to grow its business and reach its long-term goals.

Financial measures are the tools used to obtain and maintain effective financial control. Generally, financial measures should cover an organisation’s key financial outcomes and issues likely to impact achievement of financial goals: profitability, liquidity and risk.

Since liquidity and risk measures have been examined in Chapters 5–7, this section will mainly focus on profitability-based financial measures.

These measures include: revenue and gains, expenses, profit (before or after interest and taxes), return on investment (total assets, net assets or equity), residual income, economic value added (EVA ® ) and earnings per share (EPS).

Sections 8.2.4.1–8.2.4.10 provide an overview of the way that some of these measures are disclosed in the statement of profit or loss.

### 8.2.4.1 Revenues and Gains

Revenue and gains are types of income disclosed in an organisation’s profit or loss for a reporting period. They represent increases in economic benefits.

Revenue arises in the course of the ordinary activities of an organisation and is generated from the sale of goods or services. Gains may arise less frequently, for example from the sale of non-current assets, or they may arise from ancillary transactions or events, for example from hedging activities or from changes in exchange rates relating to foreign currency receivables and payables.

### 8.2.4.2 Expenses and Losses

Expenses represent decreases in economic benefits. They encompass losses and those expenses that arise in the course of the ordinary activities of an organisation, for example cost of sales, employee benefits and depreciation. Losses may arise less frequently, for example from disasters such as fire and flood or from the disposal of non-current assets. They may also arise from ancillary transactions or events, for example from hedging activities or from changes in exchange rates relating to foreign currency receivables and payables.

### 8.2.4.3 Gross Profit

Gross profit is sales revenue less the cost of sales. Gross profit is a key performance indicator. It provides an indication of whether the average mark-up on an organisation’s goods and services is sufficient to cover operating expenses and make a profit. However, care should be exercised when comparing this performance indicator with other organisations, particularly if the organisations are from different industries.

### 8.2.4.4 Profit Before Interest and Tax 
This measure is often referred to as earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) or operating profit. It is a measure of a company’s profit that includes all income and expenses recognised in the statement of profit or loss except interest expenses and income tax expenses. EBIT is used to analyse the performance of a company’s core operations without the impact of tax and the cost of debt capital. The measure is of importance to lenders, investors and managers, because it provides an indication of the capacity of a company to meet its financing costs in future periods.

### 8.2.4.5 Net Interest Income

Net interest income is the difference between the income generated by an entity from its interest-bearing assets and the interest cost incurred on its liabilities. It is a key performance indicator for financial institutions because it is a measure of a bank’s exposure to interest rate risk.

In Illustrative Example 2, in the case of Global Dairy Products, EBIT is NZ$281.001 million and net interest income is NZ$2.231 million. This shows that Global Dairy Products is in a strong financial position to service its debt in future periods.

### 8.2.4.6 Profit for the Period

This is sometimes referred to as the net profit or net income. Net profit is the amount of profit a business can extract from its total sales. Net profit margin is the percentage of revenue available after deducting all expenses recognised in the statement of profit or loss from sales. These measures reveal the underlying profitability of the company’s core operations and can be used to extrapolate current performance into the future. Net profit and net profit margin are of importance to both external stakeholders (investors and creditors) and company management because they are good indicators of a company’s financial performance and its ability to manage its assets efficiently.

### 8.2.4.7 Other Comprehensive Income and Comprehensive Income

Other comprehensive income includes gains and losses that arise in a period but are not recognised in the statement of profit or loss for the reporting period. The gains and losses are recognised in the other comprehensive income section of the statement of profit and loss and other comprehensive income. Some of these gains and losses may be recognised in the statement of profit or loss in future reporting periods if accounting standards require or permit them to be recycled from retained earnings to profit or loss.

Comprehensive income is the total of profit or loss and other comprehensive income for the period. It provides a more complete view of a company’s financial performance during a period because it includes all revenue, gains and expenses (including losses) that have been recognised by a company during the period. Comprehensive income can be used to identify changes in the overall net assets of a company and, by so doing, provide an indication of the change in the value of an owner’s interest in the company.

### 8.2.4.8 Earnings Per Share

EPS is another common measure of a company’s performance. It demonstrates the financial success of a shareholder’s investment, especially when comparing results over a period of several years. A company must be able to sustain its earnings to pay dividends and reinvest in the business to achieve future growth. Investors often look for growth in the EPS from one year to the next. EPS is calculated as net profit attributable to members of the parent company, adjusted to exclude any costs of servicing equity (other than dividends), divided by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the financial year. Diluted EPS adjusts the figures used in the determination of basic earnings per share to consider the after-tax effect of interest and other financing costs. It is important to note that EPS is a measure based on past data, and thus it may not be a good indicator of future earnings. What is more, it can be manipulated by changes in accounting policies or by mergers and acquisitions. If this measure is used in calculating management bonuses, it may be susceptible to such manipulation. EPS must be evaluated in context, for example, by comparing the results of a company over time. Investors will be interested in knowing whether EPS is growing, what is the rate of growth and whether the rate of growth is increasing or decreasing. For EPS to be a reliable basis for performance comparison, it must be calculated consistently and be disclosed in the financial statements together with comparative information presented in the financial statements.

The following example is the consolidated statement of profit or loss for Global Dairy Products, the opening case for this chapter.

### 8.2.4.9 Benchmarking

Although some of the most important information required to assess a company’s profitability is disclosed in formal financial statements, there is another important consideration: benchmarking. To be meaningful as a tool for comparison, financial results should be compared against an **appropriate yardstick**.

Examples of such yardsticks are:
• Budgeted sales, costs and profits.
• Standards in a standard costing system.
• The trend over time where the figures for various years are placed in adjacent columns (see Global Dairy Products comparative statement of profit or loss).
• The results of other parts of the business or the results of other businesses.
• Measures of the growth in the economy in general, e.g. gross domestic product (GDP).
• Future potential (for example, the performance of a new business may initially be judged in terms of breaking even rather than making significant profits).

#### Common Size Analysis 
Common size analysis, also referred to as vertical analysis, is a tool that managers, business analysts and investors frequently use to analyse financial statements. As mentioned previously, we will focus only on the statement of profit of loss.

To evaluate the performance of a company, it is valuable to benchmark its performance against other companies in the industry, particularly those companies that appear to be performing better. Common size analysis can be readily used to compare or benchmark financial performance against other firms within the same industry because percentage values provide a comparable metric between companies. Comparing financial data can reveal different companies’ strategies. For example, some companies may reduce the selling prices of their goods or services to gain a larger market share, which has the effect of increasing revenues at the expense of profit margins.

Common size analysis assesses profitability in the statement of profit or loss by expressing each line item as a percentage of the base amount for the period, usually using the sales revenue. The analysis helps understand the impact and contribution of each line item toward the company’s bottom line. It also highlights any significant changes in a company’s financial performance when compared over two or three years. For example, significant drops in the company’s gross profit in consecutive years may reveal that the company is experiencing difficulty in maintaining market share for its primary products or services.

Illustrative Example 3 expands the Global Dairy Products case to demonstrate the commonsize method.

#### Index Analysis
Assessing performance at only a particular point in time may not provide the best measure of a company’s performance. Managers, business analysts and investors may wish to compare the financial statements of a company over time by comparing the percentage change in a financial statement item over time. This involves calculating each year’s line items in the financial statements as percentages of those in the base year. The analysis is called index analysis, also known as a trend or horizontal analysis. The base year is usually selected by business analysts or management as the starting point for the trend analysis.

To undertake the analysis, the base year amounts are 100%, and percentage changes can be determined by comparing the difference between the targeted year with the base year and then dividing the difference by the base year amount. For example, if sales in 20X0 are HK$100,000 and in 20X1 they are HK$300,000, there is a 200% increase [(HK$300,000 HK$100,000)/HK$100,000)](#). By examining the magnitude of direction of a financial statement item over time, managers, analysts and investors will be able to see how an item has changed over time relative to itself and may be able to better predict future performance.

### 8.2.4.10 Common Financial Performance Ratios

There are many useful financial ratios for measuring various aspects of performance including profitability, solvency and investment return. In this section, we discuss some commonly used profitability and solvency ratios that can be identified from the statement of profit or loss, and then migrate to more sophisticated analytical techniques, such as economic value added (EVA ® ).

We will continue with the Global Dairy Products case and examine these ratios. These ratios are gross profit margin, operating profit margin, net income margin and interest coverage ratios (Exhibit 8.6). For a detailed discussion of ratios, refer to Chapter 9.
- gross profit margin
- operation profit margin (profit before interest and tax)
- net income margin (profit for the year)
- interest coverage ratio (cover profit before interest and tax)
![](DraggedImage-216.png)
These ratios can provide additional information when placed in a different context, for example, by comparing them to a competitor from the same industry or by comparing the ratios over several years. These comparisons can enhance managers’ understanding of the company’s past performance and prospects and identify areas worthy of further investigation. For example, a falling gross profit margin suggests that the company has not been able to pass on input price rises to customers or has had problems in controlling input costs.

It is worth noting that among the four performance ratios shown previously, net income margin and interest coverage ratio perhaps warrant more attention from managers than the others. Companies with a low net profit margin tend to lack flexibility and agility in pursuing their goals, while companies with a low-interest coverage ratio are more likely to be subject to risk and volatility and have difficulty in progressing towards their long-term sustainable targets.

While the above financial ratios can provide useful information for an organisation, it is impossible to fully assess profit or profit growth as measures of a company’s performance without relating the measures to the amount of funds (the investment) that has been deployed by the company in generating the profits.

So how is performance evaluated by large companies such as Microsoft or Exxon? Next, we will examine the methods used to evaluate investment centres and the performance of their managers. Managers are held accountable by stakeholders not only for maximising the company’s profit but also for utilising the invested capital as efficiently as possible. The common measures used to evaluate the performance of managers are return on investment (ROI), residual income (RI) and economic value added (EVA ® ), a registered trademark of Stern and Stewart.

#### Return on Investment (ROI)

ROI is a financial metric that enables users to determine the return (or gain) from an investment. It shows the return that has been earned from the amount of capital invested. Unfortunately, there is no single, universally accepted definition of ROI so care needs to be taken in interpreting this ratio. One key area that can differ is whether ROI is calculated on a before interest and tax basis or an after interest and tax basis. Whilst the after interest and tax basis is sometimes favoured by analysts and investors as it enables determination of the realisable return from an investment, others favour the before interest and tax approach because interest and taxation can be, to some extent at least, unrelated to operational performance. Regardless of the precise method of calculation that is used, ROI is widely adopted as one of the key performance measures because it ties in directly with the accounting process and is determinable from the statement of profit or loss and the statement of financial position. However, it does have limitations, as we will see later in this chapter.

#### Residual Income (RI)

An alternative way to measure the performance of a company is the residual income (RI) approach. Residual income is a measure of a company’s profits after deducting a notional or imputed interest cost. By using the residual income approach, a company may be able to overcome the potential dysfunctional managerial behaviour that may accompany the use of ROI.

> RI = Net income (excluding interest ) - (invested capital imputed interest rate)

The imputed interest rate used in applying this formula is normally the company’s minimum required rate of return on invested capital. However, companies may also use the company’s cost of borrowing or the weighted average cost of capital. Sometimes, companies may also have different levels of risk assigned to different imputed interest rates.

Using residual income as the guide for investment decisions will increase the opportunities for those marginal investment projects (beneficial for the organisation overall but not the division) to be undertaken, rather than being abandoned. Approval to proceed would normally be given provided that the investments are earning above the cost of capital. What’s more, residual income can be used to accommodate investments with different risk characteristics by simply adjusting the imputed interest rate.

#### Economic Value Added (EVA ®)
Economic value added (EVA ® ) is a registered trademark owned by Stern Stewart & Co. It is calculated as shown below.
> EVA ® = Net operating profit after tax (NOPAT) - Capital charge
![](DraggedImage-217.png)
EVA ® and RI share some similarities inasmuch as they both measure performance by subtracting an imputed interest cost from profit before interest and after tax, and they both put a ‘price’ on the cost of capital although each uses a different method of calculation.

However, there are also some differences between them. EVA ® is based on an ’economic profit’ that is derived by making a series of adjustments to the accounting profit. These adjustments include:

• Costs that are treated for accounting purposes as expenses but are considered to be investments for the future; for example, advertising costs and costs incurred in the research phase of research and development (R&D) projects, are treated as assets in EVA ® and added back to operating profit after tax (OPAT).

• Accounting depreciation is added back to profit, and economic depreciation is subtracted to arrive at net operating profit after tax (NOPAT) which is considered to be a charge for wear and tear or obsolescence.

• Any lease expenses are excluded from NOPAT and added to net assets as a part of the capital employed.

There are many advantages of using EVA ® : it focuses on the creation of economic value by a company, which can facilitate the alignment of managers’ interests with shareholders’ interests; being based on economic profit, it is less susceptible than other measures to potential accounting distortions; and by treating certain costs as giving rise to assets rather than expenses, for example, advertising and R&D, managers are incentivised to invest in activities that are potentially wealth creating.

However, EVA ® does have some disadvantages: it focuses on short-term performance, and hence managers may game the system at the expense of a company’s long-term development; it is derived from past data, which may not be a good indicator of future performance; a tedious adjustment process is required; and, like RI, it does not facilitate comparisons between business units of different sizes because the measure is skewed towards business units with a larger capital base.

To summarise, financial measures of the performance of a company and its managers are popular because they are based on readily available and verifiable data. However, they should be used with caution because they induce dysfunctional behaviour by managers seeking to exploit the well being of the organisation for personal gain. Hence, when selecting these measures, it is important to consider goal and behaviour congruence.

In management accounting research literature and practice, financial measures have been criticised for: dwelling in the past and not being forward-looking; having too many accounting distortions; being too rigid and aggregative to facilitate timely decision-making by management; and providing an incomplete picture of a company’s performance. To address these shortcomings, management has tended to employ a combination of non-financial measures to supplement the use of financial measures. Non-financial performance measures (NFPMs) refer to both qualitative and quantitative measures that cannot be expressed in monetary terms:

for example, staff turnover, brand awareness, absentee rates and the number of defective products. This development reflects the opinion that an organisation’s performance should not be viewed from one dimension alone (i.e. only from a financial point of view); rather, it should be assessed more holistically.

To facilitate the achievement of a company’s strategic objectives, both financial and non-financial performance measures have an important role to play. Financial measures can be used to objectively evaluate the financial performance of a company by using budget variances and various financial ratios. NFPMs can complement these measures by providing information on the quality of a company’s performance and its prospects for the future. Managers find NFPMs to be more readily available and helpful in understanding cause and effect relationships. For these and other reasons, we have witnessed an increased use of NFPMs in recent years.

In Section 8.2.5 strategic control measures are discussed. Section 8.2.6 discusses operational control measures. Non-financial (multidimensional) performance measures are discussed in Section 8.3.

## 8.2.5 Strategic Measures
The previous section introduced common financial measures adopted by companies to measure performance. This section will shed some light on how companies use strategic measures to enforce their strategic control to improve their strategic performance.

### 8.2.5.1 Strategic Control

Before discussing strategic performance measures, it is important to understand the meaning of strategic control.

When management formulates a company’s three- or five-year strategic plan, it does so based on assumptions about the environment in which the company will operate in the future. However, because both internal and external environments can change so rapidly, management needs a mechanism to be able to revisit these underlying assumptions on a timely basis. Strategic control aims to revisit the assumptions underlying the current strategy during the implementation stage, continually monitor and evaluate the strategic milestones, and take any necessary corrective actions.

At the highest level, strategic control represents the processes used by organisations to monitor and control the execution of a strategic plan by scanning and assessing higher-level, long-term issues. As such, it is a specialised form of management control, different from other forms of operational control discussed in the next section. Strategic control focuses on ‘management by objective’, which targets the organisation’s ability to achieve future goals, as opposed to evaluating past performance. It is also concerned with economic conditions, competitive environment, product life cycles, supply chains and market share and how to optimally steer the organisation through these ever-changing conditions. Finally, it serves as an early warning system by detecting problems necessitating changes to the present strategy.

To embed an effective control mechanism, management usually uses a set of measures to analyse performance and take necessary corrective actions. The same principle applies to strategic control. Strategic measures will be adopted to assess whether the strategy has been successful. The following questions would typically be addressed:

• Has the strategy been implemented as planned?
• Are the assumptions about major trends and changes correct?
• Are objectives and schedules being met?

• Do costs, revenues and cash flows verify the assumptions and match the projections?

• Based on the observed results, does the strategy need to be changed or adjusted?

• Are any operational changes necessary?

### 8.2.5.2 Types of Strategic Control

According to strategic management literature, there are four types of strategic control and their associated performance measures. Each one provides a different perspective and applies a method of analysis to test the validity of a strategy.

#### Premise Control

Premise control is designed to continually and methodically test and verify whether the assumptions from which the strategy is founded are still valid. Those assumptions are typically related to shifts in economic conditions, customer preferences or political policy. Once a false premise is identified, management should adjust the aspects of the strategy affected, including aborting the adopted strategy. The sooner the assumptions are confirmed or rejected, and as appropriate actions are taken, the better the result for the company. The responsibility of premise control generally lies with senior management. However, due to limited time and resources, only the key assumptions of the strategy will tend to be reviewed.

#### Implementation Control

During the planning stage, plans and projects and their critical timelines will be identified as milestones, at which points stop/go assessment is needed before proceeding to the next stage. As events and results unfold and milestones are reached, implementation control often involves examination of a series of meaningful thresholds (costs, market success, etc.) where expectations are compared with actual outcomes. This step-by-step or stop/go assessment is also called a milestone review, in which the strategy assessment at various intervals may trigger strategic rethinking and resource reallocation. It is worth noting that implementation control can also take place via operational control, like reviewing budgets, schedules and key performance indicators.

#### Strategic Alert Control

Strategic alert control is designed to activate a fast and rigorous strategy assessment in the light of an extraordinary event occurring. Such an event could impact the company so profoundly that it warrants an immediate and intense reassessment of its strategy by a crisis team usually formed by the strategic planning and leadership teams. Examples of the events could be anything from a natural disaster, product recall, a corporate scandal or a third party’s acquisition of a company’s competitor.

#### Strategic Surveillance Control 
Strategic surveillance control involves a broad information scan over a wide range of events happening inside and outside of the company. This practice is also known as environmental scanning. The purpose of the surveillance is to identify factors that are not currently on the company’s radar, but that may affect the strategy of the company. The surveillance may encompass the following approaches:
• Gathering data through market research;
• Having conversations with stakeholders;
• Collecting information from secondary sources, such as newspapers, trade magazines, online or social media, etc.;
• Monitoring public policy, industry trends and demographic data; and
• Benchmarking with global and domestic competitors.

### 8.2.5.3 Interactive Use of Strategic Measures

There is little disagreement that strategic performance is concerned with a company’s long-term performance. However, there is contention around the type of performance measures that can be used for strategic control, i.e. financial or non-financial.

According to Simons (1995), there is a type of control existing in companies that stimulates information searches, enables organisational learning and allows new strategies to emerge as the organisation responds to perceived opportunities and threats. Simons calls this type of control ‘interactive control’. Interactive control focuses primarily on increasing information flow to vital areas of the organisation to improve communication networks and managers’ understanding or knowledge of the issues. Control is enacted when effective dialogue is established throughout the organisation about issues such as new programmes, operational milestones and monthly progress reviews. To be effective, this will require regular follow-up of market intelligence to ensure that the need for external surveillance is maintained. Thus, senior managers signal their focus, draw subordinates’ attention to important strategic factors and maintain and activate surveillance throughout the organisation. As for the subordinates, information from these interactive communications with senior management triggers their learning about new projects and long-term reviews of current product lines.

For example, in face-to-face meetings, senior managers have the opportunity to challenge subordinate managers to explain any unforeseen changes in their areas of responsibility and the assumptions that underlie their analyses. The preparation for these meetings will require managers to learn more about changing market conditions and assist them in proposing action plans relating to the timing of, for example, new product rollouts, advertising campaigns and pricing decisions.

Many management accounting researchers have found that properly designed, implemented and monitored financial performance measures or NFPM’s can be used interactively to assert strategic control, especially in turbulent business environments. Evidencing this view, Chenhall (2003) suggests that using a combination of financial and non-financial performance measures can translate strategy more successfully and coherently whilst also facilitating organisational learning and goal congruence.

Therefore, in choosing appropriate performance measures for strategic control, it is not only a matter of whether the performance measures address the key strategic success factors, but also how effectively the performance measures are used.

In short, putting strategic control in place is critical to successful strategy formulation and implementation, as well as the achievement of sustainable superior performance. Both financial measures and non-financial measures can assist management in monitoring strategic progress, evaluating deviations and taking any necessary corrective action. The process bridges gaps and allows an organisation to adapt its strategy in response to any changes in the environmental context in which it operates.

## 8.2.6 Operational Measures
This section discusses how companies use operational control measures to improve operational performance.

Operational performance is concerned with the short-term performance of a company. Thus, in contrast to strategic controls, which require large amounts of data over a long timeframe, operational controls are designed to monitor and evaluate day-to-day actions with established standards. Meeting the short-term goals and providing post-action evaluation are their main objectives. If implemented successfully, they will flag potential risks, identify misalignments among resources, processes and systems, and implement changes to stay on course with the strategy. For example, if there are technical malfunctions of equipment that have resulted in performance below expectations, operational control will trigger actions to update the equipment or retrain the relevant employees to meet the targeted performance. Strategic control, on the other hand, might evaluate whether the hiring criteria will need adjustment to achieve long-term goals.

The notion of operational control is primarily based on the principle of ‘management-byexception’ philosophy. In this sense it aligns with Simons’s diagnostic controls, which managers use to monitor organisational outcomes and correct deviations from pre-set standards of performance. It is normally implemented when cause-and-effect relationships are well understood, and desired outcomes can be defined and measured with a reasonably high degree of accuracy (Simons, 1995).

Managers are able to use this type of control to facilitate lower-level managers’ commitment to the organisation’s strategic priorities, with quality reports, production output reports, budgets, business plans, profit and loss reports and performance reports being common examples of operational control measures.

One important benefit of operational control measures is that they allow organisations to achieve their goals without constant supervision. Once the desired outcome is set, the system is in effect self-regulating inasmuch as it enables comparison between actual performance with pre-set standards. Senior managers are only required to invest their attention when negotiating targets and goals with their subordinates, or when they receive exception reports that require further investigation or action. As a result, senior managers can conserve their limited time and focus their attention on issues as required, such as the organisation’s future development, project milestones, personal goals and plans and budgets (Simons, 1995).

Both financial and non-financial performance measures can be used as operational controls, as long as the measures address the short-term operational goals (while still aligning with the long-term strategic objectives). Some contend that non-financial performance measures are more appropriate for operational controls because, unlike financial performance measures, they focus on actions. While there may be some truth to this view, when addressing operational efficiency in terms of cost, financial performance measures are likely to be superior to NFPMs.

When selecting suitable operational performance measures, it is important to bear in mind that it is not only a matter of whether the performance measures address the short-term operational goals but also an issue of how these performance measures are to be used.

Exhibit 8.7 provides some widely adopted operational performance measures, categorised by function.

## 8.2.7 Relationship Between Various Measures of Performance
As discussed in the previous sections, the performance measurement system (PMS) is a system which gathers and uses the information to compare the organisation’s performance to expectations and determine its progress towards the pursued organisational strategies. In this system, both financial and non-financial measures, or both quantitative and qualitative measures, can be used as strategic and operational controls. They interact with each other, enabling goal obtainment while maintaining agility.

### 8.2.7.1 Leading and Lagging Indicators

Leading indicators refer to the measures that drive future financial and non-financial outcomes. Hence, identifying and measuring the leading indicators reliably is an important part of measuring performance because they are the signposts flagging progress towards meeting performance objectives. Employees consider the leading indicators as their guiding light. If they are likely to miss performance targets, they should take corrective action to get back on course.

Many leading indicators are non-financial because they are more actionable, providing a direct link to long-term organisational strategies. Examples of leading indicators are staff learning and growth measures, production efficiency measures and customer satisfaction measures. These indicators are closely related to the organisation’s ability to develop new products, reduce production costs and maintain customer loyalty.

In contrast, lagging indicators measure the outcomes of a plan or a goal and signal the effect of actions taken rather than the cause. Most financial measures are lagging indicators because they are less disputable, providing verifying links to accounting profits and market value.

It is important for professional accountants to understand the relationship between financial and non-financial measures and leading and lagging indicators because it provides a feasible roadmap to achieve goals. Through such a roadmap, organisations can directly manage the leading indicators, also known as the causes, which will ultimately lead to the lagging indicators, the effects. Organisations that can successfully establish this causal link between its performance measures are more likely to achieve their targets and generate a competitive operating profit. It is also worth noting that in a continuous business process, a leading indicator can become the lagging indicator of another leading indicator. The following example demonstrates the discussion above.

### 8.2.7.2 Tension Resulting from Strategic and Operational Control

Strategic planning teams will readily acknowledge that even the best-planned strategy can go awry. Organisations these days exist in a constantly changing environment full of uncertainty and ambiguity. Hence, it is essential that organisations pursue their financial ambitions while remaining agile and competitive.

Simons (1995) argues that organisations typically exist in an environment of multifaceted tension, resulting from the conflicting interplays between senior management’s opportunityseeking behaviour and their limited attention, the intended strategy and the emergent strategy, the current financial targets and future development. Balancing such multilevel tensions can assist organisations in maximising their current return on investment without losing the focus to develop future competitiveness. An effective performance measurement system should therefore recognise these inherent tensions and aim to balance inspiration and coercion, reward and sanction, guidance and prohibition, learning and control. The fusion of different performance measures can help an organisation achieve goals and simultaneously foster innovation.

Performance can be regarded as a trade-off or compromise between financial performance and strategic control. At times, performance can be measured quantitatively (i.e. a numeric value), for example, that profit is HK$20 million, or that 90% of customers are satisfied. At other times, performance may be considered qualitatively (and typically more subjectively), for example, the quality of a service or an organisation’s reputation. Qualitative measures are, by nature, subjective and judgemental, but they are simpler, cheaper and more flexible to operate, especially when they are derived from several different sources and are not overly dependent on judgement.

There may be a trade-off between quantitative and qualitative aspects of performance, for example, between achieving a certain level of profitability and maintaining and enhancing the organisation’s reputation. Similarly, there can be a trade-off between short-term performance and longer-term sustainable performance, whether that be financial, societal, environmental or reputational.

Despite the issues discussed above, the main objective is to ensure that the important factors are being measured. The truism, ‘you get what you measure’, is appropriate. To encourage the measurement of the right things, organisations need to recognise the following four influences on a strategic control system: the time-lag between strategic control measures and financial results, the linkages with the other businesses in a group, the risks the business faces and the sources of competitive advantage.

Strategic control measures weigh up trade-offs between current financial performance and longer-term competitive position, and between different desirable ways of building competitive strength, to see if they have the potential to grow the business. Financial control ensures that the organisation is managing its financial resources efficiently and, in so doing, minimises the risk of the organisation going into administration. Disconnected strategic planning and operational planning goals may waste resources and increase operating costs. For example, if a performance measurement system focuses principally on the measurement of costs, managers may concentrate on cost reduction and ignore other important strategic production goals, such as developing new product features that customers value.

The balanced scorecard (BSC) to be discussed in Section 8.3.1, is one of the tools that has been developed to provide a clear picture of what should be measured to achieve strategic control objectives while concurrently establishing the links between an organisation’s overall strategy and its day-to-day activities. These tools enable employees to achieve both operational control objectives and strategic control objectives within the one framework, thereby enhancing their understanding of the causality between the respective processes. Ultimately, it facilitates the embracing by employees of the organisation’s key strategies.

## 8.2.8 Changes to Control Systems
Performance measurement can be categorised into two types:

• Informational measurement – Measurement used for information purposes to improve understanding of performance.

• Motivational measurement – Measurement used for rewards and punishment to motivate employees to perform at the highest level.

Performance measurement permeates every system in an organisation and creates the basis for effective management. The truism, ‘You get what you measure’, is deeply rooted in most managers’ management philosophy. However, we have all experienced anomalous situations where performance measures are functioning in the opposite way to what was intended. Examples can be found across different geographical locations, industries and organisational sizes.

To some extent, the incidence of counterproductive behaviour is epidemic. For instance, sales employees may decide to postpone a key customer’s order to the next period because they have already reached their current quarterly sales targets to qualify for their bonus; procurement employees may purchase cheaper, inferior quality materials because their performance is measured by reference to cost savings; corporate executives may defer the incurrence of expenses on important activities, such as research and development, to subsequent periods because they are rewarded on the basis of profit generated during the current period; university academics may focus on research activities rather than teaching because research publications have a higher weighting than teaching when their performance is evaluated; tram drivers may stop at fewer stops than scheduled before the terminal because on-time service is measured; hospital surgeons may refuse to take on patients with complex injuries/illnesses because their remuneration is affected by their success rate; and, police officers may undertake breath tests on themselves in order to meet the minimum required number of roadside breath tests specified in their performance targets.

#### Illustrative Example 10

In the opening case, Global Dairy Products had appointed a local executive, Raymond Li, to manage the Asian region. Whilst the decision to establish the Hong Kong distribution centre initially appeared to be highly successful, about 18 months after its establishment the New Zealand head office started receiving complaints from several key customers from Hong Kong and mainland China about the quality of some products (in particular milk powder, the biggest selling product) and also about the pressure being applied by some of the company’s regional sales agents.

Eventually, the situation became so serious that the New Zealand-based chief executive and the Singapore-based director of research decided to visit the Hong Kong operation to investigate. To their dismay they soon discovered that in a small number of cases, milk powder shipped to Hong Kong from New Zealand had been ‘diluted’ by the addition of an inert powder, the effect of which was to reduce the purity and nutritional benefits of the product. To make matters worse, it was also discovered that Mr. Li had introduced an incentive scheme for the regional sales staff that enabled them to earn very significant cash bonuses for achieving sales targets that were considered extremely optimistic. The enormous pressure applied by senior management on the regional sales agents to reach a certain sales target resulted in counterproductive behaviour.

Performance measurement underlies every component of an organisation, possesses the power to trigger actions and directs employees’ behaviour. When it is used wisely, it can lead to effective management and business success. On the other hand, when used unwisely, it can contribute to dysfunctional behaviour, cause serious errors and operational problems, and potentially, through inadequate or poorly implemented control systems, create opportunities for fraudulent activities. Setting sales targets is a common practice for businesses and is done, amongst other reasons, to motivate employees and monitor performance, rather than commit fraud or conspiracy. Numerous factors could have contributed to the situation detailed in the case of Global Dairy Products, but it clearly reflects many of the classic elements of performance measurement mismanagement.
---- 

Illustrative Example 10 demonstrates that performance measurement has a powerful ‘dark side’; it can become dysfunctional and destructive, contrary to its intended purpose. This has prompted some to question why performance measurement systems may give rise to counterproductive behaviour. Possible areas of concern are:

• Mistrust between senior and operational management.
• Lack of understanding of the performance measures by the operational staff.
• Uncontrollability of the measures used to assess the performance of the operational staff.
• Mismatch between goals, objectives and performance measures.
• Inadequate information systems.
• Lack of standardised performance measures.
• Difficulty in linking measures to customer value.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Organisations need to develop performance measures to ensure that the needs of stakeholders are met. Management should use performance measurement to monitor progress and improve performance.

The following section identifies the major reasons why information measurement can cause a performance measurement system to be ineffective. Issues relating to motivational measurement will be discussed in Section 8.5.

### 8.2.8.1 Measuring the Wrong Things

The most common reason why information measurement can lead to an ineffective performance measurement system is requiring measurement of the wrong information. Measuring the wrong information may change employee behaviour but typically provides few benefits to the organisation. For example, assume that an organisation has a competitive advantage over its rivals because of the speed with which it can deliver its products. To maintain its competitive advantage, it needs information about its speed of delivery compared to those of its competitors. However, if its performance measurement system focuses on the cost of inventory, it will provide information about how well inventory costs are being managed but will not provide the key information it needs to establish and maintain its competitive advantage.

The most common reason why performance measurement systems are inadequate is that the system produces ‘results’ on the wrong measure(s) of success. This situation often arises due to a lack of expertise in performance measurement. Whilst executives or managers are usually well-intentioned and genuinely believe they are acting in the best interests of the organisation, when they measure the wrong information it will ultimately produce counterproductive behaviours from employees and, at times, intentional wrongdoings.

#### Illustrative Example 11

A Hong Kong-based trade organisation for professional architects prides itself on its excellent membership services. To reduce the wait time for members’ inquiries, the organisation invested in a device to measure how quickly members’ phone calls were answered; 20 seconds was set as the performance benchmark.

Responding to this performance measure, senior managers mounted a digital scoreboard on the office wall for everyone to see the number of calls coming in and the number being answered within 20 seconds. The member services unit consistently achieved a 98% successful response rate over a specified period.

The performance of the unit appeared to be outstanding and was showcased within the organisation and at meetings with members. However, the performance measure was met so consistently because members were put on hold as soon as their phone calls were answered. This practice led to an increase in members’ complaints because they felt they were being brushed off by member service officers before their issues had been satisfactorily resolved. When a new CEO took over, he identified the problem and immediately replaced the ‘response time’ measure with one that measured how successfully the issues were resolved.

### 8.2.8.2 Measuring to ‘Look Good’

Another reason why using information measurement can lead to an ineffective performance measurement system is executives or managers choosing ‘convenient’ measures to make their performance look ‘good’ in the eyes of the external stakeholders, rather than focusing on the provision of information to facilitate the management of business processes and improve customer value. Executives and managers may tend to opt for ‘convenient’ measures of performance in circumstances where it is difficult to identify appropriate performance measures, for example, non-financial measures for intangible items such as customer satisfaction.

In these circumstances, performance measures are chosen not because they count, but because they can be counted. When this happens, it is not surprising to see good news being highlighted and bad news being suppressed by the use of a string of activity measures, for example: the number of training programmes implemented; the number of patent applications lodged; the number of audits undertaken; the number of new products introduced; and, the number of female employees hired. These activity measures create an illusion of progress or achievement. The inappropriate or overuse of such measures is sometimes called the ‘activity perception trap’. That is, they may sound like wonderful, successful stories, in the short-term at least, but it is difficult or even impossible to predict if they will lead to an increase in economic benefits for the organisation, with absent relevant lagging indicators also being measured and subsequently matched.

### 8.2.8.3 Measuring that Gives Rise to Sub-optimisation

While financial measures are relatively easy to calculate and implement, they are limited in scope because they focus only on an aspect of organisational performance. Over-reliance on financial performance measures for divisional performance may lead to sub-optimisation of an organisation’s overall economic interest.

Sub-optimisation refers to the behaviour of prioritising one component of a total system without considering the impact on the other components. For example, particular financial measures may indicate that individuals and teams have performed well, but at the expense of the organisation’s long-term success. Hence, it is important not to solely rely on financial measures or at least to use them with caution. Sales measurement, cost measurement and borrowing ratios can frequently become ‘silo-based’ measurements and using them alone may encourage responsibility centres to optimise their own performance, without necessarily benefiting the organisation as the whole.

The following are common examples of sub-optimisation:

(a) Project proliferation Many organisations engage in project proliferation. When examining business cases, each project seems to add value to the organisation. However, if the projects are examined together, some projects may be found to be duplicating others, and some may be working at cross-purposes to others. Given that all projects are competing for the organisation’s scarce resources, it is essential that a holistic approach is taken when assessing individual projects to ensure that the organisation’s resources are allocated efficiently.

(b) Cost-cutting initiatives In an endeavour to better manage costs, organisations may undertake cost audits. This may result in certain divisions being reduced in size but without necessarily considering the flow-on effects across the organisation of the size reduction. For example, after undertaking a cost audit, a company reduced the size of its marketing department by hiring less marketing staff, thus saving the marketing department a significant amount in operational cost. However, these cuts resulted in the organisation’s functional divisions supplementing their marketing needs by hiring localised marketing personnel, at a cost far exceeding the original cost savings. ‘Optimising’ marketing operating expenses resulted in an overall increase in costs for the whole organisation.

Many organisations are unwittingly using division-focused, unaligned measures to quantify the performance of their divisions and the managers in charge of the divisions. Measuring elements of an interrelated system individually can lead to sub-optimisation unless the process is used in conjunction with aggregated measures that are tied back to the organisation.

### 8.2.8.4 Measuring Too Much and Not Following Up

It is self-evident that we increasingly live in an age of ‘accountability’. This suggests that accountability can be discharged by measuring performance and making the resultant measures available to the public. As a result, there is frequently a tendency for managers to measure everything that moves without properly considering whether the measures really matter. For example, every month managers from different divisions may be presented with their own scorecard, instrument panel and dashboard with idiosyncratic measures of success, resulting in organisations ending up with hundreds of disjointed sets of measures. Too often, measurement becomes an end in itself without addressing fully the causes underlying the need for the measurements. Indeed, when we measure too much and do little, the whole performance measurement exercise becomes useless and potentially harmful.

Convinced by the overly promised power of data analytics, many organisations today have been more aggressively collecting data than ever before. Eventually, it is quite likely that they will become buried in their own ‘big data’. By way of example, it has recently been reported that a supermarket chain collected 340 million different data points per week but used only 20% of the data collected. Measuring the wrong things or measuring things that are unnecessary can lead to high costs of measurement, both in terms of actual cost and opportunity cost. Further, with information overload, employees may become more confused rather than better informed. If an organisation is not going to act upon the measures collected and translate them into actions, it becomes pointless to spend the time and money in the first instance.

It is thus evident that the construction of workable and useful performance measures can be complex and difficult. Consequently, organisations may experience problems with performance measurement. These problems may be caused not by the measurement per se, but by the initial failure to consider carefully what to measure and the possible excessive use of measurement for its own sake merely because data is available. If organisations are aware of these pitfalls, they will be better placed to ensure that they measure what matters and combine those measurements with the exercise of judgement. Executed well, performance measurement can be a powerful tool that can provide real benefits and produce desirable outcomes, rather than being dysfunctional.

#### Apply and Analyse 1

SupaLens (Asia) Limited (SLA) is a Hong Kong-based manufacturer of spectacle and microscope lenses for several well-known suppliers of those products. The company has two manufacturing divisions, Spectacles (S) and Microscopes (M), both of which operate as standalone investment centres. In addition to using targets for Sales Revenue and gross margin, divisional performance (and, in part, remuneration) has always been measured based on ROI, using controllable operating profit (calculated as gross margin less controllable expenses). SLA also has a sophisticated research and development division, and a corporate office that encompasses accounting and finance, legal, human resources and IT.

Following the recent appointment of a new chief financial officer (CFO), a decision has been made to start allocating R&D and corporate costs to each of the two manufacturing divisions, and to then calculate a ‘net profit’ to be used to calculate the ROI for each manufacturing division.

For the past three years SLA has set its annual ROI target for each division at 20%. The cost of capital is estimated at 10%. Over the past three months, the S and M divisions have achieved ROIs of 22% and 23% per annum, respectively. This has meant that substantial performance bonuses have been paid to key staff.

# 8.3 Multidimensional Models of Performance
The previous section introduced different types of performance measures focusing respectively on financial, strategic and operational measures and the interrelationships between them.

This section commences by outlining the changes in performance measurement systems (PMS) over recent decades and the reasons why those changes have occurred. The emergence of more multi-dimensional and integrated approaches to performance measurement is then discussed. The section concludes with a review of three of the more widely known multi-dimensional performance measurement systems, their advantages and limitations and their usefulness in today’s increasingly competitive business world.

Multidimensional models of performance describe various frameworks used to measure organisational performance that includes a range of financial and non-financial performance measures. Traditionally, performance measurement systems concentrated only on the financial aspects of organisational performance by endeavoring to measure the ‘financial health’ of the organisation. Whilst financial measures have doubtlessly been of value in earlier times and continue to play an important role in performance measurement, over the past two or three decades the emergence of a more strategic view of business, and the growing role played by business in the wider environment has highlighted the limitations of relying primarily on financial measures as the determinants of organisational performance. Key limitations of relying solely on financial measures are that they:

• Encourage short-termism.
• Offer no control over non-financial processes.
• Focus on results, not causes.
• Do not offer a strategic perspective.

### Illustrative Example 12

The example in the Opening Case makes reference to some unacceptable business practices that collectively appear to demonstrate shortcomings in the nature of and adherence to appropriate performance measurement systems. Viewed against the shortcomings already identified, it seems reasonable to conclude that, for one reason or another, these possibly reflect governance failures present in the Global Dairy Products setting.

These kinds of shortcomings, whilst sometimes quite obvious and explicit, can frequently also be more subtle and less obvious. Either way, such shortcomings have led to considerable criticism of the usefulness of financial measures as a true measure of overall organisational performance. Because they measure past performance, a major limitation is that they cannot provide management with guidelines as to how the financial metrics and performance targets selected can actually be achieved. Without this kind of information, objective determination as to whether the targets are realistic is difficult.

Together with the (typically) short-term nature of most financial performance measures, these shortcomings and overreliance on financial information make it difficult to effectively evaluate and appropriately reward managerial performance. As an example, while a favourable financial outcome against a budget may reflect a high degree of managerial skill and judgement, it is also possible that the favourable outcome occurred as a result of other (typically external) factors unrelated to managerial capabilities and performance. Due to how these conflicting scenarios are interpreted, sound management is sometimes penalised and poor management is sometimes rewarded.

The impact of technological change, changing cost structures and globalisation of trade over the past three decades have fundamentally altered the competitive landscape faced by many organisations, with many now facing an intensity of competition far greater than ever before. Against this background, there has been a growing recognition that financial measures alone have been increasingly unable to reflect other drivers of organisational value in a business environment that requires more dynamism, innovation and quick decision-making.

Meeting these emerging needs made it necessary for organisations to review the effectiveness of their existing, traditional, finance-oriented performance measurement systems and, in many cases, identified the need to redesign them to better meet twenty-first century needs to survive in a rapidly changing competitive environment. Consequently, multi-dimensional performance measurement systems, incorporating non-financial as well as financial measures have received increasing attention in both the management accounting and strategic management literatures, and in practice.

There are several reasons that have led to this increased interest in non-financial performance measures. The more important of these may be summarised as follows:

• Focus on too limited a range of variables. If an organisation focuses almost entirely on events and outcomes that can be expressed in monetary terms, it is probable that managers will (understandably) tend to focus mainly on those measurements. As a result, management may not pay enough attention to various other important aspects of performance that cannot be directly measured in financial terms.

• Technological advances in manufacturing processes. Modern manufacturing processes, such as the increased use of robotics, and flexible manufacturing systems can frequently result in reduced set-up and throughput times, and lower inventory levels. Whilst these technological advances are all potentially beneficial, by maximising output, manufacturing managers can reduce the costs for which they are directly responsible. By focusing single-mindedly on cost reduction, there is a risk that managers may tend to pay less attention to other, more strategic, production and manufacturing goals.

• Changing cost structures. Maintaining competitiveness in an era of rapid advances in manufacturing technology and the resultant shortening of product life cycles requires very significant levels of investment in both capital expenditure and human resources. The typical cost structure for many products now requires a far greater level of ‘upstream expenditure’ than traditional manufacturing, resulting in a far greater percentage of total costs being committed (but not necessarily incurred) before production commences. Regardless of the success or failure of the product in question, many of these costs are, in effect, sunk costs.

• Non-financial performance measures are often superior pointers to the future outlook. Whilst traditional financial measures of performance show an entity’s current (or recent) financial performance, they are not usually able to identify emerging problems.

Against this background of significant change, throughout the 1980s and 1990s management accounting practitioners and academics devoted considerable time and energy to designing performance systems capable of addressing these problems.

Designing an effective performance measurement model presented them with a considerable challenge. For the model to be comprehensive it needs to contain: all organisational financial and non-financial indicators; internal and external indicators; leading and lagging indicators; and, short-term and long-term indicators, whilst simultaneously not being overly complex and unwieldly. A critically essential requirement is that the system be closely aligned with the overall organisational strategy. These issues are further discussed in Section 8.4.

In response to this challenge, several frameworks have been developed to assist organisations integrate traditional financial performance measures with non-financial performance measures (strategic and operational) to the point where a fully integrated approach, incorporating multiple dimensions, is now widely considered a standard approach to performance measurement. A multidimensional, integrated approach recognises that performance measurement should be process-oriented and encompass all key functional areas. It also recognises that a balanced set of measures, both financial and non-financial, is required to provide a more comprehensive perspective of overall organisational performance.

Despite the relatively recent widespread acceptance of this approach, it is worth noting that the concept is not as new as might be imagined. For example, an integrated performance measurement system known as the ‘Tableau de Bord’ has been in use since the 1930s in France.

Three of the more widely known models that have emerged since the 1980s are the balanced scorecard, the performance pyramid and the building block. Whilst each of these frameworks has individual characteristics, their common features are, in summary, that they:

• Include financial and non-financial performance measures;
• Are integrated with the corporate strategy;
• Include external as well as internal measures;
• Endeavour to include all important factors regardless of how easy or difficult they are to measure;
• Show clearly the trade-offs between different dimensions of performance; and
• Show how measures will motivate managers and employees.

The next sections describe the development of, and approach taken by, each of these models, and discuss their advantages and disadvantages.

## 8.3.1 Balanced Scorecard (BSC)
The most well-known and widely used multidimensional performance measurement system is the balanced scorecard (BSC).

The rationale for the development of the BSC was a growing dissatisfaction with traditional, purely financial measures of performance.

By incorporating both financial and non-financial measures, the BSC endeavours to provide management with a multi-dimensional set of information covering all relevant areas of performance in an objective and unbiased fashion.

The original Kaplan and Norton model contains four groupings of performance measures. These groupings, collectively referred to as ‘perspectives’ were considered by Kaplan and Norton to be sufficient to track the key drivers of both current and future financial performance of the firm.

The perspectives focus on the achievements of the organisation in four areas:

1. Financial: Similar to traditional performance measures, this focuses on how the organisation performs in terms of return to shareholders. Typical metrics used to assess whether the organisation’s financial objectives are being achieved and include profitability, return on investment, return on assets, liquidity and cash flow, residual income and economic value added.

2. Customer: The metrics selected for this perspective are designed to determine what the organisation must do to satisfy its customers so as to achieve its financial objectives. Metrics typically include measures of customer satisfaction, such as, market share, customer retention and customer profitability.

	These can be sub-divided into measures that drive customer satisfaction, including lead times, on-time delivery, product quality and product cost.

3. Internal processes: This perspective focuses on identifying and measuring what the organisation must excel at in order to successfully support its product/marketing strategies and thereby achieve its financial objectives.

	Typical outcome measures include those relating to innovation (product and process) and operations (cycle times, defect rates).

4. Learning and growth: These measures are designed to ascertain what infrastructure and knowledge base the firm must establish, build and maintain to create long-term growth and organisational improvement.

	In other words, what capabilities must be improved or acquired to achieve the longterm targets for the organisation and internal business process perspectives. Outcome measures typically include metrics on employee satisfaction, training and staff retention.

In constructing a balanced scorecard, careful consideration needs to be given to the selection of meaningful metrics for each of the perspectives (traditionally four, but see Section 8.3.1.1 for emerging trends toward the addition of a fifth perspective).

In selecting metrics, it is important to include an appropriate mix of ‘input’ and ‘output’ measures. Input measures (usually referred to as ‘leading’ indicators) are typically quite hard to measure but relatively easy to influence. Conversely, output measures (usually referred to as ‘lagging’ indicators’) are usually easy to measure but hard to improve.

Put another way, leading indicators usually cause some change or effect in one or more lagging indicators.

Whilst the BSC can be visually represented in many ways, a typical schematic is shown in Exhibit 8.8.
