### Apply and Analyse 2

Daphne Zhou, the CFO of EasyTrip, a medium size, family owned, Hong Kong-based travel agency with outlets in Hong Kong, Macau, Beijing, Shanghai and Chongqing, is considering introducing the balanced scorecard in her organisation. Currently, performance measurement at EasyTrip is based almost entirely on summary financial measures such as gross margin per trip, earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) and return on investment (ROI). Daphne, who is based at the head office in Hong Kong, has recently been worried about her organisation’s deteriorating financial performance and has also become aware that a number of customer complaints have been made about the quality of service at some of EasyTrips outlets. Daphne is also aware that EasyTrip’s market share appears to be deteriorating in what is a very competitive market.

Required:

(a) Identify and explain three problems associated with the use of non-financial performance measures.

(b) Distinguish between lead and lag performance measures. To illustrate, identify one lead measure and one lag measure that would be suitable for Daphne’s organisation for the customer perspective of the balanced scorecard. Justify your choices.

(c) Daphne attended a business conference last week and a CEO from another organisation was talking about cause and effect linkages within the balanced scorecard. Daphne had no idea what he was talking about. Explain to Daphne how cause and effect linkages exist between the four (traditional) perspectives of the balanced scorecard, using examples to illustrate.

Analysis

(a) Some problems associated with the use of non-financial performance measures are:

• Wide choice of non-financial measures available – selecting too many could be problematic. BSC should be kept as simple as possible to avoid it becoming unwieldy and difficult to use effectively.

• Their development can be ad-hoc and undirected – this frequently happens when new staff are appointed.

• Managers must necessarily make trade-offs between achieving some measures and not others – this can cause tensions between different parts of the organisation.

• Some measures lack integrity/accuracy of the data, creating an opportunity for manipulation.

• Some measures are not easily translated into financial outcomes.

(b) Characteristics and examples of lead and lag indicators:
(i) Lead indicators 
They are measures that drive the outcomes and provide information that is actionable and manageable.

They relate to the processes and activities of the business. Improvements in these measures should, over time, flow through to improvements in lag indicators.

Examples: Number of customer complaints, number of repeat customers, number of refund demands.

(ii) Lag indicators
They monitor progress towards the organisation’s objectives.
Examples: customer satisfaction (survey), industry market share data.

(c) Causal linkages connect objectives and measures in the balanced scorecard. In effect, they identify an interconnected pathway between non-financial measures of performance, and the ultimate and collective impact of all of those on the overall financial performance of the organisation.

In the case of EasyTrip, good performance on measures in the learning and growth perspective (i.e. improved tourism planning and vacation-sales skills) should then drive good performance in the internal business process perspectives (for example, increased margins on trips, more and longer vacations booked, more billable tourism experiences, more lucrative partnerships with hotels and tour operators). In turn, these improved service attributes should lead to good performance in relation to the customer perspective (for example by making the travel experiences more reliable, more customised, more attractive to customers etc.). Finally, this should lead to improved financial performance through increased sales, lower cancelation rates and increased repeat business and referral business that should then reflect in better margins and overall financial performance.

### 8.3.1.1 A Fifth Perspective?

In the three decades since the introduction of the BSC, there has been increasing recognition of the strategic importance of environmental, social and ethical issues. This has in turn resulted in increased interest in how to incorporate these into the traditional BSC. Extensions and modifications to the original BSC which explicitly consider environmental, social and ethical issues are often referred to as sustainability balanced scorecards.

As with the original model, there are many ways that these additional measurements can be reflected. Some organisations may choose to incorporate relevant measures into the existing BSC framework, while others may choose to introduce an additional perspective. The choice of which is more appropriate will be dependent on the extent to which sustainability measures are core to the organisation’s activities or whether they are more peripheral.

### 8.3.1.2 Advantages
Correctly designed, implemented, monitored and actioned, the BSC offers the following advantages:
1. It measures performance across multiple dimensions, rather than relying solely on a limited range of financial indicators.
2. Managers will find it difficult to distort the performance measure – poor performance is hard to disguise or hide when multiple measures are used.
3. It takes a long-term perspective in assessing organisational performance.
4. Success in each of the four perspectives should result in delivering long-term accomplishment of organisational objectives.
5. It is flexible – what is measured can be changed over time to reflect changing competitive, market and environmental conditions and organisational priorities.
6. ’What gets measured gets done’ – if managers know they are being appraised on various aspects of performance they are more likely to properly focus their energies on these and not become distracted by other, less important matters.

### 8.3.1.3 Disadvantages
Notwithstanding its potential value as a way of expressing organisation vision and strategy into specific objectives, and quantified performance measures (which have doubtlessly contributed to its widespread acceptance and adoption in many businesses), the BSC certainly has its critics, with research suggesting that some BSC implementations have not been successful. Many of the reasons for this suggested outcome relate to problems with implementation rather than conceptual validity. These problems are discussed further in Section 8.4.

From a practical perspective, the main difficulty with the BSC approach is setting standards for each of the key performance indicators (KPIs). This can prove difficult where the organisation has no previous experience of performance measurement. Benchmarking with other organisations is a possible solution to this problem, although it can be difficult to obtain the necessary information.

## 8.3.2 Performance Pyramid
Developed during roughly the same period as the BSC by Lynch and Cross (1991), the performance pyramid is another multi-dimensional performance measurement system designed to include both financial and non-financial measures. Whilst not as well known or widely used as the BSC, the performance pyramid is framed around assessing performance from two key perspectives: external effectiveness and internal efficiency.

The performance pyramid has some similarities to the BSC but also introduces an additional concept – the notion that multi-dimensional performance systems should be designed to assess performance not only at the overall organisational level, but also at key hierarchical bands within the organisation. Commencing at the apex of the organisational pyramid with the corporate vision, the hierarchical bands cascade downward through the business unit level, and ultimately to individual departments, work teams and, if appropriate, ultimately to individual employees.

The rationale for this approach assumes that each hierarchical level should apply its own capabilities to the accomplishment of the overall corporate objectives that have been established by the executive and expanded into specific and actionable targets for each hierarchical level.

The model is usually visually represented in a manner similar to that shown in Exhibit 8.9.
![](DraggedImage-220.png)
The four levels of the model operate in an interrelated and interdependent way as follows:

• Level 1: At the apex of the pyramid the corporate vision or mission describes how the organisation plans to achieve long-term success and a sustainable competitive advantage.

• Level 2: The next level of the pyramid is designed to focus on the achievement of specified success factors in terms of market-related and financial measures. Together, the marketing and financial success of an organisation constitutes the initial focus for the achievement of the corporate vision.

• Level 3: The marketing and financial strategies and measures established at level 2 must however be linked to the achievement of customer satisfaction, increased flexibility and high productivity. These are detailed at level 3 of the pyramid. In effect, these are the guiding forces (as opposed to the actual outcomes measured at level 2) that senior management believe will drive the strategic objectives of the organisation.

• Level 4: The extent to which the level 3 drivers are accomplishing their objectives can in turn be monitored using specific departmental indicators of quality, delivery, cycle times and waste.

The left-hand side of the pyramid contains measures that have an external focus, and which are predominantly non-financial. Those on the right are focused on the internal efficiency of the organisation and are predominantly financial.

### 8.3.2.1 Advantages
Proponents of the model argue that:
• It clearly links organisational strategy with day-to-day operations in a systematic manner.
• It develops agreed measures.
• It enables interdivisional comparisons.
• It promotes stakeholder accountability.
• It clarifies the objectives of the organisation.

### 8.3.2.2 Disadvantages
Critics of the performance pyramid argue that:
• It focuses on only two groups of stakeholders, i.e. shareholders and customers.
• It fails to incorporate measures relating to other stakeholders.
• It can become unwieldy in more complex organisations.

## 8.3.3 Building Block Model
The building block model is an evolution of the balanced scorecard, developed to meet the specific performance measurement needs of service organisations. It evolved from a 1996 research report entitled ‘Performance Measurement in Service Industries; Making it Work’. The rationale for developing a service sector specific model recognises that service businesses possess several characteristics that differentiate them from businesses producing physical goods and these differences can create difficulties in measuring performance (Moon and Fitzgerald, 1996).

Some key differences are:

• Inseparability/Simultaneity. This recognises that production and consumption of the service usually occur at the same time. An example of this would be a visit to the doctor, where the service provided usually cannot be separated from the service provider.

• Perishability. This reflects that the service cannot be stored and consumed later.

Examples of this include airline flights, hotel accommodation and theatre tickets. If they are not consumed, they ’perish’ – they cannot be used later.

• Heterogeneity. This lack of consistency is frequently present in services businesses because of the large number of variables involved. An example would be the difference in quality (real or perceived) provided by one law firm compared to another; the quality of service will often depend on the person who actually delivers that service.

• Intangibility. Typically, unlike goods, there are no physical aspects to a service product – no taste, no feel.

• Ownership. The provision of services does not result in the transfer of ownership from provider to consumer as no real property is exchanged. The purchase of a service only gives the customer access to or the right to use a facility, not ownership.

The building block model, like other measurement frameworks, connects an organisation’s strategic objectives to a range of forward-looking, non-financial performance measures. However, the building block model differs in that it also considers reward systems and also aims to create a framework of individual metrics, clearly understood and communicated, that aligns individual performance targets with organisational objectives.

The building block model is based on three building blocks: dimensions, standards and rewards. Diagrammatically, it is usually represented as shown below in Exhibit 8.10.
![](DraggedImage-221.png)
The dimensions building block encompasses six key outcomes, measurement of which is considered possible and valuable:

1. Financial performance – Measuring actual results.
2. Competitiveness – Includes measures such as market share and relative cost structure.
3. Quality of service.
4. Flexibility – Ability to alter output volumes or pre-service specifications quickly.
5. Resource allocation – How effectively are resources being used – for example, what percentage of available capacity in each process is being deployed at any time.
6. Innovation – Measuring improvements to products and processes, and the time and cost it takes to implement these.

The six outcomes are subdivided into two groups. The first of these, results, measures competitiveness and financial performance. The second, classified as determinants, comprises quality of service, flexibility, resource utilisation and innovation.

The rewards building block seeks to provide a framework to assess the effectiveness of performance metrics. These are:

1. Clarity – It is important to ensure that the people using the measures can easily understand them.
2. Motivation – Measures should be designed in a way that aligns and is congruent with the overall goals of the organisation.
3. Controllability – Reflecting the ‘responsibility centre’ concept, this surmises that managers and supervisors should be given appropriate authority over all factors that affect the measures for which they are going to be held accountable.

The standards building block comprises three constructs considered essential if a performance measurement system is to be effective. These are:

1. Ownership – This addresses the importance of involving those responsible for achieving defined outcomes in establishing and quantifying the measures. This reflects contemporary participative budgeting theory that has been extensively researched in the management accounting literature.
2. Achievability – Targets should be as realistic as possible to minimise the likelihood of demotivating people. It is important to note that opinions differ with regard to how achievable targets should be. Some schools of thought argue that relatively ‘easy’ targets are preferable because of the positive motivational affect that ‘budget success’ may bring. Others argue that ‘tougher’ targets are better because they are likely to foster a degree of internal competitiveness, and thereby improved overall performance. In practice, the best approach should reflect the culture of the organisation; what is appropriate for one organisation may not be at all suitable for another organisation.

3. Equity (or fairness) – This is arguably one of the most important overall characteristics of the building block model, suggesting that the overall system must be viewed by employees as being equitable, transparent and applicable to everybody in the organisation.

### 8.3.3.1 Advantages
The advantages of the building block model are that:
• It connects strategic objectives to forward-looking non-financial measures.
• It considers reward systems by establishing metrics that align individual performance with broader organisational objectives.
• It provides processes that, properly constructed and used, can motivate staff and improve employee engagement.

### 8.3.3.2 Disadvantages
As with all models, the building block model is by no means perfect. Some potential difficulties and problems are:

• Some important perspectives are missing. Issues of increasing contemporary relevance such as corporate social responsibility, risk management and performance of key business partners on whom success may be dependent are absent.
• There is a possibility that the chosen metrics may to some extent conflict with each other and thereby cause internal tensions and staff anxiety. For example, simultaneously incorporating one measure seeking to reduce costs and another seeking to improve customer service levels could prove problematic.
• The model is internally directed and has no external dimension – as such it does not attempt to assess (let alone measure) the preparedness of the organisation to respond to external threats or opportunities such as competition, technological disruption, and environmental change. However, it is not alone in this regard – neither the BSC nor the performance pyramid incorporate these factors.
• As with the other models, the costs of developing, implementing, updating and monitoring a suite of measures can, if not carefully controlled, become excessive. Similarly, there may be a risk that ‘paralysis by analysis’ emerges; managers may be distracted by the need to ‘measure’ and may take their ’eye off the ball’ in terms of concentrating on the operational tasks for which they are responsible and accountable.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> There are some limitations of conventional financial performance measures. Incorporating non-financial performance measures into an overall performance measurement system helps to create an integrated multidimensional approach to performance measurement.

#### Apply and Analyse 3
Asiatic Leisure Industries (ALI) is a rapidly growing privately owned diversified provider of leisure facilities operating throughout Hong Kong and South East Asia. Its product offering consists of cinemas, ten pin bowling alleys, ice skating rinks and indoor rock climbing.

ALI’s mission is to become the leading leisure provider in South East Asia by building the strength of its brand through consistently pleasing its customers; investing in staff training and development; delivering fresh, innovative products and value-added service; and, continually improving all aspects of organisational performance. In doing so, ALI expects to maximise shareholder value and create pride in the brand to the benefit of all stakeholders.

At present, most of the facilities operated by ALI are in properties progressively acquired over many years and owned by the founders of the business. Organisationally, ALI has to date structured its operations on a product-based divisional structure with each operation having its own divisional manager reporting to the chief executive officer (CEO). Toward the end of each financial year, divisional managers meet with the group’s CFO to develop operating budgets for the coming year. Divisional managers’ performance bonuses are based on actual profit performance against budget.

Following a recent review, ALI is considering a strategic change to its current business model. Rather than increase debt to finance planned expansion, the Board has decided to free up cash by taking advantage of the recent growth in property prices. Selected property assets will be sold and leased back. The cash generated from the sales will be used to finance planned expansion.

To assist in the management of this strategic initiative, the CEO is considering implementing the Balanced Scorecard throughout ALI. Concerned that several key staff members may perceive the BSC as just another ‘fad from the manufacturing sector’ the CEO has engaged you, as a management consultant with considerable experience in performance measurement, to assist with the development and implementation of the BSC. Your task will be to ensure that BSC adopts a multidimensional approach, integrates operational and strategic performance measures into a logical and coherent framework and clearly differentiates the differences between service and manufacturing businesses.

The first thing that you decide to do is review the preliminary work on the BSC that some of ALI’s managers have already undertaken.

This table provides details of the perspectives and performance metrics currently identified.
