BRIEFING TO THE EXECUTIVE LEADERSHIP TEAM AT AUDIO PLUS HK ENTITY LIMITED ON EFFECTIVE RISK MANAGEMENT

As a senior partner in Risk and Evaluation Consulting Group (RECG), you have been asked to assist a new client, Audio Plus HK Entity Limited (‘Audio Plus’), with reviewing different strategy options for their listed audio products business. Key considerations will be how the different options align with existing product offerings, the relative risk of the different options and forecasting their expected financial returns using their established investment evaluation methodology. Audio Plus executives are also aware of the entity being a good corporate citizen and have expressed a desire to ensure that any new product offering will take into account non-financial factors such as being environmentally and societally friendly. Lastly, as Audio Plus is a maturing entity, the executives have been working on developing an enterprise risk management system based on the COSO model and may need some assistance in finalising the framework.

Audio Plus HK Entity Limited (‘Audio Plus’) is a Hong Kong listed entity that manufactures mid-range priced technology audio products, including the ‘Hello! Wireless Smart Speaker’ range. Its market capitalisation is HK$2 billion with its significant shareholders being multi-national investment banks, some of whom are also their financiers. Their five manufacturing plants are located primarily in the Guodong province. Audio Plus have been operating for five years and have faced increasing competition from mid-range offerings from Google, Amazon, Apple and Sonos in the smart speaker market. Audio Plus’s current audio product categories are smart speakers, traditional portable ‘dumb’ speakers, DJ equipment, consumer headphones and business conference headsets. While Audio Plus’s gross margins on their audio products have been reasonably healthy, they have seen reduced gross margins across the board in all categories in the last six months due to increased price cutting by its competitors.

Audio Plus is therefore looking to diversify its product offerings further to reduce exposure risk to audio products and is considering a range of technology offerings believed to align and capitalise on Audio Plus’s existing expertise in the audio market. Audio Plus’s vision is to ‘Make consumers technology life easier’ and its stated strategy is ‘to deliver high quality, innovative, affordable consumer technology products that are easy to use’. Its key target markets are China, the European Union and the United States, with the single most important market being the European Union. Audio Plus has struggled to make inroads into the United States, given the competition from established brand offerings. Also, the pace of technological innovation and change has been faster than anticipated and consequently some of the existing product lines have experienced rapidly slowing sales and Audio Plus has had to discount them heavily to sell them, reducing their gross margins. Audio Plus wants to avoid the risk of this type of situation from occurring again.

## OVERVIEW

Risk is an ordinary part of the operations of every entity and creates both opportunity and threats to the entity arising from the different types of business activities it engages. It occurs when the entity takes, or does not take, a course of action seeking a particular outcome, despite knowing there is uncertainty, such as unpredictability and uncontrollability of that outcome. Risk can be described as the effect of uncertainty on the entity’s pursuit of achieving their strategic objectives.

Entities seek to measure the probability of uncertainty occurring and their likely consequences for the entity. When considering risk, it is important to remember that not all risk is inherently negative in terms of consequence to the entity and may in fact present opportunities to add value to the entity.

This chapter introduces students to the fundamentals of what it means to manage risk and explores common risk factors that the entity may face and how they can effectively manage these. It then introduces the concept of enterprise risk management (ERM), which is a systematic entity-wide approach to managing risk and is an integral part of the entity’s good corporate governance framework. ERM provides a framework to consistently and effectively identify, assess, qualify, quantify and manage risks identified from all the parts of the entity’s business, even when dealing with uncertainty and/or imperfect information.

When risk is identified, we will demonstrate how the risk can be assessed, treated and managed. We will consider risk and how to assess it within the process of an entity evaluating potential investment projects. Lastly, we will consider how to use the ERM to ensure the entity’s financial sustainability and prevent financial distress.

# 9.1 FUNDAMENTALS OF RISK MANAGEMENT

All entities have risk in their business. Risk can affect all parts of the entity, in similar or completely different ways, depending on the diversity of the entity’s operations. It creates opportunities for entities to be rewarded for the amount of risk that they are prepared to take on (a risk advantage) and exploit (upside risk), or how actively they minimise those risks that threaten the entity’s ability to earn rewards or cost it financially (downside risk). By its nature, risk also creates uncertainty for the entity as its likely impact is not always known; therefore it is critical for entities to be aware of, and actively manage, all risks with the potential to significantly affect their value.

Entities manage risk in two ways — either in taking action (change) or through conscious inaction (exploiting the status quo). Well-managed risk means the entity knows what risks it is exposed to and actively manages these risks to either exploit or minimise them. Poorly managed risk can lead to sub-optimal or disastrous results for the entity, including a loss of value, financial distress or bankruptcy.

Risk management should be a defined, disciplined, continuous process that provides a framework for how the entity manages all its different types of risk in its business, regardless of whether the risk is the result of internal or external events and within the entity’s control or not (Exhibit 9.1). It requires the entity to continually scan their operating environments to obtain relevant, accurate and reliable information that fully informs them of the risks it faces and understand the potential consequences of those risks in setting their strategy and in their decision making. It requires entities to be adaptive enough to be able to change their strategic objectives or business plans in order to appropriately respond to risks. Effective risk management does not mean being risk free as all entities need to take risks in order to pursue their strategic objectives. Additionally, there are different ways of ‘managing’ risk, including exploiting its positive opportunities, accepting it, seeking to mitigate its negative consequences, seeking to take advantage of positive consequences, avoiding risk by deciding not to take a course of action or possibly transferring the risk to another party. This enables the entity to manage risk to an acceptable residual level that falls within its risk appetite. By having a risk management process in place, the entity can also more readily respond to risks as and when they occur. For risks with potentially significant benefits or costs and uncertainty, risk management provides the entity with options on how to deal with such risks as they evolve. This provides the entity with the best chance of achieving its strategic objectives, adding value and not experiencing financial distress. In designing a risk response, the entity’s governance and control environment is considered to see how effective it is in managing the risk.
![](DraggedImage-223.png)
It is important that the entity embeds risk considerations into its culture, resource capabilities, tone at the top, and principles, processes and practices, at all levels, to ensure that risk management is fully integrated into the way the entity operates its decision-making processes.

Overall, the Board of Directors is responsible for setting the entity’s risk framework, including policies and procedures, and its risk tolerance and appetite.

The type of employees within the entity that typically may perform risk management vary according to the size and nature of the entity.

• In larger entities, such as multinationals, those with significant financial and legal risks (e.g. financial institutions), those trading internationally in raw commodities (e.g. miners, agribusinesses) or treasury products (e.g. financial institutions) ordinarily have a Chief Risk Officer and a specific governance and risk department to assist in risk management. The Chief Risk Officer operates across the executive leadership team function (senior management) to ensure that all risks are appropriately identified, managed, documented and reported.

• For smaller entities they may have dedicated internal risk professionals or out-source the risk function to external risk experts, with their reporting lines to the Chief Financial Officer. Regardless, members of the entity’s executive function are responsible for the strategic objectives of the entity and for conducting continual internal and external environmental scanning to identify any risks that may damage the entity’s ability to achieve its objectives.

It is important to note that while entities have areas or functions that have responsibility for risk reporting, all parts of the entity, and at all levels, are responsible for managing risk. Risk can be present anywhere within the entity and needs to be assessed by those best placed to understand its possible consequences. An entity-wide framework for risk management, called enterprise risk management (ERM), is covered in Section 9.4 and deals with the strategic decisions taken by the entity’s executive leadership team in establishing risk management within the entity (for example establishing key risk principles – risks registers, risk reporting, how risk is identified, the information used, risk appetite, individual risk tolerance and residual risk indicators). For the purposes of this section, key risk concepts that can be applied to an individual level risk are covered.

## 9.1.1 Key Steps in Managing Risk

Let’s look at the key steps in managing risk in more detail. The following discussion assumes that the entity has in place an entity-wide risk management system (called an enterprise risk management framework). This framework documents the entity’s overarching principles for what risk is, how to assess, classify and quantify its likely impact on the entity based on probability and consequence, and provides different risk response options available. These documents are ordinarily policies, procedures and processes that address risk considerations in key aspects of the entity’s operations and may or may not be designated or described as specific risk related policies within the ERM framework. It includes all governance reporting of risk and ownership and approval delegations. Refer to Section 9.4, Enterprise Risk Management, for more detail.

### 9.1.1.1 Step 1: Identifying Risks

The entity needs to scan their environment to obtain relevant (pertinent to decisions) and faithfully representational information (measures what it says it does) to identify all possible threats it faces that create risks to achieving its strategic objectives. It is important that all risks are identified, so they can be appropriately documented, assessed and, if applicable, responded to.

In identifying risk, the entity should look for both upside risks (i.e. opportunities for the entity to create and add to its value) and downside risks (i.e. the uncertainty of loss or damage to the entity) as well as for financial (directly affect the entity’s financial outcomes) and non-financial type risks (indirectly affect the entity’s financial outcomes). Environmental scanning should identify all types of risk: financial, operational, political, legal and/or business risks. These are discussed in more detail in Section 9.2, Key Risks Facing by an Entity.

It is also important when identifying risk to classify it according to the way in which it may affect the entity’s strategic objectives. To ensure consistency of classification across the entity, the entity could create a classification scheme. The complexity of the scheme will depend on the entity’s size and complexity. For example, the first level could be the entity-wide level (i.e. financial, operational, political, legal or business). The second level could be the relevant business units’ risk (i.e. finance, manufacturing), and the third level could be at the task or functional level (e.g. inventory obsolescence, fraud or internal control). The key is to ensure that the classifications are appropriate to the entity and are consistently used throughout the entity so that ‘like’ types of risks are classified in the same way. In this way, the entity has the best means of addressing such risks with appropriate risk responses.

### 9.1.1.2 Step 2: Assessing Identified Risks

Performing a risk assessment on identified risks allows the entity to prioritise identified risks so that it can direct its scarce resources in the most efficient and effective manner in addressing those risks with the most chance of occurring and having the most impact (threat) to the entity. All identified risks must then be assessed in terms of the probability of such a risk occurring (e.g. more likely than less likely) and their likely consequence (upside or downside) to the entity. For downside risks, this initial assessment excludes consideration of any internal controls the entity may have in place to safeguard against that type of risk occurring.

It is preferable that the person within the entity performing the assessment (risk assessors) understands the context of the risk within the entity so they can exercise appropriate professional judgement and make informed decisions of the probability and consequence of the risks occurring. As part of the enterprise risk management framework, there should be a standardised risk assessment template available to all risk assessors to ensure entity-wide consistency of interpretation and application to all individual risks.

Probability ratings will be set by the enterprise risk framework, based on how likely it is that the identified risk will be, or become, important. This will depend on various internal and external factors, including but not limited to the entity’s individual circumstances, the nature and type of the risk (upside or downside risk and whether it is a new risk or an existing risk), past experience and the location of the risk. To ensure consistency in the assessment, probability ratings should be defined qualitatively (descriptively) and quantitatively (numerically, e.g. percentage wise). For example, if it is expected that the risk will occur, or continue to occur, ‘rarely’ it could be assessed as ≤5% probability, ‘unlikely’ as \>5% and ≤30%, ‘possible’ as \>30% but ≤51%, ‘likely’ as \>51% but ≤90% and ‘almost certain’ as \>90%. By assigning standard ratings, the entity can easily see what risks, based on probability, it should actively manage to take advantage of possible rewards or minimise possible loss.

Once risks have been properly identified and its probabilities assessed, the entity should then look at the consequence of the risks in terms of the potential positive or negative impact on the entity. Like for probability, this will depend on various internal and external factors, including but not limited to the entity’s individual circumstances, the nature and type of the risk, past experience, the maturity of the entity (start-up or established) and the location of the risk. To ensure consistency in the assessment, the enterprise risk management framework will categorise the impact with a qualitative description. For example, upside risk may be assessed as having ‘low’, ‘medium’, ‘high’ or ‘significant’ benefits and downside risk may be assessed as having a ‘negligible’, ‘moderate’, ‘significant’, ‘catastrophic’ or ‘low’, ‘medium’ or ‘high’ costs to the entity.

The results of the probability and consequence assessment can be plotted on a simple risk assessment matrix (Exhibit 9.2). This provides an easy to understand visual to see which risks it is most necessary to respond to, and to which risks it is least important to respond to.
![](DraggedImage-224.png)
Once each risk is assessed and depending on how many risks the entity has identified and assessed, a risk heat map may be used to visualise the risk assessment results (Exhibit 9.3). One map could be created for upside risks and another for downside risks as the risk responses will likely be very different. Depending on the type and number of risks identified, the risks can be all plotted on one map or ‘like’ types of risks (e.g. financial, operational, political, legal and business risks) can be plotted together.
![](DraggedImage-225.png)

Once completed, the entity’s risk appetite (its willingness to accept or exploit risk), as determined by the Board of Directors, can be overlayed to the matrix or map to show where the entity’s risk acceptance line lies in relation to the risks (Exhibit 9.4).

![](DraggedImage-226.png)
When a risk requires more mathematical precision or sophistication (i.e. less judgement or subjectivity) in measuring the probability and consequence, quantitative method models can be used. These models convert the impact of an individual risk into numerical terms.

### 9.1.1.3 Step 3: Identifying Possible Ways of Responding to the Assessed Risk

Selecting the appropriate way of responding to the identified risk depends on the type and nature of risk that have been identified and how they have been classified as part of the risk evaluation procedure. The higher the risk assessment rating the more important the risk to either take advantage of, and exploit, upside risk or minimise/mitigate downside risk.

#### Upside Risk 
If an upside risk has been assessed as having a high impact (e.g. if it happened it could greatly benefit) and a low probability (it is unlikely to happen), then the entity would likely not pursue any action to take advantage of this risk. Alternatively, if the risk had been assessed as highly probable and of high consequence then it may be appropriate to adopt a strong proactive approach to take advantage of the circumstances creating the risk so that the entity can benefit.

A practical example is an entity that had previously identified that a popular seasonal product may be in short supply in the coming season and had planned to increase production to meet the expected increased demand. At the beginning of the season, it becomes evident that demand is even greater than expected and the entity would have to significantly increase its production levels to accommodate. To achieve this, the entity would have to make a further capital investment in the manufacturing plant. The entity would assess the benefits of increased production on expected sales against the cost of the increased capital investment. Refer to Section 9.3 for a discussion on evaluating investment projects like this for more detail.

#### Downside Risk

If a downside risk has been assessed as having a low impact (e.g. if it happened, it would not have a negligible impact) and low probability (it is unlikely to happen) on causing a threat to the entity, then the risk may be classified as acceptable and the treatment would involve no action. Alternatively, if the risk had been assessed as highly probable and of high consequence then it may be appropriate to adopt a strong avoidance policy or if not practical, a strong risk response to reduce the risk to a more acceptable level. A back-up strategy (contingency plan) may also be created to prevent the risk from causing the entity a high degree of damage.

A practical example is an entity that had previously identified that a popular technology product may be obsolete in the coming season due to new improved technology product being tested by its competitors and had planned to gradually decrease their production of the existing product to prevent excess inventory build-up and obsolescence. Midway through the beginning of the season, their competitors start selling the improved product, which was earlier than expected, and it becomes evident that initial demand for the new product is high, leaving the entity with the prospect of significant quantities of the old product being unsold, unless it is discounted heavily. In addition, they should stop producing the old product immediately and start producing the new technology product as soon as possible. To minimise the cost of poor product sales at lower gross margins and increased product obsolescence, the entity should stop manufacturing the old product immediately. Additionally, to halt further reduced profitability, the entity should start manufacturing the new product as soon as possible, assuming the entity has already assessed the benefits of producing the new product as against the cost of re-purposing their existing manufacturing plant. Refer to Section 9.3 for a discussion on evaluating investment projects like this for more detail.

#### Risk Response Options

The commonly used treatment options for how to respond to risk are:

##### • Exploit – the risk provides an opportunity to earn significant rewards/value from taking a particular course of action.
-The cost of the risk is less than the perceived benefit of the activity.
- An example is an investment evaluation that may be marginally beneficial to proceed with, that simply requires the entity increase its output by a small amount to achieve significantly increased benefits. Refer to Section 9.3, Evaluating Investment Projects, for more details

##### • Avoid – does not allow the activity creating the risk from proceeding.
° This occurs when the cost of the risk is greater than the perceived benefit of the activity.
° An example is an investment evaluation that does not meet its required rate of return criteria. Refer to Section 9.3, Evaluating Investment Projects, for more details.

##### • Tolerate – accepts the risk as is, with no mitigating actions to be taken.
° This may be because for the nature/type of risk there is no cost-effective strategy for addressing it or because the risk of impact is so low it can be accepted.
° These risks must always be monitored to ensure that the ‘tolerate’ strategy remains appropriate, particularly if events impacting the risk change in the future.
° An example is accepting that in the manufacturing process there will be some quality control issues that result in not all products being able to be sold.

##### • Enhance – increase the probability of the opportunity occurring.
° This occurs when the perceived benefit to the entity will only be realised if more resources are allocated to achieve that benefit.
° An example is an investment evaluation involving expanding an existing manufacturing plant. Refer to Section 9.3, Evaluating Investment Projects, for more details.

##### • Treat – devises an action plan to control or reduce the likelihood of the risk occurring based on its risk rating.
° This also includes putting in place contingent measures to reduce the impact of a risk if it occurs.
° An example is to test internal controls relevant to the risk to ensure they are working or implement new internal controls.

##### • Share (upside risk) – give some or all of the opportunity to a third party for mutual benefit.
° This can increase the benefit the entity receives. ° An example is entering into a partnership to build a manufacturing plant that can produce both parties’ products. Refer to Section 9.3, Evaluating Investment Projects, for more details.

##### • Transfer (share the downside risk) – transfers the source of the risk to another party.
° This can be achieved by contracting with a third party to minimise the cost of the risk to the entity.
° Examples include using sub-contractors, outsourcing some internal functions (e.g. payroll) and taking out insurance coverage.

##### • Terminate – removes the source of the risk from the entity.
° This can be achieved by amending an inherent risk process/practice to remove the risk, without materially affecting the entity.
° An example is closing a poorly performing retail location to reduce its drain on profitability.

#### Considering Internal Controls

In managing risk, it is important to consider what internal controls need to be in place to help identify, monitor and, if need be, to exploit or mitigate risk, and to ensure that those controls are operating as intended. Internal control refers to the processes the entity has in place to support the entity in achieving its objectives in operations, create entity value, minimise risk, ensure compliance with applicable laws and regulations, safeguard its assets and provide reliable financial reporting to external and internal stakeholders. Refer to Section 9.4.6, Control Framework, for more detail covering what internal control is and how it impacts risks responses. It includes a discussion on the widely applied internal control framework issued by the international Committee of Sponsoring Organisations (COSO) titled Internal Control Integrated Framework (2013).

It is also important to assess the frequency that the control operates. Effectiveness looks at whether the control operates to identify, exploit, prevent or correct for a particular risk. To place reliance on a control’s effectiveness requires that the control be tested to ensure that it was in operation during the period it was designed to be; that is, that the control worked as designed.

If the entity has an internal audit function (in-house or outsourced) and the risk is rated high enough to be important to the entity, then an internal audit should test and report the operating effectiveness of the control with sufficient regularity to provide comfort that it can be relied on as part of the risk treatment plan. If the entity does not have an internal audit function, control testing should be part of the risk treatment plan.

#### Considering Residual Risk

Whatever the risk treatment plan, the entity needs to consider the level of residual risk that likely will continue to exist after the plan has been implemented, and be comfortable with that level of risk, relative to their risk tolerance (individual risk) and overall risk appetite (entity-wide risk). Residual risk may be assessed qualitatively in terms of ‘low, medium and high’. If they are not acceptably classified, the treatment plan needs to be revised until the residual risk meets with the entity’s acceptable level.

If the risk is significant enough to the entity, the proposed risk response will have to be approved by a person other than the risk assessor. Refer to Section 9.4, Enterprise Risk Management, for more detail.

### 9.1.1.4 Step 4: Implementing the Risk Response

The risk response should be implemented in a timely manner and by appropriately qualified employees within the entity or external experts. The risk manager should then evaluate the effectiveness of the risk response in addressing the risk, amending its residual risk to acceptable levels and report results to the appropriate entity level so it can effectively be monitored as part of the entity’s enterprise risk management framework.

### 9.1.1.5 Step 5: Risk Summary

The results of the risk management process can be summarised as in the risk summary template in Exhibit 9.5.
![](DraggedImage-227.png)

### 9.1.1.6 Step 6: Evaluating the Risk Response Result

Once the risk response has been implemented, it is important that the results be considered by the risk manager to see if the designed risk response achieved the intended outcome of managing the risk. It is also important to consider if any improvements can be made to the risk management process as a result of the risk response process.

If the risk response did not achieve the desired outcome, the entity should consider alternatives for how to manage the risk and implement the preferred alternative, and then re-evaluate its success in managing the risk. No risk should be left untreated if the entity assesses the risk as requiring to be managed by one of the response options.

The results of managing the risk needs to be reported to the appropriate risk owner(s) and those responsible for overseeing the entity’s enterprise risk management framework.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Risk is a necessary part of the operations of the entity and can present both challenges and opportunities for the entity to deal with and appropriately address.

Now that we have discussed the fundamental concepts of risk, let’s consider the impact of uncertainty on risk.

## 9.1.2 Differentiating Risk and Uncertainty

Risk is any internal or external event that may affect the entity’s ability to achieve its strategic objectives. Managing risk is exceptionally challenging in situations where great uncertainty exists. This may exist when the entity cannot quantify the likelihood of the risk changing, or the potential consequences of such changes, or the speed of the change, due to a lack of relevant and representationally faithful information or a lack of experience in dealing with the risk or related information.

It is critical to note here that the events that underpin risk can impact the entity in either a positive or negative manner. The concept of risk has three key elements:

• The perception that something could happen,
• The likelihood of something happening and
• The consequences if it were to happen.

Uncertainty relates to circumstances in which the full set of potential outcomes in a given situation are not known. Those outcomes may be positive or negative and their assessment might bear little relationship to past experiences, which can make it difficult to assign probabilities to possible outcomes. Entities are faced with a range of internal and external factors and influences that gives rise to uncertainty with respect to whether the entity will be able to achieve its objectives and to what extent they will be able to do so. Nevertheless, risk management needs to systematically consider the range of possible outcomes and to reassess judgements over time as more information becomes available.

Assessing risk necessarily involves consideration of uncertainties. Risk and uncertainty are not the same principles but interact in how the entity manages risk. Risk management seeks to identify all events giving rise to uncertainty and considers how the occurrence of the events could impact the entity (both positively and negatively). Based on that impact assessment, the entity then designs an appropriate risk response to address that risk in a manner that enables the entity to pursue its objectives.

A comparison of risk and uncertainty for a potential investment project is as follows:

• Risk: the entity knows that prices are volatile in their industry as supply and demand for the product can vary significantly between seasons.
• Uncertainty: the entity has expectations about these prices, which may or may not be correct and may have to be changed when more information comes to light.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Uncertainty affects the assessment of risk as the entity does not know the outcome of the potential event. Risk management seeks to identify and respond to all such uncertainty, thereby enabling it to take advantage of opportunities aligned and creating value in the strategic objectives, while reducing those risks that are a threat to achieving those strategic objectives.

## 9.1.3 Linkage Between Strategy and Risk

With the concept of risk and uncertainty now explained, this section discusses the interaction between risk and achieving the entity’s strategy and why it is so important for risk to be an integral part of strategy considerations.

### 9.1.3.1 Establishing the Entity’s Strategy

Whether committed to paper or not, every entity has an explicit or implicit mission, vision and core values that define what it is trying to achieve and how it wants to conduct its operations. Senior Management (also called the executive leadership team) and the Board of Directors (the entity’s leaders overall) are responsible for setting the entity’s strategic direction (core mission) to ensure that the entity achieves its strategic objectives. The entity’s strategic direction establishes the entity’s core purpose for being. The entity’s leaders also have responsibility for ensuring the entity is structured, resourced (people and technology) and financially able to appropriately meet its current and future needs.

The entity’s strategy for how it is going to meet its strategic direction must be dynamic and able to rapidly and appropriately respond to risks brought about by unexpected changes in events and conditions, and the availability of more complete information. It requires the entity’s leaders to be able to anticipate or identify key trends and challenges in their industry (industries), more broadly in the economies in which they operate, and to consequentially identify future opportunities and potential threats (challenges) from those factors on the entity.

They do this by conducting strategic planning and scanning their internal and external environments (through comprehensive market research) for all events that impact the entity and create or change risks or opportunities. Examples include deciding which markets will be attractive for it to operate in and how it can offer unique value to customers in those markets by offering resources and capabilities that cannot be easily rivalled by its competitors. Being able to prioritise how it will achieve its strategy involves a trade-off between the entity’s available resources, their predictions about key industry, market and macroeconomic trends and allowing for future proofing of the entity as a going concern. The latter in Section 9.3.3.3 will include stress testing the ability of the entity to withstand unexpected shocks.

The entity’s leaders are effectively planning on the entity’s core strengths and competencies and its ability to find future areas of growth and profitability and to avoid both anticipated and unanticipated pitfalls. Getting the balance right between managing for the known and unknown is a trade-off that depends on the entity’s leader’s ability to have appropriately assess their relative risk and likely impact (uncertainty). Getting these trade-offs right ensures that shareholder value is maintained or enhanced. Getting these trade-offs wrong can mean that shareholder value is reduced or even destroyed. Examples of circumstances in which an entity might need to rebalance its strategies include risks created or enabled by new technologies, changing laws and regulations, the changing demands of current and potential customers, availability of inputs required to provide the entity’s goods/services, employees, competitor’s offerings and competition from new market entrants.

In order to achieve the entity’s strategy, the entity’s leaders formulate, prioritise and establish strategic objectives, which at a high level essentially operationalise how to achieve the strategic direction and help the entity gain and sustain a competitive advantage in all markets where it offers its products and services. This in turn adds value to the entity.

The entity’s annual business plan (or equivalent) provides more details on how the entity proposes to implement certain actions (sometimes called strategic initiatives) to achieve those strategic objectives (in order of prioritisation), their budget implications, and can change from year to year. It forms the basis for the next level individual business unit/areas business plans and budgets. Setting the entity’s strategic direction, objectives and annual business plan are the most important governance responsibilities of the entity’s board of directors and its senior management team.

By nature, events that can impact the entity’s ability to meet its strategic direction, strategic objectives and annual business plan create risks, and with that risk comes some uncertainty in terms of predicting how the entity may be impacted or how well it will respond to such events.

### 9.1.3.2 How Managing Risk Can Help

A system of effective risk management requires that the entity have a culture whereby management routinely integrates risk considerations into all key decision-making processes within the entity, including setting its strategic direction, strategy, strategic objectives and annual business plans. It also sets out accountability for risk throughout the entity. Risk management provides a defined, disciplined approach to identify events (and consequent risks) that may impact the success of their plan and then implements strategies for managing (either minimising or taking advantage of) such risks to give the entity their best chance of annual business plan success. It provides the entity with a framework in which to weigh any tradeoffs involved. It ensures the entity has well-prepared processes to manage risk (those already identified and those unknown) and uncertainty in its operations.

Annual business plans can easily fall short of entity and market expectations and high success rates of strategic initiatives can tend to be the exception rather than the norm. Consequently, entities are incentivised to increase their likelihood of achieving their annual plans through using any tools that assist them to achieve or exceed their plan, which should include identifying and actively managing any risks. Risks that are inherent in, or affect, an entity’s pursuit (formation or implementation) of its strategic direction or objectives are called strategic risks.

Risks affecting strategy can occur:
• During the development and design of the strategic objectives, including how they align with the strategic direction of the entity, business unit level strategies and available operating budgets.
• During the execution of entity-wide and divisional/business unit strategies that are designed to achieve key entity goals and objectives. For example:
(a) Actions taken or not taken from any one, or all, of an entity’s key customers, suppliers, competitors and other relevant stakeholders in response to the new strategy.
(b) From the operationalisation of new technologies that disrupt a particular area of operation that the entity may be pursuing in its new strategy.

Examples of specific risk factors that affect strategy include:
• Changes in laws and regulations that affect how the entity operates.
• Financing availability – at the appropriate level and price.
• Competitive pressures – including competitor offerings.
• Stakeholder pressures.
• Environmental and social factors.
• Availability of relevant and representationally faithful information to make informed decisions.
• Key input costs pressures – labour, materials, including availability.
• Consumer demand and buying trends.
• Type, rate, pace and cost of technological change.
• Employee capabilities and expertise.
• Macro- and micro-economic conditions and variables (interest rates, inflation, unemployment rates, exchange rates, share/stock prices and national output).
• Senior management turnover.

These risk factors affect strategy as they can affect, inhibit or threaten (due to internal and external events) the ability of the entity to achieve its strategic objectives, maintain or add shareholder value and the entity’s ongoing viability/success, and therefore must be proactively identified and managed.

Additionally, the entity can create risk by pursuing the wrong strategy or by pursuing the right strategy too late or not implementing it correctly.

Given the above, it is therefore critical for an entity to incorporate strategic risk considerations into their risk management programme. Managing strategic risks is an integral part of the entity’s Enterprise Risk Management framework, which is discussed in more detail in Section 9.4.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Effective risk management must be aligned to the entity’s strategy as it ensures that the entity focuses on those risks that have the most potential to enhance, damage or inhibit the entity’s ability to achieve its strategic direction and objectives.

## 9.1.4 Decision-Making with Imperfect Information

Risk is present when the entity is required to make decisions, and even more so when those decisions are based on information that is not complete, relevant or faithfully represented. Let’s consider how entities manage this scenario.

### 9.1.4.1 Key Types of Decisions Made by the Entity

In setting the entity’s strategy, it is important to be fully informed of all relevant information that could impact that strategy. Given that the strategy is forward-looking and essentially the entity’s best estimate (projections) for what it is going to achieve in its operations, there is already considerable uncertainty and risk involved.

To craft a realistic strategy requires the entity to obtain relevant and representationally faithful information from a wide variety of sources, inside and outside of the entity. In an ideal world, the entity would have all such information; however, in the real world this is seldom the case. Entities routinely make decisions with incomplete (partial) or very little information at all. This is called imperfect information and the entity’s task in its strategic decision making is making sense of this information given the significant degree of uncertainty and risk involved.

Having the ability to make optimal decisions when faced with significant levels of uncertainty is a key aspect of risk management. There can easily be a disconnect between the assumptions/expectations of the strategic objectives, annual business plans, the planned outcomes, and the actual outcomes. Consider, for example, is this simply the result of a bad strategy or sub-optimal implementation or are there other factors at work? While the initial strategy or implementation plan may have been optimal given the information available, the reality in which the entity is implementing the strategy may be quite different from that expected by the initial analysis and the outcomes achieved consequently significantly different from expected. If the entity is a listed entity, this can cause problems with its stock exchange forecasts of expected profit versus actual results and visibly call into question the credibility of the entity’s leaders in being able to execute their strategy.

When there is considerable uncertainty (required information is not available) in making decisions, the entity needs to take a series of actions designed to give them the best possible opportunity to use their intuition, experience, imagination and their instincts in order to make effective decisions. Information choice can play a critical role in making these decisions. Information sources abound and choosing both accurate and relevant information is an essential aspect of the decision-making process and quite often it requires experience, expertise and sound judgement to choose from the information at hand.

The decision makers can meet regularly with employees of the various levels and experiences across the entity’s business units (with varying levels of seniority) to help understand their perspectives on the risks, challenges and opportunities the entity faces. This can be one step towards the decision makers becoming more informed and contributing to them having a solid foundation on which to form their perspective as to what appropriate courses of action are required to address such challenges. Of course, the decision makers also need to consider the opinions of a wide range of external parties (e.g. analysts, financiers, investors, customers and creditors) to ensure that the foundation is solid. These communications facilitate better quality decision making. Once information has been obtained, the entity needs to consider which decision options will take it as close as possible to achieving the entity’s strategic objectives and avoid those that could be potentially harmful to meeting those objectives.

When faced with uncertainty it is essential that the decisions that need to be made are still made. This may require drawing on a considerable degree of courage as the decision may impact the members or customers of an entity in a variety of both expected and unexpected ways. However, not deciding and doing nothing may prove to be considerably worse than making the wrong decision and then having to take corrective and remedial action.

### 9.1.4.2 Information Availability and Quality

Regardless of whether the entity has all or some of the information it requires, or lacks some of the required information, the entity still has to assess if the information obtained is of sufficient quality to place reliance on it for decision-making purposes. Higher quality information is clearly preferable and less risky than lower quality or unknown quality information. Where information is limited, strategies will be needed to monitor circumstances and to identify any better information that becomes available over time, so that past decisions can be revisited when necessary.

It is clear that the entity’s key decision-making processes supporting its strategic objectives must involve an identification and assessment of the relative costs and benefits of decisions. This may need to be an iterative process, adjusting for better information when it emerges.

In the next section we will consider specifically what types of risks the entity should consider in this process.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Information available to the entity on which to base decisions is seldom perfect. The entity must make the most of the information that is available to make the best-informed decisions and be prepared to revisit decisions when better information becomes available.

#### Apply and Analyse 1

Audio Plus is preparing a revised strategy to re-position the entity as it seeks to diversify its product offerings in the face of increased competition on its core audio products. Based on the opening case facts, describe the risk-related recommendations you can make to the entity regarding the drafting of the strategy.

Analysis

There are multiple factors that Audio Plus needs to consider with respect to its business strategy, all of which are related to risk. These include:

1. Information quality – Is the quality and depth of the market research sufficient for Audio Plus to make informed decisions about the merits of each of the proposed product offerings? Poor quality, incomplete or incorrect information risks poor decisions. How certain is Audio Plus that there is a profitable market opportunity for each of the product offerings?

2. Proposed product offerings – Consider how all potential offerings identified will align to the existing vision or strategic direction of the entity. How can the offerings align with current product offerings and Audio Plus’s current technical expertise and capabilities with its employees and manufacturing plants? Are any of the offerings complementary to the current offerings or any of the other proposed offerings?

3. Competitor research – How competitive are each of the markets? Who are the competitors? Are they profitable? How will Audio Plus’s competitors react to any of the new offerings? Are they operating in the local and overseas markets that Audio Plus proposes to target with the new offerings? What about already established competitors in the new product offerings? How saturated is the current market for each of the proposed products? How can Audio Plus differentiate itself from its competitors? For example, how easily can it be innovative, offer high quality and easy to use products and maintain affordable prices? What about offering new advanced technology? Does Audio Plus think they can generate cost of scale efficiencies from its existing products with these new offerings that will distinguish it enough from its competitors?

4. Financial considerations – How much capital will it require to commence producing each of the product offerings? Can any currently unprofitable locations/product line equipment be easily and cost-effectively repurposed to produce the new offerings to save on capital investment? Can it share proprietary technical ‘know how’ from its existing products in the new products to save start-up costs? Can the required rate of return be earned by each of the different offerings? How reliable is the financial data being used to assess how profitable and cash flow positive the proposed investment is that Audio Plus would need to make to produce the new products?

# 9.2 KEY RISKS FACING BY AN ENTITY

The entity must obtain an understanding of what are the key risks that may contribute to, or prevent, it achieving its strategic objectives. These are the risks that the entity must managed through its risk management framework. The way in which it obtains this understanding requires a systematic approach to ensure that no potential risks are excluded, left unidentified, under-estimated for their consequences, or ignored, and all risks are holistically considered and assessed for their overall potential impact on the entity. Only by doing so will an entity have the best opportunity of achieving its strategic objectives and maximising its value.

Overall risk is made up of various possible risks the entity could face. Those risks can be broken down into those that it can take advantage of and exploit, those that it should share, enhance, transfer, avoid or mitigate and those that can be tolerated if good management is sustained.

It helps to categorise identified risks in terms of their potential impact on the entity, using standardised terms so that risks are consistently evaluated. Risks can generally be classified into one of five broad categories: financial, operational, political, legal and business. It is important to note that any of these categories could impact the other categories as risk often overlaps and has consequences far wider than simply one risk category or one area of the entity.

Examples of the factors that can assist in categorising risks are:
• The type of entity it is (legal and business structures) – can lead to legal, financial and political risks.
• The size of the entity – can lead to financial, political and legal risks.
• The nature of the industry (industries) it operates in – can lead to financial, political, operational and legal risks.
• The type and nature of the geographical locations it operates in – can lead to operational, political and business risks.
• The extent to which the entity is subject to laws and regulations – can lead to legal, political and financial risks.
• Its business model (e.g. its financing structure, high/low margin business) – can lead to financial, operational and business risks.
• The extent of reliance on technology to conduct its operations – can lead to operational and business risks.
• The type of staff it requires to operate (e.g. highly specialised) – can lead to operational and business risks.
• The extent of competition it faces for its products and services – can lead to financial, operational and business risks.

## 9.2.1 Financial Risk

Financial risk refers to the likelihood that the entity, its shareholders, lenders, creditors or other stakeholders of an entity may experience variability in returns or costs, gain money from financial opportunities or lose money if the entity gets into financial difficulties. Financial risk includes a broad set of specific risk factors that relate to an entity’s capital structure, financing strategies, sources of revenue and the broader financial industry. Almost all risk can create consequences of a financial nature.

Financial risk is material when it is of such significance that it could affect the entity’s ongoing viability or its ability to fund emerging opportunities. This risk could arise from the entity’s activities relating to the adequacy of its financing (equity, loan or trade credit), having adequate infrastructure to cope with changed levels of demand for product, changes in commodity availability and pricing, and changes in rates (such as interest rates and foreign exchange rates) that can result in changed levels of profitability, cash flow mismatches and the repricing of asset portfolios and other investments. It can also arise from financing provided by the entity in the form of borrowings (loans) or customer credit.

### 9.2.1.1 Credit, Market and Operational Risks

The downside risk is that the entity’s shareholders, lenders and trade creditors will lose part or all of their initial financing of the entity (either through their shares, bonds or shorter-term provisions of credit) as a result of the entity actions. The upside risk is the expectation that an entity will benefit from the increased trust that markets and suppliers have in the entity and further financing or refinancing will be easier and better priced.

This category of risk has three elements:

• Credit risk (or counterparty risk) has three components.

- Default risk, being the risk to an entity that another entity may be unable or unwilling to pay a debt (all or partially), make a settlement, or execute performance in transactions or contracts related to derivative trades, or vice versa. The entity itself has a credit risk and so do its customers and the other parties with which it contracts. Those risks can change and can impact each other (for example, a change in the credit risk of its significant customers can impact the entity’s financing from banks and other lenders, in terms of its financing costs). Credit risk can change well before any credit ratings adjustments are made.

- Credit spread risk, being the risk that the entity is exposed to volatility in their equity (shares) investments as compared to the risk-free rate of return, assuming both have the same maturity timeframes but differing credit qualities.

- Downgrade risk, resulting from a reduction in the entity’s own credit rating or in the entity in which it holds shares.

	Credit risk can be affected by efficiency of cash flow management, general economic and industry trends, shifts in the financial markets, changes in the legal environment, and the level and changes in the level of gearing. Competitive conditions can also affect the ability of an entity to be able to settle all debts as and when they fall due, due to having to accept longer settlement terms. Untoward changes in credit risk can lead to the entity experiencing financial distress. This is covered in more detail in Section 9.5, Preventing Financial Distress.

• Market risk is the downside risk of a loss in the valuation of an entity’s assets or the upside risk of a gain from an increase in valuation of an entity’s assets arising from unexpected fluctuations (volatility) in their price. Market risk can also impact upon the attractiveness of the entity’s equity (e.g. generally when markets are in downturn). The volatility addressed under the heading of market risk is caused by non-entity specific factors and affects all entities and are not risks that the entity has any control over in terms of whether they occur or not.

Market risk is often called ‘systematic risk’ as it can apply to any assets, liabilities and equity in any entity, has the potential to impact the entity’s market valuation and profitability, and can be caused by a myriad of factors. These include from economic downturn (e.g. increasing inflation gross domestic product, rising unemployment, significantly expanded or shrinking monetary supply) that causes negative market sentiment, political uncertainty or instability, changes in laws and regulations (including taxation), general industry viability concerns, share market concerns, movements in the price of commodities, changes in exchange rates, changes in interest rates, credit spreads, equities and option prices.

• Financial operational risk is the risk of financial loss from the entity’s internal processes, people, systems (technology) or from internal or external events. This is particularly relevant if the entity has designed its systems to standardise how it processes and/ or approves repetitive, small or large volume transactions, or how it deals with non-recurring transactions. If such areas are poorly designed, reviewed and/or not continuously monitored, the entity may lose significant amounts of money through fraud or error if transactions are processed that are unauthorised, or if automated transactions are continually processed incorrectly. Inadequately oversighted or poorly trained people can contribute to them making errors in transaction processing, dealing incorrectly with issues when they arise or allowing them to commit fraud. Additionally, if the entity does not have standardised processes in place to record its transactions, it risks inconsistency of treatment and financial loss.

An example of this is the entity’s process for extending trade credit to its customers when purchasing its goods or services (that is, providing those goods or services before payment is received). If the entity does not conduct and enforce an active, rigorous credit assessment process on a prospective customer’s credit worthiness before providing goods of services to that customer, the entity risks losing the value of the goods or services provided if the customer subsequently cannot or will not pay for them. This also risks losing interest rate revenue and incurring additional legal costs trying to recover payment – these are discussed below. In this example, the entity needs to manage its operational risk by having an active credit assessment process in place, operating and enforced, to minimise financial loss from this process.

Operational risk without a direct financial loss is discussed more in Section 9.2.2, Operational Risks.

### 9.2.1.2 Commodity Risk

Any entity engaged in buying or selling products whose sales price is either directly or indirectly linked to the price of a raw material or primary agricultural product (commodity) is exposed to commodity risk. This is the risk that the price of a commodity will change adversely or beneficially for the entity. Commodity risk is ordinarily managed by the entity’s treasury or finance function. Examples of commodities are wheat, rice, natural gas, iron ore, copper, coal, oil, gold and silver. Commodities are traded on special global markets and commitments to purchase or sell them are entered either on an immediate (spot) or future (forward rate) basis, so that buyers and sellers have some price and quantity certainty.

If underlying commodity prices increase or decrease significantly (e.g. as a result of weather events, production issues, employee strikes, quality issues) then this will impact the final price of the commodity/final product reliant on those commodities for their input. This in turn impacts the entity’s customers who may or may not accept the higher price for the commodity/final product and result in the entity either not selling as much of the commodity/ final product as they planned or not being able to meet existing contracts or increased demand for the product.

### 9.2.1.3 Interest Rate Risk

The entity has exposure to two types of interest rate risk:

1. Movements in interest rates causing their own trade credit interest charges to its customers or being charged by its suppliers will be higher or lower. An example of this is the entity receiving trade credit from its suppliers when purchasing raw inputs to be used in its own manufacturing process. If the entity does not ensure it pays their suppliers on time, the entity may be charged a higher interest rate on the value of the purchases, reflecting their poor credit rating. This therefore costs the entity more in interest expense. In this example the entity needs to manage its operational risk by ensuring it has the processes in place to ensure it pays its suppliers on time and minimises financial loss due to higher interest rates.

2. Movements in interest rates affecting their borrowings or investments (e.g.

repayment amount, re-financing). If the entity has significant external borrowing facilities, then it will be sensitive to even small changes in interest rates. The extent of sensitivity depends on the amount, type (short or long term) and maturity profile of the borrowings. The extent of impact will depend on the entity’s total exposure to interest rate sensitive assets and debt (e.g. those entities operating in capital intensive industries). This risk also applies to the entity’s ability to meet its borrowing covenants (entity compliance obligations required to continue to hold the borrowings). The entity needs to carefully manage its interest rate risk to ensure it can meet its borrowing obligations and prevent any financial distress.

### 9.2.1.4 Liquidity Risk

The entity’s exposure to liquidity risk depends on the type of assets the entity hold (e.g. assets readily saleable in an active market) and how quickly they can be converted to cash. The quicker the conversion (in time), the more the asset is said to be liquid, while the less quick, the more illiquid they are said to be. Examples of liquid assets are cash, marketable securities, inventory, and accounts receivable.

The entity needs to carefully manage its liquidity risk through its working capital management policy to ensure it does not experience financial distress from a sudden, unplanned lack of liquidity. This ensures it has sufficient cash and other liquid assets to meet its short-term liability obligations (e.g. borrowings and operational expenses) and comply with any applicable banking covenants. Proper management of the entity’s working capital is essential to its good financial health, growth, liquidity and operations. It is also important that the entity does not hold too much cash as this is not the most efficient use of cash (e.g. consider investments).

### 9.2.1.5 Foreign Exchange Risk (Currency Risk)

Entities can be exposed to exchange rate (currency) movements in a variety of direct and indirect ways. The entity may be affected in its transactions, translations, or economically.

Transactional – entities with significant purchases or sales transactions denominated in foreign currency (i.e. a currency other than their functional (home) currency of the entity reporting) are exposed to exchange rate risk in relation to foreign denominated receivables and payables and other cash flows resulting from those transactions. Entities can aim to match their exposures using natural hedges (e.g. by having two offsetting exposures to the same currency) or by using derivatives to change the exposure back into the domestic currency.

Translational – entities with overseas subsidiaries are also exposed to exchange rate risk on translation of the financial statements of their foreign operations for the purposes of consolidation. As exchange rates of foreign operations vary from the functional currency of the parent entity, exchange differences will be recorded on consolidation (directly in a foreign currency translation reserve). These differences may or may not be significant to the parent entity depending on whether the funds in the foreign operation are to be repatriated to the parent entity. Global entities often now exist in various domains and are not necessarily oriented to repatriation beyond dividends. Some entities hedge translation differences, but many do not. Circumstances will be important to risk management in this area.

Economically – the entity may have economic risks related to foreign exchange if its market value is able to be affected by unexpected foreign exchange rate fluctuations. Those fluctuations can affect the value of any of the entity’s foreign investments, foreign assets and the entity through their effect on its customers or suppliers.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Financial risk can come from a wide variety of external and internal factors and needs to be carefully managed if the entity has exposure to such factors.

## 9.2.2 Operational Risk

Operational risks are the likelihood of the entity experiencing upside or downside risk resulting from making changes, or not making changes, to operational processes, procedures, people, or IT systems (e.g. those related to the buying and selling goods/services) resulting in more efficient or detrimental impacts. Operational risks are very broad and the factors that cause it are often inter-related. Operational risks represents one of the most significant types of risk that the entity can face, due to the broad nature of the risk.

The sensitivity of the entity to these types of factors can mean that even if the odds of a certain risk factor occurring are low, the actual benefits or losses suffered, when they do occur, may still be substantial. An example of this is the entity manufactures a product according to a 10-step assembly process at its manufacturing plant and by reviewing the process to see if there are improvements that can be made, the entity identified that it could combine three steps, saving it 20% in costs, without comprising the quality of the product. In this example the entity needs to manage its operational risks to ensure that is has the most efficient processes in place in its manufacturing to ensure costs are minimised and benefits are maximised to the entity.

### 9.2.2.1 Process Risks

Process risks are a sub-component of operational risk reflecting the likelihood of the entity experiencing upside or downside risk resulting from making changes, or not making changes, to operational processes, resulting in more efficient or detrimental impacts. The impacts may be that the process facilitates efficiencies to be made, or fraud, errors and/or omissions to occur without immediate detection.

Some process downside risks examples include:

• Poorly designed manufacturing processes leading to inefficiencies in the use of inputs, quality control issues or poor-quality outputs.
• Lack of access to timely, accurate and relevant information by decision-makers on key decisions.
• Poor internal controls (e.g. inadequate segregation of duties, ineffective review processes and inappropriate approval processes) leading to potential for fraud, loss or error.
• Failure to recruit sufficient employees to ensure that appropriate internal control processes exist in the entity.
• Decision making of key processes is either too concentrated (in a few people) or too delegated (in too many people) to be timely and effective.
• Lacks an appropriate business continuity plan (covering loss of key employees, suppliers and customers).
• Heavy reliance on third party outsourcing for performing key processes (e.g. payroll, IT system maintenance).
• Changes in accounting standards resulting in the need to update systems and processes.
• Poor-quality assurance and compliance process leading to the potential for costly industrial accidents.
• No plans in place to respond to disaster, accidents and man-made incidents.

Process upside risks relates to the opportunities to be more efficient in the use of process than currently being achieved. It can relate to resolving any of the above examples of downside risks.

### 9.2.2.2 People Risks

People risks are the risk that the entity’s employees act or fail to act in such a way that beneficial or adverse impacts the entity. People risks may arise from any level of the entity’s employee with the ability to affect the entity’s financial outcomes.

Some people downside risks examples include:
• Inadequate or poor oversight, management or governance of the entity, or lack of skills, experience and/or integrity demonstrated by the executive leadership team.
• Inadequate, inappropriate or unenforced policies and procedures in place to deal with how employees are permitted to use social media applications during working hours or after hours.
• Remuneration or incentive programmes for key employees reward excessive risk taking or taking no risks.
• ‘Tone at the top’ or conduct of the executive leadership team is inconsistent with the entity’s communicated cultural values.
• Entity does not provide required training for its employees, leading to a poor understanding of how to perform their roles.
• Employee dissatisfaction or turnover is high, leading to failures in following required processes.
• Loss of key employees performing critical processes/tasks who have not been replaced.
• Disclosure related issues such as hiding or covering up errors and losses, misusing confidential or sensitive information (including failure to prevent data loss) and not disclosing required sensitive or regulatory related issues or events to the appropriate entity staff.
• Failure to act to prevent employees’ issues from occurring, such as employee strikes, labour disputes, compensation disputes, illness and injury, discrimination, harassment and bullying.
• Internal fraud related to accounting transactions, credit cards, employee expenses, embezzlement, unauthorised funds transfer and payment, tax fraud and money laundering. This may be either to the benefit of the employee committing the fraud or another party.
• Impact of employees stealing sensitive, private information or unauthorised information.
• Trading errors and misconduct such as insider trading, unauthorised trading, incorrect trading, market manipulation and improper pricing.

As in the case of process risk, upside risk from a process can come from rectifying any of the above examples.

### 9.2.2.3 Technology Risks

Technology risks are the likelihood that the entity experiences upside or downside risks from the entity’s technology (hardware or software) with beneficial or adverse impacts on the entity. Technology risks arise from any use of technology that the entity relies on to operate (e.g. facilitates the delivery of its products or services).

Some technology downside risk examples include:
• Impact of external cybersecurity attacks on its ability to continue operating.
• Lack of investment in ‘back office’ type processes (e.g. corporate governance, risk management, internal controls, internal audit), IT systems to support financial management and governance, and internal controls designed to protect the entity and its assets, leading to internal control weaknesses that remain unaddressed. They may result in:
° Failure of obsolete and redundant hardware. 
° Corruption or loss of data from a failure of software systems. 
° Not applying required system patches to software programs to protect and prevent known system vulnerabilities, or not applying them on a timely basis.
° Not applying required security updates to security software to protect and prevent a cyber-security attack, or not applying them on a timely basis.
° Failure to implement measures to secure required private and sensitive data in the entity’s systems compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
° IT systems failures or instability due to the systems being out of date, unsupported or not integrated.
° Failure to prioritise system management of critical systems the entity relies on to manage its business (e.g. recording sales, purchasing, paying suppliers, receiving cash from customers, foreign currency positions, commodity positions and software enabling electronic approvals).
• Not performing countermeasures to neutralise a known system computer virus or attack.
• Incorrectly configuring a system and generating incorrect transaction flows, from lack of knowledge of those flows or intentional error.
• Experiencing software or hardware issues arising from inadequate testing of new or updated software (e.g. software incompatibilities with other systems/processes and/ or failure).
• Experiencing communication system issues resulting from the failure of the phone system, e-mail or the Internet.
• Lack of a robust, tested, disaster recovery plan to ensure the entity can commence operating again within set timeframes in the event of a cybersecurity attack or critical system(s) failure.

The upside for technology risks comes from the benefits of innovation and mitigating any of the above.

### 9.2.2.4 External Risks

External risks are the likelihood of an external event in the entity’s jurisdiction beneficially or adversely affecting the way in which the entity conducts its operations.

Some examples of downside risk external risks include:
• Trading partners are unreliable or lack good business reputation.
• Effects of climate change on the entity’s ability to access required resources (e.g. water, energy).
• Being unable to source key inputs to the entity’s manufacturing processes.
• Significant competition impacting the entity’s margins and product demands.
• Large reliance/dependency on a few key suppliers or customers.
• Fraud or cyber-security attacks.
• Reputational damage caused by the entity’s products or services (e.g. adverse publicity around court cases to do with the entity’s conduct, the safety of its products or knowledge about potential adverse consequences to users of its products).
• Money laundering by a related party.
• Fraud and misrepresentation by an external party about the entity.
• Adverse weather events due to climate change causing natural disasters (e.g. hurricane, tornado, bushfires, volcanic eruption, earthquake, tsunami, flood, and drought).
• Man-made disasters (e.g. bomb threats, arson, bombings, acts of terrorism and war).

Examples of beneficial external risks include:
• The gaining of access to new markets.
• Exceptional weather in growing seasons.
• Failures of competitors.
• Tax reductions.
• Breakthroughs that enable operations.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Operational risks, like financial risks, can come from a wide variety of external and internal factors and need to be carefully managed if the entity has exposure to such factors.

## 9.2.3 Political Risks
 
Political risks are the likelihood that an entity’s operations (e.g. licenses to operate, investment activities) will be constrained or adversely affected (downside risk), or enabled (upside risk), by the actions, or threat of action, of a government. Political change or instability in a country can impact the ability of an entity to deliver its strategic and corporate objectives within that country. Changes in government (whether democratically or through military intervention and coups), key legislative bodies, foreign policy or foreign actions all have the potential to create political risks. It can also arise if the entity operates in a politically or economically sensitive industry. It can also occur if the government is highly bureaucratic in its decision-making processes and is therefore slow to consider, approve or reject proposals, policies or procedures. The level of government could be local (e.g. council, province, counties), state (region) or federal (national, whole of country), depending on the country. The government could be in the entity’s own jurisdiction or another jurisdiction where the entity trades or plans to trade.

Political change or instability in an individual country or regional part of the world can severely impact the ability of an entity to deliver its strategic and corporate objectives within that country. Resolution of political instability can, on the other hand, bring great opportunity for companies able to move quickly.

Governments generally have the capacity at any time to make a variety of decisions and policy changes and take a variety of actions and all of these can impact individual entities, industries, countries and the overall economy.

Government’s create political risks in different ways. For example, they can make decisions/ actions that impact an entity’s decisions taken to approve/not approve certain domestic projects, they can change laws and regulations (e.g. taxation) impacting the entity’s industry or operations, respond to foreign policy actions of other countries (e.g. trade tariffs, trade embargoes or restrictions on the import of certain products) with counter-measures and make broad economic decisions that impact any entity’s ability to raise capital, obtain borrowings, expand globally and trade with certain countries. Such changes can be based on new or changed political agenda, lobbying pressure received from certain constituents, or in response to worsening or improving economic circumstances (e.g. rising or falling unemployment rates), as well as whether there is an upcoming election cycle. Decisions taken do not have to be on any macro (national) or micro (entity or individual level) economic basis.

Part of political risks are geo-political, which relates to the likelihood of geographical and economics factors influencing politics and countries trade relationships. Geopolitical risks are complex, fluid and interrelated. Each part of the risk needs to be considered holistically in the context of other risks and the wider political landscape. Uncertainty in the political environment of a country (e.g. due to a minority government, military rule, collapsing economic conditions) can significantly impact the viability of planned or actual investments, or the profitability of continuing or expanding operations in that country. In some cases, the occurrence of significant man-made disasters (e.g. war, terrorism, insurrections, riots, civil war) or natural disasters that have a catastrophic impact on a country may precede that country’s government taking control of a private asset or an entire industry. Additionally, the government may introduce laws that effectively nationalise significant portions of the economy/industry back into government control, leaving private entities uncompensated for their loss of assets and/or unable to operate at all. Such an event would significantly impact the ongoing profitability of affected entities and likely reduce the value of their investments in such countries to nil.

This can all create the potential for significant uncertainty and risk to the entity’s operations that would be difficult for any individual entity to successfully manage. This is increasingly so given the globalisation of trade. Globalisation creates significant levels of complexity and uncertainty when assessing political risk, given the disconnect between an individual country government and the entities trading in more than one country (global entities). This exposes such entities to having to deal with the political decisions of many different governments, hence adding to the level of complexity involved in assessing political risk exposures for global entities.

Political risks are more prevalent in emerging economic nations (with severe gross trading deficits), those under military control or those with severe structural economic issues (e.g. hyperinflation, deflation, negative or very high interest rates or high unemployment).

Diversification of where the entity operates can help reduce political risks, but that depends entirely on whether the entity’s products or services can be diversified (industries that may struggle with that are commodities where natural resources and crops are only found/grow in certain areas).
