Political risks can impact the value of its assets, the ability of the entity to remit funds overseas, investments, debt or the entity’s actual valuation, and its ability to continue to operate in its current form, or at all.

Political risks have the potential to directly or indirectly impact all the other risks mentioned in this section – financial, operational legal and business risks due to their pervasive effect on an entity’s operations.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Political risks are pervasive and has the potential to affect the way in which the entity operates, if it can operate at all. The entity needs to carefully manage these risks.

## 9.2.4 Legal Risks

Legal risks refer to the likelihood of the entity taking advantage of its compliance with required laws, regulations, rules and contracts or from suffering damage of loss as a result of its intentional or unintentional negligence in compliance with required laws, regulations, rules and enforceable contracts/agreements. Legislative requirements and changes therein can have a considerable impact on an entity and its ability to deliver on its strategic objective. Being a good corporate citizen and following due legal process for its applications, in demonstrating compliance with requirements in all markets in which it operates, can give entity public credibility and speed up the timely resolution of legal issues and rapidly adapting to legislative changes can give it competitive advantages if its competitors are slower to react. Alternately, failure to comply with the relevant legislation in the various markets in which an entity operates can give risk to significant levels of reputational damage and legal action that can pose a significant level of risk and potential loss to an entity, either through decreased revenues on the back of a reduction in sales, penalties imposed by a government or removal of an entity’s ability to transact and operate in a particular market. Failure to adapt to legislative change can also present a significant level of risk to an entity.

Laws and regulations can affect almost every aspect of the entity’s operations and governance and can depend on the type of entity (legal structure). Non-compliance may affect the way in which the entity operates, its key supplier and customer relationships, its business and governance reporting processes and the safety of its products or services. The costs of changing current entity practices to ensure compliance may be high, as may be the enforcement of fines and penalties the entity is required to pay. However, as noted above, changing practices may also offer the entity a competitive advantage if it adapts more quickly than its competitors and enhances the entity’s reputation. Non-compliance can cause the entity to suffer significant reputational damage if their non-compliance is made public.

As with other risks discussed above, legal risks can also present opportunities. Well-informed entities may be able to qualify more quickly for licences to operate, enter into new contracts and to scale up to meet customer demand.

Legal risks can occur at any stage of business operations and includes such sub-risks as regulatory risk, contractual risk and dispute risk.

### 9.2.4.1 Regulatory Risks

Regulatory risks refer to the likelihood of the entity being advantaged or suffering damage of loss as a result of changes in the government’s laws or regulations. Laws and regulations represent a set of rules, responsibilities and obligations that the entity must comply with and can depend on the legal structure of the entity. Any entity that operates in a country where laws and regulations can change, or do change regularly, is exposed to both upside and downside regulatory risks. Laws and regulations may have economy-wide implications (i.e. applies to all entities), be specific to an industry (e.g. energy) or even an individual entity. Increased globalisation of business has resulted in a vast proliferation of global laws, regulations and rules, as well as country specific equivalents, resulting in entities requiring appropriate risk frameworks to ensure they are aware of applicable laws and regulations they must comply with, when those laws change, and be able to comply with the requirements. This has increased the compliance cost of doing business, the degree of sophistication required by entities to trade globally and the risk of non-compliance with all laws and regulations. An entity can be incentivised to minimise their compliance costs by implementing efficient processes to capture required information that it must report to or have available to report to the appropriate authorities.

Common examples of laws and regulations affecting an entity include those covering stock exchange listed entities, information security and privacy, financial reporting, taxation, governance, competition, environmental, employment, workplace health and safety, regulating prices to be charged for certain products or services, contracts related to purchase or sales of goods and services, and financing agreements.

Whilst not government regulation, some industries have also developed best practice codes of conduct (optional regulation) that specify the way in which entities in a particular industry need to conduct themselves in order to receive recognised accreditation/certification for their products or services. Additionally, some government entities require particular accreditations/ certifications in order for private sector entities to trade with them. If the entity is accredited, then they also have the risk that changes to the accreditation requirements may adversely affect the cost of the way in which the entity operates. If the entity fails to comply with accreditation, then they may experience financial penalties, removal of their accreditation and reputational damage should the non-compliance be made public.

The entity has to continuously monitor its regulatory environment for any changes made to laws or regulations that require the entity to change the way in which it conducts its affairs, including if any of these changes have advantages to the entity. The entity needs to be able to assess if the change is beneficial or more costly in nature. Regardless, if the entity does not comply when required, it may be faced with a series of penalties or a revocation of its ability to operate.

Examples of regulatory risks include:
• New law comes into effect allowing the entity to capitalise more of the cost of its investment.
• Lack of investment in a data inventory system to identify and manage private and sensitive data the entity holds that it has obtained from stakeholders (e.g. customers, suppliers) or that it has generated itself (e.g. through research and development) in order to comply with data governance laws.
• Not monitoring required compliance with applicable laws and regulation in all its markets (e.g. overseas subsidiaries with different regulatory requirements and business customs). Upside risk is monitoring the compliance and demonstrating its ‘good corporate citizen’ reputation for respecting laws and regulations.

• Individual business units’ attitude towards compliance with laws, regulations or contractual terms are not consistent with the entity’s communicated cultural values, leading to possible non-compliance with the laws, regulations or contractual terms. Upside risk is that the entity encourages and enforces individual business units to comply and acknowledges and rewards its employees.

### 9.2.4.2 Contractual Risks

Contractual risks refer to the likelihood of the entity being advantaged or suffering damage or loss as a result of contracts or agreements it holds with third parties. This may be as a result of changes proposed to the contract’s obligations or conditions, the inclusion of incentive clauses or onerous clauses, improved or poor drafting of the contract (e.g. including or lacking an appropriate safeguard for both parties) or an in-built reward to meeting its obligations under the contract or an actual or expected failure of the entity, or other party, to meet its obligations under the contract. Most entities have contracts and hence this risk is common. If one party fails to honour the contract terms, attempting to enforce the terms through legal proceedings can be expensive and time consuming, with no guarantee of success.

Examples of contractual risks include:

• Building in rewards to the entity for early delivery of required goods or services (e.g. volume discounts).
• Not having all the appropriate terms and conditions included in contracts signed on the entity’s behalf to protect the entity from loss or damage (including reputational damage). An upside risk to this is including such terms and conditions, protecting the entity from loss.
• Commercial or contractual disputes affecting key suppliers or contractors, or the ability to fulfil customer orders, leading to the inability to provide required goods/services on time. An upside risk to this is including agreed dispute resolution procedures in the contract to minimise business disruptions caused by disputes.

### 9.2.4.3 Dispute Risks

Dispute risks refer to the likelihood of the entity being advantaged or suffering damage or loss as a result of legal action by third parties for enforcement or infringement of intangible rights (e.g. copyrights, patents, trade names, franchises or trademarks) or tort claims (e.g. negligence, product liability and misrepresentation). These risks can result even if the entity does not have a contract or agreement with another entity. After mediation, the legal remedy to such disputes is a civil action and the entity can have a judgement entered against it, with financial damages awarded.

Examples of dispute related risks include:
• Suing or being sued for breach of intellectual property laws.
• Demonstration of, or failure of, a duty of care to its employees, customers, suppliers or other stakeholders.
• Maintaining the entity’s reputation when dealing with product or service issues or suffering reputational damage from failure to deal with known issues with their products or services that become public knowledge.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Legal risks also come from a wide variety of external and internal factors and need to be carefully managed by the entity to minimise the risks of loss or damage.

## 9.2.5 Business Risks

Business risks affects entities in different ways, depending on their legal structure/form. Business risks can result from any of the risks noted above in Sections 9.2.1 to 9.2.4 inclusive and may be inter-related.

For example, entities that are corporates (e.g. companies) and are for-profit pursue their strategic direction and objectives to generate a financial profit and maximise their shareholders’ value (i.e. provide adequate returns and achieve a share price that reflects the entities’ future value). Business risks directly impact the entity’s ability to achieve these objectives.

Business risks are influenced by several factors, including:
• The appeal of the entity’s products and services.
• The quality and alignment of the executive leadership team.
• The quality of decision making.
• The quality, timeliness and accuracy of information supporting key business decisions.
• The skills and capabilities of key entity employees.
• Consumer preferences, demand and sales volumes.
• The ability to change the product per-unit price and input costs.
• The level of industry competition.
• Labour conditions – availability or otherwise, remuneration levels and demands.
• The overall economic climate(s) in which the entity operates.
• The extent of government laws and regulations.
• The impact the investment has on the environment and social relationships of the location in which it is based.

The extent to which these factors are relevant to the entity will depend on the nature and type of the investment and the entity’s strategic objectives.

Examples of business risks not already discussed in prior sections are:
• Reputational (enhancement or damage to the entity’s image) caused by how the entity responds to, or does not respond to, an issue.
• Commitment to innovation (the embedding, or lack of, the entity’s products or service meeting customer demands).
• Good or poor programmes or projects management on key projects (the ability of the entity to deliver activities of high quality, on time and budget).
• High- or low-quality control on its products or services (the quality of the entity’s products or services).
• Strategy (the entity having the correct or incorrect strategy and being able to, or unable to, execute those strategies as intended).
• Having appropriate or inappropriate resources (e.g. people, technology, funds and infrastructure to operate).
• Taking advantage of or ignoring seasonal factors (e.g. the extent to which the entity is subject to seasonal weather or factors in its operations).
• Responding to, or ignoring, employee industrial action.
• Appropriate or inappropriate business model used (e.g. heavy/low reliance on low margin, high/low turnover products or a single/multiple product line(s) required for the entity’s profitability).
• Entity’s legal or business structure is compatible/incompatible with the entity’s objectives or nature of business.
• Existence of, or lack of, management plans in place to guard against a natural or man-made disaster contingency response plan, health and safety plan for employee incidents.
• Being sustainable. That is, does it allow the entity to deliver product and services-based outputs to meet people’s present needs while not disadvantaging the ability of people to meet their future needs?
• Being environmentally responsible:
° Delivering environmentally friendly benefits (e.g. energy and water efficient) that also save money.
° Designed to be ‘renewable’ in terms of how it uses the inputs it requires. For example, a factor designed to operate on a carbon-neutral basis.
° Will not significantly deplete already finite natural resources (e.g. water, minerals, energy, air quality).
° Designed in such a way that considers that the investment is located in an environmentally sensitive location (e.g. an area with known significant biodiversity).
° It will contribute to improving the natural environment (e.g. agricultural lands surrounding the project, air, water, land, minerals, forests, biodiversity and ecosystem health) rather than damage it by adversely impacting that environment.
° Will not result in high quantities of carbon dioxide and other toxic gases being emitted by its facilities.
° Able to quantify the expected cost of pollution of the investment (e.g. cost of removing/recycling any expected e-waste and values of any greenhouse gas emissions).
° Able to offset the expected cost of pollution with replacing or mitigating the loss of such resources (e.g. planting trees to improve air quality, recycling water, using solar energy, wind energy or hydroelectricity).
° If not already legally required to, the entity will voluntary commit to incur costs to rehabilitate/restore the investment’s location at the end of its economic life.
• Being socially responsible:
° Will the entity have a ‘social license’ to operate and be supported by the local community in which it is located? This could be assisted by the following: the investment will help the local community in which it is being constructed or operated in terms of employment, will provide improved employee health and well-being, community, quality and way of life, and it will offer training and skills.
° Likely to be/unlikely to be supported by the entity’s key stakeholders (e.g. institutional investors, financiers, customers and suppliers).

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Business risks can come from a wide variety of external and internal factors and needs to be carefully managed if the entity has exposure to such factors.

### Apply and Analyse 2

List and describe the key risks you think Audio Plus has in considering diversifying its existing product offerings.

Analysis

Audio Plus may have exposure to each of the key risks discussed in the above section financial, operational, political risk, legal risk and business risks.

• Financial risks – Upside aspects include that Audio Plus will have to invest capital to produce any new products. Depending on its financing, the investment it could have exposure to are capital, interest rate and liquidity risk. Downside aspects include that it may have to borrow capital required at higher interest rates than their current borrowings due to interest rate increases.

• Operational risks – Upside aspects include that Audio Plus has existing processes in place to rapidly scale-up for the new product offerings, meaning the costs of the implementation will be less and Audio Plus may achieve economies of scale through the expansion. Downside aspects include if Audio Plus does not implement appropriate processes (e.g. in relation to IT controls, training people) for operationalising the new products, it risks loss. It also cannot be certain of what competitors will do, and how this may impact their product offerings in terms of gross margin.

• Political risks – Upside aspects include that it already operates manufacturing plants in China and is familiar with the political environment, it knows the Chinese market for sales and some of the markets it wants to sell into (European Union and the United States) are relatively stable as they are not emerging economies. Downside risks are that as Audio Plus want to sell the products overseas it remains exposed to political risk in each country in which it sells them.

• Legal risks – Upside aspects include that it is already familiar with the applicable laws and regulations from manufacturing its current products and these are unlikely to be different for the proposed new product lines given they are still audio products. Downside aspects are that Audio Plus should still consider the impact of any applicable laws and regulations on the proposed product offerings.

• Business risks – Upside aspects are that they are expanding into an area they are already familiar with, and have expertise in, so the risks of manufacturing poor quality, low technology products are reduced. They have also done research to ensure that there is a market for the new offerings and consider, based on current experience, that they could earn reasonable returns on the offerings. Downside aspects are that Audio Plus is exposed to the uncertainty of not knowing if they will earn a profit on the product offerings and this could be due to external factors (e.g. competitor’s price matching or reducing prices, consumer demand, etc).

A Avoid the risk.

# 9.3 EVALUATING INVESTMENT PROJECTS

This section will cover how we should consider how risk presents potential opportunities and threats to an entity when it is considering making a significant investment in a project designed to create value.

Investment projects in this section are assumed to be long term in nature and not to be situations in which the investor controls the investee. Additionally, the investment project is assumed to be the entity making an investment in their own capital project, rather than a capital investment in another entity.

Deciding about whether to invest in a new project can be one of the most strategically rewarding and expensive decisions the entity may make. The entity may commit significant funds to an investment project in the hope that the return on these funds will result in incremental net cash inflows and consequently justify the entity’s investment. The desired outcome for most investment projects is to identify the one that is the most profitable, with the least risk or uncertainty.

Entities decide if they should invest in an investment project by performing a financial evaluation of the investment based on its financial risks and non-financial risks to determine its expected rate of return.

• Financial risk-based return – the quantitative return calculated for the financing risks aspects of the investment. This is calculated by using a forecasting model and having a dollar amount. Such returns are related to the entity’s financing risk of the investment and include, but are not limited to, the elements discussed in Section 9.2.1. These returns will ordinarily be easy to quantify as a dollar amount, although it is recognised that some elements will be difficult to quantify.

• Non-financial risk-based returns – the quantitative and/or qualitative returns calculated for all the non-financing risk aspects of the investment. These can be inputted into the forecasting model if quantifiable. Such returns are related to the entity’s operational, political, legal and business-related risks related to the investment, as discussed in Sections 9.2.2 to 9.2.5 inclusive. These returns should, as much as practical, be given a dollar amount, although it is recognised that some of these risks will be difficult to quantify and may be only qualitatively described (e.g. according to their nature).

Quantitative returns refer to those returns that can be expressed in dollar terms. Qualitative returns refer to those returns that cannot be expressed in dollar terms.

Such an evaluation is dependent on the entity making certain assumptions about the investment in terms of what it will cost the entity and what the returns will be, and its expected economic life. Together these considerations give the ‘value’ of the investment project to the entity.

Alignment with the entity’s strategic objectives requires that the entity only choose those investments that align to its pursuit of the strategic objectives. Non-aligned, incompatible, investments would be rejected regardless of the investment return offered. Strategic-based questions to ask regarding the investment include:

• Is the investment consistent with the entity’s reputation, brand and image? Will these be enhanced by the investment?

• If required by the entity, is the investment ‘ethical’ in terms of its social responsibility (e.g. individual and collective well-being) and/or environmental impacts (e.g. sustainable, carbon-neutral) in the location it will be located? Note that such ethical-based strategic objectives may not necessarily achieve value maximisation for the entity in purely financial terms.

• Will it be consistent with the types of products and services it already produces?

Entities are focused on creating and maximising the value of the investment project in meeting the entity’s strategic objectives through generating increased sustainable profits for its shareholders. It is critical to be able to consistently value different investment projects and to align them with the entity’s strategic objectives. It is up to the investor entity to determine what will create value – purely financial risk returns that maximise the entity’s value or a mix of financial risk and non-financial risk returns that may not maximise the entity’s value to the same extent. So, how to determine value?

Value depends on the type of investment being made.

• If the investment is a non-controlling share purchase in another entity, the entity as the investor’s assessment of the worth of that investment will take in the investee entity’s market value (the entity’s current share price times the total number of outstanding shares) and adjust for any insights the investor may have on the project that they do not consider already reflected in the market value. The current share price reflects market expectations on the investee’s current and future value and their reported earnings/profitability provides a ready proxy for measuring any likely variability in value. The insights that an investor considers may be their own interpretation of financial results and non-financial factors and considerations to ascertain and quantify any risks that may affect the investee’s future value.

• If the investment is an individual project within the entity, then the value will be assessed and determined in terms of its calculated forecast return on investment (i.e. expected aggregate net incremental cash flows) using a forecast model as against the entity required rate of return.

The drivers of success for the investee entity are based on the risks from which it seeks to make an appropriate return. If the investment has no risk, then theoretically it would be a risk-free investment and it would have a low return. Entities are rewarded for the amount of risk that they take on in the investment. Ordinarily investments have risks and therefore it is up to the entity to assign an appropriate value measure for what the level of risk should require in terms of a return on their investment. As noted already, the higher the risk, the higher the return required, and the lower the risk, the lower the return. Additionally, other risks may come from the relationship between the investee and investor if their objectives are not mutually compatible. For example, the investee entity may be concerned with growth and the investor entity might be seeking yield (return). Further, investor entities are likely to have imperfect information about the investee entities’ risks and decision-making. They will be uncertain when measuring those risks and may well need to make significant assumptions about key financial matters.

What creates risk in an investment project? Risk is created as the investment project evaluation relies on estimates in determining the future values of key project variables variables that include but are not limited to: what is its economic life, what will be the cost of the investment and what should be included in the cost, what are the incremental ongoing costs, what incremental cash flows will it generate from the investment and what are the other advantages and disadvantages to the investment? How likely/probable are these to occur? Virtually certain? Probable only if certain other assumptions are made? Is there a single estimate or a range of estimates possible for these variables?

## 9.3.1 Key Considerations in Evaluating Investment Projects

Entities attempt to quantify the impact of risk in preparing detailed investment evaluations, essentially forecasts. These evaluations scrutinise its expected outcomes and approve those projects that meet its required investment metrics and:
• Considers whether it meets the entity’s required rate of return by calculating all the financial risk-based returns and non-financial risk-based returns (collectively referred to as the ‘expected returns’).
• Considers how probable the expected returns are in being achieved.
• Considers and evaluate all alternative scenarios to making the investment.
• Demonstrates good governance in the evaluation process.

We will review investment project evaluations performed below using common types of evaluation methodology. We will also discuss how entities factor in and consider the probability of differing project variables using sensitivity analysis and scenario analysis.

Examples of common investments projects undertaken by entities are:
• Building a new manufacturing plant to produce different types of consumer products.
• Extending an existing manufacturing plant to increase output to meet customer demands or fulfil existing contractual supply obligations.
• Repurposing/refitting an existing manufacturing plant to change its product lines.
• Renovating an existing manufacturing plant to equip it with upgraded technology or to accommodate increased capacity.
• Purchasing a warehouse facility to store products.
• Purchasing new equipment, machinery or technology to improve outputs and/or profitability.
• Investing in research and development of potential new products.

All of the above involve risks being taken so as to achieve the entity’s strategic objectives. The outcomes of taking those risks will create some uncertain variability in those outcomes that need to be monitored. If those outcomes impact the strategic objectives, the entity’s investment decision-making outcome may need to change. Decision-making is an iterative process that is based on reducing the imperfections in information used and reassessing options as information comes to hand. There are different methodologies that can be used to evaluate an investment project, depending on the range of expected returns possible for the project.

### 9.3.1.1 Key Financial Risk Return Considerations

As noted above, financial risk returns are quantitative (expressed in dollar terms) and are calculated by using a forecasting model.

Key financial-based considerations in evaluating an investment project are to earn a rate of return commensurate with the project’s risk, and to have that risk fall within the entity’s risk appetite, seek to quantify potential financial risks and possible financial returns. Considerations include (but are not limited to):

• What is the entity’s required rate of return on the investment?
° Is the project riskier or less risky than the entity’s current portfolio of investments? Does it enhance or reduce the entity’s diversification of its investment portfolio for that class of asset?
° Is the residual risk of the investment project acceptable (i.e. does it fall within the entity’s risk appetite)?
° What is the project re-investment rate (i.e. the rate of return that the entity could alternatively earn by investing in another project)?

• How will the entity finance the project (e.g. cash reserves, equity or debt)?

• Will it be exposed to any equity, loan capital and trade credit risks (credit, market and operational), commodity, interest rate, liquidity or foreign exchange risks arising from how it proposes to finance the project? Refer to Section 9.3.1 for more details on the types of considerations to make.

• What are the possible alternatives to the investment? What are their investment returns and how do they compare to the investment project (e.g. could the entity outsource production to a sub-contractor, perform equipment maintenance or choose not to invest)?

• Is the investment able to be readily expanded in the future and save the entity money (e.g. through the entity not having to construct a totally new plant to increase output)?

• Will the investment create economics of scale with existing operations (e.g. by rationalising existing trading locations into one location or saving costs through being able to negotiate purchase contracts at higher volumes, thereby obtaining better purchase discounts for the plant and its other locations)?

• Is the investment return greater than the required rate of return?
° Is the investment return achievable given the entity’s knowledge of the type and nature of the investment?
° If there is a range of returns possible, is the lowest likely return still acceptable? 

• Are all assumptions and estimates included in the forecast model? Examples of assumptions are incremental cash inflows and outflows (based on expected increases in sales and cost of sales and operating costs), the economic life of the investment and the cost of the initial investment.
- Do they have a reasonable basis of preparation? That is, are they based on detailed research (e.g. coming from past experience from similar investments, current contract values) and consider current economic and prospective economic conditions or is it simply a ‘best guess’ based on prior years? Is the quality and reliability of the estimates reasonable? How accurate has the entity been in the past to reliably estimate the key assumptions?
- Are the assumptions and estimates able to be independently tested or reviewed?
- Is the expected economic life reasonable given the nature of the investment project? Is the timeframe to deliver the investment return too long? For example, technology related investments may have a relatively short useful life. The longer the project will take the greater the risk that the estimates involving revenue (sales), cost (to produce) and resultant cash flows and profitability may be unrealistic.
- If the investment will require related significant technological upgrades or purchases to integrate to existing systems, are these priced into the initial costs?
- Does it include any post economic life considerations of the investment (e.g. the entity may be required by law to rehabilitate the site and/or be able to remove and relocate key components/machinery)?
- Have any eligible tax concessions offered by the country in which the investment is located been factored into the cost?

• How much of the entity’s capital funds will the investment require? The higher the cost of the investment, the higher the risk that the entity could make an incorrect investment decision that impacts on the entity’s existing value and its financial sustainability in the future. This can be managed by ensuring that the entity performs an investment evaluation using a forecasting model and ensures that the investment return, commensurate with its risk, is possible.


### 9.3.1.2 Key Non-Financial Risk Return Considerations

As noted above, non-financial risk returns are calculated for operational, political, legal and business-related risks and may be quantitative (expressed in dollar terms) and qualitative (not expressed in dollar terms) in nature.

Examples of such risks include:

• Operational:
- Have entity current processes been put in place that can readily be deployed to the investment to save on set-up costs and ongoing costs? If the investment will cause disruption to existing manufacturing plants, does the entity have plans to minimise the disruption and associated costs?
- Has the entity appropriate people to monitor the investment? If applicable, will the entity be able to employ sufficient people (with the appropriate skills and capabilities) at the proposed investment location?
- Has the entity the required technology platform (software and hardware) to facilitate/deliver the investment?
- Is the investment exposed to external events/factors that are beneficial or detrimental to earning the required rate of return?

Refer to Section 9.2.2 for more detail.

• Political:
- How stable politically, socially and economically is the country/location in which the investment is located? Is the investment subject to regular government policy change?
- Does the entity have established business and government relationships in the country/location?
- Is the investment dependent on using existing sales and distribution channels for the products? Are they local or international? Is there any political risk associated with being able to continue to access those channels?

Refer to Section 9.2.3 for more detail.

• Legal:
- Is the investment in a country/location that is subject to significant regulatory oversight and laws and regulations? Can the entity meet the requirements? Are the costs too high?
- How likely is significant change to those laws/regulations?
- Can the costs of the initial and ongoing compliance be factored into the cost of the investment?

Refer to Section 9.2.4 for more detail.

• Business:
- Is the investment in a sustainable industry, with growth forecasts and continuity of inputs supply from its suppliers and ongoing customer demand? How much real demand from customers is there for this type of investment? Is it a current social trend or expected to be in demand over the life of the expected investment?
- Is the investment consistent with what the entity already does? Is it aligned to the entity’s corporate culture and values?
- Does the investment evaluation policy/process allow for possible bias in its preparation?
- Does the entity have strong experience in delivering the project? This will lower the riskiness of the entity undertaking the investment project as compared to a project that the entity has little or no experience in undertaking.
- Does it allow the entity to diversify away from core operating areas that are no longer profitable or protect its current investments or intellectual property against competition? Will the investment prevent a competitor from accessing that location, its market, and therefore preserve or improve the entity’s margins on existing products?
- Can the entity ensure the quality of any products/services delivered by the investment?
- • Will the entity be able to earn profits on other investments as a result of the proposed investment (e.g. through synergies of use of resources or use of the investment as a base on which to build other investment profits)?
- • Will key internal and external stakeholders support the investment (e.g. will it improve the entity’s relationships with key customers or suppliers (including employees) through the entity demonstrating its commitment to invest in that project type?)
- • Does the entity have the necessary intellectual property rights, technical, resource capabilities and skills to support the investment?

Refer to Section 9.2.5 for more detail.

The relative importance of the above risks is particular to the entity and the nature and type of investment project being considered and require considerable professional judgement on the part of the relevant entity employees performing the evaluation in ranking them according to their importance, or risk impact, to the investment evaluation. Also important is the sufficiency and appropriateness of the entity’s documented policies, procedures and guidance for performing investment evaluations. The entity can use different approaches in determining the importance of the risks, such as the principles in the risk assessment matrix discussed in Section 9.1, Fundamentals of Risk Management, in assessing the probability of occurrence and consequence of the risk.

### 9.3.1.3 Evaluating Investment Projects Using Financial Models

There are a number of assumptions the entity makes that are included in financial evaluation models. These are discussed below.

#### Calculating the Entity’s Required Rate of Return

The entity’s required rate of return (RRR) is the minimum return the entity will accept for a potential investment that compensates them for a given level of risk. This return, also known as the hurdle rate, adds to the entity’s value.

The entity determines this to be able to consistently assess different potential investment projects and to ensure it is optimising the use of its capital structure. Establishing the optimal capital structure for the entity will result in the minimisation of the cost of capital and in turn optimise the value of the entity. The rate of return can be equated to the entity’s own rate of return or a project rate of return.

• Entity required rate of return – This is the rate of return the entity requires to receive on its investments, reflective of the risk taken on, and is based on their total risk profile. It may equate to their weighted average cost of capital (WACC). The entity’s WACC is the return required to reflect the risk of the entity, as determined by its shareholders and financiers when investing in the entity. The WACC is an average; it comes from the perspective of external parties (meaning that it is not conditioned by private information available to the entity) and it is not usually a true measure of the risk of an individual investment by the entity. As indicated, it is important to note that the calculated cost of capital is only an appropriate proxy for the entity’s cost of capital if the investment project has a similar ‘risk profile’ as the entity’s existing investments (same level of risk). That is, the project is no riskier or less risky than the entity’s prior investments made (and reflected in the entity’s cost of capital). Nevertheless, it is often a benchmark from which the entity can determine a required rate of return for projects.

To calculate the WACC the entity needs to know:
- What is the entity’s own cost of equity? That is the rate of return needed to be earned to satisfy its shareholders. The entity’s cost of equity is necessary to factor into the cost of capital as it is one of the sources of funds for its investment projects. It generally has a higher cost than debt, as the entity’s shareholders generally expect a higher rate of return as they bear a higher risk than debt holders if the entity goes into liquidation. The way in which the entity calculates that equity rate of return is based on one of two mathematical models – the dividend valuation model (DVM) or the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). Refer to Chapter 7 on how to calculate the cost and value of equity using one of these models.
- What is the entity’s own cost of debt? That is the cost of its long-term interest-bearing external borrowings. The entity’s cost of debt is necessary to factor into the cost of capital as it is the other source of funds used for investment projects. Most entities have multiple sources of borrowings and are short (less than one year) and long term (greater than one year) in maturity. Given that the typical investment project is long term, the borrowings used for the cost of debt calculations are only interest-bearing long-term borrowings, valued at their market value. Market value is the total value of the outstanding principle and interest, discounted at the current cost of purchasing the debt at that level. The entity’s weighted average cost of all their long-term borrowing facilities becomes their cost of debt. This is then tax adjusted to give the after-tax cost of debt. Refer to Section 1 of Chapter 7 for more details on how to calculate the cost of debt.

Together the entity’s cost of equity and cost of debt are weighted to become its after-tax cost of capital. This is the proxy for the entity’s required rate of return. Refer to Section 4 of Chapter 7 for more details on how to calculate the WACC.

• What is the impact of taxation on the project? Examples of taxation impacts could be through income tax payable on the project’s investment returns, tax incentives related to any payments for research and development related to the project and capital depreciation, intangible amortisation deductions and capital works deductions (e.g. constructing buildings, extensions and improvements).

• Whether the entity wants a pre-tax or post-tax (takes the entity’s effective tax rate) included in the rate of return. This depends on the entity’s tax position.

• Project required rate of return – This is the rate of return the entity requires for an individual project given its risk profile. This is used if this investment risk profile is different from the entity’s required rate of return (above) due to the project being riskier or less risky than the entity’s overall investment portfolio. If the project return is the same as the entity’s return, it may equate to the entity’s WACC. If it is different, the entity may adjust the WACC accordingly or derive the rate of return differently (e.g. base it on the likely cost of debt to be used to fund the project).

#### Individual Investment Project Considerations

The entity also needs to obtain other information regarding the investment project. For example,

• When will the investment occur?

• How much is the initial investment and how much, if any, is the ongoing planned investment?

• What is the investment project’s (useful) economic life? That is, how many years will it operate for the investment’s intended purpose. Is there any residual value in the investment at the end of its economic life?

• What is the expected timing and amount of cash inflows and cash outflows expected to be earned over the useful life of the investment? Do they include the entity’s risk assessment about how likely they are to be earned and in what period?

• What is the entity’s expected discount rate to be applied to those cash flows to determine their present value? Is that discount rate inclusive (risk premium) or exclusive (risk-free) of risk? Is it a real discount rate (adjusted to remove the effects of inflation) or a nominal discount rate (a discount rate before taking inflation into account)? The difference in the rates will depend on the entity’s expectation of the movement in the official inflation rate over the project’s economic life.

• What is the expected economic inflation rate in the country in which the cash inflows and outflows are being earned over the life of the investment? Inflation represents the loss of purchasing power of cash. If the inflation rate is high, the entity will need to earn a higher rate of return to take account of inflation’s effective discounting of the real value of cash. If the inflation rate is low, the entity will not need to earn as much return. If inflation is rampant or its movement is unstable, it may be prudent for any entity not to adjust for inflation in its cash inflows and outflows.

#### Mutually Exclusive Investment Project Considerations

If the entity has a range of like projects (i.e. projects that achieve the same objectives) it can invest in, but will select only one for actual investment, such that acceptance of one project adversely affects the cash flows of the other project, this is referred to as a mutually exclusive investment project analysis (i.e. where all potential projects are competing against each other). Conversely, if investment projects are independent, then the cash flows of one project are not affected by the acceptance of the other investment project.

The entity, in addition to obtaining individual project information regarding the investment project, should consider/obtain additional information regarding the various investment options. For example,

• Are the various investments comparable, for example in terms of initial investment, ongoing planned investment, useful economic life, cash flows/cash outflows, same discount rate and basis, expected/required rate of return and same investment evaluation methodology used?

• Is the same investment evaluation methodology being used to evaluate the different investment projects? It is preferable that the same evaluation methodology be used to assess all competing investment projects. For example, it may be that the entity decides to use the NPV evaluation methodology to accept an investment project if its net present value (NPV) is NPV positive and reject it if the NPV is negative, or to use the internal rate of return (IRR) evaluation methodology to accept an investment project if its IRR is equal or greater than the required rate of return and reject it if the IRR is less than the required rate of return.

If different investment methodologies are used between the various investment project options (e.g. NPV and IRR – see below for more detail), then the entity needs to ensure that the expected returns of all the respective investment project options are comparable.

Now, having obtained that information, it is time to consider how to prepare the investment project evaluation.

We will now describe each of the evaluation methodologies when forecasting under certainty and re-calculate their expected rates of return using the details in Illustrative Example 1. We will then add in variability of the expected rates of return to demonstrate the impact of uncertainty of key financial risk considerations on the evaluation.

We will use the following illustrative example information to demonstrate the different evaluation methodologies that can be applied to an investment project.

#### Illustrative Example 1

The Audio Plus HK Entity Limited executive leadership team, comprising the Chief Operating Officer (who is also the Chief Risk Officer), Chief Financial Officer, Chief Marketing Officer and Chief Product Technology Officer, is considering its strategic options for product offerings into which Audio Plus could expand that offer synergies with their existing audio products, causing minimal disruption to their existing operations and offering minimal risk and maximum potential financial returns.

Any new product offerings would need to meet or exceed the established investment evaluation criteria for evaluating any new investments. The executive leadership team have been meeting with key local and overseas customers and suppliers and conducting targeted market research to understand what the possible product offerings should be. Some new product offerings that have been suggested are TV sound bars, AV receivers and home theatre surround stereo systems. Audio Plus is yet to review these suggestions in detail.

As Audio Plus has been very profitable to date, the executive team proposes funding the product expansion through a mix of equity and debt financing. The required rate of return for any new product would have to be around 30% minimum as Audio Plus has been able to achieve an average of 25% on its existing audio speaker range. Audio Plus’s cost of debt is 10% and its project re-investment rate is 12%. The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is 25%. However, it would be seeking a slightly higher return of 27%, reflecting the executive team’s assessment of the slightly higher risk of diversifying the product offerings.

Audio Plus is also considering building a new manufacturing plant in Guodong province to meet increased customer demand for its latest audio product line, the ‘Hello!’ smart speaker range. This is in addition to its product diversification plans. Based on the plant specifications and the land purchase price, it will cost HK$1,000,000 to build and take one year to construct. Output in year one post construction is expected to be increased by 20%.

Based on current sales and profitability for the speaker range, the expected net cash inflows (i.e. net of cash outflows of HK$200,000 from increased cost from running the plant) will be around HK$450,000 in the first year and then HK$500,000 per year for the following four years (assume the cash flows are earned evenly throughout the year). Audio Plus has estimated the probability of receiving the cash flows in all years from the sale of the Hello! Speakers based on their past experience. Total cash flows for the five years are HK$2.45 million (i.e. HK$450,000 + (HK$500,000 × 4)).

If customer demand for the speakers is high, there is a 20% chance of receiving cash flows equating to HK$490,000 (i.e. HK$2.45 million × 20%). If customer demand is average, there is a 50% chance of receiving cash flows of HK$1.225 million (i.e. HK$2.45 million × 50%). If demand is low, there is a 30% chance of receiving cash flows of HK$735,000

(i.e. HK$2.45 million × 30%).

Audio Plus expects to earn a profit of HK$250,000 in year one, increasing by 10% per year thereafter after tax (through increased plant efficiencies). The plant’s economic life will be around five years when it will be re-purposed to manufacture another product, assuming continued product innovations. Audio Plus’s required rate of return on its speaker range is 25%, based on its WACC. Audio Plus’s cost of debt is 10% and its project re-investment rate is 12%.

## 9.3.2 Evaluating the Returns on Investment Projects

Forecasting is the entity’s process of making predictions about a future situation based on past and current data/trends applied to the current forecast.

The entity relies on the best-available information in determining their key assumptions and inputting them to the investment project evaluation models (evaluation model) to provide consistency and rigour. One or all of these assumptions may not be correct (e.g. the timing and amount of actual cash flows) and this will impact on the actual rate of return on the project. Additionally, the entity may not have considered all the possible considerations necessary for the investment or understood their likely consequence (incorrectly considered them), and consequently underestimated/overestimated the value of the investment.

In determining the assumptions to include in the evaluation model the entity has to ensure those assumptions are robust and complete and:

• For expected future cash inflows and cash outflows, ensure that they are based on the entity’s experience, match time periods of receipt correctly and either include or exclude risk considerations:
° If they already exclude risk considerations, the future cash flows should be discounted to present value by a non-risk-free rate that reflects their risks and any uncertainty arising from their risks.
° If they already include risk considerations, the future cash flows should be discounted to the present value by a risk-free rate to ensure that their risks and any uncertainties are not double counted in their calculation.

• Be consistent in taking pre-tax or post-tax amounts from all assumptions (i.e. all pre-tax or all post-tax). This will depend on whether the investment project changes the effective tax rate of the entity – if it does, post-tax should be included; if not, pre-tax is acceptable.

• Be consistent in expressing all assumption dollar amounts in either nominal (based on today’s inflation rate) or real terms (based on expected future inflation rates over the economic life of the investment project).

There are five main methodologies used for assessing and evaluating investment projects:
• Net present value (NPV)
• Internal rate of return (IRR)
• Payback period
• Accounting rate of return (ARR)
• Return on investment (ROI)

### 9.3.2.1 Net Present Value (NPV) 
An entity can use the net present value (NPV) methodology to evaluate the investment project. Net present value discounts all expected future cash flows from the investment into their present-day using an appropriate discount rate, less the cost to acquire those cash flows. The appropriate discount rate may be the entity’s WACC (being the expected rate of return) if the risk profile of the investment is the same as the entity’s, the entity’s cost of debt or a specific project investment return that is commensurate with the entity’s assessment of the investment’s individual risk. It is the only methodology that takes account of the size and timing of all expected future cash flows. Under this evaluation methodology, an investment project is acceptable if the investment project generates a positive NPV value. A negative NPV value is unacceptable, as it implies the investment is not worth the cost and a neutral NPV (with a value of zero) generates no return, earning only what it cost.

The advantages of the NPV evaluation methodology is that it is a direct measure of the investment project’s contribution to the entity’s cash flow, by considering all cash flows and the time value of money, and considers the risk of earning/paying future cash flows. Its main disadvantage is that it cannot be used to compare projects of different sizes and there are no accepted guidelines for calculating the required rate of return.

Analysis

The formula for calculating the net present value of the proposed manufacturing plant is:
![](DraggedImage-228.png)
![](DraggedImage-229.png)
NPV = +HK$304,640

As the proposed investment in the manufacturing plan is NPV positive (+HK$304,640), it is acceptable for Audio Plus. In risk terms, the total cash inflows are greater than the total cash outflows, even when adjusted by the entity’s required rate of return (in this case WACC), meaning that the entity is being appropriately compensated by the risk it is taking on in the investment.

### 9.3.2.2 Internal Rate of Return (IRR) 
Internal rate of return (IRR) is the required rate of return (discount rate) that makes the net present value of a project zero. It therefore corresponds to the present value of the investment’s anticipated cash inflows (using the entity’s reinvestment rate) with initial cash outflows (calculated at the cost of debt rate). It excludes any external factors such as inflation or the entity’s WACC (cost of capital). This allows for competing projects to be compared using the size of the rates calculated.

IRR is often used when assessing the relative costs/benefits of an entity investing in a project to establish new operations or expanding an existing operation.

IRR is calculated on a ‘trial and error’ basis to find out the IRR and it cannot be calculated analytically like NPV methodology. The higher the IRR it is said, the better the investment project. Under this evaluation methodology, an investment project is acceptable if the calculated IRR exceeds the entity’s benchmark rate (e.g. the WACC).

The IRR is calculated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-230.png)
It is calculated using an iterative ‘trial and error’ process of trying to find the IRR value. The entity then compares the calculated IRR value to their required rate of return to see if it is acceptable or should be rejected.

IRR is often calculated in conjunction with NPV to give the entity a more realistic evaluation of the investment project. For example, an investment project using both IRR and NPV evaluation methodologies may have a low IRR and high NPV. This means that the project may generate slow returns but add value to the entity over its economic life. For projects with different economic lives, a shorter life investment project may have a high IRR (faster returns) and low NPV compared to a longer life project that has a low IRR (slower returns) and high NPV. Using IRR methodology, the shorter life project would be preferred, which would deny the entity the opportunity of receiving a higher longer term NPV return. In risk terms, it reflects the rate of return that generates a net present value of the investment as zero. It allows the entity to determine if the investment project’s internal rate of return is acceptable as compared to the entity’s required rate of return (which could be the project reinvestment rate or the cost of capital) and hence whether the entity is being appropriately compensated by the risk it is taking on with the investment.

The advantages of the IRR evaluation are that it is a simple calculation, easy to understand and interpret, and does not involve collecting huge amounts of data to calculate, including establishing the expected rate of return. Its main disadvantages are that it disregards the time value of money for longer term investments and ignores mutually exclusive projects or projects with different sizes/terms.

The disadvantage/limitations to the IRR evaluation methodology is that it assumes that interim cash flows are reinvested at the same rate of return, which may not be appropriate and may calculate multiple IRRs in some circumstances.

As the IRR (39%) is above both the entity’s cost of debt (10%) and the entity’s reinvestment rate (12%), the project is acceptable for Audio Plus to undertake. In risk terms, the IRR represents the discount rate at which the investment project makes more cash inflows than its cash outflows.
