### 9.3.2.3 Payback Period

The entity may want to calculate how long it may take for an investment project to recover the cost of the investment through its net cash inflows. This evaluation methodology focuses on cash flow and not profit. To use this methodology the entity must decide on the maximum payback period they will accept for the investment project. This methodology is often used in conjunction with another evaluation methodology as it can emphasise short term returns more, rather than longer term returns. The advantage of the payback period evaluation is that it is a simple calculation, is easy to understand and interpret, and does not involve collecting huge amounts of data to calculate.

The disadvantages/limitations of the payback period evaluation methodology are:

• It excludes discounting for the time value of the cash flow money and so the payback period is based on nominal cash flows rather than real cash flows.

• It ignores the value of further cash flows once the initial investment has been repaid (i.e. the total cash flows the investment project could earn) and if multiple investment projects are being evaluated, this will need to be taken into account (for example consider if one investment continues to earn cash flows after the payback period, while the other investment ceases to earn cash flows after the payback period).

• It preferences investment projects with the shortest payback period, rather than those with the most future cash inflows.

There are two ways to calculate the payback period:

1. Averaging method – This takes the annual expected cash inflows and divides it by the expected initial cost of the investment (works best when cash inflows are expected to be consistent in subsequent years).

2. Subtraction method – This takes the initial cost of the investment and subtracts the annual expected cash flows (works best when cash inflows are expected to be variable in subsequent years).

The entity compares the calculated payback period to their required payback period to see if it is acceptable.

#### Apply and Analyse 5

Using Illustrative Example 1, explain whether Audio Plus should invest in the investment project to construct a new manufacturing plant using the payback period calculation (using the subtraction method).

A reminder of the key details:

Audio Plus’s required rate of return (WACC) is 25%, the new plant’s life is 5 years and will cost HK$1,000,000 to build and cash flow forecasts are HK$450,000 in year one and HK$500,000 in years 2–5 inclusive. We are told to assume the cash flows are earned evenly throughout the years.

Analysis

Year one’s cash flow is stated as HK$450,000. Year two’s cash flow is HK$500,000. At the end of year two, the cash flow is HK$950,000. Another HK$50,000 is required in cash flows from year three to cover the initial cost of the investment. Assuming the stated yearly cash flows are earned evenly throughout the year, the HK$50,000 will be generated as follows: yearly cash flow of HK$500,000/12 months = cash flows per month of HK$41,667, so the full HK$50,000 will be earned in month two. The payback period is therefore three years two months. 

In risk terms, the payback period demonstrates that it takes over halfway through the useful life (5 years) of the investment project to start generating a rate of return greater than zero. The entity will have to determine if this is acceptable and that the entity is being appropriately compensated by the risk it is taking on in the investment.

### 9.3.2.4 Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)

The fourth evaluation methodology for valuing investment projects is the accounting rate of return. This focuses on determining the after-tax accounting profit (after depreciation and interest expense) to be generated by the project (expressed as a percentage) and comparing it to the entity’s cost of capital (WACC). The advantages of the accounting rate of return evaluation are that it is a simple calculation, is easy to understand, does not involve collecting huge amounts of data to calculate and focuses on the profitability of the investment project. Its main disadvantage is that it disregards the cash flows and their timing and ignores the time value of money for longer term investments.

ARR is calculated as: average after tax accounting profit/initial or average investment × 100%, where ‘accounting profit’ after tax is equal to net income (after depreciation and interest expense) and ‘average investment’ is the total of initial investment and disposal value divided by 2.

An ARR greater than the WACC would be accepted, if less it would be rejected. A limitation to this methodology is that it does not take account of the time value of money.

#### Apply and Analyse 6

Using Illustrative Example 1, explain whether Audio Plus should invest in the investment project to construct a new manufacturing plant using the accounting rate of return calculation.

A reminder of the key details:

Audio Plus’s required rate of return (WACC) is 25%, the new plant’s life is 5 years and will cost HK$1,000,000 to build and cash flow forecasts are HK$450,000 in year one and HK$500,000 in years 2–5 inclusive. We are also told that the accounting profit for the first year is HK$250,000 and this increases by 10% year on each year thereafter.

Analysis

The accounting rate of return is calculated as follows:
Year one: HK$250,000 profit after tax
Year two: HK$275,000 profit after tax (HK$250,000 × 1.10)
Year three: HK$302,500 profit after tax (HK$275,000 × 1.10)
Year four: HK$332,750 profit after tax (HK$302,500 × 1.10)
Year five: HK$366,025 profit after tax (HK$332,750 × 1.10)

Total accounting profit after tax is the sum of the five years = Year one (HK$250,000) + Year two (HK$275,000) + Year three (HK$302,500) + Year four (HK$332,750) + Year five (HK$366,025) = HK$1,526,275.

Average (yearly) accounting profit after tax = HK$1,526,275/5 years = HK$305,255

The initial investment is the cost HK$1,000,000.

The ARR is therefore accounting profit HK$305,255/Initial investment cost
HK$1,000,000 × 100% = 30.5%.

As the ARR of 30.5% is higher than the entity’s WACC of 25%, the project is acceptable to undertake. In risk terms, the accounting rate of return assumes that the entity is being compensated for the risk taken on in the investment project by the profit generated.
---- 
### 9.3.2.5 Return on Investment (ROI) 
The simple financial return on investment (ROI) concept explains the amount of return on an investment (total growth of the investment) relative to the investment’s cost. The higher the ROI, the more beneficial the investment. The advantages of the return on investment evaluation are that it focuses on the required level of investment required to earn the expected rate of return, is a simple calculation, is easy to understand and does not involve collecting huge amounts of data to calculate. Its main disadvantages are that it ignores the time value of money for longer term investments, can be difficult to agree on investment profit and quantify and ensure that the total cost of investment is included.

It is calculated as investment profit/total cost of the investment, with the result expressed as a percentage.

It ignores the time value of money and so this would need to be adjusted if comparing investment ROIs involving different investment time periods.

#### Apply and Analyse 7

Using Illustrative Example 1, explain whether Audio Plus should invest in the investment project to construct a new manufacturing plant using the return on investment (ROI) forecast methodology.

A reminder of the key details:

Audio Plus’s required rate of return (WACC) is 25%, the new plant’s life is 5 years and will cost HK$1,000,000 to build and cash flow forecasts are HK$450,000 in year one and HK$500,000 in years 2–5 inclusive. We are also told that the accounting profit for the first year is HK$250,000 and this increases by 10% on each year thereafter.

Analysis

ROI = [total profit/total cost of investment](#) − where cost of investment is initial cost plus any additional incremental cash outflows from the investment

ROI = HK$1,526,275 (sourced from the ARR calculation)/[HK$1,000,000 + (HK$200,000 × 5 years)](#)

ROI = HK$1,526,275/HK$2,000,000

ROI = 76%

As the financial ROI is strongly positive (76%), it is acceptable to undertake.

In risk terms, the simplistic return on investment percentage assumes that the risk being taken on in the investment project is being compensated through profit earned on the investment. This may or may not be the case.

### 9.3.2.6 Interpreting Results of Investment Project Evaluations

As you can see from the above Audio Plus case, the five methodologies give differing results:

NPV = +HK$304,667
IRR = 39% 
Payback period = 3 years and 2 months (out of 5 years)
ARR = 30.5% 
ROI = 76% 

In risk terms, all the forecast methodologies (using the entity’s key forecast assumptions) provide the entity with different ways of calculating the rate of return the investment project may earn to compensate the entity for the riskiness of the project. They can be compared to the entity’s required rate of return to assess whether the project is acceptable or is to be rejected. The diversity of the rate of returns for the same example shows the importance of choosing the right methodology for the investment project circumstances.

It is also important to choose the entity’s required rate of return carefully. As noted above, the entity can choose its weighted average cost of capital (WACC), cost of debt or project rate of return (reinvestment rate). The entity’s choice will depend on the characteristics of the investment project, including its risk profile, and which one it more closely approximates, and also the nature and type of investment project (e.g. its timeframe and volatility in its cash flow and profit profile).

Now that the different investment evaluation models have been discussed, let’s consider how to make changes to these to reflect various different potential outcomes in a sensitivity analysis.

### 9.3.2.7 Comparing the Different Evaluation Models

Exhibit 9.6 shows a summary of the five different methodologies.
![](DraggedImage-232.png)
As can be seen from the above evaluation models, they provide the entity with different means of evaluating and calculating the expected return of the individual investment project and its contribution, or otherwise, to the entity’s value. Some also price in the value of risk, expressed at the entity’s required rate of return, while others report a return for the entity to assess against its required rate of return.

Regardless, this required return is also an assumption, so the entity must assess its appropriateness to the individual investment project and its risk profile (i.e. less risky or more risky than other investment projects, the entity’s existing portfolio of projects or the entity’s risk appetite). The entity then selects which forecasting model is appropriate to its circumstance based on what is the outcome it wants to understand ($value, %value), the type of imperfect information available to assess the project, including how many and what assumptions have already been made about the investment project and what is important to the outcome of the evaluation (e.g. cost recovery, accounting profit, how long it will take to recover cost and how much return the entity could have and requires the project to earn). Different models are often used together to give the entity more information about the possible outcomes of the investment project using different assumptions and metrics that test the rigour and likely outcome of the project from different rate of return aspects. Given the variability of assumptions used as inputs to the evaluation, this creates risk, and is reflected in the highly variable outcome.

Each model relies on different sets of assumptions to determine that return and may be useful in different situations. It is up to the entity to decide which model is more appropriate for its individual investment project (e.g. given its length of useful life, variability of all incremental cash flows and profit contribution) and the outcome it is trying to achieve in considering the project (e.g. generate most of the cash flows in the first five years of the project, aim for consistent cash flow returns over the life of the project or minimise costs) while achieving an overall rate of return that is acceptable given the project’s risk profile. Assumptions are essentially the entity’s best-estimate for the variables required to assess the investment project, and may or may not be accurate, given they are trying to predict future outcomes that are uncertain. The more assumptions used the more risk that the entity will incorrectly estimate those assumptions, their impact on the evaluation and the overall value of the investment to the entity. The entity inherently accepts that each of the assumptions may be incorrect, and hence uses professional judgement to determine what those assumptions should be (e.g. using past experience), and in consistently allowing for/excluding a risk pricing element reflecting how certain they are of those assumptions.

## 9.3.3 Evaluating the Variability of Returns on Investment Projects

The above investment project evaluation models calculate the expected returns when forecasting under certainty. What happens when uncertainty is introduced? How does it affect the range of potential consequences and their likelihood of occurring on the expected returns? There are three common evaluation techniques that can be used to determine the effect of uncertainty:

• Sensitivity analysis
• Scenario analysis
• Probability analysis

In determining the extent to which the variability of each or all of these risky assumptions underlying the investment project evaluation may impact on the certainty of its expected return outcome, the entity can consider measuring the extent of this variability using sensitivity analysis. This analysis allows the entity to better understand the nature and range of how individual assumptions may, one at a time, impact the model.

If the evaluation assumptions are interdependent of each other (e.g. cash inflows and cash outflows), scenario analysis allows the entity to calculate how multiple assumptions may, together, impact the model and produce different expected return outcomes.

Probability analysis can further enhance the evaluation by considering for each of the different outcomes the likelihood of them occurring, based on the mean or average of all possible outcomes.

### 9.3.3.1 Sensitivity Analysis – Forecasting and Project Evaluation Under Uncertainty

Sensitivity analysis is a technique that takes an investment project evaluation and predicts the financial effects of changing certain key assumptions in the investment forecast. In doing this, the sensitivity analysis allows for the degree of risk and uncertainty in the assumptions, the relative risk inherent in those assumptions and the consequence of explored changes on the expected return of the investment project. That is, it assesses the risk associated with a capital investment project. As noted above, assumptions can include:

• The discount rate chosen.
• Initial cost of the investment.
• Expected cash inflows from revenue (volume and cash dollar values).
• Expected cash outflows from costs (volume and cash dollar values).
• Expected economic life (useful life) of the investment.
• Timing of cash flows for revenue and expenses.

Given the above discussion above regarding forecasting with uncertainty in investment project evaluation, it is critical that the entity also considers the impact of making changes in one or more of the key variable evaluation inputs that determine the success or failure of the project that are affected by uncertainty. It can help answer questions such as how reliable the assumptions in the evaluation are, what are the most significant in terms of their effect on the evaluation and what is the financial effect if the assumptions turn out to be significantly different in real life.

For example, a small change to a key variable may make the project not acceptable for the entity to pursue. It is important to determine what are the key variables. If the investment project is approved, it provides the entity with an understanding of the variables for which the investment is particularly sensitive to movements, and therefore those it needs to closely monitor as the project progresses. In other words, for risk management it is important to monitor and adjust decision-making to allow for improved information.

There are two ways in which sensitivity analysis can be performed:

• Local sensitivity analysis – Involves making changes to one variable in the evaluation. This analysis may be limited if the entity makes the wrong choice in the variable selected or the variable selected may not be correlated to overall sensitivity.

• Global sensitivity analysis – Involves making changes to more than one variable, which may or may not be interdependent with each other. This may include making sets of changes to variables and testing these sets individually or together. Again, same as local sensitivity analysis, this type of analysis will be limited if the entity makes the wrong choice of variables selected and/or makes the wrong assumption about their interdependencies.

However, more than one variable can interact and affect other variables and vice versa. It can be performed over all the investment evaluation methodologies (NPV, IRR, payback period, ARR and ROI) and can provide an indication of why an investment project may not achieve its expected forecast outcome. Sensitivity can be performed on:

• Expected sales volume, sales price, purchases volume and cost of sales price.

• Expected cost of initial investment and any capital purchases.
• Expected cash inflows or their timing (revenue).
• Expected cash outflows or their timing (expenses).
• Expected cost savings.
• Expected useful life (economic life) of investment.
• Expected residual value of investment.
• Expected inflation rates over the project life.
• Expected tax rates.
• Variations in the entity’s benchmark required rate of return (e.g. in the future weighted average cost of capital (WACC)) due to changes in its components (cost of equity, cost of debt) or any other discount rate used.

#### Key Steps in Performing a Sensitivity Analysis

The key sensitivity analysis steps are:

• Determine what the key quantitative project variables to the forecast are, based on professional judgement in their assessment of the likely impact on the investment project evaluation (e.g. their impact on NPV, payback period, ARR and ROI). That is, identify the independent variable(s) to test in the evaluation.

A simple way of understanding what variables the investment project may be sensitive to changes in is to calculate the sensitivity of each variable (expressed as a percentage). Let’s use the NPV evaluation methodology as an example:

> Sensitivity percentage = NPV/Present value of project variables

The lower the sensitivity percentage, the more sensitive the NPV calculation is to the variable (i.e. the variable only needs to change by a small amount to make the investment project less viable or potentially non-viable).

• Determine what the adjustment should be (e.g. minimum or maximum values) made to the inputs to include in the evaluation which would still ensure the evaluation remains positive. These adjustments may be based on past experience. For example, risky future cash flows can be adjusted by the estimated probability that they occur (that is, their estimated success rate).
• Make the adjustment.
• Analyse and interpret the results.

The entity then repeats the above steps for each assumption being changed.

---- 
Apply and Analyse 8
---- 
#### The advantages of performing a sensitivity analysis are:

• It is easy to observe the impact of one change to an assumption on the investment outcome.
• It identifies which key inputs (assumptions) to the evaluation have the most significance to the expected value of the investment, so that the entity can more closely evaluate the likelihood of those forecasted inputs being realistically achieved (e.g. by considering how much is within the entity’s control and how much is outside the entity’s control).
• It tests the robustness of the evaluation in the presence of uncertainty.
• It also provides greater understanding of the relationships between the input and output variables, which reduces uncertainty.

#### The disadvantages of performing a sensitivity analysis are:
• It requires considerable professional judgement (e.g. regarding the decision on what variable is the most important of potential variables in its sensitivity within the model, the degree to which they are assessed to be sensitive and the extent to which past experience is relevant).
• It only generates results based on changes made to one independent variable at a time and not all variables that could impact the evaluation (these are assumed to remain constant).
• Their total impact may not be correct (that is, variables seldom move independently).
• It does not adjust for those variables that are dependent (one variable directly affects the other) or interdependent (both variables affect each other, but potentially in different ways). This is unrealistic as in reality many of the variables are related and interdependent.
• It does not consider the probability that the sensitivities tested may occur.
• The variables chosen to change (the independent variables) may not be the right ones or the size of the changes may not be correct. This may be because the person performing the analysis does not understand the drivers in the evaluation properly, or purposely wants to avoid demonstrating that the evaluation is only positive for the entity in limited circumstances.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> It is important for all investment projects that have financial inputs in the forecasting model that are uncertain to have their relative sensitivity to variation considered before approving the project.


### 9.3.3.2 Scenario Analysis – Forecasting and Project Evaluation Under Uncertainty

Scenario analysis seeks to overcome the limitations of the sensitivity analysis (noted above). It is performed when the entity wants to understand the impact (expected value) of a possible scenario, at a point in time, on the investment project by changing the value of key variables used in the investment evaluation. In this way, the entity can quantify the total possible range of uncertainty inherent in the project evaluation. Scenarios may be highly likely or highly probable to occur; however, they give the entity a more precise insight into how much the investment project’s profitability is dependent on the underlying variables/inputs and assumptions, how this may impact the value of the entity and therefore how much risk or value the potential investment project offers.

Scenario analysis can help the entity identify future risks by looking for the best-case or worst-case scenario, or multiple scenarios, on the investment and not just the ‘theoretically’ possible. For example:
• Best case scenario – All variables set to the best possible results, with the return = X%.
• Worst case scenario – All variables set to the worst possible results, with the return = X%.
• Multiple scenarios – If one or more interdependent variables are adjusted by X% what the results would be.

#### The limitations of performing the scenario analysis are:
• Its usefulness is limited by the skills, capabilities and cognitive bias of the person preparing the scenario analysis (for example, in terms of their understanding of the investment evaluation.)
• What the range of scenarios to be considered should be.
• It takes the average of the results of the different scenarios.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> It is important for all investment projects where the financial inputs to the forecasting model are uncertain, but it is known they are dependent or interdependent on each other, that all their relative sensitivity to variation is considered before approving the project.

### 9.3.3.3 Stress Testing (Resilience Testing)

Let’s now consider the benefits of stress testing on an investment evaluation model.

Stress testing is a mathematical model, performed using computer software, that can be used for investment evaluation and simulates for a given dependent its impact on a range of independent variables. It essentially tests for the impact of risk and uncertainty in the evaluation methodology used. The model can be simple or complex depending on the scenario being tested. It is widely used in assessing the capital adequacy of financial institutions, by entities that have derivative strategies (to determine their range of effectiveness), by entities that hold substantial investments (to manage their asset portfolio risk, where individual or groups of assets held fail to meet the entity’s financial goals) and by superannuation fund entities to ensure that they have adequate investment returns to match expected payouts.

#### There are three common types of stress tests:

• Historical – Involves running simulations on the entity’s actual data, based on parameters set by a previous (historical) scenario to identify any hidden vulnerabilities in how the entity would be impacted (e.g. consider the 1987 stock market crash).

• Hypothetical – Involves running simulations on the entity’s actual data, based on parameters set by a broad artificial ‘what if’ scenario (i.e. has not occurred) (e.g. consider the likelihood of a weather event on the entity’s ability to produce goods and services).

• Stylised – Involves running simulations on the entity’s actual data, based on parameters set by a more specific artificial ‘what if’ scenario (i.e. has not occurred) (e.g. consider the likelihood of the entity’s share price losing more than 20%). It only tests one or a few variables adjusted in the evaluation at a time.

The methodology most commonly used for modelling risk stress testing, particularly in project cash flows and options pricing, is the Monte Carlo simulation (also known as multiple probability simulation). It is a stochastic model (i.e. it includes randomness into the model) and simulates multiple combinations of variables in an evaluation and calculates the probability of different expected outcomes occurring within a process that cannot easily be predicted due to the intervention of random (unrelated) variables. It does this by replacing a range of values (probability distribution) for any factor in the evaluation that has inherent uncertainty. It then calculates every possible outcome, using a different set of random values from the probability functions, to produce a distribution of all possible outcome values.

In this way Monte Carlo quantifies risk (uncertainty) in predictive/forecasting models.

The limitations of Monte Carlo are that it either uses a considerable volume of actual data to calculate probability distributions (i.e. a way of showing the probabilities of occurrence of different possible outcomes of something) or, in the absence of data, it requires assumptions to be used to calculate those probability distributions. An example of an assumption is that relating to the correlations (a connection between two or more of the evaluation variables), or otherwise, of different variables used in the simulation. This results in the output of the Monte Carlo simulation being only as accurate as the quality of the inputs. It can also have difficulty dealing with the effects of extreme one-off type events like a country or global financial crisis and behavioural economic aspects.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Stress testing of investment project evaluations is required if the evaluation is complex due to the number and size of the variables involved.

### 9.3.3.4 Post Investment Evaluation

Once a particular investment project has been approved and operationalised, it is prudent to conduct a post implementation assessment to see if the project has actually achieved its forecast cash flows that were expected in the project evaluation. Where there are significant differences between actual cash flow results and expected cash flows, these differences should be promptly investigated to understand the root cause(s) of such differences. The benefit of doing this is that it enables the entity to identify and make any required adjustments to the forecast project evaluation methodology that may have been identified from the actual results so that it increases the accuracy and/or consistency of the methodology for future project evaluations.

### 9.3.3.5 Probability Analysis

To finalise the risk considerations when evaluating an investment project, we need to consider the probability of which of the scenarios discussed using forecasting models is the most likely investment return outcome for the entity.

If the entity wants to understand how probable a scenario is of occurring versus another scenario in which the sensitivity analysis outcome is more likely, the entity can perform a probability analysis.

Probability is the extent to which something is likely to occur (that is the chance of happening or not happening of an event). Put another way, it is the ratio of the rate of occurrence of a certain event (favourable event) compared to that of equally likely events taken over a certain timeframe. It is usually expressed in both quantitative and/or qualitative terms (i.e. it is 10% likely to occur, or more likely than less likely to occur). Probability is subjective and open to judgement.

If an event has as much chance of occurring as another event, they are both said to be equally probable. If an event’s occurrence is not affected by the occurrence of another event, they are said to be independent events. Dependent events are when an events occurrence is affected by the occurrence of another event. Mutually exclusive events are when one event prevents or precludes the occurrence of another event.

Probability analysis uses mathematical techniques to consider such likelihoods. The theory of probability is that it quantifies how to measure the underlying variability caused by risk within a range of confidence about the results, thereby allowing for a more rigorous evaluation of the investment project. To reduce this degree of uncertainty and bring precision and consistency to the evaluation, a probability model is used to statistically model possible outcomes of the investment given certain parameters being tested for.

Probability analysis can be particularly useful when risk is a significant factor in the evaluation (i.e. there are significant inputs/assumptions that are simply estimates and their likely consequence is uncertain). It does this by looking at the range of effects of all possible combinations of variables. It reduces the level of uncertainty in the investment project evaluation decision, for example by considering the probability of earning that forecast outcome. The higher the confidence level, the more confident the entity can be in the probability of the outcome occurring.

A common type of model used is the Monte Carlo simulation run using the net present value methodology. It randomly simulates the effects on the variables that are heavily affected by uncertainty (imprecision). It extends a scenario analysis to produce many random but possible outcomes from changing the variables in proportion to their likelihood, as well as their volatility (degree of variation) amongst the variables. There are a number of calculations performed to support the Monte Carlo simulation:

• It calculates the mean value of a variable (simply the average of the total range of the variable being calculated possible divided by the total count of the number of ranges).

• It also calculates the standard deviation of the variable (how much the range of the variable differs from the mean value of the variable or of the range of expected variables). That is, it can calculate the probabilities of different cash flows occurring.

• Finally, it calculates the coefficient of variation value (ratio of the standard deviation of the expected net present value) and infers the degree of variation within the expected cash flows.

#### Illustrative Example 2

The Audio Plus case details in Illustrative Example 1 advised that, based on the plant specifications and the land purchase price, it will cost HK$1,000,000 to build and take one year to construct. Additionally based on current sales and profitability for the speaker range, the expected net cash inflows (i.e. net of cash outflows of HK$200,000 from increased costs from running the plant) will be around HK$450,000 in the first year and then HK$500,000 per year for the following four years (assume the cash flows are earned evenly throughout the year). Total cash flows were forecast to equate to HK$2.45 million (i.e. HK$450,000 + (HK$500,000 × 4 years)). Audio Plus has now estimated the probabilities of receiving the cash flows from the sales of the Hello! speakers based on their past experience with customer demand for new products. They are aware that total cash flows of HK$2.45 million are in an ideal/certain scenario and consider it appropriate to consider what total cash flows would be in more uncertain, real world scenarios – when sales based on customer demand are more variable and therefore cash flows received may be lower. Audio Plus have therefore estimated the probability of sales based on three different customer demand-based scenarios. The first scenario is they experience high demand for the speakers, the second is average demand and the third is low demand. Further they estimate the total probability of all scenarios occurring as follows (out of 100%): the first scenario to be 20%, the second to be 50% and the third to be 30%.

Converting this to the cash flow impacts of the different scenarios, scenario 1 (high demand – 20% probability) cash flows would equal HK$490,000 (i.e. HK$2.45 million × 20%), scenario 2 (average demand – 50% probability) cash flows would equal HK$1.225 million (i.e. HK$2.45 million × 50%) and scenario 3 (low demand – 30% probability), the cash flows would equal HK$735,000 (i.e. HK$2.45 million × 30%).

Using Illustrative Example 1, let’s perform a probability analysis, using the previously calculated NPV calculation as the base, on Audio Plus HK Entity Limited’s expected cash flows from its potential investment (constructing a new manufacturing plant). Total cash flows were previously calculated as HK$2.45 million (being HK$450,000 + (HK$500,000 × 4 years)) with an initial cash outflow of HK$1,000,000 to build the plant.

1. Calculate the total expected NPV for each of the scenarios:
	![](DraggedImage-235.png)
	Calculate the expected NPV based on the three scenarios:
	![](DraggedImage-236.png)

2. Calculate the median value of the expected NPV for each of the three scenarios using MS Excel ‘MEDIAN’ FX function: = +HK$391,392

3. Calculate the standard deviation of the three expected annual cash flows using MS Excel ‘STDEV’ FX function = HK$199,287

4. Calculate the coefficient of variation (a measure of the spread of the expected NPVs relative to their average). This is the ratio of the standard deviation to the median value (calculated as [Standard deviation/median](#)) = HK$199,287/HK$391,392 = 0.5092 or 51%. This tells us that the standard deviation of the expected NPVs is 51% of the median, which indicates variability in expected NPVs.

Given the calculated standard deviation of HK$199,287, it tells us that the project’s expected cash flows are variable. The calculated coefficient of variation at 51% additionally tells us that the standard deviation of expected cash flows are considerable (variable) relative to the expected NPV (+HK$304,640) and therefore the project is riskier.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Probability analysis is important to perform if highly variable returns are expected on an investment project evaluation.

## 9.3.4 Ethical and Behavioural Considerations When Forecasting Under Uncertainty

There are ethical issues and personal characteristics to consider when evaluating the results of forecasting under uncertainty conditions performed on an investment evaluation. A sensitivity analysis is prepared by one or more of the entity’s employee(s) and hence the analysis can be affected by that person(s) ethical judgements and behavioural traits.

Ethics are the moral principles and values that guide a person’s behaviour or the way in which they perform or react to an activity. A person’s ethics can be shaped by many things including, but not limited to, their upbringing, education, family, friend and work environment. Ethical values can lead to conscious and unconscious bias. For example, an employee might oppose the company extending into activities that the employee considers undesirable (e.g. socially or environmentally).

Behaviourally, a conservative upbringing might see downside risk being exaggerated compared to upside risk. Some analysts may be more capable/insightful than others.

A lack of ethics might see potential personal rewards from a project as an incentive for downplaying risk. A lack of judgement may well limit the usefulness of an evaluation.

Therefore, in assessing an investment project evaluation it is important to consider the preparer’s behavioural influences:

• What is the person’s known risk tolerance?
° Are they risk adverse or a risk-taker? How has this impacted the evaluation in terms of the key assumptions made or not made?

• How accurate has the person’s previous investment evaluations been in terms of actual outcomes?
° Do they have the necessary skills and experience to perform the evaluation?

• What is the entity’s culture or tone at the top?
° Does the entity actively reward or encourage employee’s taking considerable risks to achieve financial return to the detriment of other evaluation factors?
° Does it not discipline/penalise employees who do not follow the required framework or evaluation process?
° Does it reward short-term strategies and profitability to the detriment of building long-term entity value?

• What is the entity’s culture towards enforcing compliance with its own policies, procedures and guidelines, and applicable laws and regulations and can these affect the investment project?
° Are the requirements clear and unambiguous for employees? ° How much latitude does the entity’s employees have in exercising their own professional judgement?

• Does the entity have a defined investment evaluation framework (with processes, procedures and templates) that the evaluation must be prepared in accordance with? ° Has this been complied with? ° Does it require the consideration of ethical issues/risks and other non-financial factors in preparing and approving all investment projects (e.g. environmental or societal impacts)?
° Have ethical considerations of the investment been given appropriate regard in the evaluation?
° Are key inputs/assumptions documented, with their reasons for use?

• Was the person exposed to any moral hazard in preparing the evaluation?
° Is there any consequence or personal responsibility for the person regarding a poorly prepared or incorrect evaluation?

• Was the person asked to prepare the evaluation to present a particular investment outcome? 
° Were they told the ‘preferred outcome’ to arrive at before they commenced the evaluation? 
° Did they just calculate the key inputs to the evaluation backwards to achieve the preferred outcome? 
° Have credible data analytics been used to source or compile the data?

• How robust are the assumptions used to prepare the evaluation?
° Are the estimates complete? How were they calculated? Are they all documented? 
° Can the key inputs be justified, with reference to how they were derived/calculated? Are they comparable to other like projects?
° How much of an estimate are they? Do they consider any relevant entity past learnings?
° Is the economic life assessment realistic or overly confident? ° Do the estimates include any limitations on interpretation that the approvers of the investment project should be aware of?

• How invested is the person in seeing the investment project being approved or not approved?
° Is there any personal or professional incentive to do so (e.g. could the approval/ non-approval affect their remuneration/bonuses, performance appraisals or chance of promotion)?
° If there are any individual penalties for particular actions, are these outweighed by the actual rewards given to the person?

• If more than one person was involved in preparing the investment evaluation, has there been appropriate diversity of thinking and skills in inputting the key assumptions/ variables used and then in choosing and testing the sensitivity of those different variables (i.e. not groupthink)?
° Has the evaluation been quality assured by someone independent of the key variables that input to the evaluation?

• Does the person have any biases?
° Do they have an unconscious bias (that is, their judgements that do not reflect the information available)?
° Do they have confirmation bias (that is, a tendency to seek out and place more weight on information that confirms a preferred conclusion while ignoring contrary information)?
° Do they have availability bias (that is, a tendency to place more weight on readily available information in decision making)?
° Do they have framing bias (that is, a tendency to view information in the context in which it is presented)?

All the above ethical-based issues have the potential to adversely impact the investment project evaluation and therefore must be considered when reviewing the financial and non-financial inputs included in the evaluation.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Ethical and behavioural issues have the potential to introduce bias to a sensitivity analysis and consequently adversely impact the results of the investment evaluations and must be considered before finalising any investment decision based on the analysis.

# 9.4 ENTERPRISE RISK MANAGEMENT (ERM)

The international based Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO) Enterprise Risk Management Framework – Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017) defines Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) to be ’a process, effected by an entity’s board of directors, management, and other personnel, applied in strategy setting and across the enterprise, signed to identify potential events that may affect the entity, and manage risk to be within its risk appetite, to provide reasonable assurance regarding the achievement of entity objectives’.

Risk left unmanaged has the potential to prevent the entity from achieving its strategic objectives. It is therefore critical that the entity proactively manages all its risks by performing environment scanning to identify potential risks, assessing them based on how they may affect those objectives, based on reliable, accurate and timely information, and designing risk responses that meet the entity’s risk appetite. In this way, the entity minimises downside risk while maximising its opportunities for upside risk to achieve its strategic objectives and enhance its value.

Enterprise risk management (ERM) provides a framework for managing entity-wide financial and non-financial risks and is more strategic than simple risk management. Simple risk management tends to be reactive to risks (that is manage risks that occur) rather than proactive (considering potential risks that have not occurred). It takes all individual risks identified by the entity’s different areas (that may have been contained in one area) and considers how they may impact the entity in totality. For example, the overall consequence to the entity of one particular risk can be much bigger than one individual area may assess it to be. That is because the individual area will only see the risk from their own perspective (e.g. the IT department focus on technology risks, the finance team focus on financial risk, or the legal team focus on known legal risks they are dealing with), may only focus on actual risks rather than potential risks, and may fail to identify those risks that present opportunities. It is critical that each entity area contribute their risks to the ERM framework, and that these risks are then considered from an entity-wide potential impact so that the entity can effectively manage all its risk and value.

An effective ERM framework is one that is developed, maintained and continuously monitored and improved, and helps:

• Provide a framework for linking how the entity manages its identified risks to its strategic objectives to ensure that the focus and effort of its risk management activities is appropriate to the potential impact on the entity.

• Ensure that the ERM framework is not seen as merely a compliance exercise for managing risk but is considered from a strategic point of view.

• Provide a consistent methodology that aims to identify and assess for probable impact (quantification and qualification) any opportunities and threats – prioritise and weigh such risks and put in place appropriate risk response, based on how the risks may interfere with an entity’s operations and objectives. Examples of such risks include those discussed in Section 9.2, Key Risks Facing by an Entity (being financial, operational, political, legal and business risks). It also facilitates internal and external risk reporting.

• Encourages the entity to look at all possible scenarios for identified risks, not just the scenario ‘most likely’ – consider the worst-case and best-case outcomes.

• Balances risks with their financial and non-financial effects. Some risks do not have an immediate effect.

°

°

For example, the entity may be financially advantaged if it disregards compliance with applicable laws and regulations when building a new manufacturing plant; however, the damage to its reputation, when discovered, in the first instance will outweigh that advantage. Additionally, it likely will face financial fines/penalties and a cost of retrofitting the plant to ensure compliance.

For example, public damage to the entity’s reputation caused by a failure to promptly act on known safety issues with its products does not have an immediate cost the entity can easily quantify. However, it is clear that such reputational damage can cause irreparable damage to the public trust in the entity, leading to a loss in the entity’s value, loss of customers and ultimately possible financial distress.

• It accepts that some risk will always be inherent in the entity. The level of risk that the entity accepts should be commensurate with the returns it accepts. If the entity accepts higher risks, then it should accept higher returns. Conversely, if it accepts lower risk, then it accepts lower returns.

• ERM frameworks help identify which risks need to be managed and which risks can be accepted with appropriate monitoring. This helps the entity to prioritise its resources on a risk/rewards basis.

• By early identifying risk, the entity may be able to put in place a risk response that can benefit/save the entity more than if it was not identified (e.g. the need to immediately increase production at the factory to meet expected increased customer demands for higher margin products or the need to increase maintenance spend on an infrastructure asset in order to prolong the asset life rather than invest in a replacement asset immediately).

• Entities should continuously assess and prioritise potential future risks and be proactive in identifying potential future risks, particularly those that may offer great opportunities and rewards to the entity if they manage them appropriately and those that offer the greatest threat to achieving rewards if left unmanaged. The entity develops contingency plans to address such risks and measure the effectiveness of risk responses to ensure that risks are being appropriately managed.

• Facilitates identifying potential risks that create opportunities that the entity could take advantage of to achieve its objectives.

## 9.4.1 Contributors to an Effective ERM

As noted in Section 9.1, functional responsibility for risk management ordinarily falls to the Chief Financial Officer or Chief Risk Officer (for larger organisations or those in the financial services industry) with direct accountability to the entity’s board. This is also the case for an ERM. Smaller organisations (e.g. not-for-profits, small to medium sized entities) are unlikely to require/have a Chief Risk Officer, and functional responsibility for the ERM process would ordinarily be the Chief Financial Officer (or equivalent role). Regardless of the size of entity, it should be able to implement a scalable, effective ERM process. As already discussed, for the ERM to be effective it must contain risk inputs from all areas within the entity that contribute to its risk. For example:

• Governance/oversight
- °Board of directors – Can provide guidance on the high-level risks it has considered in formulating the entity’s strategy; identify, based on the nature and type of entity, if external expertise is required to help the entity identify, manage and treat its risks; and approve the entity’s risk framework.
- °Audit and risk committee – Can provide guidance to the entity on the high-level risks it considers the entity faces, setting the entity’s risk appetite, and provide advice to the board of directors on how to manage and take advantage of the different types of risk.

• Senior management
- Chief Executive Officer/Chief Operating Officer/Chief Financial Officer/Chief Risk Officer – Can help identify external threats and competitive opportunities, along with strategic initiatives to address them.
- Chief Information Officer/Chief Data Privacy Officer – Can advise on compliance with data laws and regulations, and implement strategies to ensure the appropriate classification, treatment and access protocols of data are maintained over data that the entity collects from third parties or generates itself. Can also provide what in-house data inventory is available to help the entity manage its risk.
- Chief Technology Officer (if different from the Chief Information Officer) – Can monitor and advise on what technology tools (hardware and software) the entity requires to conduct its business and safeguard its data. Also responsible for ensuring the entity’s cybersecurity and IT systems are kept up to date and appropriately backed up.
- Executive leadership team – Can review all identified risks from the business units and assess possible risk consequences across the entity (e.g. some risks may be identified in one area of the entity but affect more than that area).

• Individual business units
°Marketing – Can inform the risk management process by obtaining information from prospective and current customers on how well the entity’s products/services are meeting customer demands and reporting feedback to the appropriate entity person, together with any recommendations of changes that might need to be made in its product/service offerings.
°Finance can inform the risk management process by:
- Monitoring and ensuring the entity’s compliance with applicable financial reporting, taxation and related laws and regulations as well as professional standards (Hong Kong Financial Reporting Standards (HKFRSs)) and reporting any non-compliance outcomes to the appropriate entity person, together with a remedial plan.
	- Ensuring all financial obligations are paid on time (e.g. suppliers, leases, interest and borrowing repayments).
	- Ensuring any credit provided to customers is in accordance with the entity’s credit policy and monitor and enforce customer payment terms to help cash flow management.

	° Treasury – Can inform the risk management process by managing the entity’s cash flow position and ensuring the entity has sufficient cash available to meet business and manage any exposure risks related to treasury operations (e.g. commodity pricing or foreign exchange).

	°Legal can inform the risk management process by:
	- Managing any litigation claims.
	- Being proactive in identifying any potential matters.
	- Ensuring the entity has the required and appropriate types of insurance coverage for its operations and locations (e.g. property, public liability, transit, key executive indemnity).
	- Escalating any potential opportunities or issues to the appropriate entity person to consider, together with their advice.

	°Compliance and ethics – Can inform the risks management process by monitoring and reporting the results of the entity’s compliance with its Code of Conduct, laws and regulations (if the entity does not have a stand-alone legal function). It can also conduct fraud investigations and report the result to the appropriate entity person.

	° Risk – Can inform the risk management process by leading the facilitation of the identification, collection, analysis and reporting of all necessary information at entity level, business unit level and transaction level to identify risks that should be managed, as well as the strategies for how to effectively and efficiently manage those risks.

	° Internal audit – Can inform the risk management process by evaluating as part of their annual audit plan the effectiveness of the ERM framework and report results and make recommendations for improvement, identifying areas of potential threats to compliance, entity value, to the appropriate entity person (e.g. business units, senior management and/or those charged with governance).
	- It is important to note that an internal audit should not have direct responsibility for making any risk management decisions or managing the risk management function – they are a separate function. The internal audit annual plan of proposed audits will be based on their own prioritisations of what areas of the entity they want to audit and will refer to the ERM, current business plans, prior audit results and other strategy documents for guidance to assist them with this.

	°Human resources – Can inform the risk management process by having in place the appropriate policies and procedures to ensure employees act in accordance with those policies and procedures when making risk-related decisions, ensuring those decisions are in the entity’s best interests and also appropriately monitoring employee’s compliance with those policies and procedures. Such policies and procedures should include appropriate incentives and disincentives to reward and hold employees accountable.

	° Operations – Can inform the risk management process by ensuring the business runs day-to-day, appropriate quality control is maintained, there are no issues with products/services and any risks are reported. Any issues or potential improvements that can be made should be reported to the appropriate entity person as soon as possible.

	° Customer service – Can inform the risk management process by ensuring customer complaints and feedback are handled promptly, and any identified positive and negative customer trends are reported to the appropriate entity person for consideration.

It is important that the resources the entity allocates to assist it with developing its ERM are appropriately skilled and efficiently and effectively utilised, as the cost of all the inputs to the ERM needs to be efficient and not outweigh their benefits (financial and non-financial terms).

## 9.4.2 Key Components of an ERM

An entity’s ERM framework contains the following components:

• A common risk language/glossary – Key terms used in the entity’s risk policies, guidelines, practices.
• Defines what is risk for the entity.
• Defines the entity’s risk culture or profile, that is, what risk is acceptable or not, and communicates and informs its employees. Additionally, the entity reinforces this through publicly rewarding appropriate risk behaviours and publicly discipling inappropriate risk behaviours.
• Defines and communicates what is the entity’s overall risk appetite. Key aspects include that the risk appetite must be measurable and able to adapt over time as the entity gains experiences and maturity in managing risk.
• Defines the entity’s individual risk tolerances. Key aspects include that the risk tolerance must be measurable and able to adapt over time as the entity gains experiences and maturity in managing such risk.
• Establishes the required internal and external risk reporting. This would include what type of reporting is required (for all risks or just significant risks), how often it must be prepared and to whom it should be reported (ensuring any statutory risk reporting obligations are met).
• Establishes a process for how to identify risks – Who is involved, how often, how to document and report, and type of uncertainty/exposure the entity wants to manage.
• Details all identified risks in a dynamic ‘risk inventory’ list – Who maintains the list, how often is it reviewed and challenged to ensure it remains current and how is it approved and reported.
• Designs how risks are to be consistently rated (benchmarked) – What types of risk rating will be applied (degree of sophistication, simplicity is required) and whether it applies to all risk types, how to rate the risks (e.g. according to their likelihood and potential consequence), who will rate the risks and how often will they be revisited and how and who will review the ratings. Examples of risk ratings are moderate, significant and catastrophic).
• Defines what is acceptable residual risk. This sets consistent measurement techniques for remaining risk that may still be evident after the risk response has been implemented.
• Establishes who within the entity has functional ownership of each type of risk, who is the appropriate risk manager/owner (should be one person) and how much authority do they have for designing, implementing and monitoring risk response plans.
• Ensures that all internal controls that will be relied on in managing risk are appropriately tested to ensure the entity can rely on their effective operation. This will depend on the significance of the risk and the extent of reliance on internal control in managing/mitigating the risk (such internal controls may be tested by an internal audit).
• Designs the risk response (treatment/action plans) to manage the risk commensurate to the risk rating and the cost/benefit analysis, ensuring that all required risk parameters are considered in the design of the treatment and appropriate internal control has been considered. As noted in Section 9.1, Fundamentals of Risk Management, the entity can avoid, tolerate, treat, transfer or terminate risks.
• Designs the risk response (action plans) to take advantage of any opportunities the identified risk has identified, commensurate to the risk rating (opportunity) and the cost/benefit analysis.
• Implementing the risk response, ensuring risk owners have the necessary authority and tools to implement the approved risk response.
• Ensures risk consideration metrics are included in executive and manager level remuneration and incentive programmes (as risk owners).
• Identifies and allocates appropriate resources/training to areas requiring support risk owners in managing individual risks, ensuring that all entity areas are appropriately resourced and trained to identify, assess and report risk.
• Embed risk considerations in routine decisions (encouraging a risk culture). This ensures that all employees with decision-making powers consider any risk downside or upside in their decisions and can access any risk specialists if they need expert guidance or advice.
• Requires risk considerations to be documented in any significant investment evaluations (including cash and resource allocation), financing decisions (e.g. possible mergers, divestments and acquisitions, capital allocations, share buybacks, dividend policies and financing arrangements) or strategic decisions (e.g. new product/service offerings, diversification proposals) and ensures that the documented evaluation process for considering investments and financing considers risk, as does the approval process.
• Ensures the identification, assessment and management of risks is a transparent, continual and dynamic process within the entity and allows for the rapid identification and response to new risks and opportunities. It ensures conversations about risk are encouraged, regular training is provided to employees on understanding risk in decision making and also creates a culture that encourages employees to report any unmanaged risk they see.

• Establishes a Risk Committee and/or Chief Risk Officer (CRO) to monitor and oversight the entity’s strategic risk reporting. This would outline who is responsible for reviewing and approving the entity’s risk register, risk ratings, prioritisation of risks, proposed risk treatments for all ‘significant’ risks and above (both upside and downside risks), and co-ordinating the activities with other business units (e.g. legal, internal audit and finance).

• Explains the responsibilities (if any) of the internal audit function in conducting its compliance activities on components of the ERM.

Ordinarily the entity will have an ERM policy that explains, at the strategic level, how the entity manages its risks, with the detail supporting each key component of the ERM policy contained in separate, or related, policies and procedures.

Such detailed policies and procedures should be incorporated into how the entity sets and updates its strategic objectives (as already explained), key decision-making processes and other operational policies (governing how the entity conducts its business) to ensure risk (upside or downside) is actively incorporated into the ordinary course of managing the entity’s business.

• Examples of key decision-making processes are those related to whether the entity enters into, continues or discontinues key contractual arrangements or key stakeholder relationships, and how it evaluates possible acquisitions, disposals, mergers and other investment activities.

• Examples of operational policies include (but are not limited to) those related to corporate governance; HR policies including those related to setting executive and manager remuneration levels, explaining acceptable/unacceptable employee conduct and consequences; position descriptions for each role within the entity and the levels of responsibility and authority assigned; IT policies (including cybersecurity); legal policies on the entity’s required terms and conditions to be included in any contracts the entity enters into or how it manages contractual issues/disputes; evaluation of possible investments (i.e. acquisitions, mergers or disposals of an entity or shares in an entity) and capital investment projects; workplace health and safety policies, quality assurance policies on the entity’s products or services; and internal or external reporting on compliance, or otherwise, with required laws and regulations.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> ERM provides an entity-wide framework for the entity to proactively identify and manage any risks and to assist them achieve their strategic objectives.

There are two commonly used international ERM frameworks that we will now consider, being those issued by COSO and ISO.

## 9.4.3 COSO ERM Framework

The COSO Enterprise Risk Management – Integrating with Strategy and Performance (June 2017) focuses on the principle that ‘value is maximised when management sets strategy and objectives to strike an optimal balance between growth and return goals and related risks, and efficiently and effectively deploys resources in pursuit of the entity’s objectives’.

COSO ERM is used extensively by entities of all types, sizes and sectors and provides a standardised framework that helps them continuously identify risks, manage those risks within a defined risk appetite, support the achievement of the entity’s strategic objectives and contribute to the entity’s enhanced value. The COSO ERM Framework is principles based and adopts a heavy controls and compliance basis, along with integrating the principles of strategy, risk management, controls and governance. Its key output is to provide the entity with assurance over its ERM framework (see Exhibit 9.7 for an overview of the COSO ERM Framework expressed diagrammatically).
![](DraggedImage-237.png)
The ERM’s five inter-related fundamental components in consecutive order, together with their supporting principles are:

1. Governance and culture (mission, vision and core values). This component sets the ‘tone at the top’ of the entity in terms of ERM oversight, what is risk and what are the acceptable entity values and behaviours:

	a. Exercises board risk oversight – The board of directors oversees the entity’s strategy and performs governance responsibilities to support the executive leadership team in achieving strategy and business objectives.
	b. Establish operating structures – The entity’s structure for how it conducts its business to achieve its strategic objectives.
	c. Defines desired culture – The entity’s definition of its culture and its desired behaviours.
	d. Demonstrates commitment to core values – The entity’s core values that it wishes to uphold and achieve.
	e. Attracts, develops and retains capable individuals – The entity’s people recruited and retained to achieve its strategy and business objectives.

2. Strategy and objective-setting (strategy development). This next component focuses on using the ERM within the strategic planning process to operationalise the governance and culture values into business objectives, ensuring such objectives are aligned to the entity’s risk appetite.

	a. Analyses business context – The entity’s considerations of its trading environment and business context on its risk profile.
	b. Defines risk appetite – The entity’s desired risk appetite for creating, preserving and realising its value.
	c. Evaluates alternative strategies – How the entity evaluates different strategies for achieving its values and how these may impact its risk profile.
	d. Formulates business objectives – When establishing the entity’s business objectives to align and support its strategy.

3. Performance (business objective formulation). This next component focuses on identifying, assessing and responding to all risks that can affect the entity’s business objectives (performance), while maintain a portfolio view of the total residual risk assumed by the entity.

	a. Identifies risk – How the entity identifies risks that may impact strategy and business objectives.
	b. Assesses impact of the risk – How the entity assesses identified risk.
	c. Prioritises risks – For assessed risks, how to prioritise them based on their likelihood and consequence of occurring.
	d. Implements risk responses – Based on prioritised risks, how to select the appropriate risk response.
	e. Develops portfolio view – How the entity views its risk from a portfolio perspective (entity-wide).

4. Review and revision (implementation and performance). This next component considers how well the ERM is operating over time and whether any improvements or revisions are necessary.
	a. Assesses substantial change – How the entity identifies any changes that may impact strategy and business objectives.
	b. Reviews risk and performance – How the entity reviews its risk management performance and considers risk.
	c. Pursues improvement in enterprise risk management – How the entity makes improvements to the ERM based on its considerations of how effective it has been.

5. Information, communication and reporting (enhanced value). This component considers how the ERM shares and reports risk information obtained from internal and external sources around the entity.
	a. Leverages information and technology – How the entity uses its information and technology systems to support the ERM.
	b. Communicates risk information – How the entity communicates risk information to support the ERM.
	c. Reports on risk, culture and performance – How the entity reports risk information throughout the entity.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> COSO ERM provides a readily adaptable entity-wide framework for preparing any type and size of entity’s enterprise risk management plan.

## 9.4.4 ISO 31000 ERM Framework

The international Organization for Standardization issued ISO 31000: ‘Risk Management Principles and Guidelines’ (2018), which provides principles and guidelines on risk management. It defines risk management as ‘a process that provides confidence that planned objectives will be achieved within an acceptable degree of residual risk.’

ISO 31000 provides a principles-based, general framework for implementing risk management and is based on a management process for managing risk. It outlines the principles of what makes risk management effective, the framework in which risk management occurs and the process for managing risk. Its principles emphasise that the framework is intended to fully integrate the management of an entity’s risk into entity culture, values and strategy. Its key risk definitions are consistent with COSO ERM.

Its key principles are:

• That risk management should have net value to the entity (e.g. through generating revenue, enhancing the entity’s reputation, contributing to public safety, improving sustainability, enhancing benefits and reducing harm) and

• That risk management is fully integrated and embedded into the routine decisionmaking process of management of the entity and is no different from other tools the entity uses to manage its business (i.e. it is not an ‘add on’ step to be taken in special circumstances).

It does not provide the entity with any assurance on the results of the implementation. COSO ERM is acknowledged as a more prescriptive standard, and more focused on control, obtaining reasonable assurance on the results of implementing COSO ERM and compliance activities.

The key ISO 31000 risk process to follow is:

• Establish context (note this area is additional to the COSO ERM framework).

• Risk assessment (identification, analysis, evaluation).

• Treat risks.

• Monitor and review.

• Communication and consultation.

• Recording the risk management process.

• Accepting some residual risk (risk remaining after risk is managed) remains and regularly monitor and review the nature and extent of residual risk to ensure that it remains acceptable and within the entity’s risk appetite.

## 9.4.5 Role in Governance

The ERM framework plays a critical role in the good governance of an entity. Governance refers to a system of processes of the entity that explain the way in which the entity plans, organises, directs and controls how it operates to maximise upside risk and minimise downside risk to the entity. It also ensures compliance with all applicable laws and regulations, its culture and values in order for the entity to achieve its mission and strategic objectives and add value. Central to good governance therefore is ensuring the entity has the appropriate risk/return balance to ensure value maximisation. The ERM is central to how the entity systematically achieves this. ERM frameworks are scalable and can be as simple or as complex as the entity requires to manage its risk profile. ERM considers how the entity sets its strategy for how it operates, setting governance principles and business plans that facilitate delivery of the strategy, communicating its risk and opportunity expectations with its employees and other stakeholders, and achieving the best possible performance results. Entities with an ERM framework integrate its governance principles throughout their strategy-setting, culture, values, capabilities and business practices with the aim of proactively managing risk in creating, maintaining, delivering and enhancing value to the entity.

ERM provides an unified snapshot of the entity’s financial and non-financial risks, enabling the entity greater clarity over potential risks, threats (uncertainties) and opportunities in its business operations and allowing it to put in place strategies to most effectively manage those risks, thereby creating and enhancing value to the entity. Examples of these strategies may be to an early response to risk opportunities and implementing appropriate internal controls over key processes at risk of threatening the entity’s compliance with required laws. It also helps the entity identify those factors that do not just represent risk, but also change, and how such change may impact the entity and require the entity to be able to change its business plans or strategies. It therefore assists the entity make better, fully informed, business decisions, and to anticipate, and to respond to change. It also helps safeguard the entity from being unprepared for dealing with unexpected events, assists in identifying any potential opportunities and unforeseen risks, helps to navigate any uncertainties, and avoids any possible financial distress. These are all key aspects of ensuring the entity maintains appropriate governance and compliance processes over its operations.

Key governance benefits of ERM for the entity include:
• Improves governance reporting of risks and opportunities.
• Challenges the entity to ensure that its strategy is aligned, and remains aligned, to the entity’s mission and direction.
• Aligns key decisions to strategy.
• Aligns the entity’s risk appetite to the strategy.
• Facilitates the entity-wide risk identification and management process.
• Helps the entity achieve its strategy by minimising downside risks and maximising upside opportunities.
• Helps the entity identify and actively manage risk challenges, opportunities and improve performance in its operations.
• Links internal control to risks where appropriate.
• Results in an entity-wide risk profile and inventory – financial and non-financial with assigned risk owners and facilitates the preparation of risk treatment plans and monitoring strategies to mitigate assessed risks/costs, while enabling it to take advantage of any identified opportunities.
• Allows the entity to more readily anticipate and respond to change through continuously scanning its environment, thereby providing it with the means to be resilient, to evolve and to thrive.
• Reduces performance variability and increasing competitive advantage through actively managing any risks that may impact the achievement of results, allowing the entity to maximise its outcomes.
• Provides the entity with the basis on which to allocate appropriate resources to manage identified risks and opportunities.
• Encourages better investment decision-making, leading to better rates of return on investments and increased profitability.
• Facilitates compliance with required laws, regulations and community expectations.

Implementing an ERM helps to create trust and build confidence in the entity’s stakeholders that the entity and its senior management have a mindset and a system for actively managing the entity’s risks, is aware of how those risks may impact the entity’s ability to deliver its strategic objectives and has assessed the entity’s resilience (relative strengths and weaknesses) to meet, adapt and manage change.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> ERM provides an entity-wide framework for the entity to proactively identify and manage any risks that present opportunities or threats to the achievement of their strategic objectives.
