# 9.5 PREVENTING FINANCIAL DISTRESS

This section will look at how risk management plays a part in safeguarding the entity’s financial sustainability and preventing it going into financial distress.

## 9.5.1 Managing Financial Sustainability

The entity’s ERM framework is designed to monitor the entity’s key risks, including those already discussed in Section 9.2 on the key Risks Facing by an Entity.

Entities need to manage their operations to ensure their ongoing financial sustainability and to prevent financial distress and possible cessation of trading. Building the entity’s resilience to change and promoting effective risk management promotes its financial sustainability by ensuring it can meet its financial obligations as and when they are due. If the entity cannot meet their financial obligations, it becomes unlikely that the entity can prevent financial distress, avoid bankruptcy and ultimately failure.

An entity can manage its business for sustainability by performing the following types of activities:
• Reviewing business plans and update to make the objectives more realistic and achievable.
• Re-negotiating and restructuring or consolidating their financing facilities – including changing their short- and long-term repayment conditions, amending borrowing covenants and renegotiating their interest rate.
• Focusing on generating profit rather than just sales turnover – managing key product margins to ensure that costs are minimised (i.e. cut discretionary or variable costs) and revenue maximised (i.e. increase prices) to the extent possible.
• Paying all payables on time, to ensure that credit rating and reputation are maintained.
• Ensuring funding guarantees are in place from the parent entity if possible.
• Managing the cash flow position to ensure cash received is always adequate to cover cash required to be paid.
• More proactively managing receivable accounts to ensure that their balances are paid within the credit terms extended by the entity.
• Communicating and negotiating with key suppliers more flexible credit terms for a period to help manage the entity’s cash flow position.
• Ensuring the product/service quality remains at the level the entity is known for.
• Ensuring that investments held are compatible with the entity’s objectives and are not surplus to requirements.
• Ensuring sales of products/services generate a profit and positive cash flow.
• Ensuring that any proposed changes in the entity’s business strategy (e.g. diversification of the entity’s core products/services) are assessed using defined metrics.
• Continuously monitoring their customer’s satisfaction with the entity’s products/ services to ensure that the entity is providing goods/services that their customers want to buy.
• Ensuring the entity can manage through a temporary in economic downturn that may lead to a reduction in customer demand.
• Ensuring investment decisions are made based on the best available information that is reliable and accurate.
• Considering if there have been any actual or potential events that may create significant risks to the entity that it is not actively managing risk and adopt steps to manage those risks (e.g. allocate resources and identify and implement the risk response).

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> The entity has a responsibility to manage the entity to achieve financial sustainability.

## 9.5.2 Identifying and Preventing Financial Risk

Can all identified financial risk be prevented? The answer is no, but entities can put in place strategies to identify, manage and minimise financial risk to prevent it from causing the entity financial distress. As noted above, it is important that the entity have appropriate policies and procedures to manage their financial risk, which are usually embedded within the entity’s corporate governance framework. Refer to Section 9.2.1 for a discussion on what financial risk is.

The entity needs to assign ownership of managing its financial risks arising from its operations to risk owners, who have the appropriate skills and expertise to appropriately manage such risk. Additionally, these risk owners should be given authority to work across divisions/business units, such that the risk is managed from an entity-wide perspective. The risk owners should be subject to appropriate and timely oversight to ensure that if such risks are identified and they are significant in terms of their ability to affect the entity, that the proposed risk mitigation treatment plan is approved and monitored for effectiveness.

There are numerous ways in which financial risk can be identified and managed. Examples include:

• Implementing an enterprise risk management (ERM) framework in order to monitor and report any early indications of distress. Strategies can then be designed, on a timely basis, to address any issues to prevent actual financial distress from occurring. Refer to Section 9.4 on Enterprise Risk Management for more details.
• Monitoring and managing the budget and actual results.
• Calculating financial ratios to gauge key financial health indicators.
• Reviewing the most recent financial statements and annual report.

### 9.5.2.1 Monitoring and Managing the Budget on Actual Results

The entity’s budget is typically set annually and represents the target results the entity wants to achieve for the financial year, based on the entity’s best estimates of key financial information. Additionally, the entity should prepare periodic forecasts updating the budget to reflect the entity’s prediction for what will happen and can cover the budget period as well as a longer time period. The forecast reflects changes in key estimates (e.g. responding to changing market conditions). The entity must always be proactive in managing its budget position and in updating the forecast to help predict the actual financial results. It is important that if the forecast indicates an early risk of default on the entity’s obligations or financial distress that the entity takes steps to investigate and address them immediately. Prevention is better than forecasting failure.

This can also give the entity early indicators if the actual results are tracking significantly lower or higher than budget/forecast and they can investigate and address the reasons if possible and practical. For an entity that sells goods or provides services this is critical to manage as their overall profitability and cash flow position will be determined by volumes sold and margins achieved on those volumes. Volatility in either, or both, of these can lead the entity to experience financial distress if the situation is not carefully managed and alternate strategies employed.

### 9.5.2.2 Cash Flow Management

The entity must also proactively manage its actual cash position. For those entities with forward treasury positions and significant short- and long-term borrowings, cash positions should be managed daily. Cash management in its simplest form is ensuring that the entity has enough cash from its customers when required to pay financial obligations (e.g. banks and suppliers) and avoid any potential financial distress. The entity therefore has to ensure it receives cash from its customers when it is due (according to the trading terms) by proactively managing their accounts receivable book and ensure that it pays all suppliers and financiers when they are due (according to their trading terms and loan agreements).

### 9.5.2.3 Managing Its Key Financial Health Indicators

The entity can calculate financial ratios to identify any early warnings that may indicate a worsening profitability or cash position. A financial ratio is calculated by using historical financial information and is generally classified according to what is measured:

• Profitability (ability of the entity to generate an accounting profit for a given time).
• Liquidity (short-term ability of the entity to pay its financial obligations).
• Solvency (entity’s ability to repay borrowings and pay interest when due).
• Productivity efficiency (use of inventory and fixed assets).

The entity’s size and market capitalisation (if listed) are also important considerations, as generally a larger entity has less risk of financial distress than a smaller entity.

Used in combination, rather than isolation of each other, financial ratios can be good early indicators of issues with the entity’s financial health. They should be used in conjunction with relevant non-financial indicators to give a total view of the entity’s circumstances. Examples of these may be qualitative analysis and commentary on the entity’s financial results from operational and financial areas.

There are numerous financial ratios that may be suitable, depending on the entity’s type (listed/not listed), size (small, medium or large) and industry (goods or services), but the most common ratios are used to identify any possible deterioration in an entity’s financial health (Exhibit 9.9).
![](DraggedImage-238.png)
![](DraggedImage-239.png)

9.5.2.4 Reviewing the Financial Statements

The benefit to be had from the entity’s executive leadership team reviewing the most recent financial statements is to early identify any indicators of future financial distress. Similarly, other external stakeholders, particularly investors and financial institutions will review the financial statements if they are publicly available to ascertain the financial health of the entity. Financial statements are often the basis for actions by regulators or affected parties against directors, companies and auditors, where they identify issues that were not adequately addressed and which caused loss to investors or creditors.

Obtaining and reviewing the entity’s most recent financial statements can help identify where there may be signs of the entity being in financial distress. They can be prepared quarterly, half-yearly or annually and be audited or not. If they have been audited, this gives more credibility and reasonable assurance that they have been prepared in accordance with Hong Kong Financial Reporting Standards (HKFRS) but that will depend on the type of audit opinion (e.g. unmodified/modified). If the entity is listed on the Main Board of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, then the audited financial statements are readily obtained. However, if the entity is not listed, it can be more difficult to obtain the financial statements. The financial statements provide financial and non-financial information that is useful to help determine if the entity is suffering or could potentially suffer financial distress.

Information to consider reviewing includes:
• The Director’s Report to:
° Assess if there has been a significant change in the entity’s operations during the year.
° Review the ‘business review’ (if the entity is listed) and ascertain if there are any highlighted indicators of worsening trading conditions.

• The Statement of Cash Flows to:
° See if operating cash flows are positive or negative. Negative cash flows cannot be sustained for long without fresh capital injections.
° Review financing interest expense to see how much it is costing the entity. Increasing interest expense puts pressure on the entity’s cash flow.

• The Statement of Financial Position to:
° See if the cash at the bank is stable or deteriorating over time.
° See if payables are increasing and receivables are reducing.
° See if borrowings have increased significantly. Also review at what interest rates are being charged. If the rate has increased on the existing portfolio of borrowings compared to a prior period, this could be a sign that the financiers consider the entity at increased risk of default.
° See if inventory levels are increasing (reflecting sales have reduced) or reducing (sales increasing or the entity is not producing as much).
° Consider if working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) is declining or becoming negative.
° Assess the liquidity of assets for rapid conversion to cash, should the entity’s cash position be deteriorating.
° Consider the entity’s level of intangible assets and eliminate these from any financial ratio health measures.

• The Statement of Profit or Loss to:
° Review the profit position and ascertain how this is being generated. 

• The accompanying notes to the financial statements to:
° Assess commitments and contingencies note disclosures to understand what future commitments the entity may have and whether they can meet these. Also consider the possible outcomes of any significant legal cases pending that may affect the entity’s cash position and ultimately its ongoing viability. Examples of contingencies include potential legal claims, product warranty claims, guarantees, regulatory investigations, future borrowing or business commitments, potential acquisitions of other entities and disposals of business units or group entities that may impact the entity’s cash flows and also risks such as the entity’s reputation.
° Review short- and long-term borrowing disclosures to see when repayments are due, interest rates charged and any specific terms and conditions. Also review compliance statements that the entity must make regarding their compliance with borrowing covenants that are standard for all long-term borrowings.
° Review leasing commitments to see how long any significant leases run for. If the lease costs are significant to the entity, these are significant fixed costs that the entity is contractually committed to pay for a long time.
° Look for any recent change in auditors. This could indicate disagreements with the entity’s management about key accounting policies or the auditor assesses that the entity is likely to get into financial difficulties and does not wish to be professionally associated with the entity.
° If applicable, review the auditor’s report and consider if the opinion is clean (unmodified), lacks a material uncertainty with regards to going concern and whether there is any emphasis on matter paragraphs or other matter paragraphs the auditor has included regarding any disagreements on the entity’s accounting policy treatments, particularly those related to revenue recognition or asset valuations. Also, if the entity is listed, review the ‘key audit matters’ disclosures to understand what the areas of most significance to the auditors are in conducting their audit as they can give insights to entity areas of financial risk.
° Review the basis of preparation note to see if the entity has fully complied with the recognition, measurement and disclosure requirements of the HKFRS and the requirements of the Hong Kong Companies Ordinance (Cap.622) (for example, the entity is required to include a ‘business review’ section in their director’s report for listed entities.)
° If there have been any recent changes in HKFRS, review the entity’s note on the likely impact of such standards on the entity’s business that will create any potential future issues for the entity in terms of its borrowing covenants.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> There are various means of identifying factors that may indicate the entity is in financial distress or could potentially go into financial distress.

### Apply and Analyse 12

For Audio Plus HK Entity Limited, describe the key possible financial distress risk it could encounter with its proposed diversification plan into new product offerings and also expanding its operations by building another manufacturing plant.

Analysis

Audio Plus could financially stretch itself in having to fund two major investments concurrently that will not earn cash flow until after their construction is completed. It has to be confident it has sufficient ongoing cash flows to adopt this strategy.

Finally, let’s consider some of the factors that commonly contribute to an entity experiencing financial distress.
---- 
## 9.5.3 Factors Contributing to Financial Distress

There is a myriad of reasons why an entity can get into financial distress. Some examples include, but are not limited to, the entity:
• Not appropriately managing its financial, operational, political, legal and business risks.
• Not managing its assets or liabilities optimally.
• Having declining financial ratios (see Section 9.5.2, e.g. high debt to equity, liquidity, interest coverage, cost to sales and debtor turnover days).
• Not making use of timely, accurate and reliable information to make key decisions. Consequently, such decisions have not been optimal, and the entity has experienced poor profitability.
• Being extremely sensitive to macroeconomic variables (e.g. GDP, interest rates, inflation, employment) and these have been having an adverse effect on the entity.
• Inadequately managing their treasury risk function and has exposures to capital risk (credit, market and operational) or commodity risk, interest rate risk, liquidity risk and foreign exchange risk.
• Having an inappropriate senior management structure and/or reliance on a key person (skills, expertise, decentralisation or centralisation of management).
• Operating in a highly regulated industries which has heavy compliance costs and has imposed limitations on what prices it can charge or products it can sell, limiting profitability, growth and viability.
• Issuing inadequate or untimely profit warnings/downgrades (for listed entities).
• Being highly sensitive to changes in consumer spending or economic conditions.
• Operating in a single industry that is significantly affected by changes in customer sentiment and/or general economic conditions.
• Having experienced sharp, or consistent, share price decline (for listed entities).
• Having recently re-financed their borrowing facilities, resulting in higher borrowing costs.
• Having not managed their cash position resulting in a declining cash position or negative operating cash flows. This may be due to the entity being too slow to collect outstanding accounts receivable. The entity may not be paying all their financial obligations on time (e.g. suppliers, borrowings, employees).
• Being highly leveraged (has more debt than equity and has significant levels of borrowings to service that is taking most or all of its operating cash flows to repay).
• Having high profitability relative to low operating cash flows (suggesting a need to consider a source of profitability).
• Having a high market capitalisation value but reporting lower profits.
• Having net assets measured at an amount exceeding capitalisation of the entity.
• Experiencing poor sales growth or having decrease in sales.
• Experiencing a significant increase in production costs due to increases in key product purchase prices, which the entity has not been able to pass on to their customers.
• Having low gross margins on products/sales, which require high transaction volumes to earn a profit.
• Experiencing increased competition and reducing gross margins.
• Reducing dividends paid to shareholders.
• Undertaking recent restructuring activities (e.g. closing a business unit, incurring employee redundancies).
• Having relatively high fixed expenses relative to its revenue stream.
• Losing key management employees who cannot be readily replaced.
• Having an auditor’s opinion qualified in relation to a going concern or disagreement in accounting treatments.
• Having experienced a reduction in future committed sales or purchases.
• Being unable to obtain capital injections from shareholders or raise debt.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Financial distress can be caused by many factors, either operating in isolation or in combination.



# SUMMARY

This chapter explains the basic concepts of risk management. It also explains what an enterprise risk management framework is and how entities can benefit from implementing this as part of their governance framework. It covers:

• What is risk, identifying risk, assessing risk and responding to risk.

• The importance of considering risk to the entity’s strategic plan.

• The key types of risk affecting an entity, including financial, operational, political, legal and business risks.

• How to evaluate forecasts involving investment projects, including considering all risk types that impact the project, and how likely projects are of achieving their expected results, including using sensitivity, scenario and probability analysis.

• The key components of an effective enterprise risk management framework, including that it is a continuous governance process that can help the entity achieve its strategic objectives.

• A discussion on two of the most widely used enterprise risk management frameworks issued by COSO – Enterprise Risk Management Framework – Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017) and ISO – ISO 31000: Risk Management – Principles and Guidelines (2018).

• The identification of factors that contribute to financial distress in an entity and how to prevent financial distress.

## OPENING CASE

### BUSINESS VALUATION

HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd is a large privately owned entity operating in Hong Kong. At June 20X2, the entity has assets of HK$2.5 billion, total sales revenue of HK$910 million, EBIT of HK$417.5 million and a net profit of HK$378 million. The entity specialises in the following three segment areas in the Hong Kong ports area:

• Owns and rents refrigerated goods warehouse facilities at three locations in Hong Kong;
• Provides contracted professional stevedoring services to one of the ports in Hong Kong; and
• Provides a road-based freight forwarding service for inward cargo.

HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd is currently considering a range of alternatives to determine the best future strategic prospects for the current owners. They recently engaged HK Business Valuations Ltd to perform the following business valuation tasks for the entity:

1. Calculate the total enterprise value of HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd and assess the current fair value of its unlisted privately owned shares in preparation for setting an issue price for equity in an initial public offering of shares.
2. Calculate the total business value of each of the individual business segments of the entity and assess the current fair value of the unlisted privately owned shares allocated to each of the business units.

	Calculate the total enterprise value for the entity and the current fair value of its unlisted privately owned ordinary shares if the entity was to divest itself of:
	a. The stevedoring business and
	b. The freight forwarding service.

3. Calculate the impact on the enterprise value and its share price if it was to sell its Warehouse No. 2 from its refrigerated warehouse business.

4. Calculate the impact on the enterprise value and the share price if the entity was to repay 50% of its current debt through the issuance of redeemable convertible preference shares.

To satisfy the above broad range of business valuation requests, you could use an asset-based, earnings-based, free cash flow-based or comparable business valuation approach. None of the valuation approaches is perfect by itself, so it is important to understand their strengths and weaknesses.

## OVERVIEW

The valuation of a business is the process of determining an entity’s enterprise value or equity value, the value of an entity’s business unit or the value of individual assets and liabilities used by the entity.

Business valuations can be performed for a number of reasons including capital budgeting, financial reporting, investment analysis, merger and acquisition transactions, litigation and taxation purposes.

Before proceeding into this chapter, it is important to distinguish between an observed market price and the value determined via a valuation process. The differences between them should be distinguished so as not to be incorrectly used interchangeably:

• Price is the amount of money paid to obtain a good or service typically via an arm’s length transaction. Price varies based on supply and demand, and economic and political conditions. In other words, a price may be higher or lower than the value of the good or service acquired.

• Valuation is the estimation of an entity’s value, based on variables perceived to be related to the historical, replacement cost, fair value or net realisable value of assets, by reference to future investment returns based on earnings or cash flow or by relative analysis comparisons with similar entities. The purpose of a valuation generally determines the appropriate definition of value and thus affects the analyst’s selection of a valuation approach.

When performing a business valuation, it is important to note that valuations contain both an objective and a subjective element. The objective element reflects the value of the asset per se, that is, the value assigned to an asset in an efficient market or reflects either the relative or the intrinsic value of an asset through the use of one or more of the generally accepted valuation approaches discussed below. The subjective element is linked to the characteristics of the parties to the transaction, each of whom seeks to maximise their own benefits and brings to the transaction their particular biases arising from their own perceptions.

As discussed in Chapter 7, critical to the business valuation process is the belief that the value of an entity is equal to the value of the capital used to fund the entity. As such, the following three relationships are important for determining the enterprise value, the value of equity and debt for an entity:

• Enterprise Value:
- Enterprise Value = Value of Equity + Value of Debt + Value of Preference Shares - Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

- equity value
- Debt

Subject to any legal or regulatory constraints, when performing valuations to determine the fair value of entities, divisions within entities and individual assets analysts can apply any of the following approaches:

• Asset-based approaches – These approaches examine the value of an entity’s assets and liabilities to identify the entity’s net asset value, which is assumed equal to the entity’s equity value. This approach relies heavily on financial reporting information.

• Earnings-based approaches – These approaches rely on earnings to estimate an entity’s fundamental value. This model is based on the premise that positive income such as dividends and retained earnings leads to shareholder value creation.

• Discounted cash flow-based approaches – These approaches are based on the fundamental idea that the value of an entity is the present value of expected future cash flows arising from the operating activities of the entity. Given that entities are regarded as a series of projects involving the use of assets, the value of an entity, the divisions within entities and both assets and liabilities can be estimated using this approach.

• Comparable approaches – These approaches identify whether an entity is fairly valued relative to some benchmark or a comparable group of entities in the same sector. Also known as relative valuation methods, these approaches assume that an entity’s value is based on the value of similar entities or transactions involving comparable entities.

As shown above, there is a variety of ways to place a value on an entity, its divisions, its assets and liabilities or the shares in an unlisted entity. As such, many analysts will apply different methods of valuation and compare the values they produce so as to provide a reasonable estimate. When using a variety of methods, the results obtained may be similar to each other. However, caution needs to be exercised in interpreting the results. Each method is based on different assumptions, data and modelling approaches. Hence the value of the same entity may differ due to the different assumptions inherent for each method.

In this chapter, students will learn how to:
- • Explain potential reasons for valuing entities or business units including IPOs, mergers and acquisitions and disposals.
- • Identify and apply appropriate valuation models for the valuation of debt including irredeemable debt, redeemable debt, convertible debt and preference shares.
- • Identify and apply appropriate valuation models for the valuation of shares, including asset-based valuation models, earnings-based valuation models, cash flow-based valuation models and comparable methods.
- • Recommend an appropriate valuation/range of valuations for a given business scenario.
- • Explain the theoretical and practical limitations of the various valuation models.

## 10.1 COMMON REASONS FOR BUSINESS VALUATION

In corporate finance and management accounting, business valuation is a frequent theme. It arises whenever an entity is considering investing in a new venture or in the shares or debt of another entity. Determining the value of an entity is also a key first step in determining the value of the shares of an entity (other factors to consider include dividends, cash flow and future growth projections).

Understanding the factors that determine the value of an entity and how to estimate that value is a reasonable prerequisite for making sensible decisions regarding: the performance of an entity; whether debt or equity securities issued by an entity are fairly priced, over-priced or under-priced relative to their current estimated intrinsic value and relative to the prices of comparable securities; the value of an entity and its equity when transitioning from being privately owned to a public offering of shares; evaluating corporate events such as mergers, acquisitions, divestments, spin-offs and leveraged buy-outs; and inferring market expectations about the future prospects of the entity.

Performing business valuations will always require some degree of judgement and the use of assumptions. Differences may exist when valuing individual assets and liabilities and the overall enterprise and its equity. Analysts should consider:

• The circumstances and purpose of the valuation, which may suggest some valuation approaches are better suited than others. For example, not all valuation approaches are suitable if an entity is in financial distress or if an entity has a medium- to long-term strategy that differs from the near term.
• Any model limitations due to factors such as the data availability and limitations, the degree of model complexity and the mathematical form of the valuation models.
• The impact of sensitivity of model assumptions and judgements.

Ideally, business valuation approaches should give priority to the objective element of valuations. However, analysts will inevitably need to contend with the potential impact of the subjective element. When the analysis requires high levels of subjectivity, analysts will rely on their own experience based on cases they have dealt with in the past. Recognition of the subjective element in performing a business valuation is especially important if it can influence the choice of the valuation method and the processing of data.

Consistent with Learning Outcome 10.01.01, this section will introduce you to the most common reasons why business valuations are performed.

Business valuations can be used by both buyers and sellers – the buyer will want to know the maximum price to pay and the seller will want to know the minimum price that they would accept.

The primary reasons why business valuations are performed are: for the initial public offering of shares when an entity moves from being privately owned to publicly owned and traded on an exchange; for the purpose of assessing the impact of merger and acquisition activities on the enterprise value; and the disposal of assets or business segments arising from either an orderly sale or a liquidation process. These scenarios are discussed briefly in Sections 10.1.1–10.1.3.

Other reasons why business valuations are performed include:
• Valuing assets for use as collateral for a debt issuance.
• Valuing assets for the purpose of sale or disposal.
• Assessing the impacts of corporate restructurings.
• Valuing assets and liabilities for financial reporting purposes.
• Assessing the impacts of taxation, especially on the sale of assets or repayment of liabilities.
• Valuing the entity for dispute resolution purposes, for example, in the context of a dispute between private-equity shareholders.
• Facilitating insolvency and bankruptcy proceedings.
• Determining executive compensation where the compensation is conditional upon changes in entity enterprise value or shareholder equity value.
• Identifying how factors, such as products, business lines and the supply chain, affect the enterprise value in order to better understand which strategies are most effective.
• Assisting with the identification of where an entity might be experiencing losses or underperforming, so as to improve and streamline operations.
• Estate planning, divorce proceedings or on the death of a shareholder for reasons associated with probate and taxation.

### 10.1.1 Initial Public Offerings (IPOs)

As discussed in Chapter 7, ordinary shares in an entity can be held either as privately owned shares or publicly owned shares. If the shares are privately owned, the entity is said to be privately owned. If shares are publicly owned, the shares are typically listed and traded on an exchange and the entity is said to be a public entity.

Private entities are **usually** owned by **a small number of shareholders** (such as family members, friends, professional investors or venture capitalists). An initial public offering (IPO) is the **first public offering of ordinary shares** by an entity that was previously privately owned. In doing so the entity changes from being a private entity, which is owned by just a few people, into a public entity that is owned by a large number of shareholders. Public entities are then typically** listed on a stock exchange** to allow the trading of shares among investors.

An example of a transition from being privately owned to undertaking a public offering and listing of shares is discussed in the Opening Case of this chapter, where business valuation approaches are needed:

- • To calculate the total enterprise value of HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd and
1. • To assess the current fair value of its unlisted privately owned shares in preparation for setting an issue price for equity in an initial public offering of shares.

In Hong Kong, as is the case in most countries in the world, at the time of issuance of public shares, a prospectus must be issued – the Companies Ordinance (CO). This ordinance specifies the prospectus requirements for entities incorporated in Hong Kong (Part II), for entities incorporated outside Hong Kong (Part XI) and small entities (the Third Schedule).

The prospectus must **contain information prescribed in statutory requirements**, such as any **material contracts**, **asset valuation reports**, **accountant’s reports** and sufficient particulars and information to enable a reasonable person to form a valid and justifiable opinion of the offer price of the shares being issued and the financial condition and profitability of the entity at the time of the issuance of the prospectus.

The offer price is typically negotiated by the entity, the sponsor, the underwriters and the selling shareholders. The price discovery process may involve the preparation of pre-deal business valuation reports. The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) Code of Conduct regulates reports by analysts covering entities listed or about to be listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

The pre-deal business valuation research reports can play an important role in price discovery in the IPO process. They are typically prepared by the syndicate of underwriters to provide an analysis of a listing applicant, including its current and future business operations and prospects. Forecasts, projections and valuations may be included in the research reports if they are prepared independently, but they must not include specific valuation figures, except for valuation ranges and discussion of valuation approaches.

To facilitate the pricing of ordinary shares under changing market conditions and subtle variation in view of their valuation, the price of publicly offered shares is often disclosed as an offer price range, rather than a fixed offer price. As discussed in Chapter 7, this offer price range is set based on a broad consultation prior to the offer being made.

Also, as discussed in Chapter 7, when debt is issued via a public issuance in the form of a bond, convertible bond, floating rate note or medium-term note, the issuing entity and prospective investors will also want to value the particular financial instruments.

### 10.1.2 Mergers and Acquisitions

The concept of mergers and acquisitions (M&A) is a generic term that can be defined as a process in which two or more entities are combined to share their assets and resources.

Although potentially similar in outcome, mergers and acquisitions are actually different in their execution.

Usually mergers occur in a friendly setting where executives from the respective entities participate in a due diligence process to ensure a successful combination of all parts of the organisations. Typically, when there is a merger the capital of the merged entity is equal to the sum of the capital of the entities involved in the merger deal and a new legal entity is created from the merging of the entities, which lose their legal status as separate entities.

Structurally, a merger involves an integration among entities either as a merger by incorporation or by union.

A merger by incorporation involves the annulment of the acquired entity, when the acquiring entity incorporates the acquired entity. This can occur in one of the following ways:

• The acquiring entity pays cash for the shares of the acquired entity or exchanges new shares issued by itself for the shares of the acquired entity, according to a well-defined exchange ratio. The shares of the acquired entity are then annulled.

• The acquiring entity simply annuls the shares of the acquired entity because it already owns all the shares of the acquired entity.

• The acquiring entity, which already owns a percentage of the shares of the target entity, exchanges newly issued shares for shares of the acquired entity that it does not yet own. All of the shares of the target entity are then annulled by the acquiring entity.

A merger by union involves the annulment of all pre-existing entities and the formation of a new entity comprising the pre-existing entities. Usually in this form of merger, the entire capital of the merged entities is transferred to the new entity and the shareholders of the merged entities become the shareholders of the new merged entity.

An acquisition (sometimes also called a takeover) involves an acquiring entity buying all of the shares of a target entity, or sufficient of those shares to obtain a controlling interest in the target entity. Acquisitions can be friendly or hostile. In the latter case, the target entity does not accept the takeover bid and adopts defensive actions to avoid being acquired.

M&A operations should be differentiated from the simple acquisitions of assets or business units of an entity. In the latter cases, the payment for the acquired assets is made directly to the vendor entity, not to its shareholders.

In Hong Kong, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) administers ‘The Codes on Takeovers and Mergers and Share Buy-backs’ (Codes) that governs the conduct of public M&A activity. The Codes apply to takeovers and mergers involving public companies in Hong Kong, companies with a primary listing of their equity securities in Hong Kong and real estate investment trusts with a primary listing of their units in Hong Kong.

Other ways by which one entity can acquire another entity include:

• Leveraged buy-out – A strategy whereby an acquirer (typically a private equity entity) acquires a target entity using a combination of debt and equity to fund the purchase. The level of debt is typically greater than 50% of the asset value of the target entity.

• Management buy-out – A form of acquisition where an entity’s existing managers acquire a large part or all of the entity from either the parent entity or from the private owners.

• Proxy contest – A strategy used in a hostile acquisition whereby the acquiring entity attempts to convince shareholders to use their proxy votes to install new management that is open to the takeover.


• Tender offer – A public offer by an individual, group of individuals or by an entity who want to acquire a substantial percentage of an entity’s shares. The purpose of the acquisition is to accumulate enough ordinary shares to either get a major presence on or completely take over the entity. As such, the tender is a conditional offer to buy ordinary shares. The offer is made at a fixed price, usually at a premium over the current market price. The offer is contingent on shareholders tendering a fixed number of their shares, else the tender is void and no shares will be transferred.

Regardless of the form by which the M&A occurs, the following steps are critical to the process:
- 1. The identification and evaluation of the target entity. Once an entity has been identified as a potential candidate for a merger or acquisition, it must be evaluated to establish if it has the required characteristics to create value for the acquirer.
- 2. A valuation of the equity of the target entity is undertaken. The valuation would incorporate any estimated economies due to synergistic effects and take account of any negative factors, such as poor management and unfamiliar industry/country, that would cause a discount in the target’s market price.
- 3. The valuation from Step 2 is compared to the current market price of the target entity.

If the value is above the market price, a bid is made. Any transaction costs need to be explicitly considered.

There are two main methods to obtain control of a public entity: a general offer or a scheme of arrangement.

A general offer to purchase a target entity’s shares can occur either via cash or through a share offer. A bidder makes an offer to the target’s shareholders to acquire all of the shares not already held by the acquirer. All offers must be conditional on the bidder receiving sufficient acceptances that, together with the shares already held, result in the bidder holding more than a regulated level of the controlling rights in the target. The Hong Kong Stock Exchange Main Board Listing Rule 1.01 defines ‘controlling shareholder’ as any person who is, or group of persons who together are: permitted to exercise or control the exercise of 30% (or such other amount as may from time to time be specified in the Codes on Takeovers and Mergers and Share Buy-backs as being the level for triggering a mandatory general offer) or more of the voting power at general meetings of the issuer or in a position to control the composition of a majority of the board of directors of the issuer.

A scheme of arrangement is a statutory process through which a court can sanction proposed arrangements between an entity and its shareholders. Typically, it allows for the cancellation of all the shares in a target entity (except for those owned by the bidder) in return for a cash or non-cash consideration from the bidder.

If there is a merger, the purchase price is agreed between the acquirer and target entity along with the method used to facilitate the merger.

If there is an acquisition, shareholders of the target entity can contest the takeover bid in order to extract a higher price from the acquirer. In contrast, the entity’s managers may contest the takeover because they believe their jobs may be at risk in the merged entity even though shareholders may achieve a higher price. Such protective action by managers may lead to a management buy-out counter offer to shareholders.

Business valuation approaches are very important in determining the value of a target entity and the value of the benefits arising from the merger or acquisition. The more accurate and realistic the valuation is, the more accurate the price to be paid will be.

An example of the use of business valuations in the context of an M&A transaction is if HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd wanted to assess the impact on its enterprise value and the value of its ordinary shares if it was to expand its stevedoring operations through an acquisition or merger with another stevedoring entity.

In preparation for merger and acquisition activities, entities may engage in restructuring activities. These activities include moving assets and business activities between divisions, centralised into a single division or decentralised across the entity. For example, a restructuring may involve the sale of individual assets or divisions within the entity. The sale of assets should result in positive NPV outcomes for both the seller of the assets and the entity acquiring the assets. Entities may also need to be broken up and sold for liquidation purposes.

When an entire business unit needs to be sold, this normally occurs via either a ‘spin off’ or a ‘carve out’.

A spin off involves the creation of an independent entity formed by detaching part of a parent entity’s assets and operations. Shares in the new entity are distributed to the parent entity’s shareholders.

A carve out is similar to a spin off, except that shares in the new entity are not given to existing shareholders but are sold in a public offering.

An example of a carve out is shown in the Opening Case, where HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd wants to calculate the total enterprise value for the entity and the current fair value of its unlisted privately owned shares if the entity was to divest itself of:

• The stevedoring business and
• The freight forwarding service.

The primary motives for entering into restructuring activities include:

• To provide a sharper focus for management who may lack the skill to manage different types of businesses.
• To correct strategic mistakes of management.
• To reflect new information about the value of various parts of the entity from the perspective of another party.

Mergers and acquisitions will be discussed in greater detail in Chapter 11.

### 10.1.3 Disposals

From time to time entities engage in the disposal of assets across their business activities. Each of these will directly impact an entity’s valuation.

Disposal of assets may involve the sale, abandonment or removal of used or outdated assets. When disposing of assets, consideration needs to be given to the current value of the assets involved, the book value of the assets as recorded in the financial statements and the assets’ depreciation. Consideration also needs to be given to the taxation consequences of the disposal, subject to whether the disposal value of the asset is above or below its depreciated value.

An example of a restructuring transaction is shown in the Opening Case, where HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd wants to calculate the impact on the enterprise value and its share price if it was to sell its Warehouse No. 2 from its refrigerated warehouse business.

C Business valuations involve the use of a range of generally accepted valuation techniques to perform the valuation.

## 10.2 INFORMATION REQUIREMENTS AND LIMITATIONS FOR VALUATION

There is a wide range of information that will be needed in order to value a business. In making business valuation decisions, analysts ordinarily consider both financial and non-financial information.

In order to perform a business valuation, an analyst will typically need to understand the economy and industry within which the entity operates and the factors affecting the earnings, growth expectations and risks of the individual entity being valued. The analyst will typically require at least five years (if possible) of financial statements and may need to perform an on-site visit to check operations and the physical assets of the business. The analyst will also consider any intangible assets and the future outlook of the entity and will compare the business to similar businesses operating in the market.

Consistent with Learning Outcome 10.01.02, this section will identify information requirements for undertaking a valuation and explain the limitations of different types of information.

### 10.2.1 Information Requirements

The valuation process requires the following three fundamental steps, which are all information dependent:

• Context analysis;
• Analysis of financial statements; and
• Identification of an appropriate valuation method.

#### 10.2.1.1 Context Analysis

In performing a context analysis, the analyst will need to identify and consider: the potential impact of both external and internal factors on the value of the enterprise; divisions within the entity; individual assets; and equity and debt financial instruments.

The prospects of individual entities are directly tied to the economic environment and the industry within which the entity operates. Each of the following external factors can affect the level of aggregate business production, expected growth rates of earnings and expected rates of return on assets, debt and equity:

• Government monetary policy. This directly affects the level of interest rates, inflation levels and changes in the rate of growth of the supply of money within the local and global economy. Each country has a central bank that engages, via open market operations, in the buying and selling of government debt securities. This activity affects the level of price of these securities (and the level of interest rates), the money supply and subsequently the level of liquidity of funding within the economy.

Bond purchases by the central bank result in an increase in bond prices, lower interest rates and an increase in the money supply. In contrast, bond sales result in decreased bond prices, higher interest rates and a decrease in the money supply. Decreasing the money supply restricts the level of economic activity in the economy and is often used to fight inflation. Increasing the money supply adds to the availability of money and thereby can increase economic activity. This is referred to as the transmission mechanism of monetary policy whereby changes in the money supply will affect the level of interest rates and inflation expectations. Changes in interest rates will affect the level of economic activity in relation to savings and investments, the availability of cash flow, asset prices and levels of wealth and exchange rates. Each of these factors impact the level of gross domestic product within the economy and therefore affect the general levels of confidence in the future prospects of the economy, share prices and levels of debt.

• Government fiscal policy. This directly affects the level of government expenditure on infrastructure projects and the amount of revenue collected from taxation. Increases in government expenditure would be viewed as positive news by entities operating in areas that supply inputs to public infrastructure projects (for example, in bridge construction, providers of concrete, steel and asphalt production may benefit). Also, employees of these entities will have wages to spend on consumer goods, which can further increase the growth of the economy. In relation to taxation, changes in the corporate tax rate, depreciation allowances, sales taxes and taxation of investor profits can all impact the levels of earnings, the cost of debt, the cost of equity and the weighted average cost of capital.

Other economic factors that will affect the performance of entities and hence the valuation of entities include:

• Growth in gross domestic product;
• Changes in the rate of inflation;
• Changes in foreign exchange rates;
• Changes in the rate of unemployment;
• Changes in the level of industrial production and manufacturing;
• Introduction of economic reforms; and
• Changes in sovereign debt ratings.

Information about the state of the economy (i.e. whether the economy is in growth or recession period) and the level of interest rates can affect all valuations in an economy. A weakening economy can lead to a reassessment of economic growth rates, although the effect on cash flow and earnings is likely to be largest in entities most susceptible to changes in the economic cycle. Similarly, an increase in interest rates will affect the fair value of most investments, though to varying degrees.

An entity’s performance is generally tied directly to economic and other factors that affect its end markets (i.e. the broad underlying markets into which an entity sells its products and services). For example, an entity that sells products into the construction industry is susceptible to macroeconomic factors that affect the overall construction industry, such as the level of economic activity, interest rates and the level of unemployment.

Information also needs to be sourced and examined about the following external factors at the industry level that may affect the business valuation:

• Size and contribution to GDP of the industry;
• Maturity of the industry;
• Short-term and long-term industry outlook;
• Degree of competition in the industry;
• Opportunities for growth within the industry and factors affecting such growth;
• Barriers to entry into the industry; and
• Current and expected government legislation.

New information that signals a change that will impact at the industry level can affect the valuations of all entities in a particular industry. For example, if the government decides to legislate significant health and safety restrictions in relation to the production of pyrotechnics, this has the potential to directly affect the operating costs of those entities involved in the manufacture of fireworks and other pyrotechnic products. All entities in the industry will be affected.

Internal factors relevant to business valuations include those that will directly affect an entity’s valuation, including the entity’s history, its shareholders and its governance. In this context, analysts will require information about:

• The age and maturity of the entity;
• The entity’s strategy;
• Competitive advantages of the entity being valued;
• Details of all majority shareholders;
• Details of the entity’s organisational structure;
• Membership of the board of directors;
• Corporate executive committee structure;
• Relationships with suppliers and customers;
• Details of any current or pending legal proceedings and/or disputes in arbitration;
• Details of the entity’s compliance with environmental and/or health and safety requirements and with any licences and registrations; and
• The impact of the departure of existing business owners and/or management.

The primary sources of information about external factors include government agencies such as the Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department (C&SD), which is the provider of major social and economic official statistics in Hong Kong, and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which reports financial data. Data can be obtained from their respective web pages or from information platforms such as Bloomberg.

Industry bodies and trade associations provide detailed information about the issues relevant to their particular industries and act as lobbyists for the interests of their industries. For example, the Hong Kong Auto Parts Industry Association undertakes a number of activities to support the interests of entities within the automotive components manufacturing industry, including:

• Promoting communication, interaction and co-operation among members;
• Establishing liaison with, and conveyance of collective opinions to, government bodies and industrial or trade organisations;
• Promoting business and technical co-operation with potential partners; and
• Developing a close network and relationship with the automotive industries in mainland China and overseas.

Also, professional bodies represent the interests of professional groups. For example, the HKICPA serves the business community and public interest of Hong Kong and contributes to the sustainable development of Hong Kong as a leading international business and financial center. The HKICPA is the only professional accounting body of Hong Kong to register and issue practicing certificates to Certified Public Accountants in Hong Kong and undertakes a number of activities including providing education and training and promoting the accountancy profession both in Hong Kong and overseas.

#### 10.2.1.2 Analysis of Financial Statements and Operational Information

Through analysis of an entity’s financial statements and operational information, normally spanning the past five years, the past performance of an entity and insights regarding its future prospects can be obtained. Areas of particular interest include:

• Information about existing shareholders, including the identity of the shareholders and the type and number of shares held;
• Existing financial commitments including debt, leases and any other financial contracts including guarantees, derivative financial instruments and contingent liabilities;
• The capital structure of the entity;
• Earnings and components of earnings such as sales, gross profit, EBITDA, EBIT and net profit;
• Cash flow budgets and future budget projections;
• Details of major sales contracts including customer details, percentage of sales, amounts sold historically and amounts currently contracted and details of any embedded optionality to change major details of the contracts;
• Details of major inventory supply contracts, identifying counterparties and amounts purchased historically and currently contracted and details of any embedded optionality to change major details of the contracts;
• Accounts receivable and accounts payable aged schedules (as discussed in Chapter 6);
• Inventory, classified by type, age and usage;
• Non-current assets and their depreciation schedules, estimated useful lives and residual values; and
• Details of all intangible assets, such as R&D, customer lists, brand names, trademarks and mastheads that are not recognised in the financial statements.

Analysis of historical financial performance provides valuable insights for developing defensible assumptions for forecasting the future earnings and growth prospects of an entity as well as identifying potential risk factors. For mature entities in non-cyclical sectors, indicators such as past growth rates, profit margins, leverage, liquidity and efficiency ratios, such as inventory turnover, are usually a reliable indicator of future performance. It is often useful to review historical levels of these measures from financial data with adjustments made for nonrecurring items and recent events, as appropriate, to provide a normalised basis for projecting financial performance or alternatively obtain industry consensus forecasts. This information is used to gain an understanding of the:

• Earnings capacity of the entity;
• Entity’s ability to meet its obligations;
• Entity’s ability to generate positive cash flows;
• Profitability of the entity and the expected growth of earnings over time;
• Cost of equity and debt and the weighted average cost of capital;
• Credit quality of the entity; and
• Financial and operating risk exposures of the entity.

This list of financial and operational data is not exhaustive. The most common sources for public entity financial data are required filings with national regulatory bodies, as well as financial statements, earnings announcements, investor presentations, equity research reports, consensus estimates, press releases and current and historical share prices, all of which are available via a number of different web-based information platforms.

A number of the data providers take financial statements and restate them using pro-forma presentations that facilitate direct comparison between amounts and also compute financial ratios using assumptions that are specific to the platform. Company credit ratings can also be found on Bloomberg or alternatively can be directly sourced from the official Moody’s, S&P and Fitch websites.

Details of some current and future operational information, such as sales and supply contract information and budget projections, may not be publicly available via financial statements or in entity annual reports. This data may need to be extracted from alternative sources as identified above or via information made available when the entity is engaging in merger and acquisition activities.

#### 10.2.1.3 Choice of Valuation Approach

When identifying the valuation approach to apply, analysts need to consider the purpose of the valuation, the availability of external and internal information, the documentation required to support the analysis, the assumptions required to support the approach used and the advantages and disadvantages of each of the valuation approaches. This will be discussed in more detail in Sections 10.3–10.5 of this chapter.

Each method of valuation provides an estimate of value. It is unlikely that one method of valuation would be used in isolation and there is no ’correct’ valuation as such. Several valuations might be made, each using a different method or different assumptions.

The valuations could then be compared and a final price could be reached based on the estimates made.

What criteria should be applied when determining the valuation approach to be used? In determining the appropriate valuation technique to apply it is necessary to consider:
- • The purpose to which the valuation will be applied, especially given the characteristics of the entity being valued, and
- • The availability and quality of data available for the valuation and the amount of assumptions and judgement required to perform the valuation.

### 10.2.2 Information Limitations

All valuations require information; however, due to information gaps, information asymmetries and difficulties in predicting future outcomes when relevant future financial and non-financial information is unknown, problems can arise in the use of the information discussed in Section 10.2.1. Information gaps arise when information is not available or observable and the analyst must make accommodating assumptions regarding the information. In contrast, information asymmetries arise because of differences in the capacity of relevant parties to access information. For example, if an entity was performing a hostile takeover of another entity, the acquirer would only have access to public information for an analysis. In contrast, if two entities were merging, they would share information to perform their business valuations.

Significant differences exist between the financial information and internal context information available for public entities as opposed to that available for privately owned entities. This is principally due to the availability of broker and analyst research reports.

Regulatory agencies impose strict requirements on publicly listed entities concerning the provision of information to the public and penalties for non-compliance, including the possibility of de-listing from the stock exchange if information is not made available in a timely manner. In contrast, privately owned entities typically have a much lower threshold in terms of public information reporting requirements. Accordingly, it is much easier for an analyst to obtain financial information about a listed entity as opposed to a private entity and this can complicate the use of some of the valuation techniques.

The primary source of financial information about an entity’s assets, earnings and capital structure is the entity’s financial statements. However, there are potential limitations in using this information as a result of:
- • Limitations of prevailing accounting standards that may result in financial statements omitting information that would be relevant for business valuation purposes. For example, assets may be measured at amortised cost and certain intangible assets and liabilities, such as litigation liabilities, may not be recognised.
- • Differences in accounting standards and practices across countries may affect comparisons between entities operating in different countries.
- • Different levels of aggregation may be applied to financial information to make the information understandable to users of the financial statements (i.e. investors, creditors, etc.). This may result in the financial statements not providing information that is sufficiently granular for analysts wishing to use the information for business valuation purposes.

This section has discussed the primary information requirements for performing a business valuation and some of the limitations associated with the use of the information.

## 10.3 VALUATION MODELS FOR DEBT

As discussed in Chapter 7, entities use a range of both short-term and long-term debt financial instruments for both funding and investment purposes. Short-term debt is typically used to fund short-term working capital requirements and to fund and provide investment opportunities for liquidity management activities, whilst longer term debt is typically used to fund entities’ assets and long-term project activities.

The amount of debt used to fund an entity directly affects the capital structure and the cost of capital. High levels of debt relative to equity expose an entity to interest rate risk, liquidity risk and funding risk. When performing a business valuation, it is important to note that the value of an entity is equal to the value of the capital used to fund the entity as follows:

> Enterprise Value = Value of Equity + Value of Debt Value of Preference Shares - Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

The total value of debt reflects the sum of the value of each of the range of individual debt items used by an entity. The value of each item will be a function of:

• The type of debt financial instrument;
• The term to maturity of the debt (longer dated debt is riskier than short dated debt);
• Whether the debt is for a fixed term, in perpetuity or subject to any optionality that can result in early termination or extension of the debt maturity. Difficulty can arise in determining future cash flows if the cash flows from the debt can be altered by either the issuer or the investor changing the timing of the principal or coupon payments or through the conversion of debt into equity;
• Whether the debt principal is repayable at maturity, amortises over time or has a structured repayment schedule;
• Whether interest rates applicable to the debt are at a fixed or floating rate;
• The size of the debt relative to total assets and equity;
• The credit quality of the issuer, which will affect the credit rating and credit spread of the debt;
• Whether the debt is actively market traded or held by investors with only limited trading;
• The seniority of the debt – as discussed in Chapter 7, the seniority of the debt reflects the order in which the debt will be redeemed in the event that the entity is placed into administration, i.e. higher ranked or senior debt will be redeemed prior to lower ranked junior debt;
• Whether the debt is secured or unsecured; and
• The types of covenants applied.

The term sheet for each debt item will specify the terms of the debt and can be used by the analyst to perform the valuation. As discussed in Chapter 7, the above characteristics will affect the value of debt, which is typically valued by discounting future cash flows by the yield to maturity yield that reflects the relationship between the market price of the debt instrument and the expected cash flows payable under the terms of the instrument. The yield to maturity is equivalent to the internal rate of return of the debt assuming that it is held to maturity and that it does not default.

In contrast, a debt instrument’s expected return is less easily calculated. This return needs to consider the probability of future default and the recovery rate (i.e. the percentage of its principal that holders can expect to recover in the case of default). Very few entities experience a single default event but rather default can happen in stages, through the gradual degradation of the issuing entity’ s creditworthiness. To complicate matters further, as entities experience default often the maintenance and quality of assets held as collateral may also decline in quality, affecting the value of the assets offered as collateral.

If the yield to maturity is consistent with the market’s expectations of the probability of default of the issuer and the recovery rate, then the yield to maturity will be equal to the expected yield on the debt.

An entity’s debt can be classified as traded or non-traded debt. Traded debt will be debt available for trading in public markets either on exchanges or in the over-the-counter market. This will often include debt instruments such as coupon bonds and convertible notes. In contrast, non-traded debt is not typically available for trading and is privately held by the lenders. Examples include term bank loans, overdrafts and bonds that have been privately issued to only a few investors who plan to hold the bonds until maturity.

Long-term debt is normally reported at amortised cost in the financial statements. It is the analysts’ responsibility to calculate the fair value, which will be of major importance when calculating the entity’s total enterprise value.

The fair value of debt refers to the price that would be paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date (HKFRS 13.9).

This value will normally differ from the carrying amount of the debt instrument on an entity’s statement of financial position because debt is normally measured on an amortised cost basis rather than at fair value.

An important aspect of the valuation of debt is to consider the impact of taxation on the valuation process. If an entity issues debt, taxation benefits will arise from the tax shield attached to the interest expense. The amounts allowed as deductions when calculating an organisation’s tax liability are in effect a refund and therefore constitute a cash inflow that should be considered as part of the evaluation of any borrowing.

As discussed in Chapter 7, taxation directly affects both the value of the interest paid and the overall post-tax cost of debt. Caution is needed, however, as tax benefits may differ between jurisdictions and also be affected by the amount and timing of interest cash outflows (in most jurisdictions, tax is also payable on interest received from investments). Some analysts therefore perform debt valuation on both a pre- and post-tax basis. However, as a general rule, there should only be a small difference between the value of debt on a pre-tax and post-tax basis.

Consistent with Learning Outcome 10.01.04, this section will apply appropriate models for the valuation of debt including models for irredeemable debt, redeemable debt, convertible debt and preference shares. Prior to doing so, this section will introduce and discuss some general approaches to the valuation of debt securities.

### 10.3.1 Alternative Approaches to Debt Valuation

Valuation of debt involves calculation of the current value at which debt would be traded between market participants at the measurement date. This value should reflect the discounted value of the expected fixed and/or floating rate cash flows or coupons payable on the debt, any optionality to extend or shorten the term to maturity of the debt or the ability to convert the debt into equity. Valuation of debt requires a suitable discount rate that reflects the current yield to maturity of the debt instrument (incorporating the current credit spread for the entity).

For valuation purposes, priority should be given to using market prices and/or observed yields to maturity to value all debt instruments. However, in some cases there is no observable market price or yield to maturity for the debt, or there is a lack of liquidity in trading that affects the observed values. In such cases, it may be necessary to use either comparable data or build complex models that reflect the properties of the debt being priced.

In relation to debt valuation, the comparable approach requires the analysis of comparable market traded financial instruments. Information can be gathered about other issuances by similar entities or entities from the same or related industries with similar credit ratings. Comparable data can be obtained in one of two ways:

- • By considering comparable debt instruments issued by similarly rated entities from similar or related industries (this enables the analyst to gather prices, coupon details, terms to maturity and yields to maturity). As part of performing this analysis, the analyst will consider debt issuances by sectors, structure of the issues and the source of the issues.
- • By considering yield spreads inferred directly from derivative instruments such as credit default swaps.

In the event that market data or comparable data does not exist for valuing debt, alternative approaches can be applied, including the following:

- • Reduced form models, which attempt to model the debt directly by individually and/or simultaneously modelling the yield curve, including the level and slope of the yield curve, the level of credit risk and the credit spreads applicable and the level of applicable discount rates. These models also involve a range of assumptions in their application and can be quite complex to implement.
- • Structural models, which attempt to value the aggregate amount of debt within an entity. The models use the value of the entity’s equity or the value of the entire entity (represented by the fair enterprise value’s assets) to identify the value of debt. These models assume that debt provides the owners of the business with an option to default if the enterprise value’s assets should fall below the current value of debt. This option can be valued in a variety of ways with differing levels of complexity.

Both the reduced form and structural model approaches are advanced approaches beyond the scope of this chapter.

The following sections will focus on the use of market prices, comparable analysis and discounted cash flow analysis as the basis for calculating the value of debt.

### 10.3.2 Irredeemable Debt

Most debt securities are issued for a fixed period of time, after which the principal of the debt is redeemable either in full or in part (with the remainder having been redeemed throughout the life of the security). However, if the debt has no finite redemption date at which time the principal will be redeemed, the debt instrument will continue to pay interest (usually at a fixed rate) in perpetuity.

Due to the lack of redemption of a principal amount, this type of debt is referred to as irredeemable debt because investors in this debt do not expect to redeem a principal amount. Rather, they expect to receive an infinite series of cash payments that typically are fixed and paid at equal time intervals.

The value of a perpetuity can be estimated as:

• The fixed rate payment is the amount payable at the end of each period and is paid throughout the life of the instrument
• R = the rate of return required by bond investors

The numerator in this equation reflects the fixed rate payment determined at the date of issuance of the debt. This interest payment has been made at the end of each period to date and will be paid at the end of each period into the future.

The discount rate applied at a valuation date may differ from the rate at the date of issuance; hence the fair value of the debt at any point in time will reflect the perpetuity value using the original numerator and a revised discount rate applicable at the date of the valuation.

When determining the required rate of return to apply to the perpetuity, the rate should reflect either the current market traded rate or a rate calculated using a comparable approach involving other perpetuities issued by similarly rated entities.
