### 10.3.3 Redeemable Debt

Unlike irredeemable debt, the valuation of redeemable debt anticipates that the principal of the debt will be repaid by a finite redemptions date in accordance with the term sheet for the debt. In this section we will consider the implications for both fixed rate and floating rate coupon bonds and bank term loans.

#### 10.3.3.1 Fixed Rate Coupon Bonds

The fair value of a fixed rate coupon paying bond reflects the present value of the coupon payments until the year of redemption plus the present value of the redemption payment (i.e. the face value of the bond).

This can be estimated using the following formula:
![](DraggedImage-243.png)
The formula can be adjusted to consider the impact of taxation on the coupon payments by adjusting the coupon payment from being C to C × (1 − TC ) and adjusting the market interest rate (i) to reflect the post-tax cost of debt.

When initially issued the fair value of a fixed rate bond is normally equal to the face value of the bond. This implies that the bond is typically issued at par with the coupon rate equal to the yield to maturity.

Over time the level of interest rates may move and/or the credit quality of the issuer may change. Both of these events will affect the yield to maturity and the fair value of the bond. However, the coupon rate will remain unchanged at its original fixed coupon rate. The effect on the fair value will be conditional on the direction and degree of movement in the yield to maturity.

What happens to the fair value of a fixed rate bond if the general level of nominal interest rates should change?

If the entity borrows at fixed rates of interest and interest rates fall, the enterprise value’s liabilities will rise (again assuming no change in credit status) because the future cash outflows, which are fixed in amount, are discounted at a lower rate, that is, the nominal coupon rate exceeds the general market interest rate. Conversely, if the entity borrows at fixed rates and interest rates rise, the value of the liability will fall because the future cash flows are discounted at the higher market interest rate.

What happens if the general level of nominal interest rates remains unchanged but the credit status of the entity changes?

If an entity borrows at a fixed rate of interest, then even if there is no change in the prevailing levels of interest rates, as the credit status of the entity falls, the value of its existing liability will fall because the future cash flows will be discounted at a higher yield to maturity to reflect the increased risk. The converse will happen if the credit status improves.

#### 10.3.3.2 Floating Rate Coupon Bonds

The fair value of a floating rate coupon paying bond reflects the present value of the floating rate coupon payments until the year of redemption plus the present value of the redemption payment (i.e. the face value of the bond). Each of the floating rate coupons change over time because they are linked to a reference interest rate such as LIBOR or perhaps even HIBOR. The coupon rate will typically be expressed as:

> Floating Rate = Reference Rate + Fixed Spread

For example, a floating rate of 6-month LIBOR + 150 basis points will require the issuer to pay coupons equal to the LIBOR rate determined at the commencement of the six months period plus a credit premium of 150 basis points or 1.50%. Over the life of the bond, LIBOR will change but the fixed credit spread will remain unchanged.

The fair value of this bond can be estimated using the following formula:
![](DraggedImage-244.png)

As above, the floating rate interest cash flows (RR + CS) can be adjusted to reflect the taxation benefit as (RR + CS) × (1 − TC ).

Over time the level of interest rates may move, affecting the reference rate, and/or the credit quality of the issuer may change. A change in the level of interest rates will also affect the yield to maturity and the fair value of the bond.

The effect on the fair value will be conditional on the direction and degree of movement in the reference rate, the credit spread and the yield to maturity.

What happens to the fair value of a floating rate bond if the general level of nominal interest rates should change?

If the entity borrows at floating rates of interest and interest rates rise or fall, the value of the liability is not affected (provided the entity’s credit status has not changed) because the future cash outflows in respect of the reference rate’s rate of interest are determined at the new interest rate. Similarly, the yield to maturity will also adjust to compensate for the change in the level of interest rates.

What happens if the general level of nominal interest rates remains unchanged, but the credit status of the entity changes?

When an entity borrows at floating rates of interest and its credit quality deteriorates, the credit spread on the entity’s debt will rise if lenders are able to increase the interest margin on the entity’s debt. If lenders cannot increase the interest margin, the entity’s cash flows will remain the same but the applicable yield to maturity will still increase to reflect the rate at which the market will provide finance to the entity. This will cause the fair value of the debt to fall. The converse will occur if the credit status improves.
---- 
##### Illustrative Example 2

In 20X0, Red Prawn Seafood Shipping Company (RPSS) issued a four-year HK$2.50 million floating rate note at par. The note required RPSS to pay a coupon rate equal to the six-month LIBOR plus a credit spread of 50 basis points p.a. each six months.

In 20X2, the six-month LIBOR changed to a new level of 4.50% p.a. At roughly the same time, RPSS’s credit quality decreased and the credit margin for their debt is now 100 basis points p.a. The current tax rate is 16.50%.

Calculate the current pre-tax and post-tax value of the borrowing issued by RPSS.

Note the following inputs required for the calculation:
• Face value = HK$1,000
• Remaining term to maturity = 2 years (4 years − 2 years = 2 years)
• Coupons per year = 2
• Current six-month LIBOR = 4.50%
• Original credit margin = 50 basis points (0.50%)
• Current credit margin = 100 basis points (1.00%)
• Current tax rate = 16.50%

Answer The bond was originally issued at par (HK$1,000). However, the change in the credit margin from 50 to 100 basis points will cause the floating rate bond to be priced at a discount below par value. This is because the original quoted margin of 50 basis points p.a. is less than the margin of 100 basis points used to determine the discount rate.

The current pre-tax valuation is calculated as follows:
Pre-tax interest payments = (0.0450 + 0.0050) x 1000/2 = HK$25 
Pre-tax cost of debt = (0.0450 + 0.0100)/2 = 0.0275 or 2.75% per period

The post-tax cost of debt = (0.0450 + 0.0100) x (1 - 0.165)/2 = 2.296% per period.

#### 10.3.3.3 Amortising Bank Term Loan

At the inception of a bank loan, an amortisation schedule is determined that allows for the principal of the loan to be amortised to zero at the maturity of the loan. Each loan payment includes both interest and principal components. The principal component reflects the amount of the decrease in the amortisation schedule under the loan that allows it to be repaid in full at maturity.

Details of how to calculate loan repayments and development of a bank term loan amortisation schedule were discussed in Chapter 7.

For floating rate bank term loans, if the floating rate was to change, the fair value of the loan will remain unchanged because repayments will be adjusted to reflect the change in interest rates. The change in the repayments will allow the loan’s maturity to continue to remain unchanged. With these changes the fair value of floating rate loans should remain unchanged.

In contrast for fixed rate bank term loans, if the fixed rate was to change, then repayments will be unchanged. However, the fair value of the loan will change to reflect the direction and amount of the change in interest rates used to discount the fixed rate cash flows.

### 10.3.4 Convertible Debt

Convertible notes provide the bond holder with the option of converting notes into a specified number of other securities, normally ordinary shares of equity (stock) of the issuing entity. The conversion occurs at a pre-determined price/rate and time.

As a general rule, the price of a convertible note depends upon the relationship between the following components:

• The price of the underlying coupon bond;
• The length of time before conversion of the bond may take place; and
• The current conversion value of the bond.

Convertible notes are exposed to different sources of risk such as interest rate, equity and default risk. These factors need to be considered as part of a valuation process. The yield on the underlying coupon bond is exposed to both interest rate risk and default risk, whereas the conversion value is exposed to equity price risk.

The valuation of convertible notes can be performed using market prices and/or yields or information from comparable issuances. This information can also be included in convertible note pricing models such as the conversion value approach or the option-based approach, as discussed below. Both of these pricing models rely upon the use of inputs from observed market prices, yields to maturity or comparable entity information.

#### 10.3.4.1 Conversion Value Approach

The fair value of a convertible note is the sum of the present value of the future coupon cash flows on the convertible note at the market interest rate, assuming no conversion (the debt component), plus the present value of the note’s conversion value (i.e. the conversion ratio × the current share price).

The conversion ratio is the number of shares that can be received at the time of conversion for each note. The conversion ratio is adjusted for any equity issues or buybacks, mergers or asset distributions in order to preserve the rights of holders of the convertibles as if they were shareholders at the time of issue. The conversion ratio is equal to the par value of the debt divided by the conversion price at the date of conversion.

The conversion value approach to valuation has a limitation in that it assumes that all convertible notes are immediately exchanged for equity and ignores the time value of the conversion option. The observed market price of a convertible note generally exceeds both the value of a non-convertible note and the conversion value of a convertible note. From the perspective of the investor, a convertible security is worth at a minimum its par value.

#### 10.3.4.2 Option-Based Model Approach

Due to the convertibility of debt into equity, convertible debt should in most circumstances be observed to have a higher value than the minimum value. This is because holders of convertible debt have the option to wait and convert their debt into equity at the maturity of the debt. The time component of the option has a value over and above the present value of the conversion value. This is due in part to the possibility of equity price movements between the date of valuation and the date of conversion.

Using the option-based model approach, the fair value of convertible debt is the sum of the present value of the future coupon cash flows on the bond at the market interest rate, assuming no conversion (the debt component), plus the value of an option to convert the bond into the entity’s equity, based on the bond’s conversion value (i.e. the conversion ratio × the current share price).

All options have two components that determine their value: an intrinsic component and an extrinsic component. The intrinsic component reflects the relationship between the current conversion value relative to the expected conversion value at the time of the valuation. The extrinsic component reflects the time to conversion of the bond and the volatility of the underlying equity price.

The relationship between the value of the debt and the price of equity is shown in Exhibit 10.1, where the continuous yellow line represents the fair value of a convertible bond, showing it as a trade-off between the present value of the coupon notes (coloured in red) and the value of the entity’s equity (coloured in blue). From the figure it is possible to determine the impact on the value of a convertible note to changes in the price of an entity’s equity instruments.

Exhibit 10.1 shows that when an entity’s equity price is low, the value of the convertible note tends to be mostly influenced by the value of non-convertible debt and is therefore sensitive to changes in both the level of interest rates and the credit spread.

If the conversion value (i.e. conversion ratio × share price) is below the redemption value of the note, note holders will want to redeem the notes for cash at the redemption value rather than convert the notes to equity, given that the conversion ratio will only provide a fixed number of shares.

The opposite happens when the entity’s equity price is very high and the conversion value (i.e. conversion ratio × share price) is above the redemption value of the note. In this case, the value of the convertible note is mostly influenced by the conversion value driven by the level
![](DraggedImage-254.png)
and volatility of the equity price per share. When this relationship exists, the total value of the convertible note will be higher than the value of the present value of the coupons from the note by an amount equal to the maximum of the conversion value less the value of the present value of the coupons from the note or zero, which reflects the value of the option embedded in the instrument.

Note that when an entity’s equity price is below the conversion price at redemption, the value of the convertible note (coloured in yellow) is slightly above the present value of the redemption value. This is due to the value of the option being positive during this period. In contrast, as the equity price increases above the conversion price at redemption, the option price is dominated by the instrument’s intrinsic value, and at very high levels will converge closely to the equity price value, reflecting the dominance of the equity conversion component of the instrument.

Several factors will affect the value of a convertible note. The impact of changes in these factors are shown in Exhibit 10.2.

### 10.3.5 Preference Shares

As discussed in Chapter 7, preference shares typically pay a fixed dividend and can be issued either in perpetuity or, alternatively, may have features that allow for:

• Redemption by the issuer of the preference shares in return for cash or ordinary shares.
• Convertibility by the holder of the preference shares for cash or ordinary shares.
• Cumulative dividends whereby dividends can be delayed and paid on a cumulative basis.
• Participation in profits beyond the prescribed dividend level.

Redeemable preference shares are similar to convertible debt in that the date of redeemability is typically set at a future date and on this date the holder of the preference share can redeem the preference share for ordinary shares in the entity. Until the date of the redemption, the preference share pays a fixed dividend payment that makes it similar to a non-convertible bond paying a debt-related interest rate coupon.

The fixed dividend payments are typically in the form of a quarterly, semi-annual or yearly dividend, depending on the entity’s dividend policy, and is the basis of the valuation method for an issued preferred share. These dividends are typically fixed as a percentage of the share price or are a fixed amount. Being specified in this way, the dividend payments become a steady, predictable stream of income to the holder of the preference shares. These cash flows are discounted at the entity’s cost of equity capital.

Uncertainty in the valuation will arise if the shares are redeemable for ordinary shares, if the holder can convert the preference shares before redemption to either cash or ordinary shares and if there is uncertainty about future profitability affecting dividend payments. Each of these features can be embedded into the valuation through the use of option and probability measures.

Hence the valuation of preference shares, in the absence of market prices or reasonable comparable issuances, will require a detailed assessment not only of the cash flows and the discount rates applied but also of the future profitability and payout ratios.

Unlike debt instruments, there is typically no tax benefit from interest payments arising from preference shares. This is because the payments made during the life of the instrument are dividends and, although considered to be ‘debt like’, are typically not debt for taxation purposes.

### 10.3.6 Recommendation on Debt Valuation Models

Each type of debt has its own specification for valuation purposes. Most debt is issued either at or near par value, but the principal can be either repaid at maturity, in instalments throughout the debt instrument’s life, amortised through the life of the debt or remain in perpetuity.

Also, subject to whether the debt is short term or long term, whether the bond is coupon paying or non-coupon paying and the frequency of the coupon payments, whether the debt is fixed or floating or whether there is any optionality in the debt structure, directly affects the value of debt at any point in time.

When performing the valuation of debt securities, priority should always be given to the use of market prices if they are available, else other valuation approaches should be applied.

If no market prices are available priority should be given to using market-based input information into debt valuation models that reflect current market inputs.

This section has discussed issues that may arise in the valuation of debt. The next section discusses alternative approaches that can be used to value equity.

## 10.4 VALUATION MODELS FOR EQUITY

HKAS 32.11 defines an equity instrument as any contract that evidences a residual interest in the assets of an entity after deducting all of its liabilities, which can be expressed as:

> Equity = Assets - Liabilities

The value of equity for an entity can be determined at the group level or at the level of the controlling entity (i.e. after removing the value of any non-controlling interests) using either direct valuation, market prices or indirectly via an alternative valuation method.

The value of equity can have either an observed or unobserved share price.

### • Observable share prices
If market share prices are observable, then the value of equity is most commonly estimated as follows:

> Value of Equity = Share Price x Number of Shares Outstanding

This approach is known as the entity’s market capitalisation. It reflects the fact that the value of the most common type of equity capital available to investors is ordinary shares.

When more complex forms of equity are used, the approach used to value equity needs to be extended to incorporate their effects as follows:

> Value of Equity = Share Price x Number of Shares Outstanding 
> = Share Price x (Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding + ‘in the Money’ Share Options + ‘in the Money’ Warrants + ‘in the Money’ Convertible Notes)

In applying this approach many analysts simplify the above calculation by setting the three ‘in the money’ option components to zero. A call (put) option is considered to be ‘in the money’ if the strike price is less (more) than the share price. This is because, the ‘in the money’ value can typically only be realised after a vesting period for employee share options or at conversion or redemption dates for warrants and convertible notes.

### • Unobservable share prices

If market share prices are unobservable, there are a variety of ways in which valuations can be performed to estimate the value of equity, including the following:
- °The entity as a whole could be valued based on expected payoffs (i.e. cash flows or earnings) to all claim holders to the entity (both debt and equity).
- °Equity could be directly valued based on the flow of expected payoffs to equity holders alone (such as dividends).
- °Through the use of a comparable method approach.

If determining equity value from the value of the entity as a whole, this can be calculated by deducting the value of debt (often referred to as a deleveraged model) with an adjustment such as:

> Value of Equity = Enterprise Value - Value of Debt - Value of Preference Shares + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

Alternatively, determining the value of equity directly from the net flow of payoffs to equity holders after deducting the estimated flow of financing costs is also known as a leveraged model.

As shown in Exhibit 10.3, equity valuation techniques can be classified as asset-based approaches, income-based approaches or market-based approaches. Entities typically use one or more of these approaches to measure fair value both for financial reporting and for other purposes, discussed in Section 10.1.
![](DraggedImage-256.png)

Exhibit 10.4 provides an overview of the asset-, income- and market-based valuation approaches shown in Exhibit 10.3 and identifies a number of methods relevant to each approach. The asset-based approach encompasses a set of methods that value the entity by reference to its statement of financial position. In contrast, income valuation approaches primarily focus on the entity’s statement of profit or loss and/or the statement of cash flows and market-based approaches focus on observable market data or data from comparable entities.

### Valuation approaches
Asset-based approaches
- Asset-based approaches value an entity by valuing the entity’s assets and liabilities, usually as a going concern or on a liquidation basis to identify the entity’s net asset value, which is assumed to be equal to the entity’s equity value.
- When applying the asset-based approach to equity valuation, an accountant/analyst will use a combination of approaches including the historical book value approach, the cost-based approach (e.g. for inventory, plant and equipment) and the net realisable value approach (all discussed in Section 10.4.1).
Income-based approaches
- The income approach converts future amounts (e.g. income, expenses and cash flows) to a single current (i.e. discounted) amount. When the income approach is used, the fair value measurement reflects the discounting of future earnings or enterprise cash flows or equity cash flows.
- Approaches include dividend discount models (as discussed in Chapter 7), earnings capitalisation and residual income models (as discussed in Section 10.4.2) and free cash flow models (as discussed in Section 10.4.3).
Market-based approaches
- The market approach uses prices and other relevant information generated by market transactions involving identical or comparable (i.e. similar) assets, liabilities or a group of assets and liabilities, such as a business (HKFRS 13. B5).
- Approaches include the use of observed market prices, the value of comparable enterprises and equity multiples and comparable transactions from recent sales (as discussed in Section 10.4.4)

The above approaches are consistent with HKFRS 13 Fair Value Measurement, which identifies three widely used valuation techniques for estimating the fair value of assets, liabilities or equity instruments: the cost approach, the income approach and the market approach. Entities are required to use one or more of these approaches to measure fair value for financial reporting purposes (HKFRS 13.62).

It is important to note the following when using the above valuation methods in a financial reporting context or by reference to information provided in an entity’s financial statements:
- • The valuation technique chosen should be appropriate in the circumstances.
- • The valuation technique chosen should be one for which there is sufficient data to measure fair value (HKFRS 13.61).
- • The valuation techniques used to measure fair value shall maximise the use of relevant observable inputs and minimise the use of unobservable inputs (HKFRS 13.67).
- • If multiple valuation techniques are used to measure fair value, the results (i.e. respective indications of fair value) shall be evaluated considering the reasonableness of the range of values indicated by those results. A fair value measurement is the point within that range that is the most representative of the fair value in the circumstances (HKFRS 13.63).
- • The asset or liability measured at fair value might be either of the following:
	- a. A stand-alone asset or liability (e.g. a financial instrument or a non-financial asset) or
	- b. A group of assets, a group of liabilities or a group of assets and liabilities (e.g. a cash-generating unit or a business) (HKFRS 13.13).

Each of the approaches identified in Exhibit 10.4 has its own parametric specification and will involve choices based on assumptions made to operationalise the approach used to value equity capital. The choice between approaches should be a choice made based on the suitability of the approaches (i.e. whether they are ‘fit for purpose’) rather than a preference based on ease of measurement. These subjective choices may arise due to the purpose of the business valuation, limitations in the valuation techniques applied and problems in data input availability and forecasting.

The trade-off between alternate approaches to valuation should not be based on the concept of the determination of value (as all approaches, given perfect information, will yield the same valuation). Rather, the approach chosen should be the one that is considered to be capable of providing the best estimate of the future (unknown) payoffs. For example, income models can be specified using dividends, earnings and cash flows. Over the life of an entity, income approaches based on these inputs can be shown to be interrelated and each of the approaches can be shown to theoretically produce the same valuation result.

The following sections demonstrate models for the valuation of equity, including assetbased valuation models (Section 10.4.1), earnings-based valuation models (Section 10.4.2), cash flow-based valuation models (Section 10.4.3) and relative valuation or comparable methods (Section 10.4.4). Also, recommendations of appropriate valuation/range of valuations for a given business scenario will be covered in Section 10.4.5.

### 10.4.1 Asset-Based Models

The objective of the asset-based approach is to estimate the value of an entity’s net assets as a going concern or on a liquidation basis, based on the principle that:

> The Value of an Entity = The Value of the Entity's Total Assets (Including Tangible and Intangible Assets - The Value of the Entity's Total Liabilities (Including All Recognised and Unrecognised Liabilities)

An entity’s statement of financial position will normally contain both tangible and intangible assets. Tangible assets include both real property (such as land, building, improvements) and personal property (including machinery, equipment, motor vehicles, furniture and computer equipment). In contrast, HKAS 38 Intangible Assets requires that for an asset to be regarded as an intangible asset it must have three properties – it must be identifiable; the entity must have control over a resource; and future economic benefits must be expected to flow from the resource. Intangible assets include non-monetary assets that do not have physical substance but grant rights or economic benefits to their owners, such as trademarks, broadcast rights, patented technology and service and supply contracts.

Caution is needed when using financial statement information to perform assetbased valuations. This is because there is a range of different measurement and reporting considerations that can affect financial statement valuations.

An entity’s statement of financial position will report some but not necessarily all of an entity’s assets. For example, certain intangible assets, such as those that have arisen as a result of a research and development project, may not have qualified under accounting standards for recognition in the financial statements. In contrast, goodwill, which comprises unidentifiable non-monetary assets, is only recognised as an asset in the statement of financial position in the event of a business combination.

Similarly, an entity’s statement of financial position will report some but not necessarily all of an entity’s liabilities. For example, an entity may have incurred a liability as a result of a faulty product, but the liability may not have qualified under accounting standards for recognition in the financial statements because of, for example, measurement uncertainties.

The value attached to an individual asset and therefore to the total value of all assets in an entity’s statement of financial position can vary considerably depending on whether the assets are valued on a historical cost basis, on a current cost basis, at a liquidation value or using the market value of assets and liabilities. However, regardless of the approach adopted by an analyst for valuation purposes, there will be some reliance on the financial information provided in financial statements for which accounting standards do not prescribe a single valuation approach.

The following sections will discuss the concept of the mixed measurement model used to prepare financial statements and show how alternative cost-based approaches can be used to estimate the value of equity.

10.4.1.1 Mixed Measurement Model

Whilst we can derive values for the assets and liabilities of an entity from its financial statements, it is important to understand that they may not all be measured in current market value terms. Accordingly, it is important to understand the basis of measurement used in the financial statements.

Financial reporting does not aim to value the equities of an entity and has its reasons for using a mixed measurement model. Valuers of the equities of an entity (and, indeed, of its assets and liabilities) need to be very conscious of what the accounting information does and does not mean and the context for their valuations.

Financial statements are prepared using a mixed measurement model in which:

1. Assets may be shown at:
- • Historical cost (depreciated where assets have limited lives).
- • The lower of historical cost and net realisable value – inventories.
- • Fair value, when accounting for revaluations of non-current assets or valuing derivative financial instruments.
- • Fair value when certain elections are made to value other financial instruments.
- • Fair value less costs to sell when measuring agricultural assets at fair value.
- • The lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell if a non-current asset (or disposal group) is classified as held-for-sale.
- • The lower of a carrying amount and fair value less costs to distribute if a non-current asset (or disposal group) is held for distribution to owners.
- • The higher the value in use (discounted asset specific cash flows) or fair value less costs of disposal when accounting for impairment of non-current assets (including intangibles).

2. Liabilities may be shown at historical cost or fair value.
- • Most liabilities are shown at ‘historical cost’ (i.e. proceeds received).
- • Some such ‘costs’ will be derived from application of an effective interest rate method to contracted cash flows.
- • Some liabilities may be subject to an election to use fair value.
- • All derivative financial instruments will be measured at fair value, even options that are out-of-the-money.
- • Fair value or fulfilment/value in use may be chosen when accounting for provisions that are liabilities (e.g. restoration liabilities).

3. Equity is the residual interest in the net assets (assets minus liabilities) and is not revalued. It is a consequence of the use of the mixed measurement bases shown above.

It is beyond the scope of this chapter to explain each of these requirements. The measurement bases for financial and non-financial assets and liabilities are specified by accounting standards. They are addressed in Module 11 on financial reporting. The important point to recognise is that the above values are commonly used for valuation purposes.

The mixed measurement model highlights that the valuation of equity will involve a mix of valuation methods to value assets and liabilities and will necessitate, as relevant, the use of the cost, income and market approaches in determining fair value.

#### 10.4.1.2 Historical Book Value Approach 
The historical book value approach allows analysts to use the reported values of assets, liabilities and equity provided in an entity’s statement of financial position for valuation purposes.

The book value approach utilises and restates the accounting identity equation to measure the net asset enterprise value (and hence the value of equity) in the following way:

- Net Assets = Assets - Liabilities

The book value approach is a very unsophisticated approach for valuing assets and equity. As such, its usefulness as a valuation approach is compromised, other than as being a lower threshold against which other valuation methods can be compared. As discussed in Section 10.4.1.1, book value (or carrying value) is seldom an aggregation of consistently measured assets and liabilities.

The historical cost approach assumes that the value of the assets are equal to their historical purchase price less any depreciation and impairment.

A central problem with this approach is that the value of equity does not directly reflect a market-based approach because typically the assets and liabilities of an entity are measured on a cost basis. In some entities, the book value of assets and liabilities may differ materially from their fair value because the book values may be considerably out of date, may not reflect the effect of technological or competitive developments or may represent only a relatively small proportion of the total fair value of an entity, as, for example, in the case of service businesses. Similarly, use of book values does not reflect an earnings-based approach because it does not examine the capacity of the assets to generate income from their operational activities.

At June 20X2, HK Dragon Cargo Services Pty Ltd has assets of HK$2.5 billion and liabilities of HK$1.37 billion. The entity has 11.5 million shares on issue. Using the accounting identity equation, calculate the value of net assets and the value per share.

#### 10.4.1.3 The Cost-Based Approach

The cost-based approach is normally categorised into two approaches:
- • Replacement cost (in basic terms, the cost of replicating functionality).
- • Reproduction cost (in basic terms, the cost of recreating the asset).

An important consideration in using these approaches is that the objective is to value the remaining service potential of the existing asset, not the value of a new replacement or reproduced asset. The replacement cost of the remaining service potential of the existing asset will be based on the cost of a modern equivalent asset.

Both of these cost-based approaches to asset valuation are consistent with the economic principle of substitution. For example, assume that an entity implemented a HK$250,000 software system to manage its inventory five years ago. This system is regarded as an asset for the entity and will be recorded in the financial statements at its depreciated cost. If the system was replaced and implemented today to provide the same services, this asset would now have a replacement cost of HK$75,000.

By measuring the replacement or reproduction cost of both the assets and liabilities of the entity, the difference between them will provide the value of the entity’s equity. However, this is not as simple an exercise as it may at first seem.

Assuming each asset and liability is recognised and measured consistent with the relevant accounting standards, it will be necessary to identify the assets and liabilities to be revalued and then to perform the revaluation. In a cost-based approach appraisal, the value of the assets will be equal to the replacement or reproduction cost of the asset, plus any costs of construction or implementation, less depreciation.

Assuming that the entity will continue as a going concern, it is reasonable to apply the following approach:

1. Obtain the current statement of financial position for the entity.
2. Determine the assets and/or liabilities that need to be revalued using the replacement or reproduction cost approach.
3. Identify all intangible assets, contingent assets and contingent liabilities that may require revaluation.
4. Estimate the replacement or reproduction cost of the assets and liabilities.
5. Estimate the implied value of equity.

A complication of this approach is that while the concept of replacement or reproduction cost as a valuation basis for assets is reasonably well understood, the same cannot be said for the concept of replacement cost as a valuation basis for liabilities. For a number of liabilities, for example provisions for restoration and litigation liabilities, there will be no ‘historical cost’ as such, since they do not arise from exchange transactions.

#### 10.4.1.4 Net Realisable Value Approach

If an entity is to be broken up because of a decision to sell or liquidate the entity, it would be appropriate to value the assets at their net realisable value (i.e. disposal value less costs of disposal) and the liabilities at their settlement value.

The net realisable value of an entity is the amount that would be available to shareholders if the assets were sold and the liabilities settled. This amount will be different from the ‘going concern value’ of an entity, which is the value assuming the entity will continue to operate in the future and be able to benefit from the income generating capacity of all of its assets, including goodwill, intellectual property, brands and customer lists.

When applying the net realisable value approach, it is important to distinguish between the amount that would be generated from the sale of an entity’s assets in an orderly realisation process and the amount that would be generated from a forced sale. The valuation approach that is used in the former situation is known as the orderly realisation of assets method. This method will produce values that are generally commensurate with measurement basis fair value less costs to sell used in a financial reporting context because both assume that the sale transaction is orderly, i.e. they assume a time period to allow for marketing activities that are usual and customary for a transaction involving the relevant assets and liabilities (HKFRS 13 Appendix A).

In contrast, in circumstances where the sale is a forced liquidation or distress sale, net realisable value is likely to be lower, all else being equal. In these circumstances the entity is, in essence, an unwilling seller and is therefore unable to demand a price that would be achievable if the sale was orderly. The valuation approach that is used in these circumstances is known as the liquidation method, which is similar to the orderly realisation of assets method. Because assets are sold in a shorter timeframe, they may therefore incur larger realisation costs.

Net realisable value can be estimated as:
> Net Realisable Value = Gross Realisable Value of Assets - Settllement Value of Liabilities - Disposal Costs - Income Tax onn Assumed Sale of Assets

Generally speaking, the net realisable value approach will involve:

• Valuing the assets and liabilities at their estimated net realisable value (depending on the nature of the assets and liabilities). Sometimes this may require the use of appropriate experts to value specific assets or asset types, such as property, plant and equipment.
• Estimating realisation costs, including:
- °Operating costs during the wind-down period.
- °Any brokerage or agent fees associated with the sale of the assets.
- °Legal, accounting and other professional fees relating to the liquidation.
- °Other costs (such as severance pay).
• Allowing for any income and capital gains tax liabilities that would be incurred and other tax consequences if the assets were liquidated. Such taxes would include:
- °Income tax on the sale of assets, net of deferred taxes previously raised. The income tax on the sale of the assets may be either a rebate or cost subject to the market price relative to depreciated value of the assets involved; for example, if the fair value is less than the depreciated value this may result in a tax rebate or offset against other tax payable.
- °Income tax on the distribution of retained profits.

• Allowing for the loss of any carried forward tax losses due to the appointment of a liquidator.
• Considering the nature and marketability of the assets.
• Allowing for the time that will elapse before the proceeds of the liquidation are available and allowing for a suitable profit margin to a purchaser (recognising the fact that a purchaser would not outlay money on day one simply to get the same sum of money back in three or six months).
• Appropriate allowance for the time value of money and the risks involved, including those extra risks involved in buying in a liquidation environment. This will be discussed in Chapter 12.

#### 10.4.1.5 Application of the Asset Valuation Approach

Asset-based valuation approaches are based on an underlying assumption that a prudent buyer will pay no more for a business than it would cost to assemble all of the individual assets and liabilities that comprise the business. In doing so, asset-based valuations are particularly useful for entities with extensive physical assets such as commercial and retail property entities, especially if there is a general expectation that the value of the assets will increase in the future. However, this approach is not suitable for service-based entities such as consultancies because these entities typically do not have large holdings of property, plant or equipment and financial statements will normally exclude most of the entities’ intangible assets. The next two sections will discuss models from the income-based approach. In contrast to using asset-based approaches, including models to estimate the value of equity capital, these sections will demonstrate how both earnings-based and cash flow-based models can be applied.

### 10.4.2 Earnings-Based Models

As discussed in the introduction to this section, the income approach converts future amounts (e.g. income, expenses and cash flows) to a single current (i.e. discounted) amount. When the income approach is used, fair value measurement reflects current market expectations about those future earnings, dividends or cash flow amounts. This is typically done using a discounted cash flow method, which is applied to enterprise cash flows such as earnings or specifically to equity cash flows such as dividends.

Earnings-based models are a computationally simple approach to the estimation of both enterprise value and equity value. These models contemplate that the entity will continue to operate as a going concern and that the value of an entity is a direct function of the entity’s earnings.

In the following sections, two approaches involving earnings will be discussed – earnings capitalisation and the residual income model. These approaches can be used to estimate the value of equity.

#### 10.4.2.1 Capitalisation of Earnings Using WACC and the Return on Equity 
In finance, capitalisation of earnings involves an assessment of the value of an entity or its equity via an assessment of an entity’s current earnings and the entity’s future earnings capacity or potential.

The capitalisation of earnings method determines the entity’s value using a single measure of the expected business earnings as the numerator. This is divided by a capitalisation rate that represents the risk associated with generating these earnings outcomes in the future.

In practice, this implies that the enterprise value or the value of equity can be estimated as a perpetuity as follows:
> Enterprise Value = Earnings/Capitalisation Rate

The steps taken in applying the capitalisation of earnings approach include:
- • Determining a sustainable persistent earnings base, making the necessary adjustments, if necessary, to convert current earnings into projected earnings;
- • Developing an appropriate capitalisation rate; and
- • Applying the capitalisation rate to the earnings to arrive at a conclusion of the fair value of the entity.

When using this approach, and assuming the use of a post-tax WACC, the persistent earnings figure used should be independent of interest costs (as debt funding is used as part of the entity’s capital) and therefore the appropriate level of earnings should reflect the net operating profit after tax (NOPAT). If a pre-tax WACC was utilised, then the assessment can be made using either EBITDA or EBIT. Further, when estimated in perpetuity, the future growth rate of the persistent earnings should also be considered as part of the calculation.

The capitalisation rate should reflect the cost of capital used to finance the assets that are in use to derive the earnings. This can be expressed as either the weighted average cost of capital when determining the enterprise value or the cost of equity when determining the value of the entity’s equity capital.

Once the inputs have been selected the enterprise value can be calculated as follows:

> Enterprise Value = Persistent NOPAT/(WACC - Constant Growth Rate) + Net Redundant Assets

In this case, because the WACC incorporates the cost of debt, the persistent earnings estimate should reflect the net operating profit after tax (NOPAT) derived from the profit or loss statement. Persistent earnings should reflect the level of earnings that are expected to be sustainable and to persist into the foreseeable future. The concept of persistent earnings will be discussed in detail in Section 10.4.4.1.

Once the enterprise value is determined, the value of equity can be determined as follows:

> Value of Equity = Enterprise Value - Value of Debt - Value of Preeference Shares + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

Alternatively, the measure of persistent earnings to the net profit from the profit or loss statement can be adjusted to reflect the cost of equity capital and then the capitalised equity value will equal:

> Equity Value = Persistent Net Income/(Cost of Equity - Constant Growth Rate) + Net Redundant Assets

In this case, the persistent earnings will need to include interest costs and taxation associated with the interest tax shield. This is because equity holders are entitled to the distribution of net profit either via dividends or through reinvestment in retained profits. Hence, the appropriate measure for persistent earnings should be net profit.

This approach to estimating the equity value can also be approximated using a ratio called the earnings yield. The earnings yield measures the annual earnings per share relative to the share price, which can be expressed as:
![](DraggedImage-258.png)
In the numerator of the equation, the EPS equals net income available to ordinary shareholders, which equals net income minus preferred dividends, and the number of shares should reflect the weighted average number of shares. Over the period of any given year, entities will be engaged in buy-backs and issuance of shares. The weighted average allows for the number of shares to be weighted relative to the portion of the year during which the shares are on issue.

Using the earnings yield it is possible to capitalise the earnings per share.

Similar to earnings capitalisation, the earnings yield can then be used to estimate the fair value of the entity’s equity using the formula:
![](DraggedImage-259.png)

##### Illustrative Example 8

Aqua Drilling Ltd (ADL) is a marine engineering entity that specialises in offshore dredging maintenance activities. ADL has operated in the Hong Kong harbour for the past 15 years with no major changes in its activities, acquisitions or divestments. The entity has no significant interests in other entities.

In a recent review of the entity’s annual reports and operating activities over the past five years, it was concluded that several patents to the value of HK$23.75 million are now redundant and are not used as part of the entity’s current technological approach.

The entity’s EBIT for the current year is HK$205 million and after considering adjustments to derive future persistent earnings, an adjustment of +HK$15 million needs to be made to the current EBIT.

The entity currently has debt with a fair value of HK$640 million and its level of cash and marketable securities is HK$80 million. ADL has a WACC of 10.0% and the entity is expected to grow at a rate close to the inflation rate of 2.00%. The corporate tax rate is 16.5%.

Based on the above information:
1. Calculate ADL’s enterprise value.
2. Calculate the value of ADL’s equity.

Answer

1. To calculate the enterprise value, we need to apply the following equation Enterprise Value = Persistent NOPAT/( WACC - Constant Growth Rate) + Net Redundant Assets
	![](DraggedImage-260.png)
2. Value of Equity = Enterprise Value - Value of Debt - Value of Preference Shares - Non-controlling Interest + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

Substituting values based on the information provided for the Aqua Drilling Ltd example, the calculation of value of equity is:

Value of Equity = HK$2.320 billion - HK$640 million - 0 - 0 + HK$80 million
 = HK$1.760 billion

Based on the above calculations the enterprise value of ADL is HK$2.320 billion and the value of equity is HK$1.760 billion.

#### 10.4.2.2 Residual Income Model

When calculating the net income of an entity an adjustment is made to EBIT to reflect the interest expense associated with the cost of debt and taxation expense. The net income is available for distribution to shareholders. The distribution may be in the form of a dividend or is retained by the entity to assist with future growth opportunities or to repay debt.

Some analysts argue that the net income from the profit or loss statement approach ignores the actual cost of equity capital. This is because unlike the cost of debt, the cost of equity is not incorporated into the net income calculation.

##### Residual Income and the Equity Charge

It is possible to assess the impact of the cost of equity capital by estimating the residual income as follows:

> Residual Income = Net Income - Cost of Equity x Book Value of Equity
which can be expressed as
![](DraggedImage-261.png)
The term cost of equity x book value of equity (k E × BVt − 1 ) is known as the equity charge and represents the actual monetary cost of equity based on the level of equity at the commencement of an accounting period.

Residual income is positive if the net income generated at time t exceeds the shareholders required rate of return on book value of shares at time t – 1. This would imply the entity created positive shareholder value at time t.

In the residual income approach, an entity’s value of equity can be calculated as the sum total of its book value plus the present value of the expected future residual income, which is discounted at cost of equity, kE . estimated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-262.png)
Consistent with the entity being a going concern, this formula runs to infinity. This presents itself as difficult to measure without some simplifying assumptions.

##### Constant Growth Residual Income Model

If earnings are expected to grow at a constant growth rate in perpetuity, then the value of equity could be estimated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-263.png)
where g = the long-term growth rate in residual income.

##### Multistage Growth Residual Income Model

In practice it is unlikely that an entity’s earnings will grow at a constant rate except in the long term. This is because a range of economic, industrial and entity specific factors will affect the level of residual income during different phases of an entity’s life-cycle.

If the residual income is expected to vary in the near term and then stabilise towards a long-term earnings growth rate, then the model can be expressed as a multistage model as follows:
![](DraggedImage-264.png)
This multistage model implies that the value of the entity’s equity has three components:

• The current book value of equity;
• A stage of incremental present values of residual income that may vary over time; and
• The final stage includes the present value of the residual income assuming a long-term constant growth rate from time T in perpetuity.

The next section will discuss another income-based approach using cash flow-based models. In contrast to the use of accounting earnings, as demonstrated in this section, the next section will focus on models that use the cash flows generated by the operating activities of an entity.

### 10.4.3 Cash Flow-Based Models

The discounted cash flow method is an income-based approach to valuation that views the intrinsic value of a security or an entity as being equal to the present value of the projected cash flows of the security (for example, the price of a coupon paying bond is the present value of the future coupons and the face value of the bond) or entity. These models assume that the value of an entity or its equity is a function of three variables:
• The capacity to generate cash flows;
• The expected growth in these cash flows; and
• The risk adjusted rate of return for the security or entity.

Using this information, the present value is determined by discounting the relevant expected future cash flows for the security or entity at an appropriate discount rate that reflects the risk inherent in the cash flows being discounted as follows:
![](DraggedImage-265.png)
where
- • CF t = the relevant future cash flows from the entity or security
- • R = the risk adjusted rate of return for the security or entity

The value of equity (ordinary shares) can be derived indirectly by first using a free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) model to estimate the enterprise value and then adjusting the FCFF to arrive at an estimate of the value of equity. Alternatively, the value of equity can be valued directly by using a free cash flow to equity (FCFE) model.

The concepts of FCFF and FCFE are discussed in Sections 10.4.3.1–10.4.3.3 and show how the FCFF and FCFE can be used by an entity for business valuation purposes to estimate the value of equity.

#### 10.4.3.1 Free Cash Flow to the Firm and Free Cash Flow to Equity 
This section will introduce the concepts of free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) and free cash flow to equity (FCFE).

##### Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF) 
Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) is the cash flow available to the entity’s suppliers of capital (shareholders and debt holders) after all operating expenses (including taxes) have been paid and necessary investments in working capital and fixed capital (alternatively expressed as non-current operating assets such as property, plant and equipment) have been made. Entities can use their FCFF to pay for dividends, to buy back shares, to repay debt or to fund future expansions, including mergers and acquisitions.

In order to calculate the FCFF it is necessary to ignore the financing of the entity’s operations and focus attention on the cash flows generated by the entity’s assets after tax. The cash flows are viewed from the perspective of the entity being a going concern, taking into account the investments needed in working capital and fixed capital for the entity to maintain or expand its operations.

##### Calculating the Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF) 
FCFF can be calculated in a number of different ways, each of which will yield the same solution for both the FCFF and subsequently the value of equity. Analysts will typically choose one of the three methods as shown in Exhibit 10.5 to calculate FCFF, but the most popular approaches are the EBIT and net income approaches.

To calculate current and historical measures of FCFF, information can be extracted from the financial statements of the entity involved. For some items in the FCFF it may be necessary to utilise the notes to the accounts, which may provide supplementary information. Future levels of FCFF will require forecasting after an assessment of the impact on the future cash inflows and outflows of the entity, of the future prospects of the entity, industry and economy and factors impacting the entity’s strategy and growth prospects. Determining the future levels of FCFF will often involve a considerable degree of judgement.

Several of the components of the FCFF that will require detailed consideration are discussed below.

##### Non-cash Charges (NCC) 
Non-cash charges (NCC) include non-cash accounting items such as depreciation, amortisation, impairment (including write-downs in the value of assets arising from an entity restructure) and gains or losses on the sale of assets. Each of these items in itself does not cause an increase or decrease in the entity’s cash flows and therefore need to be identified.

![](DraggedImage-266.png)

Non-cash charges are reported in the statement of profit or loss and in the cash flow from operations in the statement of cash flows.

##### Investment in Fixed Capital (CAPEX)

Investment in fixed capital is the outflows of cash during the period for FCFF purposes for capital expenditure on physical long-term assets such as land, buildings, plant and equipment (sometimes referred to as PP&E). These outflows of cash can be for the purpose of acquisition, maintenance or improvement of the assets.

When estimating capital expenditures, both internal investments (for example, purchases of property, plant and equipment) and external investments (for example, acquisition of a subsidiary) should be included. These assets are used to support the entity’s operations by generating revenues and cash flow. Long-term assets sold during the period for cash should be deducted from investment in long-term capital.

The following two measures should be examined when interpreting the impact of changes in CAPEX:
- • Capital expenditure, which reflects capital expenditure on a gross basis and therefore reflects the actual cash paid for the internal and external assets.
- • Net capital expenditure, which reflects the capital expenditure after the impact of depreciation has been considered.

Of these two measures the preferred approach is to use the gross basis to reflect the full cash flow associated with cash expenditure on the assets. Moreover, the depreciation will be included in the non-cash charges, so to include it here would require a double counting of the impact of depreciation.

In general, it is observed that high-growth entities tend to have higher capital expenditures (both in gross and net terms) relative to earnings than low-growth entities, which may have low, and sometimes even negative, capital expenditures.

As a general rule, when determining the expected growth rate for CAPEX it is useful to consider historical levels of the ratio between the change in gross CAPEX relative to the change in sales. Similarly, the growth rate in depreciation can be expressed as the change in depreciation relative to the change in sales.

Information about investment in fixed capital can be observed in the cash flow from investing activities in the statement of cash flows or by considering the change in gross assets (i.e. before accumulated depreciation) from the statement of financial position over consecutive years.

##### Investment in Net Working Capital (Δ NWC)

In accounting, net working capital would normally be calculated as current assets minus current liabilities and the change in net working capital would simply be the change in this measurement from one period to the next. All current assets and liabilities would be included regardless of whether they were for operating, investment or financing purposes.

However, for the purpose of measuring the investment in working capital as part of the FCFF, the accounting approach will need to be limited to reflect only the cash flows associated with the operating activities of the entity.

Investment in working capital is the outflows of cash during the period for increases in the net working capital requirements of the entity arising from the operating activities of the entity and therefore items such as cash and cash equivalents and short-term debt (the cash flows relating to these items are financing rather than operating costs and result in recognition of a liability and subsequently an interest expense, for example, overdrafts, term loans, notes payable and the short-term component of long-term debt) should be excluded. If cash is added to current assets for this calculation it will lead to double counting. To avoid this, cash is excluded from the calculation. When a sale is made the sale is recorded in revenue. If cash is received from the sale, the cash is recorded in cash but if the sale is on credit the sale will be recorded in accounts receivable. In this latter case, there will be a delay in the receipt of funds until the payment date. When the payment is received in the future there will be a decrease in accounts receivable.

The change in Net Working Capital (Δ NWC) is calculated as:

> ∆NWC = (Change in Accounts Receivable + Change in Inventory + Change in Prepaid Expenses and Other Current Assets) - (Change in Accounts Payable + Change in Accrued Liabilities and Other Current Liabilities)

An increase in NWC over a given period will involve the use of cash. For a growing entity, both accounts receivable and inventory tend to increase in line with sales growth. Conversely, an increase in accounts payable represents a source of cash as it is money that has been retained (through delay in payment) by the entity as opposed to being paid out.

The concept of investment in working capital is similar to the concept of the cash conversion cycle as working cash flow discussed in Chapter 6. For the purpose of estimating the FCFF it is necessary to identify all investments in net working capital. An increase in accounts receivable or inventory for business expansion purposes needs to be funded as does a decrease in accounts payable. Both decrease the FCFF available to shareholders and debt holders.

Information about investment in working capital can be observed in the cash flow from operating activities in the cash flow statement or by considering the change in current assets and current liabilities (adjusted for cash, cash equivalents and short-term debt).

##### Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE) 
Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) is the cash flow available to the entity’s holders of equity after all operating expenses, interest and principal payments on debt have been paid or new debt raisings have been completed and necessary investments in working and fixed capital have been made.

The FCFE typically represents the cash available for payment over time in the form of dividends and share buybacks to the ordinary share equity owners of an entity.

Calculating the Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE) The FCFE can be calculated in a number of different ways, each of which will yield the same solution for both the FCFE and subsequently the value of equity. Analysts will typically choose one of the three methods shown in Exhibit 10.6 to calculate FCFE, but the most popular approaches are the EBIT and net income approaches.
![](DraggedImage-267.png)
The FCFE is the amount of money that could be paid out as dividends to ordinary shareholders, preference shareholders and other non-controlling interests. If we wanted to know the value of the FCFE attributable to ordinary share equity only, we would need to adjust for any preference shares and non-controlling or minority interests. Most entities do not issue preference shares or have minority interests, but for the ones that do, the adjustment required would be to subtract the following from the FCFE calculated using the above approaches.

> FCFE attributable to ordinary share equity = FCFE - Preferred Share Dividends - New Preferred Shares Issued + Preferred Shares Redeemed - Contributions from Minority Interests + Payments to Non-controlling Interests

#### 10.4.3.2 FCFF and the Value of Equity

Using the discounted cash flow approach, it is assumed that the value of an entity can be estimated by discounting all future cash flows expected to be generated by an entity by an appropriate risk-adjusted discount rate. When using the FCFF as the expected future cash flows, the appropriate discount rate will be the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) to reflect the expected returns of equity and debt investors providing funding.
![](DraggedImage-268.png)
Given that it is not feasible to estimate all FCFFs to infinity, analysts can either apply a constant growth model to determine the enterprise value or apply a multistage model which can map the FCFF through the phases of an entity’s life cycle.

##### Constant Growth FCFF Model

In the constant growth model, the enterprise value is assumed to be the present value of a perpetuity in which the future growth rate of the FCFF is constant. This can be specified as follows:
![](DraggedImage-269.png)
This approach to calculating an entity’s value is simple in its application. However, it assumes that the FCFF will grow at its current growth rate in perpetuity. Whilst this is a reasonable assumption for mature, established entities, it is not reasonable for entities in their early growth phase or entities going through significant transition (a change of business activity or significant growth via acquisition).

##### Illustrative Example 11
---- 

##### Multistage FCFF Model

A multistage model (typically a two- or three-state model) requires consideration of economic, industry and entity specific factors affecting the FCFF during different phases of an entity’s life-cycle. A model such as this requires acknowledgement that the behaviour of the entity’s FCFF changes over time as the entity moves from one phase to another. The complexity of the multiphase approach increases as the number of phases is increased, the point at which phases transition and because the time value of money causes long dated future cash flows discounted over long horizons to become insignificant relative to more recent cash flows.

Most analysts apply a two-state model that requires an initial period during which the entity may have a high or variable growth rate followed by a second period where the FCFF grows at a lower but constant rate.

The point of differentiation between the first and second period is selected on the assumption that all future cash flows will grow at a long-term stable rate beyond this point and that preparing detailed forecasts beyond that point in time may not be worthwhile since the level of accuracy achieved by determining a precise long-run figure for cash flow is outweighed by the uncertainty associated with a long-term forecast.

Most analysts prefer to utilise the two-state model as it allows a deeper interrogation of factors affecting the value for the entity by requiring consideration of factors affecting the FCFF during the initial and terminal periods.

Using a two-stage valuation model can mitigate the problems inherent in forecasting distant FCFF. The first stage involves identification of the FCFF for each year until the end of phase 1 (time = T). By using a constant growth rate in the second period, it is possible to estimate a terminal value (TV) or residual value. The TV captures the value of all free cash flows to the entity that exist during the second period in a single outcome.

The two-state-model can be specified as follows:
![](DraggedImage-270.png)
When estimating the terminal value (TVT ), three inputs are required: the value of the FCFF at time T, the expected growth rate (gTV ) during the second period and the WACC that will apply during the second period. The constant perpetual growth rate, together with the WACC, allows the use of a simple perpetuity model to determine the terminal value. The WACC used to calculate the terminal value may differ from the WACC used in the initial period because the risk profile of the entity may differ during the initial period and the second period.

The terminal value can be estimated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-271.png)
![](DraggedImage-272.png)
For the process of estimating the value of equity using the two-stage process, FCFF involves the following steps:

Step 1. Identification of relevant FCFF over an initial selected time horizon until such time as future growth rates are assumed to stabilise (this is usually 5 to 10 years). Some analysts refer to this as the ‘competitive advantage’ period to reflect the period when the entity has an advantage over competitors that would afford it a different growth rate or growth opportunities that will not be sustained into the long term. For mature entities in established industries, five years is often sufficient for allowing an entity to reach its steady state. If an entity is in the early stages of rapid growth or is expected to experience changing growth prospects over the next few years, it may be more appropriate to build a longer-term projection model (e.g. ten years or more) to allow the entity to reach a steady state level of cash flow.

To perform Step 1:
- a. Determine the primary strategic, entity specific and industry factors likely to affect future growth prospects and performance. Mature entities normally require a shorter initial period.
	- b. Identify an appropriate timeframe for Stage 1 based on the relationship between the expected rate of return of the incremental investment required to support forecasted growth and the cost of capital. This period should continue whilst the expected rate of return of the incremental investment required to support forecasted growth exceeds the cost-of-capital.
	- c. Forecast relevant FCFF.

	There is no prescribed formula to forecast future cash flows and therefore this will require a degree of judgement. In order to calculate future FCFF, it is necessary to estimate the amount of cash the entity will receive and pay in each period.

	As discussed in Section 10.2.1 of this chapter, historical performance can provide valuable insight for developing defensible assumptions to forecast FCFF. Past growth rates, profit margins and other ratios are usually a reliable indicator of future performance, especially for mature entities in non-cyclical sectors. It is often useful to review historical levels of these measures from financial data, with adjustments made for non-recurring items and recent events, as appropriate, to provide a normalised basis for projecting financial performance or alternatively obtain industry consensus forecasts.

	Also, for mature entities, the relationship between sales and the levels of EBIT, changes in NWC, CAPEX and depreciation typically can be expressed as a percentage that remains relatively constant over time.

	The factors likely to affect the length of the initial period, the future growth prospects and performance include the industry of the entity, the impact of economies of scale arising from lower per unit costs as the entity grows, the level of operating leverage, the impact of the business cycle and how it may impact future sales and capital investment in working capital and fixed assets, where the entity is positioned in its life-cycle and the degree of consistency between the levels of investment and expected future revenue growth rates. Some analysts will apply detailed assessment techniques such as SWOT analysis (analysing the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats to the entity), Porter’s five forces (analysing the rivalry among existing entities, threats of potential entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of suppliers and bargaining power of customers) or PESTEL analysis (analysing the external Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal factors).

	Step 2. Selection of an appropriate discount rate (for FCFF use the WACC).

	Step 3. Determine an appropriate terminal value at the end of the initial selected time horizon using a constant growth model. The determination of the perpetual growth rate is one of the most important and complex tasks of the DCF valuation process. Minor changes in this rate will have major effects on the TV and therefore on the entity value in total.

	Calculation of the TV can also be done using an enterprise value multiple such as EV/EBITDA, as discussed in Section 10.4.4.1.

	Step 4. Calculate the present value of the initial period cash flows and the terminal value.

	Step 5. Adjust the enterprise value to remove the claims of all claimants other than ordinary controlling shareholders. Recall from the introduction to Section 10.4 that the value of equity is equal to:
> Value of Equity = Enterprise Value -  Value of Debt - Value of Preference Shares + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

Common missteps that can skew the DCF valuation include the use of unrealistic financial projections and an incorrect WACC.

The results of the FCFF discounted cash flow analysis rely heavily on the assumptions made to derive the cash flows, growth and WACC observations above. Whilst the above may be regarded as a base case, analysts typically also apply sensitivity to the results obtained to assess the impact of changes in the assumptions made and develop scenarios that reflect an optimistic worst case and pessimistic scenario that reflect realistic and probable outcomes.
