##### Constant Growth FCFE Model
In the constant growth model, the enterprise value is assumed to be the present value of a perpetuity in which the future growth rate of the FCFE is constant. This can be specified as follows:
![](DraggedImage-274.png)
It is important to note that the growth rates of FCFF and FCFE need not be, and frequently are not, the same. In general, it is expected that the FCFE growth rate will be a function of the entity’s reinvestment rate and the return on equity.

##### Multistage FCFE Model

As per the multistage FCFF model, the FCFE may also require a multistage model (typically a two- or three-state model), due to changes in economic, industry and entity specific factors affecting the FCFE during different phases of an entity’s life-cycle.

Using a two-stage valuation model can mitigate the problems inherent in forecasting distant FCFE. The first stage involves identification of the FCFE for each year until the end of phase 1 (time = T). By using a constant growth rate in the second period, it is possible to estimate a terminal value (TV) or residual value. The TV captures the value of all free cash flows to the entity that exist during the second period in a single outcome.

The two-state model can be specified as follows:
![](DraggedImage-275.png)

When estimating the terminal value three inputs are required: the value of the FCFE at time T, the expected growth rate during the second period and the cost of equity that will apply during the second period. This cost of equity may differ from the cost of equity used in the initial period because the risk profile of the entity may differ during the initial period and the second period. Most analysts prefer to utilise the two-state model as it allows a deeper interrogation of factors affecting the value for the entity by requiring consideration of factors affecting the FCFE during the initial and terminal periods.

The terminal value can be estimated as follows:
![](DraggedImage-276.png)
The assumptions made to calculate the terminal value are critical because the present value of the terminal value is often a substantial portion of the total value of the equity. The long-term stable growth rate (gTV ) can be approximated by considering the long-term return on capital multiplied by the retention rate.

### 10.4.4 Comparable Methods

Comparable methods of valuation involve market-based approaches that can be used in the valuation of an entity, divisions within an entity, assets held by an entity and an entity’s equity through reference to other entities and assets that are comparable.

The approach derives a relative rather than intrinsic value for an entity and its equity through the use of comparable industry or entity data. From an entity valuation perspective, this is a particularly useful approach when the entity’s shares are not publicly quoted or when there is limited public information about the entity.

The idea underlying relative valuation is that similar assets should sell at similar prices, and the comparable method is typically implemented using enterprise multiples (ratios of enterprise value to sales, EBITDA, EBIT or FCFF) or equity price multiples (ratios of stock price to a fundamental performance measure such as earnings, book value of equity or FCFE per share).

Comparable analysis requires a systematic approach to ensure there is rigour in the identification of suitable comparable entities and in the calculations performed. The approach assumes that similar entities will provide a relative reference point for valuing a given entity or its equity. To be used in this way, the relative entities share key business and financial characteristics, performance drivers and business and financial risks. It is critical that a detailed understanding of the business and financial attributes of the entity being valued are identified and understood so as to facilitate comparisons.

Comparable methods generally fall into two categories:
• Trading comparable or multiples analysis; and
• Transactions or precedent analysis.

These two approaches are discussed in the next sections. Both approaches are quite similar in their execution, except the trading comparable approach relies upon multiples derived typically from similar existing entities that are traded on exchanges. In contrast, the transactions comparable or precedent approach relies upon data from previous transactions involving the sale of equity to third parties.

As will be discussed next, the most generic and widely used multiples employ a measure of market valuation in the numerator (e.g. enterprise value, equity value) and a universal measure of financial performance in the denominator (e.g. EBITDA, net income).

#### 10.4.4.1 Trading Comparables or Multiples Analysis

Comparable analysis involving the use of enterprise or price multiples from individual comparable entities from within an industry involves the following five steps as part of the analysis

##### Step 1. Select the universe of comparable entities

The identification and selection of comparable entities is based on professional judgement, which may vary between analysts. The purpose of the selection is to identify entities that have similar risk, growth and cash flow profiles that enhance the legitimacy of the entity comparison.

In general, the selection of comparable entities is based on a number of business and financial attributes and an assessment of whether the similarities are reasonable enough to include as a benchmark. These attributes include the following criteria as shown in Exhibit 10.7.
![](DraggedImage-277.png)
Whilst it is important that these entities exhibit similar factors affecting cash flows, growth and risk, from time to time it may be necessary to select comparable entities that are listed overseas or may operate in similar or related industries. It will be almost impossible to find two or more entities with identical financial statistics, ratios and trading multiples. Hence the analyst must apply judgement in determining which comparable entities are most suitable. Otherwise, restricting the sample to just those with almost identical features may be unnecessarily restrictive

##### Step 2. Identify necessary financial information

Once a group or ‘universe’ of comparable entities has been identified, information necessary to calculate key financial statistics, ratios and trading multiples needs to be obtained from publicly available sources such as annual reports, public announcements, press releases and information from industry bodies, equity analysts and media agencies such as Bloomberg and Reuters. This information is used to determine the profitability, growth and credit strength of the comparable entities in the next step

##### Step 3. Key statistics, ratios and trading multiples

Using information from Step 2, the analyst can calculate key financial statistics, ratios and trading multiples for the comparable entities.

Some caution is needed to ensure the ratios and trading multiples are all calculated on the same basis to allow direct comparison. Because entities report at different year ends and intermittent dates (quarterly or semi-annually) it is necessary to ensure the financial statements are all calendarised to conform to a common calendar year. This will provide a common basis for comparison of financial information and ensure that appropriate adjustments are made for non-recurring items that may otherwise distort comparative analysis

##### Step 4. Benchmark the comparable entities

Using a benchmarking approach, the characteristics of the entity being valued are compared to the key financial statistics, ratios and trading multiples for the comparable entities. This analysis allows the entity to be assessed and ranked relative to the comparable entities.

To evaluate an individual entity, the analyst can compare the enterprise or equity multiple it trades at to the average multiple computed from the comparable entities. If it is significantly different, the analyst can make a subjective judgement about whether to exclude the entity from the analysis. This allows for a stronger comparable analysis by eliminating those comparable entities that do not exhibit similar key financial statistics, ratios and trading multiples. On the basis of this analysis, outliers can be eliminated from the analysis

##### Step 5. Determine the required valuation

Descriptive statistics including mean, median, high and low value are determined from the remaining comparable analysis. The value of an entity or its equity can be derived by using the findings of this analysis – either as a range using the high and low of the comparables or as a single estimate using the mean or median of the comparables or sometimes relying on the judgement of the analyst.

#### Enterprise Value Approach

To estimate the enterprise value, the earnings model needs to consider the earnings possible from the operational assets of the entity and exclude any redundant assets that do not contribute to the entity’s expected future earnings. The calculation of the enterprise value is as follows:
![](DraggedImage-278.png)
#### Persistent Earnings

In this model, persistent earnings should reflect the level of earnings that are expected to be sustainable and to persist into the foreseeable future. Earnings persistence is a central measure of earnings quality and therefore affects the ability to forecast earnings. The following four measures that can be derived from the profit or loss statement are potential measures from which to derive persistent earnings. For example, when calculating the enterprise value, the earnings should be pre-interest expenses. When calculating the equity value directly, earnings should be net of interest expenses.

• Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA). This can be considered an approximate measure of the operating performance of an entity before considering the impacts of taxation (including depreciation), accounting adjustments (including amortisation) and the funding decisions of the entity.

• Earnings before interest and taxes (operating income). This is a more conventional measure of accounting earnings that considers both the operating and non-operating activities of the entity but is measured before income tax and the effect of funding choices.

• Earnings before interest but after taxes (NOPAT). This converts the entity’s operating profit into an after-tax value.

• Revenue (sales). In some industries such as retail and other service-based industries, or if the entity introduces a new product or develops a new franchise, sales are a major factor in determining the overall profitability and therefore Enterprise Value.

To determine the persistent earnings of an entity, it is necessary to adjust historical pre-tax reported earnings for items such as discontinued operations, one-off or abnormal earnings or income or expenses related to redundant assets.

Estimation of persistent earnings typically involves an examination of historical and current financial statements to identify any necessary adjustments and then a decision is made as to whether the earnings should reflect:
- • The arithmetic average of historical earnings.
- • A weighted average approach giving a heavier weighting to more recent historical earnings.
- • Using the last available earnings calculation as representative of future earnings, especially if there have been significant changes in the entity’s operations, significant acquisitions of new assets or divestments of activities in the past.
- • Forecasting the future earnings figure to reflect expected changes in the entity’s operations or assets.

#### Enterprise Value Earnings Multipliers

It is critical that the earnings multiple is consistent with the choice of persistent earnings. They can be estimated by using the entity’s historical, current or expected multiples for the entity or by using publicly available comparable entity multiples from a similar or related industry (Exhibit 10.8).
![](DraggedImage-279.png)

Enterprise value earnings multiples are built around valuing the entity or its operating assets. Value multiples require two inputs – an estimate of the value of an entity or its operating assets in the numerator and a measure of persistent earnings or revenue (sales) in the denominator.

The above measures of persistent earnings need to correspond directly to the enterprise value multiples that are used. Both the persistent earnings and the multiples can be calculated to reflect an entity’s historical, current or expected measures or alternatively can utilise publicly available multiples from comparable entities in the same or related industries.

The most commonly used enterprise value multiple is the EV/EBITDA multiple. Analysts have a preference towards using EV/EBITDA so as to avoid the distortions caused by non-cash items such as depreciation. This multiple relates the fair enterprise value to the earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of the entity:
![](DraggedImage-280.png)

Using the EV/EBITDA earnings multiple, the enterprise value can be estimated as follows:

> Enterprise Value = (Persistent EBITDA Earnings x Industry EV /EBITDA Multiple) + Net Redundant Assets

Subsequently the equity value can be estimated as follows:

> Value of Equity = Enterprise Value - Value of Debt - Value of Preference Shares + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

The EV/EBITDA multiple is popular with analysts because: it allows comparison between entities with differing levels of financial leverage; it allows for valuation distortions arising from the use of non-cash items such as depreciation and amortisation; and EBITDA is typically positive even if net profit and earnings per square are negative.

When using EV/EBITDA, caution should be exercised because this approach ignores capital expenditure requirements and differences in tax rates between entities and the time value of money is not fully taken into account

#### Net Redundant Assets

Net redundant assets are measured as redundant assets – redundant liabilities. If entities are operating efficiently, net redundant assets should have an immaterial amount of redundant assets and liabilities, so normally this value would be set to zero. Redundant assets include an entity’s assets that are in excess of the day-to-day operations of the business under review and could be withdrawn without impairing its ability to operate and generate the persistent earnings (for example: excess amounts of cash; marketable securities; unused land, buildings and equipment; and unused copyrights, patents and licences). Redundant liabilities include borrowings for servicing redundant assets or working capital that is excessive relative to what is needed for normal operations.

#### Equity Price Multiples Value Approach

It is also possible to estimate the value of equity directly by using the following approach:

> Value of Equity = Persistent Earnings x Price Multiples + Net Redundant Assets

In this case, the persistent earnings should reflect earnings net of interest expenses (net profit) and the earnings multiple will typically involve the use of price multiples (ratios of stock price to a fundamental performance measure such as earnings, book value of equity or FCFE per share).

#### Price to Earnings (P/E) Ratio

The price to earnings (P/E) ratio’s simplicity makes it the most widely used of all relative measure multiples (however, caution is required in its application, because without consideration of the internal context of an entity, the relationship to an entity’s financial fundamentals is often ignored, leading to significant errors in applications). In its simplest form, the P/E ratio is the ratio of the fair value of equity relative to the earnings distributed to equity holders:

![](DraggedImage-281.png)

This formula can be used to calculate a per share basis:
![](DraggedImage-282.png)
Using the the P/E ratio as an earnings multiple, the value of an entity’s equity can be derived as follows:
> Value of Equity = Maintainable Net Profit x P/E Multiple + Net Redundant Assets

In determining the P/E ratio, the numerator should reflect the current market price of the ordinary shares on issue. The denominator is the earnings per share. It should reflect the earnings available to shareholders and can be expressed in any of the following ways:
• Current earnings per share
• Trailing earnings per share or
• Forward earnings per share

Using current earnings per share involves the use of the most recently reported earnings per share. The trailing earnings per share involves the use of historical semi-annual or quarterly earnings results during the past 12 months. In contrast, the forward earnings per share is based on the estimated future earnings per share (this is particularly useful if the analyst wants to compare the impact of current versus future earnings per share, especially if there is an expectation of any material changes in earnings).

The P/E ratio can be very different between entities and over time depending on which measure of earnings per share is used, due to volatility in earnings over time, differences in the entity life-cycle, difference in industries and differences in the utilisation of leverage.

Caution is needed when calculating P/E multiples because the measurement of both the EV and the EBITDA are sensitive to differences in accounting standards, the time value of money not being fully taken into account and measures needed for normalising when earnings are erratic.

The following characteristics of the P/E ratio impact its performance as a multiple:
• The P/E ratio of a high-growth entity is a function of the expected extraordinary growth rate – the higher the expected growth, the higher the P/E ratio for an entity. Entities with a higher growth potential, lower risk and higher payout generally have higher P/E ratios.
• The P/E ratio is a function of the perceived business and financial risk of an entity. An entity with a higher cost of equity will trade at a lower multiple of earnings than a similar entity with a lower cost of equity.
• Caution is needed in interpreting the P/E ratio of an entity. It is generally regarded as an indication of relative value rather than the actual price of the entity, especially when the P/E ratios are derived from an industry average or via comparable entity analysis.

#### 10.4.4.2 Comparable Approach Using Transactions Comparables or Precedent Analysis

The transaction comparable or precedent analysis approach is similar to the trading comparable or multiples analysis approach discussed in the previous section. Both approaches rely upon external comparable data to estimate key financial statistics, ratios and multiples. The primary difference to the trading comparable approach is the source of the data that is used.

In precedent analysis the data is derived from valuations performed during merger and acquisition transactions. Entities involved in mergers and acquisitions are normally valued to include premiums due to synergies or other non-cash advantages arising from the transactions. Caution must therefore be exercised when using precedent analysis to ensure that the impact of these factors on the derived value is understood.

### 10.4.5 Recommendation on Valuation Models

As has been discussed, each of the approaches has their own advantages, disadvantages, underlying assumptions and processes for implementation. Most analysts typically use more than one approach for business valuation purposes.

Exhibit 10.9 summarises the findings of the equity valuation analysis performed in Section 10.4.3 for FCFF and FCFE and Section 10.4.4 for EV/Sales, EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT and Price/Earnings.
![](DraggedImage-283.png)
So how can the results in Exhibit 10.9 be examined to demonstrate the value of an entity’s equity?

This can be done by visualising the results using a floating bar chart, which is otherwise known as a football field chart. This can show estimates of the value of an entity using different valuation methods. The approach provides a good way to summarise these ranges and visualise any possible overlap.

The following demonstrates how we can apply a football field approach to assess the value of GNP’s equity value using FCFF, FCFE and enterprise value and price multiples. As shown in Exhibit 10.10, by layering the results in a football field visualisation, the analyst can see the comparative results.

Each of the valuation approaches gives a differing outcome with respect to not only the median but also the high and low range outcomes. Analysis of the exhibit shows that there is a common overlap between each of the approaches for the value of equity in the range of
![](DraggedImage-284.png)
HK$2.955 billion to HK$3.202 billion. This is the range in which the value of equity is most likely to be, a range similar to the FCFE range.

The FCFF and FCFE approaches require a rigorous assessment of current and future cash flows, growth opportunities and determination of appropriate discount rates. This detailed analysis adds support to the use of these approaches over the less rigorous approaches involving a single enterprise or price earnings multipliers.

The following section will extend the discussion of the business valuation approaches by considering some of the theoretical and practical limitations of the approaches.

## 10.5 LIMITATIONS OF VALUATION MODELS

Putting the valuation models into practice highlights a number of theoretical and practical limitations that should be considered when selecting an approach to perform a required analysis.

Consistent with Learning Outcome 10.01.05, this section will explain the theoretical and practical limitations of the various valuation models discussed in Section 10.4.

### 10.5.1 Theoretical Limitations

Valuation methods raise a number of theoretical questions when put into practice, including:

• How do we define fair value?
• How can fair value be validly determined in theoretical terms?
• What practical tools may be employed to determine fair value?

If it is generally accepted that valuation should reflect the fair value of a business, a business division or the assets and liabilities of a business or division of a business, then a suitable definition is needed to ensure there is commonality of belief and acceptance of the value obtained through the valuation process. How should the fair value be defined?

Accounting standards define ‘fair value’ as the price that would be received to sell assets or paid to transfer a liability, in an orderly transaction, between market participants at the measurement date (HKFRS 13.9). Whilst applying this definition is relatively straightforward for assets and liabilities that are traded on public markets, most assets and liabilities held by entities are not market traded and therefore their values cannot be directly observed. Hence the need may often arise for the analyst to apply business valuation methods to estimate fair value.

To increase consistency and comparability in fair value measurements and related disclosures, the accounting standards establish a fair value hierarchy that categorises inputs used in the measurement of fair value into three levels. The fair value hierarchy gives the highest priority (Level 1) to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities and the lowest priority (Level 3) to unobservable inputs (Exhibit 10.11) (HKFRS 13.72–90).
![](DraggedImage-285.png)
The definition of fair value for financial reporting takes a theoretical, market-based perspective that excludes any entity specific advantages/disadvantages and information asymmetries. Its determination will have involved management making judgements about the unit of account (i.e. whether to value individual items or to group them into portfolios) and the relevance of possible reference markets. Considerations regarding reference markets can include identifying whether a relevant principal market exists, choosing the most advantageous of several potential markets or, if no observable market exists, determining whether a theoretical market can be constructed.

The remainder of this section discusses the theoretical issues and limitations arising from the valuation approaches discussed in Section 10.4.

In considering the asset-based approach, analysts must consider whether the shareholder whose interest is being valued has the authority to access directly the value of the entity’s assets (for example, by exercising their rights as a controlling shareholder). As such it is necessary to assess whether an entity’s shareholders can be classified as either controlling or non-controlling shareholders:

• Controlling shareholders – shareholders that have the authority to direct the corporation to sell all or part of the assets it owns and to distribute the proceeds to the shareholder(s).

• Non-controlling shareholders – shareholders that lack the authority available to controlling shareholders and therefore cannot directly access the value of the assets. Because these shareholders cannot avail themselves of this value, the value of a corporation’s assets is not a suitable indicator of value to a shareholder.

All income-based valuation models, including earnings-based models and discounted cash flow models, are based on the notion that the value of an investment in an asset is derived from the cash flows it is expected to deliver. This is founded on the economic premise that individuals are concerned with consumption and that access to cash now or in the future buys consumption either now or in the future. Through the use of investments, current consumption can be deferred to buy future consumption, as future cash is used to buy consumption in the future.

In this context, the value of an investment is the present value of the cash that it is expected to deliver in the future. Cash given up to acquire the investment has a time value, so expected future cash must be discounted for the time value of money. Further, if there is a risk of not receiving the expected cash, the expectation must be discounted for that risk. Accordingly, the value of an investment is the present value of (discounted) expected cash flows.

In practice it is well known that there are fundamental differences in the assumptions made and results obtained from the discounted cash flow and relative valuation approaches. Whilst discounted cash flow analysis relies on examination of intrinsic value, the relative value approach relies upon relative value by considering the market value of comparable assets, liabilities and entities. If the approaches are correct in their application, it is expected that the intrinsic and relative valuations should converge. However, if the market is systematically under or over pricing, the valuations obtained from the two approaches will diverge.

The value of an entity or its equity based on a discounted cash flow valuation is a direct function of three variables: the capacity to generate cash flows as impacted by the entity’s external and internal context (as discussed in Section 10.2.1 of this chapter), the expected growth in these cash flows and the uncertainty associated with these cash flows.

Every multiple, whether it is of earnings, book value or sales, is also a function of these same three variables (as noted by Damodaran in his book Investment Valuation, entities with higher growth rates, less risk and greater cash flow generating potential should trade at higher multiples than entities with lower growth, higher risk and less cash flow generating potential).

Theoretically, it is not unreasonable to expect that if the valuations are correctly specified the approaches should converge in their estimation of implied valuations. However, in practice this will only hold if the expected earnings, growth rate and risk are expected to remain unchanged in perpetuity. In practice unless the entity is a mature stable entity it is unlikely that this relationship will hold in practice.

### 10.5.2 Practical Limitations

This section will address the practical limitations of the valuation techniques discussed in Section 10.4 of this chapter.

#### 10.5.2.1 Cost-Based Approaches

The cost-based approach to asset valuation is widely known and applied. When performing a cost-based approach to asset valuation, many of the assets are well known and can be benchmarked quite easily between entities, for example, accounts receivable, inventories (when inventory is bought and simply resold as in distribution) and equipment.

However, the approach does have a number of challenges and limitations, including the following:

• The independent appraisal of assets can become expensive if there are numerous, large or exotic assets.

• The tax effects of measuring assets and liabilities at values different from their carrying amounts in the financial statements must be estimated.

• It may be difficult to identify assets and liabilities that are not currently recognised in the financial statements of an entity and challenging to estimate their fair values.

#### 10.5.2.2 Earnings Capitalisation Approach

One of the strengths of the capitalisation of earnings method is its simplicity. It is typically estimated by using a single number representing the earnings of the entity divided by an appropriate capitalisation rate reflecting the cost of capital adjusted for a long-term growth rate. Due to the sensitivity of results from this approach, the validity of estimated values is improved when the entity’s operations are well established and reasonably stable. Due to this stability, historical results are generally a reasonable estimate of future values.

In contrast, caution is needed if:

• The entity is operating in an industry that is rapidly evolving, the entity is in its early stage, the entity is being wound down or the entity is going through a transition phase involving changes in the nature and/or location of its operations.
• Adjustments are not correctly applied to ‘normalise’ earnings used to recast the results into what the entity could have achieved under reasonably predicable operating conditions. The adjusted results are then used to build a forward-looking earnings forecast. These adjustments include:
- °Non-recurring or extraordinary costs (or income) not typically associated with ongoing operations, such as losses from asset sales.
- °Discretionary items, including expenses that are considered to be abnormal in the context of customary operations.

#### 10.5.2.3 Discounted Cash Flow Approach

As discussed in Section 10.4.3, the discounted cash flow (DCF) approach to valuation is a common tool to estimate the value of an entity or its assets and liabilities. It is also used to analyse the effects that different economic scenarios may have on an entity’s value. Using discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis provides a number of benefits to the analyst including:

• The approach is cash-flow-based and thereby requires extensive analysis of cash flows affecting the levels of the free cash flow to the firm and the free cash flow to equity. The DCF model is extremely detailed and incorporates future expectations about the entity’s performance. The detailed analysis of cash flows allows for detailed attribution and analysis.

• The approach can be used to calculate the intrinsic enterprise value and the value of an entity’s equity by considering historical and future cash flows that are likely to affect the valuation of the entity or the entity’s equity.

• Due to the long-term nature of the DCF approach, outcomes tend not to be significantly influenced by short-term market conditions or non-economic factors, especially given the impact of the terminal value as part of the analysis.

• The approach reflects a certain level of self-sufficiency in that it does not directly require information about the cash flows of other entities or relative measures such as EV/EBITDA.

• The approach allows the analyst to assess multiple financial performance sensitivities and scenarios, including improving or declining growth rates, margins, capex requirements and working capital efficiency.

However, caution is needed when applying the DCF approach. The results from the approach are highly contingent on the cash flow projections, growth rates and WACC/cost of equity used and the estimate of terminal value. Disadvantages of the DCF approach include:

• The valuation is highly dependent on the assumptions made and the quality of financial projections, especially if using multistage models. Numerous assumptions can result in the model being prone to errors if the assumptions are not validated or if the model is made overly complex.

• The valuation from the multistage models are dominated by the value of the terminal value because the Stage 1 cash flows are dominated by the terminal value. Small changes in assumptions related to the terminal value will have a significant impact on the final valuation of the entity or equity.

• The model is best suited to situations where the entity’s capital structure remains stable. Mature entities are likely to target and maintain a particular capital structure (as discussed in Chapter 7) but entities in the early phase of their development or in the latter stages of their operations are likely to have a less stable capital structure.

• Due to the possibility of overcomplexity in models derived for the DCF approach, analysts need to exercise caution in order not to suffer from an over-confidence bias in setting assumptions and interpreting results.

• The DCF approach is not very well suited in the following situations:
- °Entities in financial distress, that may suffer from declining growth and negative FCFF measures.
- °Entities with cyclical cash flows, where the cyclicity cannot be directly captured in the terminal value.
- °Entities with non-operational assets, because the DCF model assumes the assets of the entities are being fully utilised. If an entity has assets that are underutilised (and produce reduced or even no cashflows), the value of these assets will not be fully reflected in the value obtained from discounting expected future cash flows.
- °Entities in the process of restructuring activities, where it is difficult to assess the impact on future cash flows and the impact on the entity’s risk. Entities in the process of restructuring often sell some of their assets, acquire other assets and change their capital structure and dividend policy.
- °Private entities, where it is difficult to estimate the WACC/cost of equity.

#### 10.5.2.4 Comparable Analysis

There should be a reasonable basis for comparison with and reliance upon comparable entities when comparable market information does not relate to the same or a similar entity. A comparative analysis of qualitative and quantitative similarities and differences between the comparable entities and the subject entity should be performed. Adjustments based on this comparative analysis will often need to be made and must be reasonable, with the reasons for the adjustments and how they were quantified.

The value of any asset can be estimated by looking at how the market prices ‘similar’ or ‘comparable’ assets. However, caution is needed when selecting appropriate comparable entities. Using industry averages presupposes that the entity has business and financial characteristics and risks consistent with the overall average for an industry. Also, entities within the same industry tend to adopt similar accounting practices.

Selecting appropriate comparable entities can give rise to the following practical limitations that may affect their relevance and use in a relative value analysis, including the following:
- • The availability of information to perform the valuation;
- • The geographical location of the comparable entity and its economic, legal, political and regulatory environment;
- • The currency in which the financial attributes are stated relative to the functional currency of the entity being valued;
- • The age, size and specifications of assets used by the relative comparable entities and the extent to which they have been depreciated;
- • Existing profitability or profit-making capacity of the assets;
- • Historical and expected growth rates; and
- • The legal form of ownership and/or degree of ownership control.

Once identified, each of the above issues can be controlled to facilitate their use as a comparable entity. However, caution is needed as part of this process so as not to overgeneralise the results obtained. Some analysts suggest the use of a regression-based approach to smooth out any outliers that do not conform directly.

This chapter has introduced a number of different business valuation approaches to estimate the value of an enterprise, its equity and its debt. In doing so, the chapter has considered the reasons why valuations are performed, the information requirements of performing a valuation, business valuation techniques for debt and equity and theoretical and practical limitations of the valuation techniques.

The next two chapters will extend this analysis through an examination of business merger and acquisition techniques and financial reconstructions.

## SUMMARY

• Business valuation is the process of estimating the value of an entity, divisions within an entity and individual assets and liabilities of an entity, by applying generally accepted valuation methods.

• When performing a business valuation, it is important to note that the value of an entity is equal to the value of the capital used to fund the entity. Accordingly, the three valuation perspectives: enterprise value, equity value and debt value, can be expressed in terms of this equation, as follows:

° Enterprise Value: 
> Enterprise Value = Value of Equity - Value of Debt - Value of Preference Shares + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities
° Equity Value:
> Value of Equity = Enterprise Value - Value of Debt - Value of Preference Shares + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities
° Debt Value:
> Value of Debt = Enterprise Value - Value of Equity - Value of Preference Shares + Cash and Cash Equivalent Securities

• Understanding the factors that determine the value of an entity is an important prerequisite for making informed decisions regarding:
- ° The performance of an entity; 
- ° Whether debt or equity securities issued by an entity are fairly priced, over-priced or under-priced relative to their current estimated intrinsic value and relative to the prices of comparable securities; 
- ° The value of an entity and its equity when transitioning from being privately owned to publicly owned; 
- ° Evaluating corporate events such as mergers, acquisitions, divestments, spin-offs and leveraged buy-outs; and 
- ° Inferring market expectations about the future prospects of the entity.

• The primary reasons for performing business valuations are:
- ° For undertaking an initial public offering of shares when an entity moves from being privately owned to publicly owned and traded on an exchange; 
- ° For assessing the impact of merger and acquisition activities on the enterprise value; and
- ° For undertaking the disposal of assets or business segments in an orderly sale or a liquidation process.

• In making business valuation decisions, analysts ordinarily consider both financial and nonfinancial information. This includes an understanding of the economy and industry within which the entity operates and the factors affecting the earnings, growth expectations and risks of the individual entity being valued. The analyst will typically require at least five years (if possible) of an entity’s financial statements and may need to perform an on-site visit to check the entity’s operations and its physical assets. The analyst will also consider any intangible assets and the future outlook of the entity and will compare the business to similar businesses operating in the market.

• Caution is needed when performing business valuations because of information gaps, information asymmetries and difficulties in predicting future outcomes when relevant future financial and non-financial information is unknown.

• Debt can typically be broadly categorised as irredeemable or redeemable. When valuing debt, priority should be given to using market prices and observed yields to maturity to value all debt instruments. However, in cases where there is no observable market price or yield to maturity, or there is a lack of liquidity in trading, it may be necessary to use alternative valuation methods such as:
- Discounted cash flow approach – This approach involves the calculation of the value of debt based on a discounted cash flow valuation model that incorporates the expected fixed and/or floating cash flows or any optionality and applies a suitable discount rate that reflects the current yield to maturity of the debt instrument (incorporating the current credit spread of the entity).
- Comparable approach – This approach requires the analysis of comparable market traded financial instruments. Prices from these debt instruments are used to estimate cash flows, price and yield to maturity. This can be done in one of two different ways:
	- By considering comparative debt instruments issued by similarly rated entities from similar or related industries. As part of performing this analysis, the analyst will consider debt issuances by sectors, structure of the issuance and the source of the issues.
	- By considering yield spreads inferred directly from derivative instruments such as credit default swaps.

• Equity can be valued directly, using approaches that value the intrinsic or relative value of equity, or indirectly, via enterprise valuation from which equity value can be derived. The most common equity valuation techniques use alternative valuation methods, such as:
- Asset-based approaches – These approaches consider the net value of assets using historical values of assets and liabilities, a cost-based approach that assesses the cost to reproduce or replace the service capability of assets being valued, fair value or the net realisable value approach. The approaches rely heavily on financial reporting information.
- Earnings-based approaches – These approaches focus on an entity’s earnings to estimate its fundamental value. The model is based on the premise that positive economic income in the form of dividends and retained earnings leads to shareholder value creation. Typical approaches include earnings capitalisation and residual income-based approaches.
- Discounted cash flow-based approaches – These approaches are based on the fundamental notion that the value of an entity is equal to the present value of expected future cash flows arising from the operating activities of the entity. Given that entities are regarded as a series of projects involving the use of assets, the value of an entity, the divisions within entities and both assets and liabilities of an entity can be estimated using this approach. Typical approaches include free cash flow to the firm to estimate enterprise value and free cash flow to equity to estimate the value of equity.
- Comparable approaches – These approaches identify whether an entity is fairly valued relative to some benchmark or comparable group of entities in the same sector. Also known as relative valuation methods, these approaches assume that an entity’s value can be estimated by reference to the value of similar entities or transactions involving comparable entities. Enterprise valuation approaches are implemented using enterprise multiples (ratios of enterprise value to sales, EBITDA, EBIT or FCFF), whilst equity price multiples (ratios of stock price to a fundamental performance measure such as earnings, book value of equity or FCFE per share) are typically used for equity valuation purposes.

# Business combination (Business finance)

## OPENING CASE

XYZ WIDGETS

Over its decades-long history, XYZ Widgets routinely found itself the target of a merger or acquisition bid.

XYZ’s management sometimes sought buyers based on strategic compatibility. More commonly, though, the company, relying on cues from professional advisors, engaged buyers who weren’t exactly a natural fit but willing to pay up.

Founded in 1956, the family-owned widget-making company was, one decade later, acquired by a boutique investment bank. A few years after that, XYZ was sold to a conglomerate which itself was later absorbed into another conglomerate which ultimately became the target of a leveraged buyout circa the late 1980s. This was a period of heavy debt and an unsuccessful foray into non-widget activities. By the mid-1990s, XYZ was back to solely making widgets, this time under the ownership of a private equity firm. In 2005, XYZ sold shares to the public via an initial public offering (IPO). The IPO flopped.

Widget making had become overly competitive with a proliferation of players pushing prices down. Management, meanwhile, was criticised for not having a clear growth strategy. Within a few months of going public, XYZ, with its share price falling, faced a hostile takeover attempt. It proved unsuccessful. Large shareholders, with a majority of controlling interest (voting shares) refused the offer.

For a brief period in 2007, senior managers considered a global growth strategy that might involve a cross-border deal with an overseas competitor. However, turmoil in the financial markets led to austerity measures and strategic growth plans were put aside. After the crisis, XYZ, having held off on new operational investments, struggled to expand revenue sources. Profit growth was flat; large institutional shareholders were anxious. Thus, XYZ recently once again found itself a target of acquisitive organisations. These acquirers can be categorised into the following three groups:

1. Foreign competitors seeking a beachhead in a new market;
2. Domestic competitors looking primarily for intellectual property (patents); and
3. Large holding companies purely seeking to diversify.

The five highest bids, based on the current value of the cash and/or stock offered, representing all three buyer-type categories were chosen for a more thorough evaluation.

Aided by analysis done by consultants, attorneys and investment bankers, along with extensive memorandums written by senior management, XYZ’s board members spent a full day in a conference room trying to make a determination on which bid to accept. Which company, if any, will XYZ choose to combine with?

## OVERVIEW

In a world of unrelenting corporate pressures, business combinations are helpful strategies for companies to maximise shareholder value relative to all possible other investments. Business combinations can also be risky given the inherent uncertainty of future business performance.

As such, senior management of companies should continually seek to make betterinformed decisions when evaluating appropriate strategic combinations, including mergers, acquisitions and consolidations. Advisory services, which include but are not limited to professionals such as accountants, bankers, lawyers and consultants, play important roles in business combination and can support management in making strategic decisions.

Skillful evaluation of potential corporate transformations, whether in weighing formal proposals or just in terms of overall awareness of strategic options, requires a mix of quantitative and qualitative approaches. Data-based analysis and calculations need to be countered by subjective judgements. In other words, creating a framework for deciding on the proper business combination calls for a broad array of measurements and considerations.

This chapter discusses common combination schemes, including mergers and acquisitions, takeovers and hostile takeovers. This chapter covers the concept of how to advise directors on fighting off hostile takeover bids, regulations, financing options and due diligence. This chapter also covers proposal evaluation skills with an eye towards being able to identify what constitutes being in the shareholders’ best interests or not, and versus other potential factors.

## 11.1 JUSTIFICATIONS FOR BUSINESS COMBINATIONS

While the overall pace of business combinations may fluctuate over the phases of a business cycle, business combinations remain a powerful force shaping the competitive landscapes of all industries.

At least several corporate priorities drive all of this buying and selling: desire to create shareholder value; pressure for external growth; quest for synergies; and diversification. Illustrative Example 1 discusses the drivers for business combinations.

It is important to be aware of the various theories that explain the motives behind and challenges of business combinations. This section introduces the principal-agent theory (PAT), the neoclassical theory, the redistribution theory, the efficiency theory and the market power theory of mergers and acquisitions.

The PAT presents a dilemma as companies will hire agents to work on their behalf yet the agents may be motivated to act in their best interest instead of the interest of the hiring company. The PAT is relevant to mergers and acquisitions as there are several principal-agent relationships involved in the process. The purchasing company or acquirer will hire and depend on agents to perform certain tasks throughout the process, which will result in the information asymmetry problem associated with the PAT. Management may want to conceal certain information about the company that may impact the company’s valuation or perception. Information asymmetry can be a cause for mergers and acquisitions to be unsuccessful as it can lead to breaches of contracts or mistrust between two parties.

The neoclassical theory presents different challenges to management during a business combination. The neoclassical theory suggests that a successful business combination requires the consideration of human behaviour of each company in addition to the areas traditionally inspected during due diligence. Under the theory, the structure and success of a company is affected by the behaviour of its employees, for example a company whose employees exhibit exceptional communication and teamwork behaviours will likely experience higher operational efficiency.

The redistribution theory can also be called the hubris theory, as it involves the overestimation of a company’s power or position. The theory suggests that the motive for a business combination is to provide a means for efficiently redistributing the resources of a company while minimising the transaction costs.

The efficiency theory suggests that companies combine because they possess different strengths and weaknesses and are therefore efficient in different ways. The two combining companies can theoretically capitalise on the efficiencies of the other company. These combinations typically take the form of a horizontal merger, which is discussed in Section 11.2.1.

The market power theory states that business combinations are undertaken to increase the market share of the firm and thus their power in the market. It can be fair to assume that increasing market share increases market power, however it should be considered that decreasing the number of competitors in the market can lead to monopolies or increased competition amongst the remaining competitors.

### illustrative Example 1

Here are four examples of business combinations and their justifications:

1. A pharmaceutical company is in private merger discussions with a rival company. Shares of both companies surge upon news of the deal becoming public. The value of the combined company is greater than the two separate companies as it will enjoy operational synergies, greater economies of scale (reductions in fixed costs through greater purchasing power and operational efficiencies) and a more powerful negotiating position with suppliers and customers.

2. The Board of Directors of a video game manufacturer and retailer has set goals for the upcoming year including significant growth in market share. The company is performing due diligence on several companies outside of the video game industry as well as on companies within the video game industry as it seeks to achieve the expansion goal.

3. Three large banks in the region have merged recently and the management of each of them have referenced the savings expected from the operational synergies. The combined bank will require less middle- and back-office support functions than the three separate companies, which will increase the efficiency of operations.

4. A multinational conglomerate has announced the acquisition of a company that produces building supplies for residential and commercial real-estate developers. The conglomerate covers business endeavours across various industries and has acquired this company to further its diversification and add exposure in this specific sector.
---- 

Transactions take many forms, involving a myriad of ownership structures, from mundane internal restructurings to headline-grabbing tender offers.

Reaching a consensus on whether to proceed with a proposed transaction, relative to some other deal, or another entirely different type of investment, can be vexing. For management tasked with charting future growth, picking the right strategic partner is fraught with pros and cons, short-term versus long-term considerations, not to mention a long list of other crucial factors.

Some of the main considerations for evaluators of deal proposals include:
• financial statement analysis
• business model and synergies evaluation
• value-added metrics
• competitive pressures
• cultural idiosyncrasies
• macroeconomic conditions
• regulatory environments

Evaluation of deal proposals involve professionals representing several interconnected disciplines. These include: banking; accounting; consulting; legal; and risk management. If a deal is to be deemed a strategically viable and worthwhile endeavour, these advisors work alongside and support senior corporate executives who will make that determination.

The following is a checklist of business combination justifications, as seen from both a target’s and an acquirer’s perspective:

• Are shareholders’ best interests served?
• Does the price reflect fair market value?
• Are synergies identifiable and, more importantly, achievable?

One more pivotal question for the acquirer (and its advisors):
• Could capital be better deployed in some other fashion?

Companies perform thorough due diligence to assist with evaluating and verifying key facts and the valuation of potential acquisition targets. The due diligence process often involves a review and verification of the following areas:

• Legal
°Organisational structure and key management personnel.
°Litigation involving the company.
°Regulation affecting the company.
°Contracts and agreements.
°Real estate locations and agreements.
°Company policies and procedures.
°Insurance coverage.

• Commercial
°Supplier and subcontractor agreements.
°Marketing plans and materials for current and new products.
°Summary of customers and customer revenues.
°Analysis of why customers leave.
°Customer and distribution partner contracts.
°Detail on revenue streams.

• Financial
°Financial statements and off-balance sheet finances.
°Contingent liabilities.
°Capital structure, shares outstanding, warrants and convertibles and outstanding debt.
°Assessment of management controls and management representation letters.
°Tax information and tax implications.
°Investment and hedging policies.
°Bank statements and letters of credit.
°Physical assets and intellectual property.

• Operations
°Capital expenditure projects completed and planned.
°Summary of equipment leased vs capitalised.
°Human resource and employee concerns.
°Summary of employee benefits and compensation policy.
°Summary of bonuses, profit sharing, stock options and pension plans.
°Litigation brought against the company by employees.
°Court judgements related to the company.
°Employee disciplinary policies and historical proceedings.
°Headcount by geographic location and function.
°Policies governing hiring practices, including background, criminal and work eligibility checks.

### apply and analyse 1

Company A is considering purchasing Company B and is in the process of completing the due diligence review. So far, Company A has performed a detailed review of Company B’s financial statements, business model and its recent financial performance using ratio analysis. It has also considered the macroeconomic conditions, the regulatory environment and competitiveness of the industry in which Company B operates.

Describe the other information Company A might be interested in.

Analysis

The acquirer should also perform legal due diligence in addition to the types of due diligence already completed. Legal due diligence can uncover pending litigation against Company B with potential financial impact. Company A should gather all available information and consult with the appropriate experts in order to identify and evaluate the litigation to determine the likelihood of financial impact. Company A should also consider any regulatory or cultural considerations specific to Company B’s geographic location. Ultimately, a deal leading two businesses to bind together will hinge on parties agreeing to a price premium, one that reflects not only fair market value but also factors in future assumptions connected to anticipated advantages, or synergies, expected from the businesses combining.

## 11.2 TYPES OF BUSINESS COMBINATIONS

Business combinations occur in a variety of ways. A common method is a merger. There are various types of mergers depending on the specific structure of the deal, including horizontal, vertical, merger of equals and forward mergers. Another common type of business combination is the acquisition where an entity is absorbed into another entity, and no new entity is created. One other significant category is worthy of examination: unsolicited tender offers. Circumventing management and directors, such offers are inherently viewed by targets as unfriendly and therefore usually treated as hostile takeovers. Another form is a leveraged buyout (LBO) where a company is purchased with a significant amount of debt. The purchased company’s cash flow is used as collateral against the loan taken to purchase the company.

Some deals are considered strategic, such as when two rival companies combine either to gain specific skills, technology or other capabilities or to achieve specific goals, such as improved finances, removal of excess capacity in the market and accelerated growth. synergies can reduce supply chain costs and create operational efficiencies which can improve financial performance. For example, a supplier could be acquired by a manufacturer to reduce input costs or two rivals could merge and combine back-office support functions to be more operationally efficient. Other deals are deemed financial such as when a private equity firm acquires a company as a way to diversify its holdings. For example, a private equity firm may have a portfolio concentrated in a specific market sector such as pharmaceuticals and acquires a health care equipment manufacturing company in order to diversify its portfolio and reduce risk. The Hong Kong Codes on Takeovers and Mergers and Share Buy-backs (which will be covered in Section 11.3.3) provides a framework for business combinations, viewed in two categories: voluntary or mandatory.

One common form of takeover in Hong Kong is executed via what is known as a contractual general offer. This is when a bidder makes an offer to acquire all the outstanding shares in a target company not held by the acquirer already. Also, Hong Kong courts can authorise schemes of arrangement which sometimes involve financially troubled companies exploring mergers or acquisitions as a way to stave off liquidation or satisfy creditors.

### 11.2.1 mergers

mergers are one form of business combinations and involve uniting existing companies into one new company. The key distinction between mergers and acquisitions, which is introduced in Section 11.2.2, is that unlike mergers, acquisitions do not result in a new company.

Mergers amalgamate at least two (and sometimes more than two) companies into one. Two direct competitors combining would be categorised as a horizontal merger (Exhibit 11.1); while a vertical merger (Exhibit 11.2) is the combining of two companies that are involved in the same industry, like a supplier and a distributor, but are in different stages of the supply chain. An upstream merger is where a company closer to the end consumer merges with a supplier. Conversely, a downstream merger is where a supplier merges with a company lower in the supply chain. For example, a clothing retailer that merges with a textile factory would be a vertical merger as both companies operate in the same industry but at different levels of the supply chain.

![](DraggedImage-289.png)
![](DraggedImage-290.png)
While rare, there are occasions when two equally sized (assets, revenues, market share) companies will structure a deal as a merger of equals (Exhibit 11.3). In this kind of amalgamation, neither company takes on the role of acquirer.
![](DraggedImage-291.png)
In reality, many deals called mergers by participants will nevertheless involve one company as the acquirer and the other, in a position of relative weakness, as the target. A forward merger (Exhibit 11.4), also called a direct merger, is a merger in which the target company ceases to exist, and all assets and liabilities are assumed by the purchasing company.
![](DraggedImage-292.png)

A conglomerate merger (Exhibit 11.5) is a combination of two completely unrelated companies, typically done to diversify in other industries and reduce risk.
![](DraggedImage-293.png)
Finally, a reverse merger (Exhibit 11.6) is where a private company acquires a public company as a method of circumventing the lengthy process of ‘going public’. In a reverse triangular merger (Exhibit 11.7), an acquiring company creates a new subsidiary company which, after purchasing the target company, is then absorbed by the target. Target stock thus gets merged with the acquirer’s subsidiary; ultimately, the target company’s shareholders end up with stock in the acquirer.
![](DraggedImage-294.png)
Because we are distinguishing mergers from acquisitions in this section, it is worth pointing out that, more often than not, what we call mergers will invariably involve an acquisition. Technically speaking, what most people call mergers are actually consolidations.

Legally recognised consolidations distinctly result in an entirely new company in which the shareholders of both the acquirer and the target get equity, and hence the ‘merger’ connotation that consolidations carry.

In addition to a new ownership structure, the new entity also emerges with a new management structure that often comprises senior leaders of the two legacy firms (though not always necessarily). For mergers to be fully consummated, both companies’ directors, having agreed to join together, put the matter to shareholders for a (51% majority) vote of approval.

Mergers can occur between similar companies mutually finding one another at precisely the right moment and on equal footing. As mentioned, such deals are rare. More deals involve a seller, or target, making concessions to a competitively stronger, or just larger, acquirer, and agreeing to be absorbed into the acquirer. In this common scenario, the term merger is sometimes used interchangeably with the term acquisition even in cases when, in actuality, the term merger wouldn’t apply.

Regardless of language, mergers have to be paid for. They can be completed in a number of ways including cash, debt, stock or convertible loans. Each of the types of payments methods have specific tax implications, which should be considered by both the purchaser and the seller. Section 11.4.4 of this chapter provides additional detail, on the various financing methods.

Even if no cash is used in the transaction, there still can be a price paid in the form of power dilution. This occurs when board seats turn over in the first few years after a merger. Power shifts can happen even more quickly than that. In July 2012, Duke Energy (acquirer) and Progress Energy (target) combined in a deal that specifically stipulated a newly configured power-sharing arrangement, with Progress’s CEO taking over as CEO of the newly enlarged Duke. Less than an hour after the deal closed, the 18-person board (11 from Duke, 7 from Progress) voted to oust the Progress CEO, replacing him with Duke’s.

From an accounting perspective, a merger is not a thing, nor an event; rather, it is merely a way to structure a purchase.

In one basic sense, a merger is an outcome in which both the acquirer and target wind up with shared operating control of a new entity, as opposed to outright stock purchases or asset purchases, both forms of acquisitions.

Companies may experience a number of benefits or advantages resulting from a merger. Benefits include:

- • Increased market share.
- • Economies of scale; for example, larger firms typically have relatively lower costs through the purchase of raw materials in bulk, or deploy larger machines that reduce per unit costs.
- • Greater operational efficiency as merged companies can rely on single back- and middle-office functions and eliminate redundancies.
- • Higher profits which can be reinvested in the company’s research and development initiatives.
- • A company with underperforming management can benefit from a merger if the other company’s management team is better suited to lead the combined company.

However, mergers have disadvantages as well, especially for the consumers or end buyers in the market. Disadvantages include:
- • Less competition in the market.
- • Higher prices.
- • Less choices or options for consumers/buyers in the market.
- • Layoffs of employees if functions become redundant.
- • Mergers have a high risk of failure.
- • Larger companies may experience operational or organisational inefficiencies due to additional layers of procedural requirements.
- • Public perception of the company may be negatively impacted.

### 11.2.2 acquisitions

Unlike mergers (or consolidations), acquisitions do not result in a new entity. In these transactions, also commonly called takeovers, a target company is absorbed into the acquirer and ceases to be. The fact that a target company finds itself being acquired often results from the company’s management recognising the strategic and/or economic benefits of selling, and often enough targets deliberately initiate a bidding process.

There are four main types of acquisitions:
- • Horizontal acquisition – This is similar to a horizontal merger where a competitor acquires a competitor.
- • Vertical acquisition – This takes place when a company purchases an intermediary in its process, such as a supplier.
- • Congeneric acquisition – This occurs when a company acquires another company that offers a product or service in a different area of the same industry. For example, a bank may acquire an insurance provider in order to offer its customers insurance products in addition to its banking products.
- • Conglomerate acquisition – This involves companies that do not operate in the same industry, do not offer the same products, or otherwise do not have the same business model. This type of acquisition offers the benefit of diversification.

In the end, the larger acquirer continues onward, having taken over the target. In some cases, a target might just be unquestionably smaller in terms of market capitalisation or net revenue. But a target might also be burdened by some competitive disadvantage (e.g. a dying distribution model or an outsized pension benefit obligation).

Acquiring companies can follow the following process to identify potentially viable acquisition targets. The first step is to perform a comprehensive review of the industry supply chain highlights where future sources of profit exist, such as emerging or disruptive technology. Then a list of targets can be assembled based on industry analysis and company criteria, such as presence in a specific geographical area, customer base, financial performance, etc. The potential targets can be prioritised based on the potential for benefit to the company.

An acquirer can buy a target company in one of two main ways: a stock purchase or an asset purchase. In a stock purchase, the target shareholders agree to sell outstanding shares (of the legal entity which owns and operates the target business) to the acquirer.

Alternatively, the acquirer can purchase the assets and goodwill of the target business itself. Asset purchases, not surprisingly, involve assets – patents or trademarks, for example – being sold. Such acquisitions can involve all of a target’s assets or just a portion of them. Apply Inc. acquired Drive.ai, which is developing autonomous vehicles, which included the Drive.ai’s fleet of cars as well as the patents and other intellectual property.

A target that has sold its assets can continue on as a shell company. But the assets get transferred to the acquirer. Target shells ultimately are liquidated. The sale of a company’s assets and its liquidation is often associated with bankruptcy although there is also a related business discontinuation process known as an assignment proceeding. Telltale Games went through this process in 2018 as it tried to quickly sell all of its assets, including trademarks, copyrights and source code, to raise enough cash to pay creditors.

Mergers and acquisitions have a legitimate role to play from the standpoint of an ambitious company looking to grow. When evaluating any deal there is one key question: are shareholders better off?

Purchases can be financed in a number of ways depending on circumstances. This section briefly discusses the financing considerations of acquisitions and Section 11.4.4 of this chapter provides additional information on financing business combinations in general.

All-cash deals, in which the acquirer uses entirely cash to buy the majority of a target’s shares, have the inherent advantage of not involving any stock. Therefore, these deals have no impact on the equity component of an acquirer’s statement of financial position. When German drug and chemicals maker Bayer acquired Monsanto for US$66 billion in 2018, it did so entirely in cash, the bulk of it provided by a global banking syndicate, marking it the largest all-cash deal on record. An all-cash offer tends to move a deal more quickly to fruition but can put the buyer at a disadvantage if financing falls through.

All-stock deals, of course, do not carry this kind of financing risk and allow buyers to hang on to cash for other purposes; nor do they need to take on debt. But if an acquirer buys a target company in an all-stock deal, equity on the statement of financial position is impacted. Sometimes called a stock swap, these deals involve the acquirer giving target shareholders, in the case of a 1:1 all-stock deal, as many shares in the new or parent company as the shareholder held in the target. Stock deals can involve a variety of share types, including preferred, common, voting, non-voting, participating, non-participating, redeemable and convertible.

A deal can be executed via a combination of both cash and stock, depending on the financing needs and dilution preferences of the parties involved.

Debt instruments can also come into play in carrying out an acquisition. Debt can be structured to be senior or subordinated; secured or unsecured; pegged to fixed or variable rates and/or convertible.

Two additional ways that buyers can pay for a target are earnouts and warrants. Earnouts are contract provisions that require the buyer of a company to pay the seller additional compensation if certain performance measures are met. Earnouts can be used as a method to decrease the purchase price and defer additional compensation into the future but only if the company meets the agreed-upon performance. Similarly, warrants can be used as compensation in an acquisition contract that gives the seller the option to buy shares of the company at a predetermined price.

A seller may be able to more forcibly define the terms of how a purchase is transacted depending on the situation. The seller’s position is strongest when, after putting itself up for sale via a friendly takeover, the process draws multiple suitors with competing bids.

However, as will be discussed next, takeovers are not always friendly.

### 11.2.3 Hostile Takeovers

Hostile takeovers are by definition associated with target companies that view an acquirer’s uninvited bid as unwelcome and thus will seek to reject it. For an acquirer to successfully complete a hostile takeover, it must directly win over shareholders or change governance whereby new directors/managers agree to the takeover.

So-called ‘hostilities’ start with some acquirer’s tender offer to buy outstanding shares at a pre-determined above-market price. As noted, such unsolicited offers bypass management and directors and instead are communicated directly to shareholders.

Another mechanism for accomplishing a hostile takeover is by way of a corporate vote initiated by a larger shareholder or group of shareholders. These are commonly called proxy battles. This unwelcome (to management) confrontation often starts with one shareholder seeking to convince additional shareholders to band together in an effort to amass sufficient shareholder proxies to usurp authority from controlling powers. For example, shareholders with enough proxies can vote out a CEO standing in the way of a proposed takeover.

In an age of ever-intensifying shareholder activism – indeed, ‘activists’ now command their own hedge fund category – acquirers engaged in unfriendly takeovers need not necessarily be cast in a negative light. This is particularly so if they are abetted by shareholders who feel their best interests are not being served by management or who perhaps tried to previously, amicably suggest changes but were instead rebuffed.

Defining what constitutes hostile for our purposes, though, centres on the fact that the target does not want to be acquired by the bidder making the tender offer. And with this being the case, the target company will put up resistance.

Many Hong Kong companies are owned by shareholders with sizable control. This makes it hard to carry out a hostile takeover. While hostile bids are allowed in Hong Kong, they are rare.

#### 11.2.3.1 advice on Defence

Proper foresight can be a form of insulation from hostile takeovers. Management can by design insert legal clauses into articles of incorporation or association, such as one requiring a supermajority (two-thirds vote, as opposed to 51%) for any tender offer to be approved. Board seats can be staggered, i.e. set up so that tiers of different directors serve rotating one-year stints, effectively blocking the ability of an acquirer to take immediate control.

Shrewd, forward-thinking corporate executives can do their best to sidestep certain scenarios that might potentially leave their company vulnerable. One potential blind spot is dispersion of shares. Managers should be vigilant. Are shares adequately dispersed? Or has one lone, enormous private shareholder been allowed to go unchecked?

In many cases, hostile bidders seize on valid considerations. Managers should remain one step ahead, constantly scrutinising and challenging the status quo. Are there obvious inefficiencies left unaddressed, or some untapped value being overlooked?

Even seemingly positive, pragmatic measures need to be carefully weighed by leaders who, by way of one example, might prefer to reduce debt and keep cash stowed away. But is debt so low – and/or are assets so liquid – that the company is an irresistible target? Sometimes preventive deterrence measures are still too little, too late. Once a hostile takeover is launched, the target company needs to consider counteractions.

Target companies can embark on a strategy to drive up their share price (making it less attractive) by allowing shareholders to accumulate more shares at a discount. Such a move is known as a ‘poison pill’.

Some other commonly used methods of defence against hostile takeovers would include the following:

• Marshaling the support of the largest, most important shareholders;
• Waging a counteroffensive public relations campaign against the takeover;
• Buying up the shares of the bidding company, turning the tables (sometimes known as the Pac-Man defence);
• Greenmail; that is, management agrees to repurchase blocks of shares amassed by the threatening acquirer, sometimes even at a steep price, in order to get them to go away;
• Litigation or regulatory defences to prevent the acquisition on a legal basis;
• The ‘crown jewel’ defence is where the target company sells its most valuable assets to reduce its value as an acquisition target;
• Golden parachutes, which are large financial compensation arrangements for executives in the event of termination from a merger or acquisition, are another way to discourage a potential acquisition; and
• The White Knight defence includes the target company’s board or management to endorse the acquisition by a different company.

Between 2011–2013, Carl Icahn, built up a majority stake in WebMD. The implication that Icahn might force a governance change led the company to take steps to remove that mere possibility by offering to repurchase its shares from Icahn at a premium.

##### illustrative Example 2

In the opening case, the XYZ Widgets company was the target of a hostile takeover attempt in 2005. A former widget designer turned financier, Mr. Chan, declared via a public filing that his holding company, Green Island Limited, as of 15 December 2005, owned 15% of XYZ’s stock. A hostile takeover battle began. At first, XYZ’s large institutional shareholders urged the company to buy back stock to push up the price, making the deal less attractive. Ultimately, XYZ, looking to rid themselves of Mr. Chan, made an offer to repurchase a large block of his shares. Mr. Chan agreed. His takeover bid failed but netted a small profit.

Did the XYZ’s board of directors act in the best interests of its shareholders? Or was the self-tender just that, a move made to protect their own interests? Or both? The directors could argue that they are protecting a corporate strategy that aligns with the best interest of shareholders.
