## 11.3 REGULATION OF BUSINESS COMBINATIONS

Regulation of business combinations has evolved and expanded over centuries as corporate interests and those of the public converge and sometimes clash. Mergers of publicly traded companies are more closely scrutinised relative to deals involving private companies. The development of regulation for mergers and acquisitions globally and in Hong Kong has been driven by several factors, including the recognition that mergers and acquisitions can have significant impacts internally and externally to the companies involved. The need for confidentiality protection as well as adequacy of disclosures have also been key drivers in the development of the regulatory framework for mergers and acquisitions. Additionally, regulators impose anti-trust or competition regulation to prevent a company from creating a monopoly in a certain market. Further, hostile takeovers present risks to the target companies and its shareholders, therefore regulations are typically more deferential to target companies. In Hong Kong, the Competition Ordinance (Cap.619) came into full effect in 2015 to prohibit anti-competitive agreements, abuse of power and anti-competitive mergers.

Disclosure rules – mandating the release of information or spelling out when disclosure is not necessary – comprise some of the core components of the legal frameworks governing mergers and acquisitions around the world. This chapter will cover the most important filing rules and the situations in which they apply. Regulations shape, even drive, the agendas of dealmakers. In addition to an examination of global regulatory frameworks, this chapter will discuss two major prisms through which the industry and its overseers view priorities, those being the shareholder model and the stakeholder model. Additionally, the origins and effectiveness of the Hong Kong Takeovers Code and its ten general principles will be explored.

### 11.3.1 mergers and acquisitions Regulatory Framework

Globally, regulations governing mergers and acquisitions have built up and evolved over time with blind spots remedied as needed. Complex sets of new rules have emerged in the aftermath of financial crises and episodes of corporate malfeasance. Many developed and developing markets around the world have their own unique rules controlling the process by which companies combine. Merger control regimes can now be found in more than 100 countries.

When one company proposes to acquire another company there are numerous legal considerations that both the acquirer and the target (if it plans to defend against being taken over) need to take into account. These would include competition law, anti-trust laws and securities laws. State and provincial laws pertaining to corporations can represent another part of the kinds of mergers and acquisitions regulatory frameworks to be examined in this section.

In Hong Kong, the primary source of competition law is the Competition Ordinance (Cap.619). The Competition Ordinance creates a merger control regime for telecommunications, jointly administered by the Communications Authority and the Competition Commission. Business combinations in Hong Kong are guided by the Hong Kong Takeovers Code and its general principles, which are discussed in more detail in Section 11.3.3. The new Companies Ordinance (CO) (Cap.622) provides further regulatory governance related to business combinations, specifically Part 13, ‘Arrangements, Amalgamation, and Compulsory Share Acquisition in Takeover and Share Buy-Back’. The Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) (Cap.571) published by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) is also relevant as it defines inside information and provides the requirements and guidelines for disclosure of inside information.

In Hong Kong and globally, regulators develop and impose merger and acquisition regulatory frameworks to preserve the health, competitiveness and fairness of markets for the benefit of market participants and customers or consumers. Specifically, regulators enact regulatory frameworks to maintain competition in the market, ease markets entry by potential competitors, protect local companies from being at a competitive disadvantage to foreign competitors and provide for standardised processes for completing business combinations.

When companies based in two different countries combine, separate sets of domestic rules require adherence while additional legal complexities arise. Cross-border rules tend to be stricter in Asia compared to Europe which by virtue of the European Union has seen barriers lowered. Around the world, China’s role as a bidder has been at the heart of cross-border mergers and acquisitions. Much of this acquiring has been in Australian and Canadian mining sectors, although in terms of target companies those based in the US represented 43% of global M&A volume in 2018.

Non US acquirers face the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS). Chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury, this multi-agency entity in consultation with the President has authority to block transactions on the basis of national security concerns.

#### illustrative Example 3

In late 2017, XYZ Widgets, based in Hong Kong, made an unsolicited offer to acquire a US chipmaker for HK$70 a share in cash and stock, a deal totaling HK$105 billion. At the time, it represented the largest technology sector takeover in history. In addition to shareholders’ approval, XYZ Widgets’ bid faced intense scrutiny by CIFIUS. XYZ Widgets’ taking over the chipmaker was seen as opening the door for China to advance in the mobile phone chipmaking technology (5G). The deal was blocked by the CIFIUS and through a press release the committee referenced national security concerns as the reason.
---- 

Like some other Asian merger and acquisition regulatory frameworks, Chinese rules are newer, compared to Western frameworks, reflecting different heritages, and are still evolving. China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) is the primary enforcer of China’s Anti-Monopoly Law which took effect in 2008. MOFCOM reviews large deals impacting key industries.

In general, Taiwan’s Business Mergers and Acquisitions Act governs mergers and acquisitions, although there exists more specific legislation for more industries like financial services. Mergers and acquisitions by a financial institution is required to meet the requirements of the Financial Institutions Merger Act and the Financial Holding Company Act. Taiwan’s regulatory structure shares much in common with other countries or governing authorities.

Japan’s regulatory system for governing takeovers resembles the US and UK Tender offers need to be made public and a Registration Statement needs to be filed with the Kanto Local Finance Bureau. Japan’s Anti-Monopoly Law is viewed as having similarities to Hong Kong, US and other anti-trust rules.

South Korea’s Securities Exchange Law requires the public filing of a tender offer statement. Foreigners are allowed to pursue acquisitions, but unfriendly deals are discouraged: for a board seat to be turned over, two-thirds of shareholders need to approve it.

Singapore’s competition law, the Competition Act, was passed in 2004 and is similar to the United Kingdom’s regulatory framework. The Competition Commission of Singapore administers the Act and has the authority to conduct investigations into suspected infractions. The Act prohibits mergers that prevent, restrict or distort competition. It also prohibits the abuse of power by market participants and mergers that results in substantial diminishing of competition.

### 11.3.2 shareholder Versus stakeholder model

Corporate shareholders are equity owners. Corporate stakeholders, meanwhile, consist of other important constituencies connected with a company, such as its employees, customers, bondholders, vendors and suppliers. Ideally, the interests of corporate shareholders and stakeholders are aligned. But this is not always the case. Thus, two different regulatory regimes have evolved, the shareholder and the stakeholder models.

The shareholder model holds that, above all else, management’s primary responsibility is to maximise shareholder value. The stakeholder model also considers shareholder value as an objective of management but holds that management needs to act in the best interest of other stakeholders simultaneously.

The imbalance between shareholder and stakeholder interests has been exposed in recent decades. Unquestioned emphasis of shareholder value under the shareholder model has helped lead to questionable activity by managers of large companies as they were primarily measured by their quarterly financial results, i.e. the quarterly consensus estimates. This resulted in several high-profile accounting scandals during the early part of the 2000s (Enron, Global Crossing, Tyco International and WorldCom). Shareholder focus found itself challenged once again following the Global Financial Crisis of 2008–2009 as ordinary individuals looked on with skepticism as industry regulators turned to emergency policies (bailouts) to avert a feared cascade of large financial firm failures.

Over the past decade, concepts such as balanced scorecards and environmental, social and governance (ESG) reporting have gained traction. Such performance measurement systems help to re-balance management’s priorities across the various stakeholders. Globally, governance trends suggest an ongoing move towards the harmonisation of the shareholder and stakeholder models.

#### illustrative Example 4

In 2009, China’s MOFCOM blocked Coca-Cola’s bid to acquire Huiyuan, a Hong Kongregistered fruit juice company serving customers in Mainland China. One main reason for its decision to prevent the merger (which at the time would have marked the largestever acquisition of a Chinese company by a non-Chinese buyer) was MOFCOM’s view that a combination of two dominant players would result in the Chinese soft drink market becoming less competitive, subjecting consumers to higher prices. Stakeholders’ interests drove the regulatory decision more than those of shareholders.
---- 
#### illustrative Example 5

In the opening case, XYZ Widgets’ board of directors was gathered in a conference room debating the five highest bids from would-be acquirers.

Using a traditional decision-making framework – valuation, synergies and cultural fit – all five bids were found to be in the shareholders’ best interests. However, a team of analysts invited to participate in the deliberations introduced some counterweights. They ran a report looking at the various acquisition scenarios from the viewpoint of stakeholders, including rank and file employees, customers, suppliers as well as the local community, examining how these various constituents might be negatively impacted.

One by one, each acquirer was evaluated on their intentions to close factories and it became clear that even best-case scenarios resulted in large numbers of employees being put out of work. The two buyers with the highest bids were connected with the most job losses. Additionally, the analysts conducted some research to examine less obvious but nevertheless still quantifiable benefits tied to not doing any deal while shifting towards longer-term alignment with stakeholder interests (e.g. retaining talented people committed to superior quality and averting negative public relations/customer backlash).

### 11.3.3 Hong Kong’s Codes on Takeovers and mergers and share Buy-backs and its Ten General Principles

First introduced in 1975, Hong Kong’s Codes on Takeovers and Mergers and Share Buy-backs is better known as the Hong Kong Takeovers Code (and also as ‘the Codes’). It provides a framework for market participants to self-regulate deal-making activities. Central to the Codes are their ten general principles, the first of which declares, emblematically, all shareholders must be treated equally. The ten principles will be listed at the end of this section. In 2018 the SFC amended the Codes to improve the protection of shareholders and to clarify certain roles and responsibilities. Specifically, the amendment gave the Takeovers Panel the authority to require that compensation be paid to shareholders who have suffered as a result from a breach of the Codes. It clarified that the Takeovers Executive, the Takeovers Panel and the Takeovers Appeal Committee have the authority to issue compliance rulings.

Although not enforced by law, the Codes reflect a standard of conduct that Hong Kong market participants have come to expect of each other. The Codes are administered by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) in conjunction with a Takeovers and Mergers Panel that can resolve disputes, make decisions regarding breaches of the code and order restitution be made to harmed shareholders. That the Codes do not carry the force of law should not be viewed as allowing industry members to be unaccountable to authority. Anyone found to have breached the Codes can face career-harming disciplinary action from the SFC, which can include the issuance of a public statement criticism or public censure. The Takeover Panel can also require that compensation be paid to a person who has suffered as a result of a breach of the Codes.

It bears repeating that fair treatment for shareholders underpins the Codes, as illustrated by a singularly pivotal requirement according to the SFC: mandating disclosure of timely and adequate information to enable shareholders to make an informed decision as to the merits of an offer.

The Codes apply to Hong Kong public companies, companies with equity shares primarily listed in Hong Kong, as well as real estate investment trusts with a primary listing of units in Hong Kong.

The ten general principles are:

1. All shareholders are to be treated equally.

	Consider a situation in which a company presents a takeover offer that includes varying levels of compensation for the different classes of the target company’s stock. Certain classes of stock would be given a more favourable offer than other shareholders.

2. If control of a company changes, a general offer to all other shareholders is normally required.

	For example, a private equity firm has taken control of XYZ Widget from the Opening Case. When the firm took control of XYZ, it was required to present a general offer to all shareholders where it would purchase their shares of the company.

3. During the course of an offer or when an offer is in contemplation, information made available to some shareholders must be made available to all shareholders (except for some information furnished in confidence to the potential offeror or vice versa).

	All shareholders must be treated equally applies to the availability of information.

4. An offer should only be made after careful and responsible consideration.

	Takeover offers should not be made for any reason other than to promote the best interests of the shareholders.

5. Shareholders should be given sufficient information, advice and time to reach an informed decision.

	Consider an offeror who presents an offer with unfavourable terms written in complex language and requires that a decision be provided within one business day. The shareholders’ interest would be at risk as the shareholders would not have adequate time to ascertain the pertinent information of the offer to make an informed decision.

6. All persons concerned with offers should make full and prompt disclosure of all relevant information and take every precaution to avoid the creation or continuance of a false market and making statements which may mislead shareholders or the market.

	Shareholders with material interests in a company should disclose any relationship to a potential acquisition target, such as a family member being involved with the target company or a material financial stake in the target company.

7. Rights of control should be exercised in good faith and oppression of minority shareholders is unacceptable.

	Shareholders should use their voting rights or other means of influencing decisions of the company in the best interest of the shareholders. For example, it would not be an appropriate use of control to vote against measures proposed by minority shareholders in an effort to maintain control.

8. Directors should have regard for the interests of the shareholders as a whole.

	Directors should treat all shareholders equally. They should consider shareholders as a single group and not by class of shares or other categorisations of shareholders.

9. The board of the offeree should not take actions to frustrate a proposed bona fide offer or deny the shareholders the opportunity to decide on its merits.

	Offers and all pertinent information should be made available to shareholders for review and consideration without the interference by the board of directors. A board may attempt to withhold information or otherwise influence the decision of shareholders in order to preserve their position.

10. All parties concerned with takeovers and mergers are required to co-operate to the fullest extent with the Executive, the Takeovers and Mergers Panel (‘Panel’) and the Takeovers Appeal Committee.

	Executives involved with a takeover of a competitor may be less inclined to fully disclose all aspects of the offer or otherwise fully cooperate with the regulators if the offer contained impermissible benefits or different treatment for the different classes of shareholders.

### 11.3.4 Changes to Listing Rules Reverse Takeovers and Continuing Listing

In 2019, to address the misuse of shell companies to maintain listed status, the rules on reverse takeovers and continuing list criteria were amended to ensure that listed issuers maintain sufficient operations and asset values to warrant continued listing. The following summarises the key listing rule amendments and the criteria for continuing listing.

• The definition of reverse takeovers (RTOs) is amended along with modifications to existing rules:
°The RTO principle-based test codifies six assessment factors with modifications to changes in control and transactions such as acquisitions and disposals. The six assessment factors are the relative size of acquisition, fundamental change in the issuer’s principal business, nature and scale of the issuer’s business, quality of acquisition targets, change in control or de facto control of the listed issuer, and change in de facto control arising from issue of restricted convertible securities.
°The RTO bright-line test restricts disposals by issuers of substantial business within 36 months of a change in control of the issuer.
°Disallowing backdoor listing through large-scale issue of securities for cash or a change in control where the proceeds would be used to acquire new business that is substantially larger than the issuer’s principal existing business.
°Extreme Very Substantial Acquisitions are renamed Extreme Transactions and additional eligibility criteria are imposed. The issuer must operate a principal business of substantial size, or the issuer must have been under the control or de facto control of the same person(s) for a long period (normally not less than 36 months) and the transaction will not result in a change in control or de facto control of the issuer.
• Three amendments to the continuing listing criteria exist for listed issuers:
°The rule on sufficient operations requires issuers to maintain a sufficient level of operations and have assets of sufficient value. Proprietary trading is excluded when performing this evaluation.
°The rule on cash companies extends the definition of short-dated securities to include those that are easily convertible into cash and renames it as ‘short-term investments’; and confines the exemption to cash and short-term investments held by members of an issuer’s group that are banking companies, insurance companies or securities houses.
°A twelve-month transitional period from 1 October 2019 applies to listed issuers that do not comply with the amendments above on sufficient operations and cash companies.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Central to most regulatory frameworks is an overarching goal to protect the interests of shareholders and make sure they are treated equally. The main way this gets accomplished is by mandated disclosures.

### apply and analyse 3

The executive head of business development at a regional office-supply chain is under pressure by senior management to acquire a supplier in order to optimise operations and gain positive publicity ahead of the year-end earnings report.

The business development team has been screening potential acquisition targets and performing thorough due diligence for several months, and they have presented several acquisition offers but none have been accepted.

To meet senior management’s expectations, the executive decides to amend the offer to the first acquisition choice by increasing the payout to the shareholders of the company’s preferred stock. The executive sends separate offer notices to the holders of the different share classes to avoid the holders of common stock becoming aware of the discrepancy in offer price.

Analysis

The executive has breached two of the general principles as the acquisition offer has not treated all shareholders equally and information has not been made available to all shareholders. As a result of the breach of the Codes, the company faces private reprimand from the SFC, public censure and potential fines payable to the holders of common stock.

## 11.4 DUE DILIGENCE IN BUSINESS COMBINATIONS

Due diligence in business combinations is relevant to buyers and sellers of businesses as a means to inform their decisions. It involves the rigorous pre-transaction investigation that an acquirer conducts when evaluating a target company. Broad in scope and comprising many moving parts, the due diligence process attempts to find out as much material and relevant information as possible for a buyer to make an informed decision. The entire process is as critical as it is comprehensive. It weighs on whether the acquisition will be completed and can affect terms, price and financing. Business and legal risks are explored. Responsible due diligence involves thorough processes and can require an array of professionals. Among those helping to carry out due diligence are accountants, attorneys, auditors, bankers, consultants and, in some cases, private investigative firms. Due diligence is also a key factor in the process to value a company as it verifies material matters relevant to the valuation process.

Target companies do due diligence to find out if a merger partner is suitable – no one wants to find out negative information after a marriage has been consummated – but for this section, the concept of due diligence mainly will be discussed from the perspective of an acquirer.

Due diligence is also required for certain business combinations by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (AML/CTF) Ordinance. The requirements include measures to verify customers’ identity, the beneficial owner, the purpose and natures of the business and the intended relationship with the financial institution.

Section 11.4 will start by discussing the reasons for doing due diligence. Next is a full overview of the due diligence process. Then it will cover due diligence from a target’s perspective, by looking at the ways the performance of the acquirer gets evaluated. Additionally, it will discuss corporate and competitive considerations that are incorporated into the due diligence process, financing; reporting and regulatory issues. This section concludes with a summary of the roles played by accountants, attorneys, auditors, bankers, consultants and private investigative firms.

### 11.4.1 Reasons for Due Diligence

Due diligence provides a number of benefits to a firm considering a business combination. The main reason an acquirer conducts due diligence when buying a target company is to ensure all business risks are fully known prior to closing the deal. If some previously unknown weakness or liability is uncovered during the due diligence process, then a proposed merger deal could fall apart. Findings from due diligence can potentially impact price negotiations or change the deal’s structure. Firms also conduct due diligence to help inform the valuation of the target company. Due diligence can identify performance trends, contacts with customers or suppliers that are set to expire soon, or other areas of concerns that influence the valuation of the business and are not typically included in financial statements. Additionally, due diligence will fulfill compliance requirements, such as background checks on key personnel to avoid unreported conflicts of interest. This section focuses on the performance of due diligence to mitigate business risks.

Business risks fall into three broad categories: legal, financial and operational. Risk reduction (or elimination or mitigation) is the primary reason for doing due diligence. Risks can’t be reduced if they are not learned. Understanding a company top to bottom, inside and out, requires critical thought, enterprise and coordination among those doing different types of research. It’s not a check-the-boxes exercise.

A multi-pronged, beyond-the-numbers, risk-centric approach to the due diligence process is difficult, time consuming and costly. Nevertheless, carrying out the most rigorous process possible will give acquirers their best chance at avoiding a bad transaction. For deals that carry risks but might still be worth pursuing, there is an upside to unearthing risks, whether existing, easy-to-spot deficiencies or harder-to-see issues lurking below the surface. By doing so, buyers can avert paying too much.

Signals of problems, or red flags, can be spotted by doing a comprehensive audit and analysis of a company’s financial statements, such as qualified or modified audit reports, low liquidity and solvency ratios and declining profitability margins. Even if no risks are found, the process of thoroughly examining the financial data will at least allow a buyer to confirm the information is accurate. But such examinations can help avoid risk, particularly if the due diligence prevents misleading or overstated information from being factored into the bargaining conversations and especially if financial due diligence is married with operational due diligence.

An example: One team of financial analysts checking a target company’s projected sales revenue data might be inclined to cross-reference their work with another team doing operational due diligence by interviewing the target’s largest distributors. Practical, real-world research could conceivably spot a major marketplace change looming. A foreign competitor could enter into the market which would threaten the target’s market share.

It’s difficult enough for an acquirer to make an amalgamation work, even after identifying known risks. But unknown risks, those that might have been identified if more exhaustive due diligence had been performed, can ruin even the best drawn business combination plans. Due diligence helps determine if risks are acceptable or untenable by providing management or other decision makers with the information necessary to reach fair conclusions of the risks.

An overview of some of the major risks that companies look to uncover during due diligence is presented here:

• Legal risks: Lawsuits against a target company do not disappear following a merger. Responsibility is inherited by the acquirer. Consider an example of a Hong Kong based pharmaceutical company that acquires a competitor. The acquirer performed thorough adequate due diligence and identified several pending litigation matters related to one of its products. The acquirer assumed the risks of the litigation matters believing the benefits of acquiring the competitor’s assets and product offering outweighed the potential legal risks. The litigation is settled years later at a cost much higher than anticipated and further resulted in the ban of one of the major products acquired.

• Regulatory risks: Practices that are deemed non-controversial (‘business as usual’) could very quickly become a liability if rules change. Regulatory changes can lead to deal-making activity, such as when the central banks require better capitalised banks, which leads to divestitures. Shifting regulatory emphasis can lead to liabilities. For example, Hong Kong based mutual fund companies can find themselves facing heavy scrutiny from the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) following trading scandals perpetuated by one or a few of the many firms. Management can use diligence to uncover questionable or illegal back office practices and should be aware of shifts in regulatory emphasis or recent regulatory fines in the market.

• Environmental risks: Many companies, regardless of the nature of their activities, are exposed to various environmental liabilities. In Hong Kong the primary regulator of environmental risks is the Environmental Protection Department (EPD). In 2018, the EPD fined a construction contracting company, Sinochram (HK) Enterprises Limited, and the sub-contractor for discharging pollutant wastewater in a storm drain. After public complaints of discoloured water, the EPA ran tests and determined the pollutants came from a nearby rooftop resurfacing project. Environmental liability will be discussed again in Section 11.4.7.

• Financial risks: The list of potential financial risks is long, which helps explain the axiom ‘trust but verify’. Are assets inflated? Are financial statements misleading, inaccurate or incomplete? Accountants are stereotyped as boring but some have quite a creative streak – hence a need to look closely and ask whether they are perhaps a little too creative. Tying in concurrent operational due diligence again comes into the equation because there is a need to understand which individual employees are in a position to possibly falsify such information. Companies can conduct investigations into the past records of such key people. Have executives suddenly departed from past corporate positions just prior to their employers running into problems? One of the biggest risks that a buyer wants to avoid is overpaying. This is why financial due diligence involves doing some valuation analysis, or the process of determining what a company is worth. For example, consider the recent acquisition of Hong Kong Express by Cathay Pacific. The Hong Kong based Cathay Pacific undoubtedly performed valuation analysis of Hong Kong Express considering the prior periods of unprofitability. While performance by Hong Kong Express had improved prior to the acquisition, Cathay Pacific was exposed to material financial risk which should be accounted for during the valuation process.

• Operational and structural risks: This category covers numerous areas that are often complicated. Examples include: loss of key people, disparate corporate cultures, sub-optimal supply chain protocols, outdated technology, poor morale, labour disputes, structural or competitive pressures, top executives’ vulnerability to negative publicity, inadequate training, to name some examples. Consider a situation in which a Hong Kong based firm contemplates an acquisition offer from an Australian firm. In addition to the analysis of financial information and competitive advantages in the market, the operations, culture and employee related matters, such as the organisational structure of the combined firm, should also be reviewed and evaluated.

Risks found during due diligence, as mentioned, can be eliminated or mitigated.

Consider the example of a target company with an owner cashing out and leaving several top employees improperly incentivised. It would be the responsibility of the acquirer to retain the key employees, which could be done by offering retention bonuses. An acquirer who learns of a target’s outsized pension obligations can reconfigure the terms of the deal, separating out the liabilities into a subsidiary (in what’s known as a triangular transaction). Or, they can just buy the assets of a company and not the liabilities.

Risks are either going to be found acceptable or unacceptable. Risk reduction is the primary reason for due diligence – lowering the odds of a regrettable misstep. Therefore, the right questions need to be raised, particularly if a company is looking to shed a business for strategic reasons.

It means not just asking why a company is looking to sell, but, more importantly, why now?

### 11.4.2 Overview of Due Diligence Process

As we’ve indicated, proper due diligence involves many moving parts and a multitude of investment professionals working off extensive checklists. Ideally, these parties are coordinating and communicating properly.

This section provides an overview of the due diligence process, covering the timing of the process, the materials and information required to complete it, how the information gets provided and where it can be found. Additionally, this section will look at who is responsible for making sure diligence gets its due.

Timing is critical. Transactions can quickly take on a life of their own. Within a brief period of days, an acquirer’s lawyers can engage a target company, draw up non-disclosure agreements (NDAs), exchange confidential information, engage with investment bankers and sign formal letters of intent (LOis) covering a transaction’s broad strokes. LOIs are based on limited information. They can resemble memorandums of understanding, commonly used in Hong Kong. From the time these non-binding, preliminary expressions of interest are signed, and a deal team assembled – but before a definitive agreement can be publicly announced – there is a window in which to conduct due diligence. Usually it’s no more than 60 days. Even though it’s usually the case that two months is insufficient time to do proper due diligence, more often the process is compressed into an even tighter time frame.

A merger due diligence team is typically structured similarly to an audit team, where the staff performs the time-consuming and tedious tasks while those with more experience and seniority supervise, review and advise the work.

A merger due diligence team, while relying on teams of junior employees, typically will be led by experienced attorneys who are experts at what they do. Sellers own an informational edge at the start of a negotiation process. But that advantage becomes less asymmetrical as the process continues.

Teams comprise a combination of bankers and other financial advisors, lawyers, accountants and consultants.

> ### Key Learning Point
> 
> Clear communication and effective coordination among all sets of deal team participants is crucial to a meaningful, actionable due diligence.

Due diligence materials – a wide range of financial statements and other pieces of relevant information – are contained in preliminary offer documents and also in the offering memorandum that is submitted by the target company. In addition to serving as an agreed upon set of starting point terms, the deal’s LOI paperwork serves as a roadmap for the due diligence phase ahead.

Materials to be inspected could include: audited financial statements and corporate records (charters, bylaws, board minutes); client and contractor lists; key staffer resumes and organisational flow charts plus corresponding compensation schedules; contracts; stock records; compensation plans; collective bargaining agreements. Document management is assigned to junior bankers running a centralised repository for all relevant materials. For public companies, extensive amounts of information are readily obtainable. This would include annual and quarterly financial statements, auditor reports and a variety of other materials, such as corporate governance reviews or prospectuses tied to bond offerings.

There are four general categories of due diligence, and some related research tasks:

1. **Financial due diligence**. This is where valuation and business modelling will overlap with due diligence through an examination of a target company’s financial statements. The valuation aspect of financial due diligence looks at historical earnings, current cash flow, profit margins, tax liabilities, tangible and intangible assets as well as liabilities, such as outstanding debt.

	Much of what’s contained in a seller’s financial statements could be categorised as projections and assumptions extending out several quarters or years into the future and critically factor into the valuation. Do these projections jibe with approved budget plans? Are there substantial tax liabilities or tax considerations due to geographic locations/jurisdictions? What precisely underpins these assumptions and how can that information be verified? Were the financial statements audited? By a reputable auditing firm? What are the target’s identifiable assets and how are they valued? Assets can be tangible, such as property or equipment, or they can be intangible, such as intellectual property or trademarks.

	In situations where a seller may have an edge in a competitive bidding process, a buyer must be willing to factor another type of intangible asset, known as goodwill, into its offer. That goodwill, or excess purchase price, is a reflection of hard-to-quantify intangibles (e.g. reputation and brand recognition) and is calculated at a rate above the target’s net identifiable assets after fair value adjustments. Thus, if a target deemed to have HK$100,000 in fair value net assets gets acquired for HK$125,000, the economic goodwill would be equal to HK$25,000. Getting to that price level, or the process of assigning a goodwill estimate, requires scrutiny of a variety of factors. These factors include reputation and brand identity, as well as harder-to-measure impactful areas such as customer loyalty, skilled people and proprietary processes.

	The return on assets (ROA) ratio is one commonly used metric of goodwill. It’s an indicator of how profitable a company is relative to its total assets. If a company with HK$12 million in net tangible assets reports an annual net profit of HK$3 million, that equals a 25% ROA. Or put another way, the annual net profit is at least twice what the company might expect to earn if it just took all of its assets and invested in an equity index mutual fund. Embedded intangibly in that above-market return are less quantifiable attributes such as favourable reputation and loyal clients.

	Tax implications resulting from a merger or acquisition is an integral component of financial due diligence. The tax considerations can be on both the target company side or the acquirer side. Due diligence should identify all liabilities, including tax liabilities, and upcoming tax bills that may not be apparent in the financial statements. The tax implications should be valued and considered when structuring a deal. Not all tax implications are negative as some taxing authorities may offer tax credits or other benefits for a business combination. International or cross-border business combinations can introduce additional tax consequences as both tax regimes will need to be considered.

> ### **Key Learning Point**
> 
> The economic goodwill that gets created in an acquisition is calculated by taking the purchase price and subtracting the fair market value of net assets.

2. Strategic due diligence. This focuses on a target’s place in its industry and also can be an examination of the industry at large. (Competitive considerations will be covered separately in Section 11.4.3.) Other aspects of strategic due diligence – picking apart a company’s strengths and weaknesses – would include a close look at the largest shareholders as well as important stakeholders, including key employees, unions, customers and suppliers. Who are the biggest clients and what portion of the total revenue do they represent?

3. Legal due diligence. It focuses on litigation, either ongoing or potential. This component can also include research to confirm intellectual property (IP) claims and verify key customer agreements. For certain deals, such as in the technology sector, IP is the driving factor. In such cases it would be common for a specialist to be engaged specifically to handle IP due diligence. Are patents properly filed or has the target been accused on patent infringement?

4. Operational due diligence. This is the sub-part of the process where some of the most important probing takes place. Site visits and face-to-face meetings with key staffers, clients, suppliers and other relevant parties will help potential acquirers determine whether the target business is a viable acquisition. Specifically, during operational due diligence, acquirers will determine what risks they’re taking on, what additional value they can find in operations and whether the business is viable given the existing operations. This is the part of the process that could conceivably uncover a poor cultural fit or some other worrisome issue. One major operational area to scrutinise is a target’s cybersecurity. If the acquirer is subjecting itself to future data breach vulnerabilities, they will almost certainly have to take major precautions to address that additional risk.

---- 
### Apply and Analyse 4
---- 

A critical component of the business combination process is valuation. Valuation provides a methodical process to quantify the current value of a company and it can be carried out in a few ways including the asset- and income-based approaches. An asset-based approach, with a sharp focus on what physical or intellectual property assets can be sold and for how much, would be called for in a business failure or liquidation scenario. An income-based approach, fixating on revenue sources and potential for future growth, would suit a strategic buyer.

A financial buyer, looking to diversity holdings, might be more inclined to take a market-based approach contrasting the target with other players in a given industry. Details of valuation approaches are covered in Chapter 10. Due diligence results can have a material impact on valuation as it can uncover synergies between the two companies or future potential risks such as expiring contracts. Further, due diligence of legal matters can help determine the likelihood of financial impact and the amount of the impact, which will directly impact the valuation.

### 11.4.3 Corporate and Competitive Considerations

Whether an acquirer moves forward with a deal to buy a target depends on several overlapping factors and due diligence does not occur in a vacuum. Findings will be considered alongside macroeconomic and industry-specific conditions, tax issues and/or any possible regulatory implications.

Board members have to carefully weigh corporate and competitive considerations and must ultimately choose the company’s best path towards a kind of growth that improves shareholder value. The two primary factors senior management should consider are competitive forces, including economies of scale and market issues, and internal corporate considerations, including personnel and capital and organisational structures. An acquirer doing due diligence on a target company can’t afford to ignore corporate and competitive forces as these will be significantly impactful on the deal’s strategic outcome.

Competitive forces management should consider including the following:

• Market forces to take into consideration:
°Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats (SWOT) analysis.
°A heavily regulated industry that evolves into one that is less regulated, for example, will see an increase in competition from new entrants.
°Legacy players surrender market power, i.e. the ability to set and maintain higher prices. Eventually, too many new players proliferate and there is a new phase of consolidation.
°Distribution channels.
°Raw materials.
°Consumer trends.
°Rivals’ strengths.
°Marketplace idiosyncrasies.
°Does the target have a new product or technology upgrade that it is about to bring to market? On schedule? Or might a competitor’s offering be more likely to arrive first?

• Economies of scale:
°Competitors combining horizontally or vertically can provide an opportunity to obtain the benefits of economies of scale by reducing per unit costs.

Corporate factors management should consider the following:
• The future value of a combined company hinges on whether the underlying companies and their processes, assets and personnel are successfully integrated.
• The capital structure of both firms can affect the structure and the success of business combinations.
• Organisational and cultural disparities can strain business combinations, which can lead to failure.

### apply and analyse 5

A team of analysts working on behalf of a beverage company has embarked on a study of Asia’s expanding beverage market with an eye towards making an acquisition. The team has conducted extensive research on two specific targets, but the competitive landscape is rapidly shifting along with consumer tastes. Below is a description of the two targets based on the research. One is in the soft drink market and the other is in the health drink market.

The soft drink market can be considered a duopoly as the vast majority of revenue is earned by two market participants. The other soft drink makers compete for less than 10% of the overall market and the competitive landscape has not changed in several decades. The health drink market is relatively new and includes dozens of participants offering a wide variety of health drink types, such as juices, teas, flavored and sparkling waters, drinks marketed to athletes and others.

The soft drink target company is not one of the two main players. The company does enjoy around 2% of market share in Asia, which is an enormous market. The company has been profitable with steady margins for the past several years and has regularly paid a 2% dividend to shareholders. It also holds patents over their recipes and brand logo.

The health drink maker is a new entrant to the market and has so far met the analysts’ performance expectations. While it does not expect to be profitable for the current year due to significant start-up costs, current sales figures suggest the company will become profitable in the following year. The market share goal is 5% for the following year and 10% within three years. The company has a pending patent protection over its two main products, both organic juices.

The analysts present their findings and recommendation to the board of directors as they weigh a possible acquisition.

Analysis

Recommendation:

Pursue acquisition of the health drink company as it provides a better opportunity for market share and expansion. While the soft drink market is concentrated in the hands of a few dominant players, the health drink market is more fragmented.

The soft drink maker is likely to maintain its 2% market share and current levels of profitability but does not offer growth opportunities without significant further investment.

The health drink maker is riskier as it is a new entrant to the market, is not yet profitable and does not currently hold patents over its products. However, the opportunity for expansion is clear as it has demonstrated sales potential and completed the bulk of the initial start-up costs.
---- 
### 11.4.4 availability of Financing

Financing a merger or acquisition is a crucial part of the lifespan of a deal in between the earliest pitch and ultimate shareholder approval. Due diligence conductors will have turned over public documents, shared confidential data and reviewed harder-to-extract market intelligence, investigative background checks and specialist research.

All of these findings can impact the negotiation of a deal’s key terms and conditions, but financing is of particular importance. As contracts move towards finalisation, both buyer and seller will seek to make sure that availability of financing, or lack thereof, does not unexpectedly present itself as a late-stage deal breaker.

Typically, mergers and acquisitions are financed with:

• Internal funds: If a buyer can comfortably secure the target company with internal revenue, the process will be much easier.

• Exchange stocks: By exchanging stocks, the seller of a company can retain some stake in the business. This often helps the buying company as the previous owner has firsthand knowledge of how the business runs.

• Equity: Used mostly by buyers targeting companies in distressed situations.

• Cash: Covered by internal funds, paying for a merger or acquisition with cash is most common when the target company is smaller than the buyer’s and has less cash on hand.

• Debt: A common and relatively inexpensive way to finance a deal, lenders will evaluate the financial health of both companies before committing funds.

• A combination of the above: Like a leveraged buyout or integrated financing like a quasi-debt.

A deal falling through would be less relevant in an all-stock transaction but can come into play in an all-cash or partly-cash deal, in which debt is incurred. Often, deal-financing debt is restructured into various risk-tolerance-level pieces and sold to investors. As a deal tied to third-party financing comes to completion, the buyer and seller will confirm financing is secure and not be subjected to some uncertainty, such as a bank failing to properly line up a syndicate. Did one of the banks back out and, if so, why? Is someone challenging unverified information relating to the acquirer’s purported assets or the target’s forward-looking revenue prospects? To address concerns of lenders, deal makers can introduce provisions, or covenants, designed to protect the lender’s position as first-in-line creditor.

Distressed sellers, perilously running day to day operations, certainly do not want the deal to fall apart because the bidder failed to secure financing. Proper due diligence would help alleviate concerns related to the acquirer’s creditworthiness. Problems that arise amidst a general environment of shrinking credit can be harder to forecast. The extent and form of due diligence with respect to financing will depend on the scenario. For example, a company paying for an acquisition using borrowed money will want to obtain as much information as possible regarding the company they are doing business with and the conditions of the credit market.

#### illustrative Example 6

In 2007, XYZ Widgets was on the verge of acquiring an overseas rival, Horizon Widgets, giving XYZ Widgets access to new markets. During preliminary due diligence, the XYZ Widgets team reviewed the target company’s most recent financial statements and performed a series of ratio analyses to measure financial performance and position. The current, liquidity and solvency ratios analyses showed that the company was laden with high levels of debt. Further examination of disclosures related to the debt revealed that a significant portion of the debt was adjustable-rate debt with steep rates kicking in amidst tightening credit markets at the start of what would become the global financial crisis. The findings from this financial due diligence led XYZ Widgets to hold off on making a bid. As the crisis grew, XYZ Widgets decided to scrap acquisition plans and instead built up a cash cushion.
---- 
### 11.4.5 Reporting implications

Merger parties need to make sure they effectively manage all activities that carry reporting implications.

When a Hong Kong listed target confidentially agrees to give a bidder access to nonpublic information (under the auspices of due diligence), the target’s board must make sure to comply with the requirements under both the SFO and the Listing Rules on disclosure of inside information; strict confidentiality must be kept or else disclosure requirements are triggered. Due diligence information would also need to be provided to a competing bidder who asks for it.

A bidder attempting to build up a controlling stake by accumulating shares in the Hong Kong market will have to disclose the size of their position when it reaches a certain threshold (5%) and may wind up not being able to carry out a planned offer if it comes upon inside information from the target.

To determine these thresholds, there are a number of size tests, including:

• Assets ratio: Assets from acquired company against assets of listed issuer.
• Profits ratio: Profits from acquired company against profits from listed issuer.
• Revenue ratio: Revenue from acquired company against revenue from listed issuer.
• Consideration ratio: Consideration payable against the listed issuer’s market capitalisation.
• Equity capital ratio: The number of shares to be issued by the listed issuer as consideration divided by the total number of the listed issuer’s issued shares immediately before the transaction.

Depending on which ratio the buyer used, the threshold may shift. Laid out in Chapter 14 of the Hong Kong Listing Rules, there are six particular circumstances in which the company needs to inform its shareholders:

• Share transaction: All size tests result in ratios less than 5% when a listed issuer seeks to acquire the assets (excluding cash) of a company where the consideration includes securities for which listing will be sought.
• Disclosable transaction: Any size test hits 5% or above, but less than 25%.
• Major transaction: Any size test is 25% or above, but less than 75% (for a disposal) or less than 100% (for an acquisition).
• Very substantial disposal: Any size test is 75% or above.
• Very substantial acquisition: Any size test is 100% or above.
• Reverse takeover: Unique to Listing Rule 14.06(B), these acquisitions are so large that they attempt to avoid the listing requirements for new applicants.

Binding agreements to accept an offer are usually obtained from a target’s largest stakeholders and are subject to regulations under Hong Kong’s Codes on Takeover and Mergers and Share Buy-backs, which can restrict a target’s ability to enter binding agreements,  or irrevocable undertakings, which aren’t always entirely irrevocable considering that some of them carry provisions making them unbinding if a higher offer comes along. Restrictions can apply to: the timing of when a target can approach shareholders about accepting the takeover offer; the number of shareholders who can be approached; and the kind of information, provided by the bidder, that the target can give to shareholders.

When it comes time for the announcement of a firm’s intention to make an offer, the details of irrevocable undertakings must be disclosed in the offer document, including revealing any circumstances in which an agreement would cease to be binding.

Under the Codes, negotiations must be made public by the target company if an acquirer notifies a target of a firm intention to make an offer. Disclosure could also be required if there is public speculation over leaked information as to a proposed offer.

While certain disclosures of otherwise confidential information can be required by regulators, exchange rules or even court orders, there are, at the same time, limits, special circumstances and exemptions that lawyers can obtain, e.g. opinion letters.

### 11.4.6 Performance of acquirer

Just as a target provides information to an acquirer during due diligence, there is ample material pertaining to the performance of the acquirer that must be scrutinised by a target.

When indicating interest, the acquirer is routinely asked to not only communicate its reasons for seeking the deal but also to verify its financial health and ability to consummate.

Due diligence done by a target company is generally geared towards risk reduction, that is, learning everything it can about the acquirer to make an informed decision as to whether to go ahead with the deal. Consider a situation where an acquirer proposes to pay for a merger entirely or mostly using shares of its stock. Owners of a target company would regret if they did not conduct a proper due diligence on the acquirer’s performance.

### 11.4.7 Potential Regulatory issues

Acquirers need to recognise that compliance lapses inherited from a target company are their responsibility. Such failures could range from doing business in states without proper licences to erect a plant without the necessary environmental permits. Due diligence can help identify potential regulatory issues that left unchecked could possibly lead to penalties.

Gaining a clear understanding of a target’s exposure to environmental regulation is paramount during the due diligence phase. Environmental rules can be extensive. They vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. Penalties can be harsh. Environmental audits will examine a target company’s permits and licences to make sure they are valid and up to date; and such audits will review the history of correspondence between the target and regulators to see if any ongoing issues are unresolved.

If the shares of the target or acquirer trade on an exchange there can be exchange-specific regulations pertaining to mergers, e.g. subject to a shareholder vote.

As mentioned earlier while discussing reporting implications, deal participants need to take steps following the signing of a firm offer to make the proper disclosures, including the release of the news about the offer, the terms and related financial statements to the public. Extra or unique disclosure obligations, regardless of jurisdiction, should not come as a surprise after two companies enter into a definitive agreement.

The other regulatory requirement under the rubric of due diligence is getting all necessary approvals from agencies with jurisdiction over anti-trust issues or at least get a sense of what kind of legal fight might be in store should a regulator move to block a deal.

#### illustrative Example 7

In 2015, a Hong Kong-based energy company spun off most of its major chemical operations into a new entity providing shareholders with one share of the new company for every five shares owned. Then the company proceeded to merge with another chemical company. The company’s old chemical operations, meanwhile, were left with the responsibility to pay for regulator-mandated contaminated site cleanup costs that by some estimates totalled as much as HK$900 million. This predicament led a number of short sellers to put pressure on the stock. For a time, a rival chemical maker was rumoured to be looking to acquire the chemical operations which never happened. The chemical operations’ arm of the energy company was recently hit with another lawsuit over pollution issues.

### 11.4.8 Working with Professional advisors

Executing due diligence ahead of a merger deal relies on many collaborators. This section will touch on the process from the standpoint of an acquirer company working with professional advisors, outlining their basic roles.

Among those involved in due diligence are:

• Accountants: Review financial data in transaction documents, spotting issues such as tax considerations or valuation inconsistencies that can have an impact on price negotiations or how the deal is structured. Accountants unearth hidden costs while verifying financial statements of a target, such as earnings quality and projected cash flows.

• Attorneys: Assemble and lead the team responsible for making the deal. From the first non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) drawn up by an attorney to all exchanges of information throughout the deal, attorneys conduct a large portion of the due diligence process. Additional legal specialists might be called in to review specific issues, such as IP, environmental, regulatory and/or antitrust hurdles.

• Auditors: Evaluate risk associated with acquiring a new company. Integral to the acquisition process, auditors ensure that the target company’s financial reports are prepared in a true and fair view.

• Bankers: Senior bankers create strategies and identify targets; junior bankers value the target and work out financing. A target company’s bankers when ‘shopping a deal’ would evaluate potential acquirers.

• Consultants: Offer guidance and insight throughout the process of combining businesses. Consultants can help boards and managers by developing strategies to secure the deal, analysing target company performance and forecasting market reactions.

• Private investigative firms: In some cases, a company will use an investigative firm to aid in the due diligence process. These firms will collaborate with the rest of the team and assist the attorneys in gathering information.

For a team of professionals to successfully work together there must be effective coordination, delegation and measures to ensure accountability, with various people in charge of specific areas.

> #### Key Learning Point
> 
> Due diligence can reduce or mitigate risks associated with business combinations as well as measure competitive pros and cons. Additionally, the process helps parties, particularly the buyer, arrive at a valuation.


## SUMMARY

• Business combination proposals should be evaluated based on whether they help grow earnings and create shareholder value.

• The two most common forms of business combinations are mergers and acquisitions. Mergers refer to two or more companies coming together to form a new entity; an acquisition involves an acquirer taking over a target company which is then absorbed, ceasing to be. True mergers of equals are rare. Usually one firm has a dominant role as the buyer in the transaction.

• Takeover bids from unwelcome acquirers require shareholder approval and can be defended using various techniques and provisions including the well-known ‘poison pill’ strategy in which target company shares are issued at a discount to drive up the price thus making the target less attractive.

• Markets around the world have unique rules controlling the process by which companies combine. Merger control regimes are found in more than 100 countries.

• The Hong Kong Takeovers Code provides a framework for market participants to self-regulate deal-making activities. First among its ten general principles is the notion that all shareholders must be treated equally.

• Due diligence is critical to the success of a merger with risk reduction being the primary objective. The four most common types of due diligence are: financial, legal, operational and strategic. Some types of deals may involve an extra layer of environmental due diligence.

• An acquirer can’t ignore competitive forces when evaluating targets. Independent, external analysis of the competitive landscape of a particular industry, and of the target’s strengths and weaknesses within that industry, is paramount.

• Both buyer and seller need to ensure availability of financing so that it does not unexpectedly present a problem. The results of financial due diligence (e.g. confirming low debt levels) can impact how a transaction is paid for (cash versus stock).

• Under the Hong Kong Takeovers Code, negotiations must be made public by the target company if an acquirer notifies a target of a firm intention to make an offer. Disclosure can also be required if there is public speculation.

• Shareholders of companies involved in a merger not only will experience price volatility but are subject to dilution, which can result in an erosion of voting power. If a merger is properly planned and executed it can result in long-term growth and a higher return on investment.

• The SFC requires certain companies to perform specific due diligence procedures as part of the AML/CTF regulations, including verifying customers’ identity, the beneficial owner, the purpose and nature of the business and the intended relationship with the financial institution.

## OPENING CASE

### GSHM

Mr. Taiping King Wong (Mr. Wong) is an entrepreneur who has incorporated a company in Hong Kong, GSHM Limited (GSHM). The main line of business of GSHM is retailing high street fashion. GSHM rents office premises both in Kowloon and Hong Kong to sell its own-brand mid-market clothing, aimed principally at middle-class women in the 25–45 age bracket. GSHM is supplied by third-party Chinese manufacturers, which produce textiles in China where labour costs are much lower, and export them to Hong Kong. Because costs have been increasing in China, GSHM has recently begun outsourcing production to Vietnam. Mr. Wong personally owns all its brands and designs and cultivates a strong brand identity, seeking to compete in the same market as H&M and Uniqlo. That structure is, however, inefficient from a tax perspective. Mr. Wong accordingly decides to transfer all the intellectual property rights he currently holds to an offshore company, Red Lantern Limited (Red Lantern), incorporated in the Cayman Islands. Red Lantern licences the intellectual property to GSHM in exchange for an annual royalty. The operations and activities of GSHM are fairly typical for a Hong Kong undertaking: In global supply chains, manufacturing, design, retail, and intellectual property holding operations are often allocated to different jurisdictions to exploit the comparative advantages of such jurisdictions when it comes to costs, worker skills, and tax incentives. Effective tax structuring and tax mitigation options are also important to GSHM.

## OVERVIEW

This chapter will provide a comprehensive introduction to profits tax in Hong Kong. Unlike many other jurisdictions, Hong Kong does not have a general income tax. That means that income is in general not taxed unless it corresponds to one of the specific taxing schedules in the Inland Revenue Ordinance (IRO). Profits tax is the most important of those schedules and charges to tax the Hong Kong source profits (and thus not just the income) of a trade, profession or business carried on in Hong Kong. That is a deceptively simple formulation. What constitutes a trade, profession or business has been the subject of extensive judicial debate. Most importantly, the source principle, which is critical in ascertaining whether profits are taxable in Hong Kong, has become highly complex and, in certain cases, does not lend itself well to contemporary transactions. While the general rule is that one looks to what the taxpayer has done to earn its profits, and where it has done it, discounting antecedent or incidental matters, it is often difficult to apply that broad guiding principle to a globalised economy based on financial services such as that of Hong Kong. This chapter will consider in depth the essential building blocks of profits tax and consider its application in a variety of commercial scenarios, with both domestic and international elements. You will further be introduced to the specific deeming provisions that treat certain sums as taxable even when they are not charged to tax under the general charging provision in s.14 of the IRO, and to concessions and exemptions that are available to certain taxpayers and certain circumstances. After acquiring a grounding in the theory of the law underlying the charge to profits tax, you will study the relationship between law and general principles of accounting, and further apply your knowledge to tax computation. After completing your study of this chapter, you will have acquired a firm and comprehensive grounding of the law and practice of profits tax and be ready to apply this to practical commercial scenarios.

## 3.1 PROFITS TAX OVERVIEW

Unlike many other jurisdictions, Hong Kong does not have a general income tax on individuals or on corporations. The principal tax on business profits is called ‘profits tax’, which is charged on assessable profits. Profits are assessable to profits tax if and to the extent that they are the profits of a trade, profession or business carried on in Hong Kong and are sourced in Hong Kong. It is essential to understand this is a three-limbed test. In order for a charge to profits tax to arise:

• First, there must be a person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong;
• Second, they must derive Hong Kong source profits; and
• Third, those profits must be the profits of that trade, profession or business carried on in Hong Kong. Simply having a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong or deriving Hong Kong source profits is insufficient.

Each limb must be met for a charge to tax to arise. An alternative way of expressing the general charging provision is that a person must: (i) carry on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong; (ii) derive Hong Kong source profits; (iii) from that trade, profession or business carried on in Hong Kong.

Although there are exceptions, which we shall consider in detail later in this chapter, generally speaking, profits sourced from outside of Hong Kong are not taxable in Hong Kong. As you by now know, Hong Kong has a territorial tax regime: The default position is that only profits that arise in or are derived from Hong Kong are chargeable to tax. Although on its face a simple and intuitive regime, the profits tax code can give rise to difficulties both for enterprises and for practitioners. For example, when is a profit sourced in Hong Kong? Under which circumstances, if at all, can a profit be said to be sourced in Hong Kong and in another jurisdiction? What about passive income, such as dividends, interest, and royalties?

In this chapter, you will deepen your theoretical and practical understanding of the charge to profits tax, the doctrine of source and some of the principal exceptions to the general rule that only Hong Kong source profits are chargeable to tax. It is assumed that you are familiar with first principles of profits tax; you should, however, take the time to refresh your memory of s.14(1) of the IRO.

### 3.1.1 Scope of Charge

Profits tax is charged on the Hong Kong source profits of a person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong. Note the use of the term ‘profits’. Profits are different from income or turnover. A profit is a notional unit of account denoting some economic gain. Generally, a profit is computed by subtracting business expenditure from business income. The scope of the charge is, as we have indicated, territorial: a company may have extensive business income from a number of sources, but will only be charged to profits tax on its Hong Kong source profits, and not its profits sourced offshore. Other jurisdictions, such as Canada and the United Kingdom, tax on a residence basis: The general charge to income tax in those jurisdictions provides that a resident person is chargeable on its worldwide income. That is not the case in Hong Kong; whether a person is resident or otherwise in Hong Kong, it will in general only be chargeable to tax on its Hong Kong source profits. The concept of tax residence is therefore of limited importance as regards domestic Hong Kong taxation.

Profits tax is a charge to tax on assessable profits, as defined in the IRO. This is distinct from any accounting notion of profits; in practice, the two concepts often overlap. The question of what a taxable profit is always a question of law, as distinct from a question of fact or accounting. In determining whether a profit is taxable, reference must be made to the terms of the IRO and the case law on point, and not GAAP or any other applicable accounting standard.

Throughout this chapter, we will refer to ‘assessable profits’. Assessable profits are profits eligible for taxation under s.14 of the IRO.

Note that gains from the sale of capital assets are expressly excluded from being chargeable to profits tax in s.14(1) of the IRO. This is significant when we come to discuss the distinction between trading and investment income below. The distinction between revenue and capital is one of the oldest questions in tax law, and we shall consider it in greater detail when we discuss the deductions regime in ss.16–17 of the IRO.

### 3.1.2 Chargeable Persons and Tax Rates

S.14 of the IRO provides that profits tax is chargeable on the Hong Kong source profits of a person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong. The key term here is ‘person’. S.2 of the IRO defines a person as including a corporation, partnership, trustee, or body of persons. That is a broad definition: essentially, any person or entity capable of carrying on an economic activity will be treated as a person, albeit not a separate legal person at law, taxable under the IRO.

The rates of profits tax are set out in Schedules 1, 8, 8A and 8B of the IRO. Corporations (that is, bodies corporate) are charged at a standard rate of 16.5% of assessable profits, though, under certain circumstances, the first HK$2 million of assessable profits are charged at half the corporate rate, being 8.25% (effective from the year of assessment 2018/19 onward). All other taxable persons are charged to profits tax at the standard rate of 15%, or, where the two-tiered profits tax rates regime applies, at half the standard rate, being 7.5% on the first HK$2 million of assessable profits. The two-tiered profits tax rate is available subject to certain conditions, the most important of which is that in a given group of connected entities only one such entity can avail itself of the two-tiered profits tax rates regime.

In order to be eligible for the lower rate of profits tax on the first HK$2 million of assessable profits, the principal condition is that only one person within a set of connected persons is eligible for the reduced rate (s.14AAC). For example, in a group of companies, only one company can enjoy the benefit of the reduced rate, even if each other company is also chargeable to profits tax in Hong Kong. An entity for the purposes of the two-tiered profits tax rates regime includes natural persons, bodies corporate, partnerships and trusts. If a natural person carries on more than one sole proprietorship business, the person is taken to be a separate entity in relation to each sole proprietorship business.

An entity is a connected entity of another entity if:
(a) One of them has control over the other;
(b) Both of them are under the control of the same entity; or
(c) In the case of the first entity being a natural person carrying on a sole proprietorship business, the other entity is the same person carrying on another sole proprietorship business.

Generally, an entity has control over another entity if the first-mentioned entity, whether directly or indirectly through one or more than one other entity;
(a) Owns or controls more than 50% in aggregate of the issued share capital of the latter entity;
(b) Is entitled to exercise or control the exercise of more than 50% in aggregate of the voting rights in the latter entity; or
(c) Is entitled to more than 50% in aggregate of the capital or profits of the latter entity.

Thus, where there is a set of connected entities, only one of those entities can elect for the concessionary rate. All other entities within that set of connected entities will pay tax at the standard rate. The reason for this restriction is to prevent aggressive tax structuring through the fragmentation of a business between a large number of companies, with each availing itself of the reduced rate of profits tax. This is a paradigmatic example of a specific, as opposed to general, anti-avoidance provision, designed to prevent aggressive tax structuring. The Inland Revenue Department (IRD) maintains a helpful FAQ summarising the scope and effect of the two-tiered profits tax rates regime, which may be accessed by following this link: https://www.ird.gov.hk/eng/faq/2tr.htm.

> **Key Learning Point**
> 
> Profits tax is a charge on the Hong Kong source profits of a trade, profession, or business carried on in Hong Kong. It is distinct from income tax in many other jurisdictions because it is only charged on certain profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong.
> 
## 3.2 TRADE, PROFESSION OR BUSINESS

This section deals with the first limb of the s.14 charge to profits tax. First, you must consider whether a person carries on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong. If no trade, profession or business is carried on in Hong Kong, the person in question is simply not chargeable to profits tax under s.14 of the IRO. Any person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong is required to register under s.5 of the Business Registration Ordinance (Cap.310), which operates as Hong Kong’s de facto tax registration law.

### 3.2.1 Trade

Trade is defined in s.2(1) as including every trade and manufacture and every adventure and concern in the nature of trade. This is a circular definition, so one looks to the case law for clarification. A trade is an organised activity that is carried on with a view to profit. This presupposes that there must exist a profit-generating activity that is carried on with some degree of recurrence and continuity (see, for example, Kowloon Stock Exchange Ltd v CIR (1984) STC 602 and Simmons v IRC (1980) 2 All ER 798). There are certain elements one would normally expect to find in trading activities because a trade should be distinguished from an investment. The gains from an investment, which are capital in nature, are not chargeable to profits tax. In most cases, trading profits arise from the sale of assets held as trading stock (as opposed to capital assets) or from the supply of services. In deciding whether a gain derived from the sale of an asset is a trading or capital sale, the landmark decision in Marson v Morton (1986) 1 WLR 1343 found the following ‘badges of trade’ to be of particular relevance:

• Profit-seeking motive: generally speaking, trading is carried on commercially and with a view to profit. This may be contrasted with activities that are carried on for pleasure or on a charitable basis, where no subjective profit-seeking motive is identifiable.

#### Illustrative Example 1

Mr. Montgomery Withnail QC is an amateur arts collector. He enjoys hanging antique Chinese scrolls in his apartment on the Peak. One scroll he bought for HK$2 million. A friend of his subsequently suggested that he might buy the scroll from him for HK$3 million. Mr. Withnail initially refused but, on reconsideration, agreed to part with the scroll for the offered sum. Under those circumstances, the gain he derived is likely not a trading profit. Mr. Withnail simply does not habitually trade in antiques, but accepted a generous offer on an exceptional basis.
---- 
• The subject matter of the transaction: A person acquiring trading stock and realising this daily at a retail outlet will likely be trading; however, a person buying and disposing of a building will be less likely to be regarded as trading unless he uses the building as his stock-in-trade (Marson v Morton (1986) STC 463). It seems that the subjective intention of a buyer of landed property at the time of its acquisition is especially important in determining whether it is acquired as a trading asset. This can also be triggered by one of the following:
- °The nature of the asset (e.g. whether it is used for personal enjoyment, income yielding, trading, etc.);
- °The quantity of such assets; and
- °The purpose to make inference on the trading intention.

The intention to elect to begin trading can also cause the asset to cease being a capital asset and become stock-in-trade (Simmons v IRC (1980) 1 WLR 1196).
